surprises.description: Services bookings were still down 1%, with a low 1.07 book-to-bill, despite the sharp improvement from the 14% decline reported for Q1. That points to some stabilization, but the segment remained soft and the company cited the carve-out and go-to-market changes as drags.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Services bookings fell 1%, with services book-to-bill of just 1.07 hurt by the regulatory/medical writing carve-out and go-to-market changes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Services stabilization vs. software strength” and said to watch “whether services bookings show a floor”; it also reported Q1 services bookings “−14%.”

surprises.description: Normalized trailing 12-month bookings growth accelerated to 7% exiting the first half, from 0.8% exiting 2025, and the sales pipeline was up 27% year over year. The preview highlighted bookings conversion as something to watch but did not anticipate this acceleration or pipeline growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Normalized for the Chemaxon acquisition, trailing 12-month bookings growth accelerated to 7% exiting the first half, up sharply from 0.8% exiting 2025, and sales pipeline grew 27% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “second-half bookings-to-revenue conversion commentary.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a May workforce reduction of about 5% and said combined operating actions should produce roughly $13 million in run-rate savings, more than the previously identified plan. The preview did not flag these actions or savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A May reduction in force cut approximately 5% of the global workforce, and combined operational actions are expected to yield roughly $13 million in run-rate savings, an increase over the prior identified plan.”

surprises.description: Certara completed a $100 million buyback and authorized another $50 million repurchase program, an additional capital-return commitment not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed a $100 million buyback (including $17.4 million repurchased in Q2), and the Board authorized a new $50 million share repurchase program.”

surprises.description: The call reported 30 Phoenix cloud implementation wins and a first major Simcyp win in China. These were concrete adoption and market-expansion milestones not anticipated in the preview, which discussed software strength more generally.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Software now represents 53% of the business versus 40% two years ago, with 30 Phoenix cloud implementations won this year and a first major Simcyp win in China.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Software has carried growth” but gave no expectation for Phoenix implementations or a Simcyp win in China.

in_line: The company reaffirmed full-year revenue growth guidance of 0%–4%, matching the preview’s stated organic growth outlook of 0%–4% ex-divestiture.
Software remained a source of growth, as the preview expected: Q2 software revenue increased 4% and trailing 12-month software bookings rose 8%.

surprises.description: FIS lowered full-year adjusted revenue growth guidance to 4.5%-5.0%, below the preview’s 4.9%-5.5% outlook. The company also lowered its Capital Markets outlook to 3%-3.5%; management attributed the weakness to internal execution, including lower professional services and slower recurring revenue, rather than market conditions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted revenue growth guidance was lowered to 4.5%-5% from 5.1%-5.7%”; “Capital Markets guidance was cut by 225 basis points to 3%-3.5% revenue growth,” driven by “lower professional services plus slower recurring revenue,” with the miss “attributed to internal execution rather than market conditions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave FY26 pro forma revenue growth guidance of “4.9%–5.5%” and said Capital Markets was expected to grow “3.0%–4.0%.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was much stronger than the preview’s outlook: it more than tripled year over year, prompting FIS to raise full-year guidance by $100 million to $2.15-$2.25 billion. The new range starts at the preview’s former high end and extends above it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow more than tripled year-over-year to $525 million,” and management raised full-year FCF guidance “by $100 million to a range of $2.15-$2.25 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 free cash flow guidance of “$2.05–$2.15B” and flagged that range as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin expansion exceeded the top of the expected sequential range, with margins expanding 113 basis points versus the preview’s 75-110 basis-point outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Margins expanding 113 basis points, ahead of the 75-110 bps outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q2 needed a “75–110bps sequential step-up.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue and pro forma growth came in slightly above the preview’s expectations: revenue was $3.4 billion versus $3.384 billion consensus, and pro forma growth was 5.3% versus about 5.2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $3.4 billion, up 5.3% on a pro forma basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited revenue consensus of “$3.384B” and pro forma revenue growth of “~5.2%.”

surprises.description: The preview identified Capital Markets as a soft spot but anticipated that stronger ACV might convert to revenue; instead, FIS disclosed UBS/Credit Suisse client attrition that is reducing 2026 Capital Markets growth by about one percentage point, concentrated in trading and asset services. This adds a specific client-loss headwind to the weaker outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The UBS/Credit Suisse client attrition is reducing 2026 Capital Markets revenue growth by approximately 1 percentage point, concentrated in trading and asset services.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the bull case rests on the 45% ACV increase converting to revenue” and flagged Capital Markets growth as the “soft spot.”

surprises.description: Issuer Solutions showed encouraging commercial and integration progress: 72% of the Total Issuing portfolio was under contract through 2029 or beyond, large-bank win rates exceeded 85%, joint-client ACV grew 35%, and captured cost savings were tracking near the high end of the target. The preview had highlighted integration and attrition as issues to watch but did not anticipate these specific traction metrics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “72% of the Total Issuing portfolio is now under contract through 2029 or beyond (up from 65%),” win rate was “above 85%” on large U.S. bank opportunities, joint-client ACV “grew 35% year-over-year in the first half,” and “$13 million of cost savings” was captured year-to-date, tracking near the high end of the $30-$40 million target.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “early commentary on synergy capture and attrition in the acquired book feeds 2027 numbers.”

surprises.description: FIS is evaluating strategic alternatives for selected lower-growth, non-core Capital Markets products, an action not raised in the preview. Management also cautioned that sales could be complicated by integrated cost structures and tax leakage, making the potential outcome uncertain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is evaluating strategic alternatives for select lower-growth, non-core products within Capital Markets,” while management acknowledged asset sales are complicated by “integrated cost structures and tax leakage.”

surprises.description: Full-year margin expansion guidance was lower than the preview’s stated range, even though management characterized the outlook as broadly in line with prior guidance: the reported range was 85-105 basis points versus 95-110 basis points in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year margin expansion of 85-105 bps remains broadly in line with prior outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 margin expansion guidance of “95–110bps.”

in_line: Banking Solutions grew 6.1% pro forma, and FIS reiterated its full-year Banking outlook, consistent with the preview’s stated FY26 Banking growth guide of 5.5%-6.0%.
FIS reaffirmed its path to more than $3 billion of free cash flow by 2028, a target the preview had already highlighted.

surprises.description: Broadridge’s fiscal 2026 closed sales reached $305 million, above the already-reduced $240–290 million guidance range; Q4 alone set a record at $158 million. This reversed the concern that deal timing might leave sales below the reduced target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 closed sales hit a record $158 million, lifting full-year closed sales to $305 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 closed sales: $240–290M, cut from $290–330M”; the preview said Q4 implied sales of “$93–143M.”

surprises.description: Fiscal 2026 recurring revenue grew 8%, exceeding the company’s minimum 7% growth guidance. The preview’s expectation was at least 7%, so the result was better than the stated floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year recurring revenue grew 8% to $4.9 billion on 6% organic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance of at least 7% constant-currency growth.”

surprises.description: Position growth was stronger than the prior-quarter benchmarks highlighted in the preview: Q4 equity position growth was 17% versus 11% previously, and fund positions grew 7% versus 6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 equity position growth was 17% with 14% revenue-generating position growth, while fund positions grew 7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Equity records grew 11%, and fund/ETF positions grew 6%.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a material potential e-delivery effect that the preview did not flag: no expected impact in fiscal 2027, but a possible modest recurring-revenue headwind over the following 2–3 years, partly offset by new solutions. Management also expects lower low-margin distribution revenue to boost reported margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The SEC's proposed e-delivery rule is expected to have no impact in fiscal '27 but may create a modest recurring revenue headwind over 2-3 years (offset by new solutions) while boosting reported margins by reducing low-margin distribution revenues.”

surprises.description: Broadridge disclosed $25 million of expected AI-driven productivity gains for fiscal 2027, primarily in technology, but plans to reinvest them in growth initiatives rather than retain them as savings. The preview raised AI as a strategic debate but did not anticipate a quantified productivity contribution or this use of the gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company embedded $25 million in expected AI-driven productivity gains in fiscal '27, primarily in the technology organization, which it plans to reinvest to fund growth initiatives.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the next framework would be “the cleanest read on how management sees AI and tokenization risk” and that “management framing on AI and tokenization” mattered, but gave no expected productivity figure.

surprises.description: Broadridge reported much more specific tokenized-repo traction than the preview anticipated: DLR handled $360 billion of daily volume in June, three times May’s level, with nearly 20 institutions onboarding and a further 50% growth target by December.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The DLR tokenized repo platform processed $360 billion in daily volume in June (3x the prior May), with nearly 20 institutions onboarding and management guiding to 50% further growth by December.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had previously stated “tokenization expands the opportunity” and that reiterating this “with proof points matters,” but did not provide a volume, onboarding, or growth expectation.

surprises.description: The call added evidence of sales momentum beyond the closed-sales result: the year-end pipeline was up more than one-third year over year, and platform-enabled and next-generation products made up nearly 40% of closed sales. The preview had noted a pipeline up 20% at Q3 but did not anticipate this year-end pipeline growth or product mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The year-end sales pipeline was up more than one-third from a year ago, with platform-enabled and next-generation products rising over 50% and accounting for nearly 40% of closed sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported the prior-quarter “pipeline above $1B (+20%)” and said management attributed the sales slowdown to deal timing, not weaker demand.

surprises.description: The company disclosed an unusual fiscal 2027 Q1 setup not addressed in the preview: a 4-point license-revenue tailwind, but tough event-driven comparisons against Q1 FY26’s record $114 million, with Q1 expected to contribute only 11%–13% of full-year earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal '27 will benefit from a 4-point license revenue tailwind in Q1 (split evenly across Capital Markets and Wealth), but faces tough event-driven comps as Q1 FY26 had a record $114 million versus a $60-70 million quarterly average; Q1 is expected to represent 11%-13% of full-year earnings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Broadridge “does not guide quarterly” and did not set an expectation for the Q1 license tailwind or earnings contribution.

surprises.description: Broadridge returned more capital and expanded its buyback capacity: fiscal 2026 buybacks were a record $600 million, it raised the dividend 12%, and it increased authorization to $1.5 billion. The preview flagged a larger authorization as a possible confidence signal but did not anticipate its size or the reported full-year return.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Broadridge returned over $9 per share to shareholders in fiscal '26 via a record $600 million in buybacks and $443 million in dividends, and raised the dividend 12% to $4.36 while increasing buyback authorization to $1.5 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “A larger repurchase authorization would signal confidence,” without specifying an expected amount.

in_line: Fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS grew 12%, at the top of the preview’s expected 10%–12% full-year growth range.

Fiscal 2027 guidance for recurring revenue growth of 6%–8% and adjusted EPS growth of 8%–12% matched the preview’s base-case ranges, although the recurring-revenue range includes a 6% low end below the preview’s 7% anchor.
Fiscal 2027 adjusted operating income margin guidance of approximately 21% is consistent with a modest improvement from the 20%–21% fiscal 2026 margin range the preview discussed.

surprises.description: Apollo reported adjusted net income of $2.11 per share, below the preview’s primary $2.18 consensus estimate by 7 cents. The preview also cited an alternate $2.05 compilation, which the result exceeded.
surprises.fact_evidence: “total adjusted net income of $1.3 billion ($2.11/share)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ANI/share (ANI) $2.18” and “$2.18 is the number to beat”; the preview also lists an “ANI alternate compilation” of “$2.05.”

surprises.description: FRE reached $785 million, an 8% sequential increase, well above the preview’s expected 2–4% step-up from Q1’s $728 million. The result was a record, and the margin also expanded to 58.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “record fee-related earnings of $785 million ($1.26/share) … up 8% quarter-over-quarter”; “FRE margin expanded to 58.5%, up ~80 bps sequentially”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “a 2–4% sequential step gets to $745–765M.”

surprises.description: Capital Solutions fees reached a record $277 million, above the preview’s roughly $255 million base case and the cited $223 million consensus. Apollo said the fees were running ahead of its five-year Investor Day target roughly three years early.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capital solutions fees reached a record $277 million”; “running ahead of the 5-year Investor Day target roughly three years early.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ACS ~$255M” in the base scenario; the preview also flags “Capital Solutions (ACS) fees vs. $223M consensus.”

surprises.description: Q2 origination was $74 billion, below the preview’s $80–85 billion base case and only modestly above Q1’s $71 billion, despite management having said Q2 would be even stronger.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Origination hit $74 billion in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “Origination $80–85B”; the preview also says management said Q2 would be “even stronger” than Q1’s “$71B.”

surprises.description: Apollo disclosed $50 billion of signed and announced deals in addition to Q2 originations, including a $35 billion Broadcom AI financing described as the largest private credit deal ever. Fees will accrue as capital is drawn over multiple quarters, weighted toward late 2026 and the first three quarters of 2027, rather than all being recognized immediately.
surprises.fact_evidence: “an additional $50 billion in signed and announced deals (including the $35 billion Broadcom financing) set to benefit future quarters”; the Broadcom deal “will be recorded and generate fees as capital is drawn down over multiple quarters, weighted toward Q4 2026 and the first three quarters of 2027.”

surprises.description: Organic capital formation reached a record $60 billion, including $42 billion of Athene inflows in the first half, putting Athene on track for its $85 billion full-year target. The preview did not flag this level of fundraising as an expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total organic capital formation was a record $60 billion”; Athene had “$22 billion” in Q2 and was “tracking toward its $85 billion full-year inflow target ($42 billion in the first half).”

surprises.description: Apollo said its record $82 billion of dry powder includes $62 billion of future management-fee potential, about 70% from credit, equivalent to approximately $400 million of annual fees once deployed. This was not among the preview’s flagged expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “a record $82 billion of dry powder including $62 billion of future management fee potential (~70% credit), representing approximately $400 million of annual management fee income once deployed.”

surprises.description: Flagship private equity Fund XI had surpassed $12 billion through July, but associated management fees are not expected to activate until the back half of the first half of 2027 and after the capital is fully invested. The preview did not discuss this fund’s fundraising or fee timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Flagship private equity Fund XI has surpassed $12 billion through July, with management fees expected to activate in the back half of the first half of 2027 once capital is fully invested.”

surprises.description: Athene’s reported net spread improved to 114 basis points from Q1’s 97, while the preview said the Q2 pre-announced 9% alternatives return meant the spread gap would persist. At the 11% alternatives assumption, however, the resulting 124 basis points was within the 120–125 basis-point full-year outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Athene's reported net spread rose to 114 bps from 97 bps last quarter”; “adjusting to the 11% alternatives return assumption, net spread would have been 124 bps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Q2 pre-announced 9% alternatives return means the gap persists”; the preview identifies the full-year spread outlook as “120–125bps.”

surprises.description: Apollo disclosed that ADS non-traded BDC had returned 8% annualized since inception versus 4% for high-yield. The preview focused on redemptions, not this return comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ADS non-traded BDC has delivered an 8% annualized inception-to-date return (vs. 4% for high-yield).”

in_line: Apollo reaffirmed FY2026 guidance for 20%+ FRE growth and 10% SRE growth, as the preview expected.
At the 11% alternatives-return assumption, Athene’s 124-basis-point net spread was within the preview’s 120–125-basis-point full-year outlook.
ADS Q3 redemption requests running at roughly half the level seen at the same point in Q2 matched the preview’s expectation that requests would decelerate.

surprises.description: BellRing raised FY26 net sales guidance to $2.335–$2.375 billion from $2.325–$2.365 billion, a modest upward revision despite the much weaker profit outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year net sales guidance was raised to $2.335-$2.375 billion (1-3% growth) from prior flat-to-2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 net sales: $2.325–2.365B (updated May 5, 2026)” and consensus was “~$2.34B (+1.0%).”

surprises.description: Q3 net sales grew 4%, well ahead of the preview’s 1.6% growth consensus; the call also said both Premier Protein and Dymatize exceeded expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 net sales rose 4% year-over-year, with both Premier Protein and Dymatize exceeding expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (Q3) … $556.0M (Zacks), +1.6% YoY.”

surprises.description: The FY26 adjusted EBITDA outlook was cut sharply, from the preview’s cited $315–$335 million company guidance to $275–$295 million, with the company now expecting only about a 12% margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA is now guided to $275-$295 million with a margin of only about 12%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA | $315–335M (updated May 5, 2026).”

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted EBITDA margins came in below guidance, and BellRing expects Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin to fall to about 10% amid promotions and cost pressures—far from the preview’s stabilization scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margins came in below guidance”; “Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin is expected to be only about 10%, reflecting heavy seasonal promotions, commodity/freight inflation ahead of pricing, and a ~100 bp bottle-inventory headwind.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario was “Guide reaffirmed, gross margin flat-to-up,” and it asked whether “margins stabilize.”

surprises.description: Excess bottled-shake inventory was a new and substantial drag: it required a $10 million reserve, contributed 180 basis points of Q3 gross-margin pressure, and is expected to bring further Q4 markdowns and inventory-related costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An excess bottled shake inventory charge that alone was a 180 basis point headwind”; “excess bottle inventory required a $10 million reserve (2% of total inventory) plus additional Q4 promotional markdowns”; the outlook includes “$28 million of unfavorable inventory-related impacts ($21 million already recorded).”

surprises.description: Dymatize delivered a sharp sales beat, with sales up 27% on 6% volume growth and 21% favorable price/mix, although management cautioned that Q4 faces a tough comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dymatize net sales surged 27% on 6% volume growth and 21% favorable price/mix from earlier inflation-driven price increases, though it faces a tough Q4 comparison”; the call said Dymatize exceeded expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Dymatize sales had fallen 1.9% in Q2, but gave no Q3 Dymatize estimate.

surprises.description: BellRing announced a double-digit price increase on Premier shakes, its first in nearly two years, plus more powder pricing; management expects volume elasticity slightly above 1, pointing to some volume giveback.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a double-digit price increase on Premier shakes plus additional powder pricing effective Q1 fiscal 2027, marking the first shake price hike in nearly two years, with expected volume elasticity slightly greater than 1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Price/mix vs. volume” as a key issue, asking whether promotion could be pulled back “without losing Premier Protein shelf space,” but did not forecast a price increase.

surprises.description: Premier shake volume grew 3% and dollar consumption rose 6%, while price/mix remained down 2%; the call nevertheless said Premier exceeded expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Premier Protein shake volume grew 3% but price/mix declined 2%, with dollar consumption up 6%”; the call said Premier Protein exceeded expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “Price/mix vs. volume” and asked whether promotion could be pulled back without losing shelf space, but gave no Q3 Premier estimate.

surprises.description: A Q4 legal settlement payment is expected to push net leverage from 3.2x at quarter-end to approximately 4x by fiscal year-end, a material cash and leverage development not raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage stood at 3.2x at quarter-end but is expected to rise to approximately 4x by fiscal year-end due to a sizable legal settlement payment in Q4.”

surprises.description: A June organizational realignment brought a $5 million charge but is expected to save $10–$12 million in annualized operating expenses, with most savings not arriving until FY27.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A June organizational realignment incurred a $5 million charge and is expected to generate $10-$12 million in annualized operating expense savings, mostly realized in fiscal 2027.”

in_line: The preview identified the gross-margin trajectory as a key question and asked whether Q2’s 27.0% was the trough. Q3 adjusted gross margin was 27.7%, a modest sequential improvement, though still far below the year-earlier 35.1%.

surprises.description: Palvella reported that the Phase III SELVA study met its primary, key secondary, and all four prespecified secondary endpoints with high statistical significance, with 95% of patients improving on the primary endpoint at week 24. The preview did not flag these results, making the reported efficacy a substantial positive development beyond its NDA-timing focus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Phase III SELVA study met its primary endpoint, key secondary endpoint, and all 4 prespecified secondary endpoints with high statistical significance,” with “95% of patients showing improvement” at week 24.

surprises.description: The FDA declined to grant Breakthrough Therapy Designation for the cVM program based on the initial 12-week data. The preview identified a BTD grant as a possible major upside, so the denial removes that potential catalyst, although management said it does not change the development path.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FDA declined to grant Breakthrough Therapy Designation for the cutaneous venous malformation (cVM) program based on the initial 12-week data package,” but management said this “does not alter the development path.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Phase 3 initiation plus a BTD grant would be the largest positive in the quarter.”

surprises.description: Palvella raised its 2026 cash-spend guidance to approximately $85–95 million, above the preview’s roughly $80 million burn framing. The company attributed the higher spend to expanded commercial and medical-affairs investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its 2026 cash spend guidance to approximately $85-95 million due to expanded commercial and medical affairs investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Prior framing was about $80M FY26 burn with runway through launch.”

surprises.description: The Phase II TOIVA study reported improvement on the cVM-IGA in 73% of patients, more than twice the predefined success threshold. The preview discussed the planned Phase III start and BTD decision, but did not anticipate or provide an expectation for this efficacy result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Phase II TOIVA study in cVM showed 73% of patients improved on the cVM-IGA (more than twice the predefined success threshold).”

surprises.description: Management gave an orphan-drug price range of $100,000–$200,000 per MLM patient per year and cited payer research indicating strong coverage support without expected step-throughs of unapproved therapies. The preview said to watch pricing and payer commentary but offered no specific price or access expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Orphan drug pricing of $100,000-$200,000 per patient per year for MLM,” with “strong coverage support and no expected step-throughs of unapproved therapies.”

surprises.description: Palvella said QTORIN rapamycin could address more than 300,000 U.S. patients across multiple mTOR-driven indications, versus more than 30,000 MLM patients alone. The preview did not describe this broader pipeline-in-a-product opportunity or the stated 2029 cVM and 2031 angiokeratoma approval targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: The strategy “could expand QTORIN rapamycin's addressable U.S. population from over 30,000 MLM patients to over 300,000 across multiple mTOR-driven indications,” with cVM targeted for 2029 and angiokeratomas for 2031.

surprises.description: Physician survey results indicated substantial intended use across the pipeline: more than 80% would consider QTORIN as first-line therapy across all four indications, and 96% would incorporate it for angiokeratomas. The preview did not include these demand-survey findings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “More than 80% of surveyed physicians said they would consider the QTORIN candidate as first-line therapy across all four indications,” and “96% said they would incorporate QTORIN rapamycin into their practice for angiokeratomas.”

surprises.description: Beyond the indications anticipated in the preview, management said it expects to announce a third product candidate later this year. The preview had anticipated additional indication news but did not flag a third product candidate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Palvella “expects to announce ... a third product candidate later this year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Two new indications promised for 2H26, named this quarter or deferred?”

surprises.description: Management said it plans to pursue FDA Platform Designation after the first approval to expedite future programs, a regulatory strategy not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Palvella “plans to pursue FDA Platform Designation after its first approval to expedite future programs.”

in_line: The first NDA module was completed and the company remained on track for full submission in 2H 2026 and potential approval in 1H 2027, matching the preview’s stated timeline.
Q2-end cash of approximately $251 million was within the preview’s base-case range of $245–252 million.
The planned sales force of approximately 40 reps was at the upper end of the previously discussed 20–40-rep range, consistent with the preview’s 30–40-rep buildout expectation.
TOIVA Phase III initiation is expected in Q4 2026, within the preview’s expected 2H 2026 window.
The planned QTORIN pitavastatin program for DSAP, expected to enter Phase II in Q4 2026, is consistent with the preview’s expectation of additional indication news in 2H 2026.

surprises.description: Enpro’s Q2 results beat the preview’s consensus on all three headline measures: sales were $338.8 million versus roughly $323 million expected, adjusted EPS was $2.50 versus $2.30, and adjusted EBITDA was $86.9 million versus an estimated $80–82 million. EPS and EBITDA also exceeded the preview’s bull-case figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales rose 17.6% year-over-year to $338.8 million,” adjusted EBITDA was “$86.9 million,” and adjusted diluted EPS “reached $2.50 in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $322.9M – $323.7M”; “Adj. diluted EPS: $2.30”; “Adj. EBITDA: ~$80–82M.” The bull scenario was “~$332M” revenue and “~$2.48” adjusted EPS.

surprises.description: Enpro raised its 2026 sales-growth, EBITDA, and EPS ranges beyond the preview’s expected move toward the upper half of the existing EPS range. The new EPS range of $9.30–$9.80 even exceeds the preview’s bull-case range of about $9.20–$9.70 at the high end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year 2026 guidance,” with total sales growth now “14%-16%” (from “10%-14%”), adjusted EBITDA “$330-$340 million” (from “$315-$330 million”), and adjusted diluted EPS “$9.30-$9.80” (from “$8.85-$9.50”).
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A raise or narrowing to the upper half is the main binary.” The bull scenario anticipated “Raise to ~$9.20–9.70 EPS.”

surprises.description: AST’s Q2 margin improved more than the preview’s baseline expectation: it reached 23.9%, above the roughly 23.5% base case and the 22.5% level the preview said would raise concerns about Q1’s inventory-related margin. AST sales growth, by contrast, landed within the preview’s expected 18–22% range.
surprises.fact_evidence: AST had “21.8% revenue growth” and adjusted segment EBITDA “up 48.5%, expanding margins 430 basis points to 23.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected AST margin of “~23.5%”; the preview said “an AST margin below roughly 22.5%” would suggest Q1 was a stocking effect and watched for AST growth of “+18–22% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: Management described a stronger AST trajectory beyond the quarter than the preview’s mid-teens full-year growth and double-digit H2 volume outlook: it expects approximately 20% AST growth in H2, growth rates and margins approaching 25% exiting the year, and visibility extending through 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects AST to grow approximately 20% in the second half of 2026,” with “revenue growth rates and adjusted EBITDA margins both approaching 25% exiting the year,” and “visibility now extending through 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “guides mid-teens FY growth with H2 volumes up a double-digit percentage over H1” and flagged quantified backlog or order growth as something to watch.

surprises.description: Sealing’s margin was modestly above the preview’s expected range: 33.2% compared with a 32.5% benchmark and a 32.5–33% base case. It remained above 30% for a tenth consecutive quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Sealing Technologies had an adjusted EBITDA margin of “33.2%, remaining above 30% for the 10th consecutive quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “above 32.5% supports the margin thesis” and its base scenario expected “Sealing 32.5–33%.”

surprises.description: Enpro raised its 2026 capital-spending expectation to $60–$65 million from about $50 million, pulling AST cleaning-capacity investments forward. The preview flagged capital deployment but did not anticipate this higher spending or the specific capacity investments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised 2026 capital expenditure expectations to $60-$65 million (up from ~$50 million), pulling forward AST cleaning capacity investments in Arizona, Milpitas California, and Taiwan.”

surprises.description: Enpro recorded an unanticipated roughly $60 million environmental reserve for legacy Arizona uranium mines. The company said meaningful cash outflows are not expected for about three years, but remediation could continue for up to a decade.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recorded a roughly $60 million environmental reserve build tied to legacy uranium mines in Arizona,” with “no meaningful cash outflows expected for about 3 years” and remediation “potentially spanning up to 10 years.”

surprises.description: Enpro reported stronger deleveraging and cash generation than the preview had highlighted: net leverage fell from the prior-quarter 1.9x to 1.6x, after $80 million of revolving-debt repayment, and year-to-date free cash flow topped $60 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reduced net leverage to 1.6x trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA after repaying $80 million in revolving debt” and “generated over $60 million in year-to-date free cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q1 free cash flow of “$26.5M” and net leverage of “1.9x,” but did not specify an expectation for Q2 or year-to-date cash generation.

surprises.description: Although the preview expected commercial vehicles to remain weak and assumed no recovery in guidance, management added a more constructive signal: it sees early stabilization and cited forecasts for 17–18% industry growth next year.
surprises.fact_evidence: Commercial vehicle markets “remained soft” and guidance “does not assume significant recovery,” but management “sees early stabilization” and cited forecasts of “17-18% industry growth next year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said commercial vehicles “remain below normalized levels, and guidance embeds no recovery.”

in_line: AST Q2 revenue growth was 21.8%, within the preview’s expected 18–22% year-over-year range.

Commercial vehicle markets remained soft, and 2026 guidance did not assume a significant recovery, consistent with the preview’s expectation that markets would remain below normal and guidance would embed no recovery.

surprises.description: U.S. Q2 comparable sales were +0.8%, below the preview’s +0.9% to +1.1% consensus range. The shortfall was small relative to that range, though the preview also noted some lower sell-side estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: U.S. comparable sales grew 0.8%, below company expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “US comps: +0.9% to +1.1%” and “US comps against the consensus of about +0.8–1.1%.”

surprises.description: U.S. momentum weakened further after the quarter: management said same-store sales were slightly negative in July, rather than showing the acceleration the preview identified as an upside possibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. same-store sales were slightly negative in July,” signaling weak momentum entering Q3.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “May and June improved sequentially” and asked whether management would “quantif[y] a July acceleration”; its bull case also assumed “July accelerating.”

surprises.description: Management said the U.S. value strategy itself contributed to traffic underperformance: it launched the new under-$3 EDAP menu while pulling back digital offers and removing Buy One Add One for $1. The preview flagged whether value was working, but did not anticipate this specific combination of offer changes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “About two-thirds of the U.S. traffic underperformance” came from a “bad trade” in which the new under-$3 EDAP menu launched while digital offers were pulled back and Buy One Add One for $1 was removed.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Positive comps driven only by price and mix would suggest the value strategy is not working. Traffic is the number to watch.”

surprises.description: The recommended EDAP pricing architecture was implemented by only about 60% to 65% of the U.S. system, contributing to inconsistent results and lower incrementality. The preview discussed the value strategy but did not flag this limited franchisee execution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Only about 60% to 65% of the U.S. system executed the recommended EDAP pricing architecture,” contributing to inconsistent results and lower incrementality.

surprises.description: The June FIFA marketing campaign underdelivered, accounting for about one-third of U.S. underperformance; the preview did not identify this campaign as a likely drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The remaining one-third of U.S. underperformance was tied to the June FIFA marketing campaign underdelivering versus expectations.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $3.38 topped the preview’s $3.32–$3.34 consensus range, although the reported constant-currency increase included a $0.03 foreign-currency benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $3.38, up 5% in constant currency, including a $0.03 foreign currency benefit.”

surprises.description: McDonald’s lowered its full-year 2026 foreign-exchange tailwind estimate to about $0.15, below the preview’s expected $0.20–$0.30 range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company cut its full-year 2026 forex tailwind estimate to about $0.15, down from a prior range of $0.20 to $0.30.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s FY26 framework included “a $0.20–0.30 FY EPS tailwind from FX.”

surprises.description: The company pushed its 50,000-restaurant target from the end of 2027 to 2028, citing pressured consumers and higher development costs. The preview expected about 2,600 openings in 2026, but did not flag this longer-term target delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “McDonald's pushed its 50,000-restaurant target from end of 2027 to 2028,” citing pressured consumers and cumulative inflation on development costs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s FY26 framework listed “About 2,600 openings, roughly 2,100 net new.”

surprises.description: The new beverage platform was performing better than expected, with more than half of its traffic after lunch and those orders’ average checks about 50% above the full-day average; the preview did not discuss this platform.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The new beverage platform is exceeding expectations,” with “more than half of traffic coming after lunch” and average checks “about 50% above the full-day average.”

surprises.description: Sky Anderson was named U.S. President immediately, replacing Joe Erlinger, who is leaving after more than two decades; the preview did not anticipate a leadership change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sky Anderson was named U.S. President effective immediately, replacing Joe Erlinger who is leaving after over two decades.”

surprises.description: Customer satisfaction and service times declined in Q2, a negative operating development not raised in the preview’s watch list.
surprises.fact_evidence: The U.S. President change came “amid Q2 declines in customer satisfaction and service times.”

in_line: Global comparable sales grew 1.3%, within the preview’s +1.3% to +1.4% consensus range.
The company continued to target about 2,600 gross openings this year, in line with the preview’s FY26 framework.

surprises.description: Thryv cut full-year SaaS adjusted EBITDA guidance to $42–44 million from $70–75 million, a much larger reduction than the preview’s base case of holding the range and its warning that a cut below $70 million would be a key downside risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Thryv lowered its full-year SaaS ... adjusted EBITDA guidance to $42-44 million,” reflecting “first-half underinvestment in sales headcount and marketing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SaaS adj. EBITDA $70–75M”; the base scenario anticipated “FY guide held,” and the bear scenario flagged a cut “below $70M.”

surprises.description: Thryv also cut full-year SaaS revenue guidance to $453–457 million from $463–471 million, reversing the preview’s expectation that the raised Q1 range would be held.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Thryv lowered its full-year SaaS revenue guidance to $453-457 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SaaS revenue $463–471M” and the base scenario described an “FY guide held.”

surprises.description: Q2 SaaS adjusted EBITDA was $13.6 million, above the $12–13 million quarterly guide, even as full-year guidance was cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 SaaS ... adjusted EBITDA of $13.6 million (12% margin).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The Q2 company guide was “SaaS adj. EBITDA $12–13M.”

surprises.description: Seasoned net revenue retention was 90%, down from 93% in Q1, and SaaS subscribers were 95,000 versus 96,000 in Q1. That is weaker than the prior-quarter metrics, though retention landed at—not below—the preview’s roughly 90% downside threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Seasoned net revenue retention was 90%” and Thryv ended the quarter with “95,000 SaaS subscribers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 “Seasoned net revenue retention 93%; SaaS client count 96,000” and said “NRR below about 90% or a steeper client decline” would indicate uncontrolled churn.

surprises.description: The company raised the low end of full-year Marketing Services revenue guidance by $4 million, to $161–163 million, rather than leaving the prior $157–163 million range unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: Thryv planned to raise “the low end of marketing services revenue guidance to $161-163 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Marketing Services revenue $157–163M.”

surprises.description: Thryv disclosed an approximately $25 million restructuring charge, split between workforce reductions and vendor spend, with roughly $60 million of expected run-rate savings—an unanticipated near-term cost paired with substantial planned savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A restructuring charge of approximately $25 million (split evenly between workforce reductions and vendor spend) expected to yield roughly $60 million in run-rate savings.”

surprises.description: Thryv launched its AI-native Growth Platform on August 3, built with 70% new code to replace the four-year-old Marketing Center. The preview anticipated discussion of the AI transition, but did not anticipate this launch or the product’s stated development details.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Launched its new AI-native Thryv Growth Platform on August 3rd, built with 70% new code to replace the aging four-year-old Marketing Center product.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “strategic commentary on the AI platform migration” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: Thryv entered partnerships with Wix and Ooma and launched integrations with Breezy and Jobber, adding distribution channels into new customer ecosystems that the preview did not identify.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Entered strategic partnerships with Wix and Ooma and launched integrations with Breezy and Jobber to expand distribution into new customer ecosystems.”

surprises.description: The JICs reclassified Thryv as a software company, validating its transformation to a pure-play SaaS business; the preview did not anticipate this external classification.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SaaS now represents 76% of Thryv's total revenue, and the company was reclassified by the JICs as a software company, validating its transformation to a pure-play SaaS business.”

in_line: Q2 SaaS revenue was $114.5 million, within the preview’s $114–115 million company guide.
Thryv said it plans to begin migrating its existing customer base to the new platform in 2027, consistent with the preview’s focus on the AI-platform migration and 2027 framework.

surprises.description: The preview put revenue consensus at about $79–80 million and expected a possible third consecutive miss; Hut 8 reported $74.9 million, roughly 5–7% below that consensus range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue increased approximately 81% year-over-year to $74.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working consensus: revenue about $79–80M”; the preview’s base case expected revenue “at or below consensus.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on revenue potentially coming in light and adjusted EPS remaining negative, but did not forecast gross margin or adjusted EBITDA. Hut 8 reported gross margin of about 64%, up from 47%, and adjusted EBITDA excluding digital-asset mark-to-market more than doubled to $10.4 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanding to approximately 64% from 47%”; “Adjusted EBITDA excluding digital asset mark-to-market movements more than doubled to $10.4 million from $4.2 million.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated a $125–135 million digital-asset mark-to-market hit. Hut 8 reported a $138 million digital-asset loss, slightly above that estimate, although the large GAAP loss itself was anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A GAAP net loss of $177.1 million, driven primarily by a $138 million non-cash loss on digital assets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The preview's own estimate of the attributable mark-to-market hit is roughly $125–135M.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted Beacon Point financing but did not anticipate the reported improvement in its debt terms. Beacon Point notes priced one notch higher and 20 basis points inside Riverbend, were substantially oversubscribed, and had four-year rather than two-year amortization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Beacon Point notes priced one notch higher and 20 basis points inside Riverbend, were substantially oversubscribed, and extended amortization from 2 years to 4 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the market would want an equivalent equity-return figure from the “$4.25B Beacon Point financing”; it did not state an expectation for pricing, demand, or amortization.

surprises.description: The preview discussed the project-financing and equity-funding gap but did not flag how little of the reported cash would be available to the parent. Hut 8 had $7 billion of cash, of which $6.8 billion was restricted, leaving $233.6 million of unrestricted corporate cash.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The balance sheet grew to approximately $7.6 billion of total debt and $7 billion of cash, with $6.8 billion restricted to project accounts and only $233.6 million of unrestricted corporate cash.”

surprises.description: The preview raised dilution as a risk if Hut 8 used an ATM or shelf, but did not anticipate the specific conversion of its remaining parent-recourse notes into shares. The conversion eliminated that debt but issued 9.7 million shares.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company eliminated its only remaining parent recourse debt by converting $159.3 million of notes into 9.7 million shares.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any ATM or shelf language would be read as dilution risk.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag the refinancing of the $200 million facility. Hut 8 lowered its coupon from 9% to 7%, reducing the stated borrowing cost.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Refinanced a $200 million facility to lower its coupon from 9% to 7%.”

surprises.description: The preview identified third-campus progress as a possible catalyst but did not specify pipeline growth. Hut 8 reported an 8.7-gigawatt development pipeline, up about 300 megawatts from the prior quarter, across 11 sites averaging more than 650 megawatts each.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The development pipeline grew to about 8.7 gigawatts, up approximately 300 megawatts from the prior quarter, with 11 sites averaging over 650 megawatts each.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s catalyst checklist included “Third-campus progress or tenant naming.”

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss the increase in G&A expense. Hut 8 reported G&A of $76.1 million versus $30.2 million, though about $43.6 million of the increase was non-cash share-based compensation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “G&A expense rose to $76.1 million from $30.2 million, but approximately $43.6 million of the increase was non-cash share-based compensation.”

in_line: The reported 352-megawatt Beacon Point lease and the resulting total of about 949 megawatts of contracted AI data-center capacity and $26.6 billion of aggregate expected base-term contract value matched the preview’s description of the already-announced second lease and contracted backlog.

surprises.description: IDEXX reported Q2 EPS of $4.27 versus the preview’s $3.95 consensus, an approximately 8% beat. The call said EPS included $0.14 per share from share-based compensation activity and $0.06 from favorable FX.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 EPS reached $4.27” and included “a $0.14 per share benefit from share-based compensation activity and $0.06 from favorable foreign exchange.”

surprises.description: Revenue grew about 10% reported, above the preview’s 8.3% implied growth and roughly $1.20B consensus—about $1.22B using the reported growth rate and prior-year revenue. This was a modest beat against a preview that said consensus was roughly at guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue grew approximately 10% as reported and 9% organically.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $1.20B” and “Implied Y/Y | +8.3%”; the preview said “Consensus Q2 is therefore roughly at guidance, not above it.”

surprises.description: CAG Diagnostics recurring revenue grew over 10% organically, exceeding the preview’s roughly 9% guide-implied rate and reaching the preview’s bull-trigger threshold. This was achieved despite U.S. same-store clinical visits declining 1.3%, producing an approximately 1,100-basis-point growth premium over visits.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over 10% organic growth in CAG Diagnostics recurring revenues” and “an approximately 1,100 basis point CAG Diagnostics recurring revenue growth premium over clinical visits”; U.S. same-store clinical visits “declined 1.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The guide implies about 9% for the rest of the year. Sub-9% is a problem; 10% or more is a bull trigger.”

surprises.description: The full-year outlook was raised: the EPS range moved to $14.69–$14.94, with a $0.14 increase at midpoint, and revenue guidance moved to $4,700M–$4,745M. The revenue midpoint rose only slightly, from the prior $4,717.5M midpoint to $4,722.5M, while the range narrowed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year 2026 EPS outlook to $14.69-$14.94,” an “increase of $0.14 at midpoint,” and “lifted revenue guidance to $4,700M-$4,745M.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior guide was “Revenue | $4,675M – $4,760M” and “EPS | $14.45 – $14.90.” The preview said the action could be “Raise, narrow to midpoint, or reaffirm” and that “a raise is not clearly priced in.”

surprises.description: Comparable operating margin expanded 110 basis points and gross margin reached 64%, up about 120 basis points, a stronger margin outcome than the preview’s emphasis on needing the second half to carry margins after Q1’s 31.8% operating margin and against a tough Q2 comparison. Favorable product costs and easing inflation helped.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable operating margin expanded 110 basis points with gross margins reaching 64%, up ~120 basis points, aided by favorable product costs and eased inflationary pressures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 operating margin was “31.8% against a 32.1% to 32.5% FY guide, so the second half must carry the margin,” and noted “Q2'25 margin was about 33.6%, a tough comparison.”

surprises.description: CAG Diagnostics instrument revenue fell 20% organically as IDEXX lapped the prior-year inVue Dx launch, despite an 11% year-over-year increase in the installed base. The preview focused on placement acceleration but did not flag the size of this instrument-revenue decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CAG Diagnostics instrument revenues fell 20% organically as the company lapped the prior-year broad launch of inVue Dx, while the total installed base grew 11% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Global Reference Lab revenue returned to double-digit organic growth for the first time since early 2023, and Cancer Dx had surpassed 10,000 clinics, with one-fifth of its orders coming from competitive-lab practices. The preview did not identify this segment rebound or adoption as a key expected driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Global Reference Lab revenues rose over 10% organically, the first double-digit growth since early 2023,” and IDEXX Cancer Dx surpassed “10,000 global clinics” with “20% of its orders coming from competitive-lab practices.”

surprises.description: IDEXX raised its free-cash-flow conversion outlook to 90%–100% of net income, a favorable outlook change that the preview did not discuss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its free cash flow conversion outlook to 90%-100% of net income.”

in_line: Premium instrument placements totaled 5,265, including 1,602 inVue Dx analyzers, consistent with the preview’s bull-case threshold of more than 1,500 inVue Dx placements and its focus on acceleration toward the 5,500 full-year goal.

U.S. same-store clinical visits declined 1.3%, broadly in line with the preview’s assumed 1.5% full-year decline; the preview had also reported Q1 wellness visits down 2.9%, while Q2 wellness visits declined by less than 3%.
The roughly 2% year-over-year reduction in diluted shares was similar to the 2.1% reduction reported in Q1, which the preview had highlighted.

surprises.description: Vivid Seats raised the low end of its FY26 Marketplace GOV guidance from $2.2 billion to $2.3 billion and the low end of adjusted EBITDA guidance from $30 million to $34 million, while keeping the upper ends unchanged. This was a more constructive guide than the preview’s expected reaffirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised or set full-year fiscal 2026 guidance to Marketplace GOV of $2.3 billion to $2.6 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $34 million to $40 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 Marketplace GOV $2.2–2.6B and Adj. EBITDA $30–40M, reaffirmed at Q1.” The preview also listed “Reaffirm at $2.2–2.6B” as a possible guidance action.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $130 million, above the preview’s $122.1 million consensus estimate. Private-label revenue grew 16% quarter over quarter, a contributor to the stronger result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was $130 million, up 3% sequentially from $126 million, with private label revenue growing 16% quarter-over-quarter.”

surprises.description: The World Cup generated transaction volume comparable to the entire Taylor Swift Eras Tour in a single quarter, and accounted for a mid-teens percentage of Q2 GOV. The preview anticipated a World Cup boost and asked for its contribution, but did not quantify an event contribution of this scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The World Cup generated transaction volume comparable to the entire Taylor Swift Eras Tour but concentrated in a single quarter rather than spread across two years”; it was “estimated to have driven a mid-teens percentage of Q2 GOV.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The FIFA World Cup … spans Q2 and Q3”; “Explicit World Cup GOV contribution” and “Ask how much GOV came from the World Cup and at what margin.”

surprises.description: The company renewed its revolving credit facility with maturity extended through August 2029, a concrete financing development amid the preview’s focus on unresolved refinancing and lender negotiations. The call facts do not give the renewed facility’s size or other terms.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $137 million in cash and renewed its revolving credit facility with an extended maturity through August 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Capital structure / refinancing” was the preview’s top issue; it said “negotiations with other lenders continue” and called for disclosure of any signed agreement or term sheet.

surprises.description: Vivid Seats reported a greater than 99.7% successful fulfillment rate on World Cup orders, an unanticipated execution result that it contrasted with publicized fulfillment problems at a competitor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vivid Seats maintained a greater than 99.7% successful fulfillment rate for World Cup orders, positioning its customer experience against publicized fulfillment problems at a competitor.”

surprises.description: Q2 cash was $137 million, slightly below the preview’s roughly $140 million reference point, although it remained above the preview’s roughly $135 million level identified as a concerning reset to the burn trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $137 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash versus ~$140M and forward cash guidance”; the preview said “a Q2 cash figure below roughly $135M would reset the burn trajectory.”

surprises.description: Management said non-World-Cup industry volumes were softer in Q2, including theater weakness from rising competition and soft Las Vegas leisure travel among lower-end consumers. This reinforces the risk that the event-driven GOV strength did not reflect a broad demand improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industry volumes outside the World Cup were softer in Q2, with theater weakness driven by rising competitive intensity and soft Las Vegas leisure travel among lower-end consumers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned: “If Q2 looks decent only because of the World Cup, the ‘2H return to growth’ narrative breaks in Q3 and Q4.”

in_line: Marketplace GOV of $659 million was within the preview’s derived $620–660 million estimate, near its upper end; the preview also expected a World Cup boost.
Adjusted EBITDA of $12.6 million was within the preview’s derived $11–14 million estimate.
Take rate was 15.8%, close to the preview’s expectation of stabilization near 16% and above its 15.5% concern threshold, despite World Cup take rate being below the broader landscape.
Management reaffirmed a return to year-over-year growth in the second half of 2026, consistent with the preview’s stated expectation.

surprises.description: Zebra was expected to report about $1.498 billion in sales, with organic growth possibly only 4–7%; it reported more than $1.5 billion, beat the high end of its guidance, and delivered 9.2% organic growth. The revenue-dollar beat over consensus appears limited, but organic growth was notably stronger than the preview’s concern implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 sales exceeded $1.5 billion, growing 20.4% total and 9.2% organically year-over-year, beating the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus sales of “$1,498M (+15.9%)”; the preview said the guide implied “organic growth of only ~4–7%” and that organic below 5% would be a problem.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was expected around $4.35 and the guidance range topped out at $4.50; actual EPS was $6.35. That is a very large beat against both consensus and the company’s outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP diluted EPS reached $6.35, a 76% year-over-year increase, significantly exceeding the top end of the outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus was “$4.35”; company guidance was “$4.20–$4.50.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA margin was expected to be about 22%, but reached 27.7%, expanding 7.1 points year over year. The beat was helped by a $73 million IPA tariff recovery that was not included in prior guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded 7.1 points to 27.7%, boosted by a $73 million IPA tariff recovery that was not included in prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed adjusted EBITDA margin consensus at “~22% (derived).”

surprises.description: The full-year outlook moved well above the prior ranges: sales growth is now 14–16% rather than 10–14%, EPS is $20.75–$21.25 rather than $18.30–$18.70, and EBITDA margin is 23.5–24% rather than about 22%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 sales growth guidance to 14%-16% (a 3-point midpoint increase) and full-year EPS guidance to $20.75-$21.25, with EBITDA margin expected at 23.5%-24%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The May guide was “sales +10–14%, adj. EBITDA margin ~22%, non-GAAP EPS $18.30–$18.70.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted whether memory-related pricing actions were being realized or were still only planned. Zebra said it fully mitigated the roughly $120 million memory cost headwind and raised its expected pricing offset from $60 million to $90 million after strong Q2 price realization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company fully mitigated the approximately $120 million memory cost headwind, raising the pricing-driven offset expectation from $60 million to $90 million due to strong Q2 price realization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether pricing actions were “described as realized or still planned” and noted a “~200bps memory headwind embedded in FY26.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow guidance increased from at least $900 million to at least $1 billion, above the preview’s stated full-year expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow guidance was raised to at least $1 billion, reflecting roughly 100% conversion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 free cash flow guidance as “≥$900M.”

surprises.description: The Elo Touch acquisition delivered growth above expectations, and Zebra identified about $10 million in synergies. The preview did not flag this acquisition-specific result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Elo Touch acquisition delivered above-expectation growth with about $10 million in identified synergies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Above-expectation growth.”

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted EPS was $3.49, above the preview’s $3.37–$3.39 consensus range and above management’s implied $3.24–$3.36 range. The beat was modest relative to consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $3.49, up more than 20% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS $3.39 (Zacks) / $3.37 (S&P/Barchart)” and management’s implied “$3.24–$3.36” range.

surprises.description: Sales growth was stronger than the preview’s consensus-implied pace: reported sales rose 8% versus consensus revenue growth of about 5.2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 fiscal 2026 reported sales rose 8% and organic sales rose 10%, with the Sensia dissolution reducing sales by 3% and currency adding about 1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $2.26B” versus “Q3 FY25 Actual ~$2.15B,” or “+5.2%.”

surprises.description: Rockwell raised FY26 sales-growth guidance: the midpoint moved from 7% under the prior 5%–9% range to 8.5% under the new 7.5%–9.5% range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year fiscal 2026 organic and reported sales growth guidance to 7.5%-9.5% (8.5% midpoint), up 150 bps from prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company FY26 guidance” was 5%–9% growth, while FY26 revenue consensus implied “+7.5%.”

surprises.description: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance rose by $0.35 at the midpoint to $13.15, above the preview’s existing $12.50–$13.10 range and slightly above consensus. However, it was just below the preview’s stated $13.20-or-higher bullish threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $13.00-$13.30 ($13.15 midpoint) ... up $0.35 from prior midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company FY26 guidance: Adjusted EPS $12.50–$13.10”; “A raise to $13.20 or above would be the bullish outcome.”

surprises.description: Lifecycle Services remained weak and its book-to-bill fell below 1.0, matching the preview’s stated warning threshold. Organic sales declined 2%, slightly worse than the prior quarter’s roughly 1% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lifecycle Services organic sales fell 2% with a book-to-bill of 0.97, constrained by weak capital spending in Food & Beverage and process industries.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A Q3 book-to-bill below 1.0 would reopen that debate”; the preview also noted Lifecycle Services organic growth was about “-1%” in Q2.

surprises.description: The memory and inflation burden increased to a higher double-digit-million-dollar second-half drag, with Software & Control taking the greatest hit. The preview had flagged a double-digit-million-dollar headwind, but specifically called out the risk that it could be larger.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inflation is an increasing headwind, now a higher double-digit-million second-half drag, hitting Software & Control hardest via memory costs, though price/cost is expected positive in Q4 and full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether “the memory headwind is larger than the ‘double-digit million-dollar’ figure given in Q2.”

surprises.description: Enterprise operating margin was 22.3%, 20 basis points below the prior quarter’s 22.5%, rather than flat sequentially as management had framed Q3. The 280-basis-point year-over-year increase was strong, but did not change the sequential comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enterprise operating margin reached 22.3%, up 280 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had framed Q3 as having “Flat enterprise operating margin sequentially”; Q2 margin was 22.5%.

surprises.description: Software & Control delivered a particularly strong quarter, with 18% organic growth, 34.8% segment margin and roughly 50% incrementals. The preview gave no Q3 segment forecast, so this was an unanticipated area of strength rather than a beat against a stated estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Software & Control organic sales grew 18% with segment margin of 34.8% (up 320 bps) and incrementals of about 50%, driven by strong double-digit Logix growth.”

surprises.description: Growth was not confined to data centers: excluding data center, organic sales still grew 8%, alongside early double-digit recovery in Automotive and 10% growth in Life Sciences. The preview had highlighted data-center strength but did not anticipate this breadth or these recovery signs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding data center, organic growth would still have been 8% in the quarter, with early recovery signs in Automotive (up low double digits) and Life Sciences (up 10%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that data-center sales had “more than doubled YoY” in Q2, but gave no expectation for Q3 growth excluding data center, Automotive, or Life Sciences.

surprises.description: North America grew 12% and management expects it to be Rockwell’s fastest-growing region for FY26. The preview did not flag a regional growth outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North America grew 12% year-over-year, the strongest region, and is expected to be the fastest-growing region for full-year fiscal 2026.”

in_line: Adjusted EPS growth was broadly in line with the preview’s consensus-implied year-over-year growth of about 19.5%–20.2%: reported growth was more than 20%, even though the $3.49 EPS level beat consensus.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $329.5 million, below the $339.2 million consensus and even the $335 million low end of company guidance. The shortfall was attributed mainly to Machine Clothing equipment downtime and delayed defense tooling shipments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was $329.5 million… though it modestly trailed forecast primarily due to Machine Clothing equipment downtime and delayed defense tooling shipments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $339.2M”; company guidance was “$335–345M.”

surprises.description: Management now expects full-year Machine Clothing revenue to be slightly down versus 2025, rather than the full recovery from the equipment failure by year-end described in the preview. Weaker Americas demand is the stated reason.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year Machine Clothing revenue is now guided to be slightly down versus 2025 due to weaker Americas demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management expects full recovery from the equipment failure by year-end.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was a $14.5 million use of cash, contrary to the preview’s expectation that Q2 would turn cash-positive on seasonality. The inventory build for the Engineered Composites ramp and European seasonal shutdowns drove the outflow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was a net use of $14.5 million versus a $17.8 million inflow last year, driven by inventory build to support Engineered Composites ramp and European seasonal shutdowns.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 should turn cash-positive on seasonality.”

surprises.description: Machine Clothing revenue was $178.7 million, just below the $180–185 million Q2 guidance range, although its roughly 28% EBITDA margin was in line with the preview’s stability benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Machine Clothing revenue declined to $178.7 million with EBITDA roughly flat at $50 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 Machine Clothing guidance of “$180–185M” and flagged revenue “at or above $180M with a 28% margin.”

surprises.description: Engineered Composites revenue was $150.8 million, below the preview’s $155–160 million Q2 guidance range, despite record quarterly revenue and strong program ramps.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engineered Composites posted record quarterly revenue of $150.8 million…”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 Engineered Composites guidance of “$155–160M.”

in_line: Engineered Composites’ adjusted EBITDA margin was 13.3%, meeting the preview’s indicated threshold of a return above roughly 13%.
Machine Clothing’s roughly 28% EBITDA margin matched the preview’s stability benchmark.
The Salt Lake City review remained ongoing, as the preview’s base case anticipated; the company reported eight final candidates but no signed deal or named bidder.

surprises.description: Revenue was $816 million versus the preview’s $813.6 million consensus, a small beat. Organic growth of 6.6% also exceeded the preview’s roughly 5% base-case assumption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue grew 5.2% to a record $816 million, with organic revenue growth of 6.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (Q2) … $813.6M”; the base scenario expected “~5% organic.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS of $0.59 beat the preview’s $0.56 consensus by $0.03, or about 5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS increased 13.5% to $0.59.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS (Q2) … $0.56.”

surprises.description: The quarter’s adjusted EBITDA margin was 26.8%, slightly below the preview’s roughly 27% quarterly bar, although it expanded 140 basis points year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding 140 basis points to 26.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin vs. ~27% bar”; the base scenario also expected “~27.0%.”

surprises.description: Consumer profitability improved sharply: adjusted EBITDA rose 24.2% and margin expanded 310 basis points, helped by exiting lower-margin service lines and productivity. The preview focused on whether Consumer growth would accelerate but did not flag this degree of margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consumer segment adjusted EBITDA margin surged 310 basis points year-over-year to 21.3% as adjusted EBITDA grew 24.2% to $77 million, driven by exiting lower-margin service lines and higher productivity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consumer organic growth. It was 3.0% in Q1… Q2 needs to accelerate.”

surprises.description: Industrial revenue growth remained above the preview’s slowdown threshold, but Industrial margin slipped 10 basis points because of higher performance-based incentive compensation—an operating pressure the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industrial revenue rose 7.8% to $402 million (7.2% organic), but adjusted EBITDA margin slipped 10 basis points to 32.3% due to higher performance-based incentive compensation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Slowing below about 7% would suggest the trend is cooling.”

surprises.description: Certification testing grew more than 10%, primarily on volume, and management said volume contributed more than price to overall revenue growth; the preview had not identified this as a specific growth driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Certification testing grew over 10% for the quarter, driven primarily by volume, with management noting volume contributed more than price to overall revenue growth.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed that restructuring-plan business exits reduced Q2 revenue by about $6 million, or roughly 1%, implying organic growth would have been about 80 basis points higher without those exits. This was not part of the preview’s stated growth assumptions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Business exits from the restructuring plan created an approximately 1% revenue drag (about $6 million in Q2), meaning organic growth would have been roughly 80 basis points higher without them.”

surprises.description: Trailing 12-month free cash flow rose 19.8% and its margin improved to 13.9%, a favorable cash-generation update not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month free cash flow rose 19.8% to $436 million with free cash flow margin improving to 13.9% from 12.3%.”

surprises.description: Full-year capital expenditure guidance rose to about 8.5% of revenue, above the prior 7%–8% range cited in the preview and above last year’s 6.5%. Management called the increase an anomaly relative to its long-term range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year capital expenditures guidance was raised to approximately 8.5% of revenue (up from 6.5% last year), which management characterized as an anomaly versus the long-term 6%-8% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “capex 7–8% of revenue.”

in_line: The company reaffirmed its full-year outlook for mid-single-digit organic revenue growth and approximately 27% adjusted EBITDA margin, matching the preview’s base case of a reaffirmed outlook.
The Eurofins Electrical & Electronics acquisition remained expected to close in Q4 2026, as the preview anticipated.
The DQS stake sale remained on track for the second half of 2026, consistent with the preview’s timing.

surprises.description: Bruker reported Q2 non-GAAP EPS of $0.49, well above the preview’s $0.38 consensus, despite revenue landing below consensus. The call attributed the EPS and margin outperformance in part to tariff refunds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 non-GAAP diluted EPS rose 53% year-over-year to $0.49 from $0.32, beating on margins and EPS despite top-line results coming in at the low end of expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP EPS … Consensus $0.38.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $838.5 million, below the preview’s $853.6 million consensus, and organic growth was only 2.8% (3.4% excluding tariff refunds). That was a shortfall against the expected revenue level, even though organic growth turned positive as management had indicated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue grew 5.2% to $838.5 million with organic growth of 2.8% (3.4% excluding tariff refunds)” and results came in “at the low end of expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 revenue … Consensus $853.6M”; management had guided to “Low-to-mid single-digit organic growth.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating margin reached 14.1%, above the preview’s roughly 13% estimate. The comparison was against a weak prior-year quarter, and tariff refunds contributed about 200 basis points of margin, so the reported expansion was partly driven by that benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin expanded 510 basis points to 14.1%, though against a weak Q2 2025 comparison”; tariff refunds contributed “roughly 200 basis points to operating margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP operating margin … ~13% (implied).”

surprises.description: Net U.S. tariff refunds provided an unanticipated, nonrecurring boost to Q2 results: about $0.06 per share and roughly 200 basis points of operating margin. The preview did not flag this source of support.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net U.S. tariff refunds contributed about $0.06 to EPS and roughly 200 basis points to operating margin.”

surprises.description: Semiconductor demand was substantially stronger than the preview’s 20%+ bookings-growth bar: Scientific Instruments reported greater than 50% growth in semi, while semiconductor metrology orders grew over 30% in the first half. However, the call said long lead times delay conversion of those orders into revenue.
