surprises.fact_evidence: “The hypersonics business is projected to grow from ~$200 million in 2025 to ~$400 million in 2026 and at least $700 million in 2027, positioning it to become Kratos' largest segment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “hypersonics” among the program areas to watch, without giving a growth forecast or scale.

surprises.description: The company described supply-chain commitments for thousands of Spartan turbojet engines, including components for a further 5,000 engines, far more specific scale than the preview’s general mention of the Spartan ramp. It also cited major prospective multiyear demand from hypersonic and missile programs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Kratos is placing supply-chain orders for 3,000 Spartan turbojet engines to be produced in 2027 and plans components for an additional 5,000 engines for 2028, at an average selling price of ~$50,000 each.” Management also cited “the Mach-TB hypersonic program at ~$7 billion over five years” and Air Force plans for “over 11,000 JASSM/LRASM missiles and tens of thousands of low-cost cruise missiles” as engine demand drivers.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview named the “Spartan turbojet ramp” and hypersonics as program color to watch, but gave no expected engine volumes, pricing, or multiyear demand figures.

surprises.description: Kratos detailed recent awards totaling roughly $660 million across directed-energy counter-UAS, space domain awareness, and hypersonic and other funding. The preview anticipated strong bookings after July’s award flow but did not cite awards of this scale or these program details.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recent new awards include a directed-energy counter-UAS program valued at ~$160 million, a space domain awareness production award of ~$100 million, and ~$400 million in new hypersonic and other funding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “July awards should support another strong bookings print,” without specifying award values or programs.

surprises.description: The bid-and-proposal pipeline was reported at $15 billion, a significant additional indicator of future opportunities that the preview did not identify as a metric to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The bid-and-proposal pipeline expanded to $15 billion.”

in_line: Operating cash flow was negative in Q2, consistent with the preview’s expectation of guided-negative operating cash flow.
The company reported strong bookings, in line with the preview’s expectation that July awards would support a strong bookings print.

surprises.description: The preview cited consensus EPS of +$0.03, but loanDepot reported a $29 million adjusted net loss. That is a miss versus the modest profit implied by consensus, although the preview flagged that consensus as low-confidence.
surprises.fact_evidence: “loanDepot narrowed its adjusted net loss to $29 million in Q2 2026 from $34 million in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS | +$0.03”; the preview also says consensus “cover[s] only four analysts” and should be treated as “low-confidence.”

surprises.description: Q3 volume guidance came in below the Q2 ranges investors were watching: the lock range is $5.25–$7.25 billion versus Q2’s $5.75–$7.75 billion, and the origination range is $6.25–$8.25 billion versus Q2’s $7.25–$9.25 billion. This points to a lower near-term pipeline and funding pace than the preview’s key Q3 lock check was hoping to avoid.
surprises.fact_evidence: “guided Q3 origination volume of $6.25-$8.25 billion with pull-through weighted lock volume of $5.25-$7.25 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Q3 locks come in at or below the Q2 range, the market will read Q2 as a pipeline drawdown”; Q2 lock guidance was “$5.75–7.75B” and funded volume guidance was “$7.25–9.25B.”

surprises.description: Cash fell to $229 million, below the preview’s $250 million bear-case threshold, even as the company announced a roughly $10 billion servicing-rights monetization that is expected to settle later in the year. The pending proceeds are a liquidity positive, but they do not offset the reported near-term cash decline yet.
surprises.fact_evidence: “monetized approximately $10 billion of servicing rights post-quarter, expected to settle later in the year to bolster liquidity after cash fell $48 million to $229 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “Liquidity and the 2027 senior secured notes” as a key issue and described “cash below $250M” as part of its bear scenario.

surprises.description: The home-equity business’s monthly losses narrowed much faster than the preview discussed, from $15 million in April to $2 million in June excluding fair value. That indicates improving segment economics beyond the preview’s focus on HELOC mix as a driver of margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company's home equity pivot narrowed monthly losses (excluding fair value) from $15 million in April to just $2 million in June.”

surprises.description: Management issued Q3 gain-on-sale margin guidance of 360–390 basis points, above the Q2 guide’s 330–360 basis points and signaling further improvement. The preview focused on Q2 margin delivery but did not set a Q3 margin expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pull-through weighted gain on sale margin expanded to 345 basis points from 271 basis points in Q1 … with Q3 guidance of 360-390 bps signaling further margin improvement.”

surprises.description: The company bought back senior notes below par—at 90% during the quarter and 86% post-quarter—but the call facts still describe maturities as a high priority requiring outside advisers, rather than reporting a full refinancing or other resolution. This is some progress on the debt issue, but not the deliverable resolution the preview identified as important.
surprises.fact_evidence: “repurchased $16 million of senior notes at 90% of par during the quarter and an additional $27 million at 86% of par post-quarter, while flagging bond maturities as a high priority requiring outside advisers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had indicated a resolution would come “in coming months” and called a “deliverable answer” a potential rerating catalyst.

surprises.description: Purchase volume rose 44% and purchase market share increased 33%, a strong gain in a business line the preview did not specifically forecast. This adds a positive source of activity beyond the preview’s focus on HELOC-driven margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Purchase market share increased 33% in Q2 with purchase volume up 44%.”

surprises.description: Management reported sizable year-over-year improvements in loan-officer count and marketing efficiency, including higher conversion and lower marketing cost per funding, plus about $12 million of annualized savings initiatives. The preview expected expenses to rise and specifically questioned whether operating leverage would show up, so the cost and productivity actions were better than that setup implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “grew net loan officer count by 18%, increased return on marketing by 70%, boosted lead-to-funded conversion by 50%, and cut marketing cost per funding by 34%”; “initiated approximately $12 million of annualized productivity/cost savings initiatives.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Management guided expenses up” and called Q2 the first quarter in which “the operating-leverage claim can be checked against a rising expense base.”

in_line: Q2 pull-through weighted gain-on-sale margin was 345 basis points, within the company’s 330–360-basis-point guide and consistent with the preview’s expectation of a roughly 74-basis-point increase from Q1.
Q2 origination volume was $8.0 billion, within the company’s $7.25–$9.25 billion guidance range.

surprises.description: Fortune Brands recognized a substantial tariff refund in Q2, even though the preview said refunds were uncertain and the company might defer recognition. The refund added $0.52 to EPS and 700 basis points to operating margin, so the reported margin increase was not representative of underlying operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company recognized $122 million in gross tariff refunds, of which $81 million flowed to operating income, adding 700 basis points of margin and $0.52 of EPS in the quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Tariff refunds are not reliably in consensus,” and the company “may defer recognition.”

surprises.description: Fortune Brands cut full-year EPS guidance to $2.70–$3.00 from $3.00–$3.30, rather than reaffirming or narrowing the prior range as the preview expected. Management attributed about $0.20 of the midpoint reduction to incremental investments and $0.10 to service-related volume loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year EPS guidance excluding tariff benefits was lowered to $2.70–$3.00 from $3.00–$3.30, roughly $0.30 lower at the midpoint, with about $0.20 from incremental investments and $0.10 from service-related volume loss.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Reaffirm $3.00–$3.30, narrow, or reset” as the guidance debate and described the base case as “FY26 reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Water’s underlying margin was materially weaker than the preview’s key threshold: excluding tariff refunds, it fell about 700 basis points year over year, implying a margin near 17.1% versus the preview’s roughly 20% benchmark. The preview specifically warned that a result below 19% would weaken the second-half outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: Excluding tariff refunds, Water operating margin fell roughly 700 basis points year over year; about half came from price/cost, around 200 basis points from service-related costs, and the remainder from volume deleverage.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A margin above 20% supports the price/cost inflection. Below 19% weakens the H2 bridge.”

surprises.description: Water sales fell 6.5%, with volume down high-single digits because of service challenges and prior-year share losses. The preview focused on Water margin but gave no expectation of this service-related volume setback.
surprises.fact_evidence: Water sales declined 6.5% to $605 million, down 5.4% excluding China, with volume down high-single digits due to service challenges and prior-year share losses.

surprises.description: Q2 sales came in slightly above the preview’s consensus range, while the year-over-year decline was also less severe than management’s prior mid-single-digit decline guide. The upside was modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: Total Q2 sales fell 4% to $1.2 billion.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 net sales consensus was “$1.16B – $1.19B”; management had guided sales “down mid-single-digits.”

surprises.description: Security sales grew and new products contributed meaningfully to that growth, a positive segment development the preview did not specifically forecast. The reported margin surge is not a separate underlying surprise because tariff refunds accounted for most of it.
surprises.fact_evidence: Security sales grew 3.8% to $184 million, and new products added nearly 200 basis points to sales growth. Tariff refunds contributed 1,030 basis points of the 1,200-basis-point margin increase.

in_line: The $70 million annualized cost-savings target remained in place, with $15 million expected to land in 2026, consistent with the preview’s description of the program and its 2026 savings target.
The Fiberon strategic review remained underway without a reported deal or impairment, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the process was ongoing.
Management continued to expect weak 2026 end markets, consistent with the preview’s cited full-year sales outlook of down low-single digits.

surprises.description: The preview treated FY2027 revenue and adjusted operating income guidance as the main event and gave a buy-side revenue bogey of about $2.45–2.50 billion. Instead, management provided no FY2027 revenue or adjusted operating income range in the reported outlook, offering only operating assumptions such as revenue per enrollment flat to slightly higher and gross margins roughly flat.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided FY2027 revenue per enrollment to be flat to up slightly, gross margins flattish, and CapEx/SG&A ratios roughly flat.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2027 revenue and adjusted OI guidance. This is the main event”; “Buy-side bogey ~$2.45–2.50B revenue, ~$480–500M adj. OI.”

surprises.description: Enrollment signals were weaker on applications but better on conversion than the preview’s setup suggested: applications were slightly behind last year despite the preview citing strong applications, while conversion and reregistration were ahead. Management also warned that Q1 count-date comparisons will be tougher because less FY2026 enrollment carried over at year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Applications are tracking slightly behind last year, but conversion rates and reregistration activity are running ahead of the prior year”; Q1 count-date comparisons “will be tougher due to lower year-end carryover from moderated FY2026 in-year enrollment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had reported “applications were strong” and framed the question as “whether applications converted.”

surprises.description: Career Learning accelerated beyond the recent trend cited in the preview: FY2026 revenue grew 19% and enrollments rose 14%, compared with Q3 growth of 15.9% and 11.6%, respectively.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Career Learning revenue grew 19% to $1.04 billion with enrollments up 14% to 109,700.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q3 Career Learning revenue growth of “+15.9%” and enrollment growth of “+11.6%.”

surprises.description: General Education’s declines were less severe than the recent trend in the preview: FY2026 revenue fell 2% and enrollment fell 2.5%, versus Q3 declines of 3.6% and 5%, respectively.
surprises.fact_evidence: “General Education revenue declined 2% to $1.42 billion with enrollments down 2.5% to 134,200.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q3 General Education revenue down “−3.6%” and enrollment down “−5%.”

in_line: FY2026 revenue was $2.518 billion, at the top of the previously disclosed $2.49–2.52 billion guidance range; the preview noted that the result was already disclosed and largely known.

surprises.description: Q2 sales were $386.6 million, above the $377.4 million consensus, and average daily sales growth was 9.3% rather than the roughly 7% preview expectation. Management also said similar momentum was continuing into Q3, while volume and mix—not just pricing—drove the growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 7.7% to $386.6 million, or 9.3% on an average daily sales basis”; “similar momentum continuing into Q3”; “Pricing contributed about 4 points of growth while volume and mix drove the rest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | $377.4M”; “Average daily sales growth vs. ~7%.”

surprises.description: Canada grew 33.7% in local currency, accelerating from the preview’s cited 24.4% in Q1 and extending its double-digit growth streak. That was substantially stronger than the preview’s concern that Canada might slow to single-digit growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Canada revenue surged 33.7% in local currency, its fourth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Three straight double-digit quarters, with +24.4% local currency in Q1. A slowdown to single digits would weaken the growth story.”

surprises.description: The company reported approximately $26 million of IEEPA tariff refunds, including $21 million benefiting cost of sales, but excluded the refunds from non-GAAP results and said future refunds should be immaterial. The preview did not flag these refunds, so this is an unanticipated one-off rather than a recurring earnings contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $26 million in IEEPA tariff refunds ($21 million benefiting cost of sales, $4 million inventory reduction, $1 million interest income), which was excluded from non-GAAP results”; “future refunds will be immaterial.”

surprises.description: Repurchases accelerated to about 160,000 shares for $4.7 million, versus only about 22,000 shares for $0.6 million in Q1. The preview highlighted the prior quarter’s low buyback pace as something to watch, but did not forecast a specific increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased about 160,000 shares for $4.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working capital reversal and buyback pace”; “Only about 22,000 shares ($0.6M) were repurchased in Q1.”

surprises.description: Management now expects gross margins to stay around 34.7%–34.8% for the balance of 2026, offering a new indication that margins are likely to remain near the current level rather than rebound soon. The preview said the company did not issue formal financial guidance and focused on the Q2 margin estimate, so it did not anticipate this full-year margin outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margins for the balance of 2026 should remain roughly in line with the recent 34.7%–34.8% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GIC does not issue formal financial guidance.”

surprises.description: Management said it is building an M&A pipeline to accelerate its go-to-market strategy, a strategic initiative the preview did not identify as an issue to watch. No deal or financial contribution was specified, so the significance is not yet clear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is now building an M&A pipeline to accelerate its go-to-market strategy.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed substantial GPO and e-procurement scale, along with a roughly 10% increase in average order value driven by larger orders and participation in projects and GPOs. The preview did not provide expectations for these metrics, making them new operating disclosures rather than a quantified beat against a stated estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The GPO business is on pace to reach roughly $100 million in annualized sales this year”; “e-procurement connections surpassed 1,300 customers with over 50 new connections added in the first half”; “Average order value increased approximately 10%, driven primarily by a greater mix of larger orders and increased participation in projects and GPOs rather than price.”

in_line: Non-GAAP gross margin was 34.7%, close to the preview’s roughly 35% expectation and above the preview’s 34.5% downside threshold; the preview had also anticipated pressure from fuel costs and mix.
The 7.3% non-GAAP operating margin matched the preview’s roughly 7.3% estimate.
The quarterly dividend remained $0.28, consistent with the preview’s expectation that there would be no further raise this quarter.

surprises.description: LMAT missed its Q2 sales guidance by $1.1 million, despite the preview’s $71.47 million consensus and $71.5 million guidance midpoint. The company attributed the shortfall in equal thirds to a stronger U.S. dollar, Middle East war-related export delays that blocked about $400,000 of orders, and cardiac allograft supply constraints.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company missed its Q2 sales guidance by $1.1 million,” attributed “in equal thirds” to a stronger U.S. dollar, Middle East war-related export delays (“~$400,000 of orders blocked”), and cardiac allograft supply constraints.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sales” guidance midpoint “$71.5M”; consensus “$71.47M.” The catalyst checklist called for sales “at or above $71.5M.”

surprises.description: Q2 diluted EPS was $0.74, below both the preview’s $0.81 consensus and the $0.79 low end of the company’s guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fully diluted EPS grew 23% to $0.74.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 diluted EPS guidance was “$0.79 – $0.84” and consensus was “$0.81.”

surprises.description: LMAT cut its full-year outlook rather than raising or affirming it: revenue guidance is now $276.3 million versus the prior $277–$283 million range, and organic growth was reduced from 12% to 11%. The new implied EPS of $2.89 and operating income of $76.8 million are also below the preview’s prior guidance figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year revenue guidance was updated to $276.3 million,” with organic growth “cut from 12% to 11%”; full-year guidance implies operating income of “$76.8 million” and fully diluted EPS of “$2.89.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 sales guidance was “$277M – $283M”; operating income was “$79.8M”; diluted EPS was “$2.93 – $3.08.” The preview said the buy side wanted the sales line raised and flagged a sales guidance raise as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Q2 operating margin was 29%, below the preview’s 30% guidance, even though operating income reached a record $20.4 million and rose 26%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating income reached a record $20.4 million (up 26%) for a 29% operating margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 operating margin guidance was “30%.”

surprises.description: Total unit growth was 3%, short of the preview’s 4% threshold for broader growth, although growth excluding catheters was stronger at 5% units. Catheters fell 11% because of recall-driven overstocking in the prior-year period.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 organic sales grew “10% (7% price, 3% units),” but excluding catheters organic growth was “12% (7% price, 5% units),” as “catheters fell 11% due to year-earlier recall-driven overstocking.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “4% or more” unit growth would signal the story was broadening beyond price increases, and listed unit growth “at or above 4%” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Artegraft’s international ramp exceeded the preview’s near-term and full-year benchmarks: Q2 international sales reached $2.8 million, and the company now expects $11 million for 2026 rather than the preview’s $10 million target.
surprises.fact_evidence: International Artegraft sales rose from “$2.1 million in Q1 to $2.8 million in Q2” and full-year 2026 international sales are expected at “$11 million versus $4 million in 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “roughly $2.5M or more in Q2” was needed to stay on plan for a “$10M FY2026 target.”

surprises.description: Cardiac allograft supply constraints are limiting growth, an issue the preview did not flag: management said growth is slowing and is moving tissue processing to Burlington to address the constraint. This comes despite Q2 RFA revenue growth of 17% and a 39% quarter-on-quarter rise in cardiac allografts specifically.
surprises.fact_evidence: “RFA revenue grew 17% in Q2 and cardiac allografts specifically rose 39% quarter-on-quarter, but growth is slowing due to supply constraints being addressed by moving tissue processing to Burlington, Massachusetts.”

surprises.description: The FDA indicated that a clinical trial is likely required for the Artegraft Quick Stick indication, stretching the timeline to years and leaving LMAT uncertain whether to pursue it. The preview did not anticipate this regulatory hurdle.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FDA indicated a clinical trial is likely required for the Artegraft Quick Stick indication, pushing the timeline to years and leaving the company uncertain whether to proceed.”

surprises.description: The call reported substantial European gross-margin gains from the relocalization strategy—5–9 full percentage points year over year—alongside plans to open about seven new or larger warehouses across 2026 and 2027. The preview had focused on warehouse and processing-transfer costs as a margin pressure, not these reported regional gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: LMAT is opening “about 7 new or larger warehouses across 2026/2027” as part of a relocalization strategy “driving European gross margin gains of 5-9 full points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q2 gross-margin guidance “reflects Irish warehouse and tissue-processing transfer costs.”

in_line: Q2 gross margin was 72.1%, matching the preview’s 72.1% guidance; the new full-year gross-margin outlook of 72.4% was only slightly above the preview’s 72.3%.
The sales-rep count increased from 158 at Q1 to 163, while LMAT continued to target 170–180 by year-end, consistent with the preview’s staffing watch.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.01, below the preview’s $0.03–$0.05 consensus range. The shortfall came despite adjusted operating income landing close to the preview’s estimate, with the call citing higher advertising and SG&A and lower gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS dropped to $0.01 from $0.21,” driven by “higher advertising, SG&A, and lower gross margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS $0.03 (Zacks); $0.04 (AAII, 12 analysts); $0.05 (alternate compiler)”

surprises.description: Net sales growth exceeded the preview’s expected 6%–8% range: constant-currency growth was 9% and reported growth was 10%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales grew 10% as reported and 9% in constant currency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected net sales growth of “+6% to +8%.”

surprises.description: Masters of the Universe had a much stronger showing than the preview’s box-office concern suggested: year-to-date gross billings more than tripled, and the film became a major streaming hit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Masters of the Universe gross billings more than tripled year-to-date” and the film became “the #1 movie on Prime Video globally” and the most-watched movie across U.S. streaming in its first week.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the “MOTU film” as having “underperformed at the box office.”

surprises.description: Management introduced a strong 2027 outlook that the preview did not discuss: mid- to high-single-digit top-line growth, strong double-digit bottom-line growth, and Barbie returning to growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided to “2027 delivering mid- to high-single-digit top-line growth, strong double-digit bottom-line growth, and Barbie returning to growth.”

surprises.description: Management said the majority of $40 million in digital performance-marketing spend will be pushed to coincide with UNO Wild’s early-2027 launch. The delay was not flagged in the preview, although management said it would not affect 2026 guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Delaying the majority of $40 million in digital performance marketing spend to coincide with UNO Wild's commercial launch in early 2027, with no impact to 2026 guidance.”

surprises.description: Hot Wheels delivered a standout result that the preview did not address: the brand grew 12% and is approaching $2 billion in annual revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hot Wheels grew 12% in the quarter,” remains Mattel’s largest brand, and is “approaching $2 billion in annual revenue.”

in_line: Adjusted gross margin was 48.6%, in line with the preview’s roughly 48%–49% expectation and its expectation that margin would improve sequentially while staying below 50%.

Full-year 2026 guidance was reiterated at 3%–6% constant-currency net sales growth, about 50% adjusted gross margin, $580M–$630M adjusted operating income, and $1.27–$1.39 adjusted EPS, as the preview’s base case expected the guide to be reaffirmed rather than raised.
Adjusted operating income of $39 million was close to the preview’s roughly $40–$55 million estimate and its approximately $42 million reference point.
North America grew, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the region would grow in Q2.

Share repurchases remained on the preview’s expected pace: Mattel had repurchased $200 million in Q1 and a $400 million full-year target; the call reported $300 million year-to-date and said the company remained on track for $400 million.

surprises.description: Lumen announced $13 billion in new PCF deals, a major upside to the preview’s baseline, which assumed no incremental deals and described new awards as an upside catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced $13 billion in new PCF deals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said its long-term projections include no incremental deals, so any new hyperscaler, neocloud, or AI award is upside.”

surprises.description: Q2 PCF cash receipts were substantial despite collections being expected to be weighted toward the second half, suggesting more cash arrived earlier than the preview’s timing expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PCF cash received of ~$476 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Collections are weighted to the second half.”

surprises.description: PCF revenue reached about $91 million even though management had said the Q1 milestone would not recur in Q2; the quarter included a $36 million California milestone pulled forward from the second half, so the revenue strength partly reflects timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 PCF revenue of approximately $91 million (including ~$36 million of State of California milestone pulled forward from the second half).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 included a $32M PCF delivery milestone that management said ‘won’t reoccur in Q2’”; the preview also flagged Q2 PCF revenue as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Business revenue declined only 1.8%, better than the preview’s roughly 4.5% downside threshold, and strategic revenue reached 53% of the mix, above the 51% watch point. Strategic growth also accelerated to 14% from the 9.4% rate cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total business revenue declined 1.8% year-over-year”; “Strategic revenue grew 14% year-over-year and reached 53% of total business revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Business revenue Y/Y better than about −4.5%, with strategic mix above 51%”; “Strategic revenue grew 9.4% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: Legacy revenue fell about 15%, a steeper decline than the 10% year-over-year legacy decline cited for Q1 in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Legacy revenue declined about 15%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Strategic revenue grew 9.4% Y/Y against a 10% decline in legacy revenue in Q1.”

surprises.description: Management said the cost-savings program remained on track, easing the preview’s concern that planned cost reductions might not land and cause an EBITDA shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is targeting $700 million in modernization and simplification cost savings exiting 2026 and $1 billion exiting 2027, both said to be on track and central to the EBITDA inflection.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Street's stated worry going into the print is a modest EBITDA shortfall unless planned cost reductions land.”

surprises.description: NaaS adoption showed strong quarter-over-quarter growth, including more than 20% of new adopters being new to Lumen; the preview did not identify these operating metrics as an expected catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NaaS customers now exceed 3,000, with new customer adoption up 22% quarter-over-quarter, active ports up 34%, and active services up 29%, with over 20% of new adopters being brand new to Lumen.”

surprises.description: Management said Alkira could provide upside beyond Investor Day targets, with the amount to be quantified in 2027 guidance; this additional upside was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Alkira to provide upside beyond Investor Day targets, with quantification coming in 2027 guidance.”

surprises.description: Strategic 100- and 400-gig waves revenue grew nearly 11% year over year while waves sales surged nearly 35%, pointing to momentum not called out in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Strategic 100- and 400-gig waves revenue grew nearly 11% year-over-year in North American enterprise channels, while waves sales surged nearly 35% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Lumen described a portfolio shift away from enterprise voice and communications products, which contribute only a low-single-digit share of sales, and said incremental digital services could approach 80% adjusted EBITDA margins; the preview did not flag this transition or margin outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lumen is phasing out enterprise voice and communications products, which contribute only low-single-digit percentage of sales, and expects incremental digital services to approach 80% adjusted EBITDA margin.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA excluding special items was $802 million, within the preview’s $790–810 million base case and around its ~$800 million bar.
The company said total business revenue was slightly ahead of consensus and in line with company expectations.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $331 million, above the preview’s estimated $328–330 million, and the 39% margin also exceeded the ~38.3% expectation. The gap was modest, but profitability came in better than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 14% to $331 million with a 39% margin, exceeding expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$328–330M (est.)”; “Adj. EBITDA margin: ~38.3%.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $853 million, about $5 million below the preview’s live consensus of $857.7 million, although it remained within the company’s $850–860 million guide. This was a small miss against consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue was $853 million, down 1% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue: $857.7M” consensus; company guide was “$850–860M.”

surprises.description: Tinder’s near-term user trend was substantially more encouraging than the preview’s focus on gradually improving MAU: DAU declines narrowed to about 2.5% in July and were nearly positive in August, with management expecting the first year-over-year DAU growth in over three years imminently.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tinder DAU declined 4% year-over-year in Q2, its best result in 10 quarters, improving to down ~2.5% in July and nearly positive in August,” with positive year-over-year DAU expected “imminently.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “April was –6.6%” for Tinder MAU and that “Movement toward –5% would support the 2027 inflection story”; it did not give a DAU outlook.

surprises.description: Tinder’s broader MAU and payer recovery timeline looked slower than the preview’s hoped-for 2027 inflection: Q2 MAU was still down 7%, and management targeted flat MAU and a return to payer growth only by Q4 2027. The preview had identified year-over-year MAU growth as the key turnaround expectation, though management still expects 2027 Tinder revenue to exceed 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tinder MAU declined 7% year-over-year in Q2”; management “targets flat MAU by Q4 2027” and “expects payer growth to return by Q4 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Any softening of management’s target of Y/Y MAU growth and FY2027 revenue growth would be the most damaging outcome.”

surprises.description: Hinge revenue was just below the preview’s stated $205 million threshold: it reported $204 million, despite delivering the expected 22% growth. The shortfall was small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hinge delivered direct revenue of $204 million, up 22%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Hinge direct revenue. Needs at least $205M (+22% FXN).”

surprises.description: The expected 2026 alternative-payment savings improved to about $130 million, roughly $20 million above plan and above the preview’s $110 million app-store-savings assumption.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Alternative payment savings are now expected to contribute ~$130 million in 2026 (about $20 million above plan).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “the $110M app-store savings assumption.”

surprises.description: The outlook for Google-related savings in 2027 was disappointing: the new fee structure is expected to provide only about $5 million of benefit. That limits the durability of the much larger 2026 alternative-payment savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Google's new fee structure effective March 2026 offers only ~$5 million of benefit in 2027, a disappointing outcome for developers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the “$110M app-store savings assumption against the Google/Epic settlement” as a key margin issue, but gave no 2027 savings figure.

surprises.description: The projected 2026 Tinder revenue headwind from user-experience tests and product changes was cut to $30–40 million from the original $60 million estimate. The smaller-than-first-estimated drag, attributed in part to a smooth rebrand, is favorable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tinder's user experience test and product-change revenue headwind for full-year 2026 was cut to $30–$40 million from the original $60 million estimate, reflecting a smooth rebrand with no revenue impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The call cited the “original $60 million estimate”; the preview separately flagged the “$45M user-investment budget” as something to watch.

surprises.description: Match Group added a firm commitment to return all free cash flow to shareholders. The preview expected capital returns and was watching buybacks, but did not describe this broader 100%-of-free-cash-flow pledge.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “pledged to return 100% of free cash flow to shareholders.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Buyback pace is doing real work on EPS” and listed “buyback pace” among the strategic items to watch.

in_line: Tinder payers declined 5%, matching the preview’s Q1-based expectation and its –4% to –5% base-case range.
Hinge’s 22% revenue growth was in line with the preview’s expected growth rate, and management remained on track for $1 billion of Hinge revenue in 2027, as the preview anticipated.
Management maintained the expectation that 2027 Tinder revenue will exceed 2026, consistent with the preview’s focus on the FY2027 revenue-growth commitment.

surprises.description: Lattice reported Q2 revenue of $201 million, well above the preview’s $185.1–185.5 million consensus range and above the high end of company guidance. The beat was about 8% versus consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached a record $201 million” and “exceed[ed] the high end of guidance.”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP EPS was $0.53 versus the preview’s $0.44 consensus, a substantial beat. The call also described strong operating leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP EPS was $0.53,” growing “29% sequentially,” with “strong operating leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS | $0.44”

surprises.description: The Q3 combined revenue guide of $245–265 million is above the preview’s internal $228–243 million bridge, with even the low end exceeding that estimate’s high end. The standalone FPGA guide also implies about 65% year-over-year growth, answering the preview’s concern that the guide might amount to in-line standalone results plus AMI revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 combined revenue guidance is $245-265 million (midpoint $255 million), including $33-37 million of AMI”; “standalone FPGA business is guided to $210-230 million for Q3, representing approximately 65% year-over-year growth at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My bridge estimate for consolidated Q3 is about $228–243M”; the bear case was “standalone in line plus AMI arithmetic, with no real organic raise.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin came in at 71.7%, above the roughly 70% consensus, alongside substantial operating-margin expansion. This was a stronger Q2 profitability result than the preview’s central margin expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP gross margin was 71.7%, up 170 basis points sequentially and 240 basis points year-over-year,” while “operating margin expand[ed] 390 basis points to 38.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin | ~70%”

surprises.description: Management said Lattice would exceed a $1 billion annualized run rate a quarter ahead of plan, rather than merely reaffirming the preview’s year-end 2026 milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Q3 guide puts Lattice “at over $1 billion annualized run rate a quarter ahead of plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “$1B annual run rate by year-end 2026” and asked whether management would “reaffirm, raise, or soften” that target.

surprises.description: The call added a strong longer-range operating outlook for AMI: an exit-2026 revenue run rate above $200 million with high gross and EBITDA margins, followed by about 25% growth in 2027. The preview focused on AMI’s stub-period contribution and did not anticipate these exit-rate and 2027 details.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AMI is expected to exit 2026 at a revenue run rate above $200 million with gross margins above 75% and EBITDA margins above 40%, and to grow about 25% in 2027 (excluding revenue synergies).”

surprises.description: Despite the strong Q2 margin expansion, management disclosed industry-wide assembly and packaging constraints and rising costs that are pressuring margins until expected normalization in Q4. The preview had highlighted margin as a key debate but did not anticipate this specific near-term cost and supply headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industry-wide assembly/packaging supply constraints and rising costs are pressuring margins until expected normalization in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for monitoring “Q3 gross margin vs. the accretion claim” and cited a reference range of “71–73%,” without mentioning these constraints or cost pressures.

surprises.description: Backlog visibility was stronger than the preview’s description of bookings extending well into 2027: management said 2027 was essentially fully booked.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog visibility extends through the end of 2027, with 2027 described as essentially fully booked.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said bookings extended “well into 2027.”

in_line: AMI’s Q3 revenue contribution was close to the preview estimate: the call guided to $33–37 million versus the preview’s estimate of roughly $33–38 million net for the stub period.
Compute and Communications grew 18% sequentially, in line with the preview’s stated bull-case condition of growth above 15% quarter over quarter.

surprises.description: The preview expected Opendoor to reaffirm adjusted net income positive by year-end 2026. Management instead described a target of reaching adjusted net income breakeven on a 12-month go-forward basis by the end of 2026, which is a less specific and potentially later profitability milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “reaffirmed its target to reach adjusted net income breakeven on a 12-month go-forward basis by the end of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reaffirmation of adjusted net income positive by end-2026.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case anticipated Q3 would be roughly flat to modestly up sequentially. Opendoor guided to at least 20% year-over-year revenue growth and contribution profit more than doubling year over year; its 4%-4.5% contribution-margin outlook also implies a much smaller seasonal Q2-to-Q3 decline than the historical average cited on the call.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For Q3, the company guided to revenue up at least 20% year-over-year, contribution profit more than doubling year-over-year, and contribution margin of ~4%-4.5%, reflecting seasonal decline better than its historical 470 bps Q2-to-Q3 average.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … Q3 roughly flat to modestly up”; the preview also said investors wanted “Q3 revenue guide” and “CM held together.”

surprises.description: The preview centered on contribution margin of about 6.0%, while Opendoor reported 5.8%. That is a small shortfall, though the result remained within the company’s 5%-7% guidance range and the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contribution margin climbed to 5.8% … within the guided 5%-7% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Contribution margin ~6% (guide midpoint)”; the key metric to watch was “Contribution margin vs. 6.0%.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 purchases of roughly 3,500 to 4,500 based on the contract backlog, but did not anticipate the reported pace of new contracts and weekly signings. Opendoor said weekly purchase contracts had reached a multi-year high and acquisition contracts totaled 6,908.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Signing over 500 purchase contracts weekly, hitting a multi-year high of roughly 700 last week, representing a ~5x year-over-year increase”; “acquisition contracts reaching 6,908.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 purchases could land around 3,500 to 4,500 based on the Q1 contract backlog. Weekly contract data showed +12% in the week ended July 18.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged inventory funding as a concern, given the $999 million cash balance. Opendoor reported growing inventory by more than $700 million, funded largely through nonrecourse asset-backed facilities, indicating that the build was not funded primarily from cash.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $896 million in cash … and grew inventory by over $700 million funded largely by nonrecourse asset-backed facilities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Acquisition pace and inventory quality. Watch funding from the $999M cash balance and any change to the no-equity-raise commitment.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag the scale of the marketing reduction. Q2 marketing spend fell to $5 million from $19 million in Q1, and marketing fell to 0.3% of acquisition GMV from 1.6% under Opendoor 1.0.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marketing spend fell dramatically to just $5 million in Q2 (from $19 million in Q1), lowering marketing as a percent of acquisition GMV from 1.6% under Opendoor 1.0 to 0.3%.”

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate the reported AI-driven productivity gains and associated decline in per-acquisition operations expense. Home project managers and underwriters are handling substantially more work, while operations expense per acquisition fell to $3,000 from $8,400 a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Home project managers now handling ~10 renovations each (up from 3, targeting 20), underwriters doing 50+ per day (up from 20), and per-acquisition operations expense falling to $3,000 from $8,400 a year ago.”

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss Opendoor’s mortgage product attach rate. The call reported meaningful early use just six weeks after launch in Colorado and Texas, with licensing planned to expand substantially by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over half of scheduled closes in Colorado and nearly 1 in 5 in Texas (just 6 weeks post-launch) are financed through Opendoor, with plans to be licensed in 35-40 states by year-end.”

in_line: Q2 acquisitions were 4,378 homes, within the preview’s estimated range of roughly 3,500 to 4,500 purchases.

surprises.description: ACTG reported Q2 revenue of $114.6 million, far above the $50.0 million consensus estimate. The preview expected IP revenue near zero in its base case; instead, a large licensing settlement drove total revenue to more than double the year-ago level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue for Q2 2026 was $114.6 million, more than doubling from $51.2 million in the prior year period, driven largely by a significant Wi-Fi 6 licensing settlement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $50.0M”; the base scenario expected “Revenue $54–58M” with “IP near zero.”

surprises.description: IP licensing revenue was approximately $60.6 million, dramatically exceeding the preview’s expectation that little or no IP revenue was likely unless there was a material settlement. The reported revenue came primarily from a single TP-Link settlement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Intellectual Property platform generated approximately $60.6 million in licensing revenue, primarily from a single TP-Link settlement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything above roughly $10M would ‘re-rate’ the stock; $0–1M is largely priced in.” The base scenario also expected “IP near zero.”

surprises.description: Operated Segment adjusted EBITDA reached $22.8 million, well above the $6.8 million level the preview identified as the clean test for the quarter. This was a much stronger result than the preview’s operating-improvement framing implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operated segment adjusted EBITDA was $22.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operated Segment Adj. EBITDA vs. $6.8M. This is the cleanest test of whether the operating businesses are compounding.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was positive at $0.13 rather than the preview’s expected loss of $0.09. GAAP net income was nearly break-even, but the adjusted result still substantially exceeded the estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income was just $47,000 ($0.00 per diluted share) and adjusted net income was $12.8 million ($0.13 per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | ($0.09).”

surprises.description: Deflecto generated only $1.1 million of adjusted EBITDA on $27.1 million of revenue, about a 4.1% margin. That was below the preview’s hoped-for move toward a 6% or higher margin, and management pointed to softer end-market demand rather than margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Deflecto generated $27.1 million revenue but only $1.1 million adjusted EBITDA amid softer end-market demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A move from the Q1 4.3% margin toward 6%+ would support the operating-improvement story.”

surprises.description: Book value fell to $5.71 per share, below the preview’s expectation that it remain at or above about $5.85. The decline included parent expenses and a full write-off of the MalinJ1/Viamet life sciences investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Book value declined to $557 million ($5.71 per share) from $567.2 million ($5.87 per share) last quarter, pressured by parent expenses and the full write-off of the MalinJ1/Viamet life sciences investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The discount thesis holds if BVPS stays at or above about $5.85”; erosion below “about $5.70” was described as breaking the analyst’s core argument.

surprises.description: Q2 IP results included $3.7 million of legacy litigation expense that was not excluded from adjusted EBITDA. The preview flagged rising legal spend as a downside scenario, but did not anticipate this specific expense; management said it does not expect the cost to recur and hopes to recover more than the amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 IP results included $3.7 million of nonrecurring legacy litigation expense (not adjusted out of EBITDA) that management does not expect to recur and hopes to recover in excess of that amount.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bear scenario cited “IP zero with rising legal spend.”

surprises.description: The securities portfolio produced $9.4 million of gains after an investee announced an acquisition agreement, allowing ACTG to exit at an attractive return. The preview discussed deploying liquid assets but did not anticipate this specific gain and exit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The public securities portfolio contributed $9.4 million in gains as one investee announced an acquisition agreement, allowing Acacia to exit at an attractive return.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “M&A deployment of the $330M+ in liquid assets.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed an active acquisition pipeline and a possible direct ownership stake in Mycovia Pharmaceuticals. The preview raised capital deployment as a catalyst but did not flag this specific potential investment path.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management flagged “an active acquisition pipeline and possible direct ownership stake in Mycovia Pharmaceuticals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “M&A deployment of the $330M+ in liquid assets.”

in_line: Benchmark adjusted EBITDA was $9.8 million, within the preview’s expected $8–10 million range.

surprises.description: Chemours cut its FY26 adjusted EBITDA outlook: the preview cited $800–900 million, while the company now guides to $775–825 million. The sales-growth range also shifted down at the low end, from 3–5% to 1–5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year 2026 guidance calls for net sales growth of 1-5% over 2025 and adjusted EBITDA of $775-825 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 unchanged: sales up 3–5%, Adj. EBITDA $800–900M.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA exceeded expectations, even though net sales were slightly below them. The preview highlighted the $220–250 million company EBITDA guide and revenue consensus of $1.66–1.67 billion, but the call facts do not give actual Q2 results to quantify either gap.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA exceeded expectations due to stronger operations, improved APM product mix, lower corporate costs and pricing strength in Titanium Technologies, though net sales came in slightly below expectations on softer residential AC demand.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consolidated Adj. EBITDA $220–250M; Revenue $1.66B–$1.67B.

surprises.description: The TSS Q3 outlook points to a substantial sequential sales decline and weaker margins, with aftermarket destocking expected to persist into Q1 2027. The preview flagged destocking and softer residential HVAC demand as issues to watch, but did not anticipate this specific decline or the projected high-20s margin level.
surprises.fact_evidence: TSS Q3 net sales are guided to decline sequentially by mid-teens to 20% with adjusted EBITDA of $125-140 million, pressured by aftermarket destocking and lower-margin mix pushing margins into the high-20s versus the 30%+ historical level. Roughly $65 million of aftermarket refrigerant sales were pulled forward into 2025 due to AIM Act channel fill, contributing to a ~25% year-over-year drop in aftermarket volumes and destocking headwinds expected to persist through Q1 2027.
surprises.expectation_evidence: TSS volume and price, and residential HVAC destocking commentary; management flagged softer residential HVAC demand on the Q1 call.

surprises.description: Titanium Technologies pricing was a stronger contributor than the preview’s baseline discussion of whether pricing would hold: three increases since December produced about 5% year-to-date price gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: Chemours has announced three TiO2 price increases since December 2025, including a global increase effective June 1, cumulatively driving approximately 5% year-to-date price gains in Titanium Technologies.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario cited “TT price holds.”

surprises.description: APM Performance Solutions showed a specific growth driver the preview did not identify: sales rose 8% year over year on data center and semiconductor demand, and AI-related end markets now make up more than 40% of Performance Solutions sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: APM Performance Solutions net sales grew 8% year-over-year, driven by data center and semiconductor demand, and now more than 40% of Performance Solutions sales target AI-related end markets. Sales into data center, semiconductor, AI and advanced electronics end markets now represent a high single-digit percentage of total sales across APM and TSS.

surprises.description: The company repaid substantially more of its 2028 euro term loan than it had previously communicated, accelerating debt reduction beyond the preview’s stated leverage path.
surprises.fact_evidence: Chemours repaid nearly $270 million of its 2028 euro term loan in Q2, $103 million more than previously communicated.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The call states the repayment was “$103 million more than previously communicated.”

surprises.description: Despite the additional loan repayment, the year-end leverage target was described as approximately 3.8x, rather than the preview’s stated target of below 3.8x. That is a slightly less ambitious near-term target, while the company still aims for below 3x over the longer term.
surprises.fact_evidence: Chemours targets net leverage of approximately 3.8x adjusted EBITDA by year-end 2026 en route to a sub-3x long-term goal.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Net leverage below 3.8x by year-end.

surprises.description: Chemours reported early commercial traction in two-phase liquid cooling and a sharp increase in product trials, creating potential beyond its stated long-term EBITDA target; the preview did not flag these opportunities or management’s openness to transformational partnerships.
surprises.fact_evidence: Product trials increased 70% year-over-year and Chemours recorded initial nominal sales of two-phase liquid cooling products for sampling, representing upside beyond the $1 billion EBITDA target as management stated no portfolio action, including transformational partnerships, is off the table.

surprises.description: Workiva’s Q2 non-GAAP operating margin was 16.8%, well above the preview’s roughly 15% consensus and the company’s 14.5–15.0% guidance range. The 180-basis-point beat of the top of guidance was a much larger margin upside than the preview’s base case of a modest margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP operating margin reached 16.8%, a 180 basis point beat versus guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin … Street Consensus … ~15%”; the base case anticipated “modest margin and FCF raise.”

surprises.description: Workiva raised its full-year non-GAAP operating margin outlook to approximately 18% from the prior 16.0–16.5% range, reaching its 2027 medium-term target a year early. The size of the increase exceeded the preview’s expectation of a modest margin raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year 2026 non-GAAP operating margin guidance to approximately 18%, achieving its 2027 medium-term margin target a full year early.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin … 16.0–16.5% (raised 100bp)”; the base case expected “modest margin and FCF raise.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue reached $255 million, $3 million above the high end of guidance and above the approximately $252 million consensus; subscription revenue was also above the roughly $233 million estimate. This was a modest upside to the preview’s expected in-line quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue grew 19% year-over-year to $255 million, beating the high end of guidance by $3 million, with subscription revenue up 19% to $236 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue … Street Consensus … ~$252M”; “Subscription & support … ~$233M”; the base case expected “Guide met.”

surprises.description: The full-year revenue range moved up from $1.037–$1.041 billion to $1.040–$1.044 billion rather than being simply reaffirmed. The increase was modest and the new range remained close to the preview’s approximately $1.04 billion consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 total revenue is guided to $1.040-$1.044 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue … $1.037–1.041B”; the base case expected “FY revenue reaffirmed,” while the bull case called for “FY revenue raised to ≥$1.045B.”

surprises.description: Workiva increased its free cash flow margin outlook by 100 basis points to approximately 21%, above the preview’s approximately 20% guidance. This was a positive but relatively measured increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised free cash flow margin outlook by 100 basis points to approximately 21%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FCF margin … ~20%”; the base case expected a “modest margin and FCF raise.”

surprises.description: Large-contract growth remained strong, but the reported year-over-year growth rates were slower than the Q1 rates cited in the preview: contracts over $500,000 grew 33% versus 39% in Q1, and contracts over $300,000 grew 34% versus 38%. That partial deceleration was a negative contrast to the preview’s concern that slowing large-contract growth would weaken the enterprise-platform story.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contracts over $300,000 up 34% to 656 and contracts over $500,000 up 33% to 276 versus Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Large-ACV cohorts. The $500K+ tier (+39% in Q1) is the main evidence that customers are standardizing on the platform. Deceleration here would undercut that story.”

surprises.description: Net new customer additions were the strongest in seven quarters, a positive acquisition signal not anticipated in the preview’s listed key metrics. The preview had focused instead on retention, large contracts, and cRPO.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Customer count reached 6,750, up 283 year-over-year, representing the strongest quarter for net new customer additions in the past seven quarters.”

surprises.description: Multi-solution customers accounted for a larger share of subscription revenue, rising to 76% from 71% a year earlier, while customers added in the past 12 months contributed about 45% of the subscription revenue increase. This was an unpreviewed indication of both broader solution adoption and contribution from new customers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Multi-solution customers now generate 76% of subscription revenue, up from 71% in Q2 2025, while new customers added in the last 12 months accounted for approximately 45% of the Q2 subscription revenue increase.”

in_line: Full-year subscription growth remained approximately 19%, as previewed; Q2 subscription revenue grew 19%.
NRR was 111% and roughly flat on a constant-currency basis, meeting the preview’s threshold of at least 110% ex-FX rather than relying on a material FX tailwind.

surprises.description: The preview expected updated FY2026 guidance and described a realistic reinstated delivery range of 14,000–18,000 units. Instead, management warned that production and deliveries would be below current consensus, with Q3 and Q4 production below Q2 because of the move to a single shift.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management explicitly warned that both production and delivery figures will come in below current consensus estimates, with Q3 and Q4 production expected below Q2 levels due to the shift to a single-shift configuration.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance reinstatement” was the top issue to watch; the preview called 14,000–18,000 units a “realistic reinstated range.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was far worse than the preview’s roughly -75% consensus estimate and below its -90% bear-case threshold. A $300 million inventory impairment accounted for 74 percentage points of the -105% margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: Gross margin was “negative 105% including a $300 million inventory impairment that hurt margin by 74 percentage points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP gross margin ~-75%”; the preview said “worse than -90%” was the bear case.

surprises.description: Free cash flow was substantially more negative than the preview’s roughly $981 million cash-burn estimate. Management said much of the cash was trapped in inventory, which qualifies the shortfall but does not eliminate the unexpectedly large cash outflow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was negative $1.476 billion for the quarter,” with management characterizing much of it as “working capital trapped in inventory rather than permanent cash burn.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash burn ~$981M.”

surprises.description: The midsize program’s timing appears later than the preview’s H2 2026 target: the Saudi factory is expected to be production-ready in early 2027, with Cosmos volume production in the second half of 2027. Lucid also withheld formal factory guidance until year-end and cited supplier-localization and infrastructure risks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The AMP-2 Saudi factory is expected to be production-ready in early 2027 with mid-size (Cosmos) volume production in the second half,” and the company “withheld formal guidance until year-end results.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Midsize launch is targeted for H2 2026,” and the preview called a slip in midsize timing the most significant risk on the call.

surprises.description: Disclosed liquidity was below the preview’s roughly $4.7 billion expectation: Lucid reported $3 billion at quarter-end and then drew another $800 million term loan after quarter-end. Management still expects runway well into 2027, so the lower liquidity figure was partly offset by financing and the runway claim.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total liquidity stood at $3 billion as of June 30 ($800 million cash plus $2.2 billion of credit facility capacity),” and Lucid “drew an additional $800 million term loan after quarter-end, expecting runway well into 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Pro forma liquidity ~$4.7B” and said management expected it to fund operations “into the second half of 2027.”

surprises.description: Lucid gave a much more concrete cost and cash-flow improvement plan than the preview’s request for quantified cost-out. The $1.4 billion 2026 cash-flow improvement target is not all permanent savings, however, because some comes from working capital and shifting spending into future years; the workforce and shift actions separately carry $158 million in annualized savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company identified “approximately $1.4 billion of 2026 cash flow improvements” across operating costs, capital spending, and working capital, partly through “phasing spend into future years.” Early actions—a “one-fifth reduction of the U.S. workforce” and elimination of the Arizona second shift—are projected to generate “$158 million in annualized savings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said investors wanted “a dollar-quantified cost-out target and a gross-margin breakeven date.”

surprises.description: Revenue was about $405 million, well above the preview’s stated $355–370 million likely base case, although it was essentially in line with the $404.2 million Visible Alpha consensus. The $25 million of regulatory-credit sales contributed to the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached approximately $405 million,” driven partly by “$25 million in regulatory credit sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The full preview treats $355–370M as the more likely base case”; it also listed revenue consensus of “$404.2M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected robotaxi production to begin in 2026, so the stated late-2026 target was broadly consistent with that timing. But the call added a substantial, previously unflagged scale commitment: 35,000 units with Uber and Nuro, nearly 100 test vehicles, and production-validation vehicles already delivered.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Uber and Nuro program involves “a committed 35,000 units and nearly 100 test vehicles,” with “production validation vehicles already delivered,” regular production in Q4, and launch targeted for late 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gravity robotaxi production is slated to begin at Casa Grande in 2026.”

in_line: Q2 deliveries were 3,953, matching the 3,953 figure already reported in the preview.
Revenue was essentially in line with the preview’s $404.2 million Visible Alpha consensus, despite being above its stated $355–370 million likely base case.

surprises.description: Revenue was about $1.2 billion, matching the preview’s rounded dollar estimate, but declined roughly 1% year over year instead of growing 3.3%. That is a meaningful shortfall in the expected growth trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY27 revenue declined approximately 1% year-over-year to $1.2 billion.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $381 million, below the preview’s estimated $385–400 million range. Management said it would have been roughly flat without $22 million of combined headwinds from the Navarino sale and lower IP licensing revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA down 7% to $381 million, though EBITDA would have been roughly flat excluding a $22 million combined headwind from the Navarino sale ($3M) and lower IP licensing revenue ($19M).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$385–400M (derived; no clean public consensus)”

surprises.description: Fixed services revenue fell 27%, with U.S. broadband subscribers down to 115,000, and management did not expect stabilization until after ViaSat-3 Flight 2 enters service. The preview highlighted Flight 2 timing but did not flag this degree of fixed-services weakness or the wait for stabilization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fixed services revenue fell 27% as U.S. broadband subscribers dropped to 115,000 (at $111 ARPU), with stabilization not expected until after ViaSat-3 Flight 2 enters service.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ViaSat-3 F2 entry into service” was a key metric to watch; the preview said investors wanted a date and that a third timing slip would be a clear negative.

surprises.description: First-quarter free cash flow was $72 million, above the $60 million generated a year earlier, despite the preview’s concern that it could come in well below that level. The full-year $180 million outlook was reaffirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was positive $72 million (up 19%), driven by operating cash flow of $291 million (up 13%), with the company reaffirming full-year FY27 free cash flow guidance of about $180 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 FCF was +$60M a year ago and could come in well below that.”

surprises.description: Aviation grew 11%, below the preview’s informal 12%-or-more bar, and some aircraft deactivated as customers transitioned to a competing provider. The preview had flagged competition, but the reported growth did not reach the stated bar and the call quantified aircraft exits and an IFC backlog of about 850 aircraft.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Aviation revenue grew 11% with commercial aircraft in service up 10% to about 4,530, though some aircraft deactivated due to a previously announced transition to a competing provider, leaving IFC backlog at roughly 850 aircraft.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Growth of 12% or more is the informal bar.” The preview also noted that management said “increased competition may slow aviation growth.”

surprises.description: Awards rose 10% and backlog grew nearly 19% to $4.2 billion, with DAT backlog up 32%. That is stronger backlog growth than the 23% DAT backlog increase cited in the preview for the prior quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Company-wide awards rose 10% to about $1.3 billion and backlog grew nearly 19% to $4.2 billion, with DAT backlog up 32% and Communication Services backlog up 13%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “DAT grew 12% in revenue and 20% in EBITDA in Q4, with backlog up 23% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: Viasat won the next phase of the Protected Tactical SATCOM-Global program, with a $4 billion ceiling value. The preview did not anticipate this award, and the call clarified that only the awarded base order—not the full ceiling or options—is booked in backlog.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company won the next phase of the Protected Tactical SATCOM-Global (PTS-G) program, which carries a $4 billion ceiling value, though only the awarded base order (excluding options) is booked in backlog.”

surprises.description: Government SATCOM revenue growth accelerated to 10%, a positive segment result not specifically anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Government SATCOM revenue growth accelerated to 10%.”

surprises.description: Maritime revenue declined 7% as vessels in service fell, despite more than 1,700 NexusWave installations and an order book exceeding 1,400 vessels. The preview did not discuss this segment or flag a decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Maritime revenue declined 7% on lower vessels in service despite surpassing 1,700 NexusWave vessels installed and a current order book exceeding 1,400 vessels.”

surprises.description: After quarter-end, ViaSat-3 Flight 3 completed reflector and boom deployment, with service expected over Asia Pacific in late August or early September 2025. The preview focused on Flight 2 and did not anticipate this Flight 3 milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ViaSat-3 Flight 3 completed reflector and boom deployment post-quarter and is expected to enter service over the Asia Pacific region in late August or early September 2025.”

surprises.description: Leverage was approximately 3.2x, 0.4x lower year over year, aided by another $100 million transfer of cash from Inmarsat to Viasat, bringing cumulative transfers to $450 million. The preview had cited 3.1x at the prior fiscal year-end but did not anticipate these additional transfers or the year-over-year improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt to trailing EBITDA improved 0.4x year-over-year to approximately 3.2x, aided by moving an additional $100 million in cash from Inmarsat to Viasat for a cumulative $450 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “3.1x leverage” for FY26.

in_line: Management reaffirmed FY27 mid-single-digit revenue growth, with Communication Services at low-single-digit growth and DAT at mid-teens, and adjusted EBITDA flat to up slightly—the outlook already issued and described in the preview.
FY27 free cash flow guidance of about $180 million was reaffirmed, as expected in the preview.
FY27 CapEx guidance of $950 million to $1 billion matched the prior guidance cited in the preview.
The DAT strategic review remained ongoing with no decision on separation or spectrum monetization, consistent with the preview’s expectation that a procedural update might not resolve the issue.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS was $0.39, well above the $0.28 consensus and above the prior $0.27–$0.32 company range. The beat was about 39% versus consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted diluted EPS rose to $0.39”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | Consensus | $0.28”; company guidance was “$0.27 – $0.32.”

surprises.description: Bloomin’ Brands raised FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $0.90–$1.00 from $0.75–$0.90, rather than merely reaffirming the range as the preview’s base and bear cases contemplated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year fiscal 2026 adjusted diluted EPS guidance to $0.90-$1.00, up from the prior range of $0.75-$0.90.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY guidance was “$0.75 – $0.90 (reaffirmed at Q1)” and described a “flat reaffirmation” as a possibility; its bull case anticipated a raise “to about $1.00 – $1.15.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $1.02 billion exceeded the preview’s consensus band of about $999 million–$1.002 billion, rather than landing around flat year over year as expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenues of $1.02 billion (up 1%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave revenue consensus of “$999.1M (Zacks) / $1,001.5M (MarketBeat)” and summarized the Street as modeling “roughly flat revenue.”

surprises.description: U.S. comps grew 2.3%, above the preview’s roughly 1.5% consensus and the company’s 1%–2% annual comp range, although the gain did not come with stronger traffic.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. comparable restaurant sales grew 230 basis points in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed U.S. comp consensus as “~+1.5%” and prior company guidance as “+1% to +2%.”

surprises.description: The positive U.S. comp result was accompanied by a 1.9% traffic decline, which trailed the industry benchmark by 1.1 percentage points. The preview highlighted narrowing the traffic gap as important to showing a durable recovery, so the reported traffic remained a weak point despite the comp beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Traffic declined 190 basis points, with traffic trailing the Black Box industry benchmark by 110 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Narrowing the traffic gap would separate a durable turn from a pricing-driven recovery.”

surprises.description: Outback posted positive comps, but its traffic fell 2.8%, much weaker than the preview’s positive-comp/near-flat-traffic bull-case marker. Management attributed the traffic decline partly to not lapping prior-year dilutive delivery offers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Outback's comp sales rose 140 basis points while traffic fell 280 basis points,” reflecting “a deliberate decision to not lap dilutive third-party delivery offers from the prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said positive Outback comps “with traffic near flat” would support the turnaround thesis; its bull case specified “traffic at -0.5% or better.”

surprises.description: Commodity inflation was 5.7%, above the preview’s 4.5%–5.5% guidance range, yet adjusted operating margin expanded by 50 basis points. The margin outcome was resilient despite the higher-than-expected cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted operating margin expanded 50 basis points to 4.0% from 3.5%, despite commodity inflation of 5.7%, aided by favorable labor and non-guest-facing productivity gains.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said commodity inflation was guided at “4.5% – 5.5%” and identified restaurant-level operating margin as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: The turnaround investment burden was reduced: planned investments fell from $50 million to $36 million, and productivity savings left a net investment of $6 million rather than the roughly $20 million implied by the preview’s $50 million investment and $30 million savings figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total turnaround investments” were cut “to $36 million from $50 million,” with “a net investment of just $6 million after $30 million in productivity savings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “a turnaround investment of about $50M, offset by about $30M of productivity savings.”

surprises.description: Management newly guided to a Q3 per-share loss of $0.27–$0.22, driven by an approximately $5 million tax expense from the full-year tax rate. The preview did not provide a Q3 EPS expectation or flag this tax-related quarterly loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q3 2026 to a loss of $0.27 to $0.22 per share,” driven by “an approximately $5 million tax expense in the quarter.”

in_line: FY26 U.S. comparable sales outlook remained 1%–2%, matching the prior company guidance cited in the preview.

surprises.description: CVS reported Q2 adjusted EPS of $2.58, far above the preview’s $1.86–$1.87 consensus estimate. The gap was much larger than the preview’s bull scenario of at least $2.00.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EPS of $2.58, up over 40% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS $1.86 (Barchart/S&P Global) or $1.87 (Zacks)” and the bull scenario was “≥$2.00.”

surprises.description: CVS raised FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance by $0.60 to $7.90–$8.10, well above the preview’s expected raise to roughly $7.55–$7.70 and above even its bull case of at least $7.75.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CVS raised full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance by $0.60 to $7.90-$8.10, an 8% increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... Raise to ~$7.55 – $7.70”; “Bull: ... Raise to ≥$7.75.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue exceeded the preview’s $100.18 billion consensus by nearly $6 billion, with growth over 7% rather than the expected 1.3% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue of over $106 billion (up over 7%).”
