surprises.description: Management offered a directional shipment outlook, saying shipments should continue at a similar pace given current backlog, despite the preview noting that the company provided no revenue guidance and did not disclose backlog.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expecting shipments to continue at a similar pace given current backlog.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CPS does not give revenue or margin guidance and does not disclose backlog.”

surprises.description: The company reported that Army-funded tungsten warhead development runs through fall 2027 and that the Navy exercised a six-month ACV lightweighting option in June. These program updates were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Army-funded tungsten warhead development runs through fall 2027 and the Navy exercised a 6-month ACV lightweighting option in June.”

surprises.description: A backlog of SBIR/STTR proposals dating back to August 2024 is still awaiting government funding decisions, indicating a prolonged wait for those potential opportunities to advance. The preview did not mention this funding delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A backlog of SBIR/STTR proposals dating back to August 2024 still awaits government funding decisions.”

in_line: Gross margin recovered to 14.8%, within the preview’s 11–15% base-case range and consistent with the expectation of a return to the mid-teens.
Net income was about breakeven and EPS was $0.00, matching the preview’s roughly breakeven base case and the cited $0.00–$0.02 expectation range.
Combined cash and marketable securities were $19.2 million after the offering, close to the preview’s expectation that liquidity would rise to about $20 million.

surprises.description: Q1 signings were $3.9 billion, above the preview’s base scenario of roughly $3.0–$3.3 billion and its bull-case threshold of more than $3.5 billion. That was a stronger booking result than the preview’s central expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$3.9 billion signed in Q1” and trailing 12-month signings totaled “$14.2 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “signings ~$3.0–3.3B”; the bull scenario expected “Signings > $3.5B.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $3.6 billion was slightly below the preview’s $3.661 billion consensus and its $3.65–$3.70 billion base range. However, the 3% constant-currency decline was within the preview’s base scenario of a 3%–4% decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue was $3.6 billion, down 3% year-over-year on both a reported and constant currency basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 revenue | $3.661B”; the base scenario forecast “$3.65–3.70B (constant currency −3% to −4%).”

surprises.description: Kyndryl reported $152 million of workforce rebalancing charges in Q1, less than the roughly $200 million the preview expected to be incurred mostly in the quarter. The charges still materially reduced adjusted pretax income.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$152 million of workforce rebalancing charges” impacted adjusted pretax income margin “by more than 4 points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY27 guidance “includes ~$200M rebalancing, mostly in Q1.”

surprises.description: U.S. revenue grew 5% for a second consecutive quarter even as company-wide revenue declined. The preview did not set a regional revenue expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. revenue grew 5% for the second consecutive quarter.”

surprises.description: Kyndryl reported substantial growth in Consult and hyperscaler-related revenue, but the preview provided no benchmark for either business. These results add a positive growth signal beyond the company-wide revenue outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Kyndryl Consult revenue grew 14% and hyperscaler-related revenue grew 48% over the last 12 months,” with hyperscaler revenue “exceeding $530 million in the quarter and $2 billion over the trailing 12 months.”

surprises.description: The share of large-deal value coming from new scope and new logos rose to about 30%, compared with 15% in FY2025. The preview did not flag this shift in deal composition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New scope and new logos rose to approximately 30% of the value of large deals, up from 15% in fiscal 2025,” reflecting “a shift toward higher-value services.”

surprises.description: Kyndryl reaffirmed FY2028 targets of more than $1.2 billion in adjusted pretax income and $1 billion in free cash flow, supported by low-single-digit constant-currency revenue growth. The preview discussed FY2027 guidance but did not mention these FY2028 targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed its fiscal 2028 targets of more than $1.2 billion in adjusted pretax income and $1 billion in free cash flow, achievable on low single-digit constant currency revenue growth.”

in_line: The company reaffirmed FY2027 adjusted pretax income guidance of $600–700 million, free cash flow guidance of $400–500 million, and flat-to-down-2% constant-currency revenue guidance, as the preview expected.
The 3% constant-currency revenue decline was consistent with the preview’s base-case range of a 3%–4% decline.
The roughly 3-point adverse revenue headwind from changing IBM purchasing patterns was consistent with the preview’s expectation of a greater-than-3-point headwind persisting through FY2027.

Q1 was a low point in earnings and included significant workforce rebalancing charges, consistent with the preview’s discussion of the expected earnings trough and roughly $200 million of rebalancing charges.
The CFO handoff was anticipated: the preview said Ellen Johnson would become CFO after the June-quarter filing, and the facts say she starts August 6.

surprises.description: ZBH reported Q2 sales of $2.177 billion, above the preview’s $2.13–$2.14 billion consensus range, while organic constant-currency growth was 4%, above the preview’s 2.5%–3.5% base scenario. The revenue and underlying growth both came in stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales reached $2.177 billion, up 4.8% reported and 4% organic constant currency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (Q2) | $2.13B (Zacks) / $2.14B (Street)” and the base scenario expected “$2.14–2.16B (organic cc 2.5–3.5%).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $2.07 beat the preview’s $2.01 consensus estimate, though it remained within the preview’s $2.03–$2.08 base-case range. This was a modest positive difference from consensus rather than an unusually large beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $2.07.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS (Q2) | $2.01” and the base scenario expected “$2.03–$2.08.”

surprises.description: Both adjusted margins fell materially: gross margin declined 120 basis points to 71.1%, and operating margin declined 210 basis points to 25.7%. That was weaker than the preview’s expectation that gross margin would remain stable through year-end and ran counter to the focus on the operating-margin trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin fell 120 basis points to 71.1% and adjusted operating margin fell 210 basis points to 25.7%, reflecting higher manufacturing costs and channel investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided gross margin stable through year-end”; the preview also flagged the “Adj. operating margin trajectory against the 27.3% Q1 mark.”

surprises.description: Technology, Data, Bone Cement and Surgical grew 21.5%, well above the roughly 12% growth cited for Q1; U.S. technology sales increased more than 50%. The call attributed the growth to ROSA robotics rather than one-time bone-cement events.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Technology, Data, Bone Cement and Surgical segment grew 21.5%, with U.S. technology sales up over 50%, driven by ROSA robotics rather than one-time bone cement events.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited prior-quarter “Tech/Data/Bone Cement & Surgical ~+12%.”

surprises.description: The iodine core hip launch in Japan was not identified in the preview, but the call described demand outpacing supply, a 40% price premium, and conversions from both existing and competing accounts. This was an unanticipated commercial opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The iodine core hip launch in Japan (a ~$0.5 billion market) is outpacing supply, commanding a 40% price premium and converting both existing and competitive accounts.”

surprises.description: Paragon 28 is expected to contribute 110 basis points to full-year reported sales growth, 10 basis points above the initial 100-basis-point expectation. The difference was favorable but small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Paragon 28 is growing mid-teens with commercial integration largely complete, contributing 110 basis points to full-year reported sales growth versus an initial expectation of 100 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Versus an initial expectation of 100 basis points.”

in_line: Management raised the full-year organic constant-currency revenue guidance, as the preview said investors wanted the low end lifted; the new range is 2.25%–3.25%, versus 1%–3%.
Full-year adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $8.47–$8.59 from $8.40–$8.55, consistent with the preview’s expectation that a raise was largely expected.
Pricing was an 80-basis-point headwind, within the preview’s stated up-to-100-basis-point guidance range.
The full-year buyback plan is up to $1 billion, matching the preview’s note that the buyback had already been lifted to $1 billion.

surprises.description: CRL’s organic revenue returned to growth at 0.1% year over year, instead of the roughly 1%–2% decline expected in the preview. Management also said this beat its prior outlook for a low-single-digit decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue returned to organic growth of 0.1% year-over-year” and “beating the prior outlook of a low single-digit decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic revenue growth | ~−1% to −2% (est.)”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was $3.02, well above the preview’s $2.72–$2.74 consensus range. It also exceeded management’s prior floor for at least 30% sequential growth, with the call noting that over half of the beat was operational and the rest came from nonoperating items.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS of $3.02 rose 47% sequentially, well above the prior outlook of at least 30% growth, though over half the beat was operational with the remainder from nonoperating items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS | $2.72 (Zacks) / $2.74 (street)”

surprises.description: DSA bookings and book-to-bill were far stronger than the preview’s expectation of a second quarter at or above 1.0x: net bookings reached $701 million and book-to-bill was 1.9x. Backlog also rose to $1.97 billion, above the preview’s $1.9 billion hold level and the bull-scenario threshold of $1.95 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DSA net bookings grew 12.6% sequentially to $701 million with a net book-to-bill of 1.9x … the highest levels in nearly four years and the third consecutive quarter above 1x, lifting DSA backlog to $1.97 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A second straight quarter at or above 1.0x, with backlog holding at $1.9B or more”; the bull scenario specified “Book-to-bill ≥1.05x, backlog above $1.95B.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating margin reached 20.5%, above the preview’s estimated 19%–20% range, and improved 420 basis points sequentially. The call attributed part of the margin improvement to divestitures, which lifted Manufacturing segment margin to 37.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin improved 420 basis points sequentially to 20.5%, aided by divestitures that pushed the Manufacturing segment margin to 37.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP op. margin | ~19–20% (est.)”

surprises.description: CRL lifted its full-year organic revenue outlook to flat-to-1%, a stronger improvement than the preview’s prior outlook of a 0.5%–1.5% decline. The preview anticipated possible action on EPS guidance but did not flag an organic-growth guide increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lifted organic revenue growth to flat-to-1%, a 150 bps improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance: organic −0.5% to −1.5%.”

surprises.description: The EPS guidance raise was expected, but the new $11.15–$11.45 range slightly exceeded the preview’s anticipated raise toward $11.00–$11.40. The midpoint rose by $0.25.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year non-GAAP EPS guidance to $11.15-$11.45 (8%-11% growth), a $0.25 midpoint increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buy-side expects a raise toward $11.00–$11.40.”

surprises.description: The preview said Q1 was the low point for RMS and looked for sequential improvement; the call still described weak North American small-model demand, tied to flat NIH budgets. RMS’s full-year guidance remained a low-to-mid single-digit decline rather than being cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “RMS revenue declined 1.4% organically due to weak North American small model demand tied to flat NIH budgets, partially offset by strong China demand, with full-year RMS guidance unchanged at a low-to-mid single-digit decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 was called the low point for the year. If RMS does not improve sequentially, the FY organic guide is at risk.”

surprises.description: The full-year tax-rate outlook rose by about 100 basis points, creating an approximately $0.20-per-share headwind. That essentially offset a $0.19 deferred-compensation-plan gain, while a Mauritius tax-law change remained pending—an EPS bridge not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The full-year tax rate outlook rose ~100 bps to 23%-24%, creating a ~$0.20 EPS headwind that essentially offsets a $0.19 deferred compensation plan gain, with a Mauritius tax legislation change still pending.”

surprises.description: Free-cash-flow guidance was raised to $400–$420 million from the prior $375–$400 million range. The preview listed the old range but did not anticipate a higher FCF guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised free cash flow guidance to $400-$420 million.”

surprises.description: Management said DSA pricing had not materially improved and that any future pricing gains would not reach revenue until 2027 because of booking-to-revenue lags. The preview discussed DSA stabilization and the 2027 setup but did not flag this delayed pricing contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DSA pricing remains stable with no material improvement yet, and any future pricing gains would only flow through revenue in 2027 given booking-to-revenue lags.”

in_line: Management maintained the expected second-half margin ramp: the preview looked for a more-than-500-basis-point improvement over the first half, and the call projected at least 500 basis points.
The expected Q4 benefit from the NHP sourcing transition remained in the outlook; the preview had already identified a material DSA margin benefit from internal sourcing in Q4.

surprises.description: Q2 continuing-operations revenue was just under $2 billion, versus the preview’s $2.62–$2.68 billion net-sales consensus; reported growth was roughly 6%, rather than the preview’s expected 2.9% decline. The bases appear different, so the dollar gap is not a clean like-for-like comparison, but the reported growth rate was much stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 continuing operations revenue was just under $2 billion, up roughly 6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | $2.68B” (with a stated consensus range of “$2.62–2.68B” and year-over-year change of “−2.9%”).

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted operating EBITDA was $408 million, well below the preview’s roughly $538 million segment-sum bogey. The preview cautioned that this was not a clean comparison, but the reported amount was still substantially lower than the figure investors were told to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted operating EBITDA rose 6% to $408 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied adj. op. EBITDA (segment sum) | ~$538M”; the preview also says to “treat ~$538M as a segment-sum bogey, not a clean comparison.”

surprises.description: The FY2026 sales-growth outlook improved: the low end rose from 1% to 2%, and management now expects 2%–4% growth. The headline sales range of $7.4–$7.6 billion is far below the preview’s $10.5–$10.8 billion prior guidance, although the differing reported bases make the dollar ranges difficult to compare directly.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was raised to sales of $7.4-$7.6 billion (2%-4% growth, up from 1%-4%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance reaffirmed: $10.5–10.8B sales”; the preview expected guidance to be “reaffirmed at low end of sales range.”

surprises.description: The reported FY2026 EBITDA guide of $1.53–$1.60 billion is far below the preview’s expected $2.05–$2.15 billion range. Management characterized the outlook as 4%–8% growth, but the difference in reported dollar levels is substantial and the materials do not reconcile the bases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EBITDA of $1.53-$1.6 billion (4%-8% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance reaffirmed: … $2.05–2.15B adjusted operating EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Fine Fragrance finished slightly positive in Q2 despite management’s earlier expectation of a mid-single-digit decline. That was a clear near-term improvement, though management still expects a softer Q3 against a difficult comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fine Fragrance finished Q2 slightly positive despite guidance for a mid-single-digit decline”; “a softer Q3 is expected against a 20% prior-year comparable.”

surprises.description: Scent delivered stronger reported growth than the preview’s concerns about Scent weakness and Middle East Fine Fragrance suggested: Fragrance Ingredients grew more than 20%, with high-single-digit Scent growth overall. Management cautioned that the unusually strong Fragrance Ingredients result should normalize lower in H2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “High single-digit Scent growth”; “Scent's Fragrance Ingredients grew over 20%, boosted by an easy comparison … and opportunistic synthetics sales, but management expects this to normalize lower in H2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Scent segment EBITDA … fell 2% in Q1”; “Whether the disruption was truly temporary is the biggest swing factor.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a roughly $100 million stranded-cost burden after the Food Ingredients divestiture, with only about two-thirds targeted for elimination within 12 months after close and the rest by year two. The preview asked for stranded-cost figures, but had no estimate of their size or duration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $100 million in stranded corporate/functional costs temporarily pressuring segment margins,” with “about two-thirds” targeted for elimination within 12 months post-close and the remainder by the second year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Investors wanted “stranded-cost figures.”

surprises.description: IFF laid out a substantial capital-return and debt-reduction plan: a $2.5 billion repurchase authorization, with about $500 million expected before the sale closes and the remaining $2 billion afterward, alongside more than $1 billion of proceeds directed to debt reduction. The preview expected a proceeds framework but did not anticipate these specific amounts or the sequencing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board authorized a $2.5 billion share repurchase program”; “about $500 million expected in H2 2026 ahead of transaction close and the remaining $2 billion following close by end of 2027”; “more than $1 billion of divestiture proceeds” to reduce debt.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Investors want a framework covering buybacks, deleveraging, and bolt-on M&A.”

surprises.description: The company gave a specific deleveraging target: net debt to credit-adjusted EBITDA of 2.0x–2.5x by the end of 2027, compared with 4.5x at the start of 2024. This adds a quantified target beyond the preview’s request for a proceeds-use framework.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Targeting net debt to credit-adjusted EBITDA of 2.0x-2.5x by end of 2027, down from 4.5x at the start of 2024.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Investors want a framework covering buybacks, deleveraging, and bolt-on M&A.”

surprises.description: First-half free cash flow reached $378 million, up $284 million year over year, due to working-capital improvements; the preview gave no comparable first-half expectation. Management also flagged a couple-hundred-million-dollar H2 working-capital headwind from the separation, tempering the cash-flow strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half 2026 free cash flow reached $378 million, up $284 million year-over-year, driven by net working capital improvements”; “a couple-hundred-million-dollar working capital headwind [is] anticipated in H2 from the separation.”

surprises.description: Higher incentive-compensation accruals tied to the strong first half reduced Q2 EBITDA growth by a couple of percentage points, an unexpected drag on the quarter’s operating performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Growth was muted by higher incentive compensation accruals tied to strong first-half results, which management said cost a couple of percentage points of EBITDA growth.”

surprises.description: Corebridge reported Q2 operating EPS of $1.12, above the preview’s $1.08 consensus estimate. The beat was modest, despite the demanding year-ago comparison highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted pretax operating income was $664 million with EPS of $1.12.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating EPS” consensus: “$1.08.”

surprises.description: Variable Investment Income was weak and management expects it to stay below target for the rest of the year, rather than rebound in the second half. The preview flagged weak VII and said a rebound could support consensus, but did not explicitly forecast a rebound.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Variable Investment Income underperformed due to weak private equity marks and is expected to remain below target for the remainder of the year, diverging from peers guiding to second-half improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “It was weak in Q1 ($22M vs. $88M a year earlier). It swings operating EPS quarter to quarter, so a rebound would support the $1.08 consensus.”

surprises.description: Despite more than $1.4 billion of holdco liquidity above 12-month needs, management expects only about $350 million of buybacks in the second half. That implies a substantial slowdown from Q1’s $1.3 billion of buybacks and leaves 2026 buybacks at roughly $1.9 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided to only approximately $350 million in share repurchases for the second half despite holding over $1.4 billion in holdco liquidity exceeding 12-month needs, implying roughly $1.9 billion of total 2026 buybacks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buyback pace ahead of the close is a live question, given $1.4B returned in Q1.”

surprises.description: Individual Retirement sales fell both year over year and sequentially to $3.8 billion, indicating continued pressure rather than a clear stabilization in retirement activity. The strongest sales month being June provides a more encouraging late-quarter signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Individual Retirement sales fell year-over-year and sequentially to $3.8 billion amid competitive pressure, but June was the strongest sales month of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 premiums and deposits fell 10% YoY, and Institutional Markets premiums and deposits fell 45%. Retirement-business flows and spread income are the main operating signals.”

surprises.description: Institutional Markets showed a strong operating contribution, with APTOI up 36% and $1.8 billion of GIC issuances, while the preview had highlighted a 45% year-over-year decline in Institutional Markets premiums and deposits. The reported results point to a much stronger operating picture than that recent weakness suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Institutional Markets APTOI grew 36% year-over-year on 17% reserve expansion, with $1.8 billion of GIC issuances in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Institutional Markets premiums and deposits fell 45%.”

surprises.description: Life Insurance run-rate APTOI came in above the top end of guidance, an upside to the company’s own stated range. This was distinct from the reported APTOI decline of 11% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Life Insurance delivered run rate APTOI of $122 million above the top end of guidance on favorable mortality, though reported APTOI declined 11% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Run rate APTOI of $122 million above the top end of guidance.”

surprises.description: The call set out specific 2027 targets for the combined company—$5 billion of earnings, $4 billion of cash generation, and more than 15% ROE—that were not included in the preview. These add earlier-dated financial targets beyond the deal’s previously described synergy and accretion objectives.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The combined Corebridge-Equitable company targets $5 billion of earnings, $4 billion of cash generation, and over 15% ROE by 2027, supported by $500 million in cost synergies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The companies target more than $500M of run-rate expense synergies and >10% EPS accretion by end-2028.”

in_line: The merger remains on track to close by year-end 2026, consistent with the preview’s stated expected closing timing; the preview also identified regulatory approvals as the main remaining condition.
The $500 million cost-synergy target is broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of more than $500 million in run-rate expense synergies.

surprises.description: FRP cut its full-year NOI plan by about $0.9 million, to $36.2 million from $37.1 million. The preview said it had not found FY2026 guidance, so the cut was not anticipated there; management attributed it mainly to industrial lease-up delays and D.C. multifamily headwinds, partly offset by stronger mining.
surprises.fact_evidence: “lowered its full-year NOI guidance to approximately $36.2 million from an original plan of $37.1 million,” driven by “$800,000 in delayed industrial lease-up and $1 million of D.C. multifamily headwinds,” partly offset by “$850,000 of stronger mining performance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Not found in my searches. I did not locate quarterly or full-year guidance figures for FY2026.”

surprises.description: Industrial leasing had not converted into much signed space: only 20,700 square feet were signed, with 97,500 square feet still in active negotiation. That fell short of the preview’s watchpoint that prior signed/LOI space would convert into occupancy, and management said stronger tenant activity had not yet produced signed leases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Only about 20,700 square feet have been signed with 97,500 square feet in active negotiation,” and “stronger tenant activity has not yet translated into signed leases.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management cited 53,000 sq ft signed or under LOI on the Q1 call. Watch for those leases converting to occupancy.”

surprises.description: The Maryland same-store industrial properties were materially weaker than the preview’s hoped-for improvement in industrial occupancy: Hollander and Cranberry were only 70.6% occupied, down from 92% in Q1 2025, following government tenant losses and a tenant bankruptcy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Maryland same-store industrial portfolio (Hollander and Cranberry) fell to 70.6% occupancy from 92% in Q1 2025 due to lost government tenants and a tenant bankruptcy.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for those leases converting to occupancy”; the bull case expected “industrial occupancy moves up from 47.5%.”

surprises.description: D.C. multifamily collection and rent-reset problems were more severe than the preview’s general description of softness: about 8% of tenants were not paying, evictions take 12 to 18 months, and new-tenant trade-outs were 10% below prior tenants.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly 8% of tenants are not paying rent, with evictions taking 12 to 18 months due to district policies, while new-tenant trade-out rates are running 10% below prior tenants.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pro rata multifamily NOI fell 11.8% to $4.1M in Q1, with occupancy at 92.1% versus 94.0%, driven by underperforming Washington, DC assets. Management's stated 2026 priority is stabilizing DC occupancy.”

surprises.description: Management indicated that most future discretionary growth capital will go to industrial real estate, a strategic emphasis not identified in the preview. This is a shift in where FRP plans to direct growth spending while it is still working through industrial lease-up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Most future discretionary growth capital will target industrial real estate,” while the company maintains multifamily and mining.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a substantial combined industrial and multifamily development pipeline: about $506 million in total project costs for roughly $34 million of expected stabilized NOI, including about $16.6 million attributable to FRP. The preview noted an industrial pipeline addition but did not give this pipeline’s cost or NOI scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The combined industrial and multifamily development pipeline represents approximately $506 million of total project costs and about $34 million of expected stabilized NOI, of which roughly $16.6 million is FRP's share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The October 21, 2025 acquisition added 1.6M sq ft to the industrial pipeline.”

surprises.description: Shareholders, including the fourth-largest holder, pressed for buybacks, but management reiterated that development takes priority over dividends or meaningful repurchases. The preview did not discuss buybacks or this capital-allocation debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Multiple shareholders, including the fourth-largest holder, pressed hard for buybacks citing a NAV near $40 versus a ~$21.50 share price, but management reiterated it prioritizes new development capital over dividends or meaningful buybacks.”

in_line: Q2 pro rata NOI of about $9.4 million was within the preview’s expected stabilization range of roughly $8.9–$9.7 million, despite being modestly lower year over year.
Mining remained a support to results, consistent with the preview’s description of mining royalties as carrying results.
Liquidity of about $130 million was essentially unchanged from the approximately $130 million reported at Q1.

surprises.description: KHC was still losing market share, rather than reporting the share gains the preview said to watch for, but the losses narrowed to 30 bps in the first half and about 20 bps in recent weeks. That is a meaningful improvement from losses of up to 90 bps early in 2025.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Market share losses narrowed to 30 bps in the first half of 2026 (and roughly 20 bps in recent weeks), a significant improvement from losses of up to 90 bps early in 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for share gains in Taste Elevation (Heinz, Philadelphia, sauces)”

surprises.description: Management announced another $100 million of incremental spending, almost entirely on marketing, beyond the previously planned $600 million. The preview discussed investment spending but did not anticipate this additional amount; the added investment may support demand while also adding near-term cost.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management announced an additional $100 million in incremental spending—almost entirely marketing—on top of the prior $600 million, framing it as spending from a position of strength.”

surprises.description: The planned $600 million investment was substantially back-loaded: only about $200 million had been spent, with roughly $500 million remaining for the second half. The preview discussed reinvestment but did not flag that most of the spending would land in Q3 and Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Only about one-third (roughly $200 million) of the planned $600 million incremental investment has been spent, with the remaining ~$500 million weighted to the second half, split broadly evenly between Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: Despite U.S. consumption declining about 2.5% in Q2, it improved to roughly -1% in July, and management expects sequential improvement in both Q3 and Q4. The preview identified volume as the core test, but this improvement in the demand trend was not specified there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. consumption declined about 2.5% in Q2 but improved to roughly -1% in July, with management guiding to sequential improvement in Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: Heinz and U.S. condiments showed growth: Heinz was up 3% worldwide year-to-date, while U.S. condiments were up 3% year-to-date after being flat last year. The preview highlighted Taste Elevation as an area to watch but did not set an expectation for this growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Heinz grew 3% worldwide year-to-date (up 12% in emerging markets in the quarter), and U.S. condiments grew 3% year-to-date versus flat last year.”

surprises.description: KHC paid down $1.9 billion of debt during the quarter and another $1 billion after quarter-end, and raised its cash-conversion expectation while leaving free-cash-flow guidance essentially unchanged in dollars. The preview cited an approximately 100% conversion guide but did not flag this scale of debt reduction or a higher conversion expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company paid down $1.9 billion of debt in the quarter plus another $1 billion after quarter close, raised its cash conversion expectation, and kept free cash flow guidance essentially unchanged in dollar terms.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 FCF conversion: ~100%”

surprises.description: Management disclosed expected 2027 inflation of 4% to 5%, a future cost headwind not called out in the preview, while saying it is manageable and that productivity should offset as much as possible without sacrificing margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects 2027 inflation in the 4% to 5% range but stated it is manageable and intends to offset as much as possible through productivity while maintaining and strengthening margins.”

surprises.description: Management said 2026 would be the base investment year, with no investment-spending wraparound into 2027, and framed it as a margin trough ahead of 2027 growth. The preview focused on whether 2026 reinvestment would pay back but did not describe this spending or margin trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reiterated 2026 is the base investment year with no wraparound of investment spend into 2027, positioning it as the margin trough setup for 2027 growth.”

surprises.description: At the midpoint, second-half organic sales look weaker than the first half, but management’s timing adjustments change the underlying comparison: after accounting for the Q1 snowstorm benefit and Q2 shipment phasing, underlying performance improves by roughly 70–80 bps. The preview did not provide this half-to-half outlook or normalization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “At the midpoint, second-half organic sales appear weaker than the first half, but normalizing for ~0.7 pp Q1 snowstorm benefit and ~0.8 pp Q2 shipment phasing into Q3, underlying performance improves by roughly 70-80 bps.”

in_line: KHC absorbed the built-in 100 bps SNAP-related headwind in 2026 while protecting market share, as management said was anticipated.

surprises.description: BCO delivered Q2 EPS of $2.13 versus $2.05 consensus, while adjusted EBITDA was $257 million versus about $255 million and the EBITDA margin was 18.5% versus an expected roughly 18.2%. The earnings beat was positive but modest, especially on EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EPS grew 18% to $2.13”; “adjusted EBITDA up 11% to $257 million”; “Q2 EBITDA margins reached a record 18.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS $2.05”; “Adj. EBITDA ~$255M”; “Adj. EBITDA margin ~18.2%.”

surprises.description: AMS/DRS organic growth was reported at 14%, one percentage point below the preview’s key 15% threshold. That falls short of the preview’s expected 15–16% base case, even though the call also described this as the 14th consecutive quarter of mid-teens-or-better growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AMS/DRS grew 14% organically”; the segment also “delivered its 14th consecutive quarter of mid-teens or better organic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A print below 15% would break the streak”; the base case expected “AMS/DRS 15–16%.”

surprises.description: Several large AMS/DRS installations slipped from Q2 into the second half because of customer timing, and organic growth was about 2% in North America, Latin America, and Europe. The preview did not anticipate these timing delays or this regional deceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Several large AMS/DRS installations slipped from Q2 into the second half due to customer-driven timing,” contributing to “organic growth decelerating to about 2% in North America, Latin America and Europe.”

surprises.description: BCO raised full-year profit guidance, whereas the preview expected the FY26 framework to be reaffirmed. The increase was not quantified in the provided call facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year profit guidance,” with Q2 EBITDA “above the midpoint of prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether the FY26 framework was “reaffirmed, raised, or narrowed,” and its base case expected “FY framework reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: The NCR Atleos closing timeline moved forward to early Q1 2027 from the preview’s end-of-Q1 2027 expectation. The call also reported more than 99% shareholder approval and clearance in over 80% of money-transmitter jurisdictions, advancing the regulatory process the preview said still had international approvals outstanding.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The NCR Atleos acquisition closing timeline was moved forward to early Q1 2027,” with “over 99% shareholder approval” and “80%+ of money transmitter jurisdictions cleared.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the deal “will not close until end-Q1 2027” and that “International regulatory approval remains.”

surprises.description: The call announced several large customer wins that the preview did not flag: a U.S. retail DRS agreement covering 5,000 locations and nearly doubling wallet share, a European bank consortium ATM outsourcing deal, and an Indonesia Mandiri Bank AMS deal covering over one-third of its ATM estate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Key new wins include a 5,000-location U.S. retail DRS enterprise agreement (nearly doubling wallet share), a European bank consortium ATM outsourcing deal, and an AMS deal with Indonesia's Mandiri Bank servicing over 1/3 of its 13,000+ ATM estate.”

in_line: The FY26 framework of mid-single-digit organic growth and 30–50 basis points of EBITDA margin expansion was reaffirmed, as the preview’s base case expected.
Reported Q2 revenue growth was 7%, including a 3% FX tailwind; this was broadly consistent with the roughly $1.40 billion consensus revenue expectation.

surprises.description: Materion reported adjusted EPS of $1.90, well above the preview’s $1.52–$1.55 consensus and management-implied $1.58–$1.64 range. The result was also the company’s highest quarterly earnings ever.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record adjusted EPS of $1.90 in Q2 2026,” up 39% year-over-year and 50% sequentially, “marking the highest quarterly earnings in company history.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS” consensus was “$1.55 (Zacks) or $1.52 (CoinCodex)”; management’s implied level was “$1.58–$1.64.”

surprises.description: Materion raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $6.80–$7.20 from $6.00–$6.50, rather than reaffirming or making only a modest adjustment to the existing range. The new midpoint is about 12% above the prior midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $6.80-$7.20 (up from $6.00-$6.50),” a 12% increase from prior guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EPS” company guidance was “$6.00–$6.50”; the preview’s base case expected “guidance reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Quarterly value-added sales reached $308.2 million, above the preview’s implied estimate of about $300.8 million. The amount was within the preview’s bull-case range, but exceeded its consensus-based expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record value-added sales reached $308.2 million,” up 15% year-over-year and 18% sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “VA sales” consensus was “~$300.8M (implied from Zacks segment estimates).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was about $71.8 million at a 23.3% margin, above the preview’s implied roughly $64 million and 21.3% margin. The record margin included roughly $2–3 million of one-time positive items, tempering the underlying beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin exceeded 23% for the first time ever, hitting a record 23.3% ($71.8 million),” with 250 basis points of year-over-year expansion, “though aided by roughly $2-3 million in one-time positive items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA” was estimated at “~$64M, ~21.3% of VA (implied).”

surprises.description: Materion raised its full-year top-line outlook to mid-teens sales growth. The preview had no full-year sales guidance figure, so this additional outlook increase was not incorporated into its stated expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year top-line outlook to mid-teens sales growth,” the “second consecutive quarterly guidance increase.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow was $59 million in Q2, a sharp reversal from Q1’s negative operating cash flow and a strong quarterly contribution toward management’s full-year cash-flow promise. The preview specifically flagged a second negative FCF quarter as a risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated $59 million in free cash flow (~150% conversion).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “Operating cash flow –$4.3M” in Q1 and said “Two negative FCF quarters would be a problem”; management had promised “strong free cash flow for the full year.”

surprises.description: Backlog grew about 30% year-over-year, ahead of the preview’s cited 20% growth benchmark. First-half incoming orders were also up nearly 30%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record backlog grew roughly 30% year-over-year and 20% since the start of the year, with first-half incoming orders up nearly 30%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Record backlog, +20% YoY.”

surprises.description: The defense order pipeline strengthened beyond the preview’s cited $300 million in open RFQs: open RFQs exceeded $500 million, while first-half defense orders totaled $90 million. The preview did not provide a comparable first-half order expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Defense secured $90 million of incoming orders in the first half with over $500 million in open RFQs (up from ~$300 million last quarter).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$300M in open RFQs.”

surprises.description: Electronic Materials reached a 32% adjusted EBITDA margin, its fifth consecutive quarter of expansion, and management said Q2 was likely the richest mix of the year. The preview noted the prior-quarter 28.3% record but gave no Q2 margin outlook; the mix comment also qualifies how repeatable this peak may be.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Electronic Materials achieved a record 32% adjusted EBITDA margin (up nearly 900 basis points year-over-year), its fifth consecutive quarter of margin expansion,” though “management flagged Q2 as likely the richest mix of the year.”

surprises.description: Precision Optics reported a 21.4% EBITDA margin, its first time above 20% since 2021, with adjusted EBITDA up 206% on 26% sales growth. The preview did not identify this segment’s margin or earnings as an issue to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Precision Optics surpassed 20% EBITDA margin (21.4%) for the first time since 2021, with adjusted EBITDA up 206% year-over-year on 26% sales growth.”

surprises.description: Space orders doubled year-over-year and reached roughly 25% of aerospace and defense sales, a segment development the preview did not flag. The call facts provide no explicit pre-release expectation for space orders, so the surprise is the emergence of this strong operating detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Space orders doubled year-over-year and now represent roughly 25% of aerospace and defense sales.”

surprises.description: A $65 million customer-funded beryllium capacity investment will push CapEx above the disclosed $75 million forecast, but the incoming customer funds are expected to offset it. This adds spending beyond the preview’s cited capex plan while limiting the cash burden.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $65 million customer-funded beryllium capacity investment will flow through CapEx above the disclosed $75 million forecast but be offset by incoming funds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$75M capex plus $25M mine development.”

surprises.description: Q2 net sales were $510 million, about 8% above the $472.1 million consensus estimate in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Gibraltar Q2 2026 net sales rose 64.6% to $510 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q2 FY2026 Consensus | $472.1M”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $1.11, above the preview’s $1.02 consensus even with a $20.6 million net interest impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS reached $1.11 including a $20.6 million net interest impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | Q2 FY2026 Consensus | $1.02”

surprises.description: The company lowered the top of its 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance range from $326 million to $315 million, while leaving the low end unchanged. The preview described the prior range and flagged guidance action as a key debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $310 million to $315 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Low $310M | High $326M”; the preview also asked whether guidance would be “Reaffirmed, raised, or trimmed?”

surprises.description: Gibraltar raised its 2026 synergy commitment above the preview’s $26 million target and said execution is roughly a year ahead of plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its 2026 synergy commitment to $29.4 million”; “$7 million has been realized to date,” and it is “running roughly a year ahead of plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The 2026 synergy target was raised to $26M at Q1.”

surprises.description: On a combined pro forma basis, building products grew organically 15.5% even though the market declined 1.3%; the preview had highlighted residential organic growth as a concern after a negative Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On a combined pro forma basis, building products grew 15.5% organically, comprised of 9.7% price/mix and 7.1% participation gains, offsetting a market down 1.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Residential organic was −3% in Q1 and is now over 80% of revenue and EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Management reported that roofing demand was already weak and expects that softness to continue through year-end, a negative demand outlook not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Actual end-market roofing demand was down mid-single digits in the first half (with retail POS down 8% to 10%) and [management] expects this soft demand to persist through the rest of the year.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA margin expanded 350 basis points sequentially to 17.3%, and residential segment margin rose 340 basis points sequentially to 19%; the preview estimated EBITDA dollars but did not flag this margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin expanding 350 basis points sequentially to 17.3%”; residential “segment EBITDA margin improving 340 basis points sequentially to 19%.”

surprises.description: The company won a supply agreement adding 630 customer locations, taking coverage to more than 1,700; revenue is expected to begin late in Q4 and primarily benefit 2027. The preview did not flag this contract win.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company won a new supply agreement adding 630 locations to bring trims and flashings supply to over 1,700 locations for a key customer, with revenue starting late Q4 2026 but primarily impacting 2027.”

surprises.description: Ag-tech sales and margins improved, but its backlog fell sharply year over year because of project timing; the preview did not discuss this segment or its backlog.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ag-tech net sales grew 8.7% organically”; operating and EBITDA margins were “up 450 and 430 bps year-over-year,” while “backlog fell 34% year-over-year to $66.2 million on project timing.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was $88 million, within the preview’s estimated $85–90 million range.
The company reiterated 2026 net sales guidance of $1.76–$1.83 billion and adjusted EPS guidance of $3.65–$4.05, consistent with the preview’s listed ranges.
Net debt of about $1.2 billion and net leverage of 3.9x were in line with the preview’s cited figures.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $115 million, below the preview’s expected step-up from Q1: even using the preview’s clean-Q1 comparison, it implied roughly $118–125 million. The preview’s base case was $124–130 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $1.62 billion with adjusted EBITDA of $115 million, down from Q1's $124 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided Q2 to a ‘very small, modest step-up’ from Q1”; “Measured off the clean $113M, it implies roughly $118–125M.” The preview’s base scenario also put Q2 Adj. EBITDA at “$124–130M.”

surprises.description: Despite reaffirming the FY26 EBITDA range, management said revenue is now biased toward its lower end, signaling a weaker revenue outlook than an unchanged range alone would suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed at $485-$535 million, though revenue is now biased toward the lower end of the $6.4-$6.7 billion range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 revenue guidance of “$6.40–6.70B” and identified the guidance question as whether the company would “reaffirm, narrow to the lower half, or cut” the range.

surprises.description: The company raised its 2026 savings target to at least $70 million, above the previously stated $55 million target, and said executed workforce and payer actions were already offsetting much of the lower-volume headwind. This was stronger cost execution than the preview had quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its 2026 impact program savings target to at least $70 million, up from $55 million previously and $40 million originally”; workforce reductions and payer recontracting provide “$20-$30 million” against an approximately “$25 million” lower-volume headwind. SW&B grew “just 0.7%” while contract labor spend fell “42%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case described “Soft volumes offset by cost execution,” but did not anticipate a higher savings target or quantify these offsets.

surprises.description: A June payer-contract renewal is expected to add $5–10 million to 2026 adjusted EBITDA, with management also identifying a multi-year repricing opportunity across markets. The preview did not identify this contract-driven upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A single June payer contract renewal in one market is expected to add $5-$10 million to 2026 adjusted EBITDA”; rates are “below the 50th percentile across most markets” and renewals occur on “2-3 year” cycles.

surprises.description: Management indicated that the $35 million exchange headwind may be conservative because a material portion of members losing exchange coverage are moving to other insurance rather than self-pay. The headwind estimate itself was unchanged, but this migration commentary was more favorable than the preview’s uninsured-volume concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed its $35 million exchange headwind for the year,” while noting that “a material portion of members losing exchange coverage are migrating to other insurance rather than self-pay, suggesting potential conservatism.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the “$35M FY26 EBITDA headwind” and contrasted HCA’s displaced patients going uninsured “almost one for one.”

surprises.description: The company reported $13 million of Q2 buybacks and signaled a willingness to keep repurchasing shares, a concrete capital-allocation stance not specified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased $13 million of stock in Q2 with $34 million remaining under authorization,” signaling a bias to continue buybacks.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “capital-allocation changes” from the new CEO but did not specify buybacks or a repurchase amount.

in_line: FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed at $485–535 million, as the preview listed that range and explicitly identified reaffirmation as a possible outcome.
The $35 million FY26 exchange headwind was reaffirmed, in line with the preview’s stated assumption.

surprises.description: Owens Corning reported Q2 revenue of $2.8 billion, adjusted EPS of $3.93, and a 24% adjusted EBITDA margin—well above the preview’s $2.65–2.66 billion revenue consensus, $3.06–3.07 EPS consensus, and roughly 21.3% implied margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $2.8 billion with adjusted EBITDA of $660 million, delivering a 24% adjusted EBITDA margin, while adjusted EPS came in at $3.93.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $2.65–2.66B”; “Adj. EPS: $3.06–3.07”; “Adj. EBITDA margin (implied): ~21.3%.”

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook was weaker than the preview’s expectation that management would reaffirm an H2 recovery: revenue is projected at $2.6–2.7 billion, slightly below the prior year, and adjusted EBITDA margin at 20–22%, versus 24% in Q2. Iran-related cost inflation is also expected to rise from $30 million in Q2 to roughly $40 million in Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Weaker Q3 guidance, projecting revenue of $2.6–2.7 billion (slightly below prior year) and an adjusted EBITDA margin of only 20–22%”; “Iran cost impact expected to worsen to roughly $40 million in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided Q2 margin to 20–22%, with negative price/cost across most segments and recovery expected in Q3–Q4”; the preview also said “H2 catch-up needs to be reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Roofing’s Q2 EBITDA margin reached 34%, above the preview’s low-30s expectation. But management guided Q3 Roofing revenue down mid- to high single digits and its margin to about 30%, attributing weaker shipments to demand pulled forward into Q2 ahead of price increases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roofing Q3 revenue is guided down mid- to high single digits with ARMA shipments expected down high single digits due to demand pulled forward into Q2 ahead of price increases, and Roofing EBITDA margin is expected to fall to ~30% from 34% in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Roofing EBITDA margin vs. ‘low-30s’ guide”; the preview also said, “The H2 catch-up needs to be reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Q2 EBITDA received an unanticipated $25 million boost from tariff refunds, half in Doors, partly offsetting $30 million of net Iran-related cost inflation. The Iran-related cost impact was also below the preview’s roughly $60 million Q2 inflation headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 EBITDA included $25 million in tariff refunds (half in Doors) that partially offset $30 million in net Iran-related cost inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management tied about $60M of Q2 inflation to the Iran conflict.”

surprises.description: Doors EBITDA was $57 million at an 11% margin and beat guidance despite revenue falling 7% to $513 million due to strategic divestitures; the beat was largely attributable to tariff refunds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Doors Q2 revenue fell 7% to $513 million due to strategic divestitures, with EBITDA of $57 million (11% margin) beating guidance largely because of tariff refunds.”

surprises.description: Owens Corning exceeded its committed Doors acquisition synergy target, reporting $135 million in run-rate cost synergies against a $125 million target, and identified another $75 million of structural cost improvements.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company exceeded its Doors acquisition synergy target, achieving $135 million in run-rate cost synergies versus the $125 million committed, and identified an additional $75 million of structural cost improvements.”

in_line: The preview flagged the $1 billion 2026 shareholder-return commitment and the need for Q2 buybacks after none in Q1. The company reported $327 million returned in the first half, including $200 million of buybacks, and reiterated its commitment to return $1 billion in 2026.
The CFO transition proceeded as previewed: Jonathan Collins was set to take over as CFO on August 10.
The preview said Owens Corning had not engaged substantively on the Carlyle approaches. Management declined to comment on acquisition speculation, with no change in position reported.

surprises.description: Q2 earnings were well below the preview’s estimates: adjusted diluted EPS was $0.64 versus $0.93–$0.98 expected, and GAAP diluted EPS was $0.39 versus about $0.73 expected. Net income fell 38.8% to $4.7 million, while adjusted EBITDA declined 22.3% to $13.9 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS declined to $0.64 from $0.93”; “net income declining 38.8% to $4.7 million ($0.39 per diluted share)”; “Adjusted EBITDA fell 22.3% to $13.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: $0.93–0.98”; “GAAP diluted EPS: ~$0.73.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 21.5%, below the preview’s roughly 24% base-case recovery and the level it flagged as important for the full-year margin target. GCR margin fell to 14.5% and ODR margin to 24%, with the call attributing pressure primarily to the lower-margin Pioneer Power business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total gross margin compressed sharply to 21.5%”; “GCR segment margin collapsing to 14.5% from 24.7% and ODR margin falling to 24% from 29%, primarily due to the lower-margin Pioneer Power business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case anticipated gross margin would “recover partway toward 24%”; the preview also said “Below roughly 24% makes the full-year margin target hard to reach.”

surprises.description: The company lowered its FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $78–84 million from $90–94 million, a sizable cut that reflects near-term margin and execution headwinds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reset full-year 2026 guidance… lowering adjusted EBITDA to $78-84 million to reflect near-term margin and execution headwinds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA: $90–94M (company guidance, reaffirmed May 2026).”

surprises.description: ODR organic revenue declined 3.4% rather than showing the inflection the preview said was needed. The preview noted that FY guidance required ODR growth of 9–12%, after Q1 organic revenue had also declined.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ODR organic revenue actually declined 3.4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ODR organic growth… an inflection is required”; the FY guide “needs +9–12%”; the bull case said “ODR organic growth turns positive.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue missed the preview’s $177–179 million consensus, coming in at $173.5 million. The shortfall was modest relative to the forecast range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue grew 21.9% to $173.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $177–179M.”

surprises.description: Despite the weak quarter, management raised FY26 revenue guidance to $760–790 million from $730–760 million. The higher range contrasts with the preview’s uncertainty over whether guidance would be reaffirmed, narrowed, or cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reset full-year 2026 guidance, raising revenue to $760-790 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue: $730–760M (company guidance, reaffirmed May 2026)”; the preview said the range “could be reaffirmed, narrowed, or cut.”

surprises.description: The $30 million CYMCOR acquisition was a new development, funded with cash and revolver borrowings. Management expects it to generate $12 million of program management revenue and $4 million of adjusted EBITDA in 2027, but included no contribution in current guidance; the acquisition also gives Limbach access to customer project budgets exceeding $8 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company acquired CYMCOR for $30 million (funded by cash and revolver borrowings) and expects it to generate $12 million of program management revenue and $4 million of adjusted EBITDA in 2027, with no contribution included in current guidance”; “CYMCOR oversees customer project budgets with a cumulative value exceeding $8 billion.”

surprises.description: Management offered a concrete healthcare example of services pulling through much larger project bookings—roughly $3 million of professional services revenue alongside approximately $60 million of bookings—and said it aims to replicate the 20x multiple in data centers. The preview had not identified this specific proof point or target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly $3 million of professional services revenue pulled through approximately $60 million of project bookings, a 20x multiple they aim to replicate in data centers.”

surprises.description: Bookings provided a positive counterpoint to the weak reported revenue and guidance reset: management cited $182 million of quarterly bookings and $616 million over the trailing three quarters as key support for its revenue outlook. The preview asked for backlog-conversion detail but did not provide a bookings expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Strong bookings of $182 million in the quarter and $616 million over the trailing three quarters,” cited as “the key basis for confidence in its revenue guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case called for “backlog-conversion detail,” but it gave no Q2 bookings estimate.

surprises.description: Pioneer Power margins had improved about 150 basis points in the first half of 2026 versus at acquisition, while the preview described progress as expected “toward the back half.” That indicates some improvement earlier than the preview’s stated timing, although management still expects company-average margins only in 2–3 years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pioneer Power gross margins improved approximately 150 basis points in the first half of 2026 versus acquisition, with management targeting company-average margins within 2-3 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Pioneer Power margin improvement was targeted over “2–3 years,” with progress “toward the back half.”

surprises.description: Net sales were $814 million versus the preview’s $793.7 million consensus, about 2.6% higher. Sales growth was over 4% year over year, compared with the preview’s 1.8% implied growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales rose over 4% year-over-year to $814 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | $793.7M”; “Q2 FY2025 actual $780M, +1.8% implied.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $1.15, far above the preview’s roughly $0.30 consensus. Adjusted net income was $9.1 million, up roughly 64%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income was $9.1 million or $1.15 per diluted share, up roughly 64%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | $0.30 (precisely $0.2967).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $35.6 million versus the preview’s roughly $24 million estimate. Even excluding the $7.2 million duty-related benefit, EBITDA was $28.4 million, above the preview’s $27 million bogey.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased approximately 33% year-over-year to $35.6 million”; “excluding a $7.2 million duty-related benefit, adjusted EBITDA was $28.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$24M (implied)”; “Bogey: at least $27M.”

surprises.description: A $7.2 million duty-related benefit boosted reported adjusted EBITDA and gross margin; the preview did not flag this one-off item. The underlying results were still above the preview’s EBITDA and gross-margin benchmarks, but the headline figures included this benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding a $7.2 million duty-related benefit, adjusted EBITDA was $28.4 million”; gross margin was “16.3% excluding the duty benefit,” versus 17.2% reported.

surprises.description: Total gross margin was 17.2%, above the preview’s 15.3–15.6% expectation. Even excluding the duty benefit, it was 16.3%, still above that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total gross margin expanded to 17.2% from 15.3% a year ago, or 16.3% excluding the duty benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~15.3–15.6%.”

surprises.description: Specialty gross margin exceeded the preview’s 17.5–18.5% guidance range even after excluding the duty item: it was 18.7% underlying and 20% reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Specialty gross margin was 20% (18.7% excluding the duty item) versus 18.5% last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Specialty 17.5–18.5%”; “Bogey: at least 18.0%.”

surprises.description: Structural gross margin reached 10.9%, above the preview’s 9.5–10.5% guidance range and its 10.0% bogey.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Structural gross margin jumped to 10.9% from 8.2% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Structural 9.5–10.5%”; “Bogey: at least 10.0%.”

surprises.description: Multifamily and national-account volumes grew rather than matching the preview’s expectation that specialty volume would be down slightly. The reported gains were especially strong in multifamily.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Multifamily volumes grew 11% and national account volumes rose 2% year-over-year, reflecting share gains amid declining housing starts and weak repair and remodel activity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided ‘down slightly’ Y/Y”; “Bogey: flat to -3%.”

surprises.description: BlueLinx reported a new Trex distribution partnership that the preview had not anticipated. Meaningful P&L contribution is expected to build only in 2027, with upfront working-capital and hiring investments during the ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BlueLinx signed a new Trex distribution partnership covering 11 markets,” with “meaningful P&L contribution” expected to build in 2027 and upfront working-capital and hiring investments required.

in_line: Management indicated that structural margin would normalize in Q3 to 8.5–9.5%; the preview had flagged H2 softening as a key issue and noted that Q1 performance should not be expected to repeat over the balance of 2026.

Liquidity and leverage remained close to the levels highlighted in the preview: available liquidity was $655 million versus $659 million in Q1, while net debt remained $58 million and net leverage improved from 0.7x to 0.6x.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $305 million, above the preview’s roughly $297.7 million consensus estimate, even though revenue was still down year over year. The beat was modest rather than a return to growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue declined to $305 million from $312 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: ~$297.7M” for Q2 2026.

surprises.description: The Braves played 34 regular-season home games, below the preview’s estimate of roughly 35–36, and baseball event revenue fell $19 million rather than holding flat. The preview said per-game revenue needed to rise about 11% to offset the expected fewer games.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The quarter includ[ed] only 34 regular season home games versus 40 in Q2 2025”; “Baseball event revenue fell $19 million to $161 million due to six fewer home games.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 likely lands around 35–36 home games versus 40 a year ago”; “Per-game revenue needs to rise about 11% to hold baseball-event revenue flat.”

surprises.description: Mixed-use development revenue grew about 16%, from $25 million to $29 million, below the preview’s expectation of growth toward roughly 20%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The mixed-use development segment grew revenue to $29 million from $25 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 laps the April 2025 acquisitions, so growth should slow toward roughly +20%.”

surprises.description: Management said BravesVision will remain an elevated expense going forward. The preview anticipated new in-house production costs, but did not flag that the expense level would remain elevated on an ongoing basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects BravesVision to be an ongoing elevated expense going forward.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “BravesVision production costs are now in-house opex.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed that it will not recognize a full year of BravesVision distribution revenue in fiscal 2026, since the network launched April 1, and that distributor payments arrive more slowly than under the former rights-fee model. The preview flagged timing differences but did not spell out this full-year revenue limitation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Distribution revenue payments now arrive on a slower cadence than the prior rights fee model”; “since BravesVision launched April 1, fiscal 2026 will not reflect a full year of distribution revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash collection timing from distributors differs from the old RSN deal, so the line can swing about ±$25M against a ~$300M quarter.”

surprises.description: Management reported that direct-to-consumer results are already outpacing early projections, a favorable update beyond the preview’s prior statement that BravesVision was expected to meet or exceed the old partner’s economics. The call did not provide a quantified DTC metric in the supplied facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Direct-to-consumer results outpacing early projections”; management is “confident BravesVision will replicate or exceed the annualized revenue from its prior third-party local rights partner.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said BravesVision is ‘on pace to meet or exceed the economics generated under our prior RSN agreement.’”

surprises.description: The preview said management had promised more detailed BravesVision metrics in Q2, but the supplied call facts provide a qualitative DTC update rather than a quantified subscriber, reach, or ad-sales metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call facts say DTC results were “outpacing early projections” but give no quantified BravesVision KPI.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management ... promised more detailed metrics in Q2”; the preview also listed “Any quantified BravesVision KPI” as a key catalyst.

surprises.description: Higher MLB revenue-sharing costs were identified as another source of rising baseball operating costs, beyond the player-payroll and in-house production-cost pressures the preview had already flagged.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cited “increased MLB revenue sharing” among the sources of higher baseball operating costs.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Player payroll is up, and BravesVision production costs are now in-house opex.”

surprises.description: Management raised a previously unflagged issue with the Section 162m salary tax-deduction limitation, describing it as unintended and expecting a legislative or regulatory fix. The prospect of a fix is reassuring, but the limitation itself adds uncertainty.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “flagged the salary tax deduction limitation (Section 162m) as an unintended consequence they expect to resolve via a legislative or regulatory fix.”

surprises.description: Management pointed to the MLB national media deal expiring on January 1, 2029 as a growth catalyst and cited the NBA’s annual media-rights increase from $2.7 billion to $7.7 billion. This was a new long-term upside argument not raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cited “the MLB national media deal expiring 1/1/29 as a growth catalyst,” referencing “the NBA's jump from $2.7 billion to $7.7 billion annually.”

in_line: Media-related revenue was $73 million versus the preview’s roughly $74 million base-case expectation; the preview had anticipated a timing-related decline from $81 million.

Management’s confidence that BravesVision will replicate or exceed the prior partner’s annualized revenue was consistent with its previously stated expectation that the network would meet or exceed the prior RSN economics.
The preview expected player-payroll and in-house production-cost pressure; management confirmed those cost pressures.

surprises.description: BorgWarner’s adjusted EPS appears to have been about $1.42, based on the reported $0.21 increase and 17% growth from the preview’s $1.21 year-ago figure. That is well above the $1.26 consensus and even above the preview’s $1.36–$1.40 bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EPS grew 17% ($0.21) year-over-year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 FY26 consensus Adj. EPS: $1.26; Bull scenario: $1.36–1.40.

surprises.description: Adjusted operating margin reached 11.3%, 40 basis points above the preview’s roughly 10.9% expectation. The preview also questioned whether PDS’s weak Q1 margin would narrow; the call said every business unit expanded margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted operating margin expanded 100 basis points to 11.3% ... and every business unit expanded margins.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 adj. operating margin: ~10.9% (guide-implied); “whether PDS's −6.1% Q1 margin narrows.”

surprises.description: Q2 sales were slightly above the $3.58 billion consensus. The gap was small, though organic sales were also positive rather than declining year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 sales exceeded $3.6 billion, roughly flat year-over-year, with organic sales up 0.5%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 FY26 consensus revenue: $3.58B.

surprises.description: BorgWarner raised its full-year adjusted EPS range to $5.05–$5.30 instead of reaffirming the prior $5.00–$5.20 range as the preview expected. The new midpoint is roughly in line with the $5.18 Street figure, but the upper end is higher; the company attributed the increase primarily to first-half buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $5.05-$5.30 (from $5.00-$5.20) primarily due to first-half buybacks.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The Street sits at the top of the $5.00–$5.20 range, so a flat reaffirm reads as a soft print.

surprises.description: The company approved a fresh $1 billion increase to its buyback authorization, a sizable additional repurchase capacity that the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Board approved a $1 billion increase to the buyback authorization, bringing total authorization to $1.35 billion ... through 2029.

surprises.description: BorgWarner plans to add $10–$15 million of industrial R&D spending in the second half for data-center products. The call said this lowers the full-year margin midpoint to 10.6% from 10.8% excluding the spending, despite the formal 10.7%–10.9% margin guidance being maintained.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is increasing second-half industrial R&D spending by an incremental $10-15 million, lowering the midpoint full-year margin to 10.6% (from 10.8% excluding it), to accelerate data center product readiness.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Company guidance (FY26): adj. op. margin 10.7%–10.9%.

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow was $492 million, a strong contribution toward the annual target after Q1 generated only $13 million. The preview had identified Q2 as the key checkpoint for the ramp needed to reach the full-year target, but gave no quarterly cash-flow estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Generated $492 million of free cash flow during the quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 is the first real checkpoint on the back-half ramp needed to reach the FY guide”; Q1 free cash flow was only $13M against the FY26 guide of $0.9B–$1.1B.

in_line: The company maintained full-year sales guidance of $14.0–$14.3 billion and free cash flow guidance of $900 million–$1.1 billion, both within the ranges in the preview.
The formal full-year margin guidance remained 10.7%–10.9%, as in the preview; the incremental R&D spending and lower margin midpoint excluding that spending are noted separately.

The full-year organic sales outlook of down 3.5% to down 1.5% was already reflected in the preview’s company guidance. The call’s battery-business headwind detail does not provide a directly comparable new estimate against the preview’s roughly $210 million BES headwind.
The turbine-generator business remained on track for a 2027 launch, with 2 GW of announced capacity and about $300 million of first-year revenue, consistent with the preview’s stated initial plan.

surprises.description: Fubo reported a $0.25-per-share loss, worse than the preview’s roughly $0.09-per-share loss estimate. The preview cautioned that EPS estimates were inconsistent after the reverse split, so the gap is notable but less certain than the subscriber and EBITDA comparisons.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net loss was $25.7 million, or a loss of $0.25 per share.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (Q3) | ~-$0.09”; the preview also says estimates are inconsistent because of reverse-split rebasing.

surprises.description: North America subscribers reached 5.75 million, well above the preview’s derived estimate of about 5.4 million. The quarter also produced a roughly 25,000 sequential gain despite the blackout, compared with a roughly 250,000 sequential decline in the year-ago third quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total North America subscribers reached 5.75 million”; the World Cup drove a “sequential gain of about 25,000 subscribers” versus a “roughly 250,000 sequential decline” a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “North America subscribers (Q3) | ~5.4M”; the preview also flagged blackout churn and a seasonally weak June as key risks.

surprises.description: Management raised the fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA guide’s low end by $10 million, rather than reaffirming the $80–$100 million range as the preview’s base case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management raised fiscal 2026 pro forma adjusted EBITDA guidance to $90–$100 million, “up $10 million at the low end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected the guide to be “reaffirmed at $80–100M” and said a raise was the clearest bull trigger.

surprises.description: The Disney ad-server migration was already delivering double-digit CPM and fill-rate increases, with management saying integration was ahead of plan and the CPM lift was faster than expected. The preview noted integration as a topic to watch but did not anticipate these reported gains.
