surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EPS guidance rose from $0.50–0.65 to $0.58–0.72, moving the upper end above the $0.66 consensus and making the range encompass that estimate. The guidance midpoint is about $0.65, close to consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS is guided to $0.58-0.72.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed $3–4 million of expected Calabrian cost and revenue synergies, which would lower the effective purchase multiple from roughly 8x to 7x EBITDA. The preview identified synergies as an open question but had no quantified synergy estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Calabrian is expected to deliver $3-4 million in cost and revenue synergies, stepping down the effective purchase multiple from about 8x to 7x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Calabrian integration details. Any quantified synergies, purchase accounting, and whether the leverage path is reaffirmed. The June 30 close release was light on numbers.”

surprises.description: Capex guidance increased to $85–95 million from $80–90 million. That is a modestly higher spending outlook than the preview’s stated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capex now $85-95 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “$80–90M capex.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $53 million, within the company’s $50–55 million guidance and consistent with the preview’s implied consensus of about $52–53 million.

Management’s sulfur outlook was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of easing costs and possible industrial softness: it expects prices to plateau or moderate modestly and noted a risk of temporary destocking-related demand impact.
Net debt leverage was 2.0x after the Calabrian funding, in line with the preview’s pro forma leverage estimate of about 2.0x.

surprises.description: Q2 total production reached the top of Devon’s guided range, while oil production was 2% above the guidance midpoint. The preview’s base case expected volumes in the mid-to-high end, so the result was stronger than that expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Oil production 2% above the guidance midpoint at 503,000 barrels per day and total production of 1.36 million BOE/d hitting the top end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “Volumes mid-to-high end”; it also gave Q2 production guidance of 1,315–1,360 MBoe/d and oil guidance of 485–505 MBbl/d.

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow was $1.7 billion, below the preview’s estimated $1.8–2.0 billion. The shortfall was modest relative to the low end of that estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 generated $1.7 billion in adjusted free cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s gaps section estimated “FCF (~$1.8–2.0B),” noting it was derived from guidance rather than a company figure.

surprises.description: Q2 capital spending was $1.3 billion, above the preview’s estimated $1.15–1.25 billion, although it still came in below the company guidance midpoint. That is a modestly higher spend than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 capital of $1.3 billion coming in 2.4% below the guidance midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Q2 capex (~$1.15–1.25B),” while noting this estimate was derived from guidance.

surprises.description: Devon reported a substantially lower reinvestment rate—43% of cash flow—than its mid-50s level over the prior two years. The preview did not flag this improvement in spending efficiency.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The reinvestment rate improved to 43% of cash flow, down from the mid-50s over the prior two years.”

surprises.description: Devon raised its quarterly dividend by 33% and resumed share repurchases, buying back 4.3 million shares in seven weeks. The preview identified capital returns as an activist focus but did not anticipate these specific actions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Devon raised its quarterly dividend 33% to $0.32 per share … [and] resumed buybacks by repurchasing 4.3 million shares in seven weeks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said activists were pressing for “asset sales, capital-return changes, and spending discipline.”

surprises.description: Devon completed its full $1.25 billion 2026 debt-reduction target, including paying the remaining $750 million term loan in July. The preview did not identify this debt paydown as an expected result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its full $1.25 billion 2026 debt reduction target, retiring $500 million of notes and term loan in Q2 plus the remaining $750 million term loan in July.”

surprises.description: Devon disclosed a New Mexico lease purchase adding 400 Delaware locations at a headline $6.5 million per location, with management arguing the lower royalty burden brings the effective cost to about $4 million per premium location. The preview had not anticipated this acquisition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The New Mexico federal lease sale added 400 top-tier Delaware locations at a headline $6.5 million per location,” which management said equates to “an effective ~$4 million per premium location” after accounting for the lower royalty burden.

surprises.description: Management gave a distinct production-and-capital cadence: Q3 oil guidance steps up to 550,000–560,000 barrels per day, Q4 oil is expected to be similar or higher, and Q3 capital is forecast to be the year’s highest before declining in Q4. The preview modeled a Q3 total-production run rate but did not anticipate this oil and quarterly-capital guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for a meaningful step-up to 550,000-560,000 barrels of oil per day and total capital of $1.4-$1.5 billion (the year's highest), with Q4 oil expected at similar or higher levels and lower capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said its derived Q3 total-production expectation was “about 1,675” MBoe/d and described a base-case Q3 guide of “1,650–1,690”; it did not give a quarterly-capital expectation.

surprises.description: Management reported Delaware drilling-and-completion costs of $800 per foot before most merger synergies have been captured, and said it expects a more aggressive cost structure in 2027. The preview discussed synergy targets but did not flag this cost level or outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Delaware D&C costs are already at $800 per foot on a 9-12 month trailing basis before most synergies are captured, and management expects a more aggressive cost structure in 2027.”

surprises.description: Management cited a second-half capital-efficiency advantage of 24% versus the peer average on a 20:1 basis, a favorable comparison not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Second-half capital efficiency is claimed to be 24% better than the peer average on a 20:1 basis.”

surprises.description: Completion trials produced material uplift exceeding 15% at 180 days in 90% of tested wells, leading Devon to expand the surfactant program to more than 50 wells this year. The preview did not anticipate these trial results or the expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Surfactant completion trials showed 90% of tested wells with material uplift exceeding 15% at 180 days, prompting expansion to more than 50 wells this year.”

surprises.description: Devon disclosed that AI-enabled closed-loop gas lift now autonomously optimizes 1,000 wells, with more than 2,000 additional Permian wells targeted. This operating deployment was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI-enabled closed-loop gas lift now autonomously optimizes 1,000 wells with over 2,000 more targeted in the Permian.”

in_line: Devon reaffirmed at least $1 billion in annual synergies by year-end 2027, consistent with the preview’s stated $1.0 billion run-rate target by year-end 2027; no pull-forward was reported.
Full-year capital guidance remained $4.8–$5.0 billion, matching the preview’s cited guidance range.

surprises.description: The preview expected a modest or moderate full-year 2026 operating profit, but management now expects a moderate operating loss. That is a clear deterioration from the recovery outlook investors were led to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects a moderate operating loss for full-year 2026, with the most significant improvement weighted to the second half as production ramps up.
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 operating profit: “Modest/moderate” full-year profit (reiterated on Q1 call); management said Q2 is the low point for operating profit and net income.

surprises.description: Bookings were expected to show sequential growth to support a second-half inflection; instead, they rose 17% sequentially, more than doubled year over year, and reached their highest quarterly level in three years. The reported strength exceeded the preview’s broadly stated growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 bookings reached $680 million, up 17% sequentially and more than double Q2 2025, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of bookings growth and highest quarterly level in 3 years.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Bookings and backlog “need to confirm the second-half inflection”; the checklist says to “look for sequential growth that supports the H2 recovery.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 to be the low point for operating profit, but the operating loss narrowed by about $10 million from Q1 rather than worsening. This was a better quarterly operating result than that trough expectation implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: Consolidated operating loss improved to $18 million, roughly $10 million better than Q1 2026, driven mainly by the lift truck business.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management said Q2 2026 should be the “low point for operating profit and net income.”

surprises.description: Cash flow was a concern in the preview, which highlighted cash burn and the prior quarter’s negative operating cash flow. Instead, operating cash flow turned positive at $17 million, improving by about $50 million from Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: Operating cash flow turned positive at $17 million, an improvement of approximately $50 million from Q1 2026, driven by lower inventory and favorable accrued liability changes.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Cash burn and leverage” and said “cash flow and debt levels matter”; Q1 operating cash flow was listed as –$32.9M.

surprises.description: Bookings were strong, but production and shipments are not yet keeping pace: management said trucks planned for Europe are being reshored to North America and customers rescheduled deliveries after the tariff change. This conversion delay was not highlighted in the preview and tempers the expected near-term benefit from booking growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: Production growth is temporarily lagging bookings because trucks originally planned for Europe are being reshored to North America following the April Section 232 tariff change and customer delivery rescheduling; booking strength has not yet fully translated into shipments due to production lags.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said bookings and backlog should “confirm the second-half inflection” and described a second-half recovery driven by backlog rebuilding.

surprises.description: Revenue slightly exceeded the $804.6 million consensus estimate, coming in at $813 million. The beat was modest, while the reported 2% sequential increase was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of a weak quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Revenue was $813 million, up 2% sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus: $804.6M.

surprises.description: Management provided a longer-term profitability and cost-savings outlook that the preview did not identify: it expects trailing 12-month EBITDA to exceed pre-COVID levels in the second half of 2027, with footprint optimization benefits and a 7% operating-profit target over the cycle.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects trailing 12-month EBITDA to exceed pre-COVID levels in the second half of 2027, aided by manufacturing footprint optimization projected to deliver $15-$20 million in annualized benefits, and targets 7% operating profit over the cycle.

surprises.description: The quarter included an unflagged $3 million noncash valuation allowance related to Brazilian deferred tax assets, adding to the reported net loss. The preview did not mention this item.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net loss was $32 million, including a $3 million noncash valuation allowance tied to Brazilian deferred tax assets.

in_line: The 2025 restructuring program remained on pace for the $40-$45 million of annualized savings the preview said to track; management reported that about half had been captured in the first half of 2026.

Tariff refunds were broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of roughly $40 million in refund applications: the quarter included $35 million in refunds. The preview also anticipated ongoing tariff costs, while the call said refunds were largely offset by unfavorable capitalized material costs and $10 million in higher gross tariff expenses.

surprises.description: NiSource reported that the IURC declined certain gas modernization tracker recovery, a new regulatory setback not flagged in the preview. Management said it would pursue recovery through the FMCA, other trackers, or rate cases, while keeping CapEx plans and the EPS outlook unchanged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The IURC issued an order today declining certain gas modernization tracker recovery,” prompting NiSource to pursue recovery through the FMCA, other trackers, or rate cases; management stated it has “no change to CapEx plans or EPS outlook.”

surprises.description: The preview expected flat O&M and flagged weather as a swing item. Instead, NiSource said unusually high storm activity and expenses related to ongoing union negotiations pressured O&M, only partly offset by new rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Higher-than-usual storm activity from a record number of tornadoes and elevated expenses tied to ongoing union negotiations pressured O&M,” partially offset by benefits from new rates at NIPSCO Electric and Columbia Gas of Ohio and Pennsylvania.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has committed to flat O&M. Weather and the depreciation and interest drag are the swing items.”

surprises.description: NiSource reported a 9 GW data-center pipeline and said it is exploring expansion beyond that level. The preview focused on whether signed capacity would move above roughly 4 GW, but did not flag this broader pipeline scale or further expansion effort.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The data center pipeline stands at 9 gigawatts, including 4 GW signed, 3 GW in active strategic negotiations, and about 2 GW of additional potential customers,” and the company is “exploring expansion beyond 9 GW.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for energization confirmation, the Amazon +400 MW ramp, and whether signed capacity moves above the ~4 GW disclosed at Q1.”

surprises.description: NiSource disclosed over $40 million of 2026 cost-optimization initiatives, with benefits expected to continue improving its cost structure beyond 2026; the preview did not anticipate this additional cost-saving effort.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management identified over $40 million of cost optimization initiatives for 2026 that are expected to continue improving the cost structure beyond 2026.”

surprises.description: The Amazon and Alphabet data-center agreements are expected to produce about $1.4 billion in bill reductions for existing NIPSCO electric customers, or up to $124 per residential customer annually, beginning as early as Q4 2026. The preview discussed the agreements and their review, but not these customer bill reductions.
surprises.fact_evidence: The agreements are expected to deliver “approximately $1.4 billion in bill reductions for existing NIPSCO electric customers, or up to $124 annually per residential customer, beginning as early as Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed the Alphabet and Amazon agreements, their review, and data-center execution, but did not mention customer bill reductions.

in_line: Q2 adjusted EPS of $0.16 was within the preview’s base-case range of $0.16–$0.18 and close to its roughly $0.15 whisper estimate, though below the cited $0.17–$0.19 consensus range.

NiSource reaffirmed full-year 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $2.02–$2.07, as the preview expected, and said earnings would be weighted toward the second half, consistent with the preview’s discussion of the required second-half ramp.
The company reaffirmed its 9%–10% adjusted EPS CAGR through 2033, in line with the long-term growth outlook cited in the preview.
The five-year capital plan remained at $21 billion of base investment, $2 billion of upside opportunities, and $7.6 billion of GenCo capital, consistent with the preview’s capital-plan figures.
The 400 MW Amazon load increase was already embedded in guidance, consistent with the preview’s focus on the Amazon +400 MW ramp.

surprises.description: Delek’s Q2 adjusted EPS of $5.48 and adjusted EBITDA of about $639 million substantially exceeded the preview’s main consensus and implied EBITDA range. Even excluding the 50% RVO adjustment, adjusted EPS of about $3.64 and EBITDA of about $490 million remained above those estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income of approximately $344 million ($5.48 per share) and adjusted EBITDA of approximately $639 million,” and “excluding the 50% RVO adjustment, adjusted EBITDA was ~$490 million and adjusted EPS ~$3.64.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 Adj. EPS” consensus ranged from $2.02 to $2.67 among the cited estimates (excluding the preview’s identified stale Zacks figure); “Q2 Adj. EBITDA” was estimated at “~$400–425M.”

surprises.description: DKL delivered a record quarter and modestly exceeded the preview’s estimated $130–140 million logistics contribution. The reported $144 million was also described as the best quarterly result in company history.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Logistics segment (DKL) posted its best quarterly results in company history at approximately $144 million in adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Read-through puts Q2 logistics contribution around $130–140M.”

surprises.description: The call reported a Krotz Springs small refinery exemption after a prior denial and strong optimism about pending 2025 petitions. The preview expected an update on the reported 2024 exemption, including a dollar figure and share count, so the call’s update was more limited on those specifics while adding optimism about 2025 petitions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Krotz Springs was recently awarded a small refinery exemption after a prior denial,” and management “expressed strong optimism about pending 2025 SRE petitions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Delek reportedly received a full 2024 exemption, per press reporting, not confirmed against the EPA docket”; the preview asked for “a dollar figure and share count from management.”

surprises.description: Delek’s Q3 system throughput guidance was 296,000–316,000 barrels per day, and management said no turnarounds were planned for the rest of the year. The preview flagged Q3 throughput and the turnaround calendar as issues to watch but gave no expected Q3 range or calendar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for total system throughput of 296,000 to 316,000 barrels per day with no planned turnarounds for the rest of the year.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed mid-cycle free cash flow of $650–700 million, or roughly a 15%–20% yield at current prices, a cash-generation outlook not specified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management projects mid-cycle free cash flow of $650 million to $700 million including DKL distributions, representing a roughly 15% to 20% free cash flow yield at current prices.”

surprises.description: Capital returns stepped up from the preview’s description of almost no Q1 buybacks: Delek bought back about $20 million of shares in Q2, alongside $16 million in dividends. Management also said repurchases since the beginning of 2025 totaled about 10% of the company.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Returned capital during the quarter via ~$16 million in dividends and ~$20 million in buybacks,” and “has repurchased approximately 10% of the company since the beginning of 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “DK repurchased almost nothing in Q1 while peers were aggressive”; “a buyback step-up would be a clear signal.”

surprises.description: Management said crude backwardation had eased sharply and that the flatter curve should improve refining margin capture roughly one-for-one. The preview focused on Q2 capture of record cracks and did not flag this potential Q3 tailwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Crude backwardation eased sharply from $6-$7+ in Q2 to a roughly flat curve (~$1.50) in Q3,” which management said “should translate roughly one-to-one into improved refining margin capture.”

surprises.description: Delek reported lower parent-level debt after refinancing its term loan and reducing stand-alone net debt. The preview gave prior-quarter debt figures but did not anticipate this quarter’s debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Refinanced its term loan, reducing it from $920 million to $850 million, and stand-alone Delek net debt (excluding DKL) declined by $72 million in the quarter.”

in_line: DKL reaffirmed its 2026 EBITDA guidance of $520–560 million and continued to expect third-party EBITDA above 80% on a pro forma basis, consistent with the preview.
The Enterprise Optimization Plan’s annual run-rate target remained at least $220 million, consistent with the preview’s stated target.

surprises.description: Management forecasts North American phosphate applications down about 20% this year after last year’s roughly 15% decline, with a similar 30% decline in Brazil. It also estimates large accumulated nutrient deficits that could eventually spur demand, adding a sharp current-demand deterioration and a possible future rebound to the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North American phosphate application is forecast down ~20% this year on top of last year's ~15% decline, cumulatively over 30% below normal, with a similar ~30% decline expected in Brazil.” Management estimates “1.4 million tonnes of DAP-equivalent nutrient in the U.S. and up to 1.3 million tonnes in Brazil” has been removed through under-application, which may eventually pressure yields and drive pent-up demand.

surprises.description: Mosaic now expects full-year CapEx of $1.2 billion, below the preview’s cited $1.25 billion guidance. The additional reduction is a modest positive for cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reduced full-year CapEx guidance to $1.2 billion” from $1.25 billion.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY capex guidance of “$1.25B” and flagged “Whether the $1.25B capex holds.”

surprises.description: Management expects a $400 million working-capital release, mostly in the second half, providing a cash source not identified in the preview. However, Brazilian customer prepayments have fallen to near zero, tempering that support.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $400 million working capital release (range $300-$500 million) is still expected,” weighted roughly one-third in Q3 and two-thirds in Q4 as Brazil collections arrive, “though customer prepayments in Brazil fell to near zero.”

surprises.description: Despite the expected working-capital release, Mosaic now expects to be roughly $500 million short for the year after operating cash flow of about $270 million against roughly $1.5 billion of CapEx and dividends. The preview warned of weak free cash flow but did not quantify this funding gap.
surprises.fact_evidence: “With year-to-date operating cash flow of ~$270 million against ~$1.5 billion in CapEx and dividends, the company expects to be roughly $500 million short for the year,” with debt stable in Q3 before declining in Q4.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “the coverage of the roughly $280M annual dividend against weak free cash flow.”

surprises.description: SG&A costs are down 20% year over year, with further reductions expected in the second half and management describing the savings as permanent. That gives more concrete evidence of durable savings than the preview’s general cost-program expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A costs were cut 20% year-over-year and are expected to decline further in the second half,” with management characterizing the savings as “permanent.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited a “Cost program above $150M annually.”

surprises.description: Potash netbacks face pressure from higher export freight and a Canpotex-weighted channel mix, an added headwind to the segment the preview described as carrying most of current profit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Potash netbacks face pressure from higher export freight rates and a Canpotex-weighted channel mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Potash carried the quarter” and highlighted roughly 2.0 Mt at about $270/t against an $84/t cash cost.

in_line: Q2 phosphate production and sales were 1.4 million tonnes, the bottom of the 1.4–1.7 million-tonne Q2 guidance range.

The Q3 phosphate volume range of 1.1–1.4 million tonnes reflects the H2 volume reset the preview anticipated; the preview specifically warned that Q3 guidance could reset the year and its base case assumed H2 volume cuts.
Sequentially lower Q3 stripping margins from higher sulfur and ammonia costs and weaker fixed-cost absorption align with the preview’s focus on compressed stripping margins and sulfur-cost risk.
A Q3 decline in Fertilizantes EBITDA from Q2’s $60 million, because Brazilian production curtailments limit sales, is consistent with the preview’s warnings about Brazil and the July curtailments.

surprises.description: NWN reported Q2 EPS of $0.01, rather than the loss of roughly $0.05–$0.08 the preview cited as the GAAP consensus. The call also said the result was above expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total EPS was $0.01, flat year-over-year but above expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP EPS” consensus: “$(0.05) to $(0.082)” (midpoint about “$(0.06)”).

surprises.description: Management moved from the expected reaffirmation of the $2.95–$3.15 FY2026 range to expecting EPS in its top half, citing strong year-to-date performance and better second-half visibility. The range itself was not raised.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its expectation to deliver 2026 EPS in the top half of its $2.95 to $3.15 guidance range,” citing “strong year-to-date performance and improved second-half visibility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A reaffirmation is expected. Narrowing to the upper half would be the most bullish outcome.”

surprises.description: The preview expected MX3’s late-2027 NTP timing to leave the long-term growth target at 4%–6%. The call said the fully contracted project would raise the target to 5%–7% upon NTP, expected at the end of 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $300 million FERC-regulated MX3 storage expansion is fully contracted with 25-year agreements at a 12.5% ROE and 50% equity structure,” and upon NTP “would raise the long-term earnings growth target from 4%-6% to 5%-7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether NTP stays ‘by late 2027,’ which would keep long-term growth at 4–6%.”

surprises.description: Washington rate relief was expected to take effect in August, but the call added a favorable award detail: the company received over 80% of its requested increase, with a 9.5% ROE and a 50/50 equity/debt structure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In Washington, the company received over 80% of its requested revenue requirement increase with a 9.5% ROE and a 50/50 equity/debt capital structure, with new rates effective August 1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Washington rate relief (effective August 2026).”

surprises.description: SiEnergy’s backlog exceeded the preview’s 250,000-meter reference point, with more than 260,000 future meters supporting its growth outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SiEnergy's Texas operations delivered over 15% organic customer growth with a backlog of over 260,000 future meters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “backlog versus 250k meters.”

surprises.description: Water’s first-half results were modestly below plan, a shortfall the preview did not flag among its key issues or expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Water customer growth was 3.4% for the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, though first-half results were modestly below plan.”

in_line: SiEnergy organic customer growth was over 15%, within the preview’s stated 15%–20% target.
The Oregon mechanism’s new rates were expected to take effect October 31, 2026, consistent with the preview’s expected 10/31/26 timing.
The 2026 capital expenditure plan remained $500 million to $550 million, and planned ATM equity of $40 million to $50 million remained within the preview’s stated plan.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS from continuing operations was $0.45, below both the preview’s $0.47 consensus and its $0.52 estimate, even though the California catch-up was recognized in Q2. The reported $0.58 EPS includes the retroactive California revenue and does not change the adjusted-EPS shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS from continuing operations rose to $0.45”; “reported EPS was $0.58 reflecting retroactive California rate case revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 diluted EPS (cont. ops) … $0.47”; “Preview estimate: $0.52 EPS”; the preview expected the California catch-up to be recognized in Q2.

surprises.description: The Great Basin 2028 Expansion estimate rose by $600 million to approximately $2.3 billion, a substantial increase in project cost. The preview flagged capex as something to watch but did not anticipate this increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Great Basin 2028 Expansion Project capital estimate increased to approximately $2.3 billion (a $600 million rise) after switching to a 48-inch pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Also watching: Great Basin 2028 Expansion capex and whether design capacity moves above 1.0 Bcf/d”; “The question is how much capex and how it is funded.”

surprises.description: Nevada intervenors recommended an average revenue increase just under $40 million, well below the company’s roughly $74 million request. The preview highlighted the case and its timing but did not flag such a large gap between the request and intervenor recommendations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Intervenor parties converged on a 9.3% ROE and recommended an average revenue increase just under $40 million versus the company’s ~$74 million request.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Nevada GRC (about $71M requested). Rates are targeted for October 2026 (Q4).”

surprises.description: Management extended its financing assurance beyond the preview’s no-equity-in-2026 expectation, saying it expects to avoid meaningful ATM draws through 2030 by using HoldCo capacity. This is a more extended commitment to limiting equity issuance than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management anticipates no equity issuances in 2026 beyond its dividend reinvestment plan” and “expects to avoid meaningful ATM draws through 2030 by leveraging HoldCo capacity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “management guided to no equity in 2026.”

surprises.description: HoldCo interest expense fell about $8.6 million year over year after the parent repaid all outstanding debt, providing an earnings benefit not called out in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HoldCo interest expense fell approximately $8.6 million year-over-year following repayment of all outstanding parent-level debt last summer.”

in_line: The California rate-case catch-up was recognized in Q2, as the preview expected; the decision provided approximately $40 million of incremental annual revenue, close to the preview’s cited $40.1 million increase.
FY2026 guidance was reaffirmed, as expected; the preview flagged affirmation of the $4.17–$4.32 range as the base case.
The 9.5%–11.5% long-term rate-base CAGR target was reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s stated company target.
The utility’s 8.1% trailing ROE (8% adjusted) remained below its 9.89% authorized return, consistent with the preview’s description of an 8.0%–8.5% ROE versus roughly 9.5%–10% authorized.
The company reiterated no equity issuance in 2026 beyond its dividend reinvestment plan, consistent with the preview’s expectation of no equity in 2026.
The Nevada case retained its October 2026 target, consistent with the preview’s timing expectation.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS was $0.82, well above the preview’s $0.65–$0.66 consensus estimates. The preview described $0.68 or higher as the bull scenario, so the reported result exceeded even that threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS rose 52% to $0.82”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 EPS | $0.65”; alternative estimates were “EPS $0.65” and “EPS $0.66.” The bull scenario was “≥ $0.68.”

surprises.description: ONE Gas moved its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to the upper half of the prior range, narrowing it to $4.89–$4.95 from $4.83–$4.95. That is a modest upward shift from the preview’s expectation that guidance might simply be affirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management now expects full-year results in the upper half of guidance, narrowing to adjusted net income of $310-314 million and adjusted EPS of $4.89-4.95.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed adjusted EPS guidance of “$4.83–$4.95” and asked whether it would be “affirmed, raised, or trimmed”; its base scenario assumed “Guidance affirmed.”

surprises.description: Texas HB 4384 is contributing more than anticipated, with about $0.28–$0.29 of its expected $0.42 full-year adjusted EPS contribution already realized in the first half. The preview did not identify this Texas benefit as a Q2 driver or quantify it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Texas House Bill 4384 is now expected to contribute approximately $0.42 to full-year adjusted EPS, with about $0.28-0.29 already realized in the first half”; Q2 included “greater-than-anticipated Texas HB 4384 benefits.”

surprises.description: Q2 included roughly $16 million of new revenue from new rates, despite the preview expecting only about four days of Oklahoma PBRC rates in Q2 and placing Texas GRIP and Kansas HB 2435 in Q3. The reported rate-related revenue was therefore a stronger Q2 contribution than the preview’s timing discussion suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 results were supported by roughly $16 million of new revenue from new rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: For Oklahoma PBRC, the preview said “Only about four days would fall in Q2”; it said Texas GRIP and Kansas HB 2435 “land in Q3.”

surprises.description: O&M growth decelerated to 6.6% in Q2 from more than 8% in Q1, rather than delivering another high-single-digit increase as the preview identified as the main risk. Costs were still growing faster than the stated 3–4% long-term rate, so the improvement was partial.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 O&M expenses rose 6.6% year-over-year (down from 8%+ in Q1)” and management expects sequential growth in the back half to fall “meaningfully below the 3-4% long-term rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “A second high-single-digit print is the most likely source of a miss,” after Q1 O&M growth of 8.6%.

surprises.description: Three high-volume large-load projects are now under contract, representing about $15 million of annual revenue and $175 million of capital. The preview mentioned one signed Oklahoma data-center agreement, but did not anticipate three contracted projects or their associated revenue and investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Three high-volume large-load projects under contract represent roughly $15 million of incremental annual revenue and $175 million of associated capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “one signed Oklahoma data-center agreement at 20 MMcf/d.”

surprises.description: Kansas capacity-release revenue had already reached $2.8 million year-to-date, with another $1.2 million opportunity remaining in the injection season. That indicates meaningful revenue was realized before the back-half-weighted timing described in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has realized $2.8 million in Kansas capacity release revenues year-to-date (shared 50-50 with customers), with an incremental $1.2 million opportunity remaining this injection season.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had called the Kansas capacity-release benefit “back-half weighted.”

surprises.description: The large-load pipeline includes 17 additional early-stage opportunities, which the preview had not identified. At the same time, the reported five late-stage prospects are one fewer than the six cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has 5 late-stage large-load prospects plus 17 additional early-stage opportunities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Six late-stage large-load projects (~3 GW).”

surprises.description: Management described a self-funding approach and a plan for 1–2% annual dividend growth through 2030, alongside a lower implied GAAP payout ratio. The preview anticipated the quarterly dividend amount but did not flag this longer-term growth policy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The quarterly dividend was held flat at $0.68 per share, with the GAAP payout ratio down to an implied 57% from 68% two years ago as the company pursues a self-funding strategy and 1-2% annual dividend growth through 2030.”

in_line: The quarterly dividend remained at $0.68 per share, matching the preview’s stated quarterly dividend.

surprises.description: USANA lowered its FY2026 outlook, rather than leaving the wide range intact or narrowing it toward the low end. The preview had identified a cut—particularly to adjusted EPS or EBITDA—as the bear case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “USANA lowered its full-year fiscal 2026 outlook,” citing a more expensive direct-to-consumer digital marketing environment hurting HIYA's second-half sales and reduced near-term Rise Wellness sales.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The more damaging outcome would be a cut to the adj. EPS or adj. EBITDA range”; the base scenario anticipated the “full $925M–$1.0B range left intact without narrowing.”

surprises.description: HIYA's weaker performance led USANA to record a $29 million preliminary non-cash goodwill impairment. The preview warned that HIYA's guide was at risk, but did not anticipate an impairment charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An estimated preliminary non-cash goodwill impairment charge of $29 million” tied to HIYA, reflecting “weaker-than-expected performance and reduced near-term forecasts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $140–155M segment guide is at risk if subscribers do not stabilize and acquisition costs do not normalize.”

surprises.description: HIYA's customer-acquisition costs remained a problem rather than normalizing, and management described a strategic pivot toward TikTok, retail, and international markets. The preview had flagged Meta-related costs but listed normalization as a positive signal to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HIYA has faced rising customer acquisition costs due to Meta algorithm challenges,” prompting a “strategic shift toward TikTok, retail expansion, and international markets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The catalyst checklist asked whether HIYA would show “commentary that acquisition costs have normalized”; the preview also noted management had blamed “higher acquisition costs tied to Meta ad-platform disruption.”

surprises.description: A Rise Wellness packaging issue caused a substantial near-term sales and margin hit, a specific disruption the preview had not flagged. It lowered the top-line guidance range by roughly $30–40 million and created $4–5 million of margin pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Rise Wellness packaging issue lowered its top-line guidance range by roughly $30 million to $40 million and created about $4 million to $5 million of margin pressure.”

surprises.description: USANA incurred $9 million of income tax expense despite a $19 million pre-tax loss, and management expects an elevated tax rate to persist for the full year. The preview did not flag this tax burden.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$9 million in income tax expense on a pre-tax loss of $19 million,” driven by a “structural misalignment” between revenue locations and cost locations; management expects an elevated rate “through the full year.”

surprises.description: North Asia direct revenue fell 20%, with prolonged Korea weakness following a leadership transition. The preview focused on whether core actives could stabilize, but did not anticipate this pronounced regional decline or its stated cause.
surprises.fact_evidence: “North Asia direct revenue declined 20%, driven mainly by prolonged softness in Korea following a leadership transition at the start of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Sequential growth in total core actives would be the cleanest sign that the core business has bottomed.”

surprises.description: Greater China returned to sales growth, a positive outcome against the preview's concern that Q1 momentum might not hold into a seasonally softer quarter. Management cautioned that the growth was partly supported by the lingering effect of the Q1 incentive and product-launch program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Greater China, USANA's largest market, showed renewed sales growth,” partly attributed to “a lingering tail from a robust Q1 incentive and product launch program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: For Greater China actives, the preview said, “The test is whether that holds into a seasonally softer Q2.”

surprises.description: Rise Wellness had already exceeded its full prior-year sales year-to-date and expected to reach more than 4,000 retail doors by year-end. The preview anticipated a rollout of nine new retailers, but did not cite this scale of sales progress or distribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rise Wellness has already exceeded its full prior-year sales year-to-date” and expects to be “selling in over 4,000 retail doors by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had cited “nine new Rise retailers rolling out in Q2 and Q3.”

surprises.description: USANA ended the quarter with more cash and no debt, while generating $20 million of free cash flow. The preview's prior-quarter baseline was $163 million of cash and $14 million of debt, and it highlighted the possibility of resuming buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “USANA ended the quarter with $169 million in cash, zero debt, and generated $20 million of free cash flow aided by improved working capital management.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior-quarter figures were “Cash $163M; debt $14M,” and the preview asked whether there would be a “Buyback resumption” against $34 million of remaining authorization.

surprises.description: Prudential reported adjusted operating EPS of $4.08, well above the preview’s $3.35–$3.42 consensus range. That is roughly a 19%–22% beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 after-tax adjusted operating income was $1.4 billion, or $4.08 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating EPS (Q2) ... $3.42 ... or $3.35.”

surprises.description: The Japan sales-suspension impact was lower than expected for the quarter, at $105 million, rather than building as the preview warned could happen in the first full suspended quarter. Prudential nevertheless kept its $525–575 million full-year guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Prudential of Japan sales suspension impact was $105 million in the quarter (below expectations, down from $130 million in Q1), with management maintaining full-year 2026 guidance of $525-575 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 is the first full suspended quarter, and management said the impact builds non-linearly through the year.”

surprises.description: Prudential set out a substantial portfolio retrenchment not anticipated in the preview: it plans to halve its retirement and insurance footprint by exiting 6–7 emerging markets, mainly through sales, and expects to release well over $3 billion of capital over about five years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Prudential plans to cut its retirement and insurance footprint by roughly half, exiting 6-7 emerging markets (primarily via sales rather than shutdowns) to free up well north of $3 billion of capital over roughly a 5-year period.”

surprises.description: Prudential sharply raised its structural efficiency ambition: the target is now about $750 million of pretax run-rate benefits by year-end 2028, versus the original $150 million target for 2027. It also added a goal of improving the adjusted operating expense ratio by another 150 basis points over three years.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its structural efficiency target to approximately $750 million in pretax run-rate benefits by year-end 2028 (full benefit in 2029), up from the original $150 million target for 2027”; it also “expects to improve its adjusted operating expense ratio by an additional 150 basis points over the next 3 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The original $150 million target for 2027.”

surprises.description: Prudential now aims for PGIM to contribute about 25% of PFI adjusted operating income, more than double its current roughly 12% share. The preview discussed PGIM margins and flows but did not flag this contribution-mix ambition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company targets PGIM growing to about 25% of PFI's adjusted operating income, more than double its current ~12% contribution.”

surprises.description: PGIM’s margin ambition moved beyond the preview’s 25%–30% long-term range: management now aims to expand margins above its 30% multiyear target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Prudential] aims to expand PGIM margins above its 30% multiyear target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management targets ... a 25–30% long-term margin.”

surprises.description: Group Insurance delivered a strong reversal from the weakness that had made it a key concern: earnings reached a record $155 million, up 24%, after Q1 earnings had fallen to $38 million and the preview warned that another weak print could suggest a structural problem.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Group Insurance delivered record earnings of $155 million (up 24%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Group Insurance: AOI fell to $38M from $89M” and “Two consecutive weak prints would suggest the problem is structural rather than cyclical.”

in_line: Prudential maintained the Japan full-year impact range of $525–575 million, as the preview’s base case expected, and targeted resumption by November 5–6, consistent with the preview’s focus on the November 6 restart date.
PGIM remained on track for more than 200 basis points of margin expansion in 2026, in line with the preview’s stated expectation.

Management did not restore a specific numerical EPS-growth target; instead it described top-quartile growth, around the high single digits, consistent with the preview’s base case of directional guidance without a hard new numeric target.

surprises.description: The company reported $56.6 million of annualized revenue from rate cases and surcharges finalized year to date, versus the preview’s $15.1 million completed as of Q1. That is a faster pace of finalized rate relief than the preview’s latest figure suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date the company finalized rate cases and surcharges representing $56.6 million in annualized revenue, with ~78% from water and wastewater.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “$15.1M annualized already completed in 2026” as of Q1.

surprises.description: Management said full-year effective tax rates should be below 5% and noted a one-time benefit later this year. The preview did not flag either favorable tax item as an expectation for FY2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects low single-digit (under 5%) effective tax rates for the full year plus a one-time benefit later this year disclosed in the S-4.”

surprises.description: Beyond the DELCORA transaction already highlighted in the preview, management cited a broader municipal pipeline of roughly 400,000 customers. The preview flagged municipal M&A but did not identify a pipeline of that scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Signed acquisition agreements plus completed deals add roughly 200,000 customers for ~$282 million (including DELCORA), with a broader municipal pipeline of ~400,000 customers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said DELCORA was “about 198,000 EDUs, $276.5M” and listed municipal M&A as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: Management said about 55% of Pennsylvania capital spending in 2026 is DSIC-eligible, a capital-recovery detail not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately 55% of 2026 Pennsylvania capital is DSIC-eligible.”

in_line: Non-GAAP Q2 EPS was $0.38, matching the preview’s $0.38 consensus and its $0.37–$0.39 in-line range.
Management reaffirmed 5%–7% multiyear EPS growth through 2027, as the preview expected.

The company still expects the merger to close in Q1 2027; the preview identified Pennsylvania approval and close timing as key debates. The Illinois and Pennsylvania procedural details add context but do not change the stated target.
The company remains on track for $1.7 billion of 2026 infrastructure investment, consistent with the preview’s stated target.
The 5.25% dividend increase and 60%–65% payout-ratio target were consistent with the preview’s information.
The $163.2 million Pennsylvania natural gas rate-case request was already identified in the preview.

surprises.description: AFG reported core EPS of $2.82, well above the preview’s $2.32–$2.37 consensus range. That is roughly 19%–22% above the estimates, rather than the approximately 8% year-over-year growth implied by the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 core net operating earnings of $2.82 per share, a 32% year-over-year increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 EPS ... ~$2.32 ... or $2.37”; “Consensus of ~$2.32 implies roughly 8% core EPS growth.”

surprises.description: Q2 net written premiums grew 6%, above the prior 3–5% full-year net written premium growth guidance cited in the preview; gross premiums grew 7% as well. The quarter’s growth was broad, with about three-quarters of AFG’s businesses reporting higher premiums.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross and net written premiums grew 7% and 6% respectively, with roughly three-quarters of AFG's 36 businesses reporting higher year-over-year premiums.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 net written premium growth: 3–5% (Q1 2026 call, Apr/May 2026).”

surprises.description: The Specialty P&C combined ratio was 91.5%, better than the preview’s approximately 92.5% full-year target. Favorable prior-year reserve development was 3.4 points, up from 0.7 points, and catastrophe losses were lower by 1.8 points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Specialty P&C combined ratio improved 1.6 points to 91.5%, aided by 3.4 points of favorable prior-year reserve development (up from 0.7 points) and lower catastrophe losses of 1.8 points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Specialty P&C combined ratio target ~92.5%.”

surprises.description: AFG’s P&C net investment income reached a second-quarter record, with alternative investment returns rising to 7.1% from 1.2% a year earlier. The preview identified alternatives as a source of earnings volatility but did not anticipate a return level or record result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “P&C net investment income rose 23% year-over-year to a second-quarter record, driven by alternative investment returns jumping to 7.1% versus just 1.2% in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Alternative investment returns. Private equity and real estate partnership returns have been the main source of quarter-to-quarter earnings variance.”

surprises.description: Commercial auto liability produced a small underwriting profit for a second consecutive quarter, a positive result on the specialty casualty issue the preview highlighted. Management nevertheless said more rate increases are needed to reach targeted returns.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial auto liability posted a small underwriting profit for the second consecutive quarter, though management indicated more rate is needed to reach targeted returns.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sustained sub-92% prints and specialty casualty pricing commentary will drive the reaction.”

in_line: The Charleston Harbor Resort & Marina sale remained pending and was expected to close in Q3 2026, within the preview’s Q2-or-Q3 timing window; the approximately $125 million pre-tax gain was therefore not reported as a Q2 result.
AFG’s regular dividend remained $0.88 per share, as noted in the preview.

surprises.description: WTTR reported Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $93 million, well above its $77 million to $80 million company guidance range. The $13 million to $16 million gap was driven by outperformance across all three segments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA of $93 million significantly exceeded the company's guidance range of $77 million to $80 million, driven by outperformance across all three segments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: $77M to $80M (company guide)”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $396 million, above the preview’s $374 million to $380 million consensus range and its $366 million to $377 million guidance-implied range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue grew 8% sequentially to $396 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $374M to $380M”; the preview also estimated “Total: $366M to $377M (mid ~$371M).”

surprises.description: Water Infrastructure revenue reached $102 million, topping the preview’s $96 million to $99 million implied range and surpassing the preview’s $100 million bull-case marker. Its 58% gross margin also exceeded the 56.2% Q1 reference point and the preview’s concern threshold of about 54%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Water Infrastructure segment posted record revenue of $102 million … with strong 58% gross margins before D&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview implied “$96M to $99M” for Q2 Water Infrastructure and said “A print below about $95M or a margin below about 54% would break the narrative”; its bull scenario cited “Infrastructure above $100M.”

surprises.description: Chemical Technologies revenue was $96 million, above the preview’s $86 million to $90 million implied range. Gross profit also grew 35% sequentially to $19.4 million despite rising oil-based raw-material costs, strengthening the segment’s outperformance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Chemical Technologies segment posted record revenue of $96 million, up 23% sequentially, with 35% sequential gross profit growth to $19.4 million despite rising oil-based raw material costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview implied Chemical Technologies revenue of “$86M to $90M” from expected sequential growth of “+10% to +15%.”

surprises.description: WTTR raised its 2026 net capital expenditure range to $250 million to $290 million, extending the ceiling $40 million above the prior $250 million high end. The preview had flagged a further capex increase without an FCF offset as a concern; the spending is to support new infrastructure awards.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its 2026 net capital expenditure guidance to $250 million to $290 million, up from the prior $250 million high end, to support new infrastructure contract awards.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Capex is $200M to $250M with buybacks paused. A further capex raise without an FCF offset would be negative.”

surprises.description: Management said Water Infrastructure is now expected to reach the high end of its 25% to 30% full-year growth target, and projected double-digit segment revenue growth continuing into 2027 with improved free-cash-flow potential. The preview expected the 2026 range to be reaffirmed, but did not anticipate this high-end emphasis or the 2027 outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Water Infrastructure to hit the high end of its 25% to 30% full-year growth guidance and projects double-digit segment revenue growth continuing into 2027 with improved free cash flow potential.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A reaffirm is expected; any trim is a thesis break.”

surprises.description: WTTR disclosed a new seven-year agreement with a large public operator, backed by a 128 million barrel MVC and involving 14 strategic SWDs in Eddy and Lea County. The project requires $25 million to $30 million and is expected to begin generating cash flow around month 13; the preview did not identify this award.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company executed a new 7-year agreement with a large public operator supported by a 128 million barrel MVC contract, which included the conveyance of 14 strategic SWDs across Eddy and Lea County, New Mexico.” The project is expected to “cost $25 million to $30 million” and “generate cash flow starting around month 13.”

surprises.description: Management reported surfactant demand up 50% year over year, but also said adoption remains limited: less than 10% of new well completions use surfactants, with 95% of that usage concentrated in the Permian. The preview did not discuss surfactants, so the rapid growth came with a qualification about its current reach.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Surfactant demand is growing rapidly (up 50% year-over-year) but remains a small portion of chemicals revenue, with less than 10% of new well completions currently using surfactants and 95% of that concentrated in the Permian.”

in_line: Management retained the 25% to 30% full-year Water Infrastructure growth target, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the range would be reaffirmed; the call added that WTTR expects to reach the high end.

surprises.description: Revenue was $260 million, above the preview’s modeled $250–253 million, and grew 11% year over year versus the roughly 7% working bar. It also rose sequentially from $248.6 million, avoiding the decline the preview flagged as a concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 revenue reached $260 million, up 11% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled revenue of “~$250–253M (+6.5–7.8%)” and said the working bar was “about 7% revenue growth”; it also flagged a sequential drop below $248.6M as a concern.

surprises.description: Reported EPS of $0.63 exceeded the preview’s modeled $0.58–0.60, but roughly $0.07 came from one-time CERIS items, primarily a legacy receivables settlement. Subtracting that benefit implies about $0.56 of EPS excluding the items, below the preview’s clean-EPS bar of at least $0.58, although net income excluding one-time items still grew 18%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Earnings per share rose 22% to $0.63” though “roughly $0.07 came from one-time CERIS items primarily tied to a legacy accounts receivable settlement”; “excluding one-time items, total net income increased 18% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled diluted EPS of “~$0.58–0.60,” called for “EPS of at least $0.58,” and expected a “$0.02 EPS headwind” because Q4 timing-related recoveries “should not recur.”

surprises.description: Patient Management contributed about $12.5 million of revenue growth, a stronger contribution than the preview’s expectation that the product line would remain a low-single-digit grower and its identification of a PM inflection as the best available upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Patient Management and Network Solutions each contributed roughly $12.5 million of revenue growth,” with “enterprise claims TPA” driving Patient Management.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “PM grew low single digits in Q4 and is the drag,” and that “a PM inflection is the best upside surprise available.”

surprises.description: The company repurchased $21.8 million of stock, a modest step up from the $20.1 million repurchased in Q4 FY26, when the preview specifically identified buyback acceleration as something to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased 377,098 shares for $21.8 million during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported “$20.1M in Q4” buybacks and said to watch for “buyback acceleration.”

in_line: The CEO transition itself was anticipated: the preview identified Sarah Scott as CEO from July 1, 2026, and noted that this would be her first call.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $1.39, well below the preview’s $1.83 model for reported EPS including the refund. The gap is large even though the bulk of the refund was reflected in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS surged to $1.39 from $0.24”; the company recognized $15.3 million in tariff refunds, with another $3.3 million reducing inventory and $700,000 of interest income.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reported diluted EPS | ~$1.83 (includes refund)”

surprises.description: Reported gross margin reached 70.4%, far above the preview’s roughly 44% estimate, because $15.3 million of tariff refunds reduced cost of sales. Another $3.3 million reduced inventory, so the headline margin does not indicate a sustainable improvement in underlying margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated gross margin jumped to 70.4%” and was “largely inflated by $15.3 million in one-time IEPA tariff refunds recognized as a reduction to cost of sales”; $3.3 million reduced inventory.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~44.0%”; the preview also identified “Gross margin ex-refund” as a key issue.

surprises.description: The tariff rate actually increased to 12.5% on imports from China and Vietnam on July 24, creating second-half margin uncertainty. The preview anticipated replacement tariff actions after the prior rate’s scheduled sunset but did not forecast this specific higher rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The administration raised the incremental tariff on imports from China and Vietnam to 12.5% effective July 24, 2026, creating near-term gross margin uncertainty for the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Section 122 rate was scheduled to sunset around July 24, 2026, with Section 301 actions expected as a replacement for Vietnam, China, and India sourcing.”

surprises.description: Stacey Adams and Bogs returned to growth, contrary to the preview’s bear case that their declines might persist: they grew 4% and 10%, respectively. Florsheim also grew 12%, while Nunn-Busch declined 3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Florsheim (+12%), Stacey Adams (+4%), and Bogs (+10%), while Nunn-Busch declined 3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bear scenario cited “Stacy Adams and BOGS declines persist”; in Q1, Stacy Adams was down 9% and BOGS down 11%.

surprises.description: Wholesale selling and administrative expenses rose to 37% of sales from 29%, with higher employee costs pressuring underlying operating margins. The preview focused on tariff-adjusted gross margin but did not flag this expense increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wholesale selling and administrative expenses climbed to 37% of net sales from 29% a year ago, driven by higher employee costs, pressuring underlying operating margins.”

surprises.description: The company received another $17.5 million in tariff refunds in early July, increasing liquidity after quarter-end; the preview had highlighted the timing and cash receipt of refunds as unresolved. Only $1.2 million of Phase 3 entries remained outstanding, so most of this refund benefit is now behind the company.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and marketable securities stood at $98.1 million with no debt, and the company received an additional $17.5 million in tariff refunds in early July”; “Only $1.2 million of remaining Phase 3 tariff entries are outstanding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the key question was whether the refund “lands in Q2, slips to Q3 … or shows up as cash.”

surprises.description: Net sales modestly exceeded the preview’s model: $62.2 million versus $61.5 million, with reported year-over-year growth of 7% versus the modeled 5.7%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales rose 7% year-over-year to $62.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | $61.5M (+5.7% YoY)”

in_line: The preview’s base case assumed the $18.6 million refund claim would be recognized in Q2; the reported treatment totaled $18.6 million across $15.3 million reducing cost of sales and $3.3 million reducing inventory, with $700,000 of interest income.
Management plans to build inventory to roughly $70 million by year-end, within the preview’s stated $60–70 million normalization target.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $2.36, above the preview’s $2.10–$2.20 consensus range. Adjusted net income rose 31% to a record, and buybacks helped adjusted EPS grow 34%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted net income grew 31% year-over-year to a record $63.8 million ($2.36 per share vs. $1.76), with adjusted EPS growing faster at 34% due to opportunistic buybacks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS | $2.10 – $2.20”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted net income guidance was raised, as the preview expected, but the new $270–$280 million range is below the preview’s anticipated raise to roughly $272–$286 million. Its $275 million midpoint is also below the preview’s anticipated range midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 adjusted net income guidance for the third time to $270-$280 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A ninth raise to roughly $272–286M is the base case.”

surprises.description: Gross written premium reached $630.5 million, about 2% above the preview’s roughly $616 million estimate, and grew 27% rather than the preview’s implied 24% year-over-year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross written premium increased 27% to $630.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross written premium | ~$616M” and “Implied Y/Y | +24%”

surprises.description: The adjusted combined ratio was 76.7%, just above the preview’s expected range of roughly 74%–76%. It remained below the preview’s 78% bear-case threshold, but came in somewhat worse than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted combined ratio of 76.7% (up from 73.1% a year ago).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted combined ratio | ~74–76% (buy-side)”

surprises.description: The crop franchise grew faster than the preview’s already-strong Q1 comparison suggested: Q2 crop GWP nearly doubled, and management raised the full-year crop premium outlook from about $320 million to over $400 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The crop franchise nearly doubled with gross written premium up 96% year-over-year, prompting a raised full-year crop premium outlook to over $400 million (up from ~$320 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Crop GWP grew 82% in Q1, and management flagged drought pressure on winter wheat in Oklahoma and Kansas.”

surprises.description: Despite the crop growth and higher outlook, management said the 2026 crop year was currently booked near a 100% net combined ratio, indicating little underwriting margin. The preview flagged crop reserve concerns but did not anticipate this near-break-even crop-year metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2026 crop year currently booked near a 100% net combined ratio.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Crop reserve commentary. Crop GWP grew 82% in Q1, and management flagged drought pressure on winter wheat in Oklahoma and Kansas.”

surprises.description: Commercial earthquake rate decreases exceeded 20%, worse than the roughly 18% renewal declines cited in the preview; management also said some new business was priced below technical levels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial Earthquake, now 36% of the earthquake book, saw average rate decreases exceeding 20% (over 20% on large layered/shared business), with some new business priced below technical levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Commercial EQ rates renewed around -18%.”

surprises.description: The quarter included $14.3 million of favorable prior-year reserve development, including from crop and a legacy workers’ compensation fronting program. The preview focused on possible crop reserve pressure, not a favorable reserve release of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 results included $14.3 million of favorable prior-year reserve development (largely Inland Marine/Property and crop, plus casualty from a legacy workers' comp fronting program).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Crop reserve commentary. Crop GWP grew 82% in Q1, and management flagged drought pressure on winter wheat in Oklahoma and Kansas.”

surprises.description: The Board initiated a new quarterly dividend, a capital-return step not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board initiated a new quarterly dividend of $0.45 per share.”

surprises.description: Share repurchases accelerated to $41 million in Q2, compared with the $23.1 million repurchased in Q1 cited by the preview; the preview did not set an expectation for a larger Q2 buyback.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased ~369,000 shares for $41 million at an average price of $111 during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buyback: $23.1M repurchased in Q1 under a $200M two-year authorization approved May 6.”

surprises.description: Surety and Credit GWP surged following the Gray Surety acquisition, and a new treaty enabled much larger bond limits with a stated $3.5 million net retention. The preview did not discuss this business or the new capacity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Surety and Credit gross written premium surged 236% year-over-year to ~$39 million following the Gray Surety acquisition, with a new reinsurance treaty enabling $70 million bond limits at a $3.5 million net retention.”

surprises.description: Palomar added about $421 million of earthquake and hurricane limit while keeping event retentions flat, increasing total earthquake coverage to $3.92 billion. This expansion of catastrophe protection was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company maintained its earthquake and hurricane event retentions flat at $20 million and $11 million respectively while adding ~$421 million of incremental limit, bringing total earthquake coverage to $3.92 billion.”

surprises.description: Net investment income rose 49.2% to $20 million on a 4.9% yield, an earnings contributor the preview did not identify among its key metrics or expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net investment income rose 49.2% to $20 million on a 4.9% yield.”

surprises.description: Q2 net product revenue was $129.9 million, above the preview’s $118.85–$121.85 million consensus range and even the preview’s $126–$130 million bull-case range. The result beat the consensus estimates by roughly 7–9%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net product revenue reached $129.9 million,” up 23% sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue, Q2” consensus: “$118.85M” or “$121.85M”; bull scenario: “$126–130M.”

surprises.description: Arcutis raised its FY26 revenue guidance to $525–$540 million, materially above the preview’s roughly $500 million consensus and above even its bull-case guide-raise range of $500–$515 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Arcutis raised full-year 2026 net revenue guidance from $480-495 million to $525-540 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY26 consensus was “~$500.09M” and that the bull scenario assumed guidance “raised to $500–515M.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted that rolling four-week prescriptions had fallen 6% QoQ and that re-acceleration was needed; Arcutis reported record quarterly demand of more than 280,000 prescriptions. The call did not provide a directly comparable exit-rate figure, so the record quarterly total is encouraging but does not establish the degree of exit-rate re-acceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ZORYVE achieved a record quarterly demand of more than 280,000 prescriptions across all indications and formulations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said rolling four-week scripts were “down 6% QoQ” and “Re-acceleration is needed.”

surprises.description: The Chief Commercial Officer is leaving later this month, with an interim replacement during a national search. The preview discussed commercial launches and sales-force expansion but gave no indication of an impending CCO departure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chief Commercial Officer Todd Edwards is resigning effective later this month, with 30-year industry veteran Rob Lisicki stepping in as Interim CCO during a national search.”

in_line: Sequential growth resumed: Q2 revenue of $129.9 million was up 23% from Q1, consistent with the preview’s expectation that QoQ growth would resume and its implied $127–$135 million quarterly H2 run-rate.
Gross-to-net remained in the 50s, with a trajectory toward the low 50s by year-end, broadly matching the preview’s expectation that it would improve.
Operating cash flow remained positive at $12.6 million, consistent with the preview’s focus on sustaining positive OCF after Q1’s first positive quarter.

The pediatric psoriasis approval and infant atopic-dermatitis sNDA acceptance were already reported in the preview; the call’s February 23, 2027 PDUFA date for the infant indication matched the preview.
A Q4 2026 vitiligo readout was consistent with the preview’s stated Q4 timing.

surprises.description: Loan originations reached $758 million, well above the preview’s $600–640 million estimate and its roughly $600 million implied bar. That is about 19% above the top of the estimate range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 loan originations surged to $758 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own Q2 base estimate … new contract purchases ~$600–640M”; “Q2 purchases of $600M+ would indicate the March run-rate held.”

surprises.description: Net charge-offs were substantially below the preview’s expected 8.5–8.9% range, coming in at 7.28%. This was also a marked improvement from Q1’s 8.57%, rather than the preview’s base-case expectation of credit being modestly worse year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net charge-offs declined to 7.28% from 7.45%” year over year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “NCO … 8.5–8.9%” and described “credit modestly worse YoY.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $121.4 million, about 3.8% above the preview’s $117 million base estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue increased 11% to $121.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own Q2 base estimate … revenue ~$117M.”

surprises.description: Recoveries rose to 33.3% from Q1’s 31.1%, extending the improvement instead of reversing as the preview warned could happen. The higher recovery rate also accompanied lower net charge-offs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recovery rates rose to 33.3% from 30.4% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Recoveries rose to 31.1% in Q1, which flattered net losses. A reversal would flow directly into gross charge-offs.”

surprises.description: Delinquency improved year over year, contrary to the preview’s base scenario of credit being modestly worse YoY, although it rose from Q1’s 11.58% to 12.16% sequentially.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total delinquency over 30 days improved to 12.16% from 13.14% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario described “credit modestly worse YoY”; the preview also flagged delinquency as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: The company reported improving expense efficiency despite its growth investments: core operating expenses rose only 3% over six months while revenue rose 8%, and the expense-to-managed-portfolio ratio fell. This is better than the preview’s concern that expansion could make growth look bought rather than earned.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Core operating expenses grew only 3% over six months while revenue grew 8%, improving the expense-to-managed-portfolio ratio to 4.6% from 4.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that sales reps and dealers had expanded sharply and warned: “If Q2 opex runs above about $110M without an origination beat, the growth will look bought rather than earned.”

in_line: Diluted EPS was $0.27, matching the preview’s own Q2 base estimate of about $0.27.
Shareholders’ equity reached $319.2 million, broadly in line with the preview’s expectation that equity would be above $300 million.

surprises.description: Q2 sales landed at the low end of the company’s range and below the preview’s working consensus: $160.1 million versus a $162 million guidance midpoint and consensus of $162.9–164.4 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales were essentially flat year-over-year at $160.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales” consensus was “$162.9M” or “$164.4M”; the preview said to use “$162.9M” and the guidance midpoint of “$162M” as the real bar.

surprises.description: Gross margin was stronger than the preview’s roughly 60% expectation, expanding to 61.1%; the reported bridge attributed about 240 basis points to lower tariffs and 120 basis points to higher full-price selling in streetwear brands.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 360 basis points to 61.1%, with roughly 240 basis points from lower tariffs and 120 basis points from higher full-price selling in streetwear brands.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 gross margin at “~60%” and said adjusted margin below “about 59.5% would be a negative surprise.”

surprises.description: Q3-to-date sales were already growing at a high-single-digit rate overall, with US growth in double digits. That provided a stronger near-term read than the preview’s concern that H2 required a substantial acceleration after earlier softness.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3-to-date net sales growth in the high single digits overall, with the US running up double digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said H2 needed growth of “roughly +5.6% to +10.1%” to hold the annual range and identified July quarter-to-date commentary as the “most direct evidence for the H2 math.”

surprises.description: The Q3 gross-margin outlook of approximately 59% points to a step down from Q2’s 61.1% and is below the preview’s roughly 60% margin reference, with tariffs and elevated air freight cited as the pressures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for ... gross margin of approximately 59% reflecting tariffs and elevated air freight.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed gross margin at “~60%,” noted freight cost pressure, and flagged margin below “about 59.5%” as negative. It did not give a separate Q3 margin estimate.

surprises.description: The company disclosed an unanticipated one-time $3 million Q3 selling expense for a planned distribution-center relocation. It is excluded from adjusted EBITDA, but will weigh on reported selling expenses.
