surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 consensus does not work on roughly 3% industrial organic growth. Look for orders sustaining high-single or double-digit growth.”

surprises.description: FY26 free cash flow was $3.9B, above the preview’s cited company guidance range of $3.3–$3.6B. Cash from operations also exceeded $4B for the first time.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY26 cash flow from operations exceeded $4 billion for the first time at $4.4 billion (20.3% of sales), with free cash flow of $3.9 billion at 107% conversion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 free cash flow guided at $3.3–$3.6B.”

surprises.description: The company raised its long-term adjusted segment margin target to 30% by FY31 after reaching its previous 27% FY29 target early. The preview did not anticipate a higher target or early achievement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its adjusted segment operating margin target by 300 basis points to 30% by FY31, after achieving its prior FY29 target of 27% early.”

surprises.description: Orders and backlog were particularly strong: orders were up 12% on a rolling 12-month basis and 19% on a three-month basis, while backlog rose 16% to a record $12.8B. The preview looked for sustained high-single- or double-digit order growth, but the reported three-month pace and backlog growth were stronger signals than that baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 total orders were up 12% on a rolling 12-month basis (19% on 3-month), with backlog up 16% to a record $12.8 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Look for orders sustaining high-single or double-digit growth”; the preview also cited a prior-quarter record backlog of “$12.5B.”

surprises.description: Management expects leverage to peak near 3x after the pending deals close, then take about six quarters to return to 2x. That is a higher interim leverage level and a longer deleveraging path than the preview’s focus on pro-forma leverage against a roughly 2x target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt to adjusted EBITDA fell to 1.4x from 1.7x a year earlier, and management expects it to peak near 3x after the pending deals close, returning to 2x within about 6 quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch … pro-forma leverage against the roughly 2x target.”

surprises.description: The pending acquisition spending includes CIRCOR aerospace deals as well as Filtration Group, while the preview identified Filtration Group as the key pending transaction. The facts cite about $12B for the two pending deals; the additional deal expands the capital commitment beyond the one the preview highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company deployed nearly $15 billion in capital in FY26, including the $1 billion Curtis acquisition, ~$12 billion for pending Filtration Group and CIRCOR aerospace deals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Filtration Group. The $9.25B deal was cleared by the EU Commission … Closing appears imminent but was unconfirmed.”

surprises.description: Beginning in FY27, Parker will change how it reports orders for all Industrial businesses, converting them to rolling 12-month reporting. The preview did not flag this reporting-method change, which may make comparisons with the prior presentation less direct.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Beginning in FY27, Parker will convert all Industrial businesses to rolling 12-month order reporting.”

in_line: FY27 adjusted EPS guidance excludes the impact of pending acquisitions, consistent with the preview’s base case that the deal would be excluded pending close.

The preview expected strong aerospace results, including double-digit organic growth as a key Q4 metric. The supplied call facts do not provide Q4 Aerospace Systems growth or segment margin, so that expectation cannot be assessed from these facts.

surprises.description: The preview cited the $890–900 million merchandise contribution guidance and flagged tough Q3 nicotine comparisons, but management now expects merchandise contribution toward the low end of that range. Consumer budget pressure and Q1 weather-related closures add downside to the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Merchandise contribution is expected to land toward the low end of the guidance range” due to “consumer budget pressures and Q1 weather impacts that closed up to half the network during winter storms.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Merchandise contribution. FY guide $890–900M. Management flagged tough Q3 nicotine comps.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a new-store delivery shortfall, but management now expects deliveries closer to 45 units, the lower end of guidance. The high end depended on tuck-in acquisitions that are not currently in the pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New store (NTI) deliveries will come in closer to 45 units at the lower end of guidance,” and “the high end assumed tuck-in acquisitions that are not currently in the pipeline.”

surprises.description: Management expects nicotine to remain a tailwind in the second half, despite the tough Q3 promotional comparison the preview highlighted. The new value-priced Cowboy Cut product and pouch growth are expected to support that contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nicotine is expected to remain a tailwind in the second half,” driven by “the new value-priced Cowboy Cut cigarette and pouch growth,” though “Q3 faces a tough promotional comp.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management flagged tough Q3 nicotine comps.”

surprises.description: Loyalty sign-ups accelerated substantially, a development the preview did not discuss: monthly sign-ups exceeded $600,000 in every Q2 month versus about $400,000 previously, and the share of new or lapsed customers also rose.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Loyalty program sign-ups exceeded $600,000 per month every month in Q2 (up from ~$400,000 previously), with new or lapsed customers rising to nearly 46% of signees from 40% in Q1.”

surprises.description: Management described fuel-supply tightness as likely to persist well into next year, rather than resolve quickly. The preview focused on falling oil prices and possible inventory losses but did not anticipate this duration outlook; Murphy also said its supply assets benefit in the current constrained environment.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management believes “fuel supply tightness from the geopolitical conflict will not normalize until well into next year” and “does not expect a quick resolution”; the controllables portion of fuel supply earned “over $0.07 per gallon this quarter” versus “only about $0.25 last year,” reflecting an advantage from Murphy's supply assets in the current constrained environment.

in_line: Q2 same-store fuel volume grew 0.5% year over year, within the preview's flat-to-+1.5% estimate.

surprises.description: RMR said it is on pace to earn over $40 million in incentive fees in calendar 2026, versus $23.6 million in 2025. The preview gave no 2026 estimate and noted DHC as the strongest candidate, so the projected increase was not anticipated there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On pace to generate over $40 million in incentive fees for calendar year 2026,” up from “$23.6 million earned for calendar year 2025,” with DHC representing about 75% of the projected total.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “CY2025 totaled $23.6M” and identified DHC as the “Strongest incentive-fee candidate,” but gave no CY2026 total estimate.

surprises.description: The preview highlighted a buy-side desire for at least $0.52 of Q4 distributable earnings per share, but RMR guided to $0.48–$0.50. That guidance is below the stated investor hurdle.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guided to Q4 … distributable earnings of $0.48–0.50 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Buy-side wants DE ≥$0.52” for FQ4.

surprises.description: RMR reported a $19 million non-cash impairment related to OPI’s bankruptcy emergence, which the preview discussed in terms of new management agreements and fees but did not flag as an impairment risk. The 2% equity stake in the new OPI entity only partially offset the charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recorded a $19 million net non-cash impairment charge tied to OPI's bankruptcy emergence, partially offset by receiving 2% equity in the new OPI entity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed OPI’s June 17 emergence and the new five-year agreements, but did not mention an impairment charge.

surprises.description: Recurring service revenue reached $45.5 million, above the preview’s roughly $44 million guide and even above its $45 million bull-case threshold. The increase was therefore stronger than the base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring service revenues rose approximately $3.5 million sequentially to $45.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed recurring service revenue guidance of “~$44M” and a bull case of “≥$45M.”

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s expectation that a full quarter of OPI fees would benefit FQ4, RMR expects recurring service revenue to be roughly flat next quarter as Greenwich acquisition fees roll off. The offsetting fee runoff limits the expected step-up.
surprises.fact_evidence: Recurring service revenues are “expected to remain flat at roughly $45 million next quarter as Greenwich acquisition fees roll off.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “The full benefit lands in FQ4” from the OPI agreements and that “the FQ4 revenue guide matters more than this print.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged adjusted EBITDA margin above 42% as a catalyst, but management described the current margin as in the low-40% range. That indicates the hoped-for move above 42% had not clearly materialized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Current EBITDA margin sits in the low-40% range,” with management targeting a return toward 50%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s catalyst checklist said to watch for “Adjusted EBITDA margin back above 42%.”

surprises.description: RMR disclosed a completed approximately $350 million Greenwich residential JV, with a 5% GP interest and roughly $750,000 in annual management fees. The preview did not anticipate this transaction or its associated recurring fees.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Closed a ~$350 million Greenwich, Connecticut JV where RMR holds a 5% GP interest and will earn roughly $750,000 in annual asset and property management fees.”

surprises.description: Management said global real estate fundraising in the first half of the calendar year reached a nine-year low amid Middle East conflict headwinds. The preview already noted fundraising disruption, but did not describe conditions as this weak.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Global real estate fundraising in the first half of the calendar year hit a nine-year low amid Middle East conflict headwinds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Middle East conflict “disrupted fundraising” and that 2026 capital deployment was down about 50% year over year.

surprises.description: Management disclosed that private capital AUM has grown from near zero in 2020 to over $12 billion. The preview discussed RMR’s total and fee-earning AUM but did not call out this scale of private capital growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Private capital AUM has grown from near zero in 2020 to over $12 billion today.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited total AUM of $37.1B and fee-earning AUM of $25.9B at March 31, 2026, without specifying private capital AUM.

in_line: Q3 distributable earnings of $0.48 per share and adjusted EBITDA of $19.7 million met company guidance of $0.48–$0.50 and $19–21 million, respectively.
The post-bankruptcy OPI management arrangement matched the preview’s stated terms: a five-year agreement with a flat $14 million annual business management fee for the first two years.
Liquidity was broadly in line with the preview’s approximately $133 million estimate: RMR reported over $130 million in total liquidity.

surprises.description: Revenue of roughly $104.7 million beat the preview’s $93.3 million consensus estimate by about 12%, though it was below the preview’s $108 million base-case scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 revenue was roughly $104.7 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue: “$93.3M”; the preview’s base scenario listed “Revenue $108M.”

surprises.description: Realized oil pricing was about $95.45 per barrel, above the preview’s roughly $92 expectation and well above its $88 level of concern for a widening differential.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Realized oil pricing rose 38% to approximately $95.45 per barrel.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said applying the prior-quarter gap to the peer price gave “about $92,” and flagged “anything below $88” as a sign of differential widening.

surprises.description: Q2 production came in slightly below the preview’s company guidance: total sales averaged 19,990 BOE/day versus 20,200 BOE/day, and oil sales were 12,683 barrels/day versus 12,950 barrels/day.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total BOE sales averaged 19,990 BOE/day”; oil sales were “12,683 barrels/day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company guidance of “12,950 Bo/d (Q2)” for oil and “20,200 Boe/d (Q2)” for total production.

surprises.description: Ring raised its full-year 2026 capital-spending outlook to $158–$178 million from the preview’s $115 million guide, a substantial increase as the company accelerates infrastructure investment in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 capital spending guidance was increased to $158-$178 million, with $80-$100 million planned for the second half to accelerate development infrastructure investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “$115M (FY)” capex guidance and asked whether management would “keep capex discipline.”

surprises.description: Management’s second-half oil guidance implies a modest increase over the preview’s Q3 and Q4 expectations, while the company also lowered its LOE outlook midpoint by about 2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Second-half 2026 oil volume guidance” was raised to “13,000-13,950 barrels/day (midpoint up ~2%)” and LOE guidance was lowered to “$10.00-$10.60 per BOE (midpoint down ~2%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q3 oil guidance of “13,250 Bo/d,” Q4 of “13,300 Bo/d,” and Q2 LOE guidance of “$10.55.”

surprises.description: The initial 2027 outlook pairs about 10% midpoint volume growth with roughly 10% lower midpoint capital spending than the newly raised 2026 outlook, a stronger growth-and-spending profile than the preview had specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Initial 2027 guidance projects BOE volumes of 21,500-23,500/day (midpoint growth ~10% over 2026) with capital spending of $135-$165 million, a ~10% midpoint reduction versus 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “the 2027 capital signal” as a key question and asked whether management would “keep capex discipline and pushes toward the 1.25x leverage target, or adds activity,” but gave no 2027 figures.

surprises.description: The call put leverage at about 1.7x, below the preview’s roughly 2.0x current estimate, and management said it could approach the 1.25x target as early as Q1 2027; non-core asset-sale proceeds would also go to debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: The equity proceeds reduced debt to “~$360 million” and lowered leverage to “~1.7x”; management expects leverage to fall toward its “1.25x target” and plans to direct non-core asset sale proceeds to debt reduction.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “about 2.0x TTM today” and framed continued debt reduction toward the 1.25x target as a key question.

surprises.description: The company disclosed expected 2027 drilling and completion savings from infrastructure investments and longer laterals, a quantified cost reduction not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The investments and longer laterals are expected to cut costs by “at least $7.5 million across the planned 20-30 wells in 2027,” assuming “$50-$100 per lateral foot savings.”

surprises.description: Oil hedge coverage for the rest of 2026 was close to the preview’s expected level, but the call indicated lower hedge coverage in 2027, leaving more exposure to potential price upside than the preview had quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: About “70% of oil” is hedged for the remainder of 2026, while hedged exposure “loosens to ~60-64% in 2027, providing more upside participation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Ring had hedged “about 72% of 2026 oil volumes” and raised possible hedge restructuring as a question; it gave no 2027 coverage level.

in_line: Remainder-of-2026 oil hedge coverage was broadly in line with the preview’s estimate: the call reported about 70% hedged versus the preview’s roughly 72%.

surprises.description: DXP reported Q2 sales of $576.5 million, $33.5 million above the preview’s $543 million consensus. That was also essentially the result implied by the preview’s calculation for holding April’s sales-per-day pace, so the beat was against consensus rather than against that rate-hold scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total sales grew 15.6% year-over-year to $576.5 million, with organic sales up 11.1% and acquisitions contributing $49.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $543.0M”; the preview also said, “Holding that pace all quarter implies roughly $576M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $70.4 million versus the preview’s estimate of about $62 million, and its 12.2% margin was a record. The preview highlighted concern about profitability and corporate expense, but did not forecast an EBITDA margin this high.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $70.4 million with margins expanding to a record 12.2%, up from 11.5% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$62M (est.)”; the preview also said to watch “Gross margin and corporate expense” because “operating margin fell” in Q1.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $1.76, above the preview’s $1.59 consensus by $0.17. This exceeded the preview’s base-case EPS range, though it was just below the stated bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS rose to $1.76 from $1.43 in Q2 2025, with net income increasing to $28.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS $1.59”; the preview’s base scenario was “$1.60–1.70” and bull scenario was “$1.78–1.92.”

surprises.description: DXP completed four acquisitions in the first half, plus the Mico Limited deal to establish a Canadian water presence, exceeding the preview’s expectation of one or two acquisitions before quarter end. The preview did not anticipate the Canadian beachhead.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DXP completed four acquisitions in the first half for $135.6 million total consideration, plus the Mico Limited deal (funded with cash and stock) to establish a DXP Water beachhead in Canada.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided to one or two acquisitions before quarter end.”

surprises.description: First-half free cash flow was $56 million, versus negative $8.6 million in the year-earlier period, while first-half CapEx fell to $5.9 million from $30.3 million. The preview flagged cash conversion and working capital as important, but gave no forecast for either free cash flow or CapEx.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half 2026 free cash flow reached $56 million, a sharp reversal from negative $8.6 million in the prior year period”; “CapEx fell dramatically to $5.9 million for the first half of 2026 versus $30.3 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Water streak and FCF. Q1 was the 14th straight quarter of sequential water growth. FCF conversion and working capital ... matter because M&A absorbed 95% of year-to-date capital deployment.”

surprises.description: DXP Water nearly doubled first-half sales year over year, a pace the preview did not quantify or specifically anticipate; it had focused on whether the sequential-growth streak would continue. The water and wastewater mix was also approaching 70% of IPS sales, supporting higher margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DXP Water posted its 15th consecutive quarter of sequential growth, reaching $97.3 million in Q2 and nearly doubling year-over-year to $175.5 million for the first half”; “Water and wastewater is now approaching 70% of IPS segment sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Water streak and FCF”; “Q1 was the 14th straight quarter of sequential water growth.”

surprises.description: DXP’s secured leverage ratio was 2.31x, below the preview’s 2.6x reference point, and S&P Global upgraded its issuer rating from B to B+. The preview highlighted leverage as something to monitor but did not anticipate a credit-rating upgrade.
surprises.fact_evidence: “S&P Global upgraded DXP's issuer credit rating to B+ from B”; the company reported “a secured leverage ratio of 2.31x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch secured leverage against the 2.6x base.”

in_line: DXP Water continued its sequential-growth streak, reaching a 15th consecutive quarter, consistent with the preview’s focus on whether the streak would continue.

surprises.description: U-Haul reported UHAL.B EPS of $0.63, below the preview’s $0.80 base-case estimate. The result was still within the preview’s unusually wide $0.54–$0.87 consensus range, so the miss is against the base case rather than a clear consensus threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 earnings fell to $123 million ($0.63 per nonvoting share) from $142 million ($0.73 per share) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (50%) … EPS (UHAL.B) ~$0.80”; the preview also reported consensus estimates of “$0.54 / $0.75 / $0.87 (sources disagree).”

surprises.description: Equipment-rental revenue grew about 2.7% ($29 million on the prior-year $1,058.3 million base), below the preview’s 3.5% base-case growth and management’s 4.5%–5% target. Growth across both In-Town and one-way markets was positive, but the overall pace fell short of those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Equipment rental revenues rose $29 million year-over-year with transaction and revenue growth across both In-Town and one-way markets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed “Rental +3.5%”; it also said management “targets a return to 4.5% to 5%.”

surprises.description: Moving and Storage costs rose enough to reduce adjusted EBITDA margin by just over 1.5%, an unexpected pressure not called out in the preview. Freight and shipping costs are expected to remain a headwind through the rest of the fiscal year, even though management expects them to peak in July.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Moving and storage operating expenses rose $55 million, cutting EBITDA margin by just over 1.5%”; roughly “$22.5 million” was from higher freight and shipping costs, which are “expected to peak in July and remain a headwind through the rest of the fiscal year.”

surprises.description: Rental-equipment depreciation increased $13.5 million, rather than being near flat or declining as the preview said was needed. The late-quarter increase was only $800,000 after April, however, and management said no further per-unit increases are expected next year, tempering the miss and supporting the view that the headwind is subsiding.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fleet depreciation increased $13.5 million for the quarter, but only $800,000 came after April”; cargo-van depreciation-driven headwinds are subsiding, with “no further per-unit increases expected next year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 growth needs to be near zero or negative.”

surprises.description: Equipment disposals swung to a $1.9 million gain instead of the losses the preview expected, substantially better than its benchmark of losses under about $15 million. Management cautioned that the strong resale market appears temporary, so the improvement may not persist and could lead the company to hold units longer.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Losses on disposal of retired rental equipment improved by $24 million year-over-year, resulting in a $1.9 million gain”; management said the strong Q1 resale market “appears temporary” and may prompt holding units longer.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Losses under about $15M would support the story.”

surprises.description: The company had already repurchased about $48 million of stock through June and roughly $50 million more since quarter-end, exceeding the preview’s concern that zero Q1 repurchases would disappoint. The preview expected buybacks to start but did not anticipate this reported pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Under the $350 million buyback program, the company repurchased about $48 million in stock through June and roughly $50 million more since quarter-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Zero repurchases in Q1 would be a notable disappointment”; the base case assumed “buyback starts.”

surprises.description: New storage customer rates rose about 2.5% while departing-customer rates fell just under 2%, an unusually favorable spread compared with peers. The preview highlighted occupancy and storage performance but did not anticipate this pricing pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New customer storage rental rates rose about 2.5% year-over-year while departing customer rates fell just under 2%, an unusual positive spread versus industry peers seeing move-in rates below move-out rates.”

in_line: Same-store occupancy built sequentially from 86.1% in Q4 FY2026 to 88.3% in Q1, consistent with the preview’s expectation that occupancy would build off 86.1%, although it remained 456 basis points below the prior-year quarter.

surprises.description: ConocoPhillips reported Q2 adjusted EPS of $3.24, above the preview’s consensus estimates of $2.88–$2.96 by roughly 9%–13%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2… delivered $3.24 in adjusted EPS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS: $2.96” (Zacks), “$2.89–$2.90” (Street composite), and “$2.88” (Benzinga).

surprises.description: Q2 production exceeded the top of the 2.19–2.22 MMBOED guidance range, despite that range excluding Qatar. The preview identified restoring Qatar volumes as a potential bull trigger; the Q3 outlook also assumes a Qatar ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 production reached 2,248,000 boe/d, above the high end of guidance, driven by a record Permian output of 920,000 boe/d”; Q3 guidance “assumes a Qatar ramp.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 production 2.19–2.22 MMBOED, excluding Qatar”; “Folding Qatar back in would be the cleanest bull trigger.”

surprises.description: The buyback rose to $2 billion, double Q1’s amount and above the preview’s base-case expectation of roughly $1.0–$1.25 billion. Total Q2 distributions were $3 billion, within the preview’s expected $2.9–$3.2 billion range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 shareholder distributions rose to $3 billion, including a doubling of buybacks to $2 billion plus $1 billion in dividends.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “At around $100 oil, the 45%-of-CFO framework implies about $2.9–3.2B of returns versus $2.0B in Q1”; base case: “buyback held near $1.0–1.25B.”

surprises.description: CEO Ryan Lance will retire effective September 1, with Andy O'Brien taking over as President and CEO and Konnie Haynes-Welsh becoming CFO. The preview did not flag a leadership transition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CEO Ryan Lance will retire effective September 1 after 14 years, with CFO/Strategy head Andy O'Brien becoming President and CEO and Konnie Haynes-Welsh joining as the new CFO.”

surprises.description: Management said the Kirkuk acquisition would cost $300–500 million and that the new Middle East positions would be largely self-funding, addressing the preview’s open question about how the Iraq commitment would fit within the capital plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Kirkuk acquisition is expected to cost “$300–500 million” at year-end close; the new Iraq and Syria entries are “expected to be largely self-funding” and add upside beyond the 2029 free-cash-flow target.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has not yet addressed how this is funded within the capex envelope”; the bear scenario included “Iraq commitments framed as incremental to capex.”

surprises.description: The company also announced a Syria entry, which was not among the Iraq-related developments identified in the preview, and described the new Middle East positions as having roughly $30/bbl cost of supply.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New Middle East entries in Iraq (Kirkuk) and Syria feature ~$30/bbl cost of supply.”

surprises.description: ConocoPhillips said it had reached its $5 billion disposition target ahead of schedule, including $1.7 billion of noncore Lower 48 asset sales in July; the preview did not identify this target or its timing as an issue to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $5 billion disposition target was achieved ahead of schedule, including $1.7 billion of noncore Lower 48 asset sales in July.”

surprises.description: The commercial LNG portfolio expanded to 12 MTPA through two new 1 MTPA offtake deals, one in Indonesia and one on the U.S. Gulf Coast. The preview did not anticipate these deals or the associated margin sensitivity estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The commercial LNG portfolio grew to 12 MTPA via two new 1 MTPA offtake deals (Indonesia and U.S. Gulf Coast),” with “roughly $200 million of cash flow per $1/MMBtu of margin on 5 MTPA.”

in_line: Total Q2 shareholder distributions were $3 billion, within the preview’s expected $2.9–$3.2 billion range, and management reiterated a 45% of CFO target for the full year.

surprises.description: Sempra reported adjusted EPS of $1.16, well above the preview’s $1.00–$1.01 consensus range and even slightly above its $1.08–$1.15 bull scenario. The preview’s base case was calibrated around $1.00–$1.04.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EPS of $1.16 ($762 million) … up from $0.89 ($583 million) in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: $1.01 (Zacks) or $1.00 (Barchart/Yahoo)”; base scenario: “Adj. EPS $1.00–$1.04”; bull scenario: “Adj. EPS $1.08–$1.15.”

surprises.description: Sempra Texas earnings rose $138 million year over year, materially more than the preview’s model of about $295 million and 42% growth implied. The call also confirmed a roughly $50 million Oncor rate-settlement catch-up benefit in Q2, rather than deferring that benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sempra Texas earnings rose $138 million year-over-year, including a favorable ~$50 million catch-up benefit from Oncor's base rate settlement approved in April 2026 that related to Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My model puts Texas near $295M, up about 42% Y/Y”; “The key question is whether Sempra booked the full catch-up in Q2 or deferred part of it.”

surprises.description: The batch-zero load opportunity had concrete demand already on the system: about 8 GW of the 44 GW identified as eligible was connected and ramping. The preview discussed a large substantiated-load pipeline, but did not indicate that this portion was already connected and moving toward full utilization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately 8 gigawatts of the 44 GW batch zero load is already connected to Oncor's system and ramping toward full utilization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Oncor's regional plan shows 127 GW of substantiated load” and “Management has flagged about $9B of incremental Texas opportunity above the $65B plan.”

surprises.description: The batch-zero process was delayed, with ERCOT seeking a good-cause exception at the August 20 PUC meeting and capital visibility not expected until later in 2027. The preview presented a formal Texas capital-plan raise as a possible catalyst but did not flag this delay to visibility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Governor Abbott's August 3 letter calling for comprehensive audits of data centers has delayed the batch zero timeline”; “batch-related capital visibility not expected until later in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A formal capital plan raise would be a re-rating catalyst.”

surprises.description: ECA LNG Phase 1 sustained equipment damage, pushing substantial completion into Q4 2026. The preview did not flag a project delay; Port Arthur LNG Phases 1 and 2 were still reported on time and on budget.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ECA LNG Phase 1 suffered damage to equipment connected to its mixed refrigerant compressors, pushing substantial completion into Q4 2026.”

surprises.description: Management described a pronounced Texas tilt in the long-term growth mix: Texas is targeted to exceed 60% of rate base by 2030, with utility-platform growth of about 11% annually, or closer to 13% including Oncor upside, versus about 5% growth in California. The preview discussed Texas opportunities and California overhang but did not provide or anticipate this quantified growth split.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sempra targets Texas comprising over 60% of total rate base by 2030, with utility platform growing ~11% annually (closer to 13% including Oncor upside) while California rate base grows at about 5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Texas capital plan and load growth” and “California overhang,” but gave no comparable rate-base growth targets.

in_line: Sempra reaffirmed FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $4.80–$5.30 and FY2027 guidance of $5.10–$5.70, as the preview’s base case expected a flat reaffirmation.

The SI Partners sale remained on track for a Q3 close, consistent with the preview’s expected timing; the transaction is expected to displace the need for common equity in the base capital plan, consistent with the preview’s expectation of no block equity issuance through 2030.

The roughly $10 billion of incremental Oncor capital opportunities is broadly in line with the preview’s approximately $9 billion estimate, though the call described a different base-plan figure and timeframe.

surprises.description: DCO reported Q2 revenue of $224.5 million, about 4–5% above the preview’s roughly $214–215 million expectation. The preview identified revenue as the key number to watch, and the result was well above its base-case range of $214–217 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached a record $224.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anchor on revenue versus about $214M”; the base case was “Revenue of $214–217M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $1.18, roughly 20% above the preview’s $0.97–$0.98 consensus. The call also said results benefited from a one-time executive compensation clawback, a qualification to the strength of the earnings result that the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS increased to $1.18 from $0.90, though results benefited from a one-time executive compensation clawback tied to an earlier restatement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS | $0.97–$0.98.”

surprises.description: Missile revenue surged 68% in the quarter, while RPO reached a record $1.16 billion with 1.4x quarterly book-to-bill. The preview expected framework agreements to lift missile and space revenue toward late 2026 and early 2027, but did not anticipate this degree of current-quarter growth and bookings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The missile business surged 68% year-over-year in Q2”; “Remaining performance obligations hit a record $1.16 billion”; and book-to-bill was “1.4x in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The RTX and Lockheed framework agreements are expected to lift revenue toward end-2026 and early 2027. Watch for RPO growth as evidence.”

surprises.description: Commercial Aerospace grew 16% and received an incremental 737MAX aftermarket retrofit order expected to support revenue for several years, with potential future line-fit business. The preview said it had limited segment detail and did not flag this order.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial Aerospace revenue grew 16% to $89 million, aided by an incremental 737MAX aftermarket retrofit order expected to sustain revenue for several years with future line-fit potential.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “I did not open the Q1 release or call transcript in full, so segment and commercial-aero detail is limited to headline figures.”

surprises.description: Management said some second-half production and revenue had been pulled into the first half, and now expects H2 growth to moderate to low-to-mid single digits. Full-year mid-to-high single-digit growth guidance was reiterated, but the timing shift and softer H2 cadence were not flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management pulled forward some second-half production and revenue into the first half, expecting H2 growth to moderate to low-to-mid single digits while reiterating full-year guidance of mid-to-high single-digit revenue growth.”

surprises.description: Engineered product content had reached 23% of trailing-12-month revenue, up from 15% in 2022, and management identified the mix shift as an ongoing margin driver. The preview focused on margins but did not identify this source of margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engineered product content reached 23% of trailing 12-month revenue, up from 15% in 2022,” and management identified the mix shift as “a key ongoing margin driver.”

surprises.description: DCO reported $38.3 million of year-to-date free cash flow and $410 million of available liquidity, which management said positioned it for acquisitions. The preview noted acquisition potential as something to watch but supplied no expectation for cash generation or liquidity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated year-to-date free cash flow of $38.3 million (127% conversion of adjusted net income) and held $410 million in available liquidity, positioning it for acquisitions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Look for specific bookings or a deal, and for framing ahead of the September 17 Investor Day.”

surprises.description: Management said it would unveil a Vision 2032 strategy at the September 17 Investor Day. The preview anticipated the Investor Day and referenced Vision 2027 targets, but did not mention a new Vision 2032 plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A Vision 2032 strategy [is] to be unveiled at a September 17 Investor Day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Investor Day on September 17, 2026”; the preview discussed “VISION 2027 targets.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA margin was 17.1%, broadly in line with the preview’s approximate 17% reference point.
Full-year revenue growth guidance was reiterated at mid-to-high single digits, matching the guidance wording the preview said would be neutral.
The September 17 Investor Day remained on the calendar, as the preview expected.

surprises.description: Oxy reported adjusted EPS of $2.40, well above the preview’s $1.84–$1.88 consensus cluster and even above its $2.10–$2.25 bull scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 delivered adjusted EPS of $2.40”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS ... $1.84 (TipRanks), $1.88 / $1.95–$1.96 (Nasdaq, StockStory), $1.66 (Benzinga)” and the bull scenario was “$2.10–2.25.”

surprises.description: Midstream and marketing earnings reached $960 million, far above the preview’s $350–$550 million quarterly guidance range; Oxy also raised full-year segment guidance by $300 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Midstream and marketing set a record with ~$960 million in adjusted earnings, more than double guidance midpoint, prompting a $300 million increase to full-year segment guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Midstream & marketing pre-tax: $350 – $550M” for Q2 and “FY26 midstream pre-tax: $1.0 – $1.2B.”

surprises.description: Oxy announced a new goal of adding more than $4 billion in annual sustainable cash flow by 2030 versus 2025, with about half of the improvement expected by 2027. The preview did not flag a comparable multi-year cash-flow plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A plan to add over $4 billion of annual sustainable cash flow by 2030 versus 2025 (~95% annualized growth), with ~85% achievable even at much lower oil prices and no production growth required”; “roughly $2 billion (about 50%) ... captured between 2026 and 2027.”

surprises.description: The company raised its quarterly dividend 8% to $0.28 per share, a concrete increase beyond the preview’s stated $0.26 quarterly dividend and its focus on whether management would provide a broader capital-return framework.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board approved an 8% increase to the quarterly dividend to $0.28 per share, enabled by structural interest savings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dividend $0.26 per quarter, raised 8% after Q4 2025”; the preview highlighted “Capital-return framework” as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Production was at the very top of the Q2 guidance range, 23,000 BOE/day above its midpoint, rather than near the preview’s base-case expectation of 1.405–1.420 million BOE/day.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 production averaged 1.43 million BOE/day, exceeding the guidance midpoint by 23,000 BOE/day, driven by Permian and Gulf of America strength offsetting Middle East disruptions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The Q2 guidance range was “1,390 – 1,430” Mboed; the base scenario expected “Production about 1,405–1,420.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 debt could fall to $10.5–$11.5 billion, but Oxy ended at $11.8 billion. It still reduced principal debt substantially and reported large interest savings, so the gap to the estimate was modest against a positive deleveraging result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Occidental reduced principal debt by $1.5 billion to $11.8 billion” and lowered its “go-forward annual interest run rate to ~$760 million, about $630 million below 2025 levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 free cash flow could run $2.5–3.4B at about $100 oil, which could take principal debt to $10.5–11.5B. This is an estimate, not a reported figure.”

surprises.description: Oxy said buybacks would remain opportunistic and lower priority, with debt reduction to $10 billion and cash for the 2029 preferred-equity redemption taking precedence. That was more specific and more restrained on repurchases than the preview’s open question about a possible capital-return framework.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Buybacks will remain opportunistic and a lower priority,” while capital allocation prioritizes “reducing principal debt to a $10 billion milestone and building cash ahead of the ~$700 million preferred equity redemption in August 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for watching for “Any target payout, authorized repurchase size, or preferred-redemption commentary” and described “opportunistic” capital-return language as its base scenario.

surprises.description: Oxy gave a 2027 capital-spending starting point of $5.9 billion, including $5.0–$5.1 billion of sustaining capital, implying roughly flat production versus 2026; the preview discussed only FY26 capex and did not provide a 2027 spending or production outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “2027 capital spending starting point is $5.9 billion (~$5.0-5.1 billion sustaining) implying roughly flat production versus 2026, while Stratos LCV capital of ~$400 million rolls off beginning next year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 capex of “$5.5 – $5.9B” and a base scenario with “FY guide unchanged”; it gave no 2027 outlook.

surprises.description: Oxy laid out a plan to reduce its total base decline rate from about 25% to 20% by 2030 through advanced recovery projects, supporting a $900 million reduction in sustaining capital. The preview did not anticipate this operating-efficiency target or capital reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advanced recovery projects are targeted to lower the total base decline rate from ~25% to ~20% by 2030, helping cut sustaining capital by $900 million (from $5.4 billion to $4.5 billion).”

in_line: Q2 free cash flow was about $3 billion before working capital, within the preview’s estimated $2.5–$3.4 billion range at about $100 oil.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.99, well above the preview's $0.68 consensus estimate. The beat was much larger than the revenue beat, with the quarter's unusually low tax rate contributing to earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS reached $0.99” and the effective tax rate “fell to 11.2%.”

surprises.description: Revenue reached $66.3 million, about 11% above the preview's $59.9 million consensus. Product sales also came in above the preview's roughly $48 million implied estimate, at $53.8 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total net revenue rose 32.3% year-over-year to $66.3 million”; “Product sales increased 40% to $53.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net revenue | $59.9M”; the preview said consensus appeared to model “about $48M of product sales.”

surprises.description: Workforce housing shipments fell far short of the roughly 300 units implied by consensus and the preview's discussion of management's 200–300-unit range: the company shipped only 113 units on the 380-unit contract. Deliveries are expected to continue through 2026, but the reported quarter was well below the anticipated shipment pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Shipping 113 units this quarter,” with “a remaining backlog of 267 units” and deliveries expected to continue throughout 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided 200–300 units on the Q1 call, so consensus sits at the top of that range”; the preview also said consensus implied “about 300 workforce housing units.”

surprises.description: First-half operating cash flow and cash were substantially stronger than the preview's liquidity snapshot suggested. Operating cash flow more than doubled, and cash rose to $29 million versus the preview's $14.1 million figure, partly helped by customer deposits and a nonrefundable workforce-housing advance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow more than doubled to $24.4 million in the first half from $11 million a year ago”; cash was “$29 million” and customer deposits rose $10.7 million, including “a $7.1 million nonrefundable advance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash is $14.1M, with a nearly undrawn $50M revolver.”

surprises.description: The quarter benefited from an 11.2% effective tax rate, but management said the rate should move toward 21% in the second half after the energy-efficient home credit terminated. The preview did not flag this near-term tax benefit or the subsequent tax-rate headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The effective tax rate fell to 11.2% from 17.3%” due to the Section 45L credit and a reversal of uncertain tax positions; management expects it to move “toward the 21% statutory rate in the second half.”

surprises.description: Dealer inventory finance sales continued to contract sharply, falling about 74%; the preview had highlighted the decline as a core-business risk, but the reported offset came from workforce housing and commercial park sales rather than the retail and direct growth it asked investors to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory finance sales dropped about $10.1 million or 74%,” partially offset by workforce housing and commercial park sales.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether retail and direct growth offset the dealer inventory-finance decline.”

surprises.description: The matured $48.6 million mobile home park note was not repaid in full: the borrower made only a $2 million paydown and received an 18-month interest-only forbearance. Added collateral and a larger guarantee, along with management's expectation of no loss, mitigate the concern, but the outcome is a workout rather than full repayment.
surprises.fact_evidence: The note “was not repaid in full,” prompting “a $2 million paydown, an 18-month interest-only forbearance, added collateral and increased guarantee,” with management “expecting no loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $48.6M bridge note matured July 2026 at 7.9%. Q1 commentary said partial repayment and renewal were under negotiation.”

surprises.description: Management identified the July 21 ROAD to Housing Act as favorable because it removes the permanent-chassis requirement and raises FHA loan limits. The preview did not identify this policy change as a potential demand catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “flagged the July 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act—which eliminates the permanent chassis requirement and raises FHA loan limits—as favorable.”

surprises.description: Management pointed to data center construction as a new potential source of workforce-housing demand, a demand driver not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “cited data center construction as a new source of potential workforce housing demand.”

in_line: Loan-portfolio interest income was $11.5 million, roughly in line with the preview's assumption of about $11.5 million.

surprises.description: Gross margin was expected to be around 37.5%, with a print above 38% seen as an early sign of improvement. WFCF reported 40.6%, up from 37.5%, and said efficiencies across all three segments drove the expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit grew 9% year-over-year to $2.7 million, with gross margin expanding to 40.6% from 37.5%, driven by cost efficiencies across all three business segments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A print above 38% would be the cleanest sign that cost inflation is being absorbed.”

surprises.description: The preview expected RaiseWell disclosure but said the most bullish update would be a dollar figure or another retailer beyond Whole Foods. WFCF reported that Whole Foods adopted the new program and that more than 270,000 cattle are enrolled, providing concrete scale though not a dollar figure or a new retailer.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Whole Foods Market adopted the new RaiseWell Certified program for its beef supply, resulting in more than 270,000 head of cattle now enrolled by participating ranchers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any dollar figure or a second named retailer beyond Whole Foods would be the most bullish disclosure available.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated about a $68,000 pre-tax unrealized digital-asset loss for the quarter. The call cited a $240,000 negative swing from non-cash digital-asset fair-value changes as a reason net income fell; the call describes a swing, not necessarily the quarter’s standalone loss, but the reported earnings drag was larger than the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net income was hurt by “a $240,000 negative swing from non-cash fair market value changes in digital assets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bitcoin fell about 14% in the quarter, implying roughly a $68K pre-tax unrealized loss.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged buyback pace and said an accelerated repurchase would be notable. WFCF bought approximately 65,000 shares in Q2, well above the 24,469 shares it bought in Q1, indicating a faster pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased approximately 65,000 shares in Q2 and nearly 89,500 shares year-to-date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “An accelerated repurchase would signal that management sees the stock as mispriced.”

surprises.description: After roughly three years without a transaction, management said it is renewing its focus on M&A and plans to file a shelf registration within the next year. The preview did not anticipate this shift, although management said no deals are imminent.
surprises.fact_evidence: “After a roughly three-year pause since its last transaction, management is renewing its focus on M&A and plans to file a shelf registration within the next year, though no deals are imminent.”

in_line: Total revenue of $6.6 million was within the preview’s $6.4–$6.6 million base scenario; verification and certification revenue of $5.4 million met the preview’s roughly $5.4 million watch level.
EPS of $0.08 was within the preview’s $0.08–$0.10 base-case range, despite being below the prior-year $0.11.

The flagship Beef business remained pressured by fewer cattle and high beef prices, consistent with the preview’s concerns about the cattle cycle and smaller herd size. The provided call facts do not state whether management changed its expectation of stabilization later in 2026.

surprises.description: Royal Gold paid down $200 million of its revolver during Q2, another $75 million in July, and planned a further $100 million payment in mid-August. That pulls substantial repayment forward from the preview’s expectation of full repayment in Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “repaid $200 million on its revolver in Q2, plus a further $75 million in July and a planned $100 million in mid-August,” while expecting to “fully repay the outstanding balance by Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$400M was outstanding at June 30 against a commitment to repay in Q4.”

surprises.description: Copper and other metals were trending around or above the top end of guidance, despite copper being identified as the least certain volume outlook. The call attributed the strength largely to the Antamina NPI royalty, which generated $26 million in the first half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Copper and other metals are trending around or above the top end of guidance ranges,” driven largely by Antamina NPI royalty revenue of “$26 million in the first half versus $16-17 million annually in 2023-2024.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Copper looks least certain.”

surprises.description: Royal Gold funded $70 million for Hod Maden in Q2, despite the preview’s expectation that near-term capital calls would be low and not significant. The stake reduction also lowered the remaining base CapEx commitment to roughly $65 million, partly offsetting the near-term cash outlay.
surprises.fact_evidence: Royal Gold reduced its Hod Maden interest from 30% to 15% and, “after funding $70 million in Q2,” had its remaining base CapEx commitment reduced to roughly $65 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had said Hod Maden near-term capital calls would be “relatively low and not significant.”

surprises.description: Relief Canyon stream ounces were delivered earlier than originally scheduled, adding about $22 million of revenue this quarter and bringing this year’s delivered ounces 1,175 above the original schedule. The preview did not flag this timing benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The advanced delivery of Relief Canyon stream ounces added approximately $22 million in incremental revenue this quarter, delivering 1,175 more ounces this year than originally scheduled.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “1,175 more ounces this year than originally scheduled.”

in_line: Revenue was $451 million, within the preview’s pre-released range of approximately $448–453 million, even though it was below the separately cited $458.9 million consensus estimate.
Adjusted EPS of $2.56 was essentially in line with the preview’s conflicting $2.57–$2.72 consensus estimates and slightly above its $2.45–$2.55 base scenario.
DD&A was $96 million, within the preview’s expected $95–99 million range.
The Hod Maden stake reduction from 30% to 15% occurred as anticipated by the preview, which said the reduction was promised in the near term.

surprises.description: AMTX reported Q2 revenue of $62.7 million, about 7% below the $67.69 million consensus that the preview flagged as the comparison for a clean beat. The result did land within the preview’s lower $60–65 million base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 20% year-over-year to $62.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Consensus” revenue was “$67.69M”; the preview also said a result near the base case would still be “a miss versus the Street.”

surprises.description: The net loss was substantially smaller than the roughly $18.3 million loss implied by consensus EPS, and also narrower than the preview’s base-case EPS range implied. The reported $9.4 million loss was less than half the consensus-implied loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $9.4 million from $23.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave consensus EPS of “-$0.26” and an “Implied net loss @ 70.4M shares” of “~-$18.3M”; its base-case EPS range was “-$0.28 to -$0.32.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA rose well beyond the preview’s near-breakeven base case, reaching positive $9.7 million. The improvement was not solely from 45Z credits: gross profit excluding those credits also improved by more than $8 million year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved by $15.5 million to a positive $9.7 million,” versus negative $5.8 million a year earlier; “excluding these credits gross profit of $13.8 million still improved by over $8 million year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case called for “adjusted EBITDA near breakeven,” while it described a positive print as the “inflection management has been describing.”

surprises.description: Despite receiving $17.6 million of net proceeds from the 45Z credit sale, AMTX ended the quarter with only $1 million of cash. That leaves liquidity weaker than the preview’s discussion of the sale proceeds might suggest, though the preview did not forecast a quarter-end cash balance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash was just $1 million at quarter-end, though the company received $17.6 million in net proceeds from selling 45Z credits on July 9.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said AMTX had “Cash $4.8M” exiting Q1 and that the July 9 credit sale was “netting about $14.5M of cash.”

surprises.description: India biodiesel revenue fell to $2.5 million in Q2, down sharply from the $10.5 million Q1 rebound, rather than showing the India ramp the preview used to support its base case. The newly secured three-month allocation is forward-looking and does not change the weak Q2 revenue figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “India biodiesel revenue fell to $2.5 million in Q2”; separately, India secured allocations for “over 18 million liters” over three months.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 India revenue “rebounded to $10.5M as OMC shipments resumed” and its base case assumed “Sequential growth from $54.6M on the India ramp.”

surprises.description: The Q2 45Z contribution was slightly above the preview’s $5–8 million base-case range, and the July sale produced more cash than the preview’s stated $14.5 million net proceeds. These are favorable differences in both the quarter’s credit contribution and the sale proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Section 45Z credits contributed $8.6 million in Q2”; AMTX “received $17.6 million in net proceeds” from the sale.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed “45Z contribution of $5–8M” and said the July 9 sale was “netting about $14.5M of cash.”

surprises.description: Management outlined additional potential 45Z value not quantified in the preview: an ethanol catch-up of $6–24 million, $12–15 million per year from CO2 reuse, and dairy RNG credits that could rise from $15.20 to over $75 per MMBtu if DOE corrects the emissions rate. These are prospective and depend on the stated updates, rather than realized Q2 earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management anticipates “$6–24 million” from ethanol with an “18-month look-back catch-up,” “$12–15 million/year” from CO2 reuse, and dairy RNG upside; the current dairy RNG credit was “$15.20 per MMBtu” at a negative 42 emissions rate, with a DOE correction toward “negative 375–420” expected to yield “over $75 per MMBtu.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on monetizing existing 45Z credits, including the July sale, but did not identify these additional quantified credit opportunities or the potential dairy RNG rate correction.

surprises.description: The call gave a more concrete debt picture than the preview’s Q1 figures: Third Eye Capital debt was described as approximately $120 million with an effective rate near 5%, and management plans further paydowns using anticipated 45Z catch-up cash. However, the call described plans, not a completed refinancing or a closed new facility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $120 million of debt with Third Eye Capital carries an effective ~5% interest rate,” and management is “planning further paydowns using anticipated 45Z catch-up cash and refinancing more expensive debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “About $247.9M” of Third Eye Capital debt “due on demand” and said balance-sheet and refinancing language was the “highest weight” issue; a “named lender, a sized facility, or a closed muni bond” was its example of meaningful specificity.

in_line: The MVR project remains on the preview’s expected later-in-2026 schedule: management now expects it to be operational by the end of 2026 and reiterated the roughly $32 million annual cash-flow benefit from cutting natural gas use by 80%. The preview had said equipment arrived in May and the timeline was “later in 2026.”

The India allocation itself was already anticipated in the preview: more than 18 million liters over three months, worth about $17 million. The surprise was the weak Q2 India revenue, not the announced future allocation.

surprises.description: MDU reported Q2 EPS of $0.10, above the preview’s $0.08 consensus and $0.09 alternative estimate. The beat was 1–2 cents, which the preview itself described as potentially noisy for a seasonal trough quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 earnings rose to $21.3 million ($0.10 per share)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) | $0.08”; “EPS (alt. mean) | $0.09”

surprises.description: Bakken East precedent agreements reached nearly 1.2 Bcf/day, well above the roughly 40% of the 1.4 Bcf/day open-season interest previously under agreement. A negotiated option could bring contracted volumes close to the full original interest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “executed precedent agreements totaling nearly 1.2 Bcf/day, with a negotiated option that could raise contracted volumes to nearly the full original binding open season interest”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Binding open season drew 1.4 Bcf/d of interest, about 40% under precedent agreements. Watch whether that share rises materially.”

surprises.description: The Bakken East FERC filing slipped from the preview’s Q3 expectation to Q4 2026 because precedent-agreement negotiations took longer. The project’s in-service dates remain unchanged, and the final investment decision is still expected before the filing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Bakken East FERC 7(c) filing has been pushed from an earlier third-quarter expectation to the fourth quarter of 2026 due to longer precedent agreement negotiations”; “Phase 1 (late 2029) and Phase 2 (late 2030) in-service dates unchanged.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management targets FID and a Section 7 application in Q3 2026.”

in_line: MDU reaffirmed FY26 EPS guidance of $0.93–$1.00, as the preview’s base scenario expected.
The signed data-center ESA tally exceeded 1 GW, in line with the preview’s expectation of about 1,010 MW; the Applied Digital agreement remains pending regulatory approval, as anticipated.
Bakken East remains incremental to the current capital program, consistent with the preview’s description of the project as incremental to the base plan.
No Bakken East financing structure was announced; financing and partnership options remain under evaluation, consistent with the preview noting that all options were open.

surprises.description: Apyx reaffirmed FY2026 revenue guidance of $59–60 million instead of raising it toward the preview’s expected $60–62 million range. The unchanged low end was also below the preview’s stated $61 million threshold for avoiding disappointment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $59.0 million to $60.0 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus positioning is for a raise to roughly $61–62M”; “Anything below $61M at the low end would likely disappoint.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $13.9 million, about 5.5% above the $13.18 million consensus estimate. It was also within the preview’s higher $13.8–14.0 million buy-side expectation, so the beat was modest against the range of expectations described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 22% year-over-year to $13.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $13.18M”; “Buy-side expectations may sit closer to $13.8–14.0M after the Q1 beat.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 63.9%, above the preview’s expected 62–63% range, despite tariffs partially offsetting the benefit from favorable segment mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to 63.9% from 62.3% year-over-year on favorable segment mix, though this was partially offset by tariffs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~62–63% (guide)”; “Gross margin at or above 62%.”

surprises.description: Apyx reported that AYON is attracting customers who have never used Renuvion, providing the new-account growth signal the preview identified as bullish after noting that about 80% of earlier AYON units went to existing customers. The call did not quantify how many new customers AYON is attracting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AYON is attracting new customers who have never used Renuvion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “It has said only that about 80% of AYON units went to existing Renuvion customers. New-account growth would be the bullish signal.”

surprises.description: Apyx received expanded FDA clearance for power liposuction on AYON and began initial shipments in June, with a full launch expected in Q3. The preview did not anticipate this launch or the associated recurring-revenue opportunity from replacement handpieces and per-case supplies.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received expanded FDA 510(k) clearance to add power liposuction to AYON and began initial commercial shipments in June 2026, with a full commercial launch expected in Q3 2026”; management expects “north of 95%” of new AYON purchasers to include power liposuction, with handpieces replaced “2-4 times per year” and roughly “$100 of tubing and canisters per case.”

surprises.description: The OEM segment declined 12% in Q2 and is expected to fall to roughly $5 million for FY2026 from $7.5 million in 2025. The preview did not discuss this segment contraction; the call characterized it as deliberate as Apyx shifts focus to surgical aesthetics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The OEM segment declined 12% to $1.5 million and is guided to fall to roughly $5.0 million for 2026 (from $7.5 million in 2025), a deliberate trend expected to continue as focus shifts to surgical aesthetics.”

surprises.description: Operating cash burn was $3.5 million, up from $1.2 million in the prior-year quarter. The preview flagged cash burn as an issue to watch but did not specify an expected Q2 cash-burn level; Apyx also said it expects sufficient liquidity into 2028.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash burn increased to $3.5 million versus $1.2 million in the prior-year quarter”; the company expects “to maintain sufficient liquidity into 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating expenses and cash burn.”

in_line: EPS of ($0.07) was within the preview’s cited consensus range of ($0.06) to ($0.08).
FY2026 gross-margin guidance of 62%–63% and the operating-expense cap of $45 million were reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s account of the existing guidance.

surprises.description: ACV plus royalties reached $99.5 million, above the $99 million guidance ceiling and roughly $97 million consensus. The preview treated $99 million or more as a bullish outcome, so this was a positive beat against the stated guide and consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 annual contract value plus royalties reached a record $99.5 million, up 44% year-over-year, exceeding the top end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ACV + Royalties” company guidance was “$95.0M – $99.0M” and consensus was “~$97M”; the preview also listed “ACV + Royalties ≥ $99M” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Revenue was $24.1 million, exceeding both the $24.0 million guidance ceiling and the preview’s consensus estimates of $23.48–$23.71 million. The beat was modest relative to those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue was $24.1 million, up 46% year-over-year and above the top-end of the guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue” company guidance was “$23.0M – $24.0M”; consensus was “$23.48M” or “$23.71M.”

surprises.description: The non-GAAP operating loss was $4.6 million, worse than the preview’s expected $2.0–$3.0 million guidance range and roughly $2.5 million consensus. Management attributed pressure in part to an unanticipated $1.7 million French employer payroll-tax charge tied to RSU vesting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating loss was $4.6 million ... pressured by $1.7 million in unexpected French employer payroll taxes tied to RSU vesting amid a rising stock price.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP op. loss” company guidance was “$(2.0)M – $(3.0)M” and consensus was “~$(2.5)M.”

surprises.description: Although trailing 12-month royalties reached a record and grew 65%, royalties dipped slightly sequentially because of one customer’s supply-chain issues. That was a setback against the preview’s bullish scenario of a royalty step-up.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month royalties hit a record $8.6 million, growing 65% year-over-year, though royalties showed a slight sequential dip due to a customer's supply chain issues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull scenario cited “Hyperscaler expansion and royalty step-up”; it also said to watch “the quarterly royalty dollar figure.”

surprises.description: The company completed an ATM offering that raised about $72 million net, a substantial financing event not anticipated in the preview. It materially increased cash, though issuing shares also means dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its ATM program raising ~$72 million in net proceeds at an average price over $35, ending the quarter with $123 million in cash and no debt.”

in_line: FY2026 revenue guidance was raised to $95–$98 million, matching the preview’s bull-case range and exceeding its stated catalyst threshold of at least a $94 million midpoint.
Management’s expectation of first non-GAAP operating profit as early as Q4 2026 was consistent with the preview’s expectation that Q4 profitability would be reaffirmed.
The CFO transition was already noted in the preview: Saurabh Sinha was expected to succeed Nick Hawkins effective September 8, 2026.

surprises.description: A new U.S. technology customer committed more than $600 million over four years, and total multiyear cloud infrastructure commitments signed this year exceeded $2.8 billion. Management said the commitments support low-teens overall revenue growth in 2027, accelerating from single-digit growth in 2026, although the new deal is not expected to contribute materially in 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new U.S.-based technology company committed over $600 million over 4 years”; “Total multiyear cloud infrastructure services commitments signed this year now exceed $2.8 billion,” driving guidance for “low teens in 2027 from single digits in 2026.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue reached $1.1 billion, slightly above the $1.091 billion consensus and at the top of the company's guidance range. The beat was modest relative to the estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $1.1 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue was “$1,091M”; company guidance was “$1,075M – $1,100M.”

surprises.description: Security revenue outperformed the preview's estimate, growing 10% to $604 million versus an expected $597.7 million and 8.3% growth. Management also said the full security portfolio is expected to exceed $2.4 billion for the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Security revenue grew 10% year-over-year to $604 million,” and the full portfolio is expected to exceed “$2.4 billion in revenue for the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “Security at or above $597.7M (+8.3%).”

surprises.description: CIS revenue was below the preview's quarterly threshold: $99 million versus an expected $103.8 million, with growth of 39% year over year. That missed the preview's stated Q2 level to watch, though it does not establish whether the separate full-year growth expectation was met.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cloud Infrastructure Services (CIS) revenue reached $99 million, up 39% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's checklist said “CIS at or above $103.8M.”

surprises.description: Despite the Q2 CIS shortfall, management expects the business to accelerate meaningfully in Q4 and said all GPU capacity is currently sold out. The preview highlighted GPU delivery timing but did not anticipate this sold-out-capacity statement or Q4 acceleration outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: CIS “is expected to meaningfully accelerate in Q4 with all GPU capacity currently completely sold out.”

surprises.description: The full-year CapEx outlook of about 40% of revenue remained within the preview's expected 40%–42% range, but Q3 CapEx is projected at 43%–46% of revenue. GPU shipments that slipped from Q2 into July and plans for up to $500 million of additional GPU CapEx, mostly in early 2027, point to a heavier near-term and subsequent investment load than the preview spelled out.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 CapEx” is guided to “approximately 40% of revenue,” while Q3 is “$475-$525 million (43-46% of revenue)” due to GPU build-outs and shipments that slipped into July; management also plans “up to $500 million in additional GPU CapEx (mostly hitting early 2027).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected FY26 CapEx of “40% – 42% of revenue” and flagged “Capex at or below 42% of revenue.”

surprises.description: Akamai is temporarily pausing share repurchases to fund its CIS pipeline, despite having spent about $616 million buying back roughly 5 million shares year to date. The preview discussed buybacks as a contributor to EPS but did not anticipate the pause.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is temporarily pausing share repurchases to reallocate capital to its high-growth CIS pipeline” after spending “approximately $616 million buying back roughly 5 million shares year-to-date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted the company “repurchased 2,476,298 shares at $141.34” and estimated a Q2 per-share contribution from “interest income and a lower share count.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that large CIS contracts have take-or-pay commitments and specified cash gross margins in the mid-60s to mid-70s and operating margins from the low-to-mid 20s up to the low 30s. The preview discussed margin pressure from the AI build but did not provide expectations for the margins or commitment structure of these contracts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Large-scale CIS contracts are structured with take-or-pay commitments” and deliver “non-GAAP cash gross margins from mid-60s to mid-70s” and “non-GAAP operating margins ranging from low-to-mid 20s up to low 30s.”

in_line: Non-GAAP EPS was $1.59, essentially in line with the preview's $1.58 consensus estimate.
The approximately 40% FY26 CapEx outlook was within the preview's expected 40%–42% of revenue range.

surprises.description: Revenue was $51 million, well below the preview’s $58.7–$59.0 million consensus range, despite rising 48% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue rose 48% year-over-year to just over $51 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 2026 Consensus | $58.7M – $59.0M.”

surprises.description: EPS was below the preview’s $0.75 estimate: GAAP EPS was $0.72, while adjusted EPS was $0.57. The preview noted that the estimate’s accounting basis was unclear, but on the adjusted measure the shortfall was substantial.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income was approximately $27 million ($0.72 per share)”; “adjusted net income reached $21 million ($0.57 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS | $0.75”; the preview also says “GAAP vs. adjusted basis is unclear.”

surprises.description: The 2026 program is now expected to complete nine operated Cherokee wells, versus the preview’s expectation of eight completions, with two wells rolling into 2027. That implies a somewhat faster completion cadence than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 2026 capital program is budgeted at $76 million to $97 million to drill 10 operated Cherokee wells (completing nine).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The program runs one rig, with 10 operated Cherokee wells drilled, 8 completed, and 2 rolling into 2027.”

surprises.description: A step-out well below the Cherokee Shale produced strong results and opened the possibility of stacked-pay development, an opportunity the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A step-out well testing a sub-member below the Cherokee Shale delivered a 90-day average rate of approximately 11,000 Mcfe per day and over 1 Bcf cumulative production after 100 days, opening potential stacked-pay development.”

in_line: Production of 19.7 Mboe per day was within the preview’s implied FY26 guidance range of about 17.5–21.1 Mboe per day; the preview gave no separate quarterly production consensus.

The disclosed 2026 hedge coverage—about 30% of guided production, including 43% of oil and 37% of gas—matched the hedge percentages cited in the preview. The facts do not disclose whether 2027 hedges were added.

The August dividend was the expected 13-cent regular dividend, with no new special dividend declared. The 20-cent special dividend paid during the quarter was already identified in the preview as a prior-quarter special.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was $0.77, above the preview’s $0.65 consensus figure and even just above its $0.72–$0.76 bull scenario. That is a meaningful earnings beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP adjusted net income rose about 17% to $41.1 million, producing $0.77 of non-GAAP EPS, a 24% year-over-year increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS … Consensus … $0.65 (MarketBeat) or $0.62 (other aggregators)” and the bull scenario was “$0.72–0.76.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was above the preview’s estimated $52–54 million, while the full-year outlook was raised to a $221–223 million range—above the preview’s bull case of a raise toward $220 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 15.7% year-over-year to $57.7 million”; full-year guidance was raised “by approximately $6.5 million at the midpoint to $221-223 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 adjusted EBITDA at “~$52–54M” and described the bull outcome as “FY EBITDA raised toward $220M.”

surprises.description: The company raised total 2026 revenue guidance to $1.079–1.089 billion, including a $15 million increase in its hardware outlook. This was stronger than the preview’s prior total-revenue guidance and came despite its focus on tariff and memory-cost risks to hardware.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lifted total revenue guidance to $1.079-1.089 billion, including a $15 million increase in the hardware outlook.”
