surprises.description: The MatrixCare divestiture was not covered in the preview and removes a substantial amount of revenue and operating profit. Transition-service agreements are expected to largely offset stranded costs in the first year, but do not eliminate the disclosed revenue and profit loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The MatrixCare divestiture, expected to close around September 1, removes ~$220 million in revenue and $58 million in non-GAAP operating profit, with TSAs expected to largely offset stranded costs in year one.”

surprises.description: ResMed laid out a much larger FY2027 shareholder-return plan than anything quantified in the preview: over $1.85 billion returned, including $1.5 billion of buybacks and a 10% dividend increase. The preview mentioned at least $175 million of Q4 buybacks, but no comparable FY2027 plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ResMed plans to return over $1.85 billion to shareholders in FY2027 (up over 75% YoY), including $1.5 billion in buybacks (with a $450 million accelerated repurchase funded by MatrixCare proceeds) and a 10% dividend increase to $0.66/share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “At least $175M of buyback is planned for Q4” and flagged “first comments from the incoming CFO on capital allocation,” but gave no FY2027 return target.

surprises.description: New patient analysis supports GLP-1 drugs as a tailwind for PAP rather than merely leaving the preview’s GLP-1 bear-case debate unresolved: patients using both therapies were more likely to start PAP and to resupply later.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Analysis of 2.5 million de-identified patients shows those on both PAP and GLP-1s are ~11% more likely to start PAP, ~3% more likely to resupply at 1 year, and ~6% more likely at 3 years, supporting GLP-1s as a tailwind.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called US device growth “the main test of the GLP-1 bear case.”

surprises.description: Life-support device revenue plunged in both Americas and Rest of World, an unexpectedly weak result against the preview’s broader focus on device growth. Sleep devices and masks grew, so the decline was concentrated in life support rather than a broad-based device contraction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 Americas life support device revenue fell 45% and Rest-of-World fell 38%, while sleep device revenue rose 8% (Americas) and 13% (Rest of World) and masks grew 10%-12%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “US/Canada/LatAm device growth” with consensus of “+7.9% for the region.”

surprises.description: Management confirmed that Section 301 tariffs do not apply to ResMed’s products because of Chapter 98/Nairobi Protocol relief. The preview discussed margin as a key debate but did not mention this tariff protection.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ResMed reconfirmed that Section 301 tariffs do not apply to its products due to Chapter 98/Nairobi Protocol relief.”

in_line: Masks grew 10%-12%, broadly in line with the preview’s 10.5% consensus estimate.

surprises.description: WEST had expected to turn free-cash-flow positive in the second half of 2026, but generated $20.2 million in Q2 and was positive for the first half—one quarter ahead of schedule.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company turned free cash flow positive a quarter ahead of schedule, generating $20.2 million in free cash flow in Q2 and positive free cash flow for the first half of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management promised free cash flow positive in H2 2026.”

surprises.description: Q2 net sales were about $306 million, below the $318.8 million consensus estimate by roughly 4%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 net sales rose 8.8% to ~$306 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | Q2 FY26 Consensus | $318.8M.”

surprises.description: First-half adjusted EBITDA was roughly 10% ahead of WEST’s internal plan, an additional positive performance measure not quantified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half consolidated adjusted EBITDA of $47.3 million was more than double the first half of 2025, running roughly 10% ahead of the internal EBITDA plan.”

surprises.description: Beverage Solutions delivered $22.2 million of adjusted EBITDA, above the preview’s expectation of at least $20 million, alongside nearly 17% sales growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Beverage Solutions net sales grew nearly 17% year-over-year, driving segment adjusted EBITDA up 13% to $22.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Look for clean BevSol EBITDA of at least $20M, compared with $19.7M in Q2 2025.”

in_line: Q2 consolidated adjusted EBITDA was $21.3 million, within the preview’s $20–22 million base case, though below its roughly $22 million-or-more catalyst level.
WEST reaffirmed its $90–100 million FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance, as the preview expected, rather than raising it.
Secured net leverage was 3.36x, below the 4.00x covenant threshold highlighted in the preview.

surprises.description: XPOF’s same-store sales were weaker than the preview’s roughly -4% to -6% North America range and its -3% to -5% year-end recovery yardstick: overall sales fell 6.8%, while Club Pilates fell 5%. Management attributed the pressure to a weaker top of the funnel.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 same-store sales declined 6.8% overall and 5% for Club Pilates, coming in below expectations and modestly weaker than Q1 trends due to top-of-funnel pressure.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “NA same-store sales: ~-4% to -6% (buy-side)”; “Q2 needs to show roughly -3% to -5% to make the year-end path credible.”

surprises.description: Despite the weaker sales trend, consolidated revenue was $66.0 million, above the preview’s $64.4–64.5 million consensus range. The beat was modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 revenue fell 13% year-over-year to $66.0 million.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $21.9 million, just below the preview’s implied $22–24 million range, and the reported margin was 33%, down from 37% a year earlier. This was a slight shortfall against the expected EBITDA range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA dropped 22% to $21.9 million and margin compressed from 37% to 33%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Not cleanly published (~$22–24M implied).”

surprises.description: XPOF cut its full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA outlook from $260–270 million and $100–110 million to $250–260 million and $91–97 million. That is a clear reduction from the guidance the preview expected to be reaffirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year 2026 guidance, now expecting revenue of $250-260 million and adjusted EBITDA of $91-97 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 company guidance (reaffirmed May 7, 2026): Revenue $260–270M; Adj. EBITDA $100–110M.”

surprises.description: The 2026 net-new-studio outlook is now approximately 150, at the bottom of the preview’s 150–170 guidance range rather than allowing for growth toward the upper end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Global net new studio openings are now guided to approximately 150 for 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net new studios 150–170.”

surprises.description: Merchandise revenue fell by $5.1 million year over year, with most of the decline tied to the commission-only outsourced model and continuing execution problems. The preview did not flag this transition as a risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Merchandise revenue declined $5.1 million year-over-year, with $3.9 million tied to the new commission-only outsourced model and ongoing transition execution challenges hurting results.”

surprises.description: XPOF announced a new agreement with its largest franchisee for 117 Club Pilates studios across 10 states over six years, an expansion commitment not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new partnership with largest franchisee Spartan Fitness Holdings is expected to open 117 Club Pilates studios across 10 states over the next six years.”

surprises.description: The company reported that member retention improved 28 basis points year over year even as same-store sales fell and management cited top-of-funnel pressure. The preview did not anticipate this retention update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Member retention improving 28 basis points year-over-year.”

surprises.description: The preview cited $17 million payable over 12 months for the franchisee settlement, while XPOF reported $6.8 million paid in Q2 and about $11.4 million more due during the rest of 2026—roughly $18.2 million across those periods, with payments concentrated in 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “After paying $6.8 million in Q2,” the company faces “roughly $11.4 million in additional legal settlement payments in the remainder of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A $22.75M franchisee settlement ($17M payable over 12 months) adds to the pressure.”

in_line: The strategic alternatives review remained ongoing, with no further commentary—consistent with the preview’s expectation of no update absent progress.
Cash of $25.0 million remained above the preview’s roughly $20 million watch level; long-term debt of $522.4 million was also close to the $523.7 million reported for Q1.

surprises.description: The company extended its expected cash runway from the preview’s “into Q1 2027” to “into 2028,” assuming full access to a new credit facility of up to $27.5 million. The facility is non-dilutive, but $15 million is conditional on milestones and it carries a high coupon plus a 16% IRR catch-up payment.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects cash runway to extend into 2028, assuming full access to the credit facility. The facility offers up to $27.5 million, with $12.5 million available immediately and $15 million contingent on year-end milestones; it carries SOFR plus 8% (with a 4.5% floor) and a 16% IRR catch-up payment.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management guided runway “into Q1 2027.” The preview’s base scenario expected runway to be reiterated and no financing detail.

surprises.description: Dispensed applicator units reached 19,626, well above the preview’s roughly 17,600 base expectation and its 16,500 level below which the growth story would weaken.
surprises.fact_evidence: Dispensed applicator units rose over 28% sequentially to 19,626 units.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “Units about 17,600”; the preview also said “Units below about 16,500 would weaken the growth story.”

surprises.description: Despite the strong unit count, Y-CANTH revenue per dispensed unit was about $260 ($5.1 million divided by 19,626 units), below the preview’s roughly $285 expectation. The preview had expected Q2 realization to recover from Q1’s deductible-reset drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: U.S. Y-CANTH net product revenue was $5.1 million on 19,626 dispensed applicator units.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected net revenue per unit of about $285 and said Q2 “should recover” after Q1’s deductible-reset drag.

surprises.description: The reported GAAP loss per share was $0.62, worse than the preview’s $0.41 loss-per-share consensus. The size of the miss is subject to the preview’s warning that the consensus EPS basis was not confirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: GAAP net loss was $13.2 million, or $0.62 per share.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed consensus EPS of “($0.41)” and cautioned: “Confirm which EPS basis consensus uses.”

surprises.description: Cash at quarter-end was $11.2 million, below the preview’s estimate of roughly $12–13 million. The new facility and longer runway mitigate the shortfall, but do not change the reported cash balance.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cash on the balance sheet was $11.2 million as of June 30, 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected cash “near $12–13M” and used about $12.5 million as its comparison point.

surprises.description: Verica announced an Israel distribution agreement that was not anticipated in the preview, providing 60% of net selling price plus up to $8.2 million in regulatory and commercial milestones.
surprises.fact_evidence: The new Israel distribution agreement with Madomi Pharma provides Verica 60% of net selling price plus up to $8.2 million in regulatory and commercial milestone payments.

surprises.description: Verica’s share of the common-warts Phase 3 costs is payable from future Japanese transfer payments, milestones, and royalties, limiting near-term cash burn. The preview knew Torii was funding most of the program but did not specify this deferral of Verica’s cost share.
surprises.fact_evidence: Torii is funding the first $40 million (about 90%) of the program, with Verica’s cost share payable from future Japanese transfer payments, milestones, and royalties, limiting near-term cash burn.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Torii funds the first $40M (about 90%) of Phase 3 cost” and flagged confirming that the cost-share was holding.

surprises.description: The company reported a new VP315 signal in untreated basal cell carcinoma lesions: a 67% average size reduction, with three complete histological clearances. The preview mentioned the existing 97% objective response rate but did not flag this abscopal-effect finding.
surprises.fact_evidence: Phase 2 VP315 data showed a potential abscopal effect: 14 untreated lesions across nine subjects achieved a 67% average size reduction, and three reached complete histological clearance.

surprises.description: The company disclosed that top-line results from the global common-warts Phase 3 program are now expected in mid-2027 and described a potential U.S. population of roughly 22 million, over three times the molluscum population. The preview discussed trial progress but did not provide a readout date or this market-size comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: Top-line data from COVE-2/COVE-3 is now expected in mid-2027, targeting an indication affecting roughly 22 million U.S. patients—over three times the molluscum population.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue modestly exceeded the syndicated consensus estimate, although it remained within the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 total revenue was $5.9 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed total-revenue consensus of “$5.73M” and a base scenario of “$5.7–5.9M.”

in_line: The sharp year-over-year decline in total revenue was expected to reflect the absence of the one-time $8 million milestone included in Q2 2025.
Torii’s funding of the first $40 million (about 90%) of the common-warts Phase 3 program matched the preview’s stated expectation.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.52 versus the preview’s $0.36 consensus, a sizable headline beat. But $0.17 came from tariff refunds; excluding that benefit, EPS was about $0.35 and underlying EPS declined year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was flat year-over-year at $0.52,” including “a $0.17 per share benefit from $44 million in tariff refunds,” meaning “underlying EPS declined absent the refund.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS | $0.36” consensus.

surprises.description: Management signaled a weaker near-term earnings path than the preview’s expectation that tariff mitigation would land in Q2–Q3 and transformation benefits would accelerate in H2: Q3 earnings are expected below Q2 excluding the refund, and investment benefits are expected to become visible only starting in Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 earnings to fall below Q2 levels (excluding the $0.17 tariff benefit), with investment benefits expected to become visible starting in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management says tariff mitigation lands in Q2–Q3 and transformation benefits accelerate in H2.”

surprises.description: Revenue modestly beat both preview consensus figures, but the constant-currency decline was steeper than the preview’s reported-sales decline estimates implied. The decline narrows to 3.6% after adjusting for Byte and a planned dealer inventory reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $898 million,” down “6.3% on a constant currency basis,” or a “3.6% constant currency decline when adjusting for Byte and an ~$8 million planned dealer inventory reduction.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales (Zacks) | $883.9M” and “Net sales (alt. panel) | about $893M”; consensus implied “about -5.6%” to “-4.6%” year-over-year.

surprises.description: The company restarted share repurchases, buying about $12 million of stock even though the preview highlighted cash generation and the buyback pace as issues to watch. The preview did not anticipate a buyback resuming this quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased 1.3 million shares for approximately $12 million at an average price below $10 per share, marking its first buyback since Q3 2024.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A second straight negative-FCF quarter would put the dividend and buyback pace into the Q&A.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow rebounded sharply from Q1, easing the preview’s concern about another weak cash-flow quarter, although the call facts do not provide free cash flow and therefore do not establish whether FCF turned positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow more than doubled to $99 million from $48 million a year earlier,” aided by tariff refunds and improved working capital management.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Free cash flow and capital allocation” and warned that “A second straight negative-FCF quarter” would put the dividend and buyback pace into the Q&A.

surprises.description: Management gave a more constructive U.S. exit-rate outlook than the preview’s general concern about company-specific execution: it expects positive U.S. growth by year-end and less severe declines in Q3, while saying much of EDS weakness reflects European distributor destocking rather than weaker demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects the “U.S. business to exit 2026 with positive growth,” targeting “less severe declines in Q3,” and attributed most EDS weakness to European distributors cutting inventory “from 12+ weeks toward 8 weeks rather than demand softness.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said sector demand “looks healthier than XRAY’s Q1 implied, which points to company-specific execution,” and described distribution agreements as a key commercial proof point.

surprises.description: The call disclosed notable weakness across specific businesses: OIS fell sharply, SureSmile declined double digits on U.S. weakness, implants were down mid-single digits, and CTS Americas was nearly 10% lower in constant currency because of CAD/CAM capital-spending deferrals. APAC growth, including in milling systems, provided a counterpoint; the preview offered no segment-level expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OIS revenue fell 13.2% as reported (5.7% excluding Byte),” SureSmile revenue of $40 million was “declining double digits driven by U.S. weakness,” implants “declined mid-single digits,” and “CTS Americas was down nearly 10% constant currency driven by CAD/CAM CapEx deferrals,” while APAC posted double-digit growth including in milling systems.

in_line: The company maintained its FY26 net-sales guidance of $3.5–$3.6 billion and adjusted-EPS guidance of $1.40–$1.50, as the preview expected; the preview specifically said a reaffirmation without a new H2 bridge would be a “show-me hold.”

surprises.description: The preview’s buy-side expectation was roughly $68.5–68.9 million of Q2 revenue, but Weave reported $67.5 million. That was below the expected range, even though it was within the company’s $67.2–68.2 million guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 total revenue was $67.5 million, up 15.5% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Applying that pattern, the number that meets buy-side expectations is roughly $68.5–68.9M.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated a raise toward roughly $278–280 million, or at least warned that reaffirming the prior range would imply caution. Instead, Weave cut its FY2026 revenue outlook to $273–275 million, citing bookings slightly below expectations during its go-to-market transition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $273-275 million due to a go-to-market transition that caused bookings to fall slightly below expectations during May-July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A lift to about $278–280M is the bull trigger”; the preview also said “a reaffirm-and-narrow after a beat would read as implicit 2H caution.”

surprises.description: Despite the revenue outlook cut, Weave raised its full-year non-GAAP operating income guidance to $12–14 million, above the prior $10.5–13.5 million range used in the preview’s 2H ramp calculation. This was a stronger profitability outlook than the preview’s focus on the existing ramp requirement suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Despite the reduced revenue outlook, management raised non-GAAP operating income guidance to $12-14 million, reflecting improved operating efficiency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY non-GAAP operating income of $10.5–13.5M requires roughly $5.4–8.4M in 2H, after about $5.1M in 1H.”

surprises.description: The preview’s Q2 non-GAAP operating income guidance was $2.1–3.1 million, while Weave reported $3.2 million of operating income, above the guidance ceiling. The result came with improving cost leverage: sales and marketing fell as a share of revenue, and incremental operating income conversion rose to 34%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating income reached $3.2 million (4.7% margin) … above the top end of guidance”; “Sales and marketing expenses fell to 38% of revenue, a 240 basis point sequential improvement and 160 basis point year-over-year improvement”; “The company converted 34% of year-over-year revenue growth into incremental operating income.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income | $2.1M – $3.1M”; the preview also said the Q2 guided midpoint was “barely above Q1’s actual despite more revenue, which implies an opex step-up.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted AI interactions growing more than 300%, whereas Weave reported custom AI interactions up 165% year over year and Call Intelligence interactions up 143%. Usage was still growing rapidly, but the reported custom-interaction growth was slower than the figure highlighted before the release.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Custom AI interactions totaled 70 million (up 165% YoY) and Call Intelligence interactions rose 143%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adoption stats are strong (300%+ growth in AI interactions, more than 50% of locations using an embedded AI feature).”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a major step-up in Athena integration depth. Weave said it advanced from a level-one to a level-four integration, opening access to more than 160,000 specialty medical providers and creating higher-ASP potential.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The deeper Athena One integration advanced Weave from a level-one to a level-four integration, unlocking access to over 160,000 specialty medical providers and higher ASP potential.”

in_line: Payments revenue grew roughly twice as fast as total revenue, consistent with the preview’s expectation that payments would continue growing at more than twice the overall rate.
Weave added a record number of locations on both a gross and net basis, matching the preview’s expectation that record location adds would repeat.

Q2 free cash flow was clearly positive at $8.7 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Q2 needed to be solidly positive; the company also reported its first free-cash-flow-positive first half.

surprises.description: Q2 product revenue of $25.1 million landed between the preview’s two consensus estimates: it exceeded the $22.9 million estimate but fell short of the $27.8 million estimate. It was also a $6.4 million sequential increase from Q1, well above the roughly $1.2 million increase implied by management’s earlier wording.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net product revenue reached $25.1 million” and reflected “a meaningful quarter-over-quarter rebound from Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue consensus was reported as “$22.9M” by one source and “$27.8M” by another; the preview said Q2 growth would be “bigger than Q4 to Q1,” implying revenue above roughly $19.9M.

surprises.description: Liquidity was materially stronger than the preview’s estimated $145–150 million Q2 cash balance: the company reported $201.4 million pro forma after approximately $90 million of non-dilutive funding, including a $50 million royalty-financing draw and a $15 million Copiktra milestone. Management said this cash should fund operations into the second half of 2027, beyond the preview’s expected runway into the first half of 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured approximately $90 million in non-dilutive funding,” including “a $50 million initial draw” and “a $15 million Copiktra sales milestone”; pro forma cash was “$201.4 million,” expected to fund operations “into the second half of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 cash at “about $145–150M” and said management’s stated runway ran “into H1 2027.” It also flagged financing as something to watch, rather than anticipating this level of funding.

surprises.description: Q2 R&D and SG&A imply total operating expenses of about $68.7 million, slightly above the preview’s roughly $66–68 million level flagged as a runway concern. The preview expected R&D to rise, so the surprise is the modest overshoot of the total-opex threshold, not the R&D increase itself.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expenses rose to $41.3 million” and “SG&A held roughly flat at $27.4 million” (about $68.7 million combined).
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Total opex above roughly $66–68M would pressure the runway,” while noting that “R&D is rising.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed an October comprehensive VS-7375 data update across pancreatic, lung, and colorectal cohorts, including an early look at durability. The preview did not flag this near-term data event.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A comprehensive VS-7375 data update is expected in October,” with response rates across the three cohorts, “approximately 20 patients each,” plus “an early look at durability.”

surprises.description: The call described substantial VS-7375 clinical and regulatory progress not covered in the preview: all three dose-expansion cohorts completed enrollment, the drug received FDA fast-track designation for NSCLC, and the first patients were dosed in all three Phase II registration-directed studies. Management also cited an approximately 30% response rate with at least six months’ durability and favorable tolerability as its accelerated-approval guidepost.
surprises.fact_evidence: “VS-7375 completed target enrollment in all three dose-expansion cohorts,” received “FDA fast-track designation for non-small cell lung cancer,” and “has dosed first patients in all three Phase II registration-directed studies.” Management cited a “~30% overall response rate with at least six months durability” and “favorable tolerability” as the guidepost for accelerated approval.

surprises.description: Although the preview said a partnership was not expected, management reported advancing a partnership with its collaborator and considerable inbound strategic interest. The new funding also means it does not feel pressure to rush into a partnership or equity financing at the current stock price.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is “advancing a partnership” with its collaborator and reported “considerable inbound strategic interest”; it said the funding removes pressure to rush into a partnership or equity financing at the current stock price.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a RAMP 205 partnership was “Not expected, but a high-impact surprise.”

in_line: Management reiterated that the LGSOC franchise is expected to become self-sustaining by the end of 2026, consistent with the preview’s focus on the H2 2026 self-sustaining target.
The preview expected R&D to rise with the clinical program and SG&A to remain roughly flat; management reported higher R&D and said SG&A should remain stable quarterly through 2026.

surprises.description: The preview put HCI’s pro forma book value per share at roughly $120–125 based on the Exzeo mark. The call said it would exceed $150 if unrealized gains on Exzeo and real estate were included, a materially higher figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pro forma book value would exceed $150 if unrealized gains on Exzeo and real estate were included.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The preview puts HCI's stake near $1.1B, and the pro forma BVPS on today's mark at roughly $120–125.”

surprises.description: The preview was watching for gross premiums earned growth of 8% or better, but HCI reported 6% growth. Policy growth was offset by flat average premium per policy, so premium growth fell short of the preview’s stated bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross premiums earned grew 6% driven by policy growth with flat average premium per policy.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether GPE growth holds at 8% or better.”

surprises.description: The preview described CORE’s declines as a continuing concern. Instead, CORE had pivoted to residential HO3 business and was bringing in roughly $6 million of new business per month, a reversal of the decline narrative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The CORE reciprocal exchange pivoted from commercial to residential (HO3) business, ramping to roughly $6 million of new business per month over recent months since first writing HO3 policies in March.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CORE declines. Condo Owners Reciprocal Exchange GPE fell sharply for a second straight quarter. A third decline would raise questions about the reciprocal model.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a new distribution channel, but HCI signed GEICO in July and sales were already underway. Management said it could support organic policy growth by year-end without Citizens takeouts, acquisitions, or entry into new markets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed GEICO in July to distribute its new product with sales already underway, positioning HCI for potential organic policy growth by year-end without Citizens takeouts, acquisitions, or new markets.”

surprises.description: The preview expected a reinsurance cost decrease of about 10% and H2 savings, but the call described more and better coverage alongside ceded-premium cuts of over 10%, worth more than $10 million per quarter. The improved coverage makes the renewal somewhat better than the cost reduction alone anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New 2026-2027 reinsurance programs secured more and better coverage while cutting ceded premiums by over 10%, translating to more than $10 million in savings per quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The 2026–27 reinsurance program renewed June 1 at about $381.2M of net ceded premium, a 10% cost decrease”; “The margin benefit is expected in Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss capital returns. HCI reported that it had completed the $80 million buyback and repurchased about 4% of outstanding shares, but also said no new authorization was active, leaving no ongoing buyback authorization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “HCI fully completed its $80 million buyback authorization, repurchasing 504,000 shares (about 4% of outstanding shares), with no new authorization currently active.”

surprises.description: Q2 diluted EPS was $5.60, above both the preview’s $5.04 consensus and its stated $5.20-or-higher practical bar. The beat was larger than the preview’s description of an EPS beat as the base case suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS reached $5.60 in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS vs. $5.04. A beat is the base case, but the preview suggests the real bar is $5.20 or higher.”

in_line: Total revenue grew 11%, broadly in line with the preview’s consensus-implied year-over-year growth range of 8.5%–11.5%.
The combined ratio was 61%, within the preview’s base-case range of 58%–61% and the stated 60% ±5 target; the loss ratio was also within the company’s 20%–25% target.
The reinsurance savings were expected to benefit Q3 and Q4; the call’s Q3 ceded-premium expectation of about $96 million is consistent with the preview’s anticipated H2 benefit.

surprises.description: Revenue was well above the preview’s own estimate of about $373 million: INNOVATE reported $421.6 million, with Infrastructure the primary driver. The published $251.7 million consensus was flagged as potentially stale, so the company-specific model is the more useful comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue rose 74.2% year-over-year to $421.6 million, driven primarily by the Infrastructure segment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: ~$373M”; the preview also cautioned that the published $251.7M consensus “may be stale.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA substantially exceeded the preview’s estimate of about $19.5 million, coming in at $46.3 million—more than twice the expected amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total adjusted EBITDA nearly tripled to $46.3 million from $15.7 million in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA… My estimate: ~$19.5M”; the preview said no published estimate was found.

surprises.description: Instead of the expected loss, INNOVATE reported positive net income and positive diluted EPS. The preview’s own estimate was a $1.20-per-share loss, and its published consensus was a $2.18-per-share loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company swung to net income of $10.4 million ($0.71 per fully diluted share) versus a net loss of $22 million ($1.67 per share) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS… Published consensus: $(2.18)”; “My estimate: $(1.20).”

surprises.description: DBM Global’s adjusted backlog rose to $2.7 billion, well beyond the preview’s $1.8 billion checkpoint and its expectation of flat-to-up backlog. That gives the business more reported revenue visibility into 2027 and 2028 than the preview’s base case implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Infrastructure adjusted backlog grew to $2.7 billion from $1.8 billion at year-end 2025, providing revenue visibility into 2027 and 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “DBMG adjusted backlog. Flat-to-up adjusted backlog”; the catalyst checklist called for “Adjusted backlog at or above $1.8B.”

surprises.description: DBM Global delivered stronger operating performance than the preview’s qualitative expectation of “solid” execution: it reported record quarterly revenue and expanded adjusted EBITDA margin by roughly 350 basis points. The preview did not provide segment-level revenue or margin estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DBM Global posted record Q2 revenue of $414 million (up 77.6%) and adjusted EBITDA of $48.7 million, with adjusted EBITDA margin expanding roughly 350 basis points to 11.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario described “Solid DBMG execution”; it gave no DBM Global revenue or margin estimate.

surprises.description: INNOVATE reported an agreed sale of a controlling stake in Broadcasting to CONX, with INNOVATE retaining a minority interest. The preview focused on unresolved CONX/Broadcasting accounting and closing details rather than stating that the stake sale had been agreed; it had already flagged the $75 million post-close commitment as an item to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “INNOVATE agreed to sell a controlling ~75% stake in Broadcasting to CONX Corp., retaining 25% with an option to increase to 40%, while CONX committed up to $75 million of post-closing equity capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CONX/Broadcasting accounting. Whether Spectrum stays consolidated, moves to held-for-sale, or becomes discontinued operations…” The preview also said to watch the “FCC timeline, expected close, and the $75M post-close equity commitment.”

surprises.description: Life Sciences revenue fell sharply, with R2’s lower unit sales attributed to liquidity constraints. The preview highlighted R2’s past-due note and broader liquidity concerns but did not forecast this operating impact on sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Life Sciences revenue fell 31.3% to $2.2 million as R2 experienced lower Glacial FX and Glacial Spa unit sales due to liquidity constraints.”

in_line: The preview expected debt to be rising on PIK accrual; the call likewise attributed indebtedness to PIK interest at the nonoperating and Life Sciences segments.

surprises.description: Westwood reported $1.6 billion of net AUM outflows, far worse than the preview’s near-flat base case and even its bear case of $300 million or worse. Institutional outflows were $1.3 billion, concentrated in legacy large cap value amid performance challenges and a shift toward passive ETFs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Substantial net outflows of $1.6 billion in AUM during the quarter”; “Institutional net outflows totaled $1.3 billion, concentrated in the legacy large cap value business hurt by performance challenges and a client shift toward passive ETFs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The model's base case is $19.8B, which implies roughly +9% blended market appreciation with flows near flat”; the bear case assumes “flows to –$300M or worse.”

surprises.description: Ending assets were well below the preview’s $19.3 billion floor: Westwood ended with $17.9 billion in AUM and assets under advisement, including $17.0 billion of AUM. Market appreciation of $1.2 billion only partly offset the outflows.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ending at $17 billion AUM and $17.9 billion in total assets under management and advisement,” after “$1.6 billion” of outflows and “$1.2 billion in market appreciation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Ending AUM/AUA vs. $19.3B”; “Below $19.3B signals that the energy drag outweighed the value rally.” The base case was $19.8B.

surprises.description: Both earnings measures came in below the preview’s model: GAAP EPS was $0.17 versus $0.22 expected, and economic EPS was $0.33 versus $0.43 expected. The gaps were meaningful even though GAAP net income rose from the prior-year quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income rose to $1.5 million ($0.17 per share)”; “non-GAAP economic earnings were $3 million ($0.33 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s model was “GAAP diluted EPS … $0.22” and “Economic EPS … $0.43.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $25.3 million, below the preview’s $26.5 million model, though it increased from both Q1 and the year-ago quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenues of $25.3 million, up from $25 million in Q1 and $23.1 million in the prior-year quarter.”

surprises.description: Small cap value outflows were described as tied mainly to one client consolidating allocations, with a larger SMIDCAP allocation already funded in July. That makes this part of the flow weakness look more client-specific and partly offset than a broad-based loss of small-cap demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Small cap value outflows were primarily tied to a single client consolidating allocations into a combined mid cap mandate, with a significantly larger SMIDCAP allocation already funded in July.”

surprises.description: The ETF platform exceeded $400 million in assets in July, above the preview’s latest cited level of $388 million at June 29. The enhanced income ETFs accounted for more than $370 million combined.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The ETF platform surpassed $400 million in assets in July,” with MDST and WEEI “exceeding $370 million combined.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ETF net assets rose from $336M (about Apr 30) to $388M (Jun 29).”

surprises.description: Private capital added nearly $147 million in co-investment commitments and surpassed $500 million in total commitments, a concrete expansion not anticipated in the preview, which instead focused on a possible Energy Secondaries Fund III first close.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Private capital closed nearly $147 million in new co-investment commitments during the quarter, bringing the platform to over $500 million in total commitments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Energy Secondaries Fund III … has marketing running ‘through early 2027,’ and no fee economics are disclosed. A first close would extend the highest-fee part of the asset base.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed private-capital fee terms—annual management fees of 1% to 1.5% and potential carry of 10% to 15% above an 8% preferred return—where the preview said fee economics were not disclosed. However, no carry is currently reflected in the financials.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Private capital funds carry annual management fees of 1% to 1.5% plus potential carry of 10-15% over an 8% preferred return, though no carry is currently reflected in the financials.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No fee economics are disclosed.”

surprises.description: Management said three business lines launched within the past three years—managed investment solutions, ETFs, and private capital—had each reached roughly $500 million in assets, with a goal of exceeding $1 billion each. The preview did not flag this combined scale milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Three business lines that did not exist three years ago—managed investment solutions, ETFs, and private capital—have each reached roughly $500 million in assets, with a stated goal to surpass $1 billion each.”

surprises.description: Westwood announced a mid-September launch of PWRX as the first listing on the Texas Stock Exchange, an upcoming product and listing milestone not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to launch the PWRX ETF as the first listing on the Texas Stock Exchange in mid-September.”

in_line: The regular quarterly dividend remained $0.15 per share, in line with the preview’s report that the dividend was unchanged at $0.15 per quarter.

surprises.description: Progyny lowered its FY2026 revenue range to $1.36–$1.385 billion from the May range of $1.365–$1.405 billion. That is a lower midpoint and a $20 million reduction at the high end, rather than the raise or narrow-only outcome the preview highlighted as the favorable case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance projects revenue of $1.36–$1.385 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the main risk was “a second narrow without a raise” and flagged a revenue raise as a catalyst; it listed current guidance of “$1.365B – $1.405B.”

surprises.description: Management said Q3 revenue guidance reflects slightly more pronounced summer seasonality, an added near-term headwind against the preview’s emphasis on clean Q3 comparisons. Management also characterized the impact as roughly a 1% adjustment at the midpoint and said it did not change the trend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for revenue of $335–$345 million (6.9%–10.1% growth) reflecting a slightly more pronounced summer seasonality,” which management called “roughly a 1% adjustment at the midpoint and not a change in trend.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q3 comparisons are clean” and flagged low-end H2 growth as a signal of deceleration on clean comps.

surprises.description: The preview already expected favorable 2027 pipeline commentary and early commitments ahead of last year, but management went further by saying it had removed the vast majority of 2027 client-retention risk earlier than usual. That is a modestly stronger de-risking update than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management believes it has “removed the vast majority of client retention risk for 2027 earlier than usual,” largely derisking client turnover.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that the pipeline was “substantially favorable versus a year ago,” with “early commitments pacing ahead” and renewal exposure at its lowest level relative to prior years.

surprises.description: Progyny Select was not discussed in the preview, but management said the new fully-insured offering is not expected to contribute meaningfully in 2027 and that the next 12–18 months will focus on signing channel partners rather than driving volume. This sets a limited near-term contribution for a new offering, though the preview provided no specific expectation for it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Progyny Select, the new fully-insured offering, is not expected to be a meaningful contributor in 2027,” with the next 12–18 months focused on “signing channel partners rather than driving volume.”

in_line: Q2 revenue growth was broadly in line with the preview’s underlying-growth expectation: reported growth was 5.3% versus the preview’s roughly 4.7% headline estimate, while growth excluding the transition-of-care client was 11% versus roughly 10.4% derived in the preview.
The target of adding at least 1 million new lives and early commitments pacing ahead of last year were consistent with the preview’s expectation of favorable pipeline and ahead-of-year commitments.

FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $2.04–$2.10 was broadly in line with the preview’s approximately $2.06 consensus; adjusted EBITDA guidance of $233–$240 million was also broadly in line with the approximately $238 million consensus.

surprises.description: Airbnb delivered $3.6 billion of Q2 revenue, slightly above the $3.58 billion consensus and just beyond the top of its $3.54–$3.60 billion guidance range. The beat was modest rather than a large departure from expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue grew 17% year-over-year to $3.6 billion, exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue … Q2'26 Consensus $3.58B”; “Q2'26 Guide $3.54–3.60B.”

surprises.description: Gross booking value reached $27.2 billion, about 3% above the $26.42 billion consensus. That was a stronger booking-value result than the preview’s estimates implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross booking value rose 16% to $27.2 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross Booking Value … Q2'26 Consensus $26.42B.”

surprises.description: Nights and Seats Booked grew 10% and accelerated from Q1, versus the preview’s roughly 8% growth implied by guidance and its 145.4 million consensus estimate. This was better than the preview’s flagged risk of an optical miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nights and Seats Booked grew 10%, accelerating from Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Slight decel. from Q1's +9%”; “Consensus sits above what guidance implies”; “Nights & Seats Booked … Q2'26 Consensus 145.4M.”

surprises.description: Airbnb raised its full-year revenue outlook from low-to-mid-teens growth to at least mid-teens growth. That is an improvement over the framework the preview expected management to reaffirm.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year guidance, now expecting revenue growth of at least mid-teens (up from low-to-mid teens).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 framework: ‘low-to-mid-teens’ revenue growth”; the base scenario expected “FY reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: The full-year adjusted EBITDA margin floor rose to at least 35.5%, above the 35% floor the preview identified as the key margin bar. The increase came despite the preview’s focus on reinvestment pressures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin of at least 35.5% (up from 35%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA margin of at least 35%”; “Reinvestment versus discipline.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $4.69–$4.77 billion came in above the preview’s derived estimate of roughly $4.55–$4.65 billion. The guidance clears the upper end of that range, although the gap is limited.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for revenue of $4.69–$4.77 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 revenue is not published; derived estimate ~$4.55–4.65B”; the base scenario expected “$4.55–4.65B.”

surprises.description: Alongside stronger full-year margin guidance, management said Q3 adjusted EBITDA margin would be down slightly year over year because of investment timing. The preview highlighted reinvestment generally but did not forecast a quarterly margin decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin expected to be down slightly year-over-year due to investment timing.”

surprises.description: First-time bookers grew 11%, the company’s highest growth rate in four years, with acceleration across several core markets. The preview did not identify this metric or signal such a result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-time bookers grew 11%, the highest growth rate in four years, with acceleration in core markets including the U.S., France, U.K. and Australia.”

surprises.description: Hotel nights were growing about three times faster than home nights, and roughly 35% of first-time hotel guests later booked a home. The preview flagged hotels as sub-scale but did not anticipate these growth and cross-booking details.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hotel nights are growing approximately 3x faster than the homes business despite still being a single-digit percentage of nights booked, and roughly 35% of first-time hotel guests return to book a home.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Experiences and hotels remain sub-scale; watch for first hard numbers.”

surprises.description: Reserve Now, Pay Later accounted for more than 20% of Q2 GBV and was associated with more bookings, longer lead times, and higher ADR; the company expanded it to more booking types in July. The preview mentioned its effect on mix but did not set an adoption benchmark or forecast these added effects.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reserve Now, Pay Later accounted for over 20% of total GBV in Q2, driving more bookings, longer lead times, and higher ADR, and was expanded to more booking types in July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reserve Now Pay Later is pushing mix toward higher-priced homes.”

surprises.description: The single service fee already covered about half of active listings, with rollout to most remaining hosts expected by year-end. Management said the fee pressures pricing downward for competitiveness; the preview did not flag this pricing pressure or rollout.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The single service fee, which pressures pricing downward for competitiveness, now covers about half of active listings and is expected to roll out to the majority of remaining hosts by year-end.”

surprises.description: AI adoption reduced customer-support cost per booking by about 16% year over year, and nearly 45% of AI-assistant issues were resolved without a human agent. The preview did not anticipate these realized cost savings or the planned AI voice support.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI adoption cut customer support cost per booking by about 16% year-over-year, with nearly 45% of AI-assistant issues resolved without a human agent, and AI voice support planned for later this year.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a $77 million tax benefit supporting Q2 net income of $816 million. The preview did not flag this benefit, which makes part of the reported net income attributable to a tax item rather than operating performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net income was $816 million, boosted by a $77 million tax benefit.”

surprises.description: Airbnb generated $1.3 billion of Q2 free cash flow, with $4.8 billion over the trailing twelve months and a 37% margin. The preview discussed capital returns but did not provide a free-cash-flow expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Airbnb generated $1.3 billion of free cash flow in Q2 (TTM $4.8 billion, 37% margin).”

in_line: The preview flagged capital return as a focus; Airbnb repurchased $1.1 billion of stock in Q2.

surprises.description: CytomX reported Q2 revenue of just $1.4 million, far below the preview’s $11.33 million consensus estimate. The call attributed the year-over-year decline primarily to the conclusion of the BMS and Astellas collaborations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue fell to $1.4 million from $18.7 million in Q2 2025, primarily due to the conclusion of the BMS and Astellas collaborations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $11.33M” Q2 2026E consensus.

surprises.description: Preliminary PFS at Varseta-M’s top two doses was 6.8 to 7.1 months, above the call’s cited third-line CRC benchmark of about 4.5 to 5.5 months and substantially longer than the cited fourth-line benchmark of a few months. The preview anticipated dose-optimization data but did not state an efficacy expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Preliminary PFS at the top two doses (8.6 and 10 mg/kg) was reported at 6.8 to 7.1 months, compared to benchmark PFS of ~4.5-5.5 months (third line) and just a few months (fourth line).”

surprises.description: The loperamide/budesonide prophylaxis strategy brought Grade 3 diarrhea to 10%, at the low end of management’s stated acceptable range for late-line CRC. The preview did not specify an expected diarrhea rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The loperamide/budesonide prophylaxis strategy reduced Grade 3 diarrhea to 10%, at the low end of the 10-20% rate management deems acceptable for late-line CRC.”

in_line: The preview expected the Varseta-M dose-optimization update in 2H26; the call kept the comprehensive update on track for year-end 2026, including overall survival and preliminary PFS from the 40-patient optimization cohort.
The planned first Varseta-M registrational monotherapy study remains on the previewed 1H27 timeline.

The preview anticipated ratable recognition of the Regeneron payment as the base case; the call said the July $37 million payment would be recognized over several years as work progresses. The additional payment also supports the previously stated runway of at least 2H28.

The preview flagged non-CRC expansion cohorts and a 2H26 study ramp. The call described expansion into gastric/GEJ, pancreatic and biliary cancers, and a Q4 2026 second-line CRC combination study; operating expenses and R&D also rose, with R&D growth driven by Varseta-M manufacturing.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case put Q2 adjusted EBITDA at $82M–$84M; CarGurus reported $85M, at the high end of its guidance. This was a modest beat of the preview’s base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 7% year-over-year to $85 million” and “land[ed] at the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “Adj. EBITDA $82M – $84M.”

surprises.description: The preview described FY2026 adjusted EBITDA margin compression of 1.5–2.5 points as the outlook. Management instead raised the profitability outlook to just 0.5–1.5 points of compression, a meaningful improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its full-year profitability outlook, now expecting 2026 adjusted EBITDA margins to compress only ~50 to 150 basis points versus 2025, citing AI-driven efficiency gains.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin down 1.5 to 2.5 points versus 2025.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $251M, close to the preview’s roughly $249.85M consensus and within the stated ±$1–2M noise range; it also fell within the $247M–$252M guidance range.
Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin compression was about 200 basis points year over year, broadly matching the preview’s estimate of about 210 basis points at the guidance midpoint.
The company reiterated FY2026 revenue growth guidance of 10%–13%, as the preview expected.

Q3 revenue guidance of $253.5M–$258.5M was centered near the preview’s roughly $255M reference, and the indicated growth deceleration was consistent with the preview’s discussion of slower second-half growth.
CarGurus continued to add U.S. dealers, with 673 net paying dealer adds, and U.S. QARSD grew 8%; this met the preview’s key expectation of a third consecutive quarter of net dealer adds.

surprises.description: Cryoport reported $49 million of Q2 revenue, above the published $48.21 million consensus but below the preview’s $50–51 million buy-side whisper; the preview said a $48–49 million print would read as a miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue reached $49 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side whisper is therefore about $50–51M, and a print of $48–49M would read as a miss.” The preview also listed consensus of $48.21M.

surprises.description: Cryoport left its FY2026 revenue range at $192–196 million rather than raising it. The preview highlighted a higher low end of at least $194 million as a catalyst and described a raise as part of its base scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cryoport affirmed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $192 to $196 million,” citing “geopolitical and macroeconomic uncertainty as reason for conservatism.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance raised to at least $194M at the low end” was a catalyst; the base scenario assumed “FY guide nudged to $194–198M.”

surprises.description: Commercial cell and gene therapy revenue was $9.4 million, below the preview’s $10 million watchpoint, and grew 9% rather than showing a continuation of the 26% growth cited for Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial cell and gene therapy revenue grew 9% to $9.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether “commercial CGT clears $10M”; it reported Q1 commercial CGT revenue growth of “+26%.”

surprises.description: Management’s expected number of new therapy approvals for the rest of 2026 was lower than the preview’s stated expectation: five new therapy approvals, plus one label or geographic expansion, versus up to eight new approvals.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “five new therapy approvals, and one label/geographic expansion approval among clients.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “guided to up to 8 new approvals in the rest of 2026.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was positive at $0.4 million, in line with the preview’s breakeven-or-better watchpoint.
Life Science Services was approximately $27.9 million, calculated from 57% of $49 million of revenue, essentially matching the preview’s at-or-above-$28-million watchpoint.
Cryoport supported 22 commercial therapies, meeting the preview’s expectation that the count move above 21.

surprises.description: Corsair’s non-GAAP diluted EPS was $0.23, far above the preview’s $0.07 consensus; GAAP net income also turned positive at $9.1 million. The EPS gap was much larger than the preview’s in-line-to-$0.07 slowdown scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP diluted EPS rising to $0.23 from $0.01”; “GAAP net income swung to a positive $9.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS … Street consensus $0.07”; the preview also says “An in-line $0.06–0.07 would read as a slowdown.”

surprises.description: Corsair raised FY2026 guidance rather than reaffirming it: the adjusted EBITDA midpoint rose about $19 million to $121–131 million, and the revenue midpoint increased roughly $35 million to $1.4–1.47 billion. That is a substantial positive change against a preview that warned a reaffirmation could disappoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance was raised, with the adjusted EBITDA midpoint increasing about $19 million (to $121-131 million) and revenue midpoint up roughly $35 million (to $1.4-1.47 billion).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance: raise or reaffirm. With consensus already near the top of the range, a reaffirmation may read as disappointing.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $16.7 million even excluding the $14.3 million tariff benefit, above the $15.5 million high end of the quarter’s guidance. This indicates a stronger underlying result than the preview’s roughly $15 million implied expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding the $14.3 million tariff benefit, adjusted EBITDA of $16.7 million still exceeded the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA $12.5–15.5M (midpoint $14.0M)”; “Not found (implied ~$15M).”

surprises.description: Company gross margin reached a record 33.2%, above the preview’s 31–32% base case. However, about 500 basis points of the 640-basis-point year-over-year expansion came from a one-time $15.6 million tariff refund, so the headline margin was not all recurring improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin hit a company record of 33.2%, expanding 640 basis points year-over-year, though approximately 500 basis points came from a one-time $15.6 million tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … Gross margin 31–32%”; the preview also described 33%+ as the bull scenario.

surprises.description: Gaming components and systems revenue fell 9% as elevated memory prices delayed DIY PC builds. The preview discussed memory constraints and expected the segment’s margin to normalize, but did not anticipate or quantify this demand-related revenue decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gaming components and systems revenue declined 9% year-over-year to $198.5 million due to elevated memory pricing delaying DIY PC builds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management expects memory constraints through 2026 and normalization in 2027.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow rose 148% year over year, first-half cash generation exceeded the whole of 2025 and 2024 combined, and Corsair ended the quarter with about $75.1 million of net cash. The preview noted the prior-quarter cash and debt balances but did not flag such a cash-generation outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow surged 148% year-over-year to $74.8 million, with first-half cash generation exceeding all of 2025 and 2024 combined, ending the quarter in a net cash position of approximately $75.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Balance sheet: $119.7M cash vs. $119.8M total debt.”

surprises.description: Corsair acquired sim-racing hardware brand TrackRacer and made minority investments in Bitfocus, moves the preview did not anticipate. Management expects only immaterial contributions in 2026, with meaningful impact from 2027 onward, so the near-term benefit is limited.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company acquired sim racing hardware brand TrackRacer and made minority investments in Bitfocus, though management expects only immaterial contributions in 2026 with meaningful impact from 2027 onward.”

surprises.description: Management identified GTA 6’s expected Q4 2026 launch as a console and peripherals tailwind, an additional prospective demand driver not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management sees GTA 6's expected Q4 2026 launch as a console and peripherals tailwind.”

surprises.description: Corsair put a roughly $22 billion desktop AI PC market opportunity in view, but said revenue contribution is expected mainly in late 2027 and beyond. This provides a quantified market opportunity, but not near-term contribution or the pipeline/bookings detail the preview said could be a catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[Corsair is] targeting the roughly $22 billion desktop AI PC market with revenue contribution expected mainly in late 2027 and beyond.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any quantified pipeline or bookings would be a new catalyst. Vague language would be a negative.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $314.3 million was above the $307.5 million guidance midpoint and roughly in line with the preview’s $310.5 million Street consensus estimate.
Gamer and creator peripherals revenue grew 13%, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of low-teens segment growth.
Gaming components and systems gross margin was 26.3%; the preview’s base case expected it to step down to about 26%, and it flagged a drop below 26% as a concern.

surprises.description: Dropbox added 96,000 net paying users, its strongest gain in about three years and a third consecutive quarter of growth. That was well above the preview’s 25,000–40,000-user bull-case range and much stronger than the preview’s roughly 18.10 million paying-user estimate would suggest; the reported total was 18.9 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Added approximately 96,000 net new paying users sequentially to reach 18.9 million,” marking “its third consecutive quarter of paying user growth” and “its strongest gain in about three years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Paying users: ~18.10M (unguided)”; the bull scenario assumed “Paying users up 25–40K.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue beat the $625.6 million consensus estimate, but the underlying growth rate remained very weak: revenue grew just 0.1% on a constant-currency basis and 1.7% excluding Form Swift. The nominal beat was positive, while the near-flat constant-currency growth tempered the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue rose 0.9% year-over-year to $631.5 million, with growth of 1.7% excluding Form Swift, and just 0.1% on a constant currency basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $625.6M (Zacks, early Aug 2026)” and company guidance of “$624–627M.”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP operating margin came in above the 38.5% guide and the preview’s 38.5%–39% expectation. The year-over-year decline was also smaller than the roughly 300-basis-point compression anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin reached 39.7%, beating guidance of 38.5%,” and “declined roughly 180 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP op. margin | ~38.5–39%”; the preview said this implied “~300bp YoY compression.”

surprises.description: Gross margin improved from the 81.1% reported in Q1 and its year-over-year decline narrowed from Q1’s 180 basis points to 60 basis points. However, management still flagged further second-half pressure from AI compute costs, making the improvement less reassuring than a full resolution of the margin concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: Gross margin was “81.6%,” down “about 60 basis points year-over-year” due to AI compute costs; management flagged “further back-half pressure partially offset by infrastructure efficiencies.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified the “Gross margin trend” as the key tell on whether AI and infrastructure spending was “an investment cycle or a structural drag,” and cited Q1 gross margin of “81.1%, down 180bp YoY.”

surprises.description: The company raised full-year revenue guidance above the preview’s prior range and near/above the $2.51 billion consensus, but the increase was modest relative to the currency help: management said the new range included a $31 million currency tailwind and still implied only about 80 basis points of growth excluding Form Swift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year revenue guidance was raised by $13.5 million to $2.513-$2.523 billion,” implying “only about 80 basis points of year-over-year growth excluding Form Swift,” and was “aided by a $31 million currency tailwind.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026: Revenue guide $2.497–2.512B (consensus $2.51B)”; the preview noted that “a simple reaffirm may read as a cut.”

surprises.description: Full-year non-GAAP operating-margin guidance was raised by 50 basis points, taking the range above the preview’s expected 39.5%–40% range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year 2026 non-GAAP operating margin guidance by 50 basis points to 40.0%-40.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP op. margin guide 39.5–40%.”

surprises.description: Full-year unlevered free-cash-flow guidance increased by $15 million, from at least $1.055 billion to at least $1.070 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “lifted unlevered free cash flow guidance by $15 million to at or above $1.070 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Unlevered FCF at least $1.055B.”

surprises.description: Dropbox announced a new $900 million share-repurchase authorization, an additional capital-return commitment not specified in the preview. The preview had highlighted buyback pace and the concern that purchases around $34 would be less accretive than Q1 purchases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a new $900 million share repurchase authorization” and repurchased “approximately 12.6 million shares for about $315 million in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “pace and leverage commentary” and noted that “Buybacks at about $34 are less accretive than Q1's roughly $25.66 average.”

surprises.description: Teams returned to positive license growth for the first time since 2024, while the Simple SKU was the largest contributor to net new paying users. The preview discussed user growth but did not anticipate these specific product-level drivers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The ‘Simple’ SKU was the largest contributor to net new paying user growth, while Teams turned to positive license growth for the first time since 2024.”

surprises.description: Integrations with Claude and ChatGPT had already drawn more than 150,000 connected users despite minimal dedicated investment, an early sign of AI-ecosystem traction not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of Dash monetization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Integrations with tools like Claude and ChatGPT have already attracted over 150,000 connected users despite minimal dedicated investment.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $91.4 million, about 2% above the $89.63 million consensus estimate in the preview and near the top of the company’s Q2 guidance range. This was a modest upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated revenue grew 4.1% year-over-year to $91.4 million in Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus: $89.63M”; company guidance was “$87.9M – $91.9M.”

surprises.description: The company expanded its buyback authorization to $200 million and repurchased about $9.6 million of shares in Q2. The preview said an expanded authorization was possible, but the increase from $100 million to $200 million was a stronger concrete action than it had established as expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased 300,000 shares for approximately $9.6 million in Q2 and raised its buyback authorization to $200 million, leaving about $118 million available.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “About $28M remained of the $100M buyback authorization after Q1, so a new or expanded authorization is a possible catalyst.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was close to expectations, but its 52.9% margin was below the preview’s approximately 53.4% guide midpoint. Management also put full-year margins toward the low end of the range as hiring ramps, a modestly weaker margin outlook than the preview’s general expectation of a step-down for hiring.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was essentially flat year-over-year at $48.3 million (0.5% growth) with a 52.9% margin, and management guided full-year margins toward the lower end of the 50%-55% range as hiring ramps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin: ~53.4% at midpoint”; the preview expected the margin to “step[] down on hiring” and identified “below 52%” as the point where costs would have arrived faster than revenue.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a sharp sequential improvement in retention: net revenue retention rose to 103.1% from 102% in Q1. The preview did not set an expectation for retention, so this was new positive evidence about expansion within existing enterprise accounts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenue retention rate rose to 103.1%, up approximately 110 basis points sequentially from 102% in Q1, signaling successful expansion within existing enterprise accounts.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow rose about 25% year-over-year in Q2, while management expects full-year 2026 free cash flow to be approximately flat with 2025. The preview did not discuss or set an expectation for free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow rose approximately 25% year-over-year to $25.5 million, with full-year 2026 free cash flow expected to approximate 2025's $106 million.”

surprises.description: SoHo’s Q2 revenue decline narrowed substantially from the prior quarter, but management said declines of 5% to 7% are expected over the next two quarters. The preview did not provide a SoHo outlook, so this was new information: an improved current-quarter trend alongside continued near-term contraction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SoHo revenue declined only 4.7% year-over-year to $30.9 million, a marked improvement from the 9.5% decline in Q1, though management expects declines of 5% to 7% over the next two quarters.”

in_line: Corporate revenue reached $60.5 million and grew 9.3%, essentially matching the preview’s expectation of roughly $60.5–$60.7 million and about 9.6% growth.
Adjusted EBITDA of $48.3 million was close to the preview’s approximately $48 million estimate.

Management reaffirmed FY2026 guidance rather than raising it, an outcome the preview allowed for; management now expects revenue between the midpoint and high end and EBITDA/EPS slightly above midpoint.
The VA contribution was expected to be about $9 million in 2026, and the call said it should be north of $9 million.

surprises.description: Clarus reported Q2 sales of $56.2 million, well above the preview’s $51.54 million consensus anchor and its alternate estimate of about $53.3 million. Instead of the expected year-over-year decline, sales rose 1.6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 sales rose just 1.6% year-over-year to $56.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $51.54M (-6.6% YoY)” and “Revenue (alt.) | ~$53.3M (-3.4% YoY).”

surprises.description: Adventure sales fell 11.9%, a much milder decline than the preview’s roughly 22% base case and better than its -20% positive-surprise threshold. However, the full-year Adventure outlook is now about $68 million, down from the previously stated $70 million, despite the better-than-feared quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adventure down 11.9% due to weakness in North American and Australian wholesale markets”; full-year guidance has “Adventure now expected at ~$68 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Results better than about -20% would be a positive surprise”; the prior-quarter discussion says Adventure’s FY revenue guide was cut “from $80M to $70M.”

surprises.description: FY adjusted EBITDA guidance jumped to $12–13 million, versus the preview’s expected reaffirmation of $3–5 million. The increase is less indicative of stronger underlying earnings than the headline suggests: roughly $8 million comes from the tariff refund and the elimination of about $2 million in expected legal expenses.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance was raised sharply to $12-13 million from the prior $3-5 million, but roughly $8 million of the increase stems from the tariff refund and elimination of ~$2 million in expected legal expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA | $3–5M”; “FY26 guidance reaffirmation” was the base case, and the preview says about $3M of legal and regulatory expense was included in guidance.

surprises.description: The reported 48.9% gross margin was heavily boosted by the tariff refund flagged in the preview, but margin excluding the refund was 38%, modestly above the preview’s estimate of about 37%. Outdoor’s underlying margin also improved as discounting eased and the company shifted toward full-price sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reported gross margin [was] 48.9%”; “Excluding the tariff refund, consolidated gross margin was 38%, and Outdoor's underlying margin improved 160 basis points to 36.5%, reflecting less discounting and a shift to a full-price model.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~37%, not separately published”; the preview also flagged a “$6.2M IEEPA tariff refund excluded from guidance.”

surprises.description: Alongside the tariff refund the preview had identified, Clarus recognized $3 million of interest income, which the preview did not mention. This was an additional one-time benefit, distinct from the underlying margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recognized a one-time IEEPA tariff refund of $6.1 million (plus $3 million interest income) at Outdoor.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cites “a $6.2M IEEPA tariff refund excluded from guidance,” but does not mention interest income.

surprises.description: Black Diamond apparel grew 22.9%, above the preview’s expectation of double-digit apparel growth, while clearance merchandise fell 61%. The clearance decline and fifth consecutive quarter of apparel growth point to a stronger full-price mix than the preview specifically anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Black Diamond's Apparel in-line sales grew a robust 22.9% while clearance merchandise fell 61%, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of apparel growth and a healthier full-price mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “double-digit apparel growth [was] expected” and noted “full-price apparel grew 10.1%” in Q1.

surprises.description: The preview expected the Jefferies review to remain ongoing with no further comment, but management said it is exploring strategic alternatives, including a potential sale of all or part of the business. That is a more concrete update than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is exploring strategic alternatives with Jefferies, including a potential sale of all or part of the business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had announced a strategic review and “would give no further commentary”; its base case expected the review to be “ongoing.”

surprises.description: The preview described the DOJ and CPSC matters as an overhang and said it had not confirmed their status. The call reported that the DOJ closed its criminal investigation into Black Diamond's avalanche transceiver reporting on June 4, 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The DoJ closed its criminal investigation into Black Diamond's avalanche transceiver reporting on June 4, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “I did not confirm the full DOJ and CPSC matters tied to Black Diamond avalanche beacons, which the preview describes as an overhang.”

in_line: Full-year revenue guidance remained at $245–255 million, as the preview expected reaffirmation.
Cash was $28.9 million, above the preview’s roughly $22 million level flagged as a negative signal.

surprises.description: Q1 revenue was $157 million, above the preview’s $151.7 million consensus and the $152 million high end of company guidance. The roughly 3% beat versus the guidance high end was stronger than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY27 revenue reached $157 million,” “beating the high end of guidance by 3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Consensus | $151.7M | Company guidance | $151–152M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in well above the preview’s roughly $69 million expectation: $75 million, or 8% above the high end of guidance. This was a larger upside than the preview’s base case implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $75 million (48% margin), exceeding the high end of guidance by 8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$69M | Company, May 13, 2026”; guidance was “$68.5–69.5M.”
