surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue: “$206–210M”; preview “My Estimate”: “$140–155M.”

surprises.description: MARA disclosed $600 million of new Bitcoin-backed borrowings at a 7.56% weighted average cost of debt, with 54% of its Bitcoin holdings pledged as collateral. The preview flagged liquidity and debt as key issues, but did not anticipate this level of new borrowing or collateralization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “MARA entered two Bitcoin-backed credit facilities with Coinbase and Two Prime totaling $600 million in incremental borrowings at a 7.56% weighted average cost of debt, bringing 54% of its Bitcoin holdings pledged as collateral.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “Check cash, remaining convertible notes, and whether the ATM was used in Q2” and to watch “whether MARA sells more bitcoin to fund” Long Ridge.

surprises.description: Long Ridge remained a pending acquisition, but MARA said it would be funded entirely through non-dilutive financing—better than the preview’s concern about substantial incremental debt or a possible Bitcoin sale. The call also supplied expected annualized EBITDA and contracted-output details that the preview had not specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: The “pending Long Ridge acquisition” is “a $1.5 billion enterprise value deal,” expected to contribute “roughly $144 million in annualized EBITDA” with “about 70% of output under long-term contracts,” and “is being funded entirely through non-dilutive financing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “about $785M+ of incremental debt” and said investors wanted the “equity/debt split” and to know “whether MARA sells more bitcoin to fund the deal.”

surprises.description: Management was more confident about AI infrastructure leasing than the preview’s base case of repeating earlier language without new contracted megawatts: it said it expected at least two leases before year-end and that tenant demand exceeded initial expectations. No signed leases or lease economics were reported, however.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expressed confidence in signing at least two AI infrastructure leases before year-end through its Starwood partnership, and noted tenant demand has exceeded initial expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had guided to “multiple tenant leases signed by year-end” and its base case was “Management repeats Q1 language without new contracted megawatts.”

surprises.description: MARA reported a much larger prospective power portfolio than the preview had laid out: approximately 4.8 gigawatts, nearly 2.5 times its size at the start of the year, subject to pending transactions and approvals. The preview discussed the power pipeline but did not set an expectation of this scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “MARA expects its total power portfolio to reach approximately 4.8 gigawatts, nearly 2.5x its size at the start of the year, upon completion of pending transactions and approvals.”

surprises.description: MARA also acquired rights to a Texas site with potential for up to 2 gigawatts of capacity and said it would not require utility infrastructure improvements. The preview did not anticipate this site acquisition or these development advantages.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company acquired rights to a 1,200-acre Matagorda County, Texas site with potential for up to 2 gigawatts of capacity,” which “has no required utility infrastructure improvements and existing transmission lines.”

in_line: The $343 million unrealized Bitcoin mark-to-market loss was close to the preview’s roughly $350 million assumption, even though the total EPS loss was worse than its estimate.
Energized hashrate was 70.3 EH, close to the preview’s estimate of about 70.7 EH and consistent with its expectation that hashrate would be flat to down from 72.2 EH.
The preview noted that MARA had sold Bitcoin in Q1 and was adding Bitcoin in Q2; quarter-end holdings of 35,577 were modestly above the 35,303 Q1 figure, consistent with that direction.
No signed AI lease, named tenant, or lease economics were reported; the preview’s base case expected no new contracted megawatts in Q2.

surprises.description: Cloudflare was expected to deliver roughly $680 million of revenue, with buy-side estimates around $675–685 million; it reported $696.1 million, or 36% growth. U.S. revenue was especially strong, growing 41% and accounting for 51% of revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $696.1 million, up 36% year-over-year, with U.S. revenue accelerating fastest at 41% growth and representing 51% of total revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue growth vs. ~$680M (+33%). Consensus is $665M, but buy-side expectations sit near $675–685M.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS was expected to be $0.27, but Cloudflare reported $0.29 diluted EPS. That exceeded the preview’s published consensus, although it was within the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net income was $107.8 million ($0.29 diluted EPS).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS … $0.27 (Zacks, unchanged past 30 days).”

surprises.description: The preview looked for dollar-based net retention of at least 119%; Cloudflare reported 120%, accelerating two points sequentially after a two-point decline in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dollar-based net retention accelerated to 120%, up 2 percentage points sequentially and 6 points year-over-year, driven by expansion with the largest customers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dollar-based net retention at or above 119%.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged a 14% non-GAAP operating margin as the bar to watch. The reported margin was 13.8%, slightly below that level, even though it expanded 240 basis points sequentially.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin of 13.8% expanded 240 basis points sequentially but declined 30 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin at or above 14%.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated Q2 charges of $140–150 million, mostly in the quarter. The reported $151 million was just above that range, and full-year charges are now expected to reach $165 million, indicating a higher charge burden than initially estimated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Results excluded $151 million in severance and restructuring charges, with full-year charges now expected up to $165 million versus initial estimates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$140–150M of restructuring charges … land mostly in Q2.”

surprises.description: The Q3 revenue outlook implies 31% year-over-year growth, below Q2’s reported 36%, pointing to renewed deceleration after the stronger Q2 result. The preview did not give a Q3 revenue estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue guidance of $736-737 million implies 31% year-over-year growth.”

surprises.description: Gross margin improved sequentially for the first time in eight quarters, whereas Q1 gross margin had fallen sharply quarter over quarter. However, the reported 73.1% was still down 320 basis points year over year due to network cost allocation shifts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin was 73.1%, improving 30 basis points sequentially for the first time in eight quarters but down 320 basis points year-over-year due to network cost allocation shifts.”

surprises.description: Cloudflare added a record 986 large customers and accelerated their growth to 27%, from 25% last quarter. The preview did not set an expectation for large-customer additions or growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added a record 986 net new large customers … ending with 4,698 such customers, up 27% and an acceleration from 25% growth last quarter.”

surprises.description: Cloudflare added more than 80,000 paying customers in the quarter and reported 74% year-over-year paying-customer growth, figures not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cloudflare added over 80,000 paying customers in the quarter—as many as it had in total at its 2019 IPO—driving 74% year-over-year paying customer growth.”

surprises.description: The Workers platform added nearly 2 million developers in Q2 alone, more than the 1.5 million added during all of 2025. The preview did not flag this developer-adoption metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Workers platform grew to over 7.4 million developers, adding nearly 2 million in Q2 alone, surpassing the 1.5 million added in all of 2025.”

surprises.description: Management said non-human traffic exceeded human traffic on Cloudflare’s network for the first time and could reach 1,000 times human traffic within five years, while describing agentic monetization products such as cloudflare.pay. The preview had focused on AI-bot monetization but did not anticipate this traffic milestone or projection.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For the first time, over 50% of network traffic was non-human in Q2,” and management projected it “could reach 1,000x human traffic within five years,” underpinning products like “cloudflare.pay.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $2.864–2.870 billion cleared the preview’s key threshold of above $2.85 billion, broadly meeting that flagged expectation.

surprises.description: Against the preview’s $0.19 core EPS consensus, Navient reported $0.29 of core EPS. A net $0.04 benefit from one-time items brought the figure to $0.29, but adjusted core EPS was still $0.25, above consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 core EPS was $0.29,” and “excluding a net $0.04 benefit from one-time items, adjusted core EPS was $0.25.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core EPS” consensus for Q2: “$0.19 (Zacks, Aug 2026).”

surprises.description: The preview looked for legacy private credit to remain a key test after Q1 improvement. Navient reported a $23 million reserve build on the remaining private portfolio, saying credit improvement moderated as the quarter progressed, even as private charge-offs improved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded $26 million in total provisions, including a $23 million reserve build on the remaining private portfolio because credit improvement moderated as the quarter progressed.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “two clean quarters in a row are needed to rebuild confidence” and highlighted the Q3 2025 “reserve build of $138M” as the main concern.

surprises.description: Navient classified $528 million—just under 10% of its legacy private loan portfolio—as held for sale and released $19 million of associated allowance. The preview did not anticipate this portfolio reclassification, which also signals potential further reclassifications.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Navient classified $528 million (just under 10%) of its ~$5.4 billion legacy private loan portfolio as held for sale, releasing $19 million of associated allowance and signaling potential future reclassifications.”

surprises.description: The preview described CECL and origination-related costs as a drag on FY26 earnings. Navient said newly originated in-school loans will instead be accounted for at fair value starting in Q3, with no CECL allowance or provision, removing provision expense that otherwise would have affected 2026 earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Beginning Q3 2026, newly originated in-school loans will be accounted for at fair value with no CECL allowance or provision, removing near-term provision expense that would have otherwise hit 2026 earnings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said FY26 guidance was “net of a $0.35–$0.40 per-share drag from CECL and opex tied to the origination increase.”

surprises.description: Navient returned $17 million to shareholders in Q2, down from the $38 million returned in Q1, while roughly $75–76 million remained under the buyback authorization. Management attributed the slower repurchase pace to 10b5-1 plan mechanics and capital needs for growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Navient returned only $17 million to shareholders via dividends and buybacks in Q2, with ~$75-76 million remaining on its $100 million buyback authorization,” and management cited “10b5-1 plan mechanics and capital needs for growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported that “Q1 returned $38M to shareholders, including $23M of buybacks,” and flagged “Dividend and buyback posture” as a catalyst to watch.

in_line: Operating expenses were $85 million, at the low end of the preview’s roughly $85–88 million watch range, and Navient said it remained on pace for the $350 million or lower full-year outlook.

Private charge-offs improved to 1.8% from 1.91%, broadly matching the preview’s focus on further improvement from the Q1 level. Combined originations grew more than 60% year over year, consistent with the prior quarter’s 60% growth pace and the preview’s expectation of continued origination growth.

surprises.description: Gross profit was $10.4 million, below the preview’s $11.0 million-or-more watch point and the $11.1–$11.3 million base case. Gross margin was 16.3%, also below the roughly 17.7% base-case expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit was $10.4 million” and “gross margin at 16.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross profit dollars. Seasonality alone should deliver about $11.0M or more”; base case: “$11.1–11.3M / ~17.7%.”

surprises.description: The company recorded an $11 million non-cash goodwill impairment, an unexpected charge that management said was triggered by the decline in its market capitalization. Management said it did not affect liquidity, cash flow, or debt covenants, but it was a substantial unanticipated item.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded an $11 million non-cash goodwill impairment charge triggered by a decline in market capitalization,” with “no impact on liquidity, cash flow, or debt covenants.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $64.1 million, modestly above the $63.55 million consensus, and grew 8% year over year versus the preview’s 6.8% expectation. This confirmed the anticipated return to positive year-over-year growth, with a small beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $64.1 million, up 8% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $63.55M” and “Y/Y | +6.8%”; the preview also said $63.55 million “would end five-plus quarters of Y/Y declines.”

surprises.description: Management provided a constructive Q3 outlook: sequential revenue growth and gross margins flat to slightly higher as industrial volumes ramp at select large customers. The preview did not give a specific Q3 outlook to compare against.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided to sequential revenue growth in Q3 and expects gross margins to be flat to slightly up as industrial volumes ramp at select large customers.”

surprises.description: SG&A fell 11% year over year even as revenue grew 8%, indicating better expense leverage than the preview had specifically laid out for Q2. First-half SG&A was down 20% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A fell 11% year-over-year to $8.2 million despite 8% revenue growth,” and “first-half SG&A was down 20% versus the prior year.”

surprises.description: The company reported four new wallet-share wins in the quarter, including one with a large national automotive parts retailer, and said it had closed nine seven-figure opportunities since the second half of 2025. The preview identified operational indicators to watch but did not anticipate these wins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company landed four new wallet-share wins in Q2, including one with a large national automotive parts retailer,” and “has closed nine seven-figure wallet-share opportunities since the back half of 2025.”

surprises.description: Management said macroeconomic uncertainty is elongating the sales cycle for new large-brand opportunities, a negative qualification on the timing of new business that the preview had not flagged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Macroeconomic uncertainty is elongating the sales cycle for new large-brand opportunities.”

surprises.description: Working-capital indicators improved: DSOs fell to about 70 days from the mid-70s in Q1, and working-capital days dropped to 5 from 12. The preview did not identify these improvements as an expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DSOs improved to roughly 70 days from the mid-70s in Q1,” with a near-term target of the mid-60s; “working capital days dropped to 5 from 12 in Q1 and 19 a year ago.”

in_line: Gross profit increased sequentially from $9.7 million in Q1 to $10.4 million in Q2, consistent with management’s prior guidance for sequential gross-profit growth, though below the preview’s Q2 dollar expectation.
The company made another voluntary $2 million early payment on its Monroe Capital term debt, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it would make a second prepayment.

surprises.description: Q2 sales were $152.5 million, well above the preview’s roughly $129 million company guide and $136.6 million consensus, rather than flat sequentially. Sales rose 18.6% from Q1, exceeding the company’s prior expectation of flat sequential revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales were $152.5 million” and were “up 18.6% sequentially from Q1's $128 million, exceeding the company's prior expectation of flat sequential revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Company guidance (Q2) | ‘Flat sequentially,’ about $129M | Consensus | $136.6M”; the preview also says “Q2 ‘flat or slightly better’ sequentially.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.73, substantially above the preview’s $0.32 consensus. It remained below the preview’s roughly $0.95 clean Q2 FY25 comparison, which the preview said excluded the prior-year tax benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income was $16.9 million ($0.73 per diluted share),” while the prior-year figure included a “$29.2 million ($1.27 per share) tax benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS | Not found | $0.32”; the preview also gives “Clean EPS comp (Q2 FY25) ... ~$0.95 (my adjustment).”

surprises.description: Gross margin recovered more than the preview’s 24% threshold for an initial recovery signal and exceeded its 23% base case, reaching 27.1%. The sequential improvement was substantial despite margin remaining below the year-ago level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved approximately 420 basis points sequentially to 27.1% from 22.9% in Q1,” driven by “operational improvements in Wisconsin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “24% or higher would be the first real sign of recovery”; the base scenario assumed “~23%” gross margin and the bull scenario “~25%.”

surprises.description: Instead of the working-capital pressure the preview expected ahead of the second-half ramp, operating cash flow reached $56.6 million and enabled a roughly $38.8 million debt reduction during the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow surged to $56.6 million in Q2,” enabling “a total debt reduction of approximately $38.8 million during the quarter”; total debt fell from $103.4 million to about $72.6 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A working-capital build ahead of the H2 ramp is expected.” The preview also noted “$95M is drawn against $45.1M of cash.”

in_line: Management said second-half 2026 sales should be roughly in line with second-half 2025, as the preview expected; the preview said repeating “approximately in line with second half 2025” would keep the thesis intact.

Oil and gas demand remained soft, with no significant improvement expected for the rest of the year, consistent with the preview’s warning that management had said no near-term improvement was expected.
Richard Hu is due to become CEO on August 17, consistent with the leadership timing already stated in the preview.

surprises.description: Home Services reached $141.6 million, well above the preview’s roughly $120 million watch level and even above its $130 million bull-case threshold. The preview had highlighted demand exceeding capacity, while the reported 88% growth shows a substantially stronger quarter than those thresholds implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The home services vertical was 38% of Q4 revenue, growing 88% to a record $141.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether Q4 Home Services clears about $120M”; the bull scenario cited “Home Services above $130M.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue of $373.9 million exceeded the approximately $360.6 million consensus by about 3.7% and topped the company’s $370 million guidance ceiling. The preview’s base case was $358–366 million, so the reported result was a clear upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 revenue grew 43% year-over-year to $373.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus ~$360.6M”; company guidance was “$350–370M”; the base scenario was “$358–366M.”

surprises.description: FY27 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $150–160 million is above the preview’s reported buy-side anchor of $135–150 million, with even the low end matching the anchor’s high end. The preview had expected strong double-digit growth, but the company’s 38% growth outlook is stronger than that anchor implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full fiscal year 2027 guidance is… adjusted EBITDA of $150-160 million (38% growth, 10.3% margin, 160 bps expansion).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A buy-side anchor is reported at roughly $1.45–1.55B revenue and $135–150M EBITDA.”

surprises.description: Auto insurance growth accelerated to 37% year over year, despite the preview’s focus on sharply rising carrier ad spend and difficult FY27 comparisons. The preview had cited the prior quarter’s record growth of 27%, while Q4 reported a higher growth rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Auto insurance up 37% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 auto insurance was a record, +27% YoY. Carrier ad spend rose sharply in 2025, which makes FY27 comparisons difficult.”

surprises.description: Management described a longer runway for carriers’ shift to digital and performance marketing, estimating they are only about 20% through it. The preview highlighted difficult carrier-spending comparisons but did not flag this estimate of how much of the shift remains.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management… estimates carriers are only about 20% through the shift toward digital and performance marketing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “Carrier ad spend rose sharply in 2025, which makes FY27 comparisons difficult.”

in_line: Q4 adjusted EBITDA was $41.4 million, within the approximately $40 million consensus and the $37–43 million company guidance range; its 11.1% margin also met the preview’s 10.8–11.2% base-case range and exceeded the flagged 10.6% floor.
FY26 revenue of $1.3 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $112.5 million were within the prior guidance ranges of $1.25–1.3 billion and $110–115 million, respectively.
FY27 revenue guidance of $1.45–1.55 billion matched the preview’s reported buy-side anchor, and quantified the outlook at 16% growth.

Management’s expectation to close one or possibly two smaller accretive acquisitions was consistent with the preview’s flag that an acquisition could be a notable capital-allocation announcement. The preview also flagged buybacks; the company reported $14.6 million of Q4 repurchases and $31.4 million for the year.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $631 million, above the preview’s $613–619 million consensus range, and grew 2% on a constant-currency basis rather than being roughly flat. Growth was 6% excluding China.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue grew 2% on a constant currency basis to $631 million, but excluding China grew 6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$613–619M (described as flat Y/Y)” and the company had guided Q2 “roughly flat” with Q1’s $619.8M.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $129 million, well above the preview’s estimated $100–110 million, and rose 21% year over year. The 20% margin was at the high end of the preview’s anticipated range, but the EBITDA amount materially exceeded its estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 21% to $129 million with EBITDA margin expanding 310 basis points to 20% of revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$100–110M (~17% margin)” and the preview said a Q2 margin of “19–20% or higher” would support the H2 exit rate.

surprises.description: Management made a substantial FY2026 guidance reset: revenue is now $2.52–2.60 billion, adjusted EBITDA $540–560 million, and adjusted EPS $0.65–0.90, all well below the May guidance cited in the preview. The EBITDA range is also below the preview’s bear-case threshold of $600 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was revised down to $2.52-2.60 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of $540-560 million and adjusted EPS lowered to $0.65-0.90.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 guidance of “Revenue: $2.70–2.75B,” “Adj. EBITDA: $615–630M,” and “Adj. EPS: $1.80–2.00”; its bear case assumed “FY EBITDA below $600M, EPS near $1.20–1.50.”

surprises.description: China revenue fell 23% as customers cut inventories faster than anticipated amid uncertainty about proposed IVD pricing guidelines. This indicates a more immediate demand and inventory impact than the preview’s expectation that implementation would slip to mid-2027 and have a modeled 2026 impact near $30 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “China revenue declined 23% year-over-year as uncertainty around proposed IVD pricing guidelines drove customers to reduce inventories more quickly than anticipated.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the guidelines’ “implementation [was] slipping to mid-2027” and described “a company-modeled impact near $30M in 2026.”

surprises.description: Instead of maintaining the preview’s expected $100–120 million FY2026 free-cash-flow guidance, management withdrew FCF guidance. Q2 FCF was negative $136 million, including a $25 million payment to Grifols to terminate the joint business arrangement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company withdrew its free cash flow guidance for 2026 due to uncertainty around China, respiratory demand, and related working capital impacts”; “Q2 free cash flow was negative $136 million and operating cash flow was negative $111 million, including a $25 million payment to Grifols.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 FCF guidance of “$100–120M” and flagged “FCF and leverage trajectory against the $100–120M FCF guide.”

surprises.description: Leverage moved to 4.3x adjusted EBITDA, above the 4.1x level cited for Q1 and further from management’s year-end target of 3.25–3.5x. The call also reported only $123 million of cash against $250 million drawn on the revolving credit facility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt leverage stood at 4.3 times adjusted EBITDA, with only $123 million in cash against $250 million outstanding under the revolving credit facility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said net debt was “4.1x adj. EBITDA at Q1” and management “targets 3.25–3.5x by year-end.”

surprises.description: Management is assuming second-half respiratory revenue will be at the lower end of historical seasons, rather than relying on a typical seasonal uptick. That adds a demand risk to the large second-half earnings step-up implied by the preview’s guidance math.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is modeling second-half respiratory revenue at the lower end of historical seasons rather than assuming a typical uptick, citing lower US positivity rates and weak southern hemisphere data.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the existing guide implied “$401–416M” of H2 adjusted EBITDA and “a step-up of about 950bp.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin contracted even as adjusted EBITDA margin expanded: gross margin was down 130 basis points year over year, with lower China volumes worsening geographic mix. The preview discussed EBITDA-margin recovery but did not flag this gross-margin pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin fell 130 basis points year-over-year to 44.4%, pressured by unfavorable geographic mix from lower China volumes.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed strong growth in core businesses outside China: labs and triage were each up 9% in Q2, and those businesses represent about 75% of the company. The preview’s headline revenue expectation was flat and did not highlight this segment-level strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The core labs and immunohematology businesses outside China represent about 75% of the company and are expected to grow 3-5% in the second half, with labs outside China up 9% and triage up 9% in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q2 consensus revenue as “~$613–619M (described as flat Y/Y).”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin was 20%, at the high end of the preview’s 19–20% level that it said would support the H2 exit rate.

surprises.description: Net sales were $135.6 million, above the preview’s $129 million consensus and $130 million house estimate, and rose from Q1’s $132 million rather than declining sequentially. The year-over-year decline was also shallower than the preview’s estimated 15.1%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales declined 10.7% year-over-year to $135.6 million”; Q1 net sales were $132.0 million, and management framed the decline as intentional.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | $129.0M”; “Our estimate | Rev $130M”; the preview said a sequential increase “would be the largest available positive surprise.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $1.8 million, modestly above the preview’s $1.5 million house estimate, though it fell short of the preview’s +$2 million bull-trigger level. A second consecutive positive quarter itself was expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was positive $1.8 million,” the “highest adjusted EBITDA since Q3 2023” and the “sixth consecutive quarter of sequential improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Our estimate ... adj. EBITDA +$1.5M”; the preview identified “Above $0” as a pass and “Above +$2M” as the bull trigger.

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 33.2%, above the preview’s 32.5–33.0% implied range and its 32.8% house estimate. The improvement came despite tariff and freight cost pressures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded to 33.2%,” up 70 basis points sequentially and 40 basis points year-over-year, with favorable product mix and freight optimization offsetting tariff and freight cost pressures.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~32.5–33.0% (implied)” and “Our estimate ... GM 32.8%.”

surprises.description: The company received $4.4 million in IEEPA tariff claims, exceeding the preview’s stated pursuit of up to $4.3 million, and recognized $2.2 million in Q2. The benefit is partly tempered because it was reinvested in pricing and marketing, while the remaining $2.2 million is to flow through COGS in future quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $4.4 million in IEEPA tariff claims, recognizing $2.2 million in Q2 (reinvested in pricing and marketing) with the remaining $2.2 million to flow through COGS in future quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the company was “pursuing up to $4.3M in CBP claims” and that “any recognition is upside not in the numbers.”

surprises.description: The company added a new undrawn $25 million revolving credit facility maturing in March 2028, an additional liquidity backstop not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $38 million in cash, no revolver debt ... plus a new undrawn $25 million revolving credit facility maturing March 2028.”

surprises.description: The reported $3.2 million GAAP net loss was worse than the preview’s house EPS estimate of -$0.23 would imply on roughly 8 million shares, although it falls within the preview’s widely dispersed and explicitly unreliable EPS estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss narrowed sharply to $3.2 million from $12.7 million in Q2 2025,” with the difference versus adjusted EBITDA driven primarily by noncash depreciation, amortization, and share-based compensation.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Our estimate ... EPS -$0.23”; the preview also noted published EPS estimates of “-$0.85 or -$0.09” and called them “unreliable.”

in_line: A-Premium’s annualized run rate was approaching $50 million, broadly matching the preview’s near-term target of $50 million and its view that a figure below about $50 million would indicate deceleration.
Cash ended at $38 million with no revolver debt, above the preview’s $35 million-or-more benchmark; the preview’s expectation was to hold cash without new financing.
Management reaffirmed the target of being free cash flow positive in 2026, as the preview expected.
The company delivered the second consecutive positive adjusted EBITDA quarter that the preview identified as the base-case expectation.

surprises.description: Backlog rose to $271 million, well above the preview’s expectation that it would stay near $246 million or in the $245–255 million base-case range, and above the $260 million level identified as a meaningful step-up. This is a stronger-than-expected build even excluding potential future runtime-license and gainshare revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total backlog grew to $271 million, up 10% sequentially and up 16% year-over-year,” and “excludes potential future Cimetrix runtime licenses and gainshare revenues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Rosenblatt expects it to stay stable near $246M”; base case: “backlog $245–255M”; “a step-up toward $260M or more would” support the second half.

surprises.description: Gross margin was 73%, materially below the preview’s approximate 76% guided-trajectory estimate. Management attributed the quarter-over-quarter decline to higher perpetual software licenses and expects recovery next quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin fell to 73% in Q2 (down from Q1 due to higher perpetual software licenses), but management expects recovery next quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The ~76% gross margin and ~24–25% operating margin figures are estimates from the guided trajectory”; the long-term gross-margin model is 77%.

surprises.description: Operating margin reached 22%, below the preview’s estimated 24–25% trajectory and further from the 27% long-term model. The year-over-year improvement was positive, but the reported margin was weaker than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin reached 22%, roughly 300 basis points higher year-over-year, with a reaffirmed 27% target operating margin model.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The ~76% gross margin and ~24–25% operating margin figures are estimates from the guided trajectory”; the long-term model includes a 27% operating margin.

surprises.description: The company reported several substantial contract wins that the preview did not anticipate: 8-figure secureWISE and DirectScan contracts and multiple 7-figure Exensio deals. The largest secureWISE contract in company history extends across virtually all of an existing customer’s 300mm fabs, with further expansion upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured 8-figure contracts for both secureWISE and DirectScan systems, plus multiple 7-figure Exensio deals”; “The largest secureWISE contract in company history was signed with an existing equipment customer at a minimum contract value, extending across virtually all 300mm fabs with upside expansion expected.”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP EPS of $0.27 was slightly above the $0.26 consensus estimate. The beat was small, and the result was below the preview’s base-case scenario range of $0.28–$0.31.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 EPS was $0.27.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS $0.26 (consistent across sources)”; base case: “$0.28–0.31.”

surprises.description: By Q2, the company had placed three new eProbe machines and reached two-thirds of its six-machine annual goal, including placements with two new customers. That is faster progress than the one machine shipped in Q1 and the preview’s focus on whether the annual target was advancing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company placed 3 new eProbe e-beam inspection machines (2 with new customers, one a 5-year subscription), reaching two-thirds of its annual goal of 6 machines.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The company’s FY framing is … an eProbe/DFI target of six systems in 2026 (one shipped in Q1)”; the preview identified “eProbe units shipped year-to-date against the six-unit plan” as a key metric.

in_line: Q2 revenue was $61.5 million, close to the roughly $61 million consensus anchor and within the preview’s $60–63 million live band.
Management reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance of 20%, as the preview expected.

surprises.description: The preview looked for revenue of about $300–302 million and diluted EPS of $0.53; PRA reported $372 million of revenue and $1.51 per share. The results were lifted significantly by an unanticipated $349 million increase to European ERC, which the company said should add about $260 million of portfolio income over the remaining cash curves, though with only nominal net-income impact in 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income attributable to PRA rose to $58 million, or $1.51 per diluted share, aided significantly by the European ERC increase driving total revenues up 29% to $372 million.” The company increased European ERC by “$349 million” and expects “approximately $260 million of additional portfolio income over the remaining life of the cash curves.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $300.0M (MarketBeat) or $301.6M (Investing.com)” and “Diluted EPS | $0.53.”

surprises.description: Cash collections were $559 million, below the preview’s own $570–585 million estimate and its +6% year-over-year threshold for maintaining the growth trajectory. However, PRA said collections were 4% above its own expectations, making the comparison mixed rather than an unqualified miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash collections grew 4% year-over-year to $559 million” and “total collections came in 4% above the company's expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash collections (own estimate ~$570–585M)” and “Growth below about +6% Y/Y would break the two-year compounding story.”

surprises.description: PRA announced a second wave of workforce reductions and additional savings that the preview did not anticipate: this wave is expected to save about $20 million annualized, bringing the two waves to roughly $35 million in annualized savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company eliminated “100 U.S. corporate/overhead roles and 35 offshore roles,” expecting “about $20 million in annualized net savings,” with combined first- and second-wave savings of “approximately $35 million annualized.”

surprises.description: The Board authorized a new share repurchase program of up to $150 million, a step-up beyond the $10 million repurchased in the quarter and the $40 million repurchased over the past 12 months.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board authorized a new share repurchase program of up to $150 million,” following “$10 million repurchased in the quarter and $40 million over the past 12 months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Any step-up in buyback authorization or pace would be a meaningful catalyst.”

surprises.description: PRA refinanced its $730 million European credit facility and extended its maturity by five years, leaving no debt maturities until February 2028; the preview did not flag a refinancing or maturity extension.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company refinanced its $730 million European credit facility extending maturity by 5 years with no debt maturities until February 2028.”

in_line: Portfolio purchases were $297 million, within the preview’s own $280–320 million estimate and above its under-$250 million concern threshold; PRA maintained its $1.0–1.3 billion full-year investment target.

U.S. legal cash collections grew 26%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that legal collections could continue growing at 25% or more; the call also reiterated that legal-cost growth is expected to moderate, as previously guided.
Adjusted EBITDA growth outpaced collections growth, and net leverage declined to 2.67x while management continued to target the mid-2x range, consistent with the preview’s standing guidance.

surprises.description: Ironton produced about 4.5 million pounds of PureFive, down from the prior quarter, rather than the preview’s expected 9.0–9.5 million pounds or a sixth consecutive production record above Q1’s 8.4 million pounds. The planned turnaround explains the decline but does not close the gap to expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ironton produced approximately 4.5 million pounds of PureFive in Q2 2026, down from the prior quarter due to a planned turnaround.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A sixth consecutive record (above 8.4M lbs) keeps the operational story intact”; the base scenario expected “9.0–9.5M lbs.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end total liquidity was $236.9 million, far below the preview’s estimated pro forma liquidity of roughly $500–525 million after the June financing. The company did raise $432 million net, but the reported liquidity figure was substantially lower than the preview estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with total liquidity of $236.9 million (including $165.2 million cash), up from $131 million at the end of Q1,” after offerings that raised “$432 million net.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The June offerings “moved pro forma liquidity to roughly $500–525M, according to the full preview’s estimate.”

surprises.description: Full-year project spend guidance increased to $45–50 million from $39–45 million, raising the midpoint while the preview had cited the lower range as the current guide. This is an unexpected increase in planned project spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year project spend guidance was raised to $45-50 million from $39-45 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 project spend guide $39–45M, described as ‘majority discretionary.’”

surprises.description: The call reported seven new customer conversions, including a first building-and-construction application, and said New Jersey’s recycled-content approval was accelerating qualification with large food and consumer brands. The preview identified NJ conversion evidence as a key watch item but had no reported customer-conversion count or new application.
surprises.fact_evidence: “7 new customer conversions including a first building and construction application”; NJ approval was “accelerating qualification with QSR and large snack/confectionery brands ahead of a January 2027 regulatory deadline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for named brands or signed volumes since the May 14 approval.”

surprises.description: P&G’s Downy caps are now in commercial production, Tide caps are scheduled for Q3 retail, and Vicks ZzzQuil child-resistant lids are targeted for Q4. The preview mentioned faster Tide-cap ramping only as a bull-case possibility and did not flag the Downy or Vicks milestones.
surprises.fact_evidence: “P&G, which holds an offtake arrangement for up to 15% of Ironton’s capacity, now has Downy caps in commercial production, Tide caps scheduled for Q3 retail, and Vicks ZzzQuil child-resistant lids targeted for Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario cited “faster Tide cap ramp” as a possible catalyst.

surprises.description: The Thailand project advanced with Board of Investment approval and FastPass status, with groundbreaking expected in the second half of 2026 and project financing targeted to close by year-end. The preview flagged Thailand-related capex as a risk but did not anticipate these approval and execution milestones.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Thailand facility … received Board of Investment approval and FastPass status, with groundbreaking expected in the second half of 2026 … and project financing targeted to close by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Accelerated capex at Thailand or Antwerp could be read as burn,” but gave no Thailand approval or project-timing expectation.

surprises.description: The company completed the turnaround with more than 170 site projects ahead of schedule and below budget. The preview anticipated the production and ramp debate but did not set an expectation for a turnaround completed ahead of schedule or under budget.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed a turnaround with more than 170 site projects ahead of schedule and below budget.”

in_line: Revenue of about $4.5 million was at the low end of the preview’s $4.5–5.5 million base scenario and close to the $3.83 million alternative consensus, although below the $6.63 million estimate; the preview warned that headline comparisons were vendor-dependent.
Adjusted EBITDA of negative $31.7 million was within the preview’s base scenario of negative $30–33 million.
Management reaffirmed the second-half 2026 Ironton monthly cash-breakeven target, consistent with the preview’s focus on maintaining the H2 ramp and breakeven trajectory.

surprises.description: Bookings were $16.2 million, $2.8 million below the $19 million guidance midpoint and below the guidance range’s $17.1 million low end. That is a clear miss against a metric the preview identified as a key test.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bookings grew 25% year-over-year to $16.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross bookings” guidance was “$19.0M ±10% ($17.1–20.9M),” and the preview called for bookings “at or above $19.0M.”

surprises.description: The Q3 revenue outlook is weaker than the preview’s roughly $19 million expectation: the $17 million midpoint is about $2 million lower. The broad guidance range does not change that the midpoint falls short of the preview’s stated threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for revenue of $17 million (+/-10%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said double-digit FY26 growth required “about $19–19.5M in each of Q3 and Q4” and identified Q3 guidance “at or above $19M” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: The company nevertheless expects FY26 revenue above $70 million and a record Q4 above $18.7 million, a stronger full-year outlook than the roughly $69.5 million needed for double-digit growth. It also expects double-digit growth in 2027, extending the positive outlook beyond the preview’s FY26 focus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 is expected to be a record quarter (above $18.7M), driving full-year 2026 revenue above $70 million and double-digit growth in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said double-digit FY26 growth required “roughly $69.5M of revenue” and described double-digit FY26 growth as management’s prior outlook.

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating income was $635,000, above the preview’s roughly $300,000 implied profit and better than its near-breakeven expectation. This delivered the profitability milestone with more cushion than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company delivered its first non-GAAP operating profit ($635,000) since late 2024.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~Breakeven” non-GAAP operating income and “~+$0.3M implied at midpoint.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin was 86.8%, below the approximately 88% company guidance cited in the preview; it also declined sequentially because of mix. The year-over-year increase was larger than the preview’s implied improvement, but the quarter missed the margin level investors were given to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin rose over 12 percentage points year-over-year to 86.8%, though it slipped 111 basis points sequentially due to mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company guidance of “~88%” non-GAAP gross margin and an implied year-over-year increase of “~+800bps.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses came in below the preview’s guidance midpoint, and management said it had achieved the targeted $20 million in annualized spending reductions. The lower expense base helped support the stronger-than-expected operating profit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company achieved its targeted $20 million in annualized spending reductions, cutting non-GAAP operating expenses 7.8% sequentially to $14.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed non-GAAP operating expense guidance of “$15.5M ±5% ($14.7–16.3M).”

surprises.description: IP revenue and bookings reached records, and the pipeline expanded more than fourfold over the year. The preview expected a bookings recovery after the prior quarter’s sharp decline, but did not anticipate this record-and-pipeline update; the facts do not provide a bookings amount to compare with its $4 million marker.
surprises.fact_evidence: “IP revenue surged 238% year-over-year, achieving record bookings and revenue, with the IP pipeline up more than 4x over the past year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “SIP bookings fell 41% sequentially” in Q1 and that “Bookings above $4M would be encouraging.”

surprises.description: Micron invested $10 million through a convertible note that closed in Q3 and deepened its FTCO co-development partnership. The preview did not anticipate this investment or financing support.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Micron invested $10 million in a Silvaco convertible note that closed in Q3, deepening their FTCO co-development partnership.”

surprises.description: Silvaco reported a strategic partnership with Dassault Systèmes Simulia for interoperable workflows targeting AI-enabled manufacturing, a collaboration not flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed strategic partnerships with NVIDIA (GPU-accelerated physics simulation) and Dassault Systèmes Simulia (interoperable workflows) targeting AI-enabled manufacturing.”

surprises.description: Cash increased to $13 million excluding the Micron note, and operating cash burn more than halved from Q1. This is a stronger liquidity update than the preview’s expectation that a second consecutive cash build would be de-risking, although the company still reported cash burn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and equivalents grew nearly 20% sequentially to $13 million (excluding the $10M Micron note), while operating cash burn halved to $5.5 million from $11 million in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted cash and equivalents of “~$10.9M” and said “a second straight cash build would be de-risking.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $17.8 million versus the preview’s $17.9 million consensus and $18.0 million guidance midpoint, essentially in line; its 48% year-over-year growth was also close to the preview’s approximately 49% expectation.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $1.8 billion, above the preview’s $1.66–$1.70 billion consensus range and company guidance of $1.653–$1.661 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue grew 28% year-over-year to $1.8 billion in Q4 FY2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus” was “$1.66B (Zacks)” to “$1.70B (alternate aggregator)”; company guidance was “$1,653M – $1,661M.”

surprises.description: Cloud revenue grew 31% and beat guidance by $49 million, outperforming the preview’s expected growth of about 25.5%. Management attributed the result primarily to cross-sell and seat expansion, rather than data center migrations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cloud revenue accelerating 31% to $1.2 billion”; “Cloud revenue beat guidance by $49 million, driven primarily by cross-sell and seat expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cloud revenue growth” was guided at “~25.5%” and “in line” with the Q3 FY26 guidance.

surprises.description: Atlassian disclosed strong growth in its largest ARR customer tiers: customers with at least $3 million ARR grew more than 50%, and those with at least $5 million ARR grew more than 70%. The preview did not flag these enterprise expansion metrics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enterprise expansion set records with $3 million ARR customers (164 total) growing over 50% and $5 million ARR customers (69 total) growing over 70% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a $14 billion cross-sell opportunity in its installed base and said Fortune 500 penetration—85% of those companies—still represents only about 10% of revenue, adding a substantial enterprise-growth opportunity not covered in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company sees a $14 billion cross-sell opportunity within its existing customer base”; its enterprise motion is early, with “85% of the Fortune 500 penetrated representing only about 10% of total revenue.”

surprises.description: Rovo usage indicators included adoption by over 80% of the Fortune 500 and a 50% quarter-over-quarter increase in Rovo-assisted actions—specific adoption and usage metrics not anticipated by the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rovo is now used by over 80% of the Fortune 500” and “Rovo-assisted actions grew 50% quarter-over-quarter.”

surprises.description: Atlassian disclosed new Teamwork Graph metrics: more than 200 billion objects and connections, with grounded agents delivering up to 44% more accurate answers while using 48% fewer tokens. The preview did not anticipate these product-performance disclosures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Teamwork Graph now spans over 200 billion objects and connections, delivering up to 44% more accurate answers while consuming 48% fewer tokens for grounded agents.”

in_line: Data center migrations contributed only mid-to-high single digits to cloud growth, which management said was in line with expectations.

surprises.description: Revenue was slightly below the preview's $194.4 million consensus, while comparable sales fell 6.2% versus the roughly 4% decline implied in the preview. Transactions improved sharply from Q1 and were roughly flat in June, but the overall comp and its 4.2% product-mix decline were weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 revenue was $192.7 million; comparable restaurant sales declined 6.2%, including a 2% transaction decline and a 4.2% product mix decline. Comparable transactions improved from down 11.2% in Q1 to roughly flat in June.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus was "$194.4M (some sources $193M)"; same-store sales were estimated at "~–4% implied by revenue" and the preview said consensus implied a comp of roughly "–3.5% to –4.5%."

surprises.description: Restaurant-level margin was well below the preview's estimated 16–17%, at 13.1%; adjusted EBITDA also turned into a small loss rather than the expected $5–8 million profit. The margin pressure came alongside higher food, labor, and other operating costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: Restaurant-level profit margin fell to 13.1% from 18.9%, and adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $0.2 million versus a $6.4 million profit a year earlier. Food, beverage and packaging costs rose about 210 basis points, labor rose about 170 basis points, and other operating expenses rose about 150 basis points.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated restaurant-level margin at "~16–17%" and adjusted EBITDA at "~$5–8M"; it also said a Q2 margin below roughly 15.5% would make the FY margin guide difficult to reach.

surprises.description: The full-year outlook was cut much more severely than simply reaffirming the existing ranges: comparable sales are now expected to decline 8–7%, restaurant-level margin is 10.5–11%, and adjusted EBITDA is a $23–27 million loss. The preview anticipated a guide cut, but its base case described trimmed ranges rather than an outlook this far below the prior plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year 2026 guidance was lowered to comparable sales decline of 8% to 7%, restaurant-level margin of 10.5% to 11%, and adjusted EBITDA loss of $27 million to $23 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior guidance was comparable sales of "–4.0% to –2.0%," restaurant-level margin of "14.2%–14.7%," and adjusted EBITDA of "$1M–$6M." The preview said a cut was "broadly expected" and its base scenario anticipated that the FY comp and EBITDA guides would be "trimmed."

surprises.description: Wraps had a meaningful traffic and repeat-purchase response, but their lower entry price pulled down check and product mix. The preview flagged incrementality and average check as open questions, so the reported combination is a mixed outcome rather than an unambiguous traffic win.
surprises.fact_evidence: Wraps reached roughly 20% incidence and drove about 500 basis points of transaction improvement; more than half of wrap buyers returned within 30 days, while the lower entry price created meaningful check/mix drag.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed "Wraps performance: attach rate, whether they bring new occasions, and effect on average check" as a key metric to watch.

in_line: The preview expected the July cyclospora outbreak to make Q3 harder and specifically called for sizing its impact. Management reported that it cut July comparable sales by about 600 basis points and assumed continued 600–700 basis-point comp impact in Q3, with 200–300 basis points embedded in full-year guidance.

The preview anticipated that a cut to full-year guidance was broadly possible; the fact of a cut itself was therefore expected, even though the reductions were much deeper than the preview's base case implied.

surprises.description: Serve cut 2026 revenue guidance to $9–10 million from the expected roughly $26 million, far below even the preview’s downside case of a cut to the low-$20 millions. Management attributed the reset primarily to removing an assumed second-half ramp in Uber delivery volume.
surprises.fact_evidence: “slashed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance from $26 million to a range of $9-10 million,” primarily due to “removing an assumed second-half ramp in Uber delivery volume.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company guidance… FY26 revenue ~$26M”; the preview said guidance might be “trimmed to a range” and described its bear case as “FY26 cut to low-$20s or withdrawn.”

surprises.description: The company said it does not expect to renew its Uber agreement when it expires in early 2027 unless the operating model meaningfully improves. The preview anticipated an H2 Uber-volume ramp, not the possible end of a partnership whose delivery volume had grown for 17 consecutive quarters before reversing in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “does not currently expect to renew its Uber agreement when it expires in early 2027 unless the operating model meaningfully improves”; Uber delivery volume had grown “for 17 consecutive quarters before reversing in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had flagged Q2 growth would be “slower” before “accelerating in H2”; the preview described roughly $19.5 million of revenue implied in H2.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $3.2 million, below the $3.49 million consensus and further below the preview’s $3.8–4.1 million whisper estimate. Its more-than-400% year-over-year growth did not prevent a miss against those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue was $3.2 million,” up “over 400% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY26 Consensus” revenue was “$3.49M”; the preview’s “whisper is about $3.8–4.1M.”

surprises.description: GAAP loss per share was $0.80, worse than the $0.69 loss consensus. The preview cautioned that the Street’s benchmark was GAAP EPS, so the reported non-GAAP loss per share of $0.59 does not erase the GAAP shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss was $64 million (-$0.80 per share) and non-GAAP net loss was $47.1 million (-$0.59 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (loss) … $(0.69)”; the preview said aggregators benchmarked that consensus “against GAAP EPS.”

surprises.description: Gross margin improved only to negative 271%, short of the preview’s cited progress marker of narrowing toward negative 200%. Gross loss was about $8.8 million, only modestly smaller than Q1’s $9.0 million loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “gross loss of approximately $8.8 million and gross margin of negative 271%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “A narrowing from (302)% toward (200)% would be the clearest sign of operating leverage.”

surprises.description: Q2-end cash and marketable securities exceeded $240 million, well above the preview’s own estimate of roughly $150–165 million. This leaves Serve with a substantially larger cash balance than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with more than $240 million in cash and marketable securities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Q2-end cash at roughly $150–165M.”

surprises.description: DoorDash delivery volume grew nearly 50% sequentially and then another 50% from June to July, providing a rapidly growing alternative channel as Uber volume weakened. The preview did not identify this growth as a catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DoorDash delivery volume grew nearly 50% sequentially last quarter and grew another 50% between June and July, positioning it as a growing alternative to Uber.”

surprises.description: Serve lowered planned 2026 capital expenditures from about $25 million to $15–17 million. The preview did not flag a capex reduction, so this is an additional indication of lower planned spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “reduced planned 2026 capital expenditures from about $25 million to $15-17 million.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP operating expense guidance fell to approximately $140–150 million from $160–170 million, a larger reduction than the preview’s expected reaffirmation of the old range or possible revenue-guidance trim alone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “cut non-GAAP operating expense guidance from $160-170 million to approximately $140-150 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company guidance… FY26 non-GAAP opex $160–170M.”

surprises.description: Recurring revenue rose to more than half of total revenue from 47% in Q1, a higher mix than the preview’s baseline implied. The preview highlighted the Q1 recurring-revenue figure but did not forecast this increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring revenue exceeded 50% of total revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q1 recurring revenue as “$1.4M (47%).”

surprises.description: Advertising accounted for nearly half of robotic food delivery revenues, an additional monetization contribution not called out in the preview’s expectations or key debates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “advertising accounting for nearly 50% of robotic food delivery revenues.”

surprises.description: Management announced an August 17 summer update covering a new delivery marketplace partner, Beacon countertop integration, market launches, and autonomy advances. The preview did not anticipate this specific upcoming announcement or its stated topics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “plans an August 17 summer announcement covering a new delivery marketplace partner, its Beacon countertop integration device, new market launches, and autonomy advances.”

in_line: Software revenue again reached nearly $1 million, broadly in line with the preview’s Q1 software-services baseline of $1.026 million.
The reported fleet of about 2,000 robots across more than 40 cities was broadly consistent with the preview’s baseline of roughly 2,000 deployed robots across 44 cities.

surprises.description: Q2 GMV reached a record $617 million, above the preview’s $590–600 million company-guidance range and the roughly $595–600 million consensus range. That is a stronger result than the preview’s base case of $595–602 million, even clearing its $605–615 million bull scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GMV reached an all-time high of $617 million, up 22% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GMV: ~$595–600M” consensus and “$590–600M” company guide; the bull scenario was “$605–615M.”

surprises.description: Instead of merely reiterating FY26 guidance, the company raised its ranges across GMV, revenue, and adjusted EBITDA. The new ranges are above the prior ranges, with the adjusted EBITDA low end raised from $59 million to $66 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year guidance to GMV of $2.535-$2.565 billion, revenue of $788-$797 million, and adjusted EBITDA of $66-$69 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “clean reiteration” of revenue and EBITDA ranges would be positive, and listed the prior FY26 ranges as GMV “$2.42–2.47B,” revenue “$770–784M,” and adjusted EBITDA “$59–67M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $13.5 million, above the prior $11–12 million Q2 guidance and the preview’s $11.5–12.0 million consensus. It also exceeded the preview’s bull-scenario range of $13–14 million only at its lower end, showing a stronger quarter than the base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $13.5 million (7% of revenue), expanding 290 basis points year-over-year and beating prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$11.5–12.0M” consensus and “$11.0–12.0M” company guide; the base scenario was “$12.0–12.5M.”

surprises.description: Revenue reached $193 million, above the $186–189 million company guidance and approximately $187.8 million consensus. Direct revenue grew faster than consignment revenue, although the preview did not provide expectations for that split.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue grew 17% to $193 million, with consignment revenue up 15% and direct revenue up 26%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: $187.8M” consensus and “$186–189M” company guide.

surprises.description: Active buyers accelerated to 11% growth and exceeded 1.1 million, rather than slowing toward the preview’s stated bear-case concern of growth below about 8%. The fourth consecutive quarter of acceleration also extends the improvement noted in the preview’s Q1 figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trailing 12-month active buyers grew 11% year-over-year, surpassing 1.1 million, marking the fourth consecutive quarter of acceleration.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q1 active buyers at “1.083M TTM (+10%)” and identified “active buyer growth slowing below about 8%” as a bear-case tell.

surprises.description: Average order value rose 13% to $659 while orders increased only 8%, and sales of items above $1,000 rose 36% in the first half. This points to stronger demand for higher-priced goods than the preview’s concern about pressure on aspirational buyers suggested, though the preview gave no specific AOV or order-growth forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average order value grew 13% to $659 while orders increased only 8%”; “sales of items above $1,000 rising 36% in the first half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “aspirational buyers stayed squeezed” and noted REAL’s buyer base “leans aspirational-to-affluent.”

surprises.description: The quarter ended with $134 million in cash, compared with the $124 million reported for Q1, while the company said it had reduced total debt by more than $80 million over two years. This is more reassuring than the preview’s concern about another weak cash quarter and renewed financing questions, although the provided facts do not state Q2 free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $134 million in cash and has reduced total debt by over $80 million in the past two years, with continued deleveraging as a priority.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “guided Q2 to another weak cash quarter” and warned that “A burn larger than expected would reopen the financing question”; it cited Q1 cash of “$124.0M.”

in_line: Take-rate pressure continued: the reported take rate fell 200 basis points, consistent with the preview’s discussion of mix-driven declines and its expectation that lower revenue relative to GMV was embedded in Q2 guidance.
Athena’s intake progress was on track with the preview’s expectation: it was forecast to process about 50% of items by year-end, and the call said it was on track to process nearly 50%.

surprises.description: Adjusted net income per share was $0.48, below the preview’s $0.51–$0.52 consensus range despite rising from $0.40 a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net income reached $60 million or $0.48 per share, up from $0.40 a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. net income per share (ANI/sh) | $0.51–$0.52.”

surprises.description: StepStone reported a $116 million GAAP net loss attributable to the company, driven by a fair-value change related to the Private Wealth profits-interest buy-in. The preview warned that GAAP revenue headlines were not very meaningful, but did not flag this large GAAP loss or its cause.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A GAAP net loss attributable to the company of $116 million or $1.41 per share, driven by the change in fair value of the Private Wealth profits interest buy-in.”

surprises.description: Private Wealth subscriptions reached a record $2.8 billion, above the roughly $2.4 billion the preview said the buy-side needed; the platform’s assets also passed $21 billion, more than doubling NAV over the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Private Wealth generated a record $2.8 billion of subscriptions, growing total platform assets past $21 billion (more than doubling NAV over the year), with SPRING alone contributing nearly $1.7 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side needs roughly $2.4B in gross subscriptions.”

surprises.description: Gross inflows were $10 billion for the quarter and nearly $40 billion over the trailing 12 months, a company record; the preview did not set an expectation for aggregate gross inflows at this level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross inflows totaled $10 billion for the quarter and nearly $40 billion over the trailing 12 months, the best 12-month period ever, split evenly between managed accounts and commingled funds.”

surprises.description: SPRING returned 23% net in the first half, but the associated Private Wealth incentive fees are not set to be recognized until fiscal Q3, after annual crystallization at the end of December. The preview asked about SPRING marks but did not flag this fee-recognition timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SPRING delivered 23% net returns in the first half of the calendar year, with Private Wealth incentive fees set to be recognized in the fiscal third quarter upon annual crystallization at the end of December.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Software and AI mark commentary. Any disclosure quantifying software or venture marks, especially in SPRING, could reset the narrative either way.”

surprises.description: Management said SpaceX had fallen from its peak to a mid-teens share of SPRING NAV and warned that public holdings could add performance volatility as lockups expire and positions are sold. The preview had identified SPRING marks as a key issue but did not anticipate this specific concentration and volatility commentary.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The SpaceX position in SPRING has declined from its peak to a mid-teens percentage of NAV, and management expects public positions to introduce performance volatility as lockups expire and positions are exited.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Software and AI mark commentary. Any disclosure quantifying software or venture marks, especially in SPRING, could reset the narrative either way.”

surprises.description: Net accrued carry was $935 million, with more than 70% tied to programs older than five years and described as ready to harvest. That is a more concrete pool of seasoned carry than the preview’s cautious discussion of potential conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net accrued carry reached $935 million, up 19% year-over-year, with over 70% tied to programs older than five years and ready to harvest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether it is still building or starting to convert, since management is cautiously optimistic pending M&A and IPO reopening.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a $1.5 billion managed-account expiration next quarter, a specific upcoming headwind not identified in the preview’s discussion of net contributions and undeployed capital.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged a $1.5 billion managed account expiration next quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FEAUM net contributions. Net contributions below about $4B would suggest deployment is slowing.”

surprises.description: The commingled fee rate is expected to stay relatively flat because of the lower fee structure on PE secondaries funds, with growth resuming only once those funds are fully raised. The preview focused on fee growth and UFEC activation but did not flag this fee-rate constraint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A lower fee structure on PE secondaries funds will keep the commingled fee rate relatively flat before resuming growth once fully raised.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “About $2.5B of the $40.1B undeployed capital was flagged to activate over two quarters. Any slip pushes FY2027 fee revenue later.”

surprises.description: StepStone raised its quarterly dividend by 18%, from $0.28 to $0.33 per share; the preview did not anticipate a dividend increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its quarterly dividend by 18% from $0.28 to $0.33 per share.”

surprises.description: Repurchases had reached $30 million of the $100 million authorization, with more than 710,000 shares bought at an average $41.87. This is more evidence of active execution than the preview’s concern that the buyback might remain passive after only $9 million had been executed in March.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Has repurchased $30 million of its $100 million authorization, buying over 710,000 shares at an average price of $41.87.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$100M was authorized but only $9M was executed in March. A passive buyback may be read as a lack of conviction.”

surprises.description: Management outlined a plan to buy in the Private Wealth profits interest using up to 75% equity and the balance in cash, while maintaining its A+ investment-grade rating. The preview did not anticipate this transaction or its funding structure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to buy in the Private Wealth profits interest as soon as contractually able, funding up to 75% in equity (30% tradable immediately, remainder locked up over 3 years) with the balance in cash while maintaining its A+ investment-grade rating.”

in_line: Fee-related earnings were $106 million with a 39% margin, broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of roughly $100–105 million FRE and a 38–39% margin.

surprises.description: TRC reported $0.10 per share, well above the preview's $0.02 Q2 consensus, and swung to positive net income. The preview identified a land sale as a possible driver, but the reported EPS was still a substantial beat against the stated consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income attributable to common stockholders reached $2.6 million ($0.10 per share) in Q2 2026,” improving from a $1.7 million loss a year ago.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP) | $0.02”

surprises.description: The Dedeaux Properties 1B land sale was recognized in Q2, whereas the preview's base case assumed no land sale. It contributed $6.9 million of revenue and $2 million of recognized profit, though another $3 million of profit was deferred.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Dedeaux Properties 1B land sale contributed $6.9 million in revenue and $2 million of recognized profit, with an additional $3 million of profit deferred due to the company's retained ownership interest.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case assumed “no land sale”; its bull case anticipated “Land sale recognized plus sustained water sales.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end liquidity fell to about $79 million from approximately $86 million at Q1, crossing below the preview's bear-case $80 million marker. That is weaker than the preview's liquidity checkpoint and reinforces its concern about further declines.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with approximately $79 million of liquidity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Liquidity versus the ~$86M Q1 level” and described its bear case as “liquidity falls below $80M.”

surprises.description: Terra Vista improved beyond the preview's Q1 reference point: leasing moved above 80%, and the apartments swung to positive NOI. The preview had flagged summer stabilization as the milestone to confirm or watch for a slip, but the call facts do not say stabilization was achieved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Terra Vista apartments swung to positive net operating income with leasing crossing 80% this month and the strongest new leasing performance in nine months in July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: At Q1, Terra Vista was “71% leased”; management had guided to Phase 1 stabilization in “summer 2026,” which the preview said Q2 should “confirm or slip.”

surprises.description: Costs declined substantially: core corporate expenses were down 18% in the first half, and expenses excluding land and water cost of sales were down nearly 18% year to date. That is a more concrete and stronger cost reduction than the preview's general expectation that corporate costs would be held down.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding land and water cost of sales, expenses declined nearly 18% year-to-date, while core corporate expenses fell 18% over the first six months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base scenario assumed “corporate costs held down.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a planned reduction in the board from nine directors to seven by next May. The preview discussed activist pressure and capital allocation, but did not anticipate or set an expectation for this specific governance change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The board is reducing its size from 9 to 7 directors by next May.”

in_line: The 510,000-square-foot Dedeaux industrial building remained targeted for early 2027 delivery, consistent with the preview's stated early-2027 target.

surprises.description: Texas Roadhouse lowered its full-year commodity inflation outlook to approximately 5% from 6%-7%, and now expects Q3 inflation of just 2%-3% rather than the 7%-8% peak anticipated in the preview. This was a better cost outlook than the preview’s bullish scenario, which had considered a cut to 5%-6%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 commodity inflation guidance was lowered from 6%-7% to approximately 5%, with Q3 inflation now expected at just 2%-3% (versus 7% in Q2) before stepping back up to about 5% in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 commodity inflation guide (6–7%). A cut to 5–6% would be the clearest bull catalyst”; Q2 was expected to be the peak at “7–8%.”

surprises.description: Comps rose 6.2%: above the preview’s roughly 5% implied consensus, but 0.3 percentage points below the 6.5% Q2-to-date pace the preview highlighted. The result therefore beat the published benchmark but fell short of the recent run rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable sales rose 6.2% in Q2, fueled by 3% traffic growth and a 3.2% higher average check.”
