surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with only $21 million in cash and equivalents, underscoring a tight liquidity position.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash $25.5M at Q1”; “Liquidity and the remaining CPF tranche. Watch the remaining ~$40M and whether preferred dividends are paid in kind or in cash.”

surprises.description: Nebraska will remain a services-only arrangement through 2027, with P3 not taking full risk until 2028. That puts the conversion of management-services lives to at-risk later than the preview’s conversion watchpoint implied, though management described the phased approach as deliberate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Nebraska expansion remains a services-only arrangement through 2027, with full risk not assumed until 2028, reflecting a deliberate glidepath approach to geographic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “conversion of management-services lives to at-risk” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: Point-of-care technology was deployed to more than 65,000 lives, about 110% of the original year-end goal, and providers closed nearly 90% of care gaps when using it. Adoption was not universal, however: the tool opened in only about half of eligible visits.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Point-of-care technology deployment reached over 65,000 lives (roughly 110% of the original year-end goal), with providers closing nearly 90% of care gaps where the tool is used, though it opens in only about half of eligible visits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Original year-end goal” (as referenced in the call facts).

in_line: Underlying Q2 adjusted EBITDA of about $9 million was within the preview’s derived $5–12 million range, despite the much higher reported headline result.
At-risk membership was about 105,000, in line with the preview’s expected ~103–107K range and its broader 103–110K guide.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 revenue around $969 million and described company guidance as low-single-digit growth. iHeart reported $977 million, up 4.7% year over year (3.5% excluding political), modestly above both the consensus estimate and the growth guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was $977 million, up 4.7% year-over-year (up 3.5% excluding political), beating guidance of up low single digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consolidated revenue | ~$969M (+3.8% Y/Y)” and “consolidated revenue up low-single digits.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Q3 adjusted EBITDA of roughly $230 million or more to support the $800 million full-year target. The reported Q3 range of $180–220 million has a $200 million midpoint, below that threshold, even though the full-year target was reaffirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for adjusted EBITDA of $180-220 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “To keep the $800M full-year figure intact with a normal Q4 skew, Q3 would need to guide to roughly $230M or more.”

surprises.description: Digital Audio revenue grew faster than the preview’s roughly 10% growth expectation, reaching 12.4% growth. This was a modest upside to the segment outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Digital Audio Group generated $364 million in revenue (up 12.4%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Digital Audio Group up ~10%.”

surprises.description: Multi-Platform revenue declined instead of coming in roughly flat as guided. Its adjusted EBITDA also fell to $59 million, with management citing non-cash co-marketing expenses, underscoring the segment-margin concern flagged in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Multi-Platform Group's revenue fell 1.6% to $536 million (below approximately flat guidance) and adjusted EBITDA dropped sharply to $59 million from $96 million, largely due to non-cash co-marketing expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Multiplatform Group roughly flat” on revenue; the preview also flagged “Multiplatform Group EBITDA margin” as a key issue and said margin reflected cost execution.

surprises.description: Management disclosed a sizable programmatic-revenue growth plan that the preview did not discuss: approximately $200 million in 2026, up about 50% from 2025, as broadcast inventory is added to major DSPs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects programmatic revenue of approximately $200 million in 2026, up about 50% from $135 million in 2025, as it adds broadcast inventory to DSPs including Amazon, Google, and Yahoo.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed that it expects minimal cash taxes for several years, avoiding roughly $150–200 million over three years—an unpreviewed potential cash-flow benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ... anticipates minimal cash taxes for the next few years, avoiding roughly $150-200 million over three years.”

in_line: Podcast revenue grew 20.7%, in line with the preview’s expectation of low-20s growth.
Adjusted EBITDA of $152 million was slightly above the $150 million midpoint of the $140–160 million guidance range.

Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance of $800 million was reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the target would hold; the $200 million full-year free-cash-flow target was also maintained.
The preview expected year-end net leverage in the mid-fives; management repeated that expectation.

surprises.description: Getty reported Q2 revenue of $229.1 million, below the preview’s roughly $235 million expectation, and revenue declined 2.5% rather than coming in flat year over year. The decline was 4.1% currency-neutral, and about 50 basis points of reported revenue benefited from recognition timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue declined 2.5% to $229.1 million (down 4.1% currency-neutral), with results aided by roughly 50 basis points from revenue recognition timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$235M (‘flat Y/Y’ per street modeling)”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $62.3 million, below the preview’s $64–66 million estimate, and its 27.2% margin was also below the expected 27.5–28% range. The reported margin was down from 28.9% a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell 8.4% to $62.3 million with margin compressing to 27.2% from 28.9%, reflecting lower revenue and higher cost of revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$64–66M”; “Adj. EBITDA margin | ~27.5–28%.”

surprises.description: Instead of reaffirming its FY26 revenue and EBITDA ranges, Getty declined to provide any earnings guidance while it evaluates its capital structure. This also leaves the preview’s expected H2 margin progression unresolved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company declined to provide any earnings guidance due to the ongoing capital structure evaluation, signaling uncertainty around its financial outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 guidance of “$948–988M” in revenue and “$279–295M” in adjusted EBITDA, noting both were “reaffirmed at Q1.” It also said to check whether “the ~30% H2 margin language survives.”

surprises.description: Getty ended the quarter with only $51.6 million in cash and then drew another $30 million on its revolver, using the full $150 million facility. That leaves less remaining liquidity than the preview’s focus on Q2-end cash and undrawn revolver capacity suggested investors would be assessing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Getty ended Q2 with only $51.6 million of balance sheet cash (down $45 million from Q1) against $2.1 billion of total debt”; in July it “drew an additional $30 million on its revolver, maxing out the $150 million facility to bolster liquidity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “The key figures are the cash balance and undrawn revolver capacity exiting Q2,” and noted an April revolver draw of $120 million.

surprises.description: The agency business fell 13%, with management citing secular pressure and customers producing content internally with AI. The preview did not identify this degree of agency weakness as an expected Q2 issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The agency business declined 13% amid secular headwinds and AI-driven internal content production.”

surprises.description: Annual subscription revenue grew 7.1% to 58.8% of total revenue, and Premium Access revenue grew 5.5% with customer retention near 100%. That revenue resilience was not anticipated in a preview focused on falling annual subscribers and retention.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Annual subscription revenue grew 7.1% to 58.8% of total revenue, with Premium Access (over 40% of revenue) growing 5.5% and Premium Access customer revenue retention near 100%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted that “active annual subscribers fell to 258K from 318K Y/Y” and “annual subscription retention slipped to 90% LTM from 92.7%.”

surprises.description: Annual subscription retention came in at 88.4%, below the preview’s 90% figure, and active annual subscribers were 240,000. The deliberate exit from the free-trial program was expected to weigh on trends, but the retention rate fell further than the preview indicated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Annual subscription revenue retention fell to 88.4% (from 93.4%) and active annual subscribers dropped to 240,000 from 321,000, reflecting the deliberate exit from the iStock free trial program and traffic headwinds.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Active annual subscribers fell to 258K from 318K Y/Y, and annual subscription retention slipped to 90% LTM from 92.7%.”

surprises.description: Getty said iStock’s new-customer acquisition continued to be hurt by search-engine and affiliate traffic declines. The preview discussed the free-trial exit as a subscriber headwind, but did not flag these traffic sources as an additional ongoing problem.
surprises.fact_evidence: “iStock continued to suffer from search-engine and affiliate traffic declines hurting new customer acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview attributed subscriber weakness to “ending iStock’s free-trial funnel in June 2025” and said Q2 was “the first quarter fully lapping that change.”

surprises.description: Getty disclosed that the abandoned Shutterstock merger had consumed more than $100 million in professional fees and financing costs over 18-plus months. The preview noted that the merger had been terminated but did not anticipate or quantify this cost burden.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company terminated its proposed Shutterstock merger after 18+ months and over $100 million in professional fees and financing costs, citing regulatory burdens and uncertainty.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview stated, “The Shutterstock merger was terminated July 6, 2026,” and listed a termination fee as an open question, but gave no estimate of the costs already incurred.

in_line: Free cash flow was deeply negative, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Q2 would absorb the roughly $110.9 million warrant-litigation judgment payment.
Getty redeemed the $628.4 million of 10.5% Senior Secured Notes at par, as the preview expected investors to confirm.

surprises.description: Revenue was $60.1 million, below the preview’s $60.87 million consensus and the implied 2.2% year-over-year growth; reported growth was only 1%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q1 revenue was $60.1 million, up just 1% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $60.87M | Prior Year (1Q26) $59.54M | Implied Y/Y +2.2%.”

surprises.description: SDC fell 3.6% organically rather than holding roughly flat as the preview’s base case anticipated. Past-due backlog also rose about $1 million from its year-end low, weakening the case that the prior quarter’s backlog improvement was durable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SDC, the largest segment at 41% of revenue, posted a 3.6% organic decline”; “SDC past-due backlog rose about $1 million from its year-end low.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... SDC flat”; the preview also said Q4 strength “may have pulled demand forward from 1Q27” and that backlog commentary was the thing to check.

surprises.description: Adjusted operating margin reached 25.6%, above the roughly 24% implied by consensus and above the preview’s 25% threshold for a strong result. Management nevertheless cautioned against annualizing the seasonally light quarter, tempering what the beat says about durability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income excluding unusual items grew 19.5% to $15.4 million (25.6% of revenue vs. 21.7% prior year), nearly 390 basis points of margin expansion,” though management “warned against annualizing this seasonally light quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Applying 4Q26's adjusted EPS-to-AOI relationship, the $2.63 consensus implies AOI of about $14.6M, or roughly a 24.0% margin”; “A print at or above 25% would suggest the FY26 expansion is durable.”

surprises.description: GAAP net income fell sharply because of an unrealized foreign-exchange loss on an intercompany loan, an item the preview did not anticipate. The reported decline was not attributed to operating deterioration, and operating cash flow increased.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income fell 40.3% to $2.8 million ($0.49 per diluted share) driven by a $2.7 million non-operating expense swing from unrealized FX losses on an intercompany loan, not operations, while operating cash flow rose $12.8 million to $14.7 million.”

surprises.description: The company repaid $8.7 million of debt, brought net leverage to 1.85x, and set a 1.5x–1.75x year-end target while explicitly deprioritizing acquisitions. The preview’s below-2.0x leverage level appeared only in its bull scenario, and it did not anticipate the stated acquisition priority.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repaid $8.7 million of debt, lowering net leverage to 1.85x ... with a target of 1.5x-1.75x by fiscal year-end and an explicit de-prioritization of acquisitions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario included “leverage below 2.0x”; the preview said a strategic announcement was possible but had not been indicated by management.

surprises.description: Management announced a new BPD general manager and accelerated the next-generation Gyrolab launch to fiscal 2028. The preview considered strategic announcements possible but did not anticipate these specific moves, and no revenue contribution was attached to the platform.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new general manager was installed for BPD, and the next-generation Gyrolab platform launch was accelerated to fiscal 2028 (its first new platform since 2018), though no revenue was attached to it.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A strategic announcement, such as portfolio changes, restructuring, or reporting changes, is possible here. Management has not said so.”

in_line: Total core organic growth returned to positive territory at 0.4%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the company would return to positive core organic growth after Q4’s negative 0.6%.

BPD posted positive organic growth of 5%, meeting the preview’s expectation for a modestly positive recovery; management attributed much of the rebound to easier comparisons and export-control-deferred orders.
Full-year guidance was not provided, consistent with the preview’s expectation that management would provide guidance with H1 results in November.

surprises.description: AlTi reported adjusted EBITDA of just over $5 million, well below the preview’s $11–13 million base-case range. The result was also below the preview’s bear-case threshold of $8 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA exceeded $5 million, up 9% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … Adj. EBITDA $11–13M”; “Bear: … Below $8M.”

surprises.description: Instead of the continued outflows the preview identified as a risk, AlTi reported positive inflows, including about $700 million of net wealth-management flows. This is a substantial swing from the prior quarter’s $200 million of net outflows.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AUM grew to $51 billion … driven by strong investment performance and net positive client inflows”; “Wealth management generated … net flows of about $700 million in the second quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net client flows vs. −$0.2B (Q1). Continued outflows undercut both the standalone and acquirer growth stories.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $58 million, below the preview’s $60–63 million base range and $61.8 million consensus estimate, despite growing year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue reached $58 million, an 11% year-over-year increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $61.8M”; “Base | Revenue | $60–63M.”

surprises.description: AlTi disclosed an unexpected nearly $19 million unrealized loss on its stake in an external Asian Credit and Special Situations fund after that fund’s manager decided to wind it down within 12 months following the founder’s serious health event. The preview did not anticipate this loss or the event behind it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recorded an unrealized investment loss of nearly $19 million on its stake in an external Asian Credit and Special Situations fund after the manager unexpectedly decided to unwind the fund within 12 months due to the founder’s serious health event.”

surprises.description: The fund winding down will also reduce a source of future fees and distributions: the fund had contributed about 75 basis points of recurring management fees and about 650 basis points of the incentive portion of distributions year-to-date. The preview did not flag this prospective revenue impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The unwinding Asian Credit fund had contributed about 75 basis points of recurring management fees and about 650 basis points of the incentive portion of distributions year-to-date, which will now diminish.”

surprises.description: The preview expected expense normalization in the second half of 2026, but management said benefits from zero-based budgeting and vendor rationalization would accelerate into 2027. That points to a later timeline for the incremental savings described on the call, although management is targeting further cost reductions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects cost reduction benefits from zero-based budgeting and vendor rationalization to accelerate into 2027, targeting further reductions in both comp and non-comp expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided that strategic-review costs could persist into Q3, with normalization in 2H26.”

in_line: Recurring management and advisory fees were $54 million, close to the preview’s approximately $54.5 million estimate and above its $54 million threshold for supporting the fee base.
The strategic review remained at “nothing further to report,” as the preview’s base case expected.

surprises.description: The preview put Q2 revenue consensus at $121.85 million and said revenue below $110 million would make the full-year outlook hard to defend. Shimmick reported $107 million, missing consensus by about 12% and falling into the preview’s sub-$110 million bear scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was $107 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $121.85M”; “Sub-$110M would make the guide hard to defend”; the bear scenario was “<$110M.”

surprises.description: The preview cited full-year revenue guidance of $550–600 million and expected management to defend it. The reported range was $525–575 million—$25 million lower at each end, despite being described as raised—although its midpoint remains above the preview’s $520.05 million Street estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was raised to $525–575 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue guidance vs. Street”; prior guidance was “$550–600M revenue / $15–30M adj. EBITDA,” and the preview said Q2 mattered for whether management “defends the guide.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted $34 million of Q1-end liquidity and noted about $14 million of net offering proceeds. Q2-end liquidity was only $33 million, rather than showing the increase suggested by those figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Liquidity ended the quarter at $33 million, comprising $17 million unrestricted cash and $16 million of credit availability.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total liquidity was $34M at Q1-end, plus ~$14M net from the May 22 offering”; liquidity was also a catalyst to monitor.

surprises.description: Despite the revenue shortfall, backlog rose from the preview’s cited Q1 level of $944 million to $991 million, its highest level since Q1 2024. The additional $221 million in awards pending contracts and a fourth consecutive quarter of positive book-to-burn point to stronger forward work than the weak quarterly revenue alone might suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total backlog reached $991 million, its highest level since Q1 2024, with an additional $221 million in awards pending contracts”; “$138 million in new work for a 1.4x book-to-burn ratio,” the fourth consecutive positive quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “backlog $944M, book-to-burn 2.6x” for Q1 and flagged “Backlog quality” as a catalyst to check.

surprises.description: Management said noncore work is now less than 3% of backlog, a favorable backlog-composition detail the preview did not quantify and which management said should reduce future gross-margin drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Noncore work now represents less than 3% of total backlog, reducing the drag on gross margins going forward.”

in_line: Q2 consolidated gross margin was 12%, matching the preview’s key threshold of 12%.
Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $4 million, within the preview’s implied estimate of approximately $4–5 million.
Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed at $15–30 million, as the preview said management might reaffirm the guide.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 revenue of about $1.95 million (its own estimate was $1.9 million); Archer reported $5 million, a much larger result than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue grew to $5 million, a 213% increase over the prior quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $1.95M”; the preview’s own estimate was “$1.9M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss around $185 million to $186 million. Archer reported a $177 million loss, better than that expectation and at the favorable end of its guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss was $177 million, at the lower (better) end of the $170 million to $200 million guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | -$185M (guide midpoint)” and the preview’s own estimate was “-$186M.”

surprises.description: The preview said Insitu was profitable and generated more than $200 million in annual revenue, but said its cash-flow contribution had not been disclosed. Archer said Insitu is expected to generate positive free cash flow and operate on a self-funding basis after closing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Insitu is already profitable, generating over $200 million in annual revenue across 35 countries, and is expected to contribute positive free cash flow that can operate on a self-funding basis after closing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Insitu reportedly does more than $200M in annual revenue across 35 countries and is profitable. Management has not disclosed its EBITDA, margin, or backlog.”

surprises.description: Beyond Insitu’s own self-funding outlook, Archer said the acquisitions are not expected to structurally raise the company’s overall cash burn. The preview highlighted uncertainty around the Boeing deal and a possible equity raise, but did not forecast flat post-close burn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management stated the acquisitions will not structurally increase overall cash burn, targeting relatively flat cash burn post-close through synergies across Midnight, Halo/Thunder, and ZEE platforms.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether a raise is announced with the print”; the preview said Archer did not need the cash for runway, but did not set an expectation for post-close cash burn.

surprises.description: The preview described Boeing’s $55 million investment as contingent on Archer completing a qualifying offering of at least $400 million. The call instead highlighted an all-stock acquisition with a Boeing lockup, committed future equity investments, and warrants priced far above Archer’s current share price; the reported facts do not say whether the qualifying offering condition was met.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Boeing took all stock with a lockup and committed future equity investments, plus warrants with exercise prices far in excess of Archer's current share price.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Boeing's $55M investment is contingent on Archer completing a qualifying offering of at least $400M gross.”

surprises.description: The preview’s Q3 scenario range extended to a $215 million adjusted EBITDA loss and warned that a guide below $200 million would signal a steeper burn curve. Archer kept Q3 guidance at a $170 million to $200 million loss, rather than indicating a worse range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance held in the same range” of “$170 million to $200 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario anticipated Q3 guidance of “-$190M to -$215M,” and the preview said “a guide below -$200M would signal a steeper burn curve.”

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss a defense UAS business with a market opportunity of this scale. Archer said Halo/Thunder addresses a market greater than $100 billion, with first flight targeted next year and customer deliveries in 2029.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Halo/Thunder Group 5 UAS platform carries a total addressable market greater than $100 billion, with first flight targeted next year, customer deliveries in 2029, and scaling around 2030.”

surprises.description: The preview did not lay out a near-term monetization timeline for Archer’s AI businesses. Management now targets ZEE and SkyGrid becoming revenue-generating and profitable as early as next year, with a possible significant ramp in the second half of 2027 and beyond.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Archer targets its AI solutions (ZEE and SkyGrid) to be revenue-generating and profitable as early as next year, with potential for a significant ramp in the back half of 2027 and beyond.”

surprises.description: The preview said piloted transition testing was slated for the second half of 2026 and focused on how many TIA events had been completed. Archer described Midnight as already in the FAA’s fourth and final certification phase, with more than 150 piloted flights, including intercity flights over 50 miles—more operational detail and apparent progress than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Archer reports being the only industry OEM in the fourth and final phase of the FAA type certification process for Midnight, having flown over 150 piloted test flights, up to 5 times a day, including intercity flights over 50 miles.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Archer closed FAA Phase 3 in April 2026”; “Piloted transition flight testing is slated for 2H26.”

in_line: Insitu’s annual revenue of more than $200 million and its profitability matched what the preview already reported.
The Boeing acquisition itself, including equity consideration, was already announced before the release, as the preview noted.

surprises.description: APEI’s Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $20.7 million, above the high end of its $16.5–18.0 million guidance range. That is a substantial beat against the range the preview identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA grew 36.8% to $20.7 million with margin expanding 275 basis points to 12%, exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Q2'26 guidance (5/11/26) | $16.5M – $18.0M.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS of $0.52 exceeded both the preview’s cited consensus estimates and the company’s prior guidance range. The quarter also reversed the prior-year per-share loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income available to common stockholders was $9.8 million or $0.52 per diluted share, reversing a prior-year loss of $0.02 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS | Q2'26 guidance (5/11/26) | $0.34 – $0.39”; “$0.36 (Zacks, 8/4/26); $0.37 (Northland, raised from $0.35 on 5/13/26).”

surprises.description: APEI raised its full-year 2026 revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and EPS guidance above the prior ranges cited in the preview, rather than merely reaffirming or making a token increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “APEI raised full-year 2026 guidance to revenue of $690-698 million, adjusted EBITDA of $96-104 million, and diluted EPS of $2.48-2.79.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue | $686M – $696M”; “FY26 adj. EBITDA | $93M – $102M”; “FY26 diluted EPS | $2.33 – $2.68.” The preview said the key question was “raise vs. reaffirm.”

surprises.description: APEI disclosed Q3 guidance of $164.5–167 million in revenue and $14–17 million in adjusted EBITDA, with about $6 million of revenue and $4 million of EBITDA shifted into Q4. The preview provided no Q3 estimates, so this timing-related quarterly outlook was not anticipated there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance (revenue $164.5-167 million, adjusted EBITDA $14-17 million) reflects a ~$6 million revenue and ~$4 million EBITDA timing shift into Q4 due to a September 7 Military Plus start date plus nonrecurring marketing optimization costs.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $171.7 million was at the high end of guidance and slightly above the preview’s $170.79 million consensus estimate, though still within the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue grew 5.5% year-over-year to $171.7 million (7.8% excluding the divested Graduate School USA business), landing at the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2'26 guidance (5/11/26) | $170.0M – $172.0M | Consensus | $170.79M.”

surprises.description: The institutional combination was completed and, unexpectedly, lifted the Department of Education’s restriction on Rasmussen’s total enrollment growth. The preview noted the combination but did not flag removal of the restriction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its institutional combination on August 4, 2026, uniting all units under a single HLC accreditation and lifting the 2021 Department of Education growth restriction on Rasmussen's total enrollment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The institutional combination completed August 6, 2026.”

surprises.description: APEI lowered its full-year capex guidance, an unflagged revision that could mean less spending than previously planned; the preview did not provide a prior capex estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “APEI raised full-year 2026 guidance to revenue of $690-698 million, adjusted EBITDA of $96-104 million, and diluted EPS of $2.48-2.79, while lowering capex to $25-28 million.”

surprises.description: Management described a possible 40% increase in military tuition assistance that could let APEI reprice active-duty tuition while retaining its zero-out-of-pocket commitment. This potential pricing opportunity was not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A pending NDAA provision could raise military tuition assistance 40% (from $250 to $350 per credit hour), potentially allowing APEI to reprice active-duty tuition while maintaining its 23-year zero out-of-pocket commitment.”

in_line: HealthPlus enrollment was about 19,600, matching the preview’s stated level to watch.
Military Plus net course registrations were about 98,300, at the bottom of the preview’s 98,300–100,300 expected range; the preview had also flagged Middle East deployments as a headwind.

surprises.description: TELA reported Q2 revenue of $19.3 million, below both the roughly $20.0 million company guide and $20.01 million consensus. The miss was about 3.5% versus consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $19.3 million… and below company expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $20.01M”; “Company guide (Q2) | ~$20.0M.”

surprises.description: OviTex PRS revenue fell to $5.5 million from $7.3 million, with unit volume down 23% and accounting for nearly the entire revenue shortfall. The preview did not identify this product-specific collapse as an expected risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OviTex PRS revenue fell to $5.5 million from $7.3 million a year earlier, a 23% unit volume decline that drove nearly the entire revenue shortfall.”

surprises.description: TELA’s gross margin was 72%, well above the preview’s expected 66–67%. The call attributed the improvement partly to a refund of previously paid tariffs and lower excess and obsolete inventory charges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to 72% from 70%, aided by a refund of previously paid tariffs and lower excess/obsolete inventory charges.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~66–67% (no formal guide).”

surprises.description: Net loss widened to $11.3 million from $9.9 million, rather than moving in the direction of the preview’s expected improvement in per-share results. Higher interest expense from the upsized credit facility was a key contributor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $11.3 million from $9.9 million a year ago,” with “higher interest expense of $2.1 million… versus $1.2 million previously.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS | -$0.17”; prior-year EPS was “-$0.22.”

surprises.description: The call newly attributed much of the PRS weakness to a failed dedicated-representative pilot and concentrated customer exposure: fewer than 10 sites and several high-volume surgeons out on leave drove most of the decline. The preview did not flag these specific operational and customer-concentration issues.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The PRS decline was attributed to a failed dedicated-rep pilot (now discontinued) plus customer concentration risk, with fewer than 10 sites and a handful of high-volume surgeons out on leave driving most of the loss.”

surprises.description: TELA said additional fundraising would be a last resort while it tries to extend its cash runway. That stance was not specified in the preview, which highlighted cash, covenant, and dilution risks but did not report a financing plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $30.4 million in cash and stated additional fundraising would be a last resort as it seeks to extend runway.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Cash and the Perceptive covenant” and said “the bear case is severe because of covenant, delisting, and dilution risk.”

in_line: TELA withdrew its FY26 revenue guidance, consistent with the preview’s base case, which anticipated guidance being “Withdrawn or cut to ~$82–84M.”
Quarter-end cash was $30.4 million, within the preview’s estimated range of “$29–31M.”
Heather Goetz’s appointment as CEO was already known to the preview, which said “Heather Getz took over August 3.”

Global OviTex unit growth outpaced dollar growth because of a shift toward smaller, lower-priced units, consistent with the preview’s warning that unit growth was outpacing revenue and its focus on pricing and mix.
The announcement of meaningful cost reductions aligned with the preview’s expectation of a “cost-focused reset”; the preview had specifically said to listen for cost actions and targets.
International revenue growth was directionally consistent with the preview’s focus on Europe as a growth area.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $214 million, below both preview consensus figures ($215.5 million and $219.2 million), though still within the company’s guidance range. The gap was small against the lower estimate and larger against the higher one.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached a record $214 million, up 10% year-over-year, landing within guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street consensus ~$215.5M (StockStory, Aug 9) or $219.2M (MarketBeat/Quiver, Aug 3).”

surprises.description: Management disclosed material pressure on marketplace unit growth from a buyer-seller price dislocation and weaker conversion, including additional macro headwinds in June and July. The preview estimated 215–218K units and identified growth below 3% as a red flag, but the call facts do not give the actual Q2 unit result, so the size of any unit miss cannot be determined.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A 600 basis point drag on unit growth resulted from a price dislocation between sellers and buyers, driving a 300-350 basis point conversion rate contraction as macro headwinds pressured June and July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Marketplace units: ~215–218K (estimate)”; “Growth below +3% would be a red flag.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in well above the preview’s roughly $19 million expectation and the $20 million high end of guidance. EBITDA per unit also reached a record and grew 11%, whereas the preview’s key test was whether it would keep expanding.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $21 million exceeded the high end of guidance, with adjusted EBITDA per unit hitting a record, up 11% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$19M (guide midpoint)”; “Adj. EBITDA of $20M or more, with EBITDA per unit still expanding.”

surprises.description: The company expects full-year operating expense growth of about 6%, below the preview’s roughly 8% expectation, and expects about 100 basis points of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion while funding go-to-market investment. That is more favorable than the preview’s concern that incremental spending could compress margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year OPEX growth is guided to ~6% (down from 12% in 2025), enabling ~100 basis points of adjusted EBITDA margin expansion even while absorbing ~$10 million of go-to-market investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP opex growth of about 8%”; “The Q2 guide already implies margin compression from 9.6% a year earlier, because of about $11M of incremental go-to-market spend.”

surprises.description: ACV introduced a new potential growth avenue with ViPR commercially available and reported substantial early dealer interest, plus plans to build units in 2026 and target much greater volume in 2027. The preview discussed commercial and off-lease wins but did not identify ViPR or anticipate this launch and pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ViPR launched commercial availability with over 50% of the top 50 dealer groups in active conversations, 100+ units being built in 2026, and management targeting 500 to potentially 1,000 units in 2027.”

surprises.description: Five emerging regions delivered mid-teens unit growth, including one above 30%, as ACV invested in field capacity; management also expects the sales force to grow 15–20% or more by year-end. The preview focused on overall marketplace units and commercial wins but did not flag this regional growth or planned sales-force expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Five emerging regions where the company leaned into field capacity delivered mid-teens unit growth (one exceeding 30%), and the sales force is expected to grow 15-20%+ by year-end.”

surprises.description: CFO Bill Zerella is departing, with Tim Fox named as his successor. The preview did not mention an expected CFO transition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CFO Bill Zerella is departing and being succeeded by Tim Fox.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance was reaffirmed, as the preview described a reaffirmation as the minimum expected outcome.
Marketplace services revenue grew 17%, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Marketplace Services would carry growth, following 19% growth in Q1.

Non-GAAP cost of revenue rose about 300 basis points year over year due to the higher no-reserve mix, consistent with the preview’s discussion of Q1’s roughly 300-basis-point gross-margin decline and the risk of further pressure.

surprises.description: Riot signed a 20-year lease with a frontier AI lab for 191 MW at Rockdale, projected to generate $9.1 billion in contract revenue, or $16.1 billion if both extension options are exercised. The preview described AMD as the existing Rockdale tenant and noted that upside depended on leases not yet secured, so this is a major new contracted revenue source.
surprises.fact_evidence: “executed a 20-year data center lease with a leading frontier AI lab for 191 megawatts” and “approximately $9.1 billion in total contract revenue, rising to $16.1 billion if two 5-year extension options are exercised.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The sell-side upside case depends on leases that do not yet exist.”

surprises.description: Corsicana moved from having no tenant or LOI to a nonbinding LOI covering the entire site, up to 756 MW of critical IT capacity. Full deployment could generate more than $1 billion in annual rent, although the LOI is not a binding lease.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Riot entered a nonbinding LOI with a single tenant for the entire Corsicana site” and it “could generate in excess of $1 billion in annual rent upon full deployment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “There is no Corsicana tenant or LOI as of the last update.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $174 million, about 17% above the $148.7 million consensus estimate and up 14% year over year, versus the preview’s expected 2.8% year-over-year decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 14% year-over-year to $174 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $148.7M | −2.8%” year over year.

surprises.description: The GAAP loss was substantially worse than expected: diluted EPS was negative $0.68 versus consensus negative $0.39. Riot also reported a $70 million adjusted EBITDA loss, with more than $240 million of noncash items, including a $75 million Bitcoin mark-to-market loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss of $237 million ($0.68 per diluted share) and an adjusted EBITDA loss of $70 million,” driven by “over $240 million in noncash items including a $75 million Bitcoin mark-to-market loss.”

surprises.description: Engineering revenue reached $37.3 million, roughly 76% above the $21.2 million consensus estimate. Its gross margin also expanded to over 27%, from about 7%, while the preview highlighted revenue growth but did not anticipate this margin expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engineering segment tripled revenue year-over-year to $37.3 million with gross margin expanding from ~7% to over 27%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Engineering revenue | $21.2M | +100.3%.”

surprises.description: Data center segment revenue was $23.2 million, well above the preview’s roughly $8 million implied line. More importantly, recurring operating lease revenue rose to $4.9 million from Q1’s $0.9 million base, though the preview cautioned that the segment headline could include nonrecurring fit-out revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The data center segment generated $23.2 million revenue with recurring operating lease revenue of $4.9 million (up over 400% from Q1).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The implied Q2 data center line (about $8M) is a residual. Q1's $33.2M segment was $32.2M of one-time tenant fit-out and only $0.9M of recurring operating lease. Judge this line by recurring lease revenue, not the headline.”

surprises.description: Riot mined 1,587 BTC, modestly above the preview estimate of 1,527 BTC. The preview had treated that production figure as a sell-side estimate because no Q2 production update was available.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bitcoin mining produced 1,587 BTC.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bitcoin mined | 1,527 BTC.”

surprises.description: Riot reported $1.2 billion of total liquidity, including $549 million in cash and $666 million in Bitcoin, and issued no common equity during Q2. Bitcoin holdings were 11,380 BTC, down from the 15,680 BTC reported for Q1, making the liquidity picture strong overall but reflecting a reduced BTC reserve.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ended Q2 2026 with $1.2 billion in total liquidity, comprising $666 million in Bitcoin (11,380 BTC) and $549 million in cash, and did not issue any common equity during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Liquidity bridge. Q2 BTC sales and realized price, unrestricted BTC left, and whether nonrecourse financing closed. The treasury is worth roughly $1.0B at about $63.5K BTC, but a third is pledged.” Also: “Riot is funding the data center build with BTC sales and project-level nonrecourse debt … and says it is avoiding equity issuance.”

surprises.description: Riot secured a $573 million interim facility backed by the tenant’s credit while its investment-grade backstop is still being finalized. This provides near-term development funding, but the financing is an interim step rather than the finalized backstop the preview was watching for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “secured a $573 million interim financing facility from Morgan Stanley to fund near-term development CapEx while an investment-grade backstop is finalized, with the facility fully secured by the tenant's credit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “whether nonrecourse financing closed,” and Riot was “funding the data center build with BTC sales and project-level nonrecourse debt (targeting 80% loan-to-cost).”

surprises.description: The AMD financing is now expected to generate about $90 million in net new capital for the frontier AI build-out, with net equity required potentially as low as $30 million. The preview described a project-debt strategy and an aim to avoid equity, but did not indicate this specific capital recycling or the possible reduction in required equity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The AMD financing is expected to close before end of Q3 with debt proceeds nearly double Riot's initial equity, generating ~$90 million in net new capital that will be recycled to fund the frontier AI lab build-out, reducing net equity required to as little as $30-280 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Riot is funding the data center build with BTC sales and project-level nonrecourse debt (targeting 80% loan-to-cost) and says it is avoiding equity issuance.”

in_line: Riot issued no common equity during Q2, consistent with the preview’s statement that it was avoiding equity issuance.
Power curtailment credits provided support to mining economics, as the preview expected ERCOT summer curtailment credits to help; the call reported $10 million in credits.

surprises.description: B&W’s Q2 revenue was $319.7 million, far above the preview’s roughly $197 million consensus and $195–$215 million base case. The preview expected a beat from the supposedly stale consensus, but not a result this far above it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue surged 130% year-over-year to $319.7 million, exceeding both company and consensus expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $196.97M” consensus; the base scenario was “$195–$215M.”

surprises.description: B&W raised the upper end of its 2026 adjusted EBITDA target by $5 million, to $105 million, rather than reaffirming the preview’s $80–$100 million range. The increase was partly supported by Base Electron revenue being recognized ahead of schedule.
surprises.fact_evidence: “B&W raised its full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA target range to $80 million to $105 million, driven partly by ahead-of-schedule Base Electron revenue recognition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 core adj. EBITDA guidance: $80M–$100M”; the base scenario expected guidance to be “reaffirmed at $80–$100M.”

surprises.description: First-half bookings reached $2.7 billion, up more than 1,058% year-over-year. The preview highlighted the need for new awards beyond the large Base Electron contract but gave no expectation for bookings on this scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half 2026 bookings reached $2.7 billion, up more than 1,058% versus the first half of 2025, while backlog hit $2.6 billion, a 533% increase year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Ex-Base Electron bookings. Quantified third-party awards are the cleanest answer to the single-contract concern.”

surprises.description: B&W disclosed a project pipeline exceeding $14 billion, including 4–6 gigawatts of power-generation opportunities from hyperscalers, developers, and utilities. The preview did not anticipate or quantify this opportunity set.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The total project pipeline now exceeds $14 billion, including 4 to 6 gigawatts of power generation opportunities from hyperscalers, developers, and utilities.”

surprises.description: Base Electron was progressing ahead of expectations and on budget, with $131.7 million of first-half revenue. The preview noted its ramp from a $31 million Q1 contribution but focused on cash conversion and the guarantee rather than anticipating this schedule performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Base Electron data center project contributed $131.7 million of first-half 2026 revenue and is progressing ahead of expectations and on budget, with major on-site construction expected to begin in early 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base Electron is ramping from a $31M Q1 contribution”; the preview called for watching “unbilled receivables, milestone payments, and any change in guarantee language.”

surprises.description: B&W reported $382.8 million in cash and restricted cash against $276.8 million of debt, putting it in a net-cash position rather than the $42.4 million net debt reported at Q1. The preview flagged balance-sheet confirmation but did not project a move to net cash.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company held $382.8 million in cash and restricted cash against total debt of $276.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net debt $42.4M at Q1”; the preview listed “buyback start and net cash confirmation” as a catalyst to check.

surprises.description: Skilled-labor shortages increased direct costs on a construction project during Q2, requiring incentives, rehires, and delayed retirements. The preview did not flag this cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Skilled labor shortages raised direct costs on a specific construction project during Q2, prompting incentives, rehires, and delayed retirements.”

surprises.description: B&W secured reservation rights for another 1 gigawatt of Siemens Energy capacity—20 50-megawatt steam turbines—with first deliveries in 12–14 months. The preview did not mention this additional supply capacity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “B&W secured reservation rights from Siemens Energy for an additional 1 gigawatt (20 50-megawatt steam turbines) with first deliveries in 12 to 14 months.”

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $21.8 million, within the preview’s approximately $20–$22 million estimate.
The $50 million share-repurchase authorization and the planned retirement of the 2026 bonds were already anticipated in the preview.

surprises.description: Revenue was $49.6 million, below the preview’s functional bar of the $51 million guidance ceiling and below published consensus of $52.9–$53.5 million, though above the $48.5 million guidance midpoint. The print was therefore weaker than the preview’s already cautious framing implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $49.6 million, above the guidance midpoint”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has beaten its own guidance repeatedly, so landing inside the range is effectively a disappointment”; published consensus was “$52.9–53.5M.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $44–$48 million came in below the preview’s base-case range of $46–$51 million, and the forecast for adjusted EBITDA of $3–$6 million was below the preview’s base-case expectation of $5–$6 million. The preview identified Q3 guidance as the highest-information item, so this lower outlook was a meaningful negative deviation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance projects revenue of $44 million to $48 million, net income of negative $3 million to breakeven, and adjusted EBITDA of $3 million to $6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “Q3 guide $46–51M” and “adj. EBITDA $5–6M”; the preview called Q3 guidance “the highest-information item on the call.”

surprises.description: The company’s Q2 net income and adjusted EBITDA both exceeded the high end of guidance, rather than merely meeting the preview’s base-case expectations. Net income was positive for a fourth consecutive quarter, versus the preview’s reference to a third straight positive quarter after Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income of $1.4 million and adjusted EBITDA of $6.7 million (a 13.4% margin), both exceeding the high end of guidance”; this was “the 4th consecutive quarter of net income.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 guidance was net income of “-$3M to breakeven” and adjusted EBITDA of “$3–6M”; the preview described positive net income at about $48 million of revenue as a key test.

surprises.description: Nutrition and other gross margin was guided to fall further to 42%–45% in Q3, despite already being 46.7% in Q2. The preview discussed the prior-quarter margin but did not anticipate this additional margin pressure in the forward outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nutrition and other gross margin dropped about 470 basis points year-over-year to 46.7%, and Q3 guidance calls for a further decline to a 42%-45% range due to lower-priced product mix and promotions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 nutrition gross margin of “46.7%, down 640bps YoY,” but gave no expectation for a further Q3 decline.

surprises.description: Cash fell to $32.4 million and net cash to $8.8 million, while free cash flow was negative $5.7 million. This was a weaker liquidity outcome than the preview’s Q1 reference point, although cash remained above the $30 million bear-scenario marker and the $22.5 million covenant threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Beachbody ended the quarter with $32.4 million in cash against $23.6 million in total debt, for a net cash position of $8.8 million, though cash declined from $36.6 million in the prior quarter”; “Free cash flow was negative $5.7 million … driven by inventory buildup for the retail rollout and declining deferred revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q1 cash of “$36.6M against about $23.6M debt; FCF -$1.7M” and said to “Watch FCF and any retail inventory build.”

surprises.description: Nutrition subscriptions rose 16.7% sequentially to about 70,000 while digital subscriptions continued to decline. The preview focused on digital subscribers and retail traction but did not set an expectation for this sharp sequential increase in nutrition subscriptions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nutrition subscriptions rose 16.7% sequentially to approximately 70,000 but remained roughly flat year-over-year.”

surprises.description: The company reported 131 Sprouts locations, up from 90, and about 12 pending planogram decisions, adding specific expansion and pipeline details beyond the preview’s reference to 100-plus Sprouts stores. The Vitamin Shoppe count of 481 was slightly below the preview’s approximate 500-door reference, and no sell-through or reorder-rate data was provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Shakeology now in 131 Sprouts stores (up 45% from 90) and 481 Vitamin Shoppe locations, plus pending pipeline of about 12 planogram decisions expected between mid-September and end of November.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “about 500 Vitamin Shoppe doors and 100+ Sprouts stores” and said “sell-through per door and reorder rates” were the key data to watch.

surprises.description: Management said it was shifting media spending toward nutrition because customer acquisition costs are substantially lower there, with nutrition advertising also converting customers into digital subscriptions through 30-day trials. This was a new efficiency and cross-selling detail not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management shifted media spending toward nutrition advertising because customer acquisition cost through nutrition products is substantially lower than through fitness advertising, with meaningful conversion into digital subscriptions via 30-day trials.”

in_line: Digital subscriptions were 760,000, at the bottom of the preview’s 760,000–785,000 base-scenario range and above its 750,000 downside threshold; the sequential decline of 6.2% was between the preview’s roughly 5% stabilization marker and its worse-than-8% downside marker.
The Tiger Finance amendment’s $22.5 million cash-cushion threshold matched the preview’s stated covenant threshold; the preview had already noted the recent covenant amendment.

surprises.description: AAON reported Q2 net sales of $627 million, far above the preview’s consensus range of about $501–515 million. The result substantially exceeded the expected revenue level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales hit a record $627 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue … Consensus band ~$501–515M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.69, well above the preview’s $0.51–0.52 diluted EPS consensus range. The reported figure is adjusted, while the preview labels its consensus diluted EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS grew 213.6% to $0.69.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS … Consensus band ~$0.51–0.52.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin was 24.3%, below the preview’s expected range of roughly 26–27%. Memphis ramp-up costs, outsourcing, and inflationary price/cost timing contributed to the shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 24.3% from 26.6% a year ago, pressured by Memphis ramp-up costs, increased outsourcing, and inflationary price/cost timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “gross margin about 26–27%”; it also called gross margin the “swing factor.”

surprises.description: AAON- and BASX-branded sales were both much stronger than the preview’s discussion of legacy demand and data-center exposure suggested: AAON-branded sales rose 39.3% despite a soft commercial HVAC market, while BASX sales rose 216%. The preview highlighted legacy AAON demand as a stabilization question but gave no comparable brand-growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BASX-branded sales surged 216% year-over-year to a record, while AAON-branded sales rose 39.3%, reflecting market share gains despite a soft commercial HVAC market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Legacy AAON-branded demand” and said backlog growth in non-residential HVAC was a signal on whether the base business was stabilizing; it also highlighted BASX customer concentration and data-center mix.

surprises.description: The margin recovery path sounds more gradual than the preview’s broad expectation of sequential improvement in the second half: management expects only modest improvement in Q3, the high watermark in Q4, and more meaningful benefits in 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided margin improvement to be modest in Q3 and back-end weighted to Q4 (the year's high watermark), with more meaningful benefit expected in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management expected “sequential margin improvement in the second half of the year.”

surprises.description: First-half cash generation and leverage were better than the preview’s balance-sheet concern implied: operating cash flow was positive and leverage had improved, rather than the capacity build remaining only a debt-financed pressure point.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half operating cash flow turned positive at $55 million versus a $31 million use of cash a year ago, while leverage improved to 1.48x from 1.77x at year-end 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the revolver is drawn heavily against limited cash” and described the capacity build as “being debt-financed,” urging investors to watch capex and covenant headroom.

surprises.description: BASX bookings had fallen from recent elevated levels, but management attributed the decline to lumpy large-project timing rather than cancellations or a changed market opportunity. That partly addresses the preview’s concern that weaker backlog or bookings might signal softer orders, although the lower bookings themselves remain a caution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BASX bookings fell below recent elevated levels,” which management attributed to “lumpiness in large-project timing rather than any specific order cancellation or a change in market opportunity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted backlog had declined from $2.13B at Q1, said investors would want bookings, and asked whether any decline reflected timing or softer orders.

in_line: The full-year sales growth guide of 55–60% and gross margin guide of 25–26% matched the preview’s stated expectation for the revised guidance; the preview also anticipated SG&A of 13–14% of sales.

surprises.description: Cannae reported $102 million of revenue versus the preview’s $99.65 million consensus estimate, a modest beat even though revenue was down from $110 million a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue decline to $102 million from $110 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $99.65M”

surprises.description: The restaurant group incurred $45 million of non-cash impairments, up from $1 million a year earlier, as traffic weakened and O’Charley’s stores closed. The preview identified further impairments as a downside risk but did not indicate a charge of this scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Incurred $45 million of non-cash impairment charges (versus $1 million a year earlier) due to reduced traffic and O'Charley's store closures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bear (20%): … further impairments.”

surprises.description: Cannae made no Q2 repurchases while allocating about $45 million to investments in the quarter, including Exeter Rugby and additional BKFC investment. That is a weaker buyback outcome than the preview’s focus on Q2 repurchases and its warning about new sports investment while buybacks slow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased no stock in Q2 due to recently announced transactions”; “allocating approximately $45 million to investments in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch Q2 repurchases”; “Bear … new sports M&A announced while buybacks slow.”

surprises.description: Black Knight Football’s adjusted EBITDA excluding player trading rose to $34 million from $8 million, stronger underlying performance than the preview’s concern that higher wage and squad costs could offset the benefits of Bournemouth’s European qualification. The $80 million reported EBITDA also included a large player-trading contribution, consistent with the preview’s warning that trading profits are lumpy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA excluding player trading was $34 million versus $8 million”; reported EBITDA was “$80 million from $8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AFC Bournemouth qualified for its first UEFA Europa League campaign … with higher wage and squad costs to offset”; player-trading profit was described as “lumpy.”

surprises.description: The SpaceX IPO generated an $83.4 million Q2 mark-to-market gain, an earnings item the preview did not flag. Management also warned that future marks could make earnings more variable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The SpaceX IPO in June triggered mark-to-market accounting, producing an $83.4 million gain in Q2”; management warned of “future earnings variability from these marks.”

surprises.description: Cannae said it expects a $45 million federal tax refund in 2026, adding a meaningful source of future liquidity that the preview did not mention.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An additional $45 million federal tax refund expected in 2026.”

in_line: AFC Bournemouth’s qualification for its first UEFA Europa League campaign was already noted in the preview.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case was that DH would reiterate its $220–$226 million FY26 revenue range. Instead, it narrowed the range to $220–$222 million, lowering the midpoint by $2 million and signaling a weaker outlook than the expected reiteration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was tightened to $220-$222 million (an 8-9% decline).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reiterate ($220–226M) ... is the base case.”

surprises.description: The preview said bookings would need to improve for the bull case, but DH reported its strongest biopharma new-business quarter in three years outside of Q4, including four customers returning after leaving before 2025. That is stronger booking and win-back activity than the preview specifically anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The biopharma segment posted its strongest new business quarter in three years outside of Q4, including four win-back customers that had left before 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bull case needs bookings to improve, not just margins.”

surprises.description: Professional services weakened because analytics engagement bookings were lighter, and management expects that weakness to pressure the second-half top line. The preview anticipated a second-half revenue decline overall, but did not identify this specific source of pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Professional services revenue underperformed due to lighter analytics engagement bookings, a weakness expected to also pressure the second-half top line.”

surprises.description: Total RPO remained down 18% year over year, worse than the preview’s base-case expectation of a 12–15% decline and short of the hoped-for slowing in the decline. Current RPO was down 12%, however, which was closer to the preview’s cited Q1 trend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Current remaining performance obligations of $150 million declined 12% year-over-year while total RPO fell 18%, reflecting a continued shift toward single-year deals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base ... RPO still down about 12–15%”; the preview also said “A slower decline in RPO and deferred revenue is the best leading indicator that revenue can stabilize in 2027.”

surprises.description: DH raised the FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint by $1 million and indicated roughly 100 basis points of margin expansion, versus the prior $55–$59 million range. The preview had the midpoint at $57 million and did not identify a raise as its base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The adjusted EBITDA guidance midpoint was raised $1 million to $57-$59 million with margins up roughly 100 basis points.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was slightly above the top of the guided range, while adjusted gross margin expanded 100 basis points after adjusting for the prior-year one-time credit. This was a modestly stronger profitability outcome than the guidance range implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $14.6 million (26% margin), modestly above the high end of guidance”; “adjusted gross margin was 80%, expanding 100 basis points after adjusting for a prior-year one-time data contract credit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | $13.5M – $14.5M (24–26% margin).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $0.05 exceeded the preview’s $0.03 consensus estimate, although it was within the preview’s base-case range of $0.04–$0.05.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $0.05.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS ... Consensus $0.03”; the base-case scenario projected “$0.04 – $0.05.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $55.2 million, slightly below the preview’s roughly $55.5 million consensus estimate, though it remained within the company’s guided range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $55.2 million, down 9% year-over-year, but landed within the guided range on the top line.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ... Consensus ~$55.5M.”

surprises.description: Trailing-12-month EBITDA-to-cash conversion was down about five percentage points year over year. The preview did not flag a deterioration in cash conversion, so this was an unanticipated negative operating detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated $50 million of unlevered free cash flow on a trailing 12-month basis, with a 75% EBITDA-to-cash conversion rate, down about 5 points year-over-year.”

in_line: Net dollar retention improved year over year for a second consecutive quarter, as the preview said two consecutive quarters of improvement would make the trend credible.
Deferred revenue was down 12% year over year, consistent with the roughly 12% decline cited for Q1 in the preview.

DH said Turbo would have no material 2026 revenue impact, with benefits weighted toward 2027 and retention, consistent with the preview’s expectation of no 2026 contribution and late-2026 availability.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $31.5 million, below the preview’s $34.13–$34.42 million consensus, despite being more than double Q1. The miss was about 8% versus the consensus range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $31.5 million (over $30 million), more than doubling Q1 revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (Q2) … $34.13M (Zacks) or $34.42M (Investing.com); street range ~$34.4–35M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating expense excluding cost of revenues slightly exceeded the previewed Q2 ceiling, and management guided to a further step-up in Q3. The $105–$115 million Q3 range and roughly $100 million quarterly average for 2026 point to a higher expense run rate than the preview’s Q2 guide of $85–$95 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP adjusted OpEx excluding cost of revenues rose to $95.9 million in Q2 from $79.8 million in Q1, with Q3 guided to $105-115 million and full-year 2026 averaging ~$100 million per quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. opex ex-COGS (Q2) | $85–95M (Q1 call, May 2026).”

surprises.description: AST received three new U.S. government awards with more than $100 million of funded near-term value expected over 2026–2027. The preview discussed government milestones as a revenue driver but did not anticipate these specific awards or their funded value.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AST received 3 new U.S. government contract awards with funded near-term value of over $100 million expected during 2026-2027, tied to Department of War applications.”

surprises.description: A preliminary Japan J-LEO award with Rakuten could provide up to approximately $1 billion in government capital without debt or dilution—an unanticipated potential source of funding. Its preliminary status means the full amount is not yet assured.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A preliminary award from Japan's J-LEO project with partner Rakuten carries a total expected value of up to approximately $1 billion in nondilutive, non-debt government capital.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted high cash burn and the risk of needing financing; AST did raise $1.15 billion in convertible notes. The 1.625% coupon and pro forma cash above $3.7 billion provide substantial liquidity on favorable stated terms, though the convertible still carries potential dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company issued $1.15 billion of 1.625% convertible senior notes due 2034 (its lowest-ever coupon) with a capped-call conversion price of $149.20, bringing pro forma cash to over $3.7 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any hint of an equity or convertible raise is a live risk.”

surprises.description: Q3 CapEx is guided to $350–$425 million, substantially below Q2’s $610 million actual spend. That indicates a near-term spending step-down relative to the preview’s concern about a roughly $650–$750 million quarterly cash-burn pace, although the preview did not give a Q3 CapEx estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 CapEx was approximately $610 million (up from $257 million in Q1), with Q3 guidance of $350-425 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guided Q2 capex of $575–650M plus about $90M of opex implies quarterly burn of roughly $650–750M.”

surprises.description: Management said about 45 satellites would be sufficient to begin commercial service, but roughly 45–60 would be needed for continuous coverage in key markets. That makes 45 a starting point rather than a guarantee of continuous coverage across those markets, while the preview had discussed the early-2027 45-satellite milestone as the continuous-coverage target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is targeting approximately 45 BlueBird satellites in orbit by early 2027, sufficient to begin commercial service, with continuous coverage in key markets requiring roughly 45-60 satellites.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has already moved the 45-satellite continuous-coverage milestone to early 2027.”

in_line: AST reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $150–$200 million, as the preview expected.
Q2 CapEx of approximately $610 million was within the previewed $575–$650 million guidance range.
The target of approximately 45 satellites by early 2027 was consistent with the preview’s account that the continuous-coverage milestone had already moved to early 2027.

surprises.description: Revenue reached $104.3M, 3% above the high end of Q2 guidance, rather than merely landing within the guided range. Its 34% year-over-year growth also accelerated from Q1’s 25%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 34% year-over-year to $104.3 million, exceeding the high end of guidance by 3% and accelerating 9 points from Q1's 25% growth rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2'26 guidance (5/11/26) | $98.5M – $101.5M (+28.4% YoY at mid)”

surprises.description: Contribution ex-TAC was $60.2M, just below the preview’s $60.5–61M buy-side bar, although it was within company guidance and above the $59.5M midpoint. This was a small shortfall against the higher investor bar, not a miss of company guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contribution ex TAC grew 24% year-over-year to $60.2 million but came in just short of the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Contribution ex-TAC | ... ~$60.5–61M (buy-side bar)”; “Anchor to guidance on this line.”

surprises.description: The take rate was about 57.7% ($60.2M contribution ex-TAC divided by $104.3M revenue), below the roughly 59.5% the preview expected from guidance. Thus, the revenue beat did not translate into the expected contribution share of revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue ... $104.3 million” and “Contribution ex TAC ... $60.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guidance implies roughly 59.5% for Q2”; the preview also listed “Take rate holding at or above 59.5%” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $14.2M, modestly above the $14.0M high end of guidance. The preview’s buy-side bar was $14M+, so this was a slight beat rather than a large upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 26% to $14.2 million, exceeding guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Q2'26 guidance ... $13.0M – $14.0M”; “$14M+ (buy-side bar).”

surprises.description: DSP’s CTV spend grew nearly 50% and reached an all-time high, with management saying growth was multiples above the industry rate. The preview highlighted sector CTV growth and potential share shifts, but did not set an expectation for DSP’s CTV growth at this level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CTV spend surged nearly 50% year-over-year to an all-time high, accounting for over 50% of total ad spend, with growth described as multiples above the industry rate.”

surprises.description: Direct access penetration rose to over 80% of CTV spend in one quarter, from just over 50% in Q1, and management cited 35% CPM reductions for advertisers. The preview flagged Direct Access penetration as something to watch, but gave no expectation for such a rapid increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Direct access penetration jumped to over 80% of CTV ad spend in Q2 from just over 50% in Q1, with management targeting over 90% in the near future and delivering 35% CPM reductions for advertisers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch the RFP pipeline, Direct Access penetration, and ViantAI Outcomes adoption.”

surprises.description: The Iris content ID had already reached nearly 50% bidstream penetration, with launches across major streaming and distribution platforms expected to take it to about 70% of viable inventory by year-end. The preview did not discuss Iris or set an adoption expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Iris content ID reached nearly 50% bidstream penetration and is expected to hit ~70% of viable inventory by year-end via launches across Disney+, HBO Max, Peacock, Roku, DIRECTV and others.”

surprises.description: The new Outcomes AI product already represented over 5% of platform spend only six months after launch, with adoption coming from existing customers shifting performance budgets. The preview flagged Outcomes adoption but did not anticipate a level or timetable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The new autonomous 'Outcomes' AI product already accounts for over 5% of total platform spend just six months after launch, sourced from existing customers reallocating performance budgets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch the RFP pipeline, Direct Access penetration, and ViantAI Outcomes adoption.”

surprises.description: TVision pilot campaigns produced strong reported conversion results: more than 80% of 42 campaigns had higher conversion rates, averaging a 1.4x lift. The preview noted the acquisition but did not discuss pilot performance or set an expectation for these results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “42 TVision pilot campaigns saw over 80% achieve higher conversion rates with an average 1.4x lift, and outliers including a 14x lift for a home improvement brand.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that TVision was weighing on EBITDA margins by about 150 basis points in Q2 and expects a larger, roughly 200-basis-point drag in Q3. The preview noted that TVision was included in guidance and highlighted margin expansion, but did not flag this specific near-term acquisition-related headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The TVision acquisition, which closed May 1, 2026, was a roughly 150 basis point drag on Q2 EBITDA margins and is expected to be about a 200 basis point drag in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management expects ‘modest adjusted EBITDA margin expansion for the full year 2026’”; “Q2 guidance implies about 50bp of YoY compression.”

in_line: Q3 contribution ex-TAC guidance of $65M–$67M, up 25% at the midpoint, matched the preview’s derived $65–67M bar and its expected 24–26% growth range.

surprises.description: OppFi cut FY2026 revenue guidance to $600–625 million from $650–675 million and adjusted EPS guidance to $1.34–1.51 from $1.76–1.84. The cuts were substantial versus the preview’s reaffirmed guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: OppFi cut its full-year 2026 guidance to revenue of $600-625 million, adjusted net income of $115-130 million, and adjusted EPS of $1.34-1.51, citing delays in its line of credit launch and Lola system migration.
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 revenue: $650M – $675M; FY26 adj. EPS: $1.76 – $1.84. The company had reaffirmed these figures in May 2026.
