surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin versus 62%”; the preview said a third straight quarter of compression would be a negative signal.

surprises.description: The company held to its roughly 100% FY26 revenue-growth target, as expected, but said the outcome depends on the timing of one or two large orders and excluded Chile business because of a government funding gap. That makes the target more explicitly conditional than the preview’s base case of a qualitative reaffirmation suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed its target of roughly 100% revenue growth for 2026 but cautioned the outcome hinges on timing of one or two large orders and could move up or down, with Chile business excluded from the forecast due to a Chilean government funding gap.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue: Target of ~100% growth”; the base scenario assumed the “target reaffirmed qualitatively.”

surprises.description: The July ATF determination was already flagged as a post-quarter event, but the call described a specific new implication: the classification opens access to a private-security market of more than 1.2 million licensed officers, larger than the U.S. law-enforcement population.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A July ATF determination classified the BolaWrap 150 as a restraint/rescue tool rather than a firearm or weapon, unlocking access to the private security market of over 1.2 million licensed security officers—larger than the entire U.S. law enforcement population.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The ATF ruling (effective Jul 2) … all came after Q2 closed. The call will likely carry most of any re-rating case.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed exclusive U.S. and NATO rights to sensing technology for counter-drone, border, and defense markets, including detection of RF-silent drones. The preview noted a post-quarter Frenel transaction but did not describe this technology or these market opportunities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured exclusive U.S. and NATO rights to Farnell's TriCore polarimetric sensing technology, positioning it for counter-UAS, border, and defense detection markets against RF-silent drone threats.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “the Frenel transaction (Jul 10)” among post-quarter narrative events but did not specify the technology or its applications.

surprises.description: Management identified 11 active DOJ grant programs that could help customers fund products and training. The preview did not mention these programs; the opportunity is potential funding support, not reported orders or revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management identified 11 active reopened DOJ grant programs that could fund BolaWrap, body cameras, de-escalation training, and virtual training for its predominantly small and midsized department customers.”

surprises.description: Wrap said its training content library is complete and described a shift toward recurring subscriptions, adding a more concrete services strategy than the preview’s general expectation that services growth could support margins. Management also said subscription revenue is still ahead, so the model has not yet produced reported revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Wrap is shifting from one-time device sales to a recurring subscription model via its now-complete Wrap Tactics training content library, though this subscription revenue is described as still ahead of the company rather than realized.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management expected margin expansion “as services grow, without assurance on pace.”

surprises.description: Total liabilities fell to $2.0 million after the former office lease was terminated, a balance-sheet improvement the preview did not anticipate. Cash was $4.8 million at quarter-end, down from $7.3 million at March 31, so the call also reported a lower cash balance than the preview’s last cited figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents grew to $4.8 million at June 30, 2026 from $3.5 million at year-end 2025, while total liabilities fell to $2.0 million from $3.9 million after terminating the former office lease.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Cash $7.3M at 3/31” and flagged “Cash and financing” as a key issue, but did not anticipate the lease termination or liability reduction.

surprises.description: Management said it may accelerate investment and access capital markets if traction develops. The preview warned that ATM or shelf language would be a sharp negative; the call’s signal was conditional rather than a stated near-term financing plan, and management said no near-term spending increase was planned.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company operates at approximately a $3 million cash breakeven with no planned near-term spending increase, but signaled a bias toward accelerating investment and accessing capital markets if traction develops.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any ATM or shelf language would be a sharp negative.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed the roughly 100% FY26 revenue-growth target, matching the preview’s stated company guidance; the timing and Chile caveats are captured separately above.

surprises.description: The preview estimated June 30 liquidity at roughly $9.5–10 million; reported unrestricted cash at quarter-end was $10.8 million, slightly above that estimate. But ESS then disclosed only about $5.6 million in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments as of July 31, a sharp subsequent deterioration that makes the latest liquidity picture worse than the preview’s outlook implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: ESS reported $10.8 million of unrestricted cash at quarter-end, but only approximately $5.6 million in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments as of July 31, and issued a going-concern warning.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A straight-line extension puts June 30 liquidity near $9.5–10M.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on ESS’s need for financing or a strategic partner but did not anticipate a business-combination LOI with terms that would leave ESS shareholders owning only 5% to 10% of the combined company. The transaction could provide a path forward, but the stated ownership share represents substantial dilution for existing ESS holders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ESS signed a nonbinding LOI for a business combination implying a combined enterprise value of ~$515 million, with ESS shareholders expected to own only ~5% to 10% of the combined company at close.”

surprises.description: The preview said opex needed to move toward $4–5 million per quarter and highlighted whether restructuring would produce savings. Instead, Q2 opex rose 19% year over year, although first-half opex fell 12% and first-half operating cash burn improved 27%; the Q2 increase was partly attributed to a largely nonrecurring legal accrual and higher R&D.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half operating cash burn improved 27% to $22.4 million and operating expenses fell 12% to $14.5 million, though Q2 opex rose 19% year-over-year driven by a $1.5 million largely nonrecurring legal contingency accrual and higher R&D spending.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Opex needs to fall toward $4–5M per quarter for the remaining cash to matter.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $73,000 came in below the preview’s lower estimate of about $100,000 and well below its alternative $404,000 estimate. The preview cautioned that the estimates differed substantially and that revenue comparisons on this very small base were mostly noise, so the shortfall is notable but not decisive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue collapsed to just $73,000 from $2.4 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue | ~$0.1M (Stocktwits) / $404K (ChartMill)” and “a revenue beat or miss is mostly noise.”

surprises.description: ESS disclosed that it had repaid $37 million of the original $40 million Yorkville note, a substantial deleveraging action not discussed in the preview. Reducing the note is favorable, though the update does not establish how it affects the company’s near-term cash needs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has repaid $37 million of the original $40 million principal on its Yorkville promissory note, prioritizing deleveraging.”

in_line: Q2 net loss was $15.6 million, within the preview’s $13–16 million base-case range; EPS of -$0.46 was also close to the -$0.44 consensus estimate.

The Juniper and Alsym arrangements remained LOIs rather than binding orders, and the nearly $1 billion sodium-ion opportunity figure remained early-stage and unconverted, as the preview had emphasized.
The going-concern warning was consistent with the preview’s expectation that the solvency concern would remain.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $260 million, above the preview’s $245–250 million company guide and $245.98 million consensus. That is a clear beat, not just the growth implied by the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached a record $260 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $245.98M | Company Guidance $245–250M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was about $0.70 versus the preview’s $0.53 consensus, a sizeable beat even allowing for the preview’s uncertainty about whether estimates reflected the share-count change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of approximately $0.70.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS | $0.53.” The preview also cautioned that it was unclear whether consensus reflected the new share base.

surprises.description: The company raised FY2026 revenue guidance to $1.02–1.04 billion, above the prior $970 million–$1.0 billion range and beyond the preview’s bull-case threshold of a raise through $1.0 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year guidance to $1.02-$1.04 billion, crossing the $1 billion threshold for the first time.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed prior guidance of “$970M–$1.0B” and said “a raise through $1.0B is the bull trigger.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA margin reached 19.8%, well above the preview’s roughly 17% benchmark and its stated 17.5%-or-higher “clean pass” level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin hit a modern-day high of 19.8% ($51.5 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin vs. ~17%” and “a print near 17.5% or higher would be a clean pass.”

surprises.description: Bookings rose to a new all-time high of $306 million rather than normalizing after Q1’s record $290.4 million; they also substantially exceeded the preview’s roughly $248 million level for maintaining 1.0x book-to-bill.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 bookings reached an all-time high of $306 million,” following $210M, $257M, and $290M in the prior three quarters.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Bookings normalize off the Q1 record” in its base case and that bookings needed to exceed “roughly $248M” to hold 1.0x.

surprises.description: Aerospace operating margin was 21.4%, exceeding even the preview’s bull-case marker of 18% or more; Aerospace sales also reached a record, though the preview gave no segment-sales estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Aerospace segment sales grew 22.6% to a record $237.3 million with adjusted operating margin of 21.4% (up 510 bps).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull scenario said “Aerospace margin reaches 18% or more.”

surprises.description: Management now expects Test Systems margins to approach Aerospace levels once the business reaches full run rate exiting Q4. That is a stronger stated margin trajectory than the preview’s expectation that margins would merely move off breakeven.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Test Systems margins are expected to approach Aerospace levels once at full run rate exiting Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “Test Systems … operating margin moving off breakeven.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a $27.4 million MV-75 FLRAA booking, roughly $35 million of expected 2026 revenue, and the possibility that it becomes the company’s largest military program. The preview did not flag this program or its contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The MV-75 FLRAA program generated a $27.4 million booking in Q2,” is “expected to contribute roughly $35 million in revenue in 2026,” and is “potentially the largest military program in company history.”

surprises.description: A $2 million IEEPA tariff refund benefited Q2 results, contrary to the preview’s statement that no refund benefit had yet been recognized. The benefit was limited, at about 70 basis points of margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Results benefited from a $2 million IEEPA tariff refund (about 70 bps of margin).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had cited tariffs as a “~$2M Y/Y headwind with no refund benefit recognized yet.”

surprises.description: Despite the Q2 refund, management expects a recurring $3–4 million quarterly tariff burden before mitigation, while another $6–8 million of IEEPA refunds is only possible and their timing is uncertain. This leaves more ongoing cost exposure and less certain relief than the preview had quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects an ongoing tariff run rate of $3-$4 million per quarter before mitigation, with an additional $6-$8 million in future IEEPA tariff refunds possible at uncertain timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a “~$2M Y/Y headwind with no refund benefit recognized yet” and did not quantify a recurring quarterly tariff run rate or additional IEEPA refunds.

surprises.description: The preview identified a possible valuation-allowance reversal as early as Q2, but the call described a potential additional $40–50 million release as still under evaluation for the second half, not as a Q2 item already realized.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A potential additional $40-$50 million valuation allowance release is being evaluated for the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a deferred-tax valuation allowance reversal was possible “as early as Q2.”

surprises.description: Management reported that long-term debt had fallen by $24.1 million since year-end and that $253.2 million of liquidity was available. This is a favorable balance-sheet update against the preview’s concern that another negative free-cash-flow quarter could raise capital-needs questions; the call facts do not state Q2 free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Long-term debt decreased $24.1 million from year-end to $310.3 million, with $253.2 million in available liquidity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged that “a second consecutive negative-FCF quarter would be a credible bear point” and could “raise questions about capital needs.”

in_line: The $44.7 million Army 4549/T production order itself was already known before the release: the preview said it had landed in July and described the $40–50 million annual run-rate expectation. The call added that deliveries should span 18 months and similar annual orders are anticipated for the next 4–5 years.

surprises.description: The preview identified Q3 revenue and OIBDA guidance as the main driver, but NCM provided no forward guidance because the Captivate transaction is pending. Investors therefore did not get the key outlook the preview was watching for.
surprises.fact_evidence: “No forward guidance was provided due to the pending transaction.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue and OIBDA guidance. This is the main driver.”

surprises.description: NCM signed an unanticipated $275 million deal for Captivate, which had $64 million of 2025 revenue and $19.3 million of adjusted EBITDA and has grown quickly. Management expects at least $3.5 million of annual run-rate synergies, with possible additional cross-selling upside, though the preview had not flagged an acquisition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NCM signed a definitive agreement to acquire Captivate … for an enterprise value of $275 million (approximately 10x pro forma EBITDA including synergies)”; Captivate generated “approximately $64 million revenue and $19.3 million adjusted EBITDA in 2025”; management expects “at least $3.5 million of annual run-rate cost synergies within year one post-close,” excluding cross-selling upside.

surprises.description: The acquisition is to be financed with new debt, bringing expected net leverage to about 3.9x at closing. The preview had not anticipated this added leverage because it did not flag the transaction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The acquisition will be financed with $275 million of new committed term debt, resulting in net leverage of approximately 3.9x at close (below 5x before synergies).”

surprises.description: NCM will pause both its dividend and share repurchases to prioritize debt repayment, rather than maintaining the dividend or potentially increasing buybacks as the preview discussed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NCM is pausing its dividend and share repurchase programs to prioritize debt repayment following the Captivate close.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The dividend is $0.03/quarter. A buyback upsize at current prices would read as a confidence signal.”

surprises.description: Network attendance grew 19.3%, far above the roughly 6% growth assumed in the preview. The attendance gain was concentrated in lower-yielding R-rated horror films, however, limiting how much it translated into advertising yield.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Network attendance grew approximately 19.3% year-over-year,” with “strong turnout from lower-yielding R-rated horror films … [that] limited advertising yield gains.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus needs about +16% growth against attendance up only about 6%.”

surprises.description: National advertising revenue grew 9%, below the roughly 16% growth the preview said consensus required. This came despite much stronger attendance, with lower-yielding films and a FIFA World Cup budget shift limiting yield gains.
surprises.fact_evidence: “National advertising revenue rose 9% to about $45 million,” while lower-yielding film turnout and “a FIFA World Cup budget shift limited advertising yield gains.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “National advertising revenue. Consensus needs about +16% growth against attendance up only about 6%, so monetization gains must do the work.”

surprises.description: Local advertising revenue reached $9.5 million, up 48.4%, exceeding the preview’s $9.1 million estimate and its expected 42% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Local advertising revenue surged 48.4% year-over-year to $9.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Local/regional revenue. Consensus is +42% Y/Y”; “Local/regional revenue vs. $9.1M consensus.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $58.4 million came in below the $60.4 million consensus estimate, although it remained within company guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 12.7% year-over-year to $58.4 million … both within guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $60.4M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted OIBDA was $2.1 million, below the preview’s implied $2.5–3.0 million expectation, though still within the company’s guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted OIBDA tripled to $2.1 million … within guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted OIBDA | ~$2.5–3.0M (implied, not a published consensus).”

in_line: The operational savings program remained on track: the preview cited about $3 million actioned as of Q1, an $11 million annualized target, and up to $6 million in 2026; the call reported $2.7 million of savings year-to-date, approximately $11 million of annualized run-rate savings, and up to $6 million by year-end 2026.

surprises.description: Q1 FY2027 revenue guidance of $1.225–$1.275 billion and EPS of $4.05–$4.35 are well above the preview’s base-case September forecast of $1.13–$1.18 billion and $3.55–$3.85. Revenue midpoint and EPS midpoint also meet or exceed the preview’s bull-case thresholds, despite the preview noting it could not find a sourced Q1 consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 guidance of $1.225–$1.275 billion (midpoint $1.25 billion)” and “EPS guided to $4.05–$4.35.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … September guide | $1.13–1.18B / $3.55–3.85”; “Bull: … ≥$1.25B / ≥$4.10”; and “I did not find a sourced consensus for the September quarter (Q1 FY27).”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP EPS of $3.23 exceeded both the preview’s $2.97–$3.02 consensus range and the prior company guidance midpoint of $2.95. The result is also close to the preview’s bull scenario of about $3.25 and above its base case of $3.10.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 non-GAAP EPS of $3.23 well above prior guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS … Consensus | $2.97 – $3.02”; “Base | … Q4 EPS | ~$3.10”; “Bull | … Q4 EPS | ~$3.25.”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP gross margin was 50.4%, below the preview’s inferred consensus expectation of roughly 51–52%. It did cross 50% and reached the company’s target earlier than the $2 billion quarterly run-rate milestone, but the reported margin was still short of the preview’s margin bogey.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 non-GAAP gross margin crossed 50% (50.4%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus implies roughly 51–52%, which is my inference from the guided margins”; the bull scenario also assumed “gross margin above 53%.”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP operating margin reached 36.6%, above the preview’s 35.0–36.0% company guidance range and its roughly 35.5% expectation. The margin expansion was therefore stronger than the preview’s operating-margin benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 36.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin | 35.0% – 36.0% | ~35.5%.”

surprises.description: The company’s Q1 operating-margin outlook of 39.5–40.5% is already at the midpoint of its $2 billion revenue-level target model, despite much lower revenue. Management suggested raising the top of that model by 100–200 basis points—an improvement to the profitability framework beyond the preview’s discussion of margin improvement and the $2 billion revenue goal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 non-GAAP operating margin is guided to 39.5%–40.5%, already at the midpoint of the company's $2 billion revenue-level target model at much lower revenue, prompting management to suggest raising the top of that model by 100–200 bps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 framing. Lumentum guides one quarter at a time, so any directional FY27 comment or timeline for the $2B-per-quarter goal may matter”; the preview also said gross margin had “a lot of room for improvement.”

surprises.description: OCS activity accelerated: shipments doubled sequentially and Q1 guidance includes the first quarter above $100 million. The preview described OCS timing as the largest swing factor and warned of a possible slip, but did not anticipate this quantified ramp or the company’s stated position as the only merchant OCS supplier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OCS shipments doubled from Q3 to Q4,” and “Q1 guidance includes the first triple-digit (over $100 million) OCS revenue quarter”; the company is “the only merchant OCS supplier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “OCS ramp. This is tied to a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar purchase agreement with Google. Management called it ‘the biggest single tightrope.’ Ramp timing is the largest swing factor”; the bear scenario included “OCS slips a quarter.”

surprises.description: Pump-laser shipments grew more than 80% year over year, with a fourfold increase expected over coming quarters, and the company now has mostly three-year take-or-pay agreements. This is a notably stronger supply and demand outlook, and more secured contracting, than the preview’s discussion of an unanticipated pump constraint and agreements still being negotiated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pump laser shipments grew over 80% year-over-year with a fourfold increase expected over coming quarters, backed by mostly three-year take-or-pay agreements.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had called the pump constraint “unanticipated” and “relatively sudden,” and that it was “negotiating prepayment, take-or-pay and price-escalator terms.”

surprises.description: The call introduced a sizable CPO/NPO opportunity that the preview did not flag: ultra-high-power laser demand is already well beyond supply, with ELS-module and laser revenue targeted at roughly $50 million by year-end and a first triple-digit quarter in fiscal Q3. The demand is strong, but the supply shortfall and customer deployments not scaling until 2028 temper the near-term opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ultra-high-power laser chip demand for CPO/NPO has surged well beyond supply,” with revenue expected to reach “roughly $50 million by year-end” and a “first triple-digit quarter in fiscal Q3,” ahead of customer scale-up deployments in 2028.

surprises.description: Cloud transceiver progress was not part of the preview’s specific expectations: the company reported record 800-gig shipments, has begun 1.6T module production, and expects 1.6T uptake to intensify through calendar 2027 as Tier 1 hyperscalers build custom AI clusters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cloud transceivers achieved record 800-gig shipments and began 1.6T module production, with 1.6T uptake expected to intensify through calendar 2027 driven by Tier 1 hyperscaler custom AI clusters.”

surprises.description: Equitizing $1.1 billion of convertible notes generated a one-time non-cash GAAP charge of $7.8 billion and a Q4 GAAP net loss of $7.2 billion, an unexpected accounting hit. The charge is non-cash and the transaction reduced outstanding convertible debt, making the overall news mixed rather than purely negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company equitized $1.1 billion of convertible notes (about 35% of outstanding convertible debt), triggering a one-time non-cash GAAP charge of $7.8 billion and a Q4 GAAP net loss of $7.2 billion.”

in_line: Q4 revenue of $1.01 billion landed at the upper edge of the preview’s consensus range of $988 million–$1.01 billion.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $3.5 million, well below the preview's roughly $4.55 million consensus estimate. The $1.05 million shortfall was larger than the preview's base-case range and revenue decline implied by its estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 R&D revenue declined to $3.5 million from $5.1 million in Q2 2025,” driven by “the transition of BARDA work into a cost-sharing phase and completion of the MTEC contract.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue, Q2 … Consensus ~$4.55M”; the preview's base scenario was “$4.4–4.6M.”

surprises.description: Cash at quarter-end was $14 million, materially above the preview's estimate of about $8 million if Q2 burn resembled Q1. This is a substantially stronger cash position than the preview's downside-focused cash scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “As of June 30, 2026, Spectral AI held $14 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A similar Q2 burn would leave cash near $8M going into a commercial launch”; the preview also said to watch cash “against the ~$8M line.”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 31.6%, down sharply from both Q2 last year and the 50.8% Q1 level highlighted in the preview. The preview anticipated launch spending pressure on operating expenses, but the reported margin decline came from the BARDA cost-share transition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin fell to 31.6% in Q2 2026 from 45.2% a year earlier, reflecting the BARDA cost-share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Gross margin and opex” as a key metric, noted “50.8% Q1 margin,” and said “Launch spend will hit G&A and S&M before device revenue arrives.”

surprises.description: FDA clearance unlocked another $6.5 million from the Avenue Capital facility and improved the repayment schedule, with no principal due until March 2028. That is more supportive financing than the preview's concern that cash needs could lead to a dilutive raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FDA clearance triggered the drawdown of the second $6.5 million tranche of the Avenue Capital facility (full $15 million commitment) and extended the interest-only period to 24 months with no principal payments due until March 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said cash would determine whether the launch is self-funded or “the next headline is a dilutive raise,” and advised watching for “any ATM, warrant inducement, or debt facility.”

surprises.description: The call gave a concrete scale for the BARDA deployment opportunity: up to 30 systems under the current contract and a longer-term opportunity across more than 200 facilities. The preview discussed BARDA funding and timing but did not quantify this deployment footprint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to deploy up to 30 systems under its BARDA CLIN II Project BioShield contract through June 30, 2027, with a longer-term opportunity across over 200 high-value US facilities.”

surprises.description: The company said it has access to more than $60 million of additional non-dilutive BARDA funding, a larger stated funding resource than the preview's discussion of the $31.7 million accelerated Phase II award and its cost-share commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company had “access to over $60 million of additional non-dilutive BARDA funding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on “most of the $31.7M accelerated BARDA Phase II award” recognizing in 2027 and the company's “$9.7M cost-share commitment.”

surprises.description: The call provided new support for the prospective commercial margin profile: a third-party pricing study indicated the market can support margins well above current development work, alongside a model with recurring software and services revenue on minimum three-year terms. The preview flagged pricing and margins as questions but did not report this validation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The commercial model “combines capital purchases or leases with recurring software and services revenue on a minimum three-year term,” and “a third-party pricing study indicated the market will support margins well above current development work.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for evidence on “the pricing model” and said “Launch spend will hit G&A and S&M before device revenue arrives.”

surprises.description: The call identified Q4 2026 UKCA clearance as an expected route to initial sales in the UK, Australia, or Gulf Cooperation Council countries. The preview focused on first commercial sales and did not flag this international clearance and market opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “expects UKCA clearance in Q4 2026 to enable initial international sales in the UK, Australia, or Gulf Cooperation Council countries.”

in_line: FY26 revenue guidance was reiterated at approximately $18.5 million, as the preview expected.
GAAP EPS of -$0.13 was within the preview's cited consensus range of -$0.11 to -$0.15; the preview also cautioned that warrant-liability effects distort EPS.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $64,000, far below the preview’s roughly $300,000 consensus and its $250,000–$400,000 base-case range. The preview cautioned that consensus was stale, but the reported figure was also below its $150,000 bear-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was approximately $64,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$0.30M”; the base scenario expected “$0.25–0.40M,” while the bear scenario was “Under $0.15M.”

surprises.description: Pixelworks signed its first major device licensee—a multi-year certification agreement with a global manufacturer—before its planned 2026 timeline. The preview focused on possible title counts and revenue mix, but did not anticipate this device-licensing milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed its first major device licensee—a multi-year device certification agreement with an unnamed global manufacturer—ahead of its planned 2026 timeline following a six-month evaluation.”

surprises.description: The company repurchased $3.2 million of stock in Q2, making buybacks its largest cash use. That is a favorable outcome versus the preview’s concern that no Q2 repurchases would be a negative signal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pixelworks repurchased $3.2 million of common stock during Q2, its single largest cash use, with $1.8 million remaining on the buyback authorization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Zero shares repurchased in Q2 would be a negative signal about capital use.”

surprises.description: Management said Q3 revenue should increase sequentially based on business already booked, giving a near-term revenue outlook despite the Q2 shortfall. The preview said the company did not provide formal guidance; management cautioned that revenue will remain lumpy until the business reaches scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Q3 2026 revenue to increase sequentially based on currently booked licensing and motion grading business, though revenue will remain lumpy until scale is achieved.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Formal guidance | None”; “Company does not guide.”

surprises.description: Q2 cash operating use was roughly $1.7 million, below the approximately $2.0 million cash-opex run rate the preview highlighted as the key cost test. GAAP operating expenses were still $3.4 million, but had fallen from $5.2 million in Q1 after restructuring.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP operating expenses fell to $3.4 million in Q2 from $5.2 million in Q1”; “operating cash use of roughly $1.7 million in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “~$2.0M run rate per CFO on Q1 call”; “Cash opex versus the $2.0M run rate. This is the most testable claim management made.”

surprises.description: Pixelworks added an endorsement from Kannapolis Group to its exhibitor ecosystem, an addition the preview did not identify among its existing relationships or watch items. The preview had already noted the CINITY relationship, so that partnership itself was not new relative to expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pixelworks expanded its exhibitor ecosystem by securing endorsements from Kannapolis Group and a partnership with CINITY, adding to existing relationships with Marcus Theatres, Odeon, and VIEW.”

in_line: Management’s expected quarterly interest income of $400,000–$500,000 matched the preview’s cited range from the Q1 call.

No quantified H2 title count was reported in the supplied facts; the preview’s base scenario had expected the H2 slate to remain unquantified, although it flagged a title count as a potential upside catalyst.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $5.1 million, below the preview’s $5.4–5.9 million consensus range and $5.84 million estimate, despite growing more than 40% year over year. The miss was about 13% versus consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $5.1 million, up more than 40% year-over-year from $3.5 million but down sequentially from $6.7 million in Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY26 consensus $5.84M (range ~$5.4–5.9M), +65.4% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 22.6%, above the preview’s 15–19% base-case range and the 18% threshold it described as important. The preview noted that no consensus gross-margin estimate was published.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP gross margin improved to 22.6% in Q2 2026 from 18.1% in Q1, driven by a higher mix of international ESS sales and pricing discipline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base ... gross margin 15–19%”; the preview also said “Sustained margins of 18% or higher support the case for a real business.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP loss was $0.04 per share, wider than the preview’s alternative estimate of a $0.02 loss. The reported $13.1 million loss was also attributed partly to lower revenue and a bad-debt provision on a legacy EV service contract, which the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net loss was $13.1 million ($0.04/share) in Q2, wider than Q1's $11.1 million loss, hurt by lower revenue and a bad debt provision on a legacy EV service contract.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (alt.) ... –$0.02” (the preview cautioned this was “likely non-GAAP / stale”).

surprises.description: The company ended the quarter with $163 million in cash, slightly above the preview’s estimate of roughly $158–162 million if Q1’s cash burn repeated. This is a small positive versus that balance expectation, although the call facts do not state Q2 cash burn directly.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with approximately $163 million in cash, equivalents and short-term investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A repeat of Q1's ~$20M burn implies about $158–162M at Q2-end.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted quantified drone revenue as a key test, but the call facts do not give a Q2 drone-revenue figure. Instead, SES disclosed that top-five-customer drone demand exceeds current deliverable capacity, with order visibility into 2028, and plans to increase Korea cell production fivefold; this indicates strong demand but does not quantify near-term revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Drone demand from its top five large customers already exceeds 1.5 million cells annually against roughly 700,000-800,000 deliverable capacity, with order visibility into 2028”; production is expected to scale “five-fold from 200,000 to 1 million cells per year by about September, running at full speed in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Quantified drone revenue. Management has described drone shipments only qualitatively so far. A hard Q2 dollar figure matters for whether the H2 ramp is credible.”

surprises.description: SES reported Solark certification as a battery partner and said residential ESS competition had narrowed from roughly 20 players to about three. The preview did not identify this certification or competitive change as an expected catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company was certified by Solark as a battery partner, reducing residential ESS competition from roughly 20 players to about three (alongside Enphase and Tesla), aided by new restrictions on foreign-produced inverters.”

in_line: SES reaffirmed FY2026 revenue guidance of $30–35 million, consistent with the preview’s stated company guidance and its base case of a reaffirmed guide with a second-half ramp.
GAAP EPS was a loss of $0.05 per share, matching the preview’s $0.05 loss consensus.

surprises.description: QuickLogic reported Q2 revenue of $5.5 million, below the $6.0 million consensus and the $6.0 million guidance midpoint; it was also well short of the preview’s buy-side anchor near $6.5–6.6 million. The company attributed the shortfall to a delayed contract extension.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $5.5 million … but landed below the guidance midpoint due to a delayed contract extension.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $6.0M” consensus and “$6.0M ±10%” company guidance; the preview also said buy-side expectations were likely anchored to “the high end of guidance (~$6.5–6.6M).”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $5.5 million, flat sequentially, is far below the preview’s key expectation of at least $7.0 million. QuickLogic said a seven-figure contract extension and the commercial Intel 18A ASIC design opportunity have both moved to 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 revenue is guided flat at $5.5 million (±10%), as two opportunities—a seven-figure contract extension and a commercial Intel 18A ASIC design—were pushed out to 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 revenue guide at or above $7.0M” was a catalyst, and the preview said guidance below about $6.5M would undercut the FY consensus.

surprises.description: QuickLogic pushed the commercial Intel 18A ASIC opportunity out to 2027 rather than delivering the near-term award the preview identified as the cleanest bull catalyst. The preview had specifically warned that another slip would be a negative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A commercial Intel 18A ASIC design” was “pushed out to 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called confirmation of the Intel 18A award “the cleanest bull catalyst,” said a “second slip” was “the cleanest bear catalyst,” and listed an award booked in Q3 as a catalyst.

surprises.description: The full-year revenue outlook now implies roughly $23.4–$24.8 million, below the preview’s $25.5 million consensus. The 70%–80% growth range is also narrower and has a lower ceiling than the prior 50%–100% growth outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “QuickLogic narrowed its full-year 2026 revenue growth outlook to 70%-80%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “FY2026 revenue | $25.5M” consensus and prior company guidance of “+50% to +100%.”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP gross margin reached 46.8%, above the preview’s approximately 42% expectation and the 42% guidance midpoint. This is a stronger quarterly margin result than anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin rose to 46.8% in Q2 2026 from 31% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview put Q2 non-GAAP gross margin consensus at “~42%” and company guidance at “42% ±5%.”

surprises.description: Despite the Q2 margin beat, the full-year gross-margin model is now approximately 51%, well below the preview’s approximately 57% model. That is a weaker full-year margin trajectory than investors were led to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 gross margin [is] modeled at approximately 51%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “The FY non-GAAP GM model of ~57% needs H2 GM near 69–70% after H1 tracked ~41%.”

surprises.description: QuickLogic raised $9.8 million through its ATM program while reporting soft revenue guidance. The resulting cash increase strengthens liquidity, but the amount raised is a meaningful dilution concern consistent with the preview’s identified bear-case risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash grew to $13.5 million (excluding a $5 million credit line drawdown) from $3.8 million at year-end 2025, aided by $9.8 million raised through the ATM program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Cash and dilution” and said “Large ATM usage alongside soft guidance is the bear path.”

surprises.description: Management said the Q4 growth story depends heavily on the U.S. government contract, which has an $89 million total ceiling and is expected to supply a significant share of Q4 revenue. The preview did not flag this degree of reliance on one contract as a key part of the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company's Q4 growth story hinges heavily on its U.S. government contract, which carries an $89 million total ceiling and is expected to contribute a significant percentage of total Q4 revenue.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed approximately $8–10 million of second-half eFPGA-related revenue, including government NRE, and said several IP contracts are signed with others in late-stage negotiation. This provides specific near-term revenue visibility not laid out in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Second-half eFPGA-related revenue (including government NRE work) of approximately $8-10 million,” with “several IP contracts already signed and others in late-stage negotiation.”

surprises.description: Full-year non-GAAP operating expenses are expected to rise roughly 17% while revenue is expected to grow 70%–80%, indicating stronger operating leverage than the preview quantified. The preview did not provide an operating-expense outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year non-GAAP operating expenses were raised to $13.7-$13.9 million, representing roughly 17% growth against 70%-80% revenue growth, highlighting the model's operating leverage.”

surprises.description: QuickLogic now expects mature product revenue to be flat with 2025 at about $3.3 million, rather than describing growth in that business. The preview did not identify this flat outlook, though the newly funded defense qualification could create a multi-million-dollar opportunity starting in 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 mature product revenue is now expected to be flat with 2025 at about $3.3 million,” while a “newly funded small-package qualification for defense customers could open a multi-million-dollar opportunity starting in 2027.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed expectations for non-GAAP profitability and positive cash flow in the second half of 2026, consistent with the preview’s expectation of H2 profitability.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $13.8 million, above the preview’s $11.4–12.0 million working range. The reported result was about 15% above the top of that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 38% year-over-year to $13.8 million from $10 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working range $11.4–12.0M.”

surprises.description: The reported Q2 net loss and EPS were worse than the preview’s expected EPS, largely because of a one-time $11.7 million debt-extinguishment loss. Excluding that item, the net loss was $11.2 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company recognized a one-time $11.7 million loss on debt extinguishment tied to paying off its 13.5% notes, widening Q2 net loss to $22.9 million ($0.18/share)”; “excluding the one-time item, net loss was $11.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (Q2): $(0.10) (FXEmpire) or $(0.12) (GuruFocus/Yahoo).”

surprises.description: The FDA-requested top-of-tongue misadministration arm had been a concern because its median time to peak concentration was longer than for correct use. The call reported that this arm still cleared both specified concentration thresholds and showed favorable pharmacodynamic responses versus manual intramuscular administration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FDA-requested misadministration (top of tongue) arm still cleared both the 50 and 100 picograms/mL thresholds with favorable pharmacodynamic responses versus manual IM.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The top-of-tongue misplacement arm showed median Tmax of 35 minutes versus 12 minutes for correct sublingual use. Labeling handling of misplacement is a live question.”

surprises.description: The revised packaging performed strongly in the completed human-factors validation: reported opening difficulties fell from 26 participants to 1, film tearing from 6 to 0, and dose misplacement from 20 to 2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The revised packaging reduced participants showing difficulty opening from 26 to 1, film tearing from 6 to 0, and dose misplacement from 20 to 2 in the new human factors validation study.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Topline results released Aug 10 were strong,” while the preview identified “Full human factors study detail” as a key metric to watch.

surprises.description: Although the expected base case remained a six-month FDA review, management is now pushing for the possibility of a two-month Class 1 review because it views the resubmission package as succinct and focused. The shorter review is only a potential outcome, not an FDA decision.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guides to a standard 6-month FDA review as the base case but is pushing for a potential 2-month Class 1 review given the succinct, focused resubmission package.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management expects a Class 2 (6-month) review and will request expedited handling, but says classification rests with the FDA.”

surprises.description: The company reported a new $150 million Oaktree debt facility that lowers its cost of capital and extends the interest-only period, favorable financing terms not specified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company refinanced with Oaktree into a new $150 million debt facility that lowers cost of capital and extends the interest-only period.”

in_line: Aquestive completed the required human-factors and PK studies and remained on track to resubmit the Anaphylm NDA before the end of Q3 2026, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it was on track for a Q3 resubmission.
Management retained a six-month FDA review as its base case, consistent with the preview’s expected Class 2 review.
Full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $46–50 million and adjusted EBITDA loss guidance of $30–35 million were reaffirmed, as the preview expected.

surprises.description: The draft had proposed allowing unlicensed space-to-first transmissions in NextNav’s lower 900 MHz band, but the band was absent from the FCC’s final direct-to-device NPRM. That is a setback against the preview’s focus on the FCC advancing NextNav’s spectrum proposal, though it does not establish the outcome of the separate PNT-focused NPRM.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NextNav's lower 900 MHz band was ultimately not included in the FCC's final direct-to-device NPRM despite the draft proposing to permit unlicensed space-to-first transmissions in the band.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The equity value depends on whether the FCC advances NextNav's April 2024 petition to reconfigure the Lower 900 MHz band for a terrestrial 5G PNT/GPS-backup network.”

surprises.description: NextNav reported approximately 20 nanoseconds of timing accuracy across outdoor, indoor, and GPS-denied environments, which management said exceeds critical-infrastructure requirements. The preview discussed network development and commercial proof points but did not anticipate this specific performance demonstration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “NextNav demonstrated approximately 20 nanoseconds of timing accuracy over its operational 5G PNT network across outdoor, indoor and GPS-denied environments,” which management says “exceeds critical infrastructure requirements.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Contracts matter more than revenue here. Items to track include the Safran Electronics & Defense interoperability agreement (July 29, 2026), MetCom (Japan) technology licensing, tolling-industry engagement (IBTTA), and rail coexistence testing at Pueblo, CO.”

surprises.description: A new Tier 1 partner is putting NextNav’s Z-access software and reference data on its devices for 911 vertical-location services, creating an additional route to potential revenue that the preview did not identify. No revenue amount or paid contract was reported, so the commercial impact remains unquantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new partnership brings NextNav's Z-access software and reference data onto a Tier 1 partner's devices for 911 vertical location services,” advancing its device-based strategy and creating incremental revenue opportunities.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Safran, MetCom, tolling, and rail as commercial proof points to track, and said a “first revenue-bearing commercial agreement” would be a catalyst; it did not mention a Tier 1 device partnership for 911 location.

in_line: Liquidity was approximately $300 million and the company was debt-free, within the preview’s expected roughly $290–315 million liquidity range with no debt. The preview also anticipated about $170 million of warrant proceeds and estimated a share count near 165 million; the call facts do not provide the resulting total share count.

The preview already noted SpaceX’s FCC letter naming NextNav’s 900 MHz proposal, and management’s view that the letter validates demand for scarce low-band spectrum is consistent with that expected development.

The draft PNT-focused NPRM remained in interagency review, with timing still subject to ongoing reviews, consistent with the preview’s report that it was at OIRA and had not yet been formally issued or voted on.

The Safran interoperability partnership was already identified in the preview as a commercial proof point to watch; the call described integration and demonstration plans rather than reporting a paid deal.

The preview warned that Q2 GAAP results would reflect noncash fair-value marks and debt-extinguishment accounting. The reported approximately $33.8 million net loss included a roughly $32 million noncash liability fair-value loss, partly offset by a roughly $21 million debt-extinguishment gain.

surprises.description: The preview expected core R&D of about $16M or less, with the $9.25M JCR option payment potentially adding to reported expense. Q2 R&D was $27.8M, above the roughly $25.25M implied ceiling if that payment was expensed, so the spending target appears to have been missed despite lower manufacturing, materials, and CRO costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expenses fell to $27.8 million in Q2 2026,” driven by “reduced manufacturing, materials, and CRO costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Core R&D of about $16M or less ex-JCR”; the preview also says Q2 “includes a $9.25M option-exercise payment” likely expensed to R&D.

surprises.description: The preview focused on whether the late-2026 readout timing would hold, but did not flag uncertainty over trial powering. Management declined to say how the study is powered or whether each dose is independently powered against placebo, leaving the criteria for a positive readout less clear.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management declined to disclose the trial's statistical powering framework or whether each dose is independently powered against placebo, leaving uncertainty about what constitutes a positive study.”

surprises.description: The preview discussed ACU301 and ACU401 development cadence but did not anticipate a striking exposure result. New non-human-primate data showed ACU401 achieved up to 40-fold greater frontal-cortex exposure than unmodified ACU234, exceeding management’s expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ACU401 achieved up to 40-fold greater frontal cortex exposure than unmodified ACU234, exceeding management's expectations.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a safety-positioning claim about sabirnetug. Management highlighted its IgG2 format and oligomer selectivity as potential advantages over IgG1 competitors because they may reduce ARIA risk; this is a proposed differentiator, not reported clinical evidence of lower ARIA rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is positioning sabirnetug's IgG2 antibody format and oligomer selectivity as differentiating safety advantages over IgG1 competitors Kisunla and Leqembi by potentially reducing ARIA risk.”

in_line: ALTITUDE-AD topline timing remained late 2026, as the preview identified as the key catalyst and expected to be reiterated.

Cash was $110.2M and management said it should fund operations into early 2027, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of roughly $100M or more and runway into early 2027; the preview had already flagged a potential financing need around the readout.
The ACU301/ACU401 IND target remained mid-2027, consistent with the preview’s stated target.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 revenue of $1.12 million and said the quarter should show a sharp step-up from Q1. Reported Symbest commercial sales were only $0.4 million, and management described Q2 as a “rebuilding quarter.”
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 commercial sales of Symbest were $0.4 million” and management characterized it as a “rebuilding quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 total revenue” consensus was “$1.12M”; the preview also said Q2 revenue consensus “implies a sharp step up from Q1.”

surprises.description: The V012 interim analysis delivered a strong efficacy result that the preview did not anticipate: ATEV provided 91 more catheter-free days than an AV fistula and met the primary endpoint with high statistical significance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ATEV delivered 91 more catheter-free days than AV fistula” with “p-value of 0.0007, meeting the primary efficacy endpoint.”

surprises.description: The V012 trial also reported a much lower infection rate with ATEV than with an AV fistula, an additional favorable clinical finding not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “6 infections per 100 patient-years” for ATEV versus “23 infections per 100 patient-years” for AV fistula.

surprises.description: Symbest adoption plans sounded more concrete than the preview’s focus on whether existing accounts would reorder: management said at least 20 major U.S. healthcare systems were in the process of adopting it, and a national-account strategy could reach roughly 1,000 more hospitals. The low reported sales show that this prospective reach had not yet translated into strong Q2 sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “At least 20 major U.S. healthcare systems are in the process of adopting Symbest in the second half of 2026,” and the new national account strategy targets “roughly 1,000 additional hospitals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case needed “40+ units and evidence that existing accounts are ordering again,” and that the key issue was “units and cash runway more than the P&L.”

surprises.description: Q2 cost of goods sold was higher than the reported commercial sales, with a substantial portion attributed to inventory and unused capacity rather than units sold. The preview did not flag this near-term cost burden.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cost of goods sold rose to $1.2 million,” including “a $0.7 million inventory reserve and unused production capacity costs,” with “only $0.2 million tied to actual units sold.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed that a non-cash remeasurement of the contingent earn-out liability was a major driver of the first-half loss, a one-off explanation not raised in the preview. The comparison was a $54.4 million six-month net loss versus $1.5 million net income a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The six-month net loss of $54.4 million compared to net income of $1.5 million a year prior, driven largely by non-cash remeasurement of the contingent earn-out liability.”

surprises.description: The FDA accepted the IND for the CTEV coronary bypass program, with a 10-patient Phase 2a study expected to open this quarter; this additional program milestone was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FDA accepted the IND for the CTEV coronary bypass program,” and “a 10-patient Phase 2a study [is] expected to open this quarter.”

in_line: The planned November 2026 supplemental BLA filing remains within the preview’s expected H2 2026 submission window; management also laid out a possible May 2027 PDUFA date and end-of-Q2 2027 launch if priority review is granted.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA loss was $5.8 million, worse than the preview’s $5.2 million estimate and outside its $5.0–$5.4 million base range. The loss still improved year over year, but not as much as the preview modeled.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss improved 17% year-over-year to $5.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA” Q2 2026E “($5.2M)”; base scenario “($5.0M)–($5.4M).”

surprises.description: GAAP net loss was $19.8 million, materially larger than the preview’s $15.0 million estimate. It also widened sequentially as the prior quarter’s $5.2 million noncash warrant gain swung to a $1.4 million loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss narrowed to $19.8 million from $21.6 million year-over-year but widened sequentially from $12.7 million, driven almost entirely by a noncash swing in warrant liabilities from a $5.2 million gain to a $1.4 million loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled Q2 “Net loss” of “($15.0M)” and noted that Q1 included a “$5.2M non-cash warrant gain.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin fell to 27%, rather than holding at the preview’s 29% estimate. The company attributed the decline to temporary packing inefficiencies while diversifying Georgia’s channel mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin declined to 27% from 30% a year earlier and 29% in Q1, due to temporary packing inefficiencies from diversifying Georgia's channel mix that have since been resolved.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview modeled Q2 adjusted gross margin at “29%” and described the base case as “flat margin.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash was $10.1 million, below the preview’s roughly $12.0 million estimate and close to its flagged $10 million downside threshold, though it did not fall below that level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash dropped to $10.1 million from $18.8 million in Q1, reflecting operating cash burn.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Cash + restricted” at “~$12.0M” and flagged “a balance below $10M” as a key concern.

surprises.description: After quarter end, Local Bounti received a $12.5 million follow-on investment from an existing strategic investor, a capital infusion not included in the preview’s base case, which assumed no financing announcement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received a $12.5 million follow-on investment from an existing strategic investor after quarter end, adding to a $15 million March investment and prior 2025 transactions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario assumed “no financing announcement”; it also highlighted cash and financing language as a key issue.

surprises.description: The company reported additional retail rollouts beyond the Harris Teeter launch already highlighted in the preview: a five-SKU rollout across about 66 Mid-South stores and a four-SKU rollout across about 110 Rocky Mountain stores.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New retail launches include a 5-SKU rollout across ~66 Mid-South stores in July and a 4-SKU rollout across ~110 Rocky Mountain stores in early August.”

surprises.description: Local Bounti is relaunching its single-serve salad kits in a fall pilot across approximately 400 Mid-Atlantic stores with a major retailer, a product and distribution initiative not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is relaunching its single-serve salad kit line via a fall pilot across approximately 400 Mid-Atlantic stores with a major retailer.”

surprises.description: The call reported operational improvements tied to the preview’s yield-and-capacity debate: Georgia, Texas, and Washington tower upgrades are running at about 10% higher yield capacity, California investments target up to 20% higher yields, and more efficient seeding cut seed costs by roughly 20% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tower upgrades in Georgia, Texas and Washington are running about 10% higher yield capacity, California investments are targeting up to 20% yield improvement, and more efficient seeding cut seed costs roughly 20% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said growth depended on “yield, price, and mix” and described “Yield upgrades convert” as a bull-case driver.

in_line: Revenue was $13.9 million, matching the preview’s $13.9 million model and falling within its $13.7–$14.1 million base range.
The six-SKU Harris Teeter rollout across 250+ stores was already described in the preview as launched on June 15 and as a Q3 revenue event.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $19.9 million, well above the preview’s $13.06 million consensus and even above its $17–19 million bull-case range. The reported $19.8 million of goods revenue was driven mainly by higher El Fabrio sales through Chiesi.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenues rose to $19.9 million”; “Q2 2026 revenues from selling goods grew to $19.8 million … driven mainly by higher El Fabrio sales through Chiesi.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 total revenue … Consensus $13.06M”; the bull scenario projected “Revenue $17–19M.”

surprises.description: The quarter was profitable, with net income of $3.8 million and EPS of $0.05, versus consensus for a $0.01 loss. That was a substantial reversal from the expected small loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income increased sharply to $3.8 million (5 cents per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 EPS (diluted) … Consensus $(0.01).”

surprises.description: Management said Chiesi’s strong Q2 purchases largely reflected inventory management, rather than presenting them as evidence of sustained demand. The preview’s bull case had looked for early Chiesi E4W restocking, so this explanation makes the revenue beat less clearly indicative of underlying uptake.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2's strong Chiesi purchases largely reflect Chiesi's inventory management,” and quarterly revenues are “lumpy and best evaluated on a full-year basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario cited “Early Chiesi E4W restocking”; the preview also said Chiesi’s H2 order book depended on country-by-country E4W reimbursement.

surprises.description: R&D expense fell to $4.4 million, rather than continuing the increase associated with PRX-115 Phase 2 initiation noted in the preview. Management attributed part of the reduction to $2.1 million of grants recorded as a reduction in R&D expense under a new law that is available on an ongoing basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expenses fell to $4.4 million from $6 million”; this was “aided by $2.1 million in grants now recorded as a reduction of R&D expenses under a new R&D law available on an ongoing basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 R&D was “up 54% y/y to $5.4M, driven by PRX-115 Phase 2 initiation.”

surprises.description: The company reported no outstanding debt, compared with the $8.5 million of debt cited in the preview’s March 31 balance-sheet snapshot. Cash and short-term deposits were also lower, at $40.7 million versus the previously reported $51.1 million, so the overall balance-sheet change is mixed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds $40.7 million in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term deposits as of June 30, 2026, with no outstanding debt or warrants.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Cash and short-term deposits of $51.1M at 3/31/26 …; debt $8.5M.”

surprises.description: Management introduced a long-term market and share ambition for El Fabrio: a global Fabry market of about $3.2 billion by 2031 and a 15–20% share for the product. The preview did not flag this projection.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management projects the global Fabry market to reach approximately $3.2 billion by 2031, with El Fabrio positioned to capture 15-20% of that market.”

in_line: The expected PRX-115 RELEASE topline timing remained in the second half of 2027, as the preview stated.

Management’s reminder that partner-driven quarterly revenue can be lumpy was consistent with the preview’s warning that shipment timing can move quarterly revenue materially and that the results should be assessed in the context of full-year performance.

surprises.description: Trimble raised its FY2026 revenue midpoint by $50 million to $3.925 billion, above the preview’s $3.90 billion bull-case threshold, and raised EPS guidance by $0.10 to $3.65—above the old range’s $3.64 high end. This was a stronger outlook increase than the preview’s expected modest raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management raised full-year guidance, lifting the revenue midpoint by $50 million to $3.925 billion (~9% growth) and EPS by $0.10 to $3.65 (~17% growth).
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A guidance raise is closer to expectations than the upside case”; the bull scenario expected “FY revenue raised to at least $3.90B.”

surprises.description: Q2 organic revenue was $972 million, above both the $950.9–951.4 million consensus and the $963 million high end of company guidance. The result exceeded the preview’s bull-case revenue range only slightly.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 organic revenue grew 10% to $972 million, beating the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus revenue was “$950.9–951.4M”; company guidance was “$938–963M”; the bull scenario was “$965–975M.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS of $0.86 beat the preview’s $0.80 consensus and the $0.82 top of company guidance, exceeding even the preview’s bull-case range by a small amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS was $0.86, beating the guidance midpoint by $0.06.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus EPS was “$0.80”; company guidance was “$0.78–0.82”; the bull scenario was “$0.84–0.87.”

surprises.description: Trimble said it now expects to reach its 30% EBITDA margin target in 2026, a full year earlier than the 2027 goal highlighted in the preview. Q2 EBITDA margin also expanded 120 basis points to 28.6%, showing progress on the margin ramp the preview flagged as a key risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “EBITDA margins expanded 120 bps to 28.6%”; management expects to “reach its 30% EBITDA margin target a full year early in 2026, versus the prior 2027 Investor Day goal.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a “27.9–28.5%” FY non-GAAP operating margin guide and said the H2 margin ramp needed to be demonstrated; it also listed the “2027 Investor Day targets” including “30% EBITDA margin.”

surprises.description: Field Systems ARR guidance was cut to high-single-digit/low-double-digit growth because Trimble is replacing a low-margin white-label product. The resulting 400–500 basis-point segment ARR headwind is weaker than the preview’s hoped-for acceleration from Q1’s 12% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Field Systems ARR guidance was cut to high-single-digit/low-double-digit growth” due to replacing a low-margin white-label field data processing product, creating a “400-500 bps ARR headwind ($16-20M).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 Field Systems ARR growth was 12%, identified the segment as having “the least visibility,” and included “Field Systems accelerating” in its bull scenario.

surprises.description: Total organic ARR reached a record $2.509 billion, slightly above the preview’s estimated $2.48–2.50 billion range, but growth was 12% rather than the 13% or more the preview identified as supportive of the re-rating case. The dollar level modestly beat the estimate while the growth rate fell short of the preview’s aspirational threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total organic ARR grew 12% to a record $2.509 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “~$2.48–2.50B” ARR and said “At least 13% supports the re-rating thesis.”

surprises.description: Trimble confirmed a strategic review of Transportation & Logistics after receiving credible inbound acquisition interest. The preview noted an unconfirmed sale report and watched for confirmation, but the company gave no predetermined outcome or timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trimble received credible inbound acquisition interest in its Transportation & Logistics business and has launched a Goldman Sachs-advised strategic review with no predetermined outcome or timeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Axios had reported Trimble was “working with Goldman Sachs to sell T&L” and listed “any confirmation or portfolio-review language” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: The company authorized another $1 billion of share repurchases, beyond the roughly $608 million of authorization the preview expected to remain after Q1. The additional authorization is supported by low leverage, while the company also reported substantial buybacks since early 2025.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a new $1 billion share repurchase authorization and has bought back nearly $1.2 billion in stock since the start of 2025, with leverage at just 1.1x versus a 2.5x long-term target.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “About $608M of buyback authorization remains after Q1's $316.9M.”

surprises.description: Field Systems revenue rose 12% despite tariff refunds creating an approximately 300-basis-point revenue headwind. The preview flagged the segment’s tariff exposure, but did not anticipate this specific temporary effect; management said it did not affect operating income and would not recur.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Field Systems revenue rose 12% to $442 million despite a ~300 bps headwind from tariff refunds that had no impact on operating income and is not expected to recur.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Field Systems as “the most tariff- and hardware-exposed segment” and flagged tariff commentary as a key watch item.

in_line: AECO ARR grew 14%, matching the 14% growth reported in Q1 and the preview’s stated focus on whether AECO would decelerate.

surprises.description: Q2 net loss was $22.8 million versus the preview’s roughly $25 million consensus and $24–$26 million base case; EPS was a loss of $0.12 versus $0.14 expected. Both were better than forecast, with the per-share result also reflecting the larger share count the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss was $22.8 million ($0.12/share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS ($0.14)” and “Implied net loss ~($25)M”; the base scenario was “($24M) to ($26M) / ($0.14).”

surprises.description: R&D expense came in below the preview’s $19–$21 million estimate, at $18.7 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D rising to $18.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “R&D expense” estimate: “$19M to $21M.”

surprises.description: G&A expense was also below the preview’s $8.0–$8.7 million estimate, at $7.6 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “G&A rising to $7.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “G&A expense” estimate: “$8.0M to $8.7M.”

surprises.description: Beyond the AUD outcomes already highlighted in the preview, the call reported that more than twice the placebo rate of pemvidutide patients achieved zero heavy drinking days. The preview gave the primary result and WHO risk-reduction result, but not this additional registrational secondary-endpoint outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “More than double the placebo rate achieving zero heavy drinking days.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported the primary endpoint and “Two-level WHO risk reduction was 64.4% vs. 34.8%”; it did not mention the zero-heavy-drinking-days result.

surprises.description: The call added an exploratory liver-marker result in AUD: half of pemvidutide patients with baseline FIB-4 above 1.3 fell below that threshold after 24 weeks, versus 17% on placebo. The preview did not flag this liver-benefit analysis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “50% of pemvidutide patients with baseline FIB-4 above 1.3 dropped below 1.3 after just 24 weeks, versus only 17% on placebo.”

surprises.description: The call reported a statistically significant 9.1% body-weight reduction in RECLAIM, an additional efficacy result not covered in the preview’s account of the AUD topline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pemvidutide produced a statistically significant 9.1% body weight reduction from baseline versus placebo in the RECLAIM AUD trial.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s RECLAIM topline summary covered heavy drinking days and WHO risk reduction, but did not mention weight loss.

surprises.description: The call clarified that the stated cash runway through the 2029 MASH readout does not cover a potential AUD Phase 3 trial. Management plans to seek royalty, debt, or strategic-partner funding for that trial after FDA end-of-Phase-2 feedback, so the runway assurance is narrower than a reading of “operations through the 2029 readout” alone might suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The cash runway does not include a potential AUD Phase 3 trial,” which management intends to fund through “non-dilutive means such as royalty, debt, or strategic partnerships after obtaining FDA end-of-Phase 2 feedback.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “reaffirmation that $535M funds operations through the 2029 readout” and described the catalyst as “cash of at least $510M and reaffirmation of runway through the 2029 readout.”

surprises.description: Altimmune amended RESTORE’s protocol to assess liver stiffness hierarchically at both week 48 and week 24. The preview discussed enrollment timing but did not anticipate this additional assessment time point.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Amended the protocol to assess liver stiffness hierarchically at both week 48 and week 24.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s RESTORE item focused on enrollment, which was “guided to complete in Q3'26”; it did not mention a week-24 assessment.

in_line: The RECLAIM primary endpoint result matched the preview’s already-reported topline: 1.45 fewer heavy drinking days per week versus placebo.
The WHO risk-reduction result in AUD was consistent with the preview’s reported 64.4% versus 34.8% result.
PERFORMA had already been initiated before the release, as the preview noted, and the call’s 2029 52-week data expectation was consistent with the preview.
Cash of $519 million was within the preview’s $510–$520 million estimate, and the MASH Phase 3 runway through the 2029 readout was reaffirmed.
RESTORE enrollment was completed during Q3 2026, consistent with the preview’s expectation that enrollment would complete in Q3.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case was that Kontoor would reaffirm FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $5.15–$5.25, with a raise described as the bull case. Instead, the company raised the range to $5.25–$5.35, even after including about $25 million of additional brand-building investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Kontoor raised its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to $5.25-$5.35 … from the prior $5.15-$5.25”; the updated outlook “incorporates approximately $25 million of incremental brand-building investment (a ~$0.36 EPS drag).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … FY range reaffirmed”; “A raise is the cleanest bull catalyst.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted gross margin as a key debate and cited the existing FY2026 range of 48.3%–48.5%. Kontoor raised its full-year adjusted gross margin outlook to 49.8%–50.0%, a substantially higher range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year adjusted gross margin guidance to 49.8%-50% from 48.3%-48.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. gross margin: 48.3–48.5%”; the preview said to watch “Adj. gross margin and the tariff bridge.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on Lee’s sale and the planned buyback, with a near-term close and buyback start flagged as a catalyst. Kontoor instead described a $400 million accelerated repurchase to be funded upon the divestiture closing in Q4, with the remaining proceeds directed to debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fund a $400 million accelerated share repurchase upon the Lee divestiture closing in Q4, using remaining proceeds to pay down debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Lee close timing and buyback execution”; “Confirmation of a near-term close and buyback start would be a real catalyst.”

surprises.description: The preview did not describe the earnings and cost burden that would remain after the Lee sale. Management said the divestiture leaves about $0.55 of stranded or unmitigated costs and $0.90 of lost operating earnings, with a 12–18 month period to offset them and reach an EPS-neutral deal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Lee divestiture leaves ~$0.55 of stranded/unmitigated costs and ~$0.90 of lost operating earnings,” which management expects to “fully offset within 12-18 months to make the deal EPS-neutral.”
