surprises.description: The call added a large long-term deployment ambition of over 1 million units across projects, beyond the 100,000-unit 2026 target highlighted in the preview. This is an additional scale target, not a report of units already shipped or revenue secured.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SKYX expects to deploy over 1 million units across projects long-term” and reaffirmed the goal of delivering “over 100,000 units by the end of 2026,” saying it was “according to plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists the stated target as “over 100,000 units into homes during 2026.”

surprises.description: SKYX described an expanded European hotel pipeline, including an agreement with Group OTT, whose developer has 250+ hotels, and its first two European hotel deployments in France and Prague. The preview mentioned hospitality projects generally but did not identify these European agreements or deployments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SKYX expanded its European hotel pipeline via agreements with Group OTT (developer of 250+ hotels) targeting a market of over 132,000 hotels, plus its first two European hotel deployments in France and Prague.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview referred to “several hospitality projects” and said the announcements remained unquantified.

surprises.description: The call clarified that B2B project shipments were only beginning in Q2 and would continue into Q4, Q1, and 2027, so meaningful revenue from the announced pipeline remained largely ahead. The preview had flagged the lack of quantified B2B contribution as a key debate and identified quantified units as a bull-case signal; the call provided no such figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “B2B project shipments are only beginning this quarter and will continue into Q4, Q1, and 2027, meaning meaningful revenue from the announced pipeline remains largely ahead.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said B2B announcements “remain unquantified,” asked for “units shipped in H1,” and listed “quantified B2B units” as a bull-case driver.

in_line: Operating cash use fell to $3.7M from $6.0M in Q1, consistent with the preview’s view that burn needed to fall below about $4M.
Management reaffirmed the target of becoming cash flow positive as it exits 2026, as the preview expected.
The 100,000-unit target for 2026 was reaffirmed as being on plan, matching the preview’s stated company target.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in far above the preview’s implied $4–6 million range. The $11.4 million result was also a record, with a 49% adjusted EBITDA margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached a record $11.4 million (up ~300%)”; “adjusted EBITDA margin rose to 49% from 16%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$4–6M (implied)” from the H1 guide; the base scenario expected “$4–5M.”

surprises.description: Q2 EPS substantially exceeded the preview’s $0.03 consensus, coming in at $0.15 as net income reached a record $8.9 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income hit a record $8.9 million ($0.15 EPS).”

surprises.description: CuriosityStream raised its full-year guidance: revenue is now $77–82 million rather than $75–80 million, and adjusted EBITDA is $18–22 million rather than $16–20 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 guidance calls for revenue of $77 million-$82 million and adjusted EBITDA of $18 million-$22 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company guidance of “$75–80M” in FY26 revenue and “$16–20M” in FY26 adjusted EBITDA.

surprises.description: Despite the raised full-year EBITDA outlook, the company’s second-half adjusted EBITDA range is lower than the preview’s guidance-implied expectation. Management attributed the step-down from Q2 chiefly to conservative licensing assumptions and more rev-share agreements.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Second-half adjusted EBITDA guidance of $6 million-$10 million implies a step-down from Q2's $11.4 million, attributed mainly to conservative licensing assumptions and more rev-share agreements.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$16–20M,” Q1 adjusted EBITDA of “$0.9M,” and implied Q2 adjusted EBITDA of “~$4–6M”—which points to roughly $9–15M for H2.

surprises.description: Revenue exceeded the preview’s roughly $21.5 million consensus by $1.7 million, though it remained within the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 22% year-over-year to $23.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue: ~$21.5M” consensus; the base scenario projected “$21–23M.”

surprises.description: Operating leverage and cost reductions were more pronounced than the preview discussed: gross margin reached 73%, operating expenses fell, and management expects another significant reduction in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded to 73% from 53%”; “Total operating expenses fell 24.1% year-over-year,” with guidance for “an additional 18%-20% cost reduction in the second half versus the first half.”

surprises.description: Subscription revenue held roughly flat instead of continuing the decline highlighted in the preview. The company said it is prioritizing durable economics over growth-at-any-cost.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Subscription revenue was roughly flat year-over-year at $8.9 million as the company deprioritizes growth-at-any-cost in favor of durable economics.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted Q1 subscription revenue was “down about 9% y/y” and flagged the subscription trend as an issue to watch.

surprises.description: The call highlighted a specific AI-training licensing opportunity not identified in the preview: a private code corpus and 17 productized video data sets supporting licensing growth. The call did not quantify the resulting revenue opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its 880-billion-token private code corpus and 17 productized off-the-shelf video data sets support AI-training licensing growth.”

in_line: Licensing revenue was $14.1 million, essentially matching the preview’s roughly $13–14 million implied expectation.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case called for $1.5–2.5 million of orders and a $4.0–5.5 million backlog; CVD reported only about $1.2 million of orders and a $3.9 million backlog. Those figures reached the preview’s bearish threshold rather than its base case, although that downside scenario had been explicitly anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Orders during Q2 2026 totaled only about $1.2 million and backlog fell to $3.9 million as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base scenario: “Orders $1.5–2.5M; backlog $4.0–5.5M.” Bear scenario: “Orders <$1.5M; backlog <$4M.”

surprises.description: After the quarter, the customer behind a $0.8 million system order filed for Chapter 11, putting that order and backlog at potential risk. The preview discussed customer concentration and weak demand but did not anticipate this bankruptcy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The customer behind the $0.8 million system order received in Q2 filed a prepackaged Chapter 11 bankruptcy after quarter-end, putting that order and backlog at potential risk.”

in_line: Continuing-operations revenue of about $2.0 million was within the preview’s $1.8–2.1 million base estimate.
The continuing-operations loss of about $0.20 per share matched the preview’s estimate of approximately -$0.20.
Gross margin of 16.8% was broadly in line with the preview’s expectation that margin could recover toward the high teens.
The preview expected the SDC sale gain to make headline GAAP net income positive; reported total net income was about $12.6 million, including a roughly $13.5 million gain on divestiture.

surprises.description: Alpha-3 passed 80 active sites in July and management now expects about 100 by year-end, with site activation roughly six months ahead of schedule. The preview described scaling to 80+ sites but did not anticipate this faster pace or the higher year-end target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “reached its year-end goal of activating over 80 Alpha-3 clinical sites in July,” and “now expects approximately 100 active sites by year-end”; site activation accelerated “by roughly six months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “That is a 25–30% sequential increase as ALPHA3 scales to 80+ sites.”

surprises.description: The Alpha-3 interim futility analysis showed MRD clearance in a majority of patients, with no treatment-related hospitalizations and most patients treated and followed as outpatients, including at community practices without prior CAR-T experience. The preview raised MRD clearance as a possible approval lever but did not report or forecast these specific results and delivery characteristics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “cema-cel drove rapid MRD clearance in a majority of patients with no treatment-related hospitalizations,” with “most patients treated and followed entirely in the outpatient setting including community practices with no prior CAR-T experience.” Management also cited a Breyanzi study in which a “24% MRD clearance differential translated into a greater than 60% EFS improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The open question is whether MRD clearance could serve as a surrogate endpoint for accelerated approval.”

surprises.description: Management cautioned that achieving statistical significance at Alpha-3’s interim EFS analysis will require overwhelming efficacy because of the alpha allocation between interim and primary analyses. That adds a substantial qualification to the preview’s focus on MRD clearance as a possible route to accelerated approval.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Achieving statistical significance at the interim EFS analysis will require overwhelming efficacy due to how alpha was allocated between the interim and primary analyses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any sign that FDA is open to this [MRD clearance as a surrogate endpoint for accelerated approval] would be the largest upside lever on the call.”

surprises.description: ALLO-316’s optimized regimen produced a 31% confirmed response rate in CD70-high renal cell carcinoma, and none of the five confirmed responders had progressed at follow-up of 8 to over 18 months after one dose. The preview did not discuss this trial or set an expectation for these results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “the optimized regimen produced a 31% confirmed overall response rate in CD70-high renal cell carcinoma,” and “none of the 5 confirmed responders” had progressed at follow-up “ranging from 8 to over 18 months after a single dose.”

surprises.description: The call says the ALLO-329 data update will be in Q4 2025, whereas the preview expected Q4 2026. As stated, the call’s date is already past at the time of this August 2026 release, so the apparent timing difference is difficult to interpret.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The ALLO-329 RESOLUTION autoimmune trial will report a clinical and translational data update in Q4 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “next update guided to Q4 2026” and “ALLO-329 Q4 2026 timing.”

surprises.description: Management offered a reassuring view that ongoing first-line CAR-T and bispecific studies are unlikely to materially reduce post-frontline MRD positivity, and that in vivo CAR-T is likely to replace autologous CAR-T mainly in relapsed/refractory settings. The preview flagged strategic framing but did not anticipate this specific competitive assessment of Alpha-3’s niche.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects first-line CAR-T and bispecific studies to have “minimal impact on post-frontline MRD positivity rates” and views in vivo CAR-T as “likely limited to replacing autologous CAR-T in relapsed/refractory settings,” leaving Alpha-3’s community-based niche “well protected.”

in_line: Management maintained the Alpha-3 interim EFS timing around mid-2027, consistent with the preview’s mid-2027 expectation.
The FDA’s RMAT and Fast Track designations for cema-cel were already reported in the preview, so the call’s confirmation of them was not new.

surprises.description: Direct Digital reported that it was not in compliance with certain credit-facility covenants and had requested a lender waiver, with discussions still ongoing. The preview identified a further covenant breach as a serious risk, but did not establish that one had occurred.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Direct Digital was not in compliance with certain financial covenants under its credit facility and has requested a waiver from its lender, with discussions ongoing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A second breach would be a serious warning.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $7.8 million, within the preview’s $7.5–8.0 million bottom-up estimate and $7.3–8.0 million base-case range, despite being below the $9.90 million consensus that the preview cautioned against relying on.
Adjusted EBITDA loss was $2.3 million, within the preview’s base-case range of a $1.8–2.4 million loss.
The preview expected mid-single-digit buy-side growth in its base case; the reported non-DSP business grew approximately 5% year-to-date, excluding reduced DSP spending.
Cash remained very tight, consistent with the preview’s concern about quarter-end liquidity and its expectation that new funding might be needed.

surprises.description: Instead of the preview’s estimated $0.08 per-share loss, Crown Crafts reported GAAP net income of $2.1 million, or $0.19 per share. The quarter’s profit was helped by tariff-related adjustments, so it was not solely a reflection of recurring operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income of $2.1 million ($0.19 per share), reversing a prior-year loss of $1.1 million ($0.10 per share), though results benefited from tariff-related adjustments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own estimate (not Street): ... diluted EPS ($0.08) against ($0.10) a year ago.”

surprises.description: Sales were $16.8 million, well above the preview’s $15.7 million estimate, and grew 8% year over year rather than the estimated 1.3%. This was a stronger turnaround in sales than the preview’s stabilization case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 net sales grew 8% year-over-year to $16.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own estimate (not Street): Net sales $15.7M (+1.3% Y/Y).”

surprises.description: Tariff refunds had a much larger near-term effect than the preview’s prior figure of $175,000 received suggested: $3.7 million reduced cost of products sold this quarter, and about $4.7 million of the requested amount had been received. The preview noted possible refund upside, but the reported amount was substantial.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tariff refunds reduced cost of products sold by $3.7 million during the quarter, with about $4.7 million of a requested $5.6-5.7 million already received, mostly in July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Tariff refunds: $5.5M applied for, $175K received to date”; “The $5.5M applied for against $175K received is a possible one-time upside.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 25.6%, above the preview’s 24.0% estimate and its 23.5% level of concern. It remained just below the preview’s above-26% threshold for strong support of the margin-leverage thesis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded 290 basis points year-over-year to 25.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own estimate ... gross margin 24.0%”; “Below about 23.5% suggests pricing is being given back or mix is worsening. Above 26% supports the leverage thesis.”

surprises.description: The Board cut the quarterly dividend, rather than merely leaving the payout uncertain. The preview identified the existing $0.08 quarterly dividend and highlighted any hedging about it as a key signal; the cut is intended to free cash for debt reduction and growth initiatives.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Board cut the quarterly dividend to free up cash flow for debt reduction and growth initiatives, now offering an approximately 4% dividend yield.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dividend is $0.08 per quarter, reviewed quarterly by the board”; “Any hedged dividend language would likely dominate the reaction.”

surprises.description: Groovy Girls did more than provide its first-quarter shipments: the relaunched line exceeded expectations, and Canadian demand was strong enough that inventory intended for the U.S. was diverted to Canada. Amazon and European launches are also targeted for the fall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The relaunched Groovy Girls fashion doll line exceeded expectations, with such strong Canadian demand that U.S.-bound inventory is being diverted to Canada, and Amazon and European (Germany) launches are targeted for October/September.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Shipments to specialty retailers began May 1, 2026, so this is the first revenue quarter. Management said it is ‘not talking about rolling out Groovy Girls into mass.’ The sell-through and reorder commentary matters more than the sell-in dollars.”

surprises.description: Crown Crafts reduced debt from more than $14 million at the start of the fiscal year to $9.6 million at quarter-end, and net interest expense fell to $190,000. The preview discussed dividend coverage and cash flow but did not anticipate this reported debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reduced debt from over $14 million at the start of the fiscal year to $9.6 million at quarter-end, supported by $5.5 million in operating cash flow”; “Net interest expense fell to $190,000 from $283,000 a year ago due to debt reduction efforts.”

in_line: The warehouse consolidation is still planned to begin in late 2026, consistent with the preview’s expectation of moves beginning late that year. The call specified a May 2028 completion target and said related capital spending is largely deferred to the next fiscal year.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $961,000, below the preview’s $990,000–$1.03 million consensus range by roughly 3%–7%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was approximately $961,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ... Consensus ... $0.99M ... or $1.03M.”

surprises.description: The quarterly loss was worse than expected: the reported $0.06 loss per share exceeded the preview’s $0.04 loss estimate, and the net loss widened to about $2.1 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss for Q2 2026 widened to approximately $2.1 million ($0.06 per share) from $1.8 million in Q2 2025.”

surprises.description: The second-half revenue ramp needed to approach the preview’s roughly $6.78 million FY26 consensus remains unsupported by an established recurring-order ramp. Management said revenue will be lumpy, with Q2 shipments mainly filling distributor IBT Bioservices’ channel and no recurring-order ramp yet established.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management indicated product revenue will be lumpy in coming quarters,” with “Q2 marking initial channel-filling shipments to distributor IBT Bioservices and early pilot sales, and no recurring-order ramp yet established.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street expects about $6.78M for FY26. First-half revenue was $2.07M, so the second half would need about $4.71M, roughly 2.3 times the first half. Absent a large licensing or milestone event, this estimate looks at risk.”

surprises.description: A pilot run of the animal-free transferrin program delivered a substantial productivity gain and an expected cost reduction, developments the preview did not flag. The cost reduction is an expectation from the pilot result, not a reported realized saving.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The animal-free recombinant human transferrin program achieved an approximately 80% productivity increase in its pilot run, expected to reduce costs by roughly 40%.”

surprises.description: Management provided more specific non-dilutive funding avenues and some near-term debt reassurance than the preview’s financing question alone anticipated: the notes remain covenant-compliant and do not mature until the end of 2027. This does not remove the going-concern doubt, and the financing avenues described are not reported as completed transactions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Convertible notes remain in covenant compliance and do not mature until December 31, 2027,” and management is pursuing “non-dilutive capital such as licensing, milestones, and royalties,” citing “$30 million of prior non-dilutive industrial-side funding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Financing plans are the main question on the call.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed specific external program funding and eligibility not identified in the preview: a roughly $3.9 million Gates Foundation-supported grant and eligibility for up to roughly $2.4 million through the CEPI collaboration. The CEPI amount is an eligibility ceiling, not a report of cash already received.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Gates Foundation-supported program is funded by an approximately $3.9 million grant for RSV and malaria antibodies, and the CEPI-supported collaboration makes Dyadic eligible for up to approximately $2.4 million.”

surprises.description: Internal R&D spending fell sharply as Dyadic shifted toward externally funded collaborations, while G&A increased on rebranding and business development costs. The preview did not specify this divergent expense pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Internal R&D expense fell 47% year-over-year to approximately $333,000 as the company shifts toward externally funded collaborations, while G&A rose 18% to $1.7 million on higher rebranding and business development costs.”

in_line: The going-concern warning and approximately $4.8 million in cash and equivalents were in line with the preview, which already reported substantial doubt and about $4.79 million in cash and securities.

The increase in cost of revenue and negative gross margin were already flagged: the preview said cost of revenue had risen about 60% and gross margin had turned negative; the call reported cost of revenue up 60% and above quarterly revenue.
First-half revenue of approximately $2.1 million was consistent with the preview’s $2.07 million figure.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $9–10 million is below the roughly $11 million the preview said was needed to support FY26 consensus revenue. The range also falls short of the preview’s $9.5–11 million base scenario at its low end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for revenue of $9-10 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus FY26 revenue of $40.5M less the first half implies roughly $24.4M in 2H26, or about $11M in Q3 and $13.5M in Q4.”

surprises.description: The smartphone customer confirmed the cells passed the 0.2C test, but a final accelerated life test is not expected to finish until year-end, before phone field testing. That is less advanced than the preview’s hoped-for confirmation of system-level deployment in 2H26.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The lead smartphone customer independently confirmed cells passed more than 1,000 cycles on the 0.2C discharge test,” with “one final accelerated hybrid cycle life test expected to complete by end of 2026 before phone field testing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Confirmation of system-level deployment in 2H26, or any further slip.”

surprises.description: The eyewear ramp produced its first revenue and a specific shipment schedule, including about 19,000 packs expected in Q3 and completion of a 50,000-unit order in Q4. The preview identified the ramp and 50,000-unit target as key questions but had no unit-level shipment figures to confirm this progress.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enovix shipped approximately 2,100 smart eyewear batteries to a Tier 1 customer in Q2 for its first eyewear revenue and expects to deliver ~19,000 packs in Q3 … part of a 50,000-unit order to be completed in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management targets only about 50,000 A1 eyewear units in 2026”; the preview asked whether the ramp had started on schedule and called for unit figures against that target.

surprises.description: The eyewear ramp is expected to carry negative gross margins for the rest of 2026 as ramp costs move above the gross-margin line. The preview focused on eyewear shipments and the company’s run of positive overall gross margin, but did not flag negative margins for this product ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects smart eyewear to carry negative gross margins for the balance of 2026 as ramp overhead moves above the gross margin line before reaching scale.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Six straight quarters of positive gross margin”; the preview also focused on the eyewear ramp and 50,000-unit target.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $9 million, above the $8.43 million consensus and at the top of company guidance. That is a positive beat, though smaller than the preview’s bull-case revenue range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $9 million … landing at the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Consensus Revenue $8.43M”; company guide was “$8.0 – $9.0M.”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP operating loss and EPS loss were both better than expected: operating loss was below the preview’s roughly $30 million consensus, and the $0.13 loss per share was better than the $0.14 consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating loss was $28.8 million (better than the $29-32 million guidance) and non-GAAP net loss per share was $0.13, at the favorable end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS ($0.14)” and “Non-GAAP loss from ops ~($30M).”

surprises.description: Zone 1 dicing yield improved to 84% from 80%, but remained below the preview’s 90% level that it said would de-risk 2027 capacity. The primary throughput bottleneck therefore persists despite the improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Zone 1 dicing yield, the primary throughput bottleneck, improved to approximately 84% from 80% in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A stated 90% or higher de-risks 2027 capacity”; the bull scenario also assumed “dicing at or above 90%.”

surprises.description: The South Korea drone, defense, and industrial pipeline grew to about $183 million, with drones alone above $100 million and more than $40 million already in testing or design-in. The preview identified Korea-built cells as important to the second-half revenue step-up, but did not anticipate this pipeline growth or these figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The South Korea drone/defense/industrial pipeline grew 41% to approximately $183 million from $130 million in Q1, with drones alone exceeding $100 million and over $40 million already in active testing or design-in stages.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The 2H step-up therefore depends on Korea-built defense, industrial and drone cells.”

surprises.description: Management provided a plan for roughly 1 million units of new South Korea drone capacity to come online by mid-2027, a specific capacity addition and timing not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New South Korea drone capacity of roughly 1 million units expected online by mid-2027.”

surprises.description: Cash use was below the preview’s approximate $40 million-per-quarter burn concern: operating cash use plus capex totaled about $31.4 million in Q2. The company ended with $552.1 million in cash and marketable securities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with approximately $552.1 million in cash and marketable securities, used $21.8 million in operating cash, and had $9.6 million in capital expenditures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Burn near −$40M per quarter raises the 2027 financing question.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was within the company’s $8–9 million guide, even though it was above consensus.
Q2 capex of $9.6 million was within the preview’s cited $9–13 million company guide.
Overall Q2 non-GAAP gross margin remained positive at 19.9%, consistent with the preview’s note that the company had recorded six straight quarters of positive gross margin.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 revenue of about $3.47 million and 13% sequential growth. Energous reported approximately $3.1 million, roughly flat with Q1 and about 11% below consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 217% year-over-year to approximately $3.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$3.47M (+254% YoY, +13% QoQ)”

surprises.description: The preview expected gross margin near 36%, after several quarters around 35%–37.5%. Instead, first-half margin was 19%, with Q2 compressed by manufacturer retooling, higher-cost component sourcing, and costs absorbed to protect customers; management expects sequential recovery in Q3 and Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half gross margin fell to 19% (gross profit of $1.2 million), with Q2 margins compressed by one-time U.S. contract manufacturer retooling costs, higher-cost alternative component sourcing amid AI-driven supply shortages, and a deliberate choice to absorb costs to protect key customers.” Management “expects sequential margin recovery in Q3 and Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~36% (unguided, trend-implied)” and “Margin held between 35% and 37.5% for four quarters.”

surprises.description: GAAP EPS was substantially worse than the preview’s –$0.21 estimate: the company reported a $0.53-per-share loss. The reported net loss was $2.9 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GAAP net loss was $2.9 million, or $0.53 per share.”

surprises.description: The preview’s last disclosed deployment figure was about 1,500 of roughly 4,700 planned U.S. retailer locations. The rollout is now roughly 90% complete, indicating much faster progress than that starting point suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The largest deployment with a leading national retailer targeting ~4,700 U.S. stores is now roughly 90% complete.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The last disclosed count was about 1,500 of roughly 4,700 planned US retailer locations. Watch whether the install pace supports completion on schedule.”

surprises.description: In addition to the retailer-store rollout, management described a planned expansion into about 50 membership warehouse locations, with the opportunity expected to scale to roughly 550 sites in early 2027 and potentially broaden further. The preview did not identify this expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expansion into ~50 membership warehouse locations [is] planned to scale to ~550 sites in early 2027 and potentially broader in 2027.”

surprises.description: A federal agency proof of concept contributed meaningful Q2 revenue and is a potential deployment of up to 500 sites, including about 15 planned for the rest of this year. This was a new opportunity beyond the preview’s listed customer and deployment issues.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A federal government agency proof of concept generated meaningful Q2 revenue (a top-five customer) and could span up to 500 sites over two to three years, with ~15 sites planned over the remainder of this year.”

surprises.description: Management reported that enterprise sales cycles have shortened to six to nine months from 18 to 24 months two years ago, and that individual pipeline opportunities are many multiples larger than a year ago. The preview did not flag this improvement in sales velocity or opportunity size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The enterprise sales cycle has shortened to six-to-nine months from 18-to-24 months two years ago, and management says individual pipeline opportunities are now many multiples larger than a year ago.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted customer concentration risk, citing 99% of accounts receivable in three customers. The call reported that revenue was spread across five customers, which made up about 74% of Q2 revenue, versus two customers at about 94% a year earlier—an improvement in revenue diversification, though not the same measure as receivables concentration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Five customers made up ~74% of Q2 revenue, versus two customers representing ~94% a year earlier, reflecting broader commercial diversification.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Customer concentration is also notable: a prior filing flagged 99% of accounts receivable in three customers.”

surprises.description: The preview expected no Q2 revenue contribution from ProPlus because certification was after quarter-end, and sought quantified commercialization details. Management said the newly certified integrated data-plus-power product should be a meaningful second-half revenue contributor and can include recurring SaaS revenue, but did not provide units, dollars, or named customers in the facts provided.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The PowerBridge ProPlus received FCC certification in July, enabling a higher-margin integrated data-plus-power end-to-end solution (with recurring SaaS revenue) expected to be a meaningful contributor to second-half revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “PowerBridge Pro+ received FCC certification on July 29, after quarter-end, so it likely adds no Q2 revenue.” The preview also said: “Bull needs: management to quantify Pro+ with units, dollars, or named customers for H2.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed no additional ATM usage or equity financing plans for the year, consistent with the preview’s account of management’s “no plans for additional ATM usage this year” statement.
ProPlus certification occurred in July, after the quarter ended, consistent with the preview’s expectation that certification would be post-quarter and would not add Q2 revenue.

surprises.description: The preview expected 500,000 HYPE to be placed in the Skew deal and said about 300,000 HYPE still had no disclosed home, with any drag showing in Q3. Instead, management said it redeployed 1 million HYPE into Q3 partnerships with SKU and Entropy, with improved economics and rights to 5% of SKU's equity and 5% of its tokens.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Within weeks of the USDH headwind, the company redeployed 1 million hype into new Q3 house partnerships with SKU (HIP4) and Entropy (HIP3), securing improved economics plus a right to 5% of SKU's equity and 5% of its tokens.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Skew Technologies HAUS deal for 500K HYPE was not signed until July 15, leaving roughly six weeks of idle capital. About 300K HYPE has no disclosed home. Q3 is where any drag would show.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated the USDH and Felix unwinds but expected any resulting drag to show in Q3. Instead, DeFi monetization revenue was already down 36% in Q2, to $158,000 from $245,000.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The May replacement of native stablecoin USDH with USDC forced the wind-down of two core deployments (Native Markets and Felix), freeing up 800,000 hype and cutting DeFi monetization revenue 36% to $158,000 from $245,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 is where any drag would show.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses excluding stock-based compensation fell 21% quarter over quarter, and management forecast another 10–20% reduction after the legacy biotech segment runs off. The preview noted the year-end cash-flow target and a tight-enough runway, but did not anticipate these expense reductions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses excluding stock-based comp fell 21% quarter-over-quarter to $2.3 million—roughly half the $4.3 million spent in Q3 2025—with management guiding to a further 10–20% reduction after fully running off the legacy biotech segment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash burn vs. the year-end breakeven target. With about $12M cash, runway is adequate but not comfortable.”

surprises.description: The June 30 HYPE price was $65, above the preview's modeled $55–62 range, and treasury gains reached $54.8 million; net income consequently reached a record $31.0 million. The preview expected marks to dominate GAAP results, so the surprise is the higher-than-modeled token mark rather than the existence of mark-driven profit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 net income hit a record $31.0 million versus $8.8 million in Q1, while adjusted EBITDA jumped to $53.7 million from $19.5 million, driven largely by $54.8 million in treasury gains as hype's price rose”; quarter-end price was “$65.0.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Verify the June 30 HYPE mark against the release, since the modeled $55–62 range is the main uncertainty in the estimates.”

surprises.description: The company completed its first institutional credit transaction, lending $1 million USDC against natively staked HYPE at 8% APY with collateral held by Anchorage Digital. The preview focused on treasury deployment and DeFi yield but did not anticipate this institutional credit deal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its first institutional credit deal on the Avia platform, lending $1 million USDC against natively staked hype at 8% APY, with collateral custodied at Anchorage Digital.”

in_line: Adjusted gross profit was $1.2 million, at the top of the preview's $1.0–1.2 million base-case range.
Management reiterated FY2026 adjusted gross profit guidance of $5–7 million, as the preview's catalyst checklist expected.
Cash was $11.8 million, close to the preview's estimate of about $12 million.

surprises.description: The preview’s rough estimate put Q2 operating loss near $0.7 million and inferred about $3 million of cash consumption, but the company reported adjusted EBITDA of positive $39,000 and said July preliminary results were near cash-flow neutral. Management also said it had lowered the annual COGS and operating-expense run rate below $22 million, putting quarterly revenue breakeven at about $5.25 million–$5.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached essentially breakeven at positive $39,000” and “July preliminary numbers showed near cash flow neutrality”; the cost run rate was “below $22 million annually,” with “a breakeven revenue point of approximately $5.25M-$5.5M per quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own rough Q2 estimate: operating loss near ($0.7M)” and cash rose $5.1M against net financing proceeds of about $8.1–8.3M, implying “roughly $3M of cash consumed in the quarter.”

surprises.description: The reported net loss and EPS were worse than the preview’s thin single-analyst consensus of a $0.05 loss per share. The company attributed nearly all of the wider loss to convertible-debenture accounting, including about $863,000 that it described as noncash and nonrecurring, so the underlying earnings comparison was less adverse than the GAAP figure alone suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $1.6 million ($0.17 per share) versus $742,000 ($0.08) a year ago,” driven almost entirely by “$873,000 of interest expense from convertible debenture accounting,” of which “~$863,000 was noncash and nonrecurring.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 EPS –$0.05” (single analyst; “very low confidence”).

surprises.description: Bookings were within the preview’s base-case range, but backlog finished below its base-case expectation and below the preview’s $2.3 million watch level. The company said the decline reflected faster order-to-ship performance, which tempers—but does not erase—the signal that shipments exceeded incoming orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 bookings were $4.9 million (up from $4.2 million in Q1), with backlog falling to $2.1 million from $2.6 million due to faster order-to-ship performance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario forecast “$4.5–5.5M / $2.5–3.0M” for bookings/backlog; the preview also said backlog “below about $2.3M” would suggest the revenue jump came from backlog conversion rather than demand recovery.

surprises.description: The pending transformational acquisition was described as potentially nearly doubling annual revenue run rate, a scale estimate the preview did not provide. The call also said the two acquisitions together could add 60–70 active accounts, although the larger deal remains pending and exclusivity was extended.
surprises.fact_evidence: The “pending transformational acquisition” is “expected to nearly double annual revenue run rate,” and “the two acquisitions together add 60-70 active accounts as new logo and domain opportunities.”

surprises.description: The call detailed a new embedded-security asset acquisition and four potential revenue streams, which the preview had not identified. It also connected the opportunity to regulatory-driven demand, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act.
surprises.fact_evidence: The IAR acquisition adds “four new revenue streams (software platform, support contracts, licensing fees, and per-token charges)” using the existing LumenX platform, with positioning for demand such as the EU Cyber Resilience Act.

surprises.description: The company disclosed six new customer logos in the first half, including three in automotive and two in robotics, and said robotics revenue was expected to become significant in the second half of next year. The preview did not flag these customer wins or this robotics outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed 6 new customer logos in the first half (3 automotive, 2 robotics, 1 global communications), with robotics revenue expected to become significant in the second half of next year.”

in_line: Q2 net sales of $5.2 million matched the preview’s company pre-release and consensus figure of about $5.2 million.
Gross margin of 57% was essentially in line with the pre-released 57.1%; the preview had already flagged the margin’s durability and mix as a key issue.
Quarter-end cash of $10.8 million matched the pre-released figure.
Bookings of $4.9 million were within the preview’s $4.5–5.5 million base-case range.

The larger acquisition remained pending, consistent with the preview’s description of a letter of intent and unresolved financing; the preview had not expected a signed definitive agreement as its base case.

surprises.description: Q2 broadband revenue was $133.5 million, above both the $120.9 million consensus and the $125 million high end of guidance. That also exceeded the preview’s bull-case range of $126–131 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 broadband revenue grew 54% year-over-year to $133.5 million, exceeding the high end of guidance ($115-125 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus ... $120.9M | Company guidance ... $115M – $125M”; bull scenario: “Revenue | $126M – $131M.”

surprises.description: Q2 EPS of $0.21 beat the preview’s $0.168 consensus and exceeded the $0.19 top of company guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 EPS of $0.21 beating the $0.15-0.19 guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS | Consensus ... $0.168 | Company guidance ... $0.15 – $0.19.”

surprises.description: Harmonic raised FY2026 broadband revenue guidance to $505–525 million, rather than reaffirming the prior $475–495 million range. The new midpoint is above the preview’s bull-case threshold of $500 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 broadband revenue guidance [was raised] to $505-525 million, up from the prior $475-495 million range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “a simple reaffirmation of $475M – $495M would be a soft signal” and set its bull scenario at “FY revenue raised to at least $500M.”

surprises.description: FY2026 EPS guidance rose to $0.67–0.75, with a midpoint about 14.5% above the prior midpoint. The preview’s prior non-GAAP EPS range was $0.57–0.67.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 EPS guidance was raised to $0.67-0.75, up approximately 14.5% from the prior midpoint.”

surprises.description: The margin outlook was substantially better than the roughly 48.8% second-half margin implied by the preview: Harmonic guided to 51–52% for Q3 and full-year, citing customer mix and supply-chain mitigation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margins are guided at 51-52% for Q3 and full-year ... full-year margin guidance was improved due to customer mix and supply chain mitigation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied second-half gross margin is about 48.8%”; the preview’s bull case called for “second-half gross margin held at or above 50%.”

surprises.description: The unrecovered memory-cost burden was higher than the preview’s estimate: the call cited roughly $3 million per quarter, versus the preview’s approximately $2.3 million per quarter estimate. This cost pressure was present even as the margin outlook improved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margins are guided at 51-52% for Q3 and full-year, incorporating roughly $3 million per quarter in unrecovered memory costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “roughly $6M of the second-half margin hit to memory costs” and “about $2.3M per quarter.”

surprises.description: Backlog plus deferred revenue reached a record $587.6 million and 73% was expected to convert within 12 months, versus the preview’s cited $582.1 million and about 60% conversion. The total was stronger than a decline but remained below the preview’s bull-case marker of $600 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog and deferred revenue reached a record $587.6 million, up 71% year-over-year, with 73% expected to convert to revenue within 12 months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Backlog plus deferred revenue of $582.1M ... with about 60% converting within 12 months,” and a bull scenario of “backlog above $600M.”

surprises.description: Book-to-bill was well over 1.5, substantially above the preview’s reference point of 1.0, indicating stronger bookings than the preview’s baseline implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rest-of-market comprising approximately 60% of bookings and a book-to-bill well over 1.5.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to compare book-to-bill “against ... 1.0.”

surprises.description: The video-business sale brought in $137.9 million at closing, below the preview’s stated $145 million sale price. The call also gave a different closing date than the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Harmonic completed the sale of its video business to Mediakind on June 16, 2025 for $137.9 million at closing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Video was sold to MediaKind for $145M, closing June 17, 2026.”

surprises.description: Q2 free cash flow was negative $7 million because memory inventory arrived early, and the company made no buybacks during the quarter despite its ongoing $200 million program. The preview specifically flagged buyback pace as something to watch but did not state a Q2 repurchase expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 free cash flow was negative $7 million due to early memory inventory delivery, with the $200 million buyback program having $122 million repurchased but no shares bought in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Use of the $145M in Video proceeds” and “Buyback pace versus strategic M&A” as key issues to watch.

surprises.description: The call reported traction for Harmonic’s intelligence platform that the preview did not discuss: Beacon was live at approximately 20 customers, broader offerings were running with about 10 operators, and the tools were associated with more than 30% fewer subscriber service calls.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Beacon live at approximately 20 customers and broader offerings running with about 10 operators, showing over 30% reductions in subscriber service calls.”

in_line: The company had become a pure-play broadband business after the video sale, as the preview described the quarter as the first clean quarter as a broadband-only company.

surprises.description: Fossil reported Q2 sales of $211 million, well above the preview’s roughly $199–200 million consensus, and the year-over-year decline was only 4% rather than the roughly 9% decline implied by consensus. Store closures accounted for about 220 basis points of the drop.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales totaled $211 million, a 4% decline year-over-year, though this beat expectations and reflected a narrowing rate of decline, with ~220 basis points of the drop attributable to store closures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 net sales … Consensus $199.3M – $200.3M”; this “Implies -9.1% to -9.6% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin reached 62.4%, far above the preview’s expected sustainable range of 57–59% and its 57.5% threshold for supporting the full-price strategy. The reported drivers included full-price selling and supply-chain initiatives, as well as lower tariffs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 490 basis points to 62.4%, driven by the shift to a full-price selling model, supply chain initiatives, and lower tariffs versus last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A Q2 print of 57–59% without one-offs supports the de-promotion thesis. Below about 56.5% would suggest discounting has returned or tariff costs are rising”; the checklist also says “Anything at or above 57.5% supports the de-promotion thesis.”

surprises.description: Fossil raised both FY26 guidance ranges: the expected sales decline narrowed to 3–5% from 4–6%, and adjusted operating margin guidance rose to 4–6% from 3–5%. The preview identified reiterating the old ranges as the neutral outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to decline 3% to 5% (improved from 4% to 6%) and adjusted operating margin of 4% to 6% (up from 3% to 5%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists FY26 guidance of “-4% to -6%” sales and “3% – 5%” adjusted operating margin, and says “Reiterating the -4% to -6% sales range and 3–5% margin range is the neutral outcome.”

surprises.description: The company now expects positive FY26 free cash flow rather than approximately breakeven, a better outlook than the preview’s baseline expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company now expects to generate positive free cash flow for full-year 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 free cash flow was expected to be “~breakeven.”

surprises.description: Traditional-watch wholesale performance was stronger than the preview’s mid-single-digit wholesale-growth expectation: Fossil’s traditional-watch business grew 12% globally and 16% in US wholesale. The newly reported regional picture was mixed, with EMEA weakness attributed to Middle East geopolitical impacts and reduced travel retail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fossil brand traditional watch business grew 12% globally in the wholesale channel, with US wholesale traditional watch growth of 16%”; “mid-single-digit growth in the US and strong double-digit growth in India, offset by weakness in EMEA due to Middle East geopolitical impacts and reduced travel retail.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bull case needs wholesale to hold mid-single-digit growth.” The preview did not flag the EMEA or India regional outlook.

surprises.description: Store reductions appear to be proceeding faster or on a larger scale than the preview’s estimate of about 15 planned closures for 2026: Fossil reported 17 net store reductions in Q2 alone, with two more planned. Eleven of the Q2 reductions were transitions to a South Africa distributor rather than closures, and management said portfolio optimization is nearing completion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fossil closed 17 net stores in Q2 (6 closures plus 11 transitioned to a South Africa distributor), plans two more closures, and expects to end the year with approximately 178 locations as portfolio optimization nears completion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “about 15 planned for 2026” and noted seven stores closed in Q1.

in_line: Management reaffirmed the expectation of a return to top-line growth in Q4, as the preview expected that growth inflection to be confirmed.

The FY26 gross-margin outlook in the upper 50s, assuming no additional tariff refunds, was broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation that mid-to-upper-50% margins were sustainable and that the Q1 tariff-refund benefit would not recur.

surprises.description: Marchex guided to Q3 revenue of $16 million to $16.5 million, above the preview’s roughly $15 million quarterly run-rate benchmark. The guide reflects a full quarter of Arcania operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance projects revenue of $16 million to $16.5 million”; the sequential jump “largely reflect[s] a full quarter of Arcania operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Combined-company Q3 target of roughly $15M quarterly revenue run rate”; “Confirmation of the ~$15M quarterly run rate is the main test.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $11 million, slightly below the $11.20 million consensus estimate. It nevertheless rose sequentially from Q1, as the preview expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $11 million, up sequentially from $10.6 million in Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus: $11.20M.”

surprises.description: Management described a longer-term opportunity to reach a $100 million-plus revenue run rate, beyond the preview’s prior Q3 combined-company benchmark of roughly $60 million annualized. The timing is qualified as being “over time.”
surprises.fact_evidence: The acquisition positions the combined company to “potentially reach a targeted $100 million-plus revenue run rate over time.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Combined-company Q3 target of roughly $15M quarterly revenue run rate ($60M annualized).”

surprises.description: The Q3 adjusted EBITDA guide of $2.3 million to $2.5 million implies a stronger profitability outlook than the preview’s prior target of 10% or more adjusted EBITDA margins on roughly $15 million of quarterly revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance projects … adjusted EBITDA of $2.3 million to $2.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior combined-company Q3 target was “10%+ adj. EBITDA margins.”

surprises.description: Cash fell to $8.2 million from $9 million, contrary to the preview’s expectation that cash should build if Q2 adjusted EBITDA was near its $1.7 million guide. Management attributed the decline primarily to transaction and organizational realignment costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash declined to $8.2 million at the end of Q2 from $9 million in Q1, primarily due to transaction expenses and organizational realignment costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If adj. EBITDA is near $1.7M, cash should build even after deal costs.”

surprises.description: Management cited a home-services customer whose annualized analytics contribution more than doubled after adopting AI verified outcomes. This is a concrete expansion case beyond the preview’s general focus on bundle penetration.
surprises.fact_evidence: A client generating “~$500,000 in annualized analytics revenue” adopted AI verified outcomes, “more than doubling its contribution to over $1 million annually.”

surprises.description: Management said a double-digit number of customers could each represent at least seven figures of incremental revenue, with many potentially reaching multi-millions annually. The preview discussed bundle adoption but did not anticipate this scale of stated customer opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management believes “a double-digit number of customers each have potential for seven figures or more of incremental revenue,” with many potentially delivering “multi-millions per year over time.”

surprises.description: Management articulated a “rule of 30 to rule of 40” trajectory, a more ambitious combined growth-and-margin aspiration than the preview’s prior 15–20% growth and 10%+ margin targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is targeting a “rule of 30 to rule of 40” trajectory, aided by “a lower cost structure and improving margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior combined-company Q3 target was “15–20% growth, and 10%+ adj. EBITDA margins.”

in_line: Q2 revenue increased sequentially from $10.6 million to $11 million, as the preview flagged sequential growth as a key catalyst, although the result was slightly below consensus.

The top-100-customer bundle update was broadly in line with the preview’s prior figures: those customers represent about 90% of revenue, and roughly one-third had received presentations, with about half of that group buying on a recurring or paid-pilot basis.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $55.7 million, well below the preview’s implied $78–82 million expectation. The shortfall was about 28–32%, as lower sales volume and gross-margin pressure weighed on results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell 31.7% to $55.7 million from $81.6 million a year ago, reflecting lower sales volume and gross margin pressures.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA: ~$78–82M (implied)”

surprises.description: Sales were $458.5 million, about 6% below the $490.1 million consensus, and declined 8.4% year over year rather than the expected 2.1% decline. Comparable sales fell 6.2%, with lower traffic and transactions, rather than sustaining the recent positive-comp momentum the preview was watching.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 fiscal 2026 total sales declined 8.4% year-over-year to $458.5 million, with comparable sales down 6.2% driven primarily by lower customer traffic and transactions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | $490.1M | $500.3M | (2.1)%”; the preview also said, “Positive comps with positive gross-margin dollars would suggest the turnaround is real.”

surprises.description: Leslie’s withdrew its full-year FY2026 sales and adjusted EBITDA guidance and provided no replacement outlook. The preview’s base case anticipated a trim to the low half of the range, although withdrawal was identified as a downside scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Leslie's withdrew its full-year fiscal 2026 sales and adjusted EBITDA guidance and declined to provide an updated outlook, citing weak peak-season traffic and macro uncertainty.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (~45%): ... guide trimmed to low half”; the preview also said, “Withdrawal would be a restructuring signal in this balance sheet.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 36.5%, 200–300 basis points below the preview’s estimated 38.5–39.5% range. The 310-basis-point year-over-year contraction was also deeper than the preview’s anticipated 100–200-basis-point inventory-related hit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin contracted 310 basis points to 36.5% from 39.6%, hurt by fewer sales of higher-margin specialty chemicals, unfavorable mix, and higher distribution and manufacturing costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~38.5–39.5%”; the preview also noted, “Management guided to a 100–200bp inventory-related margin hit in Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end liquidity was stronger than the prior-quarter position the preview highlighted: the revolver draw was $30 million rather than $99 million, and total availability was about $207 million versus $97.1 million in Q2. The preview had flagged potential ABL repayment as an important question but did not specify an expected amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company carried $753 million of net long-term debt plus $30 million drawn on its revolver, with only about $207 million of total available liquidity at quarter end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Liquidity: $16.9M cash, $99M drawn on the $250M ABL, $97.1M total availability”; and, “Q3 is the main cash-generating quarter, so revolver repayment from the $99M drawn will determine how much runway remains into the seasonal trough.”

surprises.description: SG&A fell 17.9% and improved as a share of sales, but a $17.5 million one-time interchange-fee settlement contributed to the decrease and to the reported net-income improvement. The preview did not anticipate this settlement, so part of the favorable expense and earnings picture was nonrecurring.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A dropped 17.9% ($23.2 million) to $106.4 million, improving 270 basis points to 23.2% of sales on lower labor and store costs plus the interchange settlement”; “Net income improved $26.1 million to $47.8 million, but the gain was aided by a one-time $17.5 million credit card interchange fee settlement recorded in SG&A.”

surprises.description: The company reported a 15% year-over-year inventory reduction while maintaining strong in-stock levels, alongside the closure of 80 underperforming stores. The preview discussed inventory-related margin pressure but did not flag this degree of inventory reduction or the store closures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Inventory declined 15% year-over-year to $233.4 million, reflecting optimization efforts and the closure of 80 underperforming stores while maintaining strong in-stock levels.”

surprises.description: Online comparable sales were positive and reactivated lapsed customers grew, but those gains had not translated into physical-store traffic gains. This was a mixed channel signal against the preview’s focus on whether the turnaround momentum would hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Leslie's delivered positive comparable sales on Leslies.com and growth in reactivated lapsed customers, but has yet to translate this into physical store traffic gains, which management now views as its central challenge.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 ... comps +6.6%; customer count +8%; reactivated customers +25%”; and, “Positive comps ... would suggest the turnaround is real.”

in_line: The company’s exploration of strategic alternatives was broadly anticipated: the preview said Leslie’s was weighing strategic options, including a potential Chapter 11 filing, and identified capital structure risk as the leading issue to watch.

surprises.description: After the preview expected FY26 same-store sales to decline at a low-single-digit rate, management said Q4-to-date comps were positive in the low single digits and it now expects full-year comps to be flat to slightly up. That is a substantial improvement to the sales outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4-to-date same-store sales have turned positive in the low single-digit range,” and management “expects full-year comps to be flat to slightly up.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 system SSS: ‘Low single-digit decline’ (May).”

surprises.description: Operating EPS of $0.96 exceeded the preview’s $0.89–$0.90 consensus range. The result was a clear beat of the stated estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating EPS was $0.96.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 operating EPS (non-GAAP) … $0.89–$0.90.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $61.2 million, above the preview’s $54–$57 million base scenario and at the top of its $58–$61 million bull scenario. That was stronger than the preview’s central expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose to $61.2 million from $57.1 million on lower G&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario put adjusted EBITDA at “$54–$57M”; its bull scenario was “$58–$61M.”

surprises.description: The full-year restaurant-level margin outlook was updated to about 16.5%, below the preview’s roughly 17% FY target. That indicates a weaker full-year margin outcome than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management updated FY2026 guidance to “~16.5% restaurant-level margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 restaurant-level margin | ~17%.”

surprises.description: The updated adjusted EBITDA range is $225–$230 million rather than the prior $225–$235 million range the preview expected to be reaffirmed. The range still includes the old low end, but its upper end has been reduced.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management updated FY2026 guidance to “$225-230 million adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed company guidance of “$225–$235M” and said “Reaffirmation is the baseline.”

surprises.description: Franchise-level margin guidance moved to about $265 million, the bottom of the preview’s prior $265–$275 million range. The quarter’s franchise-level margin was also pressured by lower sales, fewer restaurants, and higher bad debt.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management updated FY2026 guidance to “~$265 million franchise-level margin”; quarterly franchise-level margin was “$60.3 million (37.4% of franchise revenues) … hurt by ~$1.7M lower same-store sales, ~$1.5M fewer restaurants, and ~$1M higher bad debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 franchise-level margin | $265–$275M.”

surprises.description: The FY26 SG&A outlook fell to $112–$115 million, below the preview’s $115–$125 million guidance range. This is a favorable cost outlook relative to expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management updated FY2026 guidance to “$112-115 million SG&A.”

surprises.description: Q3 same-store sales declined 1.1%, just worse than the preview’s warning threshold of about -1% and short of management’s “approaching flat” marker. The miss was slight, but it undercut the expected sequential improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 fiscal 2026 same-store sales declined 1.1% overall,” primarily due to lower transactions partially offset by pricing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management’s marker was “Approaching flat” and that “Anything worse than about -1% would undercut the sequential-improvement story.”

surprises.description: The Hot Ones promotion underperformed because the products were overly spicy and polarizing and checks were lower, leading the company to change the menu and end the promotion early. The preview did not flag this weakness.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Hot Ones promotion underperformed due to polarizing, overly spicy products and lower checks,” prompting less-spicy builds, replacement of value panels with higher-priced core items, and an early end to the window.

surprises.description: Management said elevated restaurant closures are likely to continue into 2027 and 2028 as franchisee profitability remains under pressure, extending the closure challenge beyond the FY26 plan discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “closed 40 restaurants year-to-date and expects 10-20 more in Q4,” with “elevated closures now anticipated to extend into 2027 and 2028 as franchisee profitability remains under pressure.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the FY26 plan as “50–100 closures” and said the closure pace “needs to accelerate in H2.”

surprises.description: Leverage improved to 6.3x from 6.9x, and the company fully paid down the August 2026 debt tranche through a summer refinancing. This was better than the preview’s 6.9x leverage baseline and expected higher interest burden suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “fully [paid] down the August 2026 debt tranche,” cut debt by “$244 million since Jack on Track began,” and lowered net debt/EBITDA “to 6.3x from 6.9x.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said net debt/adjusted EBITDA was “6.9x at Q2” and noted the new notes “replac[ed] roughly 4.476% debt” with “about +$23M of annual interest expense.”

in_line: Q3 restaurant-level margin was 17.6%, within the preview’s 17.5%–18% base-scenario range; the preview also identified Q3 as the peak beef-cost quarter.
The preview expected 50–100 FY26 closures and said closures needed to accelerate in H2; 40 closures year-to-date plus 10–20 expected in Q4 implies about 50–60 for the year, within that range.
The updated FY26 restaurant count of about 2,100 is at the upper end of the preview’s 2,050–2,100 range.

surprises.description: The preview looked for revenue to stabilize after the Q1 decline of 10.3%, but Q2 revenue fell 17% to $67.8 million, a further deterioration in the year-over-year trend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net revenue declined 17% year-over-year to $67.8 million,” driven by “a 17% drop in total orders placed and higher return rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A print that stabilizes the decline would support the recovery narrative.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA cleared the preview’s $0.5 million reference bar by reaching $1 million. The preview identified this as the quarter’s explicit commitment, so the result was better than the stated threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA doubled year-over-year to $1 million (1.5% margin) from $0.5 million (0.6%) in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Positive, above prior-year period (bar: >$0.5M)” and “Adjusted EBITDA above $0.5M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 48.6%, up 330 basis points and the company’s highest Q2 level since 2021. The preview gave no Q2 gross-margin expectation, making this a favorable result it had not anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 330 basis points to 48.6%, the company's highest Q2 gross margin since 2021, aided by higher-margin sales mix and freight cost savings.”

surprises.description: Markdown sales fell substantially, especially in casual apparel, as the company shifted toward regular-price selling. The preview described a reset to clear casual apparel and footwear but did not anticipate this degree of markdown reduction or the stronger regular-price mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total markdown sales fell 38% versus Q2 2025, including a 65% decline in casual apparel markdowns, reflecting a deliberate shift toward regular-price selling.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “a deliberate reset: new product launches cut more than 50% to clear casual apparel and footwear.”

surprises.description: The wholesale channel grew sharply, with LTM revenue up 130% and same-account revenue up 61%, plus expanded department-store distribution and new accounts. The preview did not flag this growth or expansion as an expected driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The wholesale channel nearly doubled in the quarter, with LTM wholesale revenue up 130% and same-account revenue up 61%, expanding to all Nordstrom doors and 100 Dillard's prom doors plus 2 new major accounts in Q3.”

surprises.description: New occasion-wear categories produced double-digit year-over-year top-line growth on strong regular-price sales. The preview did not identify these categories as a source of growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New occasion wear categories—bridal, bridesmaids, formal and day event—delivered double-digit year-over-year top-line growth supported by strong regular-price sales.”

surprises.description: Despite fewer casual-apparel and footwear launches, units transacted per new launch increased year over year and sequentially. The preview discussed launch cuts in the prior quarter but did not anticipate the higher productivity per launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Casual apparel and footwear new product launches were cut 48% year-over-year, while units transacted per new launch rose 28% versus Q2 2025 and 29% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1’s reset included “new product launches cut more than 50% to clear casual apparel and footwear.”

surprises.description: The company secured new financing, including a $4.5 million equity line with an option for another $5.5 million. The preview flagged liquidity as a watch item but did not anticipate this financing; the added funding is offset by the uncertainty inherent in an equity-line structure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Secured new financing including a $4.5 million equity line of credit with an option for an additional $5.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Liquidity” and asked whether Q2 seasonal cash burn would reverse Q1 deleveraging.

in_line: The company reaffirmed FY2026 guidance for adjusted EBITDA to inflect positive and revenue trends to improve, as the preview expected the positive adjusted EBITDA outlook to be reaffirmed.

The strategic review was already known before the release: the preview said the board had formed a Special Committee to review alternatives, including a possible transaction. The call facts repeat the committee’s formation but report no new transaction or review-status detail.

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 adjusted EBITDA of about $4.5 million ex-Movies, but SCOR reported just $1.3 million, with margin at 1.7%. The shortfall was much worse than the preview’s bear-case threshold of less than $3 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA collapsed 85% to $1.3 million with margin falling to 1.7% from 10% a year ago”; management said largely fixed data and compensation costs make top-line underperformance disproportionately affect the bottom line.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (ex-Movies) … My Q2 2026E … $4.5M”; the preview’s bear case was “<$3M.”

surprises.description: Cross-Platform revenue was $12.5 million and declined 2.1%, far below the preview’s $14.0 million estimate and expected 22% growth. That also missed the preview’s warning threshold of roughly 15% growth for sustaining the offset narrative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cross-platform revenue declined 2.1% to $12.5 million, hurt by lower usage of Proximic activation products” amid broader weakness across major buying platforms.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cross-Platform … My Q2 2026E … $14.0M … +22%”; “Growth below about +15% would undercut the offset narrative.”

surprises.description: Research and Insight Solutions revenue fell to $11.5 million, below the preview’s $12.3 million estimate, as renewals and delivery timing weighed on the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Research and Insight Solutions revenue dropped 9.2% to $11.5 million due to lower renewals and delivery timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Research & Insight Solutions … My Q2 2026E … $12.3M.”

surprises.description: The reinstated FY2026 outlook implied substantially weaker profitability than the preview’s post-Movies run-rate reference: management guided to only a low-to-mid-single-digit adjusted EBITDA margin and said it did not anticipate near-term growth. The preview put FY2025 pro forma adjusted EBITDA at about $28–30 million on roughly $318–322 million of revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management lowered full-year 2026 guidance to revenue of $315–325 million with an adjusted EBITDA margin only in the low-to-mid single digits, and explicitly does not anticipate near-term growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate for FY25 pro forma adj. EBITDA is about $28–30M”; the preview identified guidance reinstatement as the key deliverable and estimated post-Movies FY25 revenue of “about $318–322M.”

surprises.description: The new CEO outlined investment priorities and a potential data-monetization initiative that the preview had not identified: local TV measurement, creator media, activation, AI, and negotiations to monetize opt-in panel prompt data with AEO/GEO firms. These are prospective initiatives, with no reported financial contribution yet.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new CEO who joined in June is directing investment toward local TV measurement (testing a next-gen platform this year), creator media, activation expansion, and AI, including monetizing opt-in panel prompt data via negotiations with leading AEO/GEO firms.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $79.2 million, close to the preview’s own ex-Movies estimate of about $78.3 million; the preview cautioned that the $87.2 million consensus figure was stale and pre-divestiture.
The ROI realignment plan’s $20–25 million annual run-rate savings and $7–9 million of one-time charges matched the preview’s cited plan.
Eliminating about $40 million of debt with proceeds from the Movies sale was consistent with the preview’s account of the sale and debt repayment.

surprises.description: Revenue was $30,000, below the preview’s roughly $70,000 estimate, though it landed at the bottom of the preview’s $30,000–$70,000 base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was just $30,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ~$70K”; the base scenario also projected “$30–70K.”

surprises.description: The loss and operating expenses were higher than the preview’s estimates: net loss was $9.1 million versus an estimated $7.5–8.0 million, and operating expenses of $10 million were above the preview’s $9.4 million comparison point.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $9.1 million”; “operating expenses of $10 million versus $9.3 million in the prior year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net loss ~$7.5–8.0M”; the catalyst checklist asks “Opex vs. $9.4M.”

surprises.description: The preview treated Illinois implementation as an unresolved potential catalyst, but management’s ramp outlook points to little near-term revenue: penetration is expected to be only 1–2% in 2027 and no more than 5% by year three, with minimal impact in 2026. Management also said payer contracting typically takes 6–9 months before utilization scales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Illinois penetration should reach only single-digit levels—about 1-2% in 2027 (year 1), 2-4% in year 2, and up to 5% by year 3—implying minimal 2026 revenue impact”; “payer contracting alone typically tak[es] 6-9 months before utilization begins to scale.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the open question is timing” and advised watching for “an effective date, fee schedule, and rate”; its bull case looked for “a concrete Illinois reimbursement rate and start date.”

surprises.description: The CE marking submission slipped from its midyear target to Q4 2026, adding a delay to the European milestone the preview said was due for confirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “European CE marking submission was pushed to Q4 2026 (from midyear)” while the company completes additional assay performance and sample stability testing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The CE mark dossier was targeted for mid-2026, so confirmation of submission is now due.”

surprises.description: The company reported a broader payer-opportunity funnel than the preview’s focus on 13 covered payers across 15 states: it is engaging more than 20 payer opportunities across more than 20 states and exceeded its goal of doubling payer discussions. The update describes opportunities and referrals, not a reported first contracted payer.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company exceeded its 2026 goal of doubling payer discussions, now engaging over 20 payer opportunities across more than 20 states, driven largely by payer referrals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “Payer coverage count (13 payers / 15 states)” as a key metric and said “the bull case needs the first contracted commercial payer, not just a wider funnel.”

surprises.description: A newly reported PRIME analysis in first-time mothers showed substantial reductions in NICU admissions and severe neonatal morbidity; the preview did not flag this subgroup result.
surprises.fact_evidence: The July-published subgroup analysis showed a “22% reduction in NICU admissions,” a “30% reduction in severe neonatal morbidity,” and a “number-needed-to-screen-and-treat of 28.”

in_line: Cash and securities ended the quarter at $80.3 million, near the preview’s $78–80 million estimate, and management reiterated that the funds support operations through milestones into 2029, consistent with the preview’s expected runway language.
The fourth commercial partnership program launched this quarter, as the preview expected from the stated cadence of about one program launch per quarter.

surprises.description: Consolidated revenue was stronger than the preview’s $9.44 million consensus: the reported 13% sequential increase from Q1’s $8.72 million implies roughly $9.85 million, about 4% above consensus.
