surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin, ≥42% needed”; “Pre-announced EBITDA implies roughly 43–44% gross margin”; the preview said a Q2 margin “in the 30s” would weaken the one-time-cost explanation.

surprises.description: Management gave a stronger near-term quarterly outlook than the preview’s concern about a possible FY26 revenue cut suggested: Q3 is expected to be the largest quarter ever, Q4 significantly larger still, with quarterly revenue targeted above $25 million and approaching or exceeding $30 million. No explicit FY26 total was provided, so this does not confirm the preview’s $101.6 million full-year consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 will be the company's largest revenue quarter ever, with Q4 expected to significantly exceed Q3,” and management “targets quarterly revenue north of $25 million approaching or exceeding $30 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called FY26 guidance “the most fragile item,” cited “$101.6M” consensus, and said “A trim to roughly $85–90M is a plausible outcome.”

surprises.description: The auditors concluded the going-concern qualification is no longer needed and it will be removed from the Q2 10-Q, resolving a key risk the preview explicitly flagged after prior filings carried substantial-doubt language.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The auditors concluded the going concern qualification is no longer needed and it will be removed from the Q2 10-Q.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said removal “would be a clear positive” and listed whether the language was “retained or removed” as a key issue to watch.

surprises.description: ARR was $20.5 million, below the preview’s expected range of roughly $21–$22 million, despite a modest increase from the prior quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Annual recurring revenue rose modestly to $20.5 million from $20.1 million last quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ARR versus about $21–22M.”

surprises.description: The preview cited an approximately 10,000-screen retail media network award and questioned whether it had converted to contracts. The call identified Albertsons as the client and said 3,000 screens were live, confirming deployment but reporting a smaller live screen count than the preview’s cited award size.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management named Albertsons as its “large retail media network client,” with “2,200 stores, 3,000 screens live running 1 million ads/day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “whether the retail media network award (~10,000 screens) has converted to contracts.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed $3.5–$5 million of SaaS backlog scheduled to turn on January 1, 2027, with potential to lift composite margin by about two points—specific future revenue and margin visibility not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An additional $3.5 million–$5 million in SaaS backlog [is] set to turn on January 1, 2027, potentially lifting composite margin by about 2 points.”

surprises.description: The company said it had already realized about 75% of its targeted annualized CDM integration synergies, while the remaining portion is expected in 2027. This is concrete integration progress not discussed in the preview, though the remaining timing is later than an immediate margin recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has realized approximately $7.5 million (75%) of its targeted $10 million in annualized CDM integration synergies, with the remainder expected to show up in 2027.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was $2.0 million, at the low end of the company’s preliminary $2.0–$2.2 million range.

surprises.description: NUWE’s Q2 gross margin reached 76%, well above the preview’s 65–69% estimate and its 68% structural-margin threshold. The 7-point gap above the top of the estimate range was a substantial upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded dramatically to 76% in Q2 2026 from 56% a year earlier,” driven by higher selling prices, favorable product mix, and the shift to contract manufacturing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin” Q2 estimate: “65–69%”; the preview also said “Holding at least 68%” would show the margin gain is structural.

surprises.description: Cash at June 30 was about $3.9 million, below the preview’s $4.2–4.8 million estimate and its stated $4.0 million downside threshold. That was weaker than the expected cash bridge, despite the company having no debt.
surprises.fact_evidence: “As of June 30, 2026, the company held only about $3.9 million in cash and cash equivalents with no debt,” and remained dependent on capital raises.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Cash (period end)” at “$4.2–4.8M” and said a figure “near $6M or below” would mean its bridge was wrong; its bear scenario was “<$4.0M.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses were lower than the preview expected: $4.7 million versus an estimate of $5.0–5.5 million. They also fell sequentially from $6.3 million as management aligned spending with priority programs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses of $4.7 million rose year-over-year from $3.9 million but declined sequentially from $6.3 million in Q1 2026 as management aligned spending with priority programs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 operating expense at “$5.0–5.5M” and said a burn-reduction program was starting.

surprises.description: The net loss was about $4.8 million, slightly worse than the preview’s $3.8–4.5 million range. The $1.7 million warrant valuation expense helps explain the miss, although the preview had already warned of warrant-related noise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed sharply to approximately $4.8 million from $12.6 million in the prior-year quarter, though it included $1.7 million of warrant valuation expense tied to the June 2026 financing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Net loss” at “$(3.8)–(4.5)M” and noted “warrant and deemed-dividend noise from June financing.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $1.97 million narrowly exceeded the preview’s $1.90–1.95 million estimate. The difference was small, and the 14% year-over-year growth rate had already been pre-announced.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 14% year-over-year to $1.97 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Revenue” at “$1.90–1.95M” and noted “Pre-announced +14% Y/Y (Jul 27).”

surprises.description: The preview hoped for an explicit, dated reaffirmation of the 50% cash-burn reduction target. The supplied call facts instead report a target of consistent double-digit revenue growth, without formal guidance, and do not report a dated burn-reduction reaffirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management was “targeting consistent double-digit revenue growth without formal guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s catalyst checklist called for an “Explicit, dated reaffirmation of the 50% burn-reduction target”; it also described the existing target as “50% cash burn reduction by Q4 2026.”

surprises.description: NUWE plans to submit an FDA label expansion in Q4 2026 to lower the minimum patient weight for Aquadex use from 20 kilograms to 5 kilograms. The preview highlighted pediatric metrics but did not identify this specific regulatory step.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to submit an FDA label expansion in Q4 2026 to broaden Aquadex use to patients weighing 5 kilograms and above (from the current 20 kilograms), potentially expanding its pediatric market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged the “Pediatric franchise” and said to watch center count, console placements, and per-center utilization; it did not mention a label-expansion submission.

surprises.description: The call facts report that Mike McCormick is becoming CEO, a leadership transition not identified in the preview. The supplied information gives no details on the transition’s implications.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company reported “a new CEO transition (Mike McCormick).”

surprises.description: NUWE said its acquired ClarityPrime kidney-monitoring product is expected to launch in 2027, a future product milestone the preview did not discuss.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “expects its acquired ClarityPrime kidney monitoring product to launch in 2027.”

in_line: The reported 14% year-over-year Q2 revenue growth was in line with the preview’s pre-announcement reference of +14%; first-half revenue growth of 20% also matched the preview’s H1 cross-check.

surprises.description: SPAR lowered its 2026 revenue range to $130–138 million, below the preview’s $143–151 million range. A cut was anticipated, but the new range is materially lower than the preview’s scenario of trimming guidance toward the low end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $130–138 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 net sales guidance of “$143–151M” and said its base scenario was “guidance trimmed toward the low end.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.1 million, above the preview’s base range of $1.3–1.6 million and the $1.3 million year-ago hurdle; it was within the preview’s bull case. This was a stronger step-up than the base scenario anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated adjusted EBITDA rose 63% year-over-year to $2.1 million from $1.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario was “Adj. EBITDA $1.3–1.6M”; its bull scenario was “$2.0–2.5M.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow worsened sharply instead of showing the working-capital normalization the preview said to watch for. SPAR used $8.7 million in operating cash in Q2, versus $3.9 million used in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash used by operating activities was $8.7 million for the quarter, reflecting working capital timing tied to growth in the merchandising business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q2 should show working-capital normalization after Q1's –$3.9M.”

surprises.description: SPAR reported positive GAAP net income of $409,000, its first profitable quarter since Q1 2025, rather than another loss or break-even result. The preview noted a Q1 loss but did not forecast Q2 GAAP profitability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SPAR Group returned to profitability in Q2 2026 for the first time since Q1 2025, posting GAAP net income of $409,000 ($0.02 per diluted share) versus break-even in the prior year.”

surprises.description: Full-year SG&A guidance fell to $21–24 million, below the preview’s $25.5–26.5 million benchmark, indicating a lower expected expense level for the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $130–138 million … while maintaining gross margin guidance of 21.5%–23.5% and SG&A of $21–24 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 SG&A guidance of “$25.5–26.5M.”

surprises.description: The full-year gross-margin range was 21.5%–23.5%, above the preview’s listed 20.5%–22.5% range. That is a more favorable margin outlook than the preview’s benchmark, even though Q2’s actual margin was below the year-ago level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Maintaining gross margin guidance of 21.5%–23.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY2026 gross margin guidance of “20.5%–22.5%.”

surprises.description: SPAR disclosed a $151,500-per-month agreement with Repositrak to re-platform technology and develop a scan-based trading proposition, a new cost and strategic initiative the preview did not identify. The potential capability benefit is paired with a material ongoing expense, so the shareholder implication is mixed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SPAR entered an IT agreement with Repositrak costing $151,500 per month to re-platform its technology and develop a scan-based trading proposition.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed ongoing legal matters involving Robert Brown, which the preview had not flagged. Management said the matters were non-material, so the disclosure is unexpected but its implications are unclear from the provided facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Disclosed ongoing legal matters involving Robert Brown that management deemed non-material.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $36.9 million, down 4.5% year over year: close to the preview’s bull-case range of $36.5–37.5 million and above its buy-side hurdle of $34.5 million.
Q2 gross margin was 22.8%, within the preview’s base-case range of 22.5%–23.0% and above its buy-side threshold of 22.5%.
Q2 SG&A was $6.8 million including $543,000 of one-time costs, or about $6.3 million excluding those costs—roughly in line with the preview’s target of less than $6.5 million ex-items.
The preview already noted that SPAR had been delisted from Nasdaq and was trading on OTCQB; the call’s confirmation of OTCQB trading under SGRP was not new.

surprises.description: The preview highlighted liquidity and upcoming covenant tests as key risks, with cash at $16.5M after Q1. In Q2, operating cash flow exceeded $36M, the revolver was fully repaid, and cash ended at $35.4M, substantially strengthening the reported liquidity position.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow exceeded $36 million during the quarter, enabling full repayment of the revolver and ending the period with $35.4 million in cash and no material debt maturities until 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Covenant and liquidity disclosure. Leverage, fixed-charge coverage, and minimum-liquidity covenants begin testing in Q3 2026. Cash was $16.5M and PIK interest of $5.8M was capitalized in Q1.”

surprises.description: The preview's recovery thesis depended partly on retailer orders shifting into Q2 and Chubbies reaching about $44M, but Chubbies sales declined 8.6% year over year; the call did not provide a dollar figure to confirm whether it fell below $44M. The segment picture was mixed: Stove sales fell 14.7%, while water sports surged 59%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Stove segment, the company's largest, saw sales fall 14.7%, while Chubbies declined 8.6%, though the newly-separated water sports segment surged 59%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Chubbies net sales. If Q2 Chubbies comes in below about $44M, the ‘orders shifted to Q2’ story fails.” The base scenario also assumed “Chubbies ~$44M; Solo Stove ~$32M.”

surprises.description: The preview's bull case called for positive July/August datapoints, while management reported that weaker DTC sales softened notably in June and continued into July. That commentary points to demand weakness continuing after the quarter rather than clear evidence of a rebound.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Weaker DTC sales ... softened notably in June and continued into July.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bull: Management gives specific July/August datapoints and confidence on the Q3 covenant test.”

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate the scale of the international growth or the new distributor wins. International sales rose 46% to $9.8M, with help from a Chubbies partnership in India, and the company signed three new distributor contracts, including a European partner with Yeti experience.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International sales grew 46% year-over-year to $9.8 million, aided by a favorable India partnership for Chubbies, and the company signed three new distributor contracts including a Yeti-experienced European partner.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a substantial distribution and sourcing overhaul that the preview had not identified: it plans to reduce its U.S. distribution footprint from five facilities to one by Q4 and move Oru from Mexico manufacturing to a sourcing model. The potential efficiency benefit is not quantified in the reported facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is consolidating its U.S. distribution footprint from five facilities in 2025 to just one by the fourth quarter, closing a U.S. distribution center and shifting Oru manufacturing from Mexico to a sourcing model.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag how much new products were contributing to Solo Stove DTC sales. Management said launches accounted for nearly half of the channel's sales and described a fall/holiday pipeline including the Infinity Flame propane fire pit and a Chubbies denim line.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New product launches accounted for nearly half of Solo Stove's DTC channel sales in the quarter,” with a “robust fall/holiday pipeline” planned.

in_line: Net sales were $88.5M, within the preview's roughly $85–92M guidance-math range and above its $85–88M key-metric range.
Adjusted EBITDA was $13.5M, within the preview's implied $10–14M range, though above its $12M base-case estimate.
Gross margin was 59.9%, within the preview's expected recovery range of 57–60% and above its 56% catalyst threshold; the call also identified tariff refunds as an offset to a one-time write-off.

surprises.description: NAV per share reached $8.25, above the preview’s implied $7.85–$7.95 range. The increase included $0.17 per share of accretion from below-NAV repurchases and $0.08 of unrealized appreciation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net asset value per share rose $0.35 to $8.25,” driven in part by “$0.17 of accretion from below-NAV share repurchases” and “$0.08 of unrealized appreciation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “NAV/share | No formal consensus (~$7.85–7.95 implied)” and “NAV per share vs. $7.90. This is the main valuation debate.”

surprises.description: Total investment income was $8.7 million, above the $8.0 million consensus estimate, even though it declined from Q1. Management attributed the sequential decline largely to Q1’s non-recurring income, including the Bloom exit fee.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total investment income declined to $8.7 million from $9.8 million in Q1, largely due to $1.8 million of non-recurring other income including a $1.5 million exit fee from the Bloom repayment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (total investment income) | Q2 2026 Consensus | $8.00M.”

surprises.description: AFC executed a substantial portion of its buyback authorization rather than making no repurchases: it bought about 839,000 shares for roughly $2.8 million, with $2.2 million still available.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased about 839,000 shares at a weighted average $3.29 for roughly $2.8 million, with approximately $2.2 million remaining under the $5 million buyback program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Leverage and buybacks… Zero repurchases in Q2 would be a negative signal.”

surprises.description: Reported yield was 13.2% excluding non-accruals, above the preview’s cited guidance that portfolio yields would move down into the low double-digit range.
surprises.fact_evidence: The portfolio had “a 13.2% weighted average yield excluding non-accruals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided portfolio yields down ‘into the low double-digit range.’”

surprises.description: Deployment was lumpy and the pipeline was lower than the prior-quarter figure cited in the preview: Q2 commitments were less than Q1’s roughly $80 million, while the pipeline stood at $1.3 billion versus the prior “above $1.5B” level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date new lower middle market commitments totaled approximately $102 million, with originations described as lumpy—about $80 million in Q1 versus less in Q2.” The pipeline was “$1.3 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pipeline quoted above $1.5B” and “Deployment and yield. Management guided yields lower… Watch the trade-off between yield compression and credit quality.”

surprises.description: AFC reported two DMA dispensaries closed in July, an adverse development in the legacy cannabis portfolio that the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Two of three DMA dispensaries closed in July.”

surprises.description: AFC disclosed concrete progress on Debbie: it had recovered $58 million of principal and signed a binding term sheet to sell two assets for $12.5 million, backed by a $2 million hard deposit. The preview did not anticipate this resolution detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Debbie has recovered $58 million of principal to date and signed a binding term sheet with a $2 million hard deposit to sell two assets for $12.5 million (AFC holds ~80% participation).”

in_line: NII was essentially in line with the $0.153 consensus estimate at $0.15 per weighted average share.
The quarterly distribution remained $0.05, matching the preview’s stated amount.
Justice Grown remained in maturity default, and AFC identified a foreclosure path—one of the outcomes the preview said to watch for. The call facts provided no specific mark or restructuring.

surprises.description: Tecogen’s Product gross margin rose to 48.5% from 29.3% as price increases and product mix improved. The preview focused on continued overall gross-margin compression, and did not flag this sharp product-margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Product gross margin expanded dramatically to 48.5% from 29.3% year-over-year due to price increases and favorable product mix,” lifting overall gross margin to 37.8% from 33.8%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin floor. Service-territory cost reductions were promised to show up ‘by Q3.’ Another quarter of compression without that improvement would weaken the services-annuity part of the bull case.”

surprises.description: Services margin faced an unexpected one-time hit: a catastrophic electric chiller failure and other costs totaling about $300,000 reduced the margin by roughly 7 percentage points. That adds a near-term margin headwind beyond the preview’s focus on service-territory cost reductions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service margin was reduced roughly 7 percentage points by about $300,000 in one-time costs including a catastrophic electric chiller failure.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Service-territory cost reductions were promised to show up ‘by Q3.’”

surprises.description: Management said capital constraints are shaping its inventory build: Tecogen is preparing chillers and power modules to shorten lead times, but timing production around expected orders and shipments. The preview highlighted cash runway and financing risk, but did not anticipate this specific constraint on inventory and production planning.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management has begun building inventory of dual-power source chillers and power generation modules to compress lead times, while managing capital constraints by timing production to expected order and shipment dates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash runway and financing. $6.78M at Jun 30 and $2.55M burned in Q2 imply roughly 2 to 2.5 quarters at current burn.”

in_line: The backlog update broadly matched the preview: the base business backlog exceeded $8 million, with another $2 million to $3 million in projects expected to close in coming months. Management said this supports anticipated Q3 revenue growth, consistent with the preview’s expectation that Q3 product revenue would be above Q1 and Q2, though no specific Q3 figure was provided.

The data-center pipeline remained qualitative rather than converting into a disclosed order or revenue figure. The call cited 12 demonstrations and substantial data-center capacity, but no named customer with a dollar-valued order, consistent with the preview’s description of the pipeline as having no disclosed revenue.
Operating expenses declined about $400,000 sequentially after service-center headcount reductions, consistent with the preview’s focus on cost reductions expected to begin showing up.

surprises.description: Q2 net ZEVASKYN revenue was $11.4 million, below the preview’s consensus range of about $12.2–$13.3 million. It was still within the preview’s $11–$13 million base-case scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net ZEVASKYN revenue of $11.4 million,” up 31% sequentially from $8.7 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net product revenue” consensus: “~$12.2M” to “~$13.3M”; base scenario: “$11–13M.”

surprises.description: The quarterly loss was larger than expected: Abeona reported a $20.2 million net loss and EPS of –$0.35, versus preview estimates of a $13–16 million loss and EPS of –$0.23 to –$0.28.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss of $20.2 million ($0.35 per share), widening from a $17.1 million loss ($0.30 per share) in Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP EPS” consensus: “–$0.23” to “–$0.28”; “Net loss” of “~$13–16M implied.”

surprises.description: Some treatments did not generate revenue because of manufacturing batch problems: a low-yield batch affected Q2 and an out-of-spec batch affected Q3-to-date treatments. The preview identified manufacturing delay as a downside risk, but did not anticipate these specific batch failures or their impact on revenue recognition.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue was not recognized on multiple treatments due to a low-yield batch in Q2 and an out-of-spec batch in Q3.” Batches yielding “fewer than 4 sheets” trigger “no revenue recognition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bear scenario cited “manufacturing or scheduling delay”; the base case expected “one or two treatments slip to July.”

surprises.description: Two of the six Q2 biopsies previously scheduled were cancelled at the last minute because patients’ health deteriorated. Unlike the preview’s expectation that one or two treatments might slip into July, the cancelled slots could not be filled by another patient.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Two scheduled biopsies were cancelled last-minute in Q2 due to patient health deterioration,” and “cancelled slots cannot be refilled by other patients.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior call had “six biopsies scheduled for Q2,” and the CFO said “1 or 2” could “slip into July.”

surprises.description: Cash and short-term investments ended June at $146.8 million, below the preview’s approximate $152 million cash-exit reference.
surprises.fact_evidence: Abeona “held $146.8 million in cash and short-term investments as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s catalyst checklist said to compare the “Cash exit balance against about $152M.”

in_line: Abeona treated five patients in Q2, matching the preview’s base case of four to five treatments.
The seventh qualified treatment center, Cincinnati Children’s, was consistent with the preview’s expectation that seven QTCs would be live, including Cincinnati.
CMS NTAP status was already reported in the preview as granted effective October 1, 2026.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $2.9M, below the preview’s $3.9–4.5M base case. The roughly 29% sequential decline was steeper than that range implied, even though the preview expected revenue to fall as contract manufacturing wound down.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 revenue declined approximately 29% sequentially to about $2.9 million from $4.1 million in Q1 2026, reflecting the intentional wind-down of contract manufacturing volume.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case Q2'26” net revenue: “$3.9–4.5M.”

surprises.description: Cash ended the quarter at $6.1M, below the preview’s already-wide $7–10M range and below its $6.5M downside marker. The supplied facts do not mention a concurrent financing.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended Q2 with $6.1 million in cash and cash equivalents and no outstanding debt.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash” base case: “$7–10M (wide; June warrant inducement proceeds not quantified)”; the catalyst checklist says “Below ~$6.5M makes the next financing close to certain.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $3.5M, worse than the preview’s expected $2.3–2.7M loss. That is also just beyond the preview’s bear-case range, which extended to a $3.4M loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: Adjusted EBITDA worsened to negative $3.5 million in Q2 2026 from negative $2.6 million in Q1 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case Q2'26” adjusted EBITDA: “$(2.3)–(2.7)M”; the bear scenario gave “$(2.8)–(3.4)M.”

surprises.description: The reported $0.3M gross loss was within the expected range, but the improvement included a substantial non-recurring benefit: a $692,000 excise tax recovery, partly offset by a $196,000 inventory write-off. That makes the headline improvement less representative of recurring gross-margin performance than the preview’s range alone conveyed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 gross margin benefited from a one-time $692,000 MSA NPM excise tax recovery, partially offset by a $196,000 one-time write-off of aged inventory; both were deemed non-recurring.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case Q2'26” gross profit/(loss): “$(0.3)–(0.6)M.”

surprises.description: Management said price increases have pushed some customers to lower-cost suppliers and that gross-margin improvement has been slower than planned. The preview expected gross-loss narrowing from the contract-manufacturing exit but did not flag this customer-retention and margin-execution problem.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management acknowledged that pricing increases have caused some customers to leave for lower-cost suppliers and that gross margin improvement has been slower than planned.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Revenue falling while gross loss narrows is the intended outcome” of exiting low-margin contract-manufacturing work.

surprises.description: The preview looked for a Q2 retail count of 2,200–2,600 stores, but the call described the expansion as starting from approximately 2,000 stores. The year-end goal was described as roughly 5,000, rather than the preview’s “>5,000” target; the facts do not provide a precise Q2 store count.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management targets expanding retail presence from approximately 2,000 stores across 20 states to roughly 5,000 stores across 35 states by year-end 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a Q2 count in the “2,200–2,600 range” would matter and described the year-end target as “>5,000.”

surprises.description: Operating loss was $3.3M, slightly worse than the preview’s $2.8–3.2M base-case range. The supplied facts also report a $3.3M net loss from continuing operations, but the preview said EPS was not forecastable on a usable basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: Operating loss and net loss from continuing operations each rose to $3.3 million in Q2 from $3.0 million in Q1 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base case Q2'26” operating loss: “$(2.8)–(3.2)M.”

surprises.description: Management newly expected branded product shipments in the second half to be significantly larger than in the first half, positioning the business for a stronger 2027. The preview did not provide a second-half branded-shipment expectation to compare against.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects second-half branded product shipments to be significantly larger than the first half of 2026, positioning for a stronger 2027.

in_line: Q2 gross loss was $0.3M, at the favorable end of the preview’s expected $0.3–0.6M loss range; narrowing gross loss as low-margin contract-manufacturing volume winds down was an anticipated outcome.

Management’s plan to substantially wind down most legacy CMO volume by year-end 2026 or early Q1 2027 was consistent with the preview’s expectation that the company was exiting low-margin contract-manufacturing work.

surprises.description: The preview gave no response-rate or durability forecast for Clover-WM, but the call reported a 79.2% major response rate and 87.5% overall response rate in patients treated immediately after BTK inhibitors. It also reported 17.8 months of median durability at 12-month follow-up, with a 14.5% very good partial response/complete response rate in late-line refractory patients.
surprises.fact_evidence: “79.2% major response rate, 87.5% overall response rate, 100% clinical benefit rate, and 16-month median duration of response” in patients treated immediately following BTK inhibitor therapy; full 12-month follow-up showed “a median durability of 17.8 months” and a “very good partial response/complete response rate rising to 14.5% in late-line refractory patients.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 R&D expense at $3.3–3.8 million, but Cellectar reported $4.6 million, well above the top of that range. The company attributed the increase to greater clinical activity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “R&D expenses nearly doubled to $4.6 million from $2.4 million due to increased clinical activity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full preview estimate: $3.3–3.8M (Q1'26: $3.0M)”

surprises.description: The preview said CLR-125 Phase 1b data were guided for mid-2026 and might be reported on the call; instead, the first patients have now been dosed and initial data are expected later in 2026 or early 2027. The trial has started, but the data timing has moved out.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company dosed the first patients in its Phase 1B trial of CLR-125 in triple-negative breast cancer, with initial dosimetry, safety, and efficacy data expected later in 2026 or early 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CLR 125 Phase 1b (TNBC) dosimetry and safety data. Guided for mid-2026 and not yet released. Either it comes on this call or it slips.”

surprises.description: The preview cited an early-2027 NDA target, while the call described the filing as targeted for mid-2027, with a March–April timeframe. That is a modest move later, although the stated six-month review expectation still points to a 2027 decision window.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plans to submit its NDA…in mid-2027 (targeting a March-April timeframe), with an approximate six-month review expected due to breakthrough designation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “NDA submission guided for early 2027”; the preview also described “approval in 2H 2027.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Phase 3 initiation in late Q4 2026, but the call said first dosing could be as late as early 2027. Opening sites in the coming months and aiming to have 10–20 open by NDA submission show progress, but the dosing window leaves room for a slight delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First Phase 3 confirmatory trial sites” are expected “in the coming months,” with “first patient dosing anticipated late 2026 or early 2027,” and 10–20 sites open by NDA submission.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Phase 3 confirmatory trial guided for initiation in late Q4 2026.”

surprises.description: The reported loss per share was slightly larger than the preview’s consensus and alternate estimate: $0.57 per share versus expected losses of $0.52–$0.55. The preview cautioned that EPS could be distorted by warrant-share treatment and was not the main focus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss widened to $6.9 million ($0.57 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS | -$0.52”; “Alternate aggregate: -$0.55.”

surprises.description: The preview described warrant calls as requiring the share-price threshold to hold for 20 sessions, but the call also specified a minimum average daily liquidity condition. That adds a further hurdle to calling the milestone warrants.
surprises.fact_evidence: The warrants are callable only if VWAP reaches at least $3.45 for 20 consecutive trading days “with minimum $500,000 average daily liquidity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Warrant calls require the stock to trade above about $3.45 (130% of $2.65) for 20 consecutive sessions.”

in_line: Cash was approximately $34.0 million at June 30, within the preview’s estimated range of approximately $32–34 million.
G&A expense was $2.6 million, at the low end of the preview’s $2.6–2.9 million estimate.
The May financing terms were broadly as previewed: $35 million upfront plus up to $105 million in milestone warrants.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case put revenue at $1.1–1.4 million and looked for a seasonal rebound, but Q2 revenue was $0.9 million and was down $1.2 million year over year. Management said cautious operator spending at $55–$60 oil prices is pushing several anticipated Gulf projects into 2027 and beyond.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $0.9 million” and management expects operators' cautious spending at “$55-$60 oil prices” to push “several anticipated Gulf projects into 2027 and beyond.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Preview's own base case (not consensus): revenue $1.1–1.4M”; the preview also asked, “Revenue: did the seasonal rebound happen?” and said the offshore wind project “should contribute in Q2/Q3.”

surprises.description: GAAP net loss was $11.1 million, above the preview’s $7.5–9.0 million base-case range. The call attributed most of the widening to non-cash losses on debt extinguishment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $11.1 million in Q2 2026 from $9.3 million in Q1 2026 and $7.4 million in Q2 2025, driven mostly by non-cash losses on debt extinguishment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Preview's own base case (not consensus): ... GAAP net loss $7.5–9.0M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted net loss was $7.0 million, slightly worse than the preview’s $5.8–6.6 million base-scenario range, despite improving slightly year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted net loss improved slightly to $7 million versus $7.4 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “Adj. net loss ... ($5.8–6.6M).”

surprises.description: Nauticus formally released its Toolkit software, but the reported milestone was a product release to fleet operators rather than the preview’s hoped-for first named license with dollars attached; management expects recurring revenue to begin in 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nauticus formally released its Toolkit software for ROVs to energy and defense fleet operators, expecting it to generate recurring, predictable revenue starting in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the key milestone would be a first named licensing customer with dollars attached” and identified a “first monetized ToolKITT license” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: The company reported reducing debt by $5.5 million through debt-to-equity exchanges, more than the roughly $4.0 million exchange the preview identified. The call also cited an equity line of credit and Series D designation, though it gave no proceeds or dilution figures here.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reduced outstanding debt by $5.5 million through debt-to-equity exchanges and completed financing initiatives including an equity line of credit and Series D designation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “the June 26 exchange of about $4.0M in secured convertible term loans and accrued interest into 4,800 shares of Series C Preferred.”

surprises.description: Management described a shift to an international primary-contractor model using fixed-price contracts and vessels of opportunity, rather than relying on long-term charter commitments. The preview discussed international expansion but did not flag this specific commercial model.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is shifting to a primary contractor model internationally using fixed-price contracts and vessels of opportunity to capture autonomy-driven margins while avoiding long-term charter commitments.”

surprises.description: Management said a reverse stock split is not required to maintain the Nasdaq listing because the share price has recovered, addressing a shareholder concern the preview did not identify as an imminent requirement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management stated a reverse stock split is not required to maintain its NASDAQ listing given recent share price recovery.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $278.7 million, above the preview’s working range of $225–246 million and even its $265 million-plus bull case. The preview expected a sharp playoff-driven lift, but the reported result was substantially higher than that bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 total revenues jumped to $278.7 million from $204 million a year earlier,” with event-related revenues up 43%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Use the $225–246M range as the working bar”; the bull scenario was “$265M+.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating income reached $39.6 million, above the preview’s $10–20 million base case and its $30 million-plus bull case. The title run therefore flowed through to operating income more strongly than the preview’s concern about playoff costs absorbing much of the gain implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 adjusted operating income swung to a positive $39.6 million from an adjusted operating loss of $16.8 million,” aided by championship-driven revenue gains; incremental playoff costs were approximately $11 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario put AOI at “$10–20M”; the bull case was “$30M+.” The preview also said playoff expenses “could absorb much of the gain.”

surprises.description: Management gave a specific end-of-October target to complete the Rangers spin-off, whereas the preview’s base case anticipated “on track, no timetable.” That is a more concrete and earlier-defined schedule than the preview led investors to expect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects to complete the spin-off of its Rangers business from its Knicks business by the end of October”; it had confidentially filed a Form 10 in May and planned to publicly file an updated Form 10 this week.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No timetable has been set”; the base scenario expected spin-off commentary of “on track, no timetable.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed an additional tax expense from new tax-law changes that the preview did not discuss. The estimated $16 million expense is for fiscal 2028, and management also expects combined tax expense across the two companies to be higher after separation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New tax law changes are estimated to add approximately $16 million in additional income tax expense in fiscal year 2028 (excluding spin-off effects), with combined tax expense across the two companies expected to be higher post-separation.”

in_line: The preview identified season-ticket renewals and post-title pricing as key forward indicators. Management said combined renewal rates are expected to again exceed 90%, raised Knicks season-ticket prices, and did not raise Rangers prices.

surprises.description: Q2 results were far worse than the preview’s expectations: revenue was $113.3 million versus $190 million consensus, while diluted loss per share was $1.55 versus an expected $0.33 loss. A $102.3 million non-cash revenue reversal and a $93.6 million unfavorable legacy claims adjustment drove a $71.2 million gross loss and negative $73.4 million EBITDA; management called the reassessment one-time but said the timing and ultimate recovery remain uncertain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell to $113.3 million” due to a “$102.3 million non-cash revenue reversal”; gross loss was “$71.2 million” primarily from a “$93.6 million unfavorable legacy claims adjustment”; net loss was “$84.3 million, or $1.55 per diluted share,” and EBITDA was “negative $73.4 million.” Management characterized the reassessment as “a one-time adjustment,” though “timing and ultimate resolution of recoveries remain uncertain.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Revenue | $190M” and “EPS | -$0.33”; its base scenario expected revenue of “$172–182M” and EPS of “-$0.30 to -$0.40.” The bear scenario anticipated “New legacy dispute charge” and EPS of “-$0.75 or worse.”

surprises.description: Financing moved beyond the preview’s base case of an agreement merely advanced but not closed: the senior credit facility was amended, providing about $27 million of cash debt-service relief over the next 12 months, and the company set a deadline to convert approximately $151 million of surety financing into perpetual, non-convertible preferred shares. The conversion is still prospective, so the financing package is not fully completed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Southland expects to convert “approximately $151 million of non-bonding surety financing into perpetual, non-convertible senior preferred shares” by September 30, 2026. The credit facility was amended to “a fixed 4% PIK interest rate with suspended amortization and early-termination premium,” delivering “roughly $27 million of cash debt service relief over the next 12 months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “signed and closed deal would give the stock runway” and described the base case as “financing advanced but not closed”; it warned that continued “in progress” language would signal slippage.

surprises.description: Surety partners provided another $70.6 million during the quarter, and repayment of advances under indemnity agreements is not required before at least August 13, 2027. This adds near-term funding flexibility, while also leaving substantial surety-related payables outstanding.
surprises.fact_evidence: Surety partners “advanced approximately $70.6 million during the quarter,” bringing advances under indemnity agreements to “$209.8 million” and total surety payables to “$298.9 million”; repayment is “not required before at least August 13, 2027.”

surprises.description: Management said it expects bidding activity to ramp up now that surety bonding support is formalized, a more constructive operating outlook than the preview specifically described.
surprises.fact_evidence: Southland “expects bidding activity to ramp up now that surety bonding support is formalized.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on whether long-term financing would close or remain “in progress,” and did not anticipate a stated ramp in bidding activity.

in_line: Backlog was $1.68 billion, close to the preview’s expected print near $1.7 billion; about 38% is expected to convert to revenue over the next 12 months, matching the preview’s cited 38% conversion rate.
The $190 million share of the Winnipeg project was booked in Q3, consistent with the preview’s note that the Winnipeg award was guided into Civil backlog in Q3 rather than Q2.

surprises.description: YETI’s Q2 adjusted EPS was $0.67, far above the preview’s $0.52–$0.54 consensus range; the preview expected EPS to fall roughly 18%–21% year over year, but it rose 2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS grew 2% to $0.67 in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS $0.52–$0.54”; “Implied Y/Y –18% to –21%.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin reached 59.5%, well above the preview’s roughly 54%–55% expectation. The reported margin included an $8.2 million IEEPA tariff refund benefit that the preview said was not modeled, despite 110 basis points of higher realized tariff costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin expanded 170 bps to 59.5%, including an $8.2 million (170 bps) benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds, partially offset by 110 bps of higher realized tariff costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. gross margin ~54–55%”; “YETI’s refund receivable is not modeled”; “IEEPA refund quantification. Management has not included it in guidance, so sizing it would be a surprise.”

surprises.description: YETI raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $2.94–$3.00 instead of merely reaffirming the prior $2.83–$2.89 range, as the preview expected at least a reaffirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted EPS guidance was raised to $2.94–$3.00 (19%–21% growth) from prior $2.83–$2.89.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year EPS guidance ($2.83–$2.89). A straight reaffirmation may be read as a soft outcome.”

surprises.description: Full-year gross-margin guidance was raised to 57.5%–58%, reversing the preview’s expectation that the 56.5%–57.0% range required a strong second-half recovery and implied a 60-basis-point decline for the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year gross margin guidance was raised 100 basis points to 57.5%–58%, implying a 40 bps year-over-year increase versus a prior expected 60 bps decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin 56.5–57.0%”; “the full-year 56.5–57.0% range requires roughly 58%+ in H2.”

surprises.description: U.S. Drinkware was flat, rather than delivering the additional consecutive quarter of category growth the preview said would strengthen the U.S. inflection story. Management also disclosed that three SKUs are creating an approximately 600-basis-point drag on 2026 U.S. Drinkware growth, expected to fully lap by year-end and reset the base for 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Drinkware grew only 2% to $241 million with U.S. Drinkware flat”; “a roughly 600 basis point drag on 2026 U.S. Drinkware growth from just 3 SKUs, expected to fully lap by year-end and reset the base heading into 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 was the second straight quarter of category growth. A third quarter would be a stronger signal of the U.S. inflection.”

surprises.description: Adjusted SG&A rose 19% and deleveraged 410 basis points, with the brand campaign shifted from last year’s Q4 into this Q2 and higher incentive compensation adding to the expense. The preview focused on tariff and mix pressure but did not flag this Q2 expense increase or campaign timing shift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted SG&A rose 19% and deleveraged 410 bps to 45.4% of sales, largely due to the brand campaign shifting from Q4 last year into Q2 this year plus higher incentive comp.”

surprises.description: YETI raised its full-year adjusted operating-margin outlook to approximately 14.9%, up 30 basis points from the prior 14.6% guidance, rather than the reaffirmation the preview expected; management also projected second-half margins up roughly 280 basis points year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 adjusted operating margin guidance was raised to approximately 14.9% (up 30 bps)”; “second-half margins up roughly 280 bps year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted operating margin ~14.6%”; “Full-year guidance action. Consensus expects at least a reaffirmation”; “Base: … FY reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: YETI repurchased $130 million of shares in Q2, exceeding the preview’s roughly $100 million of buybacks embedded in the full-year outlook, and reported more than $600 million of buybacks since 2024.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repurchased 2.8 million shares for $130 million in Q2, bringing total buybacks since 2024 to over $600 million, with roughly $370 million remaining on authorization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Roughly $100M of buybacks embedded against a $500M authorization.”

in_line: Q2 sales were approximately $484 million, up 9% year over year, essentially matching the preview’s $483.8 million consensus and 8.5% implied growth.

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EPS was a loss of $0.01, sharply below the preview’s $0.38–$0.40 expectation. The call attributed the loss to a 67.8% effective tax rate after resolving two dividend-withholding matters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Q4 effective tax rate spiked to 67.8% due to resolution of two dividend withholding matters, driving an adjusted loss of $0.01 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 adj. EPS” consensus was “$0.38–$0.40”; the preview says the consensus is an adjusted figure.

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted operating margin was 4.9%, above the preview’s 4.4%–4.6% guidance range and roughly 4.5% expectation. That was a better quarter-end margin than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 adjusted operating income was $18.1 million (4.9% of sales).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 adj. operating margin” consensus was “~4.5%,” with company guidance of “4.4%–4.6%.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue came in slightly below the preview’s $373.4 million consensus, although it remained within the company’s stated $370–$380 million range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 net sales were $371.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 revenue” consensus was “$373.4M”; company guidance was “$370–380M.”

surprises.description: Q4 gross margin reached 8.9%, above the preview’s 8%-or-more benchmark for a constructive outlook. The preview had cited 7.9% in Q3, so the reported improvement was also larger than that benchmark implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 gross margin improved 90 basis points year-over-year to 8.9%, driven by favorable mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q4 at 4.6% with gross margin of 8% or more supports a constructive FY27 outlook,” and reported Q3 gross margin of “7.9% (+70 bps YoY).”

surprises.description: The FY27 operating-margin guide is modestly above the preview’s base-case range: the company guided to 4.4%–4.7% versus the preview’s 4.3%–4.6% scenario. The ranges overlap, but both ends of the company’s range are 10 basis points higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 operating margin [is] guided to 4.4%-4.7%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “margin 4.3%–4.6%.”

surprises.description: Management said medical sales should approach 35% of company sales in FY27. The preview anticipated continued double-digit medical growth but did not forecast that share of total sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Medical sales grew over 10% for the full fiscal year (normalized for last year's consigned inventory sale) and are expected to approach 35% of total company sales in fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Medical growth. Three straight double-digit quarters, driven by respiratory care, imaging, and drug delivery.”

surprises.description: Borrowings were $116.6 million and leverage was near 1x EBITDA, a strong balance-sheet position that the preview had identified as something to assess after the Helvoet acquisition but had not forecast at this level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Borrowings fell to $116.6 million, the lowest level in over 4 years, down 21% year-over-year, leaving leverage near 1x EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “$163M net debt at Q3” and said to watch “pro forma net leverage.”

surprises.description: Q4 operating cash flow was $42.4 million, with cash conversion days at their best level in 17 quarters. The preview did not flag these cash-generation metrics, so this was an unanticipated positive operating update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash from operations was a robust $42.4 million in Q4, marking the tenth consecutive quarter of positive cash, with cash conversion days improving to 82, the best in 17 quarters.”

in_line: FY27 revenue guidance of $1.535 billion–$1.56 billion is within the preview’s $1.50 billion–$1.56 billion base-case range; the preview said there was no published FY27 consensus.
Medical sales grew at a double-digit rate, consistent with the preview’s expectation of continued double-digit medical growth.

The preview anticipated a 40–50 basis-point Indianapolis ramp headwind and relief not expected until FY28; the call reported a FY27 drag of roughly $6.5–$7 million and said new-program production would not start until the end of calendar 2026.
Automotive weakness tied to EV-program pressure was anticipated: the preview flagged North American EV program de-content as a concern, while the call reported weaker EV volumes and a 3% Q4 decline.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue was $26.7 million, above the top of management’s $24–26 million guide and the preview’s $22.6–24.0 million consensus range. The beat over the company’s guide was modest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 fiscal 2026 revenue grew approximately 11% year-over-year to $26.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company Q3 revenue guidance | $24M – $26M”; consensus was “$22.6M – $24.0M.”

surprises.description: GAAP diluted EPS of $0.25 was above the preview’s $0.23–$0.24 consensus. This was a small beat over the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income rose to $4.5 million ($0.25 diluted EPS).”

surprises.description: Excluding F-16 revenue and acquisitions, the organic business grew over 40%, stronger than the preview’s concern that weak book-to-bill could raise questions about organic growth. The steep F-16 comparison—$5.7 million versus $12.6 million a year earlier—masked that underlying growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding F-16 revenue and new acquisitions, the organic business grew over 40% year-over-year in Q3”; “F-16 revenue was $5.7 million this quarter versus $12.6 million a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Sub-1.0x book-to-bill would raise questions about organic growth.”

surprises.description: The Liberty flight deck won its first OEM contract with a Japanese eVTOL developer, with more than 400 aircraft orders. The preview mentioned an eVTOL development agreement, but not an OEM award or this order base.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company won its first OEM contract for the Liberty flight deck with a Japanese eVTOL developer, holding over 400 aircraft orders.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “eVTOL display and avionics development agreement announced Aug 12.”

surprises.description: Backlog was approximately $83 million, down from $87.0 million in Q2, rather than roughly flat as the preview’s base scenario anticipated. It was still up $5.5 million year-over-year, making the signal mixed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog at approximately $83 million, up $5.5 million year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base | ... backlog roughly flat”; the preview also cited Q2 backlog of “$87.0M.”

surprises.description: Net leverage was 1.4x despite more than $35 million deployed on acquisitions and capex, below the prior 1.7x level even as the preview expected the Aydin cash outlay to affect the balance sheet. This was a better leverage outcome than that context suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt of $43.8 million and modest net leverage of 1.4x despite over $35 million deployed on acquisitions and capex.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net leverage 1.7x after $33M of acquisition spend”; “Aydin Displays ($24.5M cash) closed July 21, after quarter-end, so it is not in Q3 but will affect the Q4 balance sheet.”

in_line: Gross margin was 51.7%, broadly matching the preview’s expectation that a print near 51% would be a positive mix result.
The $250 million long-term revenue target was reaffirmed, as the preview noted it had been reiterated in the prior quarter.
The July Aydin Displays acquisition had closed after quarter-end, as the preview expected.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.43, below the preview’s working consensus of about $0.50 and even below its cited published estimates of $0.47–$0.54. The preview anticipated dilution from the rights offering, but the reported per-share result still came in materially weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS fell to $0.43 from $0.53 due to a higher share count following the April 2026 rights offering.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working consensus: revenue ~$14.8M, EPS ~$0.50”; published EPS estimates were “$0.47 / $0.53 / $0.54.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 41.2%, well below the preview’s 45.0% base case and beneath the 43–46% long-term target range it highlighted. The preview specifically flagged a result below 43% as a break from the new framework.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margins declined to 41.2% from 43.6% a year earlier,” weighed down by “roughly $0.5 million of non-cash stock-based compensation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario projected “Gross margin” of “45.0%”; the preview cited a “43–46% long-term target” and said “Sub-43% would break the new framework.”

surprises.description: The company gave a second-half gross-margin outlook of roughly 41.5–43.5%, likely near the midpoint, below the preview’s 43–46% target framework. The preview also said the company did not issue quarterly or annual guidance, so a specific margin outlook was not expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company guided second-half gross margins to a range of roughly 41.5% to 43.5%, likely landing near the middle, with a ~1-point drag from rapid ramping of new programs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guidance: none. The company does not issue quarterly or annual guidance”; the preview cited a “43–46% long-term target.”

surprises.description: Net income included a substantial non-cash stock-compensation charge tied to accelerated vesting of the 2025 annual bonus, which was absent in the prior-year period and was not identified in the preview. This was an unanticipated earnings headwind alongside the expected share-count dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income included a $1.0 million non-cash stock compensation expense tied to accelerated vesting of the 2025 annual bonus, absent in prior-year periods.”

surprises.description: Recently introduced products drew $12 million of orders for 2026–2027 production despite only about $200,000 in sales during 2025. The preview did not anticipate this scale of orders for the new products.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recently introduced products generated $12 million in new orders for 2026-2027 production despite selling only about $200,000 in 2025.”

surprises.description: New seven-year defense framework agreements are expected to produce their first purchase orders only in Q1 2027, for 2028 production, with a more meaningful revenue contribution in 2028. The preview did not discuss these agreements or this delayed timing of their revenue contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The first purchase orders from newly signed 7-year defense framework agreements are expected in Q1 2027 for 2028 production, with more meaningful revenue impact anticipated in 2028.”

in_line: Revenue was $15.1 million, matching the preview’s $15.1 million base case and exceeding its cited consensus estimates of $14.7–$15.04 million.
Adjusted EBITDA was $3.4 million, matching the preview’s $3.4 million base case.
Backlog was $84 million, at the top of the preview’s $78–84 million base-case range.

surprises.description: Saga's operating income was $623,000, well above the preview's estimated $1.1 million operating loss. The result was a substantial positive gap despite the weaker-than-estimated station operating income.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating income dropped to just $623,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating income” base estimate: “-$1.1M.”

surprises.description: Digital revenue grew 60.8%, far faster than the 10.2% growth cited in the preview as management's latest pacing. At the same time, every traditional revenue line fell by double digits, with national down 25%, revealing a much sharper split between digital and traditional advertising than the preview's headline revenue estimate conveyed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Blended digital revenue surged 60.8% in Q2”; “local down 11.2%, national down 25%, and nontraditional down 16.4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said on the May 7 call that Q2 was ‘pacing down high single digits with digital up 10.2%.’”

surprises.description: Station operating income came in at $3.0 million, below the preview's $3.4 million estimate, while quarterly station operating expense rose 5.4% rather than the roughly 2% increase assumed. The company attributed the added expense in part to hiring nine sales and digital campaign managers.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Station operating income fell to $3 million”; “Station operating expense rose 5.4% in Q2 (3.9% excluding noncash tower rent), driven by hiring 9 sales managers and digital campaign managers, adding roughly $357,000 in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Station operating income” base estimate: “$3.4M”; “Station opex rises about 2%.”

surprises.description: Saga's full-year corporate G&A guide fell to $11.8–$12.0 million, below the preview's $12.3 million assumption. This points to lower overhead costs than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Corporate G&A to fall to $11.8-$12 million from $12.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Corporate G&A is about $3.1M per quarter, per the $12.3M annual guide.”

surprises.description: Saga repaid its full $5 million revolver and terminated its credit agreement, leaving cash and short-term investments at $22.9 million, down from $27.8 million at June 30. The preview listed the $5 million of debt and $27.8 million cash position but did not anticipate the repayment or the resulting cash reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company terminated its credit agreement after repaying the full $5 million revolver, reducing cash and short-term investments to $22.9 million as of August 10 from $27.8 million at June 30.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash and short-term investments $27.8M as of May 4, 2026; long-term debt $5.0M.”

surprises.description: Saga reported substantial noncore property monetization, including six property sales for over $4 million since Q4 2025 and $10.5 million in cash from a tower sale. These asset sales were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has monetized noncore assets, selling 6 properties for over $4 million since Q4 2025 (including a $1.7 million Sarasota house and a $1 million Portland tower site), plus $10.5 million cash from the tower sale.”

in_line: Q2 net revenue was $26.4 million, slightly above the preview's $26.1 million base estimate.
Full-year station operating expense guidance remained at the preview's expected 1.5%–2.5% increase.
Capital expenditure guidance of $3–$3.5 million was broadly in line with the preview's roughly $3.5 million assumption.
The $0.25 quarterly dividend was paid, consistent with the preview's base case that the dividend would be held.

surprises.description: Quarterly revenue was $20.8 million, above the preview’s own bottoms-up estimate of about $19.7 million, although revenue still declined year over year. The reported figure reached the top of the preview’s $20.3–$20.8 million bull range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated revenues fell to $20.8 million for the quarter (down 15%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own bottoms-up model is not consensus. It estimates Q3 revenue of about $19.7M (-20% Y/Y).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $570,000, well above the preview’s estimate near $200,000 and its $100,000–$300,000 base-case range. It also exceeded the preview’s bull-case threshold of $500,000.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved to $570,000 for the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA near $200K”; the base case was “EBITDA $0.1–0.3M,” while the bull case was “EBITDA above $0.5M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 39.9%, 1.6 percentage points above the preview’s 38.3% estimate. The preview had anticipated improvement, but not this level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded significantly to 39.9% for the quarter (up 450 basis points).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own bottoms-up model is not consensus. It estimates … gross margin of about 38.3%.”

surprises.description: GEE Group reported one cent of diluted EPS rather than the preview’s expected $0.00. The preview specifically judged a one-cent result unlikely, although the reported net income was below the roughly $1.1 million the preview said would be needed for that EPS level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income of $566,000 (one cent per diluted share) for Q3 FY2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS will likely print $0.00 in almost every scenario”; “$0.01 of EPS requires roughly $1.1M of net income.”

surprises.description: The strategic review produced an indication that a decision is expected soon, rather than the silence the preview warned would be negative. However, no transaction or defined timeline was reported, and management said it was suspending further acquisitions until the review concludes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GEE Group has engaged Roth Capital Partners to evaluate strategic alternatives including a potential M&A transaction, describing interest as robust and expecting a decision soon, while suspending further acquisitions until the review concludes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “After three months, the market wants a timeline or a transaction, not adjectives. Silence is a negative.”

in_line: Direct hire placement revenue grew for a third consecutive quarter, as the preview expected; the preview did not set a Q3 growth-rate estimate.
Cash was $20.3 million, matching the preview’s stated reference balance of about $20.3 million.
Contract revenue excluding the lost account declined 11% for the quarter, within the preview’s watch range of stabilizing near 8% down or worsening beyond 12% down.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $12 million, well above the $10.71 million consensus and the preview’s $10.4–$10.6 million estimate. The roughly 12% beat came alongside about 30% Ameluz unit-volume growth and a Q4 2025 price increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net product revenue grew 33% year-over-year to $12 million, driven by ~30% growth in Ameluz unit volume plus a Q4 2025 price increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 consensus” revenue “$10.71M”; “My estimate: Revenue $10.4–10.6M (+16–18%).”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in near breakeven at a $0.2 million loss, far better than the preview’s expected $3.0–$3.6 million loss. The improvement exceeded even the preview’s bull case of a $2.0 million loss or better.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA reached negative $0.2 million (near breakeven).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: … adj. EBITDA $(3.0)–$(3.6)M”; bull scenario: “$(2.0)M or better.”

surprises.description: GAAP results were substantially better than the preview’s estimate: EPS was a $0.05 loss versus an estimated $0.34–$0.38 loss, and the net loss was $0.6 million versus $5.3 million a year earlier. The preview’s stale consensus was a $0.07 loss, so the beat against that figure was smaller.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $0.6 million ($0.05 per share) in Q2 2026 versus a net loss of $5.3 million ($0.57 per share) in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: … GAAP EPS $(0.34)–$(0.38)”; consensus GAAP EPS “$(0.07)” (noted as stale).

surprises.description: Cash was $4.7 million, below the preview’s expected $5.5–$6.5 million base-case range and below the roughly $5 million watch level. The going-concern qualification remained, as expected, but the lower cash balance was worse than the preview’s base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents fell to $4.7 million as of June 30, 2026 … prompting a going-concern qualification.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base case: “cash ~$5.5–6.5M, going concern retained”; key issue: “Cash below ~$5M would likely pull forward a capital raise.”

surprises.description: An ITC exclusion order unexpectedly bars the current Rodolet XL lamp and restricts Ameluz sales for use with it, affecting 243 of 801 installed lamps. Management says this should shift order timing rather than reduce total demand; a modified lamp has FDA clearance, but customs approval is still pending and remediation is estimated at about $500,000.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An ITC exclusion order effective July 7 bars import and sale of the current Rodolet XL lamp and restricts Ameluz sales for use with it, affecting 243 of the 801 installed lamps”; the order is expected “to shift order timing rather than reduce total demand”; remediation is “~$500,000” with “customs/border approval still pending.”

surprises.description: Management maintained full-year 2026 revenue goals despite the new ITC restriction. The preview said the company had declined to give formal FY guidance, so this was a reaffirmation not anticipated there, although no goal amount is provided in the call facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management maintains full-year 2026 revenue goals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The company has declined to give formal guidance all year”; preview also cited FY2026 revenue consensus of “$45.65M–$47.69M.”

in_line: Gross margin was approximately 80%, in line with the preview’s expectation that it should hold near 80%.
The going-concern qualification remained, as the preview expected.
The sBCC sNDA was accepted and has a September 28, 2026 PDUFA date, consistent with the preview’s focus on that date.
The planned AK extremities/neck/trunk sNDA filing remains on track for Q3 2026, consistent with the preview’s expectation.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $17.8 million, about 19% above the $14.99 million consensus, rather than near the preview’s roughly $15.0–$15.2 million base case. The call attributed $2.1 million to unregulated ICFA revenue recognized when GW Hassayampa’s first wastewater plant entered service, a contributor the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue rose 24.8% year-over-year to $17.8 million,” partly driven by “$2.1 million of unregulated ICFA revenue recognized when GW Hassayampa's first wastewater plant went into service.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 2026 Consensus | $14.99M”; the preview also said “Revenue above $15.2M would be the most likely positive surprise.”

surprises.description: Q2 diluted EPS of $0.10 substantially exceeded the $0.03 consensus, which implied a decline from the prior-year quarter. The call also reported first-half EPS of $0.08, already equal to the preview’s FY2026 consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income rose to $2.7 million ($0.10 per diluted share) from $1.6 million ($0.06) in Q2 2025,” while “year-to-date EPS was flat at $0.08 versus prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP) | Q2 2026 Consensus | $0.030”; the preview listed “FY2026 EPS | $0.08.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $7.9 million, above the preview’s estimated $7.0–$7.2 million and even its approximately $7.5 million bull-case level. The increase was materially stronger than the preview’s modeled 2–4% year-over-year growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 15% to $7.9 million in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Not found (model ~$7.0–7.2M)”; the bull scenario was “~$7.5M.”

surprises.description: The Santa Cruz rate case contemplated a smaller annual revenue increase than the preview’s approximately $2.3 million expectation: about $1.9 million, a reduction of roughly $0.4 million. The November 1 effective date remains contemplated, but final Commission approval is still pending.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The GW Santa Cruz rate case settlement contemplates net increased revenues of approximately $1.9 million effective November 1, 2026, pending final Commission approval later this year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The GW-Santa Cruz settlement (about $2.3M annual revenue increase) is effective Nov 1, 2026.”

surprises.description: GW Palo Verde’s rate recovery was pushed out, with new rates now not expected until 2028, delaying recovery of a major wastewater investment. The preview did not flag this specific recovery delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GW Palo Verde's rate recovery, including the recommissioned Southwest reclamation plant, was delayed with new rates now not expected until 2028, deferring recovery of that major wastewater investment.”

surprises.description: The preview watched for depreciation and amortization to plateau near $4.3–$4.4 million per quarter, but the call reported a $1.1 million Q2 increase in depreciation, amortization and accretion that pressured net income. The call does not provide the Q2 absolute amount or a sequential comparison, so the size of the gap from the anticipated plateau is not fully quantifiable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Depreciation, amortization and accretion increased $1.1 million in Q2 (and $2 million year-to-date), pressuring net income due to Arizona's historical test-year regulatory lag on 2025 capital investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether D&A plateaus near $4.3–4.4M per quarter.”

surprises.description: Organic growth accelerated to 3.2% over the last three months, a level management said had not been seen in several years. The preview highlighted organic growth as a key watch item and cited 1.9% annualized growth in Q1, but did not anticipate this acceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management indicated organic growth accelerated to 3.2% over the last three months, a level not seen in several years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic growth and building permits matter more than the total”; the preview cited Q1 “Organic connection growth [of] 1.9% annualized.”

surprises.description: Phoenix-area building permits fell only 4.7% year over year, much less than the preview’s concern about a second straight double-digit decline. This was a less negative signal for the Phoenix growth outlook than the preview’s stated risk case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Phoenix MSA [single-family] building permits declining 4.7% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A second straight double-digit permit decline would challenge the Phoenix growth thesis”; the preview also referred to “about 19% permit declines.”

in_line: Total active service connections were 69,429, within the preview’s expected range of about 69.3–69.6 thousand.
The Santa Cruz rate increase remains contemplated for November 1, 2026, matching the preview’s expected effective date, although the contemplated increase is smaller.

surprises.description: Aethlon reported operating expenses of about $1.6 million, below the preview’s $1.70–$2.10 million range and roughly $250,000 below its $1.85 million estimate. The lower spending was attributed to reduced professional fees, G&A, and preclinical costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated operating expenses fell 11.9% to approximately $1.6 million,” driven by “lower professional fees and reduced G&A and preclinical costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Our own estimate (not company guidance): Total opex about $1.85M (range $1.70–2.10M).”

surprises.description: The preview noted that Cohort 2 replicated Cohort 1’s biomarker direction, but the call described signals that were more consistent across participants and lasted longer—up to eight weeks, versus two to three weeks in Cohort 1. That is a stronger and more durable biomarker result than the preview had indicated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cohort 2 (two treatments) showed biomarker signals that were more consistent across participants and persisted longer—up to the 8-week mark—compared with cohort 1 (single treatment), which showed changes in only 2 of 3 participants lasting 2-3 weeks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Jul 13, 2026: Cohort 2 replicated Cohort 1 biomarker direction.”

surprises.description: The preview left Cohort 3 enrollment and timing as open questions; the call reported that the first participant had been treated and only two more participants were needed to complete the trial. Management also targeted completion of treatments and the eight-week follow-up by the end of 2026 or early 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Australian oncology trial has enrolled and treated the first participant of its third and final cohort, with only 2 additional participants needed to complete the trial.” Management aims to finish treatments and the “8-week follow-up measurement period by the end of calendar 2026 or early 2027.”
