surprises.description: KULR reported Q2 revenue of $2.1 million, far below the preview’s $5.2–6.0 million base case and even below its $4.8 million bear-case threshold. The preview also cited a third-party consensus estimate of about $8.5–9.0 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $2.1 million,” down significantly from both the prior year and Q1.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario revenue: “$5.2–6.0M”; “Bear” scenario: “Under $4.8M.” The preview also listed total-revenue consensus of “~$8.5–9.0M.”

surprises.description: Instead of the gross margin of at least 25% flagged as the key test, KULR produced a gross loss in Q2. That is a substantial deterioration from the preview’s 24–29% base-case margin range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The quarter produced a gross loss, missing management's expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for attention to “gross margin at or above 25%,” gave a “Base” scenario of “24–29%,” and said the bear case was “Under 20%.”

surprises.description: The preview expected a roughly $9–11 million noncash Bitcoin charge for Q2, while KULR reported about $31.4 million of mark-to-market losses on digital assets for the first half. The reported figure covers a different period, so it does not establish the Q2 charge by itself, but the first-half amount was much larger than the preview’s anticipated charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: KULR reported an approximately “$51 million net loss in the first half,” including “about $31.4 million” of noncash mark-to-market loss on digital asset holdings.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected “a non-cash charge of roughly $9–11M” from the Bitcoin decline.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated a sale of about 333 Bitcoin to repay the Coinbase facility and expected KULR to retain roughly 724–760 Bitcoin afterward. Instead, the Board authorized management to sell any and all remaining Bitcoin, signaling a full exit from the crypto treasury.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Board “authorized management to sell any and all remaining Bitcoin holdings,” signaling “a full divestment of the crypto treasury to focus on the operating business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the July sale of “about 333 BTC to retire the $20M Coinbase Credit facility” and estimated “Holdings afterward” at “about 724 to 760 BTC.”

surprises.description: KULR said supply-chain bottlenecks and long lead times delayed planned Q2 battery shipments, with recovery pushed into the second half. The preview highlighted the production ramp and Q3 start but did not anticipate these shipment delays.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New program supply chain bottlenecks and long lead times delayed planned Q2 battery shipments,” which management expects to recover “in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said new lines were installed in Q2, with production expected to start in Q3 at 10,000 packs per month.

surprises.description: KULR ended with approximately $60 million on its balance sheet and no debt, a stronger liquidity position than the preview’s cited $19 million cash figure from May 13. The preview had flagged June 30 cash and post-repayment liquidity as open questions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended with approximately $60 million on its balance sheet and no debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Cash was $19.0M at May 13” and listed “Cash at June 30 and pro-forma liquidity after the Coinbase facility was retired” as a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: Beyond the revenue and production outlook discussed in the preview, KULR disclosed a defense drone battery opportunity exceeding $5 million. This was a new commercial opportunity not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: KULR “secured a defense drone battery opportunity exceeding $5 million.”

in_line: KULR sold about 333 Bitcoin and repaid the $20 million Coinbase credit facility, as the preview had anticipated.

The new facility’s expected Q3 operational start is consistent with the preview’s expectation that production would start in Q3; the reported facts do not confirm the preview’s 10,000-packs-per-month figure.

surprises.description: Management now expects 2026 revenue to be slightly below 2025 if the large customer completes its planned volume reduction, a sharp reversal from the preview’s expectation of 8.3% annual growth and its reference to expected back-half acceleration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Assuming the large customer completes its planned volume reduction, management expects total 2026 revenue to be slightly lower than 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 revenue consensus: “$24.55M (+8.3% y/y)”; the preview also said management “has pointed to back-half acceleration.”

surprises.description: A customer responsible for about 29% of first-half revenue is considering a multi-vendor IDV approach, creating substantial revenue risk that the preview did not flag. The immediate picture is less severe than the customer’s warnings: management said reductions so far were far smaller than the “doomsday scenario,” and the customer recently placed a new order and plans to migrate to the newest API.
surprises.fact_evidence: The customer “represent[s] approximately 29% of first-half revenue” and “has begun evaluating a multi-vendor IDV approach”; actual reduction so far was “far less severe than the ‘doomsday scenario,’” and it “recently signed a new purchase order” and intends to migrate to the newest API.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $5.9 million, above the $5.67 million consensus and the preview’s $5.55–$5.60 million base scenario, despite management’s prior flattish-quarter steer. It was up 7% year over year, a solid beat against those expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $5.9 million, up 7% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus: “$5.67M”; preview base scenario: “$5.55–5.60M,” with management having steered to a “flattish” Q2.

surprises.description: Excluding the large concentrated customer, the rest of the customer base grew about 19% in the first half across all verticals. The preview expected banking to carry growth but did not anticipate this degree of growth across the broader base.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding the large concentrated customer, the rest of the customer base grew approximately 19% year-over-year in the first half across all verticals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Banking needs to keep carrying growth while retail declines,” but gave no expectation for growth across the customer base excluding the large customer.

surprises.description: A previously dormant large social media customer has resumed activity, with more than 99% of its data now processable. The company still assumes zero revenue from this customer in its current forecast, so the potential contribution is not included in the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: The customer “has resumed activity with over 99% of data now processable,” but the company “includes zero revenue from them in its current forecast.”

surprises.description: Title-related mortgage loan originations rose 14% year over year, an encouraging operating detail not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Title-related mortgage loan originations rose 14% year-over-year.”

in_line: Retail remained weak but was down only about 2% year over year, consistent with the preview’s concern about retail declines.
Banking and lending continued to be an important growth area, consistent with the preview’s expectation that banking would carry growth.

surprises.description: Proteus was expected to launch at the end of 2026, but management pushed the launch to Q2 2027 to add an integrated instrument design cycle before production. This is a substantial delay against the preview’s base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Delayed its Proteus platform launch from end of 2026 to Q2 2027,” adding “an additional integrated instrument design cycle to de-risk manufacturing before production.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said announcing 18 amino acids would “de-risk the end-2026 launch”; its bear scenario flagged a launch slip into “1H27.”

surprises.description: The early access program, which the preview said was expected in summer 2026, has not begun and is now expected in early 2027. This pushes customer access back along with the launch delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Proteus early access program has not yet begun and is now expected to shift to early 2027,” contingent on completing the additional design cycle by year-end 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed early-access sites live versus the “summer 2026” commitment as a key catalyst and said named sites and a site count would confirm the thesis.

surprises.description: Despite the later launch, the planned launch detection count improved beyond the preview’s 17–18 amino-acid expectation: management now expects 19 or 20 at launch and says all 20 will be demonstrated in 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects Proteus to launch detecting “either 19 or 20 amino acids,” up from 18 previously planned, with “all 20 to be demonstrated in 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “17–18 amino acids,” and said the launch requires 18 of 20.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was above the roughly $0.30 million consensus, although it remained below the year-ago level. The beat was modest relative to the consensus figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 revenue was “$344,000” versus “$591,000 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus was “~$0.30M (TradingView, $302K).”

surprises.description: After the announced cost reductions, management extended the cash runway to Q4 2028, beyond the preview’s expectation of runway into Q2 2028.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company said its “$169.9 million in cash and investments” would fund operations “into Q4 2028 after the cost-cutting actions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 guidance section stated “runway into Q2 2028”; the preview also said reaffirming runway into Q2 2028 mattered most.

surprises.description: The company announced a substantial workforce reduction and associated savings, neither of which the preview anticipated. The savings improve the cost outlook, while the reduction itself signals a significant pullback.
surprises.fact_evidence: A reduction in force of “approximately 20% of total headcount” is expected to generate “roughly $12 million in annualized operating expense savings” starting in the second half of Q4 2026.

surprises.description: The preview looked for commercial conversion evidence such as evaluation commitments, while management reported a sizable but softer funnel: institutions with stated interest and companies identified as potential users, rather than early-access placements or commitments.
surprises.fact_evidence: Quantum-Si had “qualified more than 250 unique institutions with stated interest in Proteus” and identified “over 150 biotech and pharma companies developing AAV gene therapies as a potential application market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said roadshow conversion into “evaluation commitments” was a commercial proof point to watch and that named early-access sites would confirm the thesis.

in_line: Full-year 2026 guidance was reiterated at approximately $1 million in revenue, adjusted operating expenses of $98 million or less, and total cash usage of $93 million or less, matching the preview’s stated guidance.
The $169.9 million cash-and-investments balance was broadly in line with the preview’s expected $167–169 million.

surprises.description: CODX’s net loss narrowed to $6.3 million, and EPS was -$1.46 versus the preview’s -$3.06 consensus estimate. That was better than the preview’s expectation that dollar losses would be flat to worse, with lower operating expenses contributing to the improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $6.3 million ($1.46 per share) from $7.7 million ($7 per share) a year earlier, driven mainly by lower operating expenses”; “Total operating expenses fell to $6.3 million from $8.2 million year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A headline EPS beat could therefore be a share-count artifact. Net loss in dollars is the better comparison, and it looks flat to worse.” The preview also noted: “If R&D does not step down from $5.93M, the burn picture worsens.”

surprises.description: The preview cited an expectation of TB commercialization in India by the end of Q3, but management described additional Indian and WHO TB regulatory submissions planned for later this year. The call facts therefore point to regulatory steps still ahead rather than confirming that the expected Q3 commercialization timing is on track.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans additional TB regulatory submissions later this year, including India's CDSCO and the WHO's Expert Review Panel for Diagnostics (ERPD).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 call: TB commercialization in India by end of Q3'26.”

surprises.description: The preview already said the flu, RSV and flu assay’s 510(k) had been submitted, but it did not flag a simultaneous CLIA waiver application. The call also gave substantial validation details supporting the submission.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company submitted a dual 510(k) and CLIA waiver application to the FDA”; it was backed by “27 analytical validation studies with over 10,000 PCR test runs” and a clinical study of “more than 1,400 symptomatic patients across 9 U.S. sites.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Clinical enrollment is complete and the 510(k) was submitted Aug 6.”

surprises.description: NGO partners are funding much of the TB validation work for the WHO assessment, reducing CODX’s cash burden for that program. The preview anticipated generic efforts to seek funding, but did not mention this specific partner support.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Certain TB validation study costs for the ERPD assessment are largely being funded by NGO partners, reducing the company's cash burden for that program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bull case requires a named non-dilutive source with a dollar figure”; the preview otherwise described “exploring equity, debt, and partnerships” as already discounted.

surprises.description: The call reported a completed direct-from-plasma Ebola proof-of-concept assay and fulfillment of a request for 200 Bundibugyo tests. The preview did not anticipate these platform-expansion developments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed its first blood-based (direct-from-plasma) Ebola proof-of-concept assay and fulfilled an Indian government-related request for 200 Bundibugyo tests.”

in_line: Revenue was $166,000 versus preview consensus of about $169,830, broadly in line with the estimate.
Cash of $3.6 million was at the top of the preview’s modeled $2.4–3.6 million range.
The preview already reported that the flu/RSV 510(k) had been submitted, so that filing itself was not unexpected.
Management’s continued pursuit of equity, debt, strategic transactions, partnerships and grants was consistent with the preview’s expectation that financing remained unresolved.

surprises.description: FitLife’s gross margin was 37.0%, below the preview’s roughly 38% estimate. Irwin’s margin was 32.8%, down from 34.0% in Q1 despite the preview noting management’s target of 300–400 basis points of Irwin margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin fell to 37.0% from 42.8% a year earlier”; Irwin’s gross margin was 32.8%, versus 34.0% in Q1 per the preview’s prior-quarter facts.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 gross margin: ~38% (model estimate)” and “Management targets 300–400bps of Irwin margin improvement from supply-chain work.”

surprises.description: Legacy FitLife revenue declined 23% year over year, slightly worse than the 22% decline in Q1 rather than moderating. Its revenue was roughly flat sequentially, however, indicating some stabilization within the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Legacy FitLife revenue declined 23% year-over-year to $12.4 million” and “was roughly flat sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Legacy FitLife revenue fell 22% in Q1. Watch whether the drop moderates.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $3.7 million, just above the preview’s $3.4–$3.6 million model estimate. The beat was modest and also at the top of the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 10% to $3.7 million year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 adj. EBITDA: ~$3.4–3.6M (model estimate)”; the base case projected “$3.4–3.7M.”

surprises.description: Management said it had approved three-year shelf-life formulas for 85% of Irwin’s products, targeting a reduction in the roughly $2 million of inventory written off annually. The preview discussed stock-outs but did not anticipate this specific product-shelf-life initiative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management has approved 3-year shelf-life formulas for 85% of Irwin's products, targeting a reduction in the roughly $2 million of inventory written off annually.”

surprises.description: The company reported sequential SG&A reductions and plans further cuts, a cost-control development not flagged in the preview. The reported decline amounted to about $0.8 million in annualized savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A fell 3.8% sequentially to $4.8 million, equivalent to roughly $0.8 million annualized savings, with further reductions planned for the rest of the year.”

surprises.description: Management reported that Amazon subscribers had recovered to about 94,000 after bottoming above 90,000 in mid-April. The preview focused on Amazon sales run rate and did not flag subscriber counts or this recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Amazon subscriber count bottomed above 90,000 in mid-April and has since recovered to approximately 94,000.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of $26.5 million was close to the $26.0 million consensus estimate and at the top of the preview’s $25.5–$26.5 million base case.
Lost revenue from out-of-stock situations fell by over 50% sequentially, consistent with the preview’s expectation that an inventory fix would provide some Q2 tailwind.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $33.7 million, above the preview’s $31.33–$31.95 million consensus range and the base scenario’s $30–$33 million range, though just below the bull scenario’s $34 million threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 revenue was $33.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $31.95M”; “Total revenue (alt) | $31.33M”; base scenario: “Total rev | $30–33M”; bull scenario: “Total rev | $34M+.”

surprises.description: Commercial adoption was stronger than the preview’s general expectation that demand would hold: U.S. NEPI market share doubled year over year, while unique prescribers more than tripled. Share gains were especially pronounced in targeted areas, reaching 8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total U.S. NEPI market share reaching 5%, doubling from 2.5% in the prior-year quarter”; “Within the field sales targeted universe, NEPI market share rose to 8% from 4% a year ago”; “Unique NEPI prescribers exceeded 16,000 in Q2, representing more than a three-fold increase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Bull scenario: “Demand holds.”

surprises.description: The CSU Phase 2b interim readout slipped from the preview’s expected Q4 2026 timing to Q1 2027, because patients need more time to log three separate flare episodes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The CSU Phase 2b interim data readout has been delayed from end of 2026 to Q1 2027 due to the time required for patients to log three separate flare episodes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “CSU Phase 2b interim expected Q4 2026.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a sizable planned reduction in cash-based spending: second-half cash-based SG&A and R&D are guided to $100–$110 million, with cash-based SG&A down more than 40% from the first half and the trend expected to continue through 2027. The preview anticipated cost discipline but did not specify a reduction of this scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guided second-half 2026 cash-based SG&A and R&D expenses to $100-110 million, driven by a more than 40% reduction in cash-based SG&A from the first half, with the trend expected to continue through 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base scenario: “cost discipline”; key issue: “Scope of restructuring.”

surprises.description: Management described a shift away from broad direct-to-consumer TV advertising toward lower-cost, targeted provider-focused channels, a specific strategic change not anticipated in the preview’s discussion of the new CEO’s priorities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is pivoting away from broad direct-to-consumer TV advertising toward lower-cost, targeted provider-focused channels like social media and search to improve SG&A efficiency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Casale's ‘updated strategic priorities.’ Scope of restructuring, sales-force sizing (148 reps), and pipeline prioritization.”

in_line: Management continued to project cash flow break-even by the end of 2027, consistent with the preview’s focus on the 2027 breakeven claim; the reported $143.8 million of cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments was also broadly consistent with the preview’s stated financing-risk context.

surprises.description: The preview expected revenue of $43.5–45.0 million and a year-over-year decline of 12%–15%; PETS reported $41 million, down 19.9%. The decline was worse than the preview’s bear-case trigger of a decline worse than 18%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 2027 net sales declined 19.9% year-over-year to $41 million from $51.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base estimate: $43.5–45.0M (-12% to -15% YoY)” and “A decline worse than -18% would undercut it.”

surprises.description: The preview expected gross margin of 30%–31%, but PETS reported 27.6%, below even the preview’s bear-case marker of below 28%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 27.6% from 28.1% year-over-year, mainly due to lower manufacturer rebates partially offset by lower freight costs per order.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin: … My base estimate: 30–31%” and “GM below 28%” in the bear scenario.

surprises.description: The preview’s base EPS estimate was a loss of $0.14–$0.17 per share, but PETS reported a loss of $0.28. The net loss narrowed sharply from a year ago, largely because last year’s impairment charge did not recur, but the reported loss per share was still materially worse than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed sharply to $6.1 million ($0.28 per diluted share) from $34.2 million ($1.65 per diluted share) a year ago, largely due to the absence of last year's goodwill and trade name impairment charge.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS … My base estimate: -$0.14 to -$0.17.”

surprises.description: The preview expected quarter-end cash of $16–18 million, but PETS ended with $13.1 million, below the preview’s bear-case marker of less than $15 million. The company did have no debt.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $13.1 million in cash and no debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … cash $16–18M” and “cash below $15M” in the bear scenario.

surprises.description: The preview estimated an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2–3 million, while PETS reported a $3.4 million loss. The loss also widened from the prior-year period.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss widened to $3.4 million from a $2.7 million loss in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA … My base estimate: -$2M to -$3M.”

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate the reported customer acquisition results: PETS acquired approximately 70,000 new customers while lowering customer acquisition cost by 15% to $60. That indicates better acquisition efficiency than the reported prior-year comparison.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company acquired approximately 70,000 new customers in Q1 while reducing customer acquisition cost 15% to $60 from $71 a year earlier.”

surprises.description: The preview did not forecast the increase in recurring sales mix; autoship and membership revenue reached 61.5% of total gross sales, versus 57.6% a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring net sales, including autoship and membership revenue, grew to 61.5% of total gross sales from 57.6% a year ago.”

surprises.description: The preview did not forecast the scale of the expense reductions: advertising fell 30.2% and G&A fell 13.5%. The lower spending is favorable, although adjusted EBITDA loss still widened.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advertising expenses fell 30.2% to $4.2 million and G&A expenses fell 13.5% to $11.2 million, reflecting elimination of unproductive media and lower professional fees.”

in_line: The Delray Beach sale-leaseback was still described as a $37 million transaction expected to close within roughly 120 days, consistent with the preview’s stated terms and timing.
The Rural King co-branded pharmacy launched in July, as the preview said it had; the preview also expected its Q1 revenue impact to be negligible.
The $3-per-share Silver Cape proposal was already disclosed in the preview. The call reported no determination and no assured transaction, rather than a change in the board’s stance.

surprises.description: MDB is backing away from its previously announced goal of launching three to five companies annually and returning to a selective “rifle-shot” approach, citing unfavorable microcap conditions. This is a retreat from the earlier growth plan, which the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Scaling back its previously announced plan to launch three to five new companies per year, reverting to a selective ‘rifle-shot’ approach due to unfavorable microcap market conditions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The call says the company had previously announced a plan to launch “three to five new companies per year.”

surprises.description: The Public Ventures self-clearing platform has advanced beyond the preview’s base case of timelines being repeated without progress: MDB has LOIs and is in discussions with four to five potential partners or buyers. However, no deal is signed, and management is targeting a close only within the next quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: MDB is in “active discussions with four to five parties,” has “received letters of intent,” and is “aiming to close a deal within the next quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “signed partnership for the self-clearing platform” would be the most useful surprise; its base case assumed spin-out timelines would be “repeated but not advanced.”

surprises.description: Paulex’s expected offering has moved later than the preview’s September 2026 target: management now expects a fourth-quarter offering, although the IPO registration statement is close to filing. The preview also anticipated a September IPO date as a key confirmation.
surprises.fact_evidence: Paulex is “close to filing its IPO registration statement” with an “expected fourth-quarter offering”; key clinical readouts are anticipated in early 2027.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Paulex’s IPO as “targeted for September 2026” and asked whether management would confirm that timing and the S-1 status.

surprises.description: PatentVest is being reframed as an AI-enabled Alternative Business Structure patent law firm in Arizona and is planned to spin out as an externally funded independent entity, so MDB would no longer bear its development costs. The preview flagged the delayed spin-out but did not describe this positioning or funding structure; management’s $750 million comparable is illustrative, not a PatentVest valuation or completed financing.
surprises.fact_evidence: PatentVest “will be spun out as an independent, externally funded entity so MDB no longer bears its development costs”; management cited an AI-enabled immigration law firm funded at a “$750 million pre-money valuation” as a comparable.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said PatentVest’s spin-out timeline “has slipped” and its base case expected timelines to be “repeated but not advanced.”

surprises.description: eXoZymes raised only about $6 million in a financing, well short of its target. The preview modeled an offering of about $5.95 million, but did not flag that the raise had missed a larger target; the shortfall is a negative update about MDB’s portfolio company.
surprises.fact_evidence: eXoZymes “recently completed a financing that raised only around $6 million, well short of its target.”

surprises.description: eXoZymes is nearing a strategic contract-manufacturing partnership, a potential commercial development not raised in the preview. It remains a prospective partnership rather than a completed agreement.
surprises.fact_evidence: eXoZymes is “nearing a strategic contract manufacturing partnership.”

in_line: Management’s approximately $5–6 million annual operating-expense target is broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of fixed OpEx falling to about $6 million after the PatentVest spin-out, although the call makes achievement dependent on the spin-out and partnering off the clearing platform.

The limited near-term transaction outlook is consistent with the preview’s base case of a thin fee quarter: MDB completed two transactions in the first half and expects up to two more in the second half.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $4.3 million, well below both the preview’s roughly $5.2 million company guide and $4.85 million consensus. The result missed the company guide by about 17%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $4.3 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Company guidance ... ~$5.2M” and “Consensus ... $4.85M”

surprises.description: Despite the Q2 shortfall, management forecast Q3 revenue of $5.0–$5.4 million, or roughly 16–26% sequential growth. The preview highlighted the need for another quarter of sequential growth but gave no comparable Q3 revenue range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company guided Q3 2026 revenue to $5.0-$5.4 million, implying sequential growth of roughly 16-26% driven by new customer launches and a Tier 1 contract extension.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side needs a second consecutive sequential growth quarter and a path to non-GAAP breakeven.”

surprises.description: June 30 cash was $2.8 million, above the preview’s roughly $2.0 million reference point and its $2.5 million bull-case threshold, easing the immediate liquidity concern relative to expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company held only $2.8 million in cash and cash equivalents as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash vs. about $2.0M” and the bull scenario specified “Cash at 6/30 >$2.5M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected a newly signed carrier contract to be delivered by the end of Q2; management instead described two new customer deployments as expected to launch by month-end, after Q2 had ended. Both have executed contracts, and the call did not establish whether either deployment was the carrier launch anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects to launch two new customers by month-end—one a SafePath OS device deployment and one a SafePath Connect deployment in Europe—both with fully executed contracts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The guided driver is one new carrier contract signed in Q1, with delivery expected by end of Q2.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a significant multi-year extension with an existing Tier 1 customer that was close to signing and expected to drive revenue growth beginning in Q3. The preview did not identify this extension as an anticipated growth driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A significant multi-year contract extension with an existing Tier 1 customer is within days of signing and is expected to generate revenue growth beginning in Q3 2026.”

surprises.description: Management plans to increase Q3 non-GAAP operating expenses by up to 6% sequentially to add engineering headcount. That is a spending ramp against the preview’s focus on a path to non-GAAP breakeven, although it is intended to support the pipeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating expenses fell 26% year-over-year to $4.4 million in Q2 2026, but management guided to a sequential increase of up to 6% in Q3 to add engineering headcount to support the pipeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side needs ... a path to non-GAAP breakeven.”

surprises.description: Management highlighted new SafePath SDK/API offerings for carrier super apps, including one contract near signing and further opportunities in a growing senior-focused pipeline. The preview did not flag this potential high-margin growth avenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New SafePath SDK/API offerings targeting carrier 'super apps' reaching tens of millions of subscribers are described as a high-margin future growth driver, with one contract near signing and additional opportunities including a growing senior-focused pipeline.”

in_line: Q2 gross margin was 81.3%, within the previewed 81%–83% company guidance.
GAAP loss per share was $0.52, close to the preview’s split-adjusted consensus estimate of a $0.50 loss.
The June warrant inducement raised $1.6 million, in line with the preview’s description of the transaction as having raised about $1.6 million.

surprises.description: Revenue was $2.3 million, far below the preview’s $4.6–5.0 million consensus range and below Q1’s $3.4 million despite the expectation of sequential improvement. The company sold 11 units, versus the preview’s 16–18 units considered healthy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue dropped approximately 68% to $2.3 million” and the company sold “11 units versus 19 units a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $4.60M”; alternative consensus “$5.03M.” The preview also said “Q2 above Q1” was the minimum and “roughly 16–18 would be healthy.”

surprises.description: The reported loss per share was much worse than expected: $0.53 versus the preview’s $0.11–$0.13 loss range. A $5.7 million valuation allowance against deferred tax assets drove most of the reported net loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss of $8.7 million ($0.53 per share)” versus a “$1 million loss ($0.06 per share)” a year earlier, driven largely by “a $5.7 million valuation allowance against net deferred tax assets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat consensus as a band: roughly $4.6–5.0M revenue and −$0.11 to −$0.13 EPS.”

surprises.description: Despite the weak Q2 unit count, management guided to more than 20 units in each of Q3 and Q4—stronger than the preview’s 16–18 units described as healthy and its expectation of only modest improvement in the base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management reaffirmed sequential unit growth, guiding to “20-plus units in each of Q3 and Q4” following 14 units in Q1 and 11 in Q2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Roughly 16–18 would be healthy”; the base case expected “sequential improvement” to be modest.

surprises.description: Eight units missed Q2 recognition because a third-party bank had not completed financing approval by quarter-end, but they have since been approved and sold and are expected to be recognized in Q3. That creates a Q3 catch-up opportunity not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: A bank’s failure to complete approval before June 30 “prevented recognition of 8 units in Q2”; the units “have since been approved, sold, and will be recognized in Q3” at an expected average selling price of about $250,000 each.

surprises.description: Management cited a proposed 26% increase in Level 1 radiation hospital reimbursement as support for SRT economics, a potential tailwind the preview did not discuss. The increase is proposed, so the facts do not establish that it has taken effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A proposed 26% increase in Level 1 radiation hospital reimbursement supports SRT economics.”

surprises.description: Management said it is expanding higher-margin CensusLink software subscriptions to nearly all new customers and existing installed systems, adding a recurring-revenue initiative not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is “expanding higher-margin recurring CensusLink software subscriptions to nearly all new customers and existing installed systems.”

in_line: Gross margin was 34.8%, close to the preview’s roughly 35% consensus implication.
Cash declined to $15.2 million, broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of a further burn leaving cash near $15 million, and remained above the preview’s $14 million level of concern.

The former largest customer was not expected to resume purchases in the preview’s base expectations: it said management had excluded SkinCure Oncology from its model and treated any reorder as upside.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue came in at $12.7 million, slightly above Rekor’s $12.6 million pre-announcement but below the preview’s cited $13.32 million consensus. The release therefore confirmed the company’s preliminary figure but did not meet the higher published consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose 2% year-over-year to $12.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company (Q2, pre-announced 7/15/26) ~$12.6M”; “Consensus (varies by source) $13.32M (Benzinga, pre-print)”; the preview cautioned that consensus “may be stale.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 56%, one percentage point above the roughly 55% level previewed from the pre-announcement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded to 56% in Q2 2026 from 50% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. gross margin ~55%.”

surprises.description: The adjusted EBITDA loss was about $1.2 million, modestly narrower than the roughly $1.3 million loss in the preview’s operative preliminary figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss narrowed 79% year-over-year to approximately $1.2 million, driven mainly by lower payroll costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~($1.3M) loss.”

surprises.description: Recurring revenue grew substantially faster than total revenue, with the reported figures showing a stronger recurring-revenue mix than the preview quantified. This adds a favorable revenue-quality detail beyond the preview’s expectation that the quarter’s revenue would not be driven by a large one-time software deal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring revenue grew 14% in the quarter to $6.7 million and 21% in the first half to $13.3 million, outpacing total revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The CFO said the sequential jump was not driven by a large one-time software deal. Check whether the ~$12.6M holds after final close.”

surprises.description: Management added a new source of expected savings beyond the previously cited workforce-related reductions: several million dollars of annualized savings from non-workforce efficiencies, with execution in Q3 and a noticeable effect in Q4 and 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects several million dollars of additional annualized cost savings from non-workforce efficiencies, to be executed in Q3 with noticeable impact in Q4 2026 and into 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~$7.5M of annualized opex reduction from a 20% headcount cut and overseas engineering consolidation.”

surprises.description: The call reported a sharp improvement in cash consumption, a metric the preview had not quantified: quarterly operating cash burn was $2.4 million, and first-half cash used from operations improved by $9.6 million, or 61%, year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating cash burn [was cut] to $2.4 million,” and “improved first-half cash used from operations by $9.6 million (61%).”

surprises.description: Q2 operating income included a $2.8 million non-cash lease-liability remeasurement gain. The preview did not anticipate this one-off benefit, so reported operating income was helped by an item that is not recurring cash earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 operating income was aided by a one-time, non-cash $2.8 million gain from the remeasurement of a lease liability tied to operational realignment.”

surprises.description: Rekor reported a product-commercialization step not covered in the preview: GoSecure video authentication launched in June, was extended to audio, and initial launch-partner commercial terms are targeted for completion in Q3. The product launch is progress, although partner terms remain unfinished.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Rekor launched GoSecure video authentication in June, extended it to audio, and aims to finalize initial launch partner commercial terms during Q3 2026.”

in_line: Period-end cash was slightly above $10 million, broadly matching the preview’s approximately $10 million expectation.
Management reiterated the target of adjusted EBITDA profitability in H2 2026, as expected; it did not specify a quarter or tighten the timing to Q3.
The prime revenue-sharing-notes refinancing remained pending, consistent with the preview’s base case that refinancing would still be in progress rather than signed.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $1.1 million, well below the preview’s $1.502 million consensus and even below its bear-case threshold of $1.2 million. The decline was driven by lower M400 sales and discontinued smart glasses products.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue declined 14% year-over-year to $1.1 million from $1.3 million, driven by lower M400 unit sales and discontinued smart glasses products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Q2 FY2026 Consensus | $1.502M”; the bear scenario was “Below $1.2M.”

surprises.description: The combined engineering-services and OEM-product line was only $0.2 million and fell 8%, far below the preview’s roughly $400,000 engineering-services level to watch. The reported fact combines engineering services and OEM sales, so it does not establish the engineering-services figure alone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Engineering services and OEM product sales dropped 8% to $0.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Below $400K would mean the defense wins are still announcements, not revenue”; the catalyst checklist also flagged engineering services against “about $400K consensus-implied level.”

surprises.description: Product sales slipped to $0.9 million from $1.0 million, rather than remaining flat as in Q1. The preview had flagged another product-sales decline as a bear-case risk, and that weakness contributed to the much larger-than-expected revenue miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Product sales fell to $0.9 million from $1.0 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1 product revenue as “flat at $1.042M” and listed “Product sales down again” as a bear-case driver.

surprises.description: The GAAP loss per share was $0.09, better than the preview’s $0.11 loss estimate. However, the net loss attributable to common shareholders stayed flat at $7.7 million, and the per-share improvement came from a larger share count rather than lower losses.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss attributable to common shareholders was flat at $7.7 million, though loss per share improved to $0.09 from $0.10 due to a larger share count.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP) | Q2 FY2026 Consensus | $(0.11)”; the preview noted that consensus “looks stale on share count.”

surprises.description: The gross loss widened from Q1’s $378,000 to $600,000, instead of moving toward the near-breakeven or positive gross result the preview identified as the strongest potential datapoint. It was still improved year over year, but the sequential trajectory disappointed the preview’s stated focus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Q2 2026 gross loss improved 15% to $0.6 million from a $0.8 million gross loss in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A near-breakeven or positive gross line would be the strongest datapoint in this print”; the preview cited Q1 gross loss of “$(378)K.”

surprises.description: Operating cash use rose to $6.6 million, above the preview’s $5–6 million quarterly-burn range and its bear-case trigger of burn above $6 million. Cash also fell from $20.2 million at the end of Q1 to $17.3 million at the end of Q2, rather than printing higher as the preview said could happen.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net cash used in operating activities rose to $6.6 million from $4.8 million a year earlier”; the company ended Q2 with “$17.3 million in cash” and “no debt outstanding.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to check “runway well into 2027” against “a $5–6M quarterly burn,” and noted “Cash could print higher despite the burn.”

surprises.description: Collins Aerospace’s drone waveguide display advanced from development into initial production, with more orders expected in the second half and 2027 described as a strong production year. The preview framed defense and waveguide wins as still needing evidence of monetization, so this was concrete production progress beyond that concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Collins Aerospace waveguide AR display program for drones has moved from development into initial production, with more production orders expected in the second half and 2027 seen as a strong production year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Above $600K would be the first real evidence the pivot is monetizing” and that below $400K would mean “the defense wins are still announcements, not revenue.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed new inbound interest in planar waveguides for optical interconnects in AI data centers, a potential application the preview did not identify. The update was interest rather than a reported order or revenue commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vuzix disclosed new inbound interest in its planar waveguides for optical interconnect in AI data centers.”

surprises.description: The Amazon relationship expanded to next-generation Ultralight Pro glasses for AI-driven data-center maintenance, a broader update than the preview’s focus on initial EVT-based shipments. The reported facts do not provide shipment volumes or a production timeline, leaving the preview’s key commercialization question unresolved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its Amazon relationship expanded to next-generation Ultralight Pro smart glasses for AI-driven data center maintenance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had indicated Q2 would see “initial EVT-based shipments” and identified whether management would give “a production timeline or unit figure” as the key question.

surprises.description: SoundThinking cut FY2026 revenue guidance to $99–100 million from $109–111 million, rather than reaffirming the range. It attributed about 70% of the reduction to timing pushouts into 2027 and 30% to slower sales growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “cut full-year 2026 revenue guidance from $109-111 million to $99-100 million,” with “about 70% attributed to timing/pushouts into 2027 and 30% to slower sales growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue: $109.0–$111.0M”; the preview says to watch whether management “reaffirms the $109–111M range.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $23.9 million, well below the $25.76 million consensus and the company's roughly $25.9 million H1 pacing target. The preview's base case anticipated an in-line quarter around $25.5–26.2 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell to $23.9 million” and missed the “$25.9 million half-year pacing target by about $2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue | $25.76M”; base scenario: “$25.5–26.2M.”

surprises.description: The company cut its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA margin outlook to 8–9%, far below the 16–18% guidance the preview expected to remain in place. Q2 adjusted EBITDA was also $1.2 million versus $3.4 million a year earlier, though it improved from roughly negative $100,000 in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA dropped to $1.2 million from $3.4 million in Q2 2025,” and “full-year adjusted EBITDA margin guidance was reduced to 8-9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 adj. EBITDA margin | 16–18%, reaffirmed”; the preview also says to watch performance “vs. the 16–18% guide.”

surprises.description: GAAP loss per share was $0.37, substantially worse than the preview's expected loss of about $0.18–$0.20 per share. The GAAP net loss also widened from $3.1 million to $4.8 million year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss widened to $4.8 million ($0.37 per diluted share) versus a $3.1 million loss ($0.24 per share) in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 2026 EPS (GAAP) | -$0.177”; the preview also cites an alternative estimate of “-$0.20.”

surprises.description: Management said ShotSpotter performance was deteriorating because both bookings and go-lives were weak, with lengthening sales cycles and internal sales execution underperformance. The preview noted ARPA funding wind-down and higher assumed attrition, but did not anticipate this explicit combination of weak execution and go-live performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “deteriorating ShotSpotter performance driven by both weak bookings and go-lives,” including “elongating sales cycles” and “admitted internal sales execution underperformance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says guidance assumes “higher attrition than historical, tied to budget pressure and the end of ARPA funds.”

surprises.description: The Puerto Rico ShotSpotter recapture was removed entirely from 2026 guidance, rather than remaining a possible H2 contributor. The preview identified the contract as embedded in the H2 ramp and said a slip into 2027 would undermine the guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Puerto Rico ShotSpotter contract recapture (originally ~$1.5 million) was removed entirely from 2026 guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says Puerto Rico was “embedded in the H2 ramp” and that “A slip into 2027 would undercut it.”

surprises.description: SafePointe deployment delays reduced expected revenue by about $2 million even though nearly 90 new lanes were booked in Q2. That contrasts with the preview's expectation for SafePointe revenue to grow from $3.6 million to $6.5 million or more.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SafePointe deployment delays reduced expected revenue by about $2 million despite nearly 90 new lanes booked in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue is expected to grow from $3.6M to $6.5M or more.”

surprises.description: The update put ARR entering 2027 at over $100 million, below the preview's roughly $110 million exit-2026 expectation. The stated increase from $95.4 million is positive, but it does not reach the preview's anticipated level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “reaffirming ARR growth from $95.4 million to over $100 million entering 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Exit-2026 ARR | ~$110M (from $95.4M entering 2026).”

surprises.description: Cash fell to $6.4 million from the $14.2 million reported at Q1, while $4 million remained drawn on the credit facility. The preview had highlighted the earlier cash balance and draw, but did not flag a further cash decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with only $6.4 million in cash, $4 million drawn on its credit facility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reports “Cash of $14.2M, $4M drawn on the revolver” for Q1.

surprises.description: Management disclosed that the Chicago ShotSpotter RFP decision could be delayed until February 2027 and excluded any renewed Chicago contract revenue from guidance. The preview did not flag this timing risk; management also cited a ballot referendum and pro-detection mayoral candidates as potential support for a later comeback.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Chicago ShotSpotter RFP decision could extend to February 2027, and guidance assumes no revenue contribution from any renewed Chicago contract,” while a “November ballot referendum and pro-detection mayoral candidates support a potential comeback.”

surprises.description: SoundThinking announced workforce and business optimization actions, including cutting about 28 positions, with approximately $4 million in annualized savings. The savings are favorable, but $900,000 of restructuring costs were recognized in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “cutting about 28 positions,” expected to deliver “approximately $4 million in annualized structural savings,” with “$900,000 in restructuring costs recognized in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “Any cost action or strategic review of SafePointe would be a potential catalyst.”

in_line: The company closed over $23 million in total contract value across multiyear renewals, consistent with the preview's note that announced Q2 renewals totaled more than $23 million.

The approximately $2.5 million annual recurring revenue Texas Crime Tracer statewide deal was won, consistent with the preview's expectation of a roughly $2.5 million state contract and its focus on whether the deal would be signed.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $1.3 million, about 16% below the preview’s $1.54 million consensus estimate. The 127% year-over-year growth and record second-quarter revenue did not prevent a meaningful miss against the expected level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $1.3 million, up 127% year-over-year, marking the highest second quarter revenue in the company's history.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Q2 consensus | $1.54M”; the preview also flagged “Revenue ≥$1.54M” as a catalyst-checklist item.

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin was 64%, below the preview’s roughly 68% expectation and under its stated 65% threshold for avoiding a reversal of the margin trend. This contrasted with the preview’s expectation of expansion toward 70%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin expanded to 64% from 43% a year ago”; gross margin was “66% versus 44%” for the first half.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~68% (est.)”; “Management guided to expansion past 70%. A drop below 65% would reverse the cleanest positive trend.”

surprises.description: The Q2 net loss was $4.1 million, versus the preview’s expected $2.9–3.0 million, and loss per share of $12.35 was worse than the split-adjusted consensus loss of $8.40. The reported loss included $0.9 million of non-cash convertible-note interest expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net loss widened to $4.1 million ($12.35 per share) from $2.8 million, partly driven by $0.9 million of non-cash interest expense from convertible note amortization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS, post-split | -$8.40”; “Net loss | ~$2.9–3.0M.”

surprises.description: The company received FDA 510(k) clearance for the Catamaran SI joint fusion system just after quarter-end. The clearance reclassifies certain instruments from disposable to reusable, which management expects to reduce per-procedure costs and lift margins beginning in Q3—an unanticipated potential margin tailwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On July 2, the company received FDA 510(k) clearance for the Catamaran SI joint fusion system, reclassifying certain instruments from disposable to reusable, which is expected to reduce per-procedure costs and boost margins beginning in Q3.”

surprises.description: Physician and distributor training events rose 98% in the first half of 2026 versus the second half of 2025, driven largely by the new Tampa training facility. The preview discussed converting trained surgeons into repeat users but did not anticipate this scale of increase in training activity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Physician and distributor training events increased 98% in the first half of 2026 versus the second half of 2025, driven largely by the newly opened Tampa training facility.”

surprises.description: Management reported a record case-value month in July, after the reported quarter, providing a new indicator of business momentum beyond the preview’s focus on the H2 ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reported a record case value month in July.”

surprises.description: Management said an enhanced Symmetry Plus system was expected to become clinically active in Q3 and a novel posterior-approach technology was approaching FDA submission. These near-term product developments were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[The company is] nearing multiple product launches, including an enhanced Symmetry Plus system going clinically active in Q3 and a novel posterior-approach technology approaching FDA submission.”

in_line: June 30 cash was $1.7 million, within the preview’s estimated $1.5–2.5 million range.
The $4.2 million gross-proceeds public offering closed July 1, as the preview had noted; it was subsequent to quarter-end.

surprises.description: Revenue was $9.1 million, above the preview’s $8.3 million house estimate and the $8.5 million level it highlighted as a meaningful run-rate hurdle. That is a clear upside gap, although there was no published sell-side consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 consolidated revenue rose 23% year-over-year to $9.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “House estimates for Q1 FY27: revenue $8.3M (+12% YoY)” and “Revenue at or above $8.5M” was a catalyst to watch.

surprises.description: Consolidated gross margin appears below the preview’s 17.5% estimate: $1.4 million of gross profit on $9.1 million of revenue implies a margin of about 15.4%. Gross profit rose year over year, but the margin outcome was weaker than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated gross profit up 36% to $1.4 million” on revenue of “$9.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “House estimates for Q1 FY27: ... gross margin 17.5%.”

surprises.description: Stadco’s revenue and gross profit improved substantially, but the segment was still not profitable. That leaves the turnaround incomplete against the preview’s focus on Stadco reaching breakeven and management’s stated expectation that the programs would be profitable in FY27.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Stadco revenue increased 22% to $4.1 million with gross profit up 65% (a $300,000 increase), though the segment remains not yet profitable.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Stadco gross profit turning positive” was the top issue to watch; the preview said management expected the programs “will be profitable in fiscal 2027” and described its base case as “Stadco near breakeven at gross profit.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed more than $24 million in fully funded Navy submarine-program grants to expand Ranor’s manufacturing capacity. The preview mentioned possible additional Navy grant money but did not anticipate support on this disclosed scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has received more than $24 million in fully funded Navy submarine program grants, representing over 50% of its $48 million market cap, to build out Ranor manufacturing capacity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “whether Ranor books more Navy grant money.”

surprises.description: Cash fell to $279,000 from $431,000 even though the company reported $1.9 million in net cash from operating and investing activities. The preview already emphasized tight liquidity, but the further cash decline underscores that concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash balance declined to $279,000 as of June 30, 2026, down from $431,000 on March 31, 2026, despite $1.9 million net cash from operating and investing activities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “$431K of cash at March 31, 2026” and flagged liquidity and the capital plan as key issues to watch.

surprises.description: Debt declined from $7 million to $5 million during the quarter, with $2 million in financing-activity paydowns. The preview highlighted debt and investment needs as a liquidity issue but did not forecast this amount of debt reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total debt was cut from $7 million to $5 million during the quarter, funded partly by $2 million in financing activity paydowns.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management wanted to “invest in Stadco equipment and pay down debt at the same time.”

surprises.description: Management said less than half of Stadco’s business was still operating under legacy loss-making contracts and described price-adjustment requests and new estimate-to-complete gates. The preview focused on contract-loss risks and the turnaround, but did not flag this specific progress in addressing legacy work.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Less than 50% of Stadco's business is now operating under legacy loss-making contracts, with management using price adjustment requests and new estimate-to-complete gating processes to improve margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged Stadco contract-loss provisions as a bear-case risk and identified Stadco’s turnaround as the top issue to watch.

in_line: EPS was a loss of $0.02 per share, matching the preview’s house estimate of a $0.02 loss.
Funded backlog of $52 million was within the preview’s $50–54 million estimate range.
Management reaffirmed FY27 guidance, as the preview identified reaffirmation as the baseline expectation.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $38 million, well below the preview’s roughly $42–43 million consensus estimate, even though it was slightly higher than the prior-year quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue rose modestly to $38 million from $37.3 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$42–43M (not broadly published; derived)”

surprises.description: DHS awarded a six-month CWMS 2.5 bridge during the protest, providing continuity despite the preview’s note that no bridge had been publicly disclosed. This addresses the preview’s main concern about a gap in CWMS work.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DHS awarded a six-month CWMS 2.5 bridge contract with a $113 million ceiling on August 6 to ensure business continuity and no ordering gaps during the protest period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No stop-work order or bridge extension has been publicly disclosed.” The preview also said the call needed to confirm “whether a bridge is in place and whether task-order performance continues uninterrupted.”

surprises.description: The call put a margin and earnings figure on the additional CWMS 3.0 opportunity: management expects about $150 million in additional annual work, concentrated in managed services and solutions at an 8%–10% net profit margin. The preview noted the contract award but did not lay out this incremental earnings opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects the ~$150 million in additional annual CWMS 3.0 opportunity to be concentrated in managed services/solutions work carrying an 8%-10% net profit margin, materially strengthening future earnings once fully scaled by end of 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “DHS was 77% of FY2025 revenue under the CWMS 2.0 IDIQ” and “CWMS 3.0 ($3.1B) was awarded.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $635,000, below the preview’s modeled $800,000–$1.0 million range, although it was more than triple the year-earlier figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to $635,000 from $183,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$0.8–1.0M (no formal consensus) | Modeled”

surprises.description: The carrier SaaS contract is now expected to go live by year-end, later than the preview’s expectation that it would be fully ramped by December 2026. That points to a slower near-term ramp than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $45 million, five-year ATV SaaS carrier contract (~$9 million/year at ~70% gross margin) is expected to go live by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guidance called for go-live in H2 2026, fully ramped by December 2026.”

surprises.description: WidePoint was also named a prime contractor on NASA’s SEWP VI vehicle, a new long-term route to federal orders that was not identified in the preview; ordering is expected to start in November, with a possible ramp from Q1 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “WidePoint was named a prime contractor under Category A of NASA's 10-year $60 billion SEWP VI vehicle, with the ordering period starting November 1 and ramp expected as early as Q1 2027.”

surprises.description: Management said it expects WidePoint to prevail in the CWMS 3.0 protest, adding an optimistic view of the outcome to the preview’s discussion of the pending GAO decision.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects to prevail based on winning all three prior predecessor contract protests.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Turning Point Global Solutions protested on June 29; GAO must decide by Oct 7, 2026.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed that the CWMS 3.0 award will bring one-time incentive payments, which it flagged as a near-term expense headwind not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company flagged upcoming one-time CWMS 3.0 incentive payments” as a near-term expense headwind.

surprises.description: The call flagged accelerated SEC-filer compliance costs as another near-term expense headwind that the preview did not identify.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company flagged ... accelerated SEC filer compliance costs ... as near-term expense headwinds.”

surprises.description: Management also identified capital investment in post-quantum cryptography as a near-term expense headwind, an investment not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company flagged ... post-quantum cryptography capital investments as near-term expense headwinds.”

surprises.description: The chief revenue officer announced he will retire at year-end after ten years with the company, a leadership transition not raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Chief Revenue Officer Jason Holloway announced his retirement at the end of the year after 10 years.”

surprises.description: Management cited possible expansion of the carrier service into state and local government and Fortune 500 customers that could double the covered device count. This adds potential beyond the federal rollout discussed in the preview, though it was presented as an opportunity rather than a commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: The carrier contract covers “2-2.5 million federal devices, with potential expansion into state/local and Fortune 500 clients possibly doubling device count.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the carrier agreement as targeting “$40–45M of recurring SaaS revenue over five years” and did not mention state/local or Fortune 500 expansion.

in_line: Q2 EPS was $0.01, within the preview’s $0.01–$0.02 estimate range; the quarter’s return to positive net income was therefore not a surprise against the stated EPS expectation.
Backlog was approximately $219 million, essentially flat with the roughly $218 million figure cited in the preview.

surprises.description: Management did not reaffirm the $50 million FY2026 revenue guidance, citing timing shifts in an international 5G deployment. The preview expected the guidance to be reaffirmed, even if with softer wording.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management declined to reaffirm its prior full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $50 million, citing timing shifts in an international 5G deployment, while insisting no backlog orders have been canceled.
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 revenue guidance: “At least $50M,” reaffirmed May 2026. The preview called the key question whether it would be “reaffirmed verbatim, softened, reframed as a run rate, or withdrawn.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin was 27.9%, far below the preview’s 40–44% base case and its expectation that margins might hold near Q1’s 48% as revenue rose. Management attributed the sequential decline to product mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 gross margin was 27.9%; sequentially, margin fell from roughly 48% in Q1 to 28% due to product mix.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “40–44%” gross margin, and the preview said holding “near 48% at higher revenue would be a positive sign.”

surprises.description: Instead of nearing operating breakeven as the preview’s base case anticipated, AMPG reported a $3.2 million operating loss and a $3.09 million net loss. SG&A nearly doubled and R&D more than doubled year over year, including substantial 5G development spending.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company posted a Q2 operating loss of approximately $3.2 million and a net loss of approximately $3.09 million, driven by deliberate investments ahead of revenue. SG&A nearly doubled to about $4.08 million, while R&D more than doubled to $1.37 million, including $1.08 million of 5G development.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “near operating breakeven”; the preview estimated quarterly opex of about $4.3–4.4 million and said breakeven was roughly $9.0 million of revenue at 48% gross margin.

surprises.description: The company said orders from the customer associated with the original $40 million LOI have already exceeded that LOI amount, a concrete order milestone not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company stated its original $40 million LOI has already been exceeded in orders from the same customer.

in_line: Q2 revenue of about $8.1 million was broadly in line with the preview’s $8.0 million consensus, and the 51% sequential increase matched the expectation that Q2 would be much higher than Q1. The year-over-year decline was also anticipated given the difficult Q2 2025 comparison.

The $6 million of July follow-on purchase orders and the continued activity around the large LOI were broadly consistent with the preview’s mention of more than $6 million in July orders and deployment timing delays.

surprises.description: Revenue was well above the preview’s roughly $4.0 million implied estimate: VirTra reported $5.8 million, within the preview’s bull-case range and above the level it said would change the narrative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $5.8 million,” up sharply from $3.5 million in Q1.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Analyst-implied ~$4.0M (my derivation)” and “Above $5M would change the narrative.”

surprises.description: The loss per share was substantially smaller than the preview’s consensus estimate, at -$0.02 versus -$0.10 expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company posted a Q2 net loss of $0.3 million ($0.02 per share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 EPS … -$0.10 (MarketBeat, Aug 2026).”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 59%, below the preview’s 60–64% base-case range and below 60% despite the sharp revenue recovery. The preview had flagged sub-60% margin alongside improved revenue as a concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin compressed to 59% from 69% a year earlier, reflecting lower revenue volume and increased content production investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … margin 60–64%” and “A revenue improvement with margin still below 60% would suggest pricing pressure or a lower-margin mix.”

surprises.description: Cash declined from the $17.9 million reported at Q1 to $14.3 million, a larger drop than the preview’s cited $0.8 million Q1 cash burn. The Orlando acquisition was already known, but the reported decline also reflected inventory investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and equivalents declined to $14.3 million from $18.6 million at year-end 2025, reflecting inventory investment and the Orlando facility acquisition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “about $0.8M burned in the quarter” and said to “Watch whether burn accelerated.”

in_line: Bookings were $5.5 million, within the preview’s $5–6 million base-case range and close to its roughly $5 million reference point.
Backlog was approximately $24.9 million, essentially flat with the preview’s $25.2 million Q1 figure and near its $25–26 million base-case range.

The U.S. Army Marketplace acceptance was not new: the preview already noted the July 30 acceptance and characterized it as a storefront position rather than an order; the call described access across three categories.

surprises.description: Platform revenue was $3.7 million, below the preview’s $4 million minimum buy-side bar and its $4.2–4.7 million base range. Caliber attributed the decline to development and construction fees from project financings shifting to later periods, rather than arriving in Q2 as the preview suggested could happen with Steamboat-related fees.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Platform revenue declined approximately 10% year-over-year to $3.7 million from $4.1 million, driven by lower development and construction fees due to the timing of project financings shifting to later periods.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side bar is the company's own metrics: platform revenue of at least $4M”; the base scenario projected “$4.2–4.7M,” and the preview said Steamboat fees were “the most likely source of an upside surprise.”

surprises.description: Platform adjusted EBITDA turned positive at about $0.3 million, better than the preview’s base-case expectation of a $0.1–0.3 million loss and at the top of its bull-case range. The preview focused on reaching breakeven, so the positive result exceeded that central bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Platform adjusted EBITDA turned positive at approximately $0.3 million, a roughly $0.4 million improvement from a $0.1 million loss in the prior year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “-$0.1 to -$0.3M”; its bull case was “+$0.1 to +$0.3M.” It described “platform Adj. EBITDA versus breakeven” as the core issue.

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s base scenario anticipating that Caliber might narrow its FY2026 revenue guide toward the low end, the company reaffirmed the full $18–22 million range and positive adjusted EBITDA outlook. It also specified that expected revenue growth is weighted toward project-level financings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed its full-year 2026 guidance of $18–22 million in revenue and positive adjusted EBITDA, with ~60% of revenue growth expected from project-level financings and ~40% from capital formation and asset management.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario anticipated the “guide reaffirmed but narrowed toward the low end”; the preview also said Q2 guidance language could “reaffirm at $18–22M, narrow, or cut.”

surprises.description: Platform expenses rose even as platform revenue fell, with increased reserves for uncollectible development and construction fees driving the increase. The preview emphasized profitability but did not anticipate this bad-debt pressure on expenses and collections.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Platform expenses rose approximately 11% to $5.9 million from $5.3 million, primarily due to increased bad debt charges from additional reserves on uncollectible development and construction fees.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified platform adjusted EBITDA versus breakeven as the core issue, but gave no expectation for bad-debt charges or expense growth.

surprises.description: The preview noted that the PURE tokenized offering had gone live, but the call described a broader planned rollout: Caliber completed its first fund tokenization and intends to extend tokenization across an initial slate of roughly $100 million in managed assets. The call did not report whether the tokenization brought in incremental capital.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Caliber completed its first fund tokenization (Pure Pickleball and Paddle) and plans to expand tokenization across an initial slate of roughly $100 million in managed assets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the offering “went live” and asked whether it would “bring[] in incremental capital or only re-plumbs existing distribution.”

surprises.description: Caliber disclosed a near-term unsecured-note maturity burden alongside refinancing and equity conversions: $21 million of approximately $26 million in note principal matures within 12 months. The preview flagged financing and dilution as issues but did not specify this maturity concentration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Caliber has 148 unsecured notes totaling ~$26 million principal, of which $21 million matures within 12 months, and it has refinanced $6.4 million into a 36-month program and converted ~$5.3 million into equity securities through August 13th.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Watch the Q2 share count and any new financing” and cited corporate cash “against $42.4M of platform notes payable.”

surprises.description: Caliber sold LINK tokens for $2.5 million and said it redeployed the proceeds into its real estate platform. The preview flagged LINK’s carrying value as relevant to EPS, but did not anticipate a quarter sale or this capital redeployment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company sold approximately 278,357 LINK tokens for $2.5 million in proceeds during the quarter and held 229,204 LINK tokens valued at $1.7 million at quarter-end, redeploying capital into its real estate platform.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “check the LINK token carrying value at June 30, which affects GAAP EPS.”

surprises.description: The call reported hotel-platform progress not identified in the preview: an eight-asset CHT acquisition pipeline, a new management model for six hotels, and the purchase of a site for a Hyatt Studios. These are additional operating and development initiatives beyond the preview’s discussion of the Steamboat project.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Caliber grew its CHT hotel acquisition pipeline to eight assets with one under executed letter of intent, transitioned six hotels to a new owner-centric management model, and purchased a 2.5-acre Hyatt Studios site near TSMC's $265 billion Phoenix semiconductor investment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview discussed the Steamboat Springs Hyatt Studios acquisition and construction financing, but did not mention this CHT pipeline, management transition, or site purchase.

in_line: Caliber reaffirmed the previously stated FY2026 revenue range of $18–22 million and its positive adjusted EBITDA goal.

surprises.description: Revenue was $12.3 million, below the preview’s Q2 consensus range of $13.29–$13.70 million and its $13.0–$13.5 million base-case scenario. That is a shortfall of roughly $0.7–$1.4 million versus the consensus figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue declined about 14% to $12.3 million in Q2 2026 from $14.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $13.29M (MarketBeat) / $13.70M (Investing.com)” and the base scenario expected “$13.0–13.5M.”

surprises.description: The Industrial Assets Division produced only about $600,000 of operating income, with management citing no larger auctions and more small-scale deals.
