That was weaker than the preview’s expectation for a seasonally strong Q2 and its view that core operating income above about $2.5 million would support the asset-services business, although the preview did not give a separate Industrial Assets forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Industrial Assets Division's operating income fell to roughly $600,000 in Q2 2026 from $1.3 million a year earlier, hurt by an absence of larger auctions and prevalence of smaller-scale deals.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 is seasonally the strongest quarter” and “Core operating income above about $2.5M would support a profitable asset-services story.”

in_line: The $21.7 million non-cash write-down was within the preview’s expected $18–24 million charge range and below the $23.7 million nonaccrual balance it flagged.
The Boston Note transaction was already disclosed as closing after quarter-end; the preview correctly noted it would add nothing to Q2.

surprises.description: Elutia finished Q2 with $19.9 million in cash, below the preview's $22–24 million base-case estimate and even below its bear-case threshold of $21 million. That is a weaker quarter-end cash position than expected, although the company also announced substantial future funding.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Elutia ended the quarter with $19.9 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management's base-case model implies cash of $22–24M at 6/30”; the bear case assumed “cash ≤$21M.”

surprises.description: Despite the lower-than-expected quarter-end cash balance, Elutia secured a $15 million Avenue facility and expects up to $11 million from the Simpliderm sale, with no equity offering. Together with other expected proceeds, the company put current and projected cash sources at about $54 million and said runway extends through at least 2028—well beyond the preview's concern about funding the 2027 launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured up to $26 million in new capital without an equity offering,” including “a $15 million Avenue Capital credit facility ($10 million already received) and up to $11 million from the Simpliderm sale ($8 million cash at closing).” It expects “up to $34 million more from signed transactions,” for “about $54 million” in current and projected sources and “runway through at least 2028.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Burn above about $7.5M in Q2 would shorten runway before first revenue and make a financing likely,” and its base case expected “no new capital raised.”

surprises.description: Q2 net sales of $2.4 million were below the preview's roughly $3.0 million as-reported estimate. The preview also flagged a roughly $1.0 million cardiovascular-only figure if Simpliderm were classified as discontinued operations, so the comparison depends on presentation; the call attributed the decline to a production disruption at Simpliderm's contract manufacturer.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales of $2.4 million,” including “a $0.7 million decline in Simpliderm (from a contract manufacturer production disruption)” partly offset by “a $0.4 million cardiovascular gain from returning to direct sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (as-reported) | ~$3.0M”; alternatively, “Revenue (if SimpliDerm is in discontinued ops) | ~$1.0M.”

surprises.description: Elutia reported a substantial year-over-year improvement in gross margins, although the preview gave no margin estimate. Adjusted gross margin rose 8 percentage points and GAAP gross margin rose 6.7 points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded 8 percentage points to 70.7% from 62.7%, while GAAP gross margin rose to 59.6% from 52.9%.”

surprises.description: Elutia reported strong initial surgeon interest in NXT 41X that the preview did not quantify or anticipate: nearly all surveyed surgeons expressed adoption interest, and all said they would use it for high-risk patients.
surprises.fact_evidence: In a “blinded, independent survey of 50 board-certified plastic surgeons,” “96% expressed interest in adopting NXT 41X,” “92% said they would champion it at their hospital's value analysis committee,” and “100% would use it for high-risk patients.”

surprises.description: Elutia said its existing facility can support at least $300 million of NXT 41X revenue at launch and set a target for gross margins above 80% at scale. The preview did not provide expectations for manufacturing capacity or product-level margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Elutia expects at least $300 million of revenue capacity at NXT 41X launch from its in-house Gaithersburg GMP facility,” with further expansion “requiring only added personnel and shifts,” and “targets gross margins above 80% at scale.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed the preview's expected NXT 41 clearance timing in Q4 2026 and NXT 41X clearance in the first half of 2027, with a soft launch in the second half of 2027. The call added a full commercial launch target in 2028.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $1.7 million, slightly above the preview’s acquisition-adjusted build of $1.50–$1.68 million. The gap was small; the preview cautioned that the $1.20 million consensus did not account for EngineRoom and that a headline beat was largely mechanical.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew approximately 79% sequentially to about $1.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A rough build of organic Q2 revenue (about $0.90–1.00M) plus roughly one month of EngineRoom (about $0.60–0.68M) gives about $1.50–1.68M”; “A headline beat is therefore close to mechanical.”

surprises.description: Cash at quarter-end was $11.7 million, well above the preview’s estimated Q2 exit range of $6–8 million. That is a meaningful cash cushion versus the preview’s concern that a low balance could require another raise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company held $11.7 million in cash as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate of Q2 exit cash is $6–8M”; “Cash below about $5M would likely force another raise.”

surprises.description: Cash EBITDA loss narrowed to $2.68 million, while operating expenses rose only 5.6% despite 79% sequential revenue growth. This was better than the preview’s downside case of burn above $3.5 million and indicates stronger cost leverage than that risk scenario implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash EBITDA improved modestly to negative $2.68 million in Q2 from negative $3 million in Q1, while operating expenses rose only 5.6% against 79% revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bear scenario cited “burn above $3.5M”; it also highlighted Q1 operating expenses of about $4.2M against about $0.79M of gross profit.

surprises.description: Management put a date on its breakeven goal: the second half of 2027, followed by profitable growth. The preview said a breakeven date was expected at the investor forum but did not specify one, so the timing is now clearer, though it remains a future target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targets breakeven in the second half of 2027 followed by profitable growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management … has discussed a path to EBITDA breakeven, with a date expected at the investor forum.”

surprises.description: CXApp reported a new three-year multimillion-dollar financial-services deal won through a competitive RFP, along with renewals from two Fortune 500 customers and an expected revenue uplift from new enterprise wins. The preview did not anticipate these specific customer wins or quantify an uplift of roughly one-third.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed a new 3-year multimillion-dollar financial services deal via competitive RFP and secured renewals from two Fortune 500 customers, with new enterprise wins expected to add roughly one-third revenue uplift.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed several product and deployment milestones not covered in the preview: Sky 2.0 entered production deployment, the Events module is due for general availability in September, and BEAT is expected to launch in Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sky 2.0 moved into production deployment, a new Events module reaches general availability in September, and the personal productivity product BEAT is expected to launch in Q4.”

in_line: EngineRoom contributed only one month of revenue in Q2, with the full three-month impact expected in Q3, consistent with the preview’s estimate that roughly one month of acquired revenue would be included in Q2.
Combined annualized revenue above $12 million was consistent with the preview’s expectation that EngineRoom would take the revenue run-rate above $12 million.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $8.1 million beat the $7.55 million consensus and fell less than the roughly 19% year-over-year decline implied by consensus. However, it was below the preview’s $9.0–$10.5 million base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 GAAP revenue fell 13.5% year-over-year to $8.1 million from $9.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (Q2) … Consensus $7.55M … Implies about −19% YoY”; the base scenario forecast “$9.0–10.5M.”

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed the $45–$50 million full-year revenue guide, whereas the preview’s base case expected a trim to roughly $40–$45 million or steering toward the low end. Holding the guide is more constructive than that scenario, although it leaves a substantial second-half revenue burden.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $45 million to $50 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario anticipated “guide trimmed to ~$40–45M or steered toward the low end”; the preview also said a cut or low-end language would be the key negative signal.

surprises.description: Only $14 million of contracted revenue was expected in the second half, while the guide requires substantial additional revenue beyond the $8.1 million Q2 result. That leaves the company reliant on new business and pipeline conversion to deliver the reaffirmed target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contracted revenue totaled $32.3 million for the first half of 2026, with $17.3 million already recognized, $14 million expected in the second half, and $1 million in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q2–Q4 revenue needed to average “$12.1–13.7M per quarter” and that contracted revenue plus Q1 reached only about $31.7M, requiring in-year wins not yet contracted.

surprises.description: Cash was $6.5 million, substantially below the preview’s $10.3 million Q1 balance and below the roughly $9 million balance implied by one quarter of the preview’s cited $1.3 million adjusted-EBITDA burn. AR days also rose sharply, adding a collection and working-capital concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents declined to $6.5 million from $8.1 million a year ago, while AR days rose sharply to 55 days in the first half from 20 days in the prior-year period due to the carrier transition.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash $10.3M” and “roughly $1.3M per quarter of adjusted EBITDA burn”; the preview flagged cash and financing as a key issue.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a $66.3 million revenue pipeline, but $64.4 million remained uncontracted and carried only a 15%–40% expected conversion rate. This gives the company potential to fill the contracted-revenue gap, but the conversion range makes that support uncertain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pipeline revenue stood at $66.3 million as of July 31, of which $1.9 million was already contracted and the remaining $64.4 million carries a 15%-40% expected conversion rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the company “must win in-year business not yet contracted as of mid-May.”

surprises.description: Management said switching to an A-rated stop-loss carrier, expected within 30 days, could lift projections by 20%–30% by opening access to large brokerages that require A-rated carriers. The preview did not anticipate this specific potential source of upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is switching to an A-rated stop-loss carrier, expected within 30 days,” which management believes “could lift projections by 20% to 30%” by unlocking business from large “alpha” brokerages.

surprises.description: Q2 net loss was $2.5 million, or $0.04 per diluted share, one cent worse than the preview’s $0.03 loss consensus, although it was within the preview’s base-case loss range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net loss was $2.5 million ($0.04 per diluted share) compared to net income of $0.6 million ($0.01 per diluted share) a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS, diluted (Q2) … Consensus $(0.03)”; the base scenario expected “$(0.03)–$(0.04).”

surprises.description: The company said its HitRix large-group stop-loss marketplace was due to launch within two to three weeks, a near-term product launch the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to launch its HitRix large-group stop-loss marketplace within 2-3 weeks.”

surprises.description: Management cited an anticipated flow of roughly 30 monthly submissions from municipalities and government agencies under the rate stabilization program. The preview expected at least one signed contract, but did not flag this prospective submission volume.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “secured its first employer group under its 3-year rate stabilization program, with an anticipated pipeline of roughly 30 submissions per month from municipalities and government agencies.”

in_line: The first employer group under the Three-Year Rate Stabilization Program met management’s previewed expectation of “at least one” signed contract in Q2.
Q2 adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $1.3 million, matching the preview’s cited approximate quarterly adjusted-EBITDA burn.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $4.7 million, far below the preview’s $14.30 million consensus, with just 30 units delivered. Management attributed the shortfall to orders deferred into future quarters.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell sharply to $4.7 million on 30 units delivered” as “multiple orders were deferred into future quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 Consensus” revenue of “$14.30M.”

surprises.description: Xos cut its FY2026 revenue and delivery guidance: revenue moved from $40–50 million to $35–43 million, and units from 350–500 to 250–350. The non-GAAP operating-loss range was widened rather than simply cut, from $11.9–13.3 million to $11.4–13.7 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management cut full-year guidance to “revenue of $35-43 million, unit deliveries of 250-350 units, and non-GAAP operating loss of $11.4-13.7 million,” reflecting shifted delivery timing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Standing FY2026 guidance: “Revenue: $40–50M,” “Units: 350–500,” and “Non-GAAP operating loss: $11.9–13.3M.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin fell into the teens, well below the preview’s base-case range of 28–33%: GAAP margin was 12.1% and non-GAAP margin was 7.2%. The preview had identified a margin starting with a 1 as a bear-case outcome, but it was materially worse than the central expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 gross margin deteriorated sequentially to 12.1% GAAP (7.2% non-GAAP) from 38.9% GAAP (38.2% non-GAAP) in Q1 2026,” driven by lower volume and delivery mix.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “gross margin 28–33%”; the preview also said “a gross margin starting with a 1” would be a bear-case signal.

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash was $13.2 million, above the preview’s $9–12 million base case and the $12 million bull-case threshold. The balance was supported by $7.6 million of net equity proceeds, including an ATM offering, rather than reflecting cash generation alone.
surprises.fact_evidence: Xos closed Q2 with “$13.2 million in cash, up about 35% from $9.8 million at Q1-end,” after raising “$7.6 million net via a $2.2 million ATM offering and $5.4 million registered direct offering.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “cash $9–12M”; the bull scenario expected “cash above $12M.”

surprises.description: The PowerHub flagship was reported at 3.1 MWh, larger than the 2.5 MWh unit cited in the preview. The launch timing itself was expected, but the reported capacity was higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: Xos launched its PowerHub line in June, featuring a “flagship 3.1 MWh unit delivering 1.5 MW of continuous AC power.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “the 2.5MWh Power Hub” as launched June 2.

surprises.description: The call reported more than 250 MWh of energy storage deployed across North America and record production of 29 hubs in Q2—operating scale not quantified in the preview. However, some hubs remained in the factory awaiting pickup, so production did not necessarily translate into deliveries in the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Xos has “over 250 MWh of energy storage deployed across North America” and “produced a record 29 hubs in Q2,” though “not all counted as deliveries since some remain in the factory awaiting pickup.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management “needs to show a dollar backlog or pipeline, not just a data-center narrative.”

surprises.description: System-level UL certification was still incomplete, with some standards potentially slipping into 2027. Management said this would not gate customer deliveries, which limits but does not remove the timing risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full UL system-level certification is incomplete,” with one standard expected within weeks and others “potentially slipping into 2027,” though management said this was “not gating customer deliveries.”

surprises.description: Xos disclosed that Q2 hub cells and packs were sourced domestically from its Illinois facility to meet U.S.-content requirements for defense and other customers, a compliance-related operating detail not raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 hub cells and packs are sourced domestically from Goshen's Illinois facility to meet U.S. content requirements for defense and other customers.”

surprises.description: The Bluebird partnership had generated more than 100 powertrain orders since its Q2 2025 launch, providing a cumulative demand figure beyond the preview’s Q1 unit count. Bluebird’s acquisition of a Detroit chassis facility also creates a potential future customer-capacity opportunity, though it is not a disclosed Xos order.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bluebird has ordered over 100 powertrains since the partnership launched in Q2 2025,” and its acquisition of Ford's Detroit Chassis facility, with capacity of about 20,000 units per year, is “a potential future EV powertrain growth opportunity for Xos.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that Bluebird powertrains were “63 of 95 Q1 units” and said to watch for “a second named OEM.”

surprises.description: Ending ARR was $11.6 million, far below the preview’s $15.6–$16.1 million base range and $15.9 million year-ago benchmark. The preview looked for another sequential gain; ARR instead fell sharply year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ending ARR fell to $11.6 million” from $15.9 million a year ago, following a $3.1 million contract expiration and a $2.6 million contract reduction, partly offset by $1.5 million of net ARR growth.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Ending ARR vs. $15.9M”; the base scenario was “ARR $15.6–16.1M,” and the key metric discussion said Q2 needed about “+6% sequentially” to produce the first positive YoY ARR since the contract losses in 2025.

surprises.description: Management withdrew its original goal of significant ARR growth by year-end 2026, rather than reiterating the goal or giving the quantified ARR or breakeven outlook investors wanted. The stated reasons were the contract reduction, no committed upsell, and limited time left in the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “withdrew its original target for significant ARR growth by year-end 2026,” citing the contract reduction, an absent committed upsell, and limited time remaining.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the base signal was “‘significant ARR growth’ repeated without quantification” and that investors wanted an ARR target or breakeven timeframe from the new CEO.

surprises.description: Secure gift card revenue and meaningful ARR contribution are now pushed beyond the 2026 holiday season: no incremental gift card revenue is committed for the rest of 2026, with meaningful ARR growth deferred to late Q4 2026 or early Q1 2027. That is weaker near-term conversion than the preview hoped for, even though some pilots and broader deployments are scheduled.
surprises.fact_evidence: Meaningful gift card ARR growth “has been deferred a few quarters to late Q4 2026/early Q1 2027,” with “no incremental gift card revenue committed for the balance of 2026 including the holiday season.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether pipeline opportunities “convert before holiday season,” and identified a second gift-card slip as the most likely bear catalyst.

surprises.description: The GAAP loss per share was much worse than the preview’s rough GAAP-like consensus, widening to $0.54 from $0.38 a year earlier. The call attributed much of the loss to stock-based compensation and severance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss per diluted share widened to $0.54 from $0.38,” largely due to $5.4 million of stock-based compensation and $700,000 of severance for the former CEO.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 EPS consensus of “–$0.33” and said to read it as “roughly GAAP,” while cautioning that the basis was ambiguous.

surprises.description: On the non-GAAP basis, the loss per share was better than the preview’s comparable expected range: $0.08 versus roughly $0.10–$0.15. This contrasts with the much worse GAAP result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net loss per share improved to $0.08 from $0.11.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the “Non-GAAP comparable is closer to –$0.10 to –$0.15.”

surprises.description: The company reported a much broader secure gift card opportunity than the preview had described: the pipeline expanded from one retailer to more than 31, and two additional retailers committed to deployments. This is encouraging evidence of customer interest, though it has not yet produced committed 2026 revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: The pipeline “has grown over 30x since the start of the year, from a single retailer to more than 31 large and midsized retailers”; two additional retailers committed to deployments, one later in August and one in October.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on whether the existing retailer rollout was on track and whether opportunities would convert before the holiday season; it did not describe a pipeline of more than 31 retailers or these two new commitments.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue modestly exceeded the preview’s consensus range, despite declining from a year earlier. The beat was supported by higher service revenue while subscription revenue fell.
surprises.fact_evidence: Total revenue was “$7.4 million,” down from $8.0 million a year earlier; subscription revenue fell by $900,000 to $3.7 million, while service revenue increased by $300,000 to $3.6 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave Q2 revenue estimates of “$7.09M” or “$7.32M” and a base scenario of “$7.1–7.3M.”

surprises.description: The company plans to direct more than 90% of capital-raise proceeds to building go-to-market teams and programs, indicating a substantial commercial rebuild rather than simply conserving cash. The preview had flagged the possibility that rebuilding sales capacity would push operating expenses back up.
surprises.fact_evidence: With $8.8 million in cash and short-term investments and no debt, the company is “planning a capital raise with over 90% of proceeds earmarked for building out go-to-market teams and programs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “whether rebuilding sales capacity pushes operating expenses back up” and noted that a $17.5 million ATM program was already in place.

surprises.description: The new CEO has already hired a Chief Revenue Officer and a VP of Retail Solutions, with the senior leadership team expected to be complete by the end of Q3. The preview wanted to hear the new CEO’s plan but did not anticipate these specific hires or that timetable.
surprises.fact_evidence: Paul Carreiro was “only 30 days into the role” and had already hired a Chief Revenue Officer and a VP of Retail Solutions; management expects the full senior leadership team to be complete by the end of Q3 2026.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said investors wanted an ARR target or breakeven timeframe from the new CEO and flagged rebuilding sales capacity, but gave no leadership-hiring timeline.

surprises.description: Digimarc is narrowing direct commercial focus to retail and CPG and moving pharma, life sciences, media, technology, and government to a partner-led approach. This is a concrete change in go-to-market strategy that the preview did not identify.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is “narrowing its commercial focus to retail and CPG” while shifting pharma, life sciences, media, technology, and government verticals to a partner-led approach.

surprises.description: Ending cash was slightly above the preview’s estimate, although the company still plans a capital raise. The cash result was better than the estimate, but the balance remained limited.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended the quarter with “$8.8 million in cash and short-term investments and no debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “about $8.5M at 6/30 excluding ATM sales.”

surprises.description: The preview expected FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $215–$235 million; KinderCare cut it to $200–$220 million. The new range’s midpoint is $15 million below the previous midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was updated to… adjusted EBITDA of $200–$220 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA | Guidance $215–235M (raised from $210–230M).”

surprises.description: FY26 adjusted EPS guidance fell to $0.05–$0.15 from the preview’s cited $0.15–$0.25 company range and $0.20 consensus; the new range’s midpoint is half the consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was updated to… adjusted EPS of $0.05–$0.15.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA was $63 million, below the preview’s base-case range of $70–$75 million, although it landed within the preview’s bear-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA fell to $63 million from $82 million a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base… Adj. EBITDA $70–75M”; the preview’s bear case was “$60–66M.”

surprises.description: The preview looked for enrollment to improve to -2% or better, but enrollment declined 4% year over year, indicating a weaker trend than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total enrollment declined 4% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Enrollment trend. Needs to improve to -2% or better to validate the trajectory.”

surprises.description: Full-year free cash flow is now expected to be less than $10 million, far below the preview’s $35–$40 million guide, largely because of elevated optimization and lease-exit costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow for the year is now expected to be less than $10 million due to elevated optimization costs, including ~$20–25 million of lease exit payments tied to about 36 identified lease exits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY FCF guide is $35–40M.”

surprises.description: KinderCare disclosed a much larger closure program than the usual 15–20 centers: it closed 49 in Q2 and expects 80–85 closures by year-end. The preview had flagged that the count was pending, but did not anticipate a program of this size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “KinderCare closed 49 centers in Q2… and expects total closures to reach 80 to 85 by year-end, mostly in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management plans to close more than the usual 15–20 centers, with counts pending lease negotiations.”

surprises.description: The new FY26 revenue range of $2.66–$2.70 billion is below the preview’s $2.70–$2.75 billion company guide and $2.71 billion consensus; its midpoint is about $45 million below the prior guide’s midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was updated to revenue of $2.66–$2.7 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue | $2.71B (FY guide $2.70–2.75B).”

surprises.description: Management said tuition’s contribution to revenue growth for the year had been lowered to about 2.5% because state subsidy reimbursement increases were slower than expected; the preview had not flagged this specific growth driver or constraint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tuition contribution to revenue growth lowered to ~2.5% for the year due to slower state subsidy reimbursement increases.”

surprises.description: Insurance and legal reserve adjustments unexpectedly accounted for about $5 million of the Q2 EBITDA decline, and the FY26 outlook includes about $8 million of incremental self-insurance costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “About $5 million of the decline [in adjusted EBITDA] driven by insurance and legal reserve adjustments”; FY guidance includes “~$8 million of incremental self-insurance costs.”

surprises.description: The company quantified the financial trade-off from the footprint optimization: about $57 million of annual revenue headwind in exchange for roughly $8 million of adjusted EBITDA benefit, $7 million lower rent expense, and a 150-basis-point occupancy improvement. The preview flagged closures and charges but did not provide an expected estimate of these effects.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Once fully completed, the footprint optimization is estimated to be a ~$57 million annual revenue headwind but a ~$8 million adjusted EBITDA benefit, cut rent expense by ~$7 million, and improve occupancy by roughly 150 basis points.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $698 million, essentially matching the preview’s $697.98 million consensus.
Q2 adjusted EPS was $0.08, matching the preview’s $0.08 consensus.
Same-center occupancy was 68.6%, within the preview’s expected 68–69% range and its stated 68% bar.
Champions revenue grew 13%, above the preview’s roughly 12% threshold for maintaining the offset to core weakness.

surprises.description: Q2 sales were $41.3 million, well above the $29.91 million consensus and above the preview’s $38 million-plus bull-case threshold. The preview cautioned that consensus might not fully reflect Terrasoul, but the reported result still exceeded that expectation substantially.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net sales surged 244% year-over-year to $41.3 million,” driven primarily by the Navitas and Terrasoul acquisitions plus organic wholesale expansion.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (Q2) | $29.91M”; the bull scenario was “$38M+.”

surprises.description: The company kept its full-year sales and adjusted EBITDA ranges unchanged, rather than narrowing guidance toward the low end as the preview considered likely in its base case. Management also expressed confidence in achieving at least the midpoint of the revenue range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed full-year 2026 guidance of $138 million to $148 million in net sales and $8 million to $12 million in adjusted EBITDA”; the CFO said she would be “personally disappointed” if full-year revenue landed below the midpoint.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called guidance the “highest-variance item” and described its base case as “EBITDA … guide narrowed to low end”; it also said “$148M looks like a stretch.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $3.0 million, above the preview’s base-case range of $0.5–1.5 million and its roughly $1 million threshold for straining the full-year guide. It was at the bottom of the quarterly run rate implied by the existing annual guidance, rather than comfortably above it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA jumped to $3.0 million in Q2 2026 from just $0.1 million a year earlier,” reflecting acquired-business contributions and early synergy realization.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “EBITDA $0.5–1.5M”; the preview said “A Q2 print below about $1M would strain the guide” and estimated the required quarterly amount at “about $3.0–4.4M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 30.3%, below the preview’s 31–33% base-case range and down from the 33.3% Q1 level the preview used as a benchmark. Management also set low-30s as the appropriate go-forward range, weaker than the preview’s cited low-to-mid-30s H2 outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin compressed 9.6 percentage points to 30.3%”; management flagged “low-30s% as the appropriate go-forward gross margin range,” reflecting Terrasoul’s lower profitability.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario had “GM 31–33%”; it said to watch “Gross margin versus 33.3%” and cited management’s H2 guidance of “low-to-mid 30s.”

surprises.description: GAAP loss per share was much worse than the consensus estimate, despite the strong adjusted EBITDA result. The reported loss included substantial business-combination and integration costs and intangible amortization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net loss widened to $1.8 million (-$0.25 per share) … driven by $3.5 million of business combination/integration costs and $1.1 million of intangible amortization.”

surprises.description: The Walmart rollout had reached more than 1,000 stores, but essentially none of its revenue was expected in Q2; the contribution was pushed to Q3 and Q4. That is later than the preview’s expectation that the Walmart and Target expansions would begin to show in the results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company launched 5 coffee and creamer SKUs into more than 1,000 Walmart stores nationwide, with essentially all revenue impact expected in Q3 and Q4 rather than Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Walmart and Target expansion “should start to show.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case put revenue around $105 million, while Q3 revenue was $108.9 million. That was a modest upside to the preview’s rough base estimate, though close to its $110 million bull-case figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue declined 3.2% year-over-year to $108.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: Revenue ... Around $105M (about –7% YoY)” and “Bull: Revenue ... Around $110M (about –2% YoY).” The preview notes these were its own rough estimates, not Street numbers.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case expected approximately breakeven EPS and its bull case expected positive EPS, but the company reported a loss of $0.34 per share. The result was below even the preview’s base-case expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company swung to a net loss of approximately $1.1 million (loss per share of $0.34).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... EPS ... About breakeven” and “Bull: ... EPS ... Positive.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted a possible moderation in Retail-Flooring’s decline, but the segment’s revenue fell 29.4%, worse than its 26.2% decline in Q2. This points to continued, rather than easing, deterioration in the segment the preview identified as the main drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retail-Flooring segment revenue fell 29.4% to $21.4 million due to continued weakness in new home construction and home refurbishment markets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A slower decline would matter more than the absolute revenue figure”; the bull scenario also cited “Retail-Flooring decline moderates.”

surprises.description: Nektar reported a Q2 net loss of $40.6 million, or $1.23 per share, versus the preview’s estimate of a roughly $55–60 million loss and EPS of about –$1.65 to –$1.80. The loss was materially smaller than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss was $40.6 million ($1.23 per share)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Preview estimate for reference: net loss of roughly $55–60M, EPS of about –$1.65 to –$1.80”

surprises.description: The finalized alopecia areata registrational plan is a single Phase III study, as the preview’s preferred outcome anticipated, but it will enroll 850 patients rather than the roughly 600-patient study described in the preview’s bull case. The larger study is a meaningful difference in trial scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nektar finalized its single registrational Phase III ZENITH-AA study in alopecia areata (850 patients, primary endpoint SALT ≤20 at week 52)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The bull case needs FDA to accept a single ~600-patient, 52-week registrational study.”

surprises.description: Nektar raised its year-end cash guidance to $815–840 million, above the prior $800–825 million range, and said its $1.02 billion cash and investments provide runway into Q3 2028, past the initial AD data readouts. The preview had expected runway only “into 2028.”
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 2026 with $1.02 billion in cash and investments and no debt, with runway extending into Q3 2028 past the initial AD data readouts”; “Nektar raised its year-end 2026 cash guidance to approximately $815 million to $840 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “year-end cash guide is $800–825M”; management’s prior runway guidance was “into 2028.”

surprises.description: The reported Q2 noncash royalty revenue was $10.1 million, below the preview’s Q2 revenue estimate of about $10.7–10.9 million. However, the full-year revenue outlook remained at $40–45 million, as expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 noncash royalty revenue was $10.1 million, with full-year 2026 revenue still expected at $40-45 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ~$10.7–10.9M”; “Company guide $40–45M.”

surprises.description: New prescriber research was favorable: 150 of 151 high-volume physicians said injection-site reactions were not a prescribing barrier, and physicians favored REZPEG’s mechanism given no increased infection risk and no observed conjunctivitis. The preview did not flag this market-research result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Market research with 151 high-volume prescribers found 150 of 151 physicians said injection site reactions were not a barrier to prescribing, and physicians favored REZPEG's novel T-reg mechanism given no increased infection risk and no conjunctivitis observed.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a federal jury trial scheduled for September 8, 2026, and management declined further comment because litigation is ongoing. The preview mentioned securities class actions and investigations, but not this scheduled trial.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A jury trial in federal court in San Francisco is scheduled for September 8, 2026, on which management declined to comment further citing ongoing litigation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “Securities class actions were filed” and that “securities investigations weighed on the stock,” but did not mention a scheduled trial.

in_line: The AD program’s initial two studies were enrolling 510 patients each after starting in July, and the third study was expected to start by September; this was consistent with the preview’s enrollment and timing watchpoints.
The REZOLVE-AA 24-week off-treatment data remained expected in Q4 2026, as the preview had flagged.
FY26 R&D guidance of $210–230 million remained within the prior $200–250 million range and reflected the anticipated Phase III ramp-up.
Full-year 2026 revenue guidance remained $40–45 million, matching the company guidance cited in the preview.
The alopecia areata Phase III study is planned to start in early 2027, consistent with the preview’s base case.
No partnership was disclosed; the preview identified silence on business development as the base case.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $46.1 million, well above the preview’s roughly $33 million consensus, a gap of about 39%. The company attributed the increase primarily to higher volumes, with pricing also contributing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $46.1 million,” driven primarily by “higher volumes ($35.8M)” and secondarily by “pricing ($3.3M).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 revenue | $32.85M” and “Q2 revenue | $33.18M.”

surprises.description: Production averaged 6,800 BOE per day, below the preview’s 7,000–7,300 base-case range. The 16% sequential decline was steeper than that base case, although the preview did expect volumes to moderate from Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Production averaged approximately 6,800 BOE per day,” a “16% sequential decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario forecast “Volumes 7,000–7,300”; the preview also flagged Q2 volumes versus the 8,091 BOE/d Q1 level and said volumes were expected to moderate.

surprises.description: First-half adjusted EBITDA was $36.8 million, below the preview’s estimate that H1 would track near $42.5 million. That leaves a lower first-half starting point for the reaffirmed full-year target than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bringing first-half adjusted EBITDA to $36.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “H1 adjusted EBITDA tracks near $42.5M.”

surprises.description: Realized oil price was $94.07 per barrel, above the preview’s roughly $85 Q2 WTI reference despite the expected hedge constraints. This indicates better-than-anticipated price realization against the benchmark cited in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average realized oil price rose 53% year-over-year to $94.07 per barrel.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “roughly $85 Q2 WTI average” and noted that legacy swaps and collars were below that level.

surprises.description: The company repaid $13 million of debt, taking its revolver balance to $85 million and net funded debt to about $73 million. The preview focused on the borrowing-base redetermination and potential availability rather than an anticipated debt repayment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company repaid $13 million of debt,” reducing the revolving credit facility balance “to $85 million from $98 million” and net funded debt to “approximately $73 million.”

surprises.description: Resolution of Wyoming BLM litigation unlocked permitting for top-tier Powder River Basin wells and expanded the second-half development program beyond prior expectations. Management said it plans to drill and participate in over 20 gross wells, though contributions are not expected until late 2026 and early 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Resolution of BLM litigation in Wyoming unlocked permitting for top-tier Powder River Basin wells, expanding the second-half development program beyond prior expectations”; management plans to “drill and participate in over 20 gross wells.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “whether the D-J Basin DUC completes on schedule and whether the Permian San Andres program is sanctioned.”

in_line: The company reaffirmed full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $60 million to $70 million, matching the preview’s stated base case.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $1 million, far below the preview’s $3.42 million consensus and the roughly $3 million quarterly level it said was implied by the December run-rate target. Accelsius contributed only $0.9 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated Q2 2026 revenue was $1 million”; “Accelsius contributing 96% ($0.9 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 consensus” revenue of “$3.42M”; the preview also said “Q2 ~$3M” was implied by the December target.

surprises.description: Management suspended all Accelsius revenue targets and withdrew the expectation that it would exit 2026 near a $100 million annualized run rate with positive operating cash flow. The preview treated that target as current guidance, though it warned a reframe or delay was possible.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management suspended all Accelsius revenue targets” and “no longer expects it to exit this year near cash flow breakeven at a ~$100 million annualized run rate, extending breakeven beyond 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dec 2026 target: ~$100M annualized Accelsius run rate, positive operating cash flow”; the preview said to watch whether this was “reaffirmed, softened, or reframed.”

surprises.description: Innventure abandoned its prior goal of consolidated positive cash flow by 2028, a company-level target not identified in the preview as at risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Innventure abandoned its prior goal of consolidated positive cash flow by 2028 due to Accelsius's delayed path to profitability.”

surprises.description: A DarkNX purchase order was removed from the 2026 forecast after the customer lost its development site, adding a specific order setback not anticipated in the preview. Management expects a transfer to another location, but gave no firm timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The DarkNX purchase order was removed from the 2026 forecast after the customer lost its development site due to power envelope constraints”; transfer to an alternate location is expected “on an uncertain timeline.”

surprises.description: Management said hyperscalers are now the target customers and that their two-to-three-year adoption cycles leave no 2027 revenue visibility. That contrasts with the preview’s FY27 revenue estimate of $161.92 million and was not part of its discussion of the adoption timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Accelsius is now targeting large hyperscalers rather than small early adopters,” but “hyperscaler adoption cycles run two to three years, making 2027 revenue visibility unavailable.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “FY27 revenue / EPS” estimates of “$161.92M / -$0.06.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a $13 million SEPA raise and signaled possible additional dilutive raises in the second half. The preview had flagged financing and dilution as risks, but did not forecast this specific raise or the signal of further issuance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Accelsius raised approximately $13 million through its standby equity purchase agreement at an average price of $6.21,” and Dave “signaled potential additional dilutive capital raises in the second half of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “Cash, burn, and financing,” noted “~$66.6M remaining” on the SEPA, and said management should be pressed on its dilution framing.

surprises.description: A third-party benchmark reported strong NeuCool cold-plate performance on a Dell/NVIDIA B200 server, including cooler GPUs at much lower coolant flow and support for warmer facility water. The preview did not anticipate this specific technical validation.
surprises.fact_evidence: GPUs ran “9–14°C cooler using roughly one-third of the coolant flow”; viable facility water temperatures extended from “~45°C to 54°C and beyond.”

surprises.description: The two-phase market forecast was raised to $9 billion by 2030, an upside market-size update not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The two-phase market forecast raised to $9 billion by 2030.”

in_line: Quarter-end cash and implied Q2 operating cash use were broadly in line with the preview’s estimate: cash was $46.5 million versus its projected $40–47 million range absent new capital, and Q2 operating cash use was about $25.5 million based on $59.5 million year-to-date use and $34.0 million in Q1, within its $25–30 million estimate.
The handoff to Bill Grieco effective October 1 and John Hewitt’s role as Accelsius CEO were already reflected in the preview.

surprises.description: Revenue was reported at $15.1 million, about 40% above the preview’s $10.8 million model, but roughly $4.4 million of the total came from newly grossed-up pass-through electricity costs. Excluding that presentation change, revenue was about $10.7 million, essentially matching the model rather than delivering a comparable underlying beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $15.1 million, up 145% year-over-year on a reported basis, but only 73% excluding a new gross presentation of pass-through electricity costs that added ~$4.4 million to both revenue and cost of revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (my model) | ~$10.8M (+75% YoY, +15% QoQ) | My model.”

surprises.description: The preview’s implied net-loss expectation was roughly $14–15 million, while the reported loss widened to $22.6 million. The gap reflected, among other items, $9.4 million of noncash stock compensation, $3.2 million of interest expense, and a $4.2 million debt-extinguishment loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $22.6 million from $7.8 million a year earlier, driven by $9.4 million of noncash stock compensation, $3.2 million interest expense, and a $4.2 million loss on debt extinguishment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A $(0.11) EPS on about 130M shares implies a net loss of roughly $14–15M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was a $1.6 million loss, worse than the preview’s $1.0 million-loss base model, although it was better than the preview’s bear case. The reported sequential improvement does not change that it fell short of the base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $1.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base | Adj. EBITDA ~$(1.0)M (my model).”

surprises.description: Gross profit fell to $766,000, with newly acquired Briscoe Wind Farm posting a $787,000 gross loss after front-loaded turbine repairs, alongside Kati 1 ramp costs. The preview discussed hosting ramps and mining economics but did not anticipate these Briscoe repair costs or this gross-profit pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit compressed 35% year-over-year to $766,000, hurt by new-site ramp costs at Kati 1 and roughly $1.5 million of front-loaded turbine repairs at the newly acquired Briscoe Wind Farm, which posted a $787,000 gross loss.”

surprises.description: Soluna raised substantial capital through its ATM and ended Q2 with $113 million in cash, exceeding the preview’s stated concern threshold of about $55 million. The funding strengthens liquidity, though the ATM issuance was dilutive and the preview had already flagged ATM use as a major risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised $159.4 million in Q2 (primarily $113.5 million via ATM) plus an additional $23.6 million through the ATM since quarter-end”; it ended Q2 with “$113 million cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash below about $55M with no financing path would be a concern”; the preview also said “About 45M shares were issued since April under the $500M ATM shelf.”

surprises.description: Management gave a more specific financing framework for future AI builds than the preview had described: it expects project-level debt to cover 70–80% of build costs, raised after a lease is signed. This was a plan rather than a committed Kati 2 financing facility, so the financing issue was not fully resolved.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For each 100 MW AI build-out estimated at $1.2–1.3 billion, the company plans to fund 70–80% with project-level debt raised within 8–12 weeks of a signed lease.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A top-tier investment bank has been engaged, but no structure has been disclosed.”

surprises.description: The renewable-power pipeline had grown to more than 6.3 GW, with more than 1.6 GW of AI capacity in development and 192 MW operating. The preview noted 147 MW under management and site construction progress, but did not flag this larger pipeline or the AI development figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The renewable power pipeline grew 47% this year to over 6.3 gigawatts, with 192 MW currently operating, 14 MW under construction (targeting 206 MW by end of summer), and over 1.6 GW of AI capacity in development.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “147 MW under management.”

surprises.description: Soluna resolved the Series B preferred shares through conversion into about 6.5 million common shares and paid $2.1 million of accumulated dividends. The preview identified a possible preferred resolution as a dilution risk, but the actual conversion and retirement occurred in the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management fully retired all 62,500 Series B preferred shares (converting into ~6.5 million common shares at $0.96) and paid $2.1 million in accumulated dividends.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Preferred dividends in arrears. $32.4M Series A and $1.8M Series B as of 3/31. Any resolution, exchange, or conversion would be a dilution event.”

in_line: Underlying revenue excluding the newly grossed-up pass-through electricity costs was about $10.7 million, essentially in line with the preview’s $10.8 million model.
Kati 2 remained in lease negotiations rather than reaching a signed lease, consistent with the preview’s base case of negotiations continuing.
Proprietary mining revenue fell as hash price weakened, in line with the preview’s warning about weak, volatile hash price and mining economics.

surprises.description: XBP reported normalized EBITDA of $21.9 million, above the preview’s $17–19 million base case and close to its $22 million bull threshold. Instead of another year-over-year decline, EBITDA rose 8.4% year over year and 40.6% sequentially.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 normalized EBITDA reached $21.9 million, up 8.4% year-over-year and 40.6% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “$17–19M”; it also warned that “a fourth straight YoY decline would break the stated plan.”

surprises.description: Revenue was $191.3 million, about 3.2% below the $197.7 million consensus, and fell 14% year over year on a pro forma basis versus the preview’s derived estimate of about an 11% decline. The reported decline was attributed to expected legacy contract exits and volume reductions from prior restructuring.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue was $191.3 million, down 14% year-over-year on a pro forma basis, attributed to expected legacy contract exits and volume reductions from prior restructuring.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Revenue | $197.70M” consensus and said this “implies about -11% YoY on a derived pro forma comp.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin reached 24.9%, exceeding the preview’s 24.5%+ bull-case level and its 23.3–24.0% base-case range. The preview expected another margin expansion to be tested, but the reported expansion was stronger than those scenarios.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin expanded for the fourth consecutive quarter to a record 24.9%, up 290 basis points year-over-year and 140 basis points sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case listed “24.5%+” gross margin, while its base case listed “23.3–24.0%.”

surprises.description: New ACV bookings reached $36 million, above the preview’s roughly $27–30 million trailing average and its bull-case threshold of more than $32 million. This was a stronger bookings inflection than the preview’s minimum stabilization requirement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New ACV bookings reached $36 million, up 57% year-over-year and 32.1% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said H2 growth required new ACV “to inflect above the roughly $27–30M trailing average” and listed “new ACV above $32M” in its bull case.

surprises.description: Management raised its annualized operational-efficiency target to $65–75 million from the previously stated $55–60 million range, and expects about $35 million of benefit during 2026. That is a larger savings target and a more specific in-year benefit than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised its targeted annualized operational efficiency range to $65-75 million (up from $55-60 million), with an expected in-year 2026 benefit of approximately $35 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “the $55–60M annualized target” and said it was “about half implemented as of Q1 but not yet visible in the P&L.”

surprises.description: The technology segment returned to year-over-year revenue growth and sharply expanded its gross margin, despite the preview highlighting a steep Q1 revenue decline and a 52.4% margin. The recovery was stronger than the preview’s general expectation of revenue stabilization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The technology segment grew revenue 9.8% year-over-year to $24.5 million with adjusted gross margin expanding 690 basis points to 64.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q1 Technology revenue of “$18.7M (-26.4%, 52.4% gross margin)” and described the base case as “Revenue stabilizes.”

surprises.description: XBP said it had engaged a financial advisor for the strategic-alternatives process, a concrete step beyond the preview’s account of an ongoing review with no news since May. The preview had identified adviser engagement as evidence that the process was live.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects a revenue inflection in the second half of 2026 and has engaged a financial advisor for its previously announced strategic alternatives process.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said there had been “no news since May” and that “named advisers, a signed LOI, or a disposal such as Technology” would matter.

surprises.description: Management now expects revenue to inflect in the second half of 2026, a stronger outlook than merely stabilizing revenue. The preview treated stabilization as the base case and flagged whether management would maintain H2 growth language.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects a revenue inflection in the second half of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case said “Revenue stabilizes,” and its catalyst checklist asked whether “H2 growth language is kept or softened to ‘stabilization.’”

in_line: The approximately 20% workforce reduction by year-end 2026 was consistent with the preview’s reference to a 20% headcount cut.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $24.3 million, about 14–16% below the preview’s $28.3–28.9 million consensus range and just below the preliminary $25 million low end. The call attributed the shortfall to delayed DoD public-sector spending diverted to the Iran conflict.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $24.3 million” and was “slightly short of expectations due to delayed DoD public sector spending diverted to the Iran conflict.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$28.3–28.9M”; company preliminary framing was “$25–30M+.”

surprises.description: The FY2026 guide was cut, as the preview anticipated, but its $100–150 million range has a $125 million midpoint—above the preview’s base-case expectation of a trim to roughly $105–120 million. The wide range nevertheless includes a lower floor than that scenario and is below the prior $130–145 million guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Veritone lowered full-year 2026 revenue guidance to $100 million-$150 million (17% growth at midpoint),” primarily due to federal delays and reduced VDR contribution expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a cut was more credible than maintaining $130–145 million and gave a base scenario of “FY guide trimmed to ~$105–120M.”

surprises.description: Cash ended June at $12.7 million, above the preview’s conditional $5–8 million estimate if little ATM stock was sold, but below its $20 million relief threshold. The balance came despite $9.4 million of ATM proceeds and $22.1 million of operating cash outflow, so the update was better than the preview’s low-cash case but still showed heavy cash use.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and restricted cash dropped to $12.7 million from $27.7 million at year-end 2025, after $22.1 million in operating cash outflows and $9.4 million raised via ATM at an average price of $1.68 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said cash could be “roughly $5–8M” if little was sold, that “Cash above $20M with disclosed ATM proceeds would be relief,” and that below $8 million would be a crisis.

surprises.description: The preview focused on whether roughly $20 million of active VDR pipeline could close in Q2; the call instead described $15 million of additional active pipeline as potentially closing in Q3/Q4, with only 2–3 months of delivery visibility. That points to conversion being later and less certain than the preview’s Q2 opportunity suggested, even though the broader pipeline and bookings remained above $65 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “VDR near-term sales pipeline and bookings exceed $65 million, with an additional $15 million active pipeline potentially closing in Q3/Q4 2026,” while “timing remains outside the company's control with only 2-3 months of delivery visibility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had cited a near-term pipeline “over $68M” and “about $20M of active pipeline that could close in Q2”; the preview said “Recognized revenue, not pipeline, is the test.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin was 63.7%, down from 67.7% in Q1 and 72.6% a year earlier, as lower-margin VDR revenue weighed on the mix. The preview provided no Q2 margin estimate, so the size of this decline was not directly benchmarked there, but it disclosed a markedly weaker margin outcome alongside the VDR conversion debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 non-GAAP gross margin fell to 63.7% from 72.6% a year earlier, an 890 basis point decline driven by revenue mix, with lower-margin VDR pressuring profitability versus SaaS products.”

surprises.description: Management now targets non-GAAP breakeven as early as the first half of 2027, at $125–130 million of annualized revenue, and said this shifts the profitability timeline from earlier expectations. The preview did not give a breakeven date, so the call’s stated delay is new negative guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management targets breakeven non-GAAP profitability as early as the first half of 2027 at $125 million-$130 million in annualized revenue (about 11% growth), shifting the profitability timeline from earlier expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The call says the timeline is shifting from “earlier expectations”; the preview supplied no breakeven timetable.

surprises.description: The company reported a substantial reduction in debt and annual interest carry costs, a positive update against the preview’s focus on the November converts. However, the call facts do not identify a named, sized solution for the remaining roughly $45 million of debt, and more than $40 million remains available under the ATM.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total debt was reduced to approximately $45 million (accruing 1.75% interest) from about $130 million a year earlier, an $85 million improvement and over $13 million in reduced annualized carry costs, with over $40 million remaining under the ATM.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Any named, sized refinancing, exchange, secured facility, or asset sale matters more than revenue. Silence would be a bear catalyst,” referring to the $45.6 million notes due Nov. 15, 2026.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a large cost-reduction program and workforce restructuring not flagged in the preview: $11.3 million of annualized savings already implemented, with a $15–20 million target by fiscal year-end and up to 30% total savings by early 2027. The savings come with a $4.5 million one-time severance and transition charge after eliminating 62 jobs, roughly 14% of the workforce.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Approximately $11.3 million in annualized cost savings” has been implemented, targeting “$15 million-$20 million by end of fiscal 2026 and up to 30% total savings by early 2027”; the restructuring eliminated “62 full-time employees, roughly 14% of the workforce,” with a “$4.5 million one-time severance and transition charge.”

surprises.description: The call reported multiyear public-sector wins with the California Highway Patrol and a Washington state agency, plus a public-sector pipeline above $200 million that could grow further with pending international and federal awards. These concrete wins and pipeline figures were not highlighted in the preview, although the awards remain future-dependent and federal spending was delayed in Q2.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured multiyear public sector wins including the California Highway Patrol and a Washington state agency,” and reports “a public sector pipeline north of $200 million that could double with pending international and federal awards expected to impact fiscal 2027.”

in_line: A reduction to FY2026 revenue guidance was anticipated: the preview judged a maintained $130–145 million guide less credible and modeled a base case with a trim. The actual range and midpoint differ from that scenario, as noted above.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $35.1 million versus the preview’s $47.1 million consensus, a much larger shortfall than the preview’s already-expected procurement pullback suggested. Procurement revenue was $18.2 million, well below the roughly $30 million implicitly assumed in the preview’s consensus framing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue declined 20% year-over-year to $35.1 million”; Procurement revenue fell “from $33 million to $18.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $47.1M”; the consensus framing says it “implicitly assumes procurement steps down to about $30M.”

surprises.description: Systems Integration revenue was $13.9 million, below the preview’s $15–17 million base scenario and slightly below Q1’s $14.1 million, rather than continuing to build sequentially. Its 46% year-over-year growth and increased share of revenue were strong, but the quarter did not meet the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Systems Integration revenue grew 46% year-over-year to $13.9 million” and represented 39% of revenue.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “SI $15–17M”; the preview also said SI revenue “well below Q1’s $14.1M would undercut that narrative.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $4.5 million, below the preview’s $5.0–5.5 million base scenario, despite growing year over year. The full-year guide was reaffirmed toward the upper end, as expected, but the quarterly result was softer than the preview’s base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased 12% year-over-year to $4.5 million in Q2”; management reaffirmed full-year guidance “toward the upper end of the $20-22 million range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario listed “Adj. EBITDA $5.0–5.5M”; the preview expected the “higher end” language to be kept.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $0.05, below the $0.06 consensus. Net income was essentially flat to slightly lower, with higher tax expense following the removal of the deferred tax valuation allowance contributing to the shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income was essentially flat to slightly down at $1.4 million ($0.05 per diluted share) versus $1.5 million ($0.06) a year ago,” with income tax expense of $413,000 versus $69,000.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS | $0.06.”

surprises.description: The revenue decline came with a sharp improvement in blended gross margin and higher gross profit: margin rose 640 basis points and gross profit increased 11% despite lower sales. The preview anticipated favorable mix, but did not set an expectation for this degree of consolidated margin and gross-profit resilience.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Blended gross margin improved 640 basis points to 22.8% from 16.4%, and consolidated gross profit rose 11% to $8 million despite the overall revenue decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “good mix and steady EBITDA,” but gave no consolidated gross-margin or gross-profit target.

surprises.description: The preview flagged a possible cash drop into the low $50 millions as a financing concern during the capex program. Instead, cash was $67.7 million at quarter-end, above Q1’s $66.0 million, while only $7–8 million of the planned $17 million investment had been completed.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company had “$67.7 million in cash and only $16.1 million in total debt”; “$7-8 million” of the approximately “$17 million” investment was completed by quarter-end.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned that “Cash falling into the low $50Ms would likely bring financing questions” and described the $17 million program as expected to complete in Q3.

surprises.description: Management gave a stronger near-term procurement outlook than the preview’s general expectation of a recovery: Q3 orders already exceeded Q2 levels, with revenue expected to return to the historical $30–40 million range. That points to a sharper second-half rebound than the preview’s base case of weak headline revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 Procurement orders already exceed Q2 levels, with revenue expected to revert to the historical $30-40 million range, signaling a stronger second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case anticipated “weak headline revenue”; it described procurement recovery as a bull-case driver rather than its base expectation.

surprises.description: The previously known $17 million capacity investment was expected to finish in Q3, but the call added a specific expectation that the NVIDIA Vera Rubin buildout would drive incremental recurring revenue mainly in Q4. The preview did not specify this platform-linked revenue timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is investing “approximately $17 million” to build capacity for “NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform,” expected to be completed by mid-September and to “drive incremental recurring revenue mainly in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “$17M next-generation capex program is expected to complete in the third quarter,” but did not identify Q4 revenue contribution.

surprises.description: Facilities Management revenue grew sharply, an outcome not discussed in the preview, but the growth was driven by discrete project work rather than stronger recurring maintenance: maintenance revenue declined as customers did not renew agreements on older MDCs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Facilities Management revenue grew 84% year-over-year to $2.7 million”; maintenance revenue fell to “$746,000 from $1 million,” while discrete project work rose to “nearly $2 million.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted validation-test capacity as a possible constraint on Systems Integration scaling. Management instead said Georgetown had two to three times the capacity required by its contractual minimum and identified supply-chain constraints, not demand, as the primary growth bottleneck.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Georgetown facility has 2x to 3x capacity above the contractual minimum,” with “supply chain constraints (rather than demand)” the primary factor limiting Systems Integration growth.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s bull case said SI could scale “faster than validation-test capacity,” identifying capacity as a potential constraint.

in_line: Management reaffirmed FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $20–22 million and continued to expect performance toward the higher end, consistent with the preview’s stated expectation.

surprises.description: Acurx ended Q2 with $10.7 million in cash, above the preview’s roughly $9.5 million estimate, and management said that cash funds the PATHFINDER trial and operations for at least a year. That is better than the preview’s base case of $9.0–9.8 million and unchanged going-concern concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Acurx ended Q2 2026 with $10.7 million in cash” and management says it “funds the Pathfinder trial and operations for at least one year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate … cash at 6/30 about $9.5M”; base case: “Cash @ 6/30 $9.0–9.8M” and “going-concern doubt unchanged.”

surprises.description: The FDA indicated it may consider the totality of evidence after one Phase III trial plus PATHFINDER, particularly if efficacy is robust. This creates a possible route to review that could reduce reliance on funding the larger ASPIRE trial, which the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FDA indicated it is open to reviewing the totality of evidence at a pre-NDA meeting after completion of a single Phase III trial (Ibez ASPIRE) plus the PATHFINDER study, particularly if efficacy results are robust.”

surprises.description: PATHFINDER enrollment is now anticipated in Q4 2026, later than the preview’s expected first enrollment by August. The trial is funded, but the start has slipped beyond the preview’s expected timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 20-patient open-label PATHFINDER trial … is fully funded, with enrollment anticipated to begin in Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided to first enrollment by August 2026 for the 20-patient open-label study.”

surprises.description: Despite the delay, PATHFINDER is fully funded, a more secure funding position than the preview’s tight-budget setup suggested. The preview warned that funding constraints could reach the clinic, but the call said the study is funded.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 20-patient open-label PATHFINDER trial … is fully funded.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Slippage would show the funding constraint reaching the clinic”; the preview also characterized the setup as one of a “tight budget.”

surprises.description: The Q2 EPS loss of $0.53 per share was better than the $0.57 consensus estimate, but the $2.3 million net loss exceeded the preview’s $1.9–2.1 million estimate. Higher R&D spending drove the larger loss, partly offset by lower G&A.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss widened to $2.3 million ($0.53 per diluted share)”; “R&D expenses more than doubled to $1.1 million” while “G&A expenses fell to $1.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus Q2 FY26 EPS: “−$0.57”; preview estimate: “Net loss $1.9–2.1M, EPS about −$0.50.”

surprises.description: Acurx reported that it has enough API and formulated product to support PATHFINDER and begin the international ASPIRE trial, with sites expected in Western and Eastern Europe. This is readiness progress beyond the preview’s status-quo framing of ASPIRE as subject to funding, though the trial still needs financing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management confirmed sufficient API and formulated product to support the PATHFINDER trial and to begin the international ASPIRE trial, with sites expected in Western and Eastern Europe.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said ASPIRE “can only start ‘subject to funding availability’” and called for “IBZ-ASPIRE start-up details.”

in_line: The pivotal ASPIRE trial still requires additional funding, and management has not secured it; this matches the preview’s expectation that the trial remained “subject to funding” and its base case of no named funding path.

surprises.description: Stardust Power’s Q2 net loss was $3.9 million, $0.6 million less than the preview’s $4.5 million estimate. That is a modestly better result, though still within the preview’s estimated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a Q2 net loss of $3.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net loss: $(4.5)M (range $(3.5)M to $(6.5)M)”

surprises.description: Loss per share was $0.35, less than the preview’s estimated loss of $0.44 per share. The call attributed the improvement primarily to a higher weighted average share count following capital raises, rather than to a comparable improvement in the underlying loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Basic and diluted loss per share improved to $0.35 from $0.59 a year earlier, primarily due to a higher weighted average share count following capital raises.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Loss per share: $(0.44) (range $(0.34) to $(0.63))”

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash was approximately $0.5 million, below the preview’s point estimate of $0.8 million. It was within the preview’s wide estimated range, but leaves less cash on hand than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash and cash equivalents falling to approximately $0.5 million as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash at quarter end: ~$0.8M (range $0.3M to $2.0M)”

surprises.description: The company reported about $2.9 million in net proceeds from its ATM after quarter end. The preview noted the existing $5 million ATM and expected incremental dilution, but did not anticipate this specific post-quarter funding amount; the proceeds improve liquidity while adding dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A separate $5 million ATM equity program with BTIG Securities raised about $151,000 during the quarter and an additional approximately $2.9 million in net proceeds subsequent to quarter end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Three live vectors: the Lind $15M convertible note, the B. Riley equity line … and a $5M ATM”; the base scenario anticipated “incremental dilution.”

in_line: Stardust Power remained pre-revenue, as the preview modeled Q2 revenue of $0.0 million.

The preview identified cash runway, the Nasdaq cure deadline, and the possibility of further dilution as central risks. The call reported that the company still depends on raising additional capital, has not announced a cure, and is evaluating alternatives for Nasdaq’s continued-listing requirements.

The preview expected no binding project-financing announcement and anticipated that feedstock and offtake arrangements could remain non-binding. The call reported construction financing remained the priority, with no material developments in feedstock, offtake, or strategic-financing discussions.
The preview estimated operating cash burn at about $2.0 million per quarter; the reported first-half operating cash use of $4.0 million is broadly consistent with that pace.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $836,000, far below the preview’s roughly $1.79 million consensus and $1.7–2.2 million bottom-up estimate. The reported amount was less than half the preview’s low-end estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue reached $836,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 revenue | ~$1.79M”; “total revenue of about $1.7–2.2M.”

surprises.description: Liabilities were reported at roughly $278 million, above the preview’s $230 million Q1 benchmark rather than showing progress below it. Management still targets under $100 million within three to four quarters, as the preview expected, but the reported balance is higher than that benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total liabilities declined about $61 million to roughly $278 million,” with management targeting “under $100 million within the next three to four quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Q2 figure versus $230M at Q1” and noted the goal of “under $100M in 3–4 quarters.”

surprises.description: The company reported $70 million in new institutional commitments during Q2, exceeding the preview’s modeled $45 million institutional raise. However, $42.5 million was classified as restricted cash, so the headline commitment does not translate directly into available liquidity.
