surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured $70 million in cumulative new institutional commitments during Q2, including $45 million in secured notes and $25 million in convertible notes, though $42.5 million was classified as restricted cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s cash estimate was “derived from … a $45M institutional raise,” and it highlighted cash under about $15 million “with no committed facility” as a key risk.

surprises.description: FFAI committed to a $5-per-share conversion floor on outstanding convertible notes, resolving the preview’s key uncertainty in favor of honoring the floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company committed to setting a $5-per-share conversion floor on outstanding convertible notes.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked “whether the $5.00 convert floor is honored or waived” and described “$5 floor held” as a bull-scenario driver.

surprises.description: The company canceled about 5.36 million Class A warrants in July, bringing cumulative permanent cancellations to about 49.9 million units. The preview discussed dilution and the share count but did not anticipate these cancellations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Canceled approximately 5.36 million Class A warrants in July, bringing cumulative permanent warrant cancellations to about 49.9 million units since December 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Share count” and the $300 million shelf and $90 million ATM, but did not mention warrant cancellations.

surprises.description: Q2 shipments were about 220 units (242 cumulative at quarter-end versus 22 in Q1), modestly above the preview’s bottom-up estimate of 195–210 units. The full-year 2,000-unit target was reaffirmed, while the 394 cumulative units through July matched the preview’s stated figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cumulative robot sales and shipments grew from 22 units in Q1 to 242 by end of Q2 and 394 by end of July 2026, with the company reaffirming a full-year target of 2,000 units.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “about 195–210 EAI robot units shipped” in Q2 and noted “394 units through July”; its base scenario expected the “2,000-unit target reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: The company reported a $10.7 million gross loss, showing aggregate gross-margin weakness. The preview highlighted robotics gross margin as a key issue and identified negative gross margin as a bear-case trigger, although the reported figure does not specify robotics margins separately.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross loss narrowed to $10.7 million from $26.9 million in Q2 2025,” with cost of revenue of $11.54 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Robot gross margin and ecosystem mix” and listed “Negative gross margin” as a bear-case trigger.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a new EAI Data Factory business with targets of 2,100 qualified real-world data collection hours per month by end-August and 20,000 per month by December, plus a 50,000-hour full-year target and a potential order worth over $400,000. This opportunity was not discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The EAI Data Factory targets monthly production of 2,100 qualified real-world data collection hours by end of August, scaling to 20,000 hours by December and 50,000 hours for the full year, with a top customer order potentially worth over $400,000.”

surprises.description: Management cited the FCC’s addition of foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots to its covered list as a structural tailwind for its U.S.-based manufacturing strategy. This policy development and potential advantage were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “On July 28, 2026, the FCC added foreign-made humanoid and quadruped robots to its covered list, which management frames as a structural tailwind for its U.S.-based ‘built-in USA’ three-phase manufacturing strategy.”

in_line: The 1-for-150 reverse split had already taken effect, and Nasdaq compliance had been regained, as the preview stated.
The full-year robot target remained 2,000 units, as the preview expected; cumulative sales and shipments of 394 units through July also matched the preview’s figure.

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 67.2%, well below the preview’s roughly 72% expectation and even below the preview’s 68% bear-case threshold. Management attributed the decline to product and customer mix and higher costs, including tariffs on imported components.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 67.2% from 69.6% year-over-year, pressured by product/customer mix and increased costs including tariffs on imported components.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin: ~72% (Q1'26: 72.3%)”; the preview also said “Below 68% breaks the breakeven math.”

surprises.description: Management guided Q3 revenue down sequentially to $2.3 million–$2.5 million, explaining that Q2 included about $500,000 of international upside, including a large dental order that is not expected to recur, alongside seasonal summer slowness. The preview did not flag this near-term sequential decline, despite expecting 2H revenue to be roughly flat with 1H.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guided Q3 2026 revenue down sequentially to a range of $2.3 million to $2.5 million due to non-recurring international orders and seasonal summer slowness”; Q2 “benefited from approximately $500,000 in international upside, including a large dental order that management does not expect to recur in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $9.8–10.2M range needs $4.8–5.2M in 2H, roughly flat half-over-half.”

surprises.description: Management reaffirmed the $9.8 million–$10.2 million full-year revenue range rather than raising it after the Q2 revenue beat. The preview noted that a bare reaffirmation after the beat could be viewed as soft.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $9.8 million to $10.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance: $9.8M – $10.2M”; “After a revenue beat, a bare reaffirm would read as soft.”

surprises.description: The loss and expense trend was better than the preview’s concern about possible opex re-acceleration: Q2 net loss narrowed, and first-half operating expenses declined substantially year over year. The preview highlighted loss reduction as important but did not forecast this first-half expense decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $1.1 million from $1.5 million in Q2 2025, with six-month operating expenses down 20% (about $1.4 million) year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any opex re-acceleration would undo” the loss reduction; the preview also noted that “The loss reduction, not revenue, drove the stock's re-rating.”

surprises.description: The company reported that CompuFlo reimbursement is established under Novitas and First Coast fee schedules at $325, covering three regions and 13 states. This is concrete reimbursement progress on an issue the preview framed as needing evidence beyond submitted claims, though the reported fact does not establish how many claims were actually paid.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CompuFlo has secured $325 Medicare reimbursement payments under Novitas and First Coast fee schedules covering 3 regions and 13 states, representing roughly 30% to 35% of the population, with Palmetto and western MACs being pursued next.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Paid claims with dollars, not submitted claims, across First Coast, Novitas, Palmetto, and others.”

surprises.description: Management said it is not currently planning another capital raise following the April private placement, a reassuring financing update that the preview identified as a risk to watch. The reported $2.1 million cash balance itself was within the preview’s estimate, so the surprise is the stated financing plan rather than cash exceeding expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds $2.1 million in cash, $3.7 million in working capital, and $466,000 in convertible debt, and stated it is not currently planning to raise additional capital following its $2.51 million April private placement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash at 6/30 versus the ~$2.0–2.5M estimate. Below ~$1.5M implies a raise within two quarters”; the preview also listed “raise or ATM signaled” in its bear scenario.

surprises.description: A new Red One Medical distribution agreement opens federal healthcare markets serving more than 18 million veterans and military beneficiaries, with first orders targeted for Q4 2026. The preview did not identify this agreement or channel expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new distribution agreement with Red One Medical opens access to federal healthcare markets serving over 18 million veterans and military beneficiaries, with the first orders targeted for Q4 2026.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $2.8 million, up 22% year over year, matching the preview’s already-public ~$2.8 million estimate and its approximately 21% growth figure.
First-half revenue reached $5.0 million, up nearly 10% year over year, in line with the preview’s ~$5.0 million and +9% estimate.
Cash was $2.1 million at quarter-end, within the preview’s estimated $2.0 million–$2.5 million range.

surprises.description: Gross profit was positive at roughly $0.6 million, despite the preview’s base case expecting margins to remain negative after two consecutive quarters of negative gross profit. That is a clear reversal of the anticipated gross-profit sign.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit stayed essentially flat at roughly $0.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... gross margin still negative”; the preview also noted “Two consecutive quarters of negative gross profit.”

surprises.description: Revenue was approximately $3.6 million, about $0.22 million (6.5%) above the $3.38 million consensus estimate. The beat was positive but not large relative to the estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 12.8% year-over-year to approximately $3.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $3.38M”

surprises.description: Net loss was approximately $3.3 million, better than the preview’s roughly $4.0 million estimate and below its base-case loss range of $4.0–$5.5 million. The loss improved even though gross profit was essentially flat, alongside lower SG&A.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss improved to approximately $3.3 million”; “SG&A expenses declined approximately $0.9 million or 21.5% to $3.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implied net loss ~$4.0M”; base case: “Net Loss $(4.0)–(5.5)M.”

surprises.description: The Prairie Hills funding came with a much larger debt balance and very little unrestricted cash: debt rose to about $14.2 million, while roughly $10 million of $10.7 million cash and restricted cash was earmarked for the facility, leaving about $0.7 million for operations. The preview highlighted the funding question but did not anticipate this combination of financing and constrained operating liquidity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total debt rose to approximately $14.2 million from $1.9 million at year-end, reflecting $13.5 million of new financing for the Prairie Hills facility”; “about $10 million is restricted for the Iowa facility, leaving only about $0.7 million available for operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked “how the planned 400,000 sq ft Prairie Hills facility ... will be funded” and flagged June 30 cash as a key issue.

surprises.description: Management said co-manufacturer production would begin at the end of Q4 2026, later than the preview’s September 2026 start timing. That pushes the planned early production ramp back by roughly a quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management plans to begin production through a co-manufacturer at the end of Q4 2026 to capture demand early.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “RTD co-manufacturer production (guided to start September 2026).”

surprises.description: Management reported that 100% of the Prairie Hills facility’s capacity was already presold across owned brands and private label. The preview discussed the facility and its production timing but did not indicate that its full capacity was already committed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Prairie Hills RTD facility is being built for over 100 million beverage units annually ... with 100% of capacity already presold across owned brands and private label.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow remained positive for a second consecutive quarter, with about $0.9 million generated in the first six months versus $6.8 million used in the prior-year period. The preview noted the first positive quarter in five during Q1, but did not establish that positive cash flow would continue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow was positive for a second consecutive quarter at approximately $0.9 million for the first six months, versus $6.8 million cash used in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q1 operating cash flow of “+$251K, the first positive quarter in five.”

in_line: Fresh cut remained a major growth driver, consistent with the preview’s focus on whether growth would continue to be Cut Herb-led: fresh cut sales increased more than 42% year over year.

surprises.description: Combined cash ended the quarter at $43 million, above the preview’s $40 million target and even its $42 million bull-case threshold. The company also reported no debt.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Combined cash across the company and JV was $43 million with no debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The target is at least $40M combined”; the bull scenario expected “Above $42M.”

surprises.description: AirJoule raised its 2026 cash-spend guidance to $27–28 million from about $25 million, rather than holding to the previous guide. Management tied the additional spending to accelerated JV commercialization and deployments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 cash spend guidance was raised slightly to $27-28 million (from $25 million), with the incremental spend directed toward accelerated JV commercialization and deployments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 combined cash spend is guided at about $25M”; the checklist expected burn “tracking to the ~$25M guide.”

surprises.description: The first full-scale Prime system is operating around the clock, tracking toward a target of up to 2,000 liters per day, and is slated for a European data-center waste-heat deployment this quarter. The preview discussed data-center prospects but did not anticipate this specific operating system and deployment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The first full-scale Prime system, commissioned in Newark in May and running 24/7, is tracking toward its target of up to 2,000 liters per day and will ship to Europe this quarter for a data center waste-heat deployment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had named “hyperscale data centers” but had not put units or dollars on the pipeline, and listed “any quantified pipeline” as a key item to watch.

surprises.description: AirJoule described a Core DH dehumidifier product aimed at an estimated 1.2 million installed conventional desiccant-wheel systems, with a targeted 2027 timeline. This product and its stated target market were not in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Core DH dehumidifier product targets an estimated 1.2 million installed base of conventional desiccant wheel systems, focusing on facilities operating at 30%-50% relative humidity, with a targeted 2027 product timeline.”

surprises.description: The company said it is preparing for contract manufacturing targeted for 2027 and exploring partners to reduce its internal CapEx needs, a manufacturing approach not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is advancing contract manufacturing preparations targeting 2027” and “is exploring partners to reduce internal CapEx needs.”

in_line: Management said liquidity is sufficient into 2028, consistent with the preview’s reference to funding operations “into 2028.”

The Kubota update described two Core systems deploying in Texas and California starting later in the quarter, consistent with the preview’s expectation of two Kubota units deploying in Q3 2026 in that territory.
The expectation of only modest paid deployment revenue in 2026, with more meaningful revenue in 2027, is consistent with the preview’s pre-commercial framing and base case of about $0 revenue.

surprises.description: The preview described Project Permian Phase 1 as an 80 MW project using gas turbines with Entropy carbon capture. Management instead said near-term capital is shifting to unabated gas generation, with Permian redesigned for 1–1.5 GW across phases and no post-combustion capture in the initial phase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Redirecting near-term capital toward unabated natural gas power generation while retaining carbon capture as an optional later-phase add-on”; Project Permian is being redesigned for “approximately 1 to 1.5 gigawatts across multiple phases,” and “post-combustion carbon capture will not be deployed in the initial phase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Project Permian Phase 1 rescoped to 80 MW using Siemens A35 turbines and Entropy amine-based capture.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged a signed PPA or term sheet as a key possibility to watch for by the call. Management said there is still no signed offtake agreement and expects to share more only within the next couple of months.
surprises.fact_evidence: “It has no signed offtake agreement yet but expects to share more within the next couple of months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Offtake status versus the expectation of a signed or term-sheeted agreement by this call.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the Entropy joint development agreement to be finalized in Q2. Instead, the relationship is being restructured for possible deployment in later phases, with no near-term capital commitment for carbon capture.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Entropy carbon capture relationship is being restructured into a revised framework for potential deployment only in later phases, with no near-term capital commitment for CCS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Entropy Joint Development Agreement. Guided to finalize in Q2. Signed would be positive; continued ‘advancing diligence’ would be negative.”

surprises.description: Cash and investments ended Q2 at about $310 million, above the preview's estimated $250–275 million. The company also reported no debt.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 2026 with approximately $310 million in cash, cash equivalents and investments and no debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash & investments (est.): ~$250–275M.”

surprises.description: The preview centered on an 80 MW first phase, but management said it is working with a potential customer to secure another 120 MW of gas equipment, which would bring first-phase secured capacity to nearly 200 MW. The additional 120 MW is still being pursued, not yet secured.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Working with a potential customer to secure an additional 120 megawatts of gas power equipment,” which “combined with already-secured turbines would bring total secured capacity to nearly 200 megawatts for the first phase.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Project Permian Phase 1 rescoped to 80 MW using Siemens A35 turbines.”

surprises.description: Management said customers will not have to pay upfront for clean or carbon-capture power, and that dropping capture from the initial deployment frees capital to roughly double installed megawatts for behind-the-meter use. The preview did not anticipate this customer-payment approach or the stated capacity effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “It does not expect to require customers to pay for clean/carbon-capture power upfront,” and dropping post-combustion capture “frees capital to roughly double installed megawatts for behind-the-meter deployment.”

surprises.description: The preview described a Phase 1 configuration using Siemens turbines but did not flag a reliability constraint. Management said one large turbine cannot meet the three-nines reliability target because of maintenance downtime, so the plan is to combine batteries, reciprocating engines and gas turbines to target 99.9% reliability on a 2028 timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Targeting three 9s (99.9%) reliability using a mix of battery storage, reciprocating engines, and gas turbines, on a 2028 timeline”; “a single large turbine unit cannot meet the three 9s reliability target due to maintenance downtime.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Project Permian Phase 1 rescoped to 80 MW using Siemens A35 turbines”; the preview gave a target “COD early 2029.”

surprises.description: Management said the power shortage and grid constraints could persist from the early 2030s through 2040 and beyond, with ERCOT queues already backed up into the 2030s. The preview did not flag this extended demand window.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The power shortage/grid-constraint environment could persist from the early 2030s at the earliest to 2040 and beyond, with ERCOT queues now backed up into the 2030s.”

in_line: The need for project-level financing, partner capital or equity was already anticipated: the preview discussed a $125–175 million equity check and identified project financing as dependent on offtake.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $9 million, well below the preview’s $12–14 million estimate and $13.10 million consensus, even though first-half revenue was up 13% year over year. The quarter’s revenue was essentially flat year over year, rather than reaching the level expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $9 million, essentially flat versus $9.1 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The full preview's own estimates are revenue $12–14M”; Q2 consensus was “$13.10M.”

surprises.description: Cash and restricted cash ended June at $48.9 million, far above the preview’s $22–26 million estimate. The increase was primarily funded by common-stock issuance, so the stronger liquidity position came with an equity-financing component amid the preview’s concern about dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash rose to $48.9 million at June 30, 2026 from $17.1 million at year-end 2025, primarily due to proceeds from common stock issuance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “quarter-end cash $22–26M” and identified “Cash and restricted cash at 6/30/26” as “the decisive line”; it also described dilution as the market’s main concern.

surprises.description: LanzaTech reinstated full-year 2026 guidance despite having issued no FY26 guidance previously. The $50–55 million revenue outlook would require $29–34 million in the second half after $21 million in the first half, while the company also guided to a $22–26 million adjusted EBITDA loss and $51–55 million of operating expenses.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reinstated full-year 2026 guidance of $50-$55 million in revenue, an adjusted EBITDA loss of $22-$26 million, and operating expenses of $51-$55 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview stated “Company guidance (FY26): None issued” and noted “No FY2026 financial guidance issued” in Q1.

surprises.description: The company reported progress toward a first sale of ISCC-EU certified ethanol at its China facility, with management expecting certified sales to begin supporting demand and pricing improvement from Q4. This was a new commercial catalyst beyond the preview’s discussion of revenue mix and segment recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LanzaTech is undergoing the world's first ISCC-EU certification for recycled carbon fuels at its China facility,” which “could unlock certified ethanol sales expected to begin driving demand and pricing improvement starting in Q4”; it is “in active negotiations for its first sale of ISCC-EU certified ethanol.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses fell further than the preview’s expectation that costs would hold: Q2 expenses were down to $11.7 million from $13.5 million in Q1, as well as down sharply year over year. The reductions included especially large cuts to R&D, while SG&A also declined year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell 67% year-over-year in Q2 to $11.7 million from $35.1 million”; R&D was “$2 million in Q2 2026 from $14.9 million” and SG&A “fell 54% to $8.8 million from $19.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario said “costs hold,” after noting Q1 operating expenses of $13.5 million.

surprises.description: LanzaTech’s retained Shougang-LanzaTech JV stake was valued at roughly $110 million, substantially above the preview’s roughly $63 million estimate. The reported JV market capitalization was about $1.32 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LanzaTech's 8.3% retained stake in the Shougang-LanzaTech JV” was “valued at roughly $110 million as of August 12, with the JV's market cap at approximately $1.32 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated the stake at “roughly $63M against an ~$81M market cap.”

surprises.description: The call gave a valuation reference for LanzaJet: LanzaTech’s 46% stake was associated with a recent funding-round valuation of approximately $650 million. The preview flagged the stake and its carrying value for attention but did not give a comparable valuation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds a 46% stake in LanzaJet, which was recently valued at approximately $650 million in its latest funding round.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch the “LanzaJet stake and carrying value,” including possible “equity-method losses, impairment” and changes to agreements.

in_line: Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss was $7.6 million, within the preview’s estimated $7–9 million loss range and close to the Q1 loss of $7.9 million.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case expected $4–5 million of cash at quarter-end, but PAVmed reported $3.8 million. That is below the base-case range, though still within the preview’s broader $3.5–5.5 million research estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “PAVmed ended Q2 2026 with only $3.8 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (50%): Cash $4–5M”; the research estimate was “$3.5–5.5M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the Lucid mark to push the GAAP loss to roughly $11–14 million, but PAVmed reported a $6.6 million net loss before NCI and preferred dividends. The fair-value charges were much smaller than the preview’s implied mark-to-market loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net loss narrowed to $6.6 million (before NCI and preferred dividends) from $12.3 million a year earlier,” with “smaller non-cash fair value charges of $3.1 million versus $10.8 million prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “That could push the GAAP net loss to roughly $11–14M, wider than Q1's $7.0M.”

surprises.description: PAVmed’s adjusted loss was lower than the preview’s expected range: non-GAAP net loss was $1.7 million, or $0.27 per share, versus the preview’s $0.35–$0.45 expected loss per share. The preview cautioned that per-share comparisons could be affected by the larger share count.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP net loss was $1.7 million, or $0.27 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP adj. EPS … -$0.35 to -$0.45”; the preview also noted that a per-share “beat” could “reflect share count, not operating improvement.”

surprises.description: The Veris implantable monitor’s submission target moved later than the preview’s late-2026 expectation, to early 2027. That also pushes the FDA-clearance-linked $2.5 million Veris warrant proceeds beyond the timeline the preview was watching.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Veris' implantable physiologic monitor is targeting an early 2027 FDA 510(k) submission”; the $2.5 million warrants are “callable upon FDA clearance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Implantable monitor targeting a late-2026 510(k) submission”; the preview said a slip past year-end 2026 would delay the “$2.5M Veris warrant trigger into 2027.”

surprises.description: Despite the later submission target, Veris reported engineering progress beyond the preview’s identified battery-life hurdle: battery life now exceeds the two-year target, and design freeze is expected this month.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Battery life now exceeding the two-year target and design freeze expected this month.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Battery optimization is the gating engineering item.”

surprises.description: Port IO may use a faster, less capital-intensive 510(k) route rather than the de novo pathway previously expected. First-in-human results also showed 100% device patency and 90% completion in the 10 patients reported.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Port IO may qualify for a faster, less capital-intensive 510(k) pathway rather than the previously expected de novo pathway,” following results showing “100% device patency and 90% completion across 10 patients.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Previously expected de novo pathway.”

in_line: The preview identified the $30 million Series D warrant as contingent on positive Lucid coverage-related news; the call likewise described the proceeds as dependent on warrant exercises tied to positive Lucid ESA guard coverage publication.

surprises.description: Management gave a first-12-month post-U.S.-launch net revenue target of $50–75 million, with Europe contributing about 10–15%. It also said the ramp would be backloaded: about 10% of first-year revenue in the first three months and about 50% in the fourth quarter; the preview had no launch-year revenue target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “first 12-month post-U.S.-launch total net revenue of $50–75 million,” with “Europe contributing about 10–15%,” and “roughly 10% of first-year revenue in the first three months rising to about 50% in the fourth quarter.”

surprises.description: Management projected more than $500 million in peak U.S. annual LightNava sales by 2030, plus roughly $300 million of additional upside if the compounded/repackaged bevacizumab market is disrupted. The preview cited the size of the U.S. retina market but gave no LightNava sales forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LightNava could generate more than $500 million in peak U.S. annual sales by 2030,” assuming repackaged bevacizumab remains available, with “roughly $300 million of additional upside” if that market is disrupted.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited an “$8.5B US retina opportunity” but provided no LightNava sales projection.

surprises.description: The company disclosed a specific WAC target below $500 per vial and said it aims to be competitive with biosimilars and other anti-VEGF therapies. The preview said pricing had not yet been disclosed, so the target resolves a key open question, though it does not establish how the price compares per dose with compounded Avastin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The WAC price for LightNava is expected to fall below $500 per vial,” targeting competitiveness with biosimilars and other anti-VEGF therapies.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pricing. Not yet disclosed.”

surprises.description: NORS 2 showed a higher proportion of LightNava-treated patients achieving at least a 15-letter gain than ranibizumab, a clinical result the preview did not discuss. The reported rates were 41.7% versus 23.1% at month 11.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In the NORS 2 registration trial, 41.7% of LightNava-treated patients gained at least 15 letters at month 11 versus 23.1% for ranibizumab.”

surprises.description: Management put the permanent J-code timeline at April 2027, indicating that a permanent code is not expected immediately around launch. The preview flagged reimbursement as a key adoption issue and described having a code in hand as part of its bull scenario, but gave no expected date.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “anticipates a permanent J-code in April 2027 to accelerate adoption.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Without a permanent or temporary J-code, uptake is likely slow” and listed “reimbursement code in hand” in the bull scenario.

surprises.description: Management outlined a substantial commercial build-out: about 30 customer-facing commercial personnel and about 20 field reimbursement personnel, alongside an expansion of medical affairs. The preview specifically asked for sales-force size but had no expected headcount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to hire approximately 30 customer-facing commercial personnel, about 20 field reimbursement personnel, and expand medical affairs to support the U.S. launch.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “the size of the retina sales force” but did not provide an expected headcount.

surprises.description: Management forecast quarterly SG&A to roughly double from current levels by the end of calendar 2026, then rise by about another 10% in 2027. The preview discussed launch staffing but did not anticipate or quantify this expense trajectory.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects quarterly SG&A to roughly double from current levels by end of calendar 2026 with a further ~10% increase in 2027.”

in_line: The FDA approval was already known before the call: the preview said LightNava was approved July 24, 2026, and the call reported approval three weeks before the call.

The $55 million offering was expected to close on the morning of the report, and the call said it was expected to close; the reported June 30 cash of $11.2 million also matched the preliminary figure noted in the preview.

surprises.description: The preview put Q2 gross revenue at about $3.43 million, implying 14% year-over-year growth; the company reported about $3 million, essentially flat year-over-year and sequentially. That is a meaningful shortfall against the preview’s revenue estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 gross revenue was approximately $3 million, essentially flat both year-over-year and sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross revenue | ~$3.43M (+14% YoY)”

surprises.description: The preview modeled gross margin at 36–38% and warned that the lower-margin Misfits mix could pull it toward 32%; instead, gross margin rose to 41%. Net revenue also increased sequentially to $1.24 million from $1.08 million, above the preview’s Q1 gross-profit-dollar reference of $1.077 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenue increased 16% sequentially to approximately $1.24 million from $1.08 million in Q1, while gross margin improved to 41% from 36% in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | No published consensus (preview’s model ~36–38%)”; “If revenue beats on Misfits while margin falls toward 32%, gross profit dollars may be flat”; “Watch gross profit, not revenue (Q1: $1.077M).”

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash and investments were below the preview’s expected range: about $6.7 million versus $7.3–7.9 million. The figure was still above the preview’s roughly $6.5 million level that it said would suggest accelerating burn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with approximately $6.7 million in cash and investments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The preview estimates about $7.3–7.9M”; “Below ~$6.5M would suggest burn is accelerating.”

surprises.description: Despite the shelf registration and Aegis settlement steps raising dilution concerns, management said it does not anticipate needing to raise additional capital. This reiterates the earlier no-raise stance but offers reassurance against the financing risk highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “[The company] stated it does not anticipate needing to raise additional capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “An S-3 shelf went effective August 11”; the Aegis settlement steps “conflict with the Q1 statement that no raise was planned. Management’s answer on this is the key moment of the call.”

surprises.description: Weighted pipeline per seller rose about 57% from Q1 to approximately $2.8 million, providing a concrete positive indicator for the 2H revenue build the preview said would be needed. The preview had not quantified this pipeline-per-seller improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Weighted pipeline per seller rose about 57% to approximately $2.8 million at the end of Q2, up from roughly $1.78 million at Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “To reach the low end of Street FY26 revenue, 2H needs about $7.6M, roughly a 15%+ step-up on the 1H run-rate. Management has not quantified this.”

surprises.description: The company said it completed the Misfits Ads acquisition without increasing its cost base and now has fewer employees than before the acquisition. That is favorable integration and cost discipline relative to the preview’s concern about Misfits’ lower-margin revenue mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Super League completed the May 2026 acquisition of Misfits Ads assets without increasing its cost base, with total headcount now below pre-acquisition levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Misfits Ads is programmatic revenue, which carries lower margin than Super League’s custom work.”

surprises.description: Billable utilization of the cost-of-goods team rose about 30% versus Q1, a productivity improvement the preview did not identify as an expected Q2 result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Billable client utilization of cost-of-goods team capacity increased approximately 30% relative to Q1.”

surprises.description: Super League eliminated all outstanding preferred stock, further simplifying its capital structure after eliminating debt the prior year. The preview discussed dilution and financing but did not anticipate this preferred-stock elimination.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company eliminated all preferred stock outstanding for the first time in several years, building on last year’s debt elimination to simplify its capital structure.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed adjusted EBITDA profitability in Q4 2026, consistent in timing with the preview’s expectation that management would maintain its fiscal-year-end breakeven target, though the preview described it as cash-EBITDA breakeven.

surprises.description: Gross margin was far weaker than the preview’s 43.5% estimate, falling to 33.9% and well below its 42% warning threshold. Management attributed the decline to lower manufacturing output, scrap, and the Re-Tain cost shift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin fell to 33.9% in Q2 2026 from 43.7% a year earlier, and declined 11.1 points sequentially,” driven by “7.5 points from lower manufacturing output, 2.1 points from ~$150,000 of scrap, and 1.9 points from the Re-Tain cost shift.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate” for gross margin was 43.5%; the preview also said “Below 42% is a problem.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was substantially above the preview’s $1.05–1.15 million estimate, reaching $2.7 million for the quarter. The call said the figure included the $2 million legal settlement, so the large reported gap included a one-off benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.7 million in Q2 2026 (up from $1.4 million) … including the $2 million settlement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s estimate for “Adj. EBITDA” was “$1.05–1.15M.”

surprises.description: GAAP EPS was $0.20, below the preview’s $0.26 estimate for the case where the settlement was booked, even though the $2 million settlement boosted both quarterly and six-month results. It was nevertheless above the preview’s $0.04 ex-settlement estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income was $1.8 million ($0.20 per share) … though both quarter and six-month results were boosted by a $2 million legal settlement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “EPS (GAAP, if settlement booked)” at “$0.26” and “EPS (ex-settlement)” at “$0.04.”

surprises.description: The expansion plan was more fully specified and larger than the preview’s identified $3.5 million phase-one project: the company described approximately $8 million of freeze-drying and liquids-processing investment. It said the work would more than triple capacity and be financed mostly with cash on hand, addressing the preview’s concern about a possible equity raise while requiring a larger investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is investing approximately $8 million ($3.5 million in freeze-drying plus $4.5 million in liquids processing) to more than triple current capacity,” with the investment “financed mostly with cash on hand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “the $3.5M phase-one expansion plus a phase two” and said “an equity raise is a live risk.”

surprises.description: First Defense gained share: the portion of animals treated with a biological scours preventative rose from about 15% to 19%, while its share of producer spending increased from about 29% to 38%. The preview did not identify these market-share gains as an expected outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First Defense's U.S. market share of animals treated with a biological scours preventative rose from ~15% in December 2025 to ~19% by June 2026, lifting its share of producer spending from ~29% to ~38%.”

surprises.description: Distributor out-the-door volume grew 28% year over year in Q2, considerably faster than the 11.5% growth in product sales highlighted in the preview. The different measures mean this is not a direct forecast comparison, but sell-through was a stronger demand signal than the reported sales growth alone suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Distributor out-the-door volume growth was 21% in Q1 and 28% in Q2 2026 year-over-year, averaging 24% for the first half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited pre-announced Q2 product sales of “$7.2M (+11.5% Y/Y).”

surprises.description: Sales were sharply divided by geography: domestic sales grew 27.7%, while international sales fell 38.9%, mainly reflecting the prior year’s Canadian backorder-clearing orders. The preview gave an overall sales figure but did not flag this regional divergence.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Domestic sales grew 27.7% to $6.2 million in Q2, while international sales fell 38.9% to about $1 million, mainly due to Canada's 2025 backorder clearing.”

in_line: Q2 product sales were $7.2 million, matching the preview’s $7.20 million estimate; the 11.5% year-over-year increase had already been pre-announced.

surprises.description: Lantern reported a GAAP loss of $0.57 per share, much worse than the preview’s -$0.38 to -$0.39 consensus, even though operating expenses fell. A $3.6 million warrant-related expense from the May offering drove the net loss higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A May 2026 registered direct offering raised approximately $4.4 million in gross proceeds but triggered a $3.6 million warrant-related expense, driving net loss to $7.1 million ($0.57/share) versus $4.3 million ($0.40/share) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP) … Consensus … -$0.38 (Investing.com) or -$0.39 (TipRanks)”

surprises.description: Despite a quarter-end cash balance within the preview’s expected range, management singled out obtaining additional funding as a top priority. That is more financing-focused than the preview’s base case of reaffirming runway into the middle of Q1 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities declined to approximately $7.4 million at June 30, 2026 from $10.1 million at December 31, 2025, with management flagging additional funding as a top priority.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Runway: ‘Into the middle of Q1 2027’”; “Base: … runway reaffirmed”; “Cash and runway vs. ‘middle of Q1 2027.’ Reaffirmation is neutral; extension is positive; contraction is negative.”

surprises.description: Lantern gave more specific terms for the OMAI separation than the preview had: OMAI is wholly owned for now, plans to raise its own capital, and could eventually list separately, with a possible share distribution to Lantern holders. The plan creates potential standalone value but does not yet provide cash to Lantern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lantern established Open Medicine AI (OMAI) as a separate, 100%-owned entity in August 2026 that intends to raise its own capital and eventually become a separately listed company, with Lantern remaining a large shareholder and potentially distributing shares to Lantern holders.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Not yet disclosed: Lantern's retained ownership, consolidation status, any cash flowing back to Lantern, and any outside capital raised by OMAI.”

surprises.description: The LP-300 study is now planned around a narrower L858R group, eight treatment cycles rather than six, and about 15–16 additional patients over the next four to six months. The preview expected 2H 2026 readouts, so this enrollment plan leaves less clarity that the anticipated timing will hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Following a successful Type C FDA meeting, Lantern narrowed the LP-300 trial to L858R patients, extended treatment from 6 to 8 cycles, and switched to a lower-cost single-arm design, expecting ~15-16 additional patients over the next 4-6 months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Further readouts are guided for 2H 2026”; “HARMONIC 2H26 readout timing and enrollment.”

surprises.description: Lantern reported several new LP-184 advances that the preview had not identified: clearances for small bladder and triple-negative breast cancer trials, plus a notice of allowance for a patient-selection patent spanning four tumor types.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LP-184 advanced on multiple fronts, receiving EMA clearance for a 39-patient dual-biomarker bladder cancer trial in Denmark, FDA clearance for a ~40-patient triple-negative breast cancer trial, and a notice of allowance on a 3-gene patient-selection patent across four tumor types.”

surprises.description: Management introduced a substantial valuation claim around Starlight: Lantern has four potential priority review vouchers and cited recent voucher transfers at $150–200 million or more each. The preview did not flag these potential assets or their cited values.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company holds four potential priority review vouchers via its Starlight pediatric brain cancer program (STAR-001), noting such vouchers recently transferred for $150–200 million or more each.”

surprises.description: Management newly put a large market opportunity around OMAI’s AI tools, estimating the AI-enabled drug-discovery market at $9–10 billion or more by 2030–2031 and saying Open Medicine’s tools could reach several hundred million dollars standalone. The preview discussed OMAI’s separation but not these market or revenue-potential estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management estimates the AI-enabled drug discovery market could reach $9–10+ billion by 2030–2031, with Open Medicine's AI tools potentially growing to several hundred million dollars standalone.”

surprises.description: Lantern also made new claims about the economics and reach of its AI-driven clinical pipeline: over $15 billion in combined annual market potential and first-in-human progress in under three years at $2–3 million per program, versus the stated industry norm of five to ten years and $25–100 million. These claims were not part of the preview’s expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The AI-driven clinical pipeline spans solid tumors, blood cancers and pediatric oncology with combined annual market potential estimated at over $15 billion, and management claims it reached first-in-human trials in under 3 years at roughly $2–3 million per program versus an industry norm of 5–10 years and $25–100 million.”

in_line: Cash and marketable securities were $7.4 million at quarter-end, within the preview’s $6.8–$7.4 million base-case range and close to its estimate of roughly $7.2 million.
Operating expenses were down 25% year over year, consistent with the preview’s expectation that losses would narrow year over year and opex would remain near the Q1 run rate.
The HARMONIC L858R six-cycle subgroup’s 8.9-month median PFS was already reported in the preview as earlier data; the result was not new relative to that expectation.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $1.1 million, below the preview’s $1.30 million estimate and well below the $1.80 million consensus figure. The preview already allowed for the Judith Ripka divestiture, so the reported revenue was weaker than its own estimate as well as consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue declined to $1.1 million from $1.3 million a year earlier,” primarily due to the Judith Ripka divestiture.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate: Revenue $1.30M”; consensus revenue was “$1.80M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected the Judith Ripka sale to push GAAP results near breakeven or positive, but Xcel reported a Q2 net loss of about $2.5 million. The loss was narrower than a year ago, but much worse than the preview’s stated expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss for Q2 2026 narrowed to approximately $2.5 million (-$0.40 per share) from a $4 million loss” in the prior-year quarter.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 likely carries a gain on the Ripka sale, which could push GAAP results near breakeven or positive.”

surprises.description: One influencer-led brand launch was deferred to 2027, whereas the preview specifically highlighted fall 2026 launches as an important timing catalyst. The rest of the balance is still expected to launch this fall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Xcel launched 2 influencer-led brands … in Q1 2026, with the balance launching this fall except one deferred to 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Fall 2026 launch timing” and said “A slip pushes the first real revenue ramp into 2027.”

surprises.description: Xcel reported that its influencer-led brands had expanded the portfolio’s social following to more than 46 million in under a year, a scale metric the preview did not anticipate. The figure is an audience measure rather than evidence of royalties or sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: Influencer-led brands grew the portfolio’s social media following “from 5 million to over 46 million in under a year,” with a goal of 100 million.

surprises.description: Management set a long-term target for each of Xcel’s eight existing brands to average $7 million a year in royalty income by the end of 2030. The preview discussed the portfolio and new launches but did not give this brand-level revenue target.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “targets each of its 8 existing brands generating an average of $7 million per year in royalty income by the end of 2030.”

surprises.description: Management said most current interest is being paid in kind, with no cash payment due until 2027. This provides a near-term cash-flow cushion not described in the preview, although the preview had already identified the equity line as a potential dilutive funding source.
surprises.fact_evidence: Liquidity levers include “a majority of current interest being paid in kind (no cash payment until 2027)” and “a $15 million committed equity line available over the next 2 years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified the “dilutive equity line” as a visible financing tool.

surprises.description: Interest and finance expense was substantially lower than a year earlier, but management attributed much of the comparison to the absence of a prior-year debt-extinguishment loss. That favorable expense comparison was not highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Interest and finance expense dropped to approximately $0.9 million in Q2 2026 from $2.3 million a year earlier,” aided by the absence of a prior-year “$1.9 million debt extinguishment loss.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA loss was about $480,000: close to the preview’s $550,000 estimate and within its $400,000–$700,000 base-case range. It also narrowed sequentially from Q1’s $700,000 loss, as the preview was watching for, although it widened year over year on the reported comparison.

Unrestricted cash of about $400,000 was very low, but consistent with the preview’s warning that cash below $1 million could force financing; the preview also identified the equity line as a likely funding tool.

The Judith Ripka sale was already anticipated in the preview, which noted it had been sold. The reported sale multiple of approximately 6x gross royalty income was consistent with the multiple on the prior Isaac Mizrahi divestiture.

surprises.description: Q3 revenue was $14.4 million, $1.1 million below the preview’s $15.5 million model and below the $15.4 million year-ago comparison. The preview identified revenue below roughly $15 million as making the full-year growth goal difficult.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 FY2026 revenue declined to $14.4 million from $15.4 million a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 FY26 (model estimate) $15.5M”; “Q3 revenue under about $15M makes full-year growth very hard to hit.”

surprises.description: Service revenue fell to $4.5 million, well below the preview’s $5.3 million comparison and its $5.4 million level for supporting the managed-cloud thesis. Management attributed the decline to vendor delivery delays.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue falling to $4.5 million from $5.3 million due to vendor delivery delays.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “At or above $5.4M supports the managed-cloud thesis; below $5.0M puts it at risk”; the catalyst checklist also flagged “Service revenue at or above $5.3M.”

surprises.description: The quarter produced a $0.09-per-share loss rather than the preview’s modeled $0.04-per-share profit, a 13-cent-per-share shortfall. The loss also widened from $0.03 per share a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 net loss of $846,000 ($0.09 per share), widening from a net loss of $264,000 ($0.03 per share) in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) … Q3 FY26 (model estimate) $0.04.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 30.1%, 1.9 percentage points below the preview’s 32.0% model. Product gross margin improved sharply, but service gross margin fell, and the overall result did not reach the preview’s margin threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall gross margin expanded more than 100 basis points to 30.1% of sales, driven by product gross margin rising to 20.7% from 15.7%, even as service gross margin dipped to 51.2% from 53.9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin … Q3 FY26 (model estimate) 32.0%”; the preview also flagged “Gross margin of 32% or higher alongside revenue growth.”

surprises.description: Technology Solutions backlog was up 65% year over year, but hardware delivery times have stretched from 30–60 days to more than 200 days, and management expects the supply constraint to last at least another year. This adds a prolonged delivery risk not identified in the preview and helps explain the revenue and service shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Technology Solutions backlog is now 65% higher than a year ago because hardware vendor delivery times have stretched from a historical 30-60 days to over 200 days, a supply constraint management expects to persist for at least a year.”

surprises.description: AZT Protect showed strong customer retention: every site that reached its one-year renewal point renewed, and management said no customer has experienced a breach. The preview described AZT Protect as a narrative driver but did not anticipate these retention and security outcomes.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AZT Protect achieved a 100% renewal rate on all customer sites reaching their one-year mark, and no AZT Protect customer has experienced a breach to date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dollars are small, so this is more a narrative driver than a Q3 numbers driver.”

surprises.description: The company reported two sizable managed-service wins: a six-year, seven-figure agreement with a professional sports team and a three-year food-distributor deal expected to generate mid-six-figure annual recurring revenue. The preview anticipated AZT Protect as a narrative catalyst but did not flag contracts of this scale or provide comparable booked-revenue expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed a 6-year, 7-figure managed service agreement with a nationally recognized professional sports team and a 3-year deal with a food distributor expected to generate mid-6-figure annual recurring revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AZT PROTECT … Dollars are small, so this is more a narrative driver than a Q3 numbers driver.”

surprises.description: Management described long sales cycles of 18–24 months for large enterprise AZT Protect deals, although smaller wastewater deals can close in six weeks. One major opportunity has narrowed to two finalists, which signals progress but also suggests that large opportunities may take considerable time to convert.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Large enterprise AZT Protect deals carry 18-to-24-month sales cycles, with one major opportunity having narrowed from 15 competing products down to a final two, while smaller wastewater deals have closed in as little as 6 weeks.”

surprises.description: Cash increased to $24.7 million from the $23.1 million reported at the prior quarter-end, rather than showing the further meaningful cash draw the preview warned about. The company also reported continuing repurchases and a dividend.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $24.7 million in cash and cash equivalents”; it also “continued returning capital by repurchasing approximately 13,000 shares and declaring a $0.03 per share dividend.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash $23.1M at 3/31/26”; “A further meaningful cash draw would weaken the valuation floor.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a couple hundred thousand dollars of costs tied to the U.K. pension buyout/sale, an expense the preview did not flag. This was an unanticipated cost alongside an already loss-making quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Incurring a couple hundred thousand dollars in costs from the U.K. pension buyout/sale.”

surprises.description: Management gave a nearer-term AZT Protect/Coronis integration milestone, targeting completion by October 1 and a fall launch, but could not quantify expected revenue from the partnership. The preview had not mentioned this partnership or its timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AZT Protect integration with Coronis (Cronos) software is targeted for completion by October 1 with a fall product launch, though management could not yet quantify expected revenue from the partnership.”

in_line: The $0.03-per-share dividend was declared as expected; the preview also modeled a $0.03 dividend.

surprises.description: BayFirst’s identified one-time and asset-resolution charges were $43.8 million, modestly above the preview’s $40.1 million estimate. Despite the higher charges, the $32.7 million net loss was slightly less severe than the preview’s forecast range.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call reported “$43.8 million in one-time asset resolution and nonrecurring charges” and a “Q2 2026 net loss of $32.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Pre-announced charges” of “−$40.1M” and a net loss of “−$33M to −$45M.”

surprises.description: BayFirst reserved much more heavily against its risky unguaranteed SBA portfolios than the preview’s roughly 13% coverage estimate: BOLT was at 33% and FlashCap at 25%. That creates a substantially larger loss cushion, though it came with a sharp increase in the quarter’s credit-loss provision.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call said the “$60 million BOLT portfolio” had a “33% reserve” and the “$29 million FlashCap portfolio” a “25%” reserve; provision for credit losses rose to “$29.7 million in Q2” from “$3.4 million in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the roughly “$100M” of higher-risk BOLT and FlashCap loans were “reserved at about 13%”; its bull scenario contemplated lifting reserves to “18–20%.”

surprises.description: Tangible book value per share finished at $4.82, above the preview’s estimated pro forma range of $3.50–$4.05, even after the asset-resolution charges and preferred-share conversion dilution.
surprises.fact_evidence: Tangible book value per share was “$4.82” at quarter-end, down from “$14.22” at the end of Q1.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “pro forma TBV at about $3.50–$4.05 per share.”

surprises.description: Reported NIM was slightly above the preview’s estimated range, and management’s normalized figure was considerably higher still. The reported 3.48% exceeded the 3.25–3.45% estimate by only a few basis points, while normalized NIM was 4.07%.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call reported normalized net interest margin of “4.07%” versus reported NIM of “3.48%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated Q2 net interest margin of “3.25–3.45%.”

surprises.description: Management said the rights offering was delayed by the restatement, with the offering now set to launch in August. The preview noted the offering’s proceeds and results were unverified but did not anticipate a restatement-driven delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call said “the rights offering” was “delayed by the restatement” and “is set to launch in August.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Final rights offering results (subscription rate and proceeds on up to $14.4M at $3.50) were not verified.”

surprises.description: Management described a plan to rebuild the retail footprint with a new South Tampa branch in September while shifting away from SBA 7(a) lending toward commercial and consumer lending and treasury services. The preview emphasized a shrinking balance sheet and very low community-bank loan production but did not flag this branch opening or strategic repositioning.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call said BayFirst is “pivoting from SBA 7(a) lending” toward “traditional commercial and consumer lending and treasury services” and plans a “new South Tampa branch in September” to return to 12 retail locations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described a “Shrinking balance sheet” and noted community banking loan production of “$1.6M” in Q1 2026.

in_line: The $32.7 million net loss was within the preview’s $33–$45 million loss range and marginally less severe than its best-case end.
Total capital was 12.77%, within the preview’s estimated 11–13% range.
Deposits fell $97 million, close to the $98 million Q1 decline; the preview specifically flagged another quarter of similar runoff as a key risk.

surprises.description: DTST reported Q2 revenue of $359K, below the preview’s $400K consensus estimate. It was nevertheless within the preview’s $355–375K base-case range, and the preview cautioned that consensus might not have been rebased to the post-sale business.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue from continuing operations (Nexus) grew 9.3% year-over-year to $359,000 for Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus | $400K”; the preview also gave a “Base” scenario of “$355–375K, +5–10% YoY” and cautioned that the consensus “does not appear to have been rebased to Nexxis-only revenue.”

surprises.description: Gross margin came in at 47%, below the preview’s expected 52–56% range for Nexxis. The company did expand margin year over year, but not to the level the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanding to 47% from 42.1%, attributed to favorable sales mix and operating leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Nexxis grows at 52–56% gross margin” in the preview’s base scenario.

surprises.description: The net loss widened to $1.2M, substantially worse than the preview’s base-case EPS loss estimate of $0.13–$0.18 per share. The call facts do not provide reported EPS, so the precise per-share miss cannot be quantified here.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss attributable to common shareholders widened to $1.2 million from $732,000 in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected EPS of “$(0.13)–(0.18)”; even its bear case was “$(0.22)–(0.30).”

surprises.description: Rather than normalizing, SG&A rose 33.2% to $1.5M, above the preview’s bear-case threshold of $1.4M or more. The increase was attributed mainly to higher non-cash stock compensation and professional fees.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A expenses increased 33.2% to $1.5 million, primarily from a 99.1% ($328,000) jump in non-cash stock-based compensation and a 26.2% rise in professional fees.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch whether SG&A “normalizes,” and listed “SG&A at or above $1.4M” as a bear-case driver.

surprises.description: Management gave a specific near-term acquisition-search timetable and described a substantial screened pipeline: it aims to sign a non-binding LOI in 45–60 days and close an acquisition by late 2026 or early 2027. The preview had flagged acquisition spending as a risk, but did not anticipate this pipeline disclosure or timetable; management also said capital is constrained and many target valuations are unrealistic.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “evaluated roughly 124 companies and screened over 15 reverse-merger proposals”; the CEO set an objective to “sign a non-binding LOI within 45–60 days” and “close an acquisition by the end of Q4 2026 or in Q1 2027.” Acquisitions would use “upfront cash plus earn-outs,” with the CEO noting “capital constraints” and unrealistic valuations among many targets.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “Funding a speculative AI build or an acquisition” as a risk, but its milestone discussion focused on SaiS initial customer agreements by “Q4 2026 or early 2027” and a possible “named design partner, LOI, or product milestone.”

in_line: Nexxis revenue grew 9.3% year over year, within the preview’s 5–10% base-case growth range.

Cash and marketable securities were approximately $9.3M, within the preview’s $9.2–9.5M base-case estimate; the company also had no long-term debt, consistent with the preview’s debt-free balance-sheet framing.

surprises.description: Volition reported operating expenses of $4.6 million, down 32% year over year, and said its cost program included a 27% headcount reduction. The preview’s base case assumed in-line burn, so the extent of the expense reduction was a positive operating development, although the reported expense figure was still just above the preview’s bull-case threshold of less than $4.5 million in burn.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell 32% year-over-year to $4.6 million,” including “a 27% headcount reduction versus 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed “in-line burn”; its bull case required “burn cut below $4.5M.”

surprises.description: Four agreements with multibillion-dollar companies are now signed, whereas the preview described more than a dozen companies as still in discussions and said a signed agreement could change the funding picture. No upfront payment or other deal economics were disclosed in the call facts, so the agreements do not establish the funding benefit the preview highlighted.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Volition now has four signed agreements with multibillion-dollar companies (Werfen, Sysmex, Revvity, Hologic).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management had cited “more than a dozen” companies in discussions; “A signed agreement with a disclosed upfront would change the funding picture.”

surprises.description: The preview’s revenue expectation was met overall, but Discover Services produced no Q2 revenue because of project timing, with higher Nu.Q Vet revenue offsetting the shortfall. That zero-services quarter is a negative segment-level development not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 revenue was “approximately $0.4 million, flat” year over year, as “higher Nu.Q Vet revenue was offset by lower Nu.Q Discover services revenue”; Discover Services revenue was “$0 in Q2 due to project timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview implied Q2 revenue of “roughly $0.4–0.5M” and gave a base-case range of “$0.30–0.45M.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed about $3 million of noncash Lind-note accounting charges as the primary reason the net loss widened, rather than simply describing Lind as a dilution or conversion risk. Lower operating expenses partly offset the charges, so the loss increase does not by itself establish an operating deterioration of the same size.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net loss widened to $7.3 million from $6.3 million,” driven primarily by “approximately $3 million in non-cash accounting charges related to Lind convertible notes,” partly offset by “$2.1 million in lower operating expenses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview focused on “Going-concern language and Lind note conversions” and described the conversion terms and “dilution spiral risk.”

surprises.description: A lateral-flow fingerprint sepsis assay showed approximately 90% correlation with Volition’s CE-marked automated Nu.Q NETs assay, adding a point-of-care and low-income-country application that the preview did not discuss. This is a promising prototype result, not evidence of a commercial launch.
surprises.fact_evidence: The prototype “demonstrated approximately 90% correlation with its CE-marked automated Nu.Q NETs assay,” potentially expanding the market into “point-of-care and low-income countries.”

surprises.description: The call described Capture-Seq as targeting estimated annualized markets of about $23 billion for multi-cancer early detection and more than $13 billion for minimal residual disease. The preview did not discuss this technology or quantify these markets; the figures are addressable-market estimates, not reported sales or contracted revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capture-Seq liquid biopsy technology targets an estimated annualized total addressable market of approximately $23 billion for multi-cancer early detection and over $13 billion for minimal residual disease.”

surprises.description: Management said a Mayo Clinic i10 analyzer placement is expected this quarter, a near-term placement milestone not mentioned in the preview. The placement was still expected, not reported as completed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A Mayo Clinic i10 analyzer placement [is] expected this quarter.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of approximately $0.4 million was within the preview’s implied $0.4–0.5 million range and its $0.30–0.45 million base-case range; first-half revenue of $1.4 million was also consistent with the Q1 actual plus the expected Q2 level.
Quarter-end cash of approximately $2.8 million was within the preview’s $2.3–3.2 million estimate. The preview also anticipated continued reliance on ATM and other financing.
Management gave no 2026 revenue guidance, consistent with the preview’s finding that no company guidance was available.
The feline lymphoma publication and associated $5 million milestone payment remained pending; the preview’s base case anticipated the milestone would still be under review.

surprises.description: BIO-key reported Q2 revenue of $1.92 million, well below the company’s approximately $2.8 million guidance. Management attributed the miss to a large hardware order slipping from Q2 into the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 total revenue grew 13% to $1.92 million, but results missed expectations due to a large hardware order that slipped from Q2 into the second half of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company guidance (Q2, 18 May 2026): Revenue ~$2.8M”; the preview says actual revenue was about 31% below guide.

surprises.description: Instead of the profitability expected for both Q2 and the first half, BIO-key reported a $577,000 Q2 net loss and a $782,000 first-half net loss. Management is now targeting profitability in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss improved 51% to $577,000 ($0.56 per share) in Q2, and improved 59% to $782,000 for the first half; management is targeting profitability for the second half of 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists Q2 guidance of “Net income: Profitable” and “EPS: Positive,” and first-half guidance of “Net result: Profitable.”

surprises.description: Gross margin rose to 87% from 73%, a sharp expansion not anticipated in the preview. Management said the higher license mix and sales of previously fully reserved inventory, which carry 100% gross profit, boosted the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded sharply to a record-like 87% from 73% a year ago, boosted by the higher-margin license mix and sales of previously fully-reserved inventory that carry 100% gross profit.”

surprises.description: License fee revenue jumped 53% on new customer agreements, an unexpectedly strong product-line result; the preview discussed new customer announcements but did not forecast this revenue growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “License fee revenue jumped 53% to $1.2 million on new customer agreements.”

surprises.description: Service revenue fell 28% to $231,000, a contraction the preview did not flag or quantify.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue dropped 28% to $231,000.”

surprises.description: Management gave a more concrete potential scale and timing for the Central Bank of Jordan initiative than the preview had: it could build over the next two to three quarters toward ARR comparable to a South African bank customer generating over $1 million. This is a potential, not a reported contract value or committed ARR.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Central Bank of Jordan initiative was won sole-source in a competitive bid and could scale over the next two to three quarters toward ARR comparable to a South African bank customer generating over $1 million in ARR.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the new logos’ “Dollar values, timing, and whether any of these are in 2H guidance were not disclosed.”

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s concern that cash runway looked like two to three quarters absent improvement and its warning about possible further raises, management said no further dilution was expected. The statement is tempered by the fact that roughly 300,000 warrants from the recent financing had already been exercised.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management stated no further dilution is expected, though roughly 300,000 of the newly issued 1.2 million warrants (held under a 9.9% ownership blocker) have already been exercised in the days following the raise.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said cash runway “looks like two to three quarters absent improvement” and listed a bear scenario in which management “signals further raises.”

surprises.description: Management also reported a growing EMEA pipeline across government, defense, financial services, and education, a breadth-of-pipeline update not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged growing EMEA pipeline deals across government, defense, financial services, and education.”

in_line: The hardware-order deferral into the second half was already flagged in the preview as roughly $800,000 of hardware revenue that had slipped from Q2; the call again cited a hardware order slipping into the second half.
The August warrant inducement and roughly $2.3 million in net proceeds were already described in the preview; the call reported $2.5 million gross proceeds and current cash above $4.5 million.
Nasdaq resumption after the reverse split was already noted in the preview, which said the stock returned to Nasdaq on July 8.

surprises.description: TOMI reported a Q2 loss of $0.05 per share, narrower than the preview’s cited $0.11-per-share loss estimate. That is a roughly $0.06-per-share beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss improved 69% to approximately $382,000, or $0.05 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS | $(0.11), H.C. Wainwright (A. Dayal), Aug 3, 2026.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 61.7%, well below the 70% implied by the July 9 pre-announcement framing. The preview had already identified that level as a risk, but the reported shortfall was still substantial.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin improved to 61.7% from 50.3% in Q1 2026, though it remained below the 65.7% recorded in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | 70% implied by July 9 pre-announcement | 61.7% | Miss vs. pre-announced framing.”

surprises.description: Management added a specific expectation that TOMI will reach breakeven comfortably by Q4 2026, a favorable operating milestone not mentioned in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating loss narrowed 78% year-over-year to approximately $244,000, and management stated it expects to reach breakeven comfortably by Q4 2026.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted the $10 million merger-financing condition as a key open question; the call said it was still under negotiation, rather than reporting that the financing had been committed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $10 million minimum concurrent financing condition [is] still under negotiation before closing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Whether the ≥$10M is committed or still ‘in discussions’ is the most important disclosure.”

surprises.description: Q2 operating expenses included about $300,000 of elevated advisory, legal, and diligence costs for the pending merger, an expense not flagged in the preview. Management expects these costs to decline after closing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 operating expenses included roughly $300,000 in elevated advisory, legal, and diligence costs tied to the pending Carbonium Core merger, which management expects to decline once the deal closes.”

surprises.description: The call cited a broader commercial pipeline of approximately $35 million in support of the $12 million revenue guide. This adds potential coverage beyond the booked and expected completions discussed in the preview, though it does not establish that the pipeline will convert.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance of at least $12 million, supported by booked orders and expected completions exceeding $6.2 million and a broader commercial pipeline of approximately $35 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Backlog of $2.6M plus $6.2M of booked or expected orders gets to about $10.1M, roughly $1.9M short. The guide is achievable but not yet backed by orders.”

in_line: Q2 revenue of about $2.25 million was in line with the preview’s approximately $2.3 million expectation.
The company reaffirmed its at-least-$12-million FY2026 revenue guide, as expected.
Applicator sales of $355,000 versus $13,000 a year earlier matched the preview’s cited increase.
Backlog reached $2.6 million currently, consistent with the preview’s $2.6 million figure; the call also reported $2.2 million at quarter-end.

Cash remained about $0.3 million, consistent with the preview’s liquidity concern. The call added that TOMI raised $1.92 million net during the quarter and had approximately $18.1 million of ELOC capacity remaining, while liquidity still depended on the ELOC.
