surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate a Hart-Hanks acquisition. Star agreed to buy it for about $30 million, funded half in cash and half in preferred stock, and said the deal should be accretive with $10 million of cost synergies; closing is targeted for Q4, subject to approvals.
surprises.fact_evidence: Star Equity announced a merger agreement to acquire Hart-Hanks for $5 per share (~$30 million on a fully diluted basis), funded half in cash and half in Star preferred stock, with no common shares issued and no external capital needed. Management is targeting $10 million in cost synergies and expects the deal to be accretive.

surprises.description: The preview expected delayed Building Solutions projects to close in Q2, backlog to rebuild above $12 million, and book-to-bill to reach at least 1.0x. Instead, revenue was $14.6 million versus $20.4 million pro forma, backlog was $10.6 million, and Q2 orders of $17.3 million remained below the $20 million normal run rate; a large project's revenue shifted to Q3.
surprises.fact_evidence: Building solutions materially underperformed with revenue of $14.6 million (down from $20.4 million pro forma), hurt by market softness and a large project whose revenue shifts to Q3. Backlog rose to $10.6 million with Q2 orders of $17.3 million, still below the $20 million normal run rate.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for backlog above $12M and book-to-bill of at least 1.0x”; the preview also said management expected “delayed projects would close in Q2 and backlog would rebuild.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Business Services to convert the strong Q1 new-business wins into gross profit in Q2. Revenue grew 2%, but gross profit fell 4% and adjusted EBITDA declined to $1.6 million from $2.2 million, with management citing higher growth investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: Business services revenue grew 2% to $36.4 million, but gross profit declined 4% to $17.8 million and adjusted EBITDA fell to $1.6 million from $2.2 million, driven by $1.5 million in growth investments versus $0.8 million a year ago.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 new-business wins were strong, but the segment still lost about $0.3M of adj. EBITDA. Q2 is when that business should convert to gross profit.”

surprises.description: The preview did not call out Energy Services as a key debate or provide a segment forecast, but the segment reported strong growth: revenue rose 19%, gross profit 75%, and adjusted EBITDA 126%.
surprises.fact_evidence: Energy services delivered strong growth with revenue up 19% to $3.9 million, gross profit up 75% to $1.9 million, and adjusted EBITDA up 126% to $1.2 million.

surprises.description: Hudson merger synergies reached about $3 million, above the original $2 million projection. The preview noted the Hudson merger but did not flag this higher-than-planned synergy realization.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Hudson merger cost synergies reached approximately $3 million, exceeding the originally projected $2 million; corporate costs fell to $3.6 million for the first half from $5.1 million pro forma a year earlier.

surprises.description: Business Services new-logo wins were only $2.1 million in year-to-date annual contract value, below the much higher expectation referenced on the call. The preview had noted strong Q1 new-business wins but did not flag this weaker year-to-date figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: New logo wins in business services were weak at just $2.1 million year-to-date annual contract value versus a much higher expectation.

surprises.description: Cash ended Q2 at $8.9 million, including restricted cash, below the preview's $9 million bear-case threshold; working capital excluding cash also declined from year-end. This points to weaker liquidity than the preview's watchlist was concerned about.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended Q2 with $8.9 million in cash (including $2.1 million restricted) and working capital excluding cash of $21.5 million, down from $22.4 million at year-end.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's bear scenario included “cash falls below $9M.”

surprises.description: Star repurchased about $0.2 million of shares and plans to continue buybacks, an unanticipated use of capital given the preview's focus on liquidity and preferred ATM usage. The company said it believes its stock is undervalued.
surprises.fact_evidence: Star repurchased about $0.2 million of shares in Q2, with $1.6 million remaining on its $3 million authorization, and plans to continue buybacks believing its stock is undervalued.

surprises.description: Barfresh cut its FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA outlook from positive $3.2–$3.8 million to a loss of $1–$2 million, and now expects the second half to range from a $500,000 loss to breakeven. This is a much larger reversal than the preview’s base case of trimming the outlook to the low end or its bear case of a cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management cut full-year 2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance to negative $1 million to $2 million, and now expects back-half Adjusted EBITDA of negative $500,000 to breakeven.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA $3.2M – $3.8M”; the base scenario anticipated it might be “trimmed to low end,” and the bear scenario anticipated a “FY cut.”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to negative 3.2%, a gross loss, rather than showing the recovery the preview expected after management said Arps startup inefficiencies would be mostly behind the company by the end of Q2. The reported result was also far below the preview’s 20%–24% base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company swung to a gross loss of $150,000 (negative 3.2% of revenue) … driven by startup costs and low productivity at the Arps facility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Management said inefficiencies would be “mostly behind us by end of Q2”; the base case expected “gross margin 20%–24%.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $4.7 million missed the company’s $5.2–$5.6 million guide, not just the higher stale consensus. The shortfall was about 10% below the bottom of the company’s range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 190% year-over-year to $4.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Company guidance (Q2) | $5.2M – $5.6M”; the preview said this was “the operative bar.”

surprises.description: The company lowered FY2026 revenue guidance to $23–$26 million from $28–$32 million. Even the new range’s high end is below the prior range’s low end, and the cut was deeper than the preview’s base case of a trim to $26–$29 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was set at $23 million to $26 million … lowered partly due to removal of ice cream mix production and slower recovery from prior school-year supply issues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue: $28M – $32M”; the base scenario anticipated “FY trimmed to low end or $26M–$29M.”

surprises.description: Q2 Adjusted EBITDA loss was approximately $1.2 million, far worse than the preview’s expected quarterly loss of $200,000–$300,000. The reported loss was roughly four to six times the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA loss doubled to approximately $1.2 million from $600,000 in the prior-year period.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Company guidance (Q2) | -$0.3M to -$0.2M.”

surprises.description: Barfresh removed its higher-margin ice cream mix business from the Arps facility because the aging facility could not reliably produce it alongside other products. Management quantified the lost ice cream business at $800,000 as a driver of the EBITDA outlook shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Barfresh removed its higher-margin ice cream mix business from the Arps facility because aging infrastructure could not reliably run both product lines simultaneously”; management cited “$800,000 lost ice cream business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance was “$3.2M – $3.8M” and it described Arps inefficiencies as expected to be “mostly behind us by end of Q2.”

surprises.description: The legacy Barfresh business grew only 9%, with customer recovery pushed into the 2026–2027 school year. That weak recovery conflicts with the sharp second-half ramp the preview said was needed to support the original full-year outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The legacy Barfresh frozen beverage and food segment grew only 9% year-over-year,” with “customer recovery” pushed into “the 2026-2027 school year”; management cited “$600,000 delayed legacy Barfresh recovery” as an outlook shortfall driver.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the FY range required “roughly $17M–$21M in H2” and that this “implies a sharp step-up from the current run-rate.”

surprises.description: Management identified $800,000 of material cost increases as a driver of the Adjusted EBITDA outlook shortfall, an additional cost headwind beyond the startup and production issues already affecting the business.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management quantified “$800,000 material cost increases” among the drivers of the Adjusted EBITDA guidance shortfall.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$3.2M – $3.8M.”

surprises.description: Management said $600,000 of expected synergies had not been realized, adding another shortfall driver to the outlook. The preview’s prior positive FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance did not flag this risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management quantified “$600,000 in unrealized synergies” as a driver of the Adjusted EBITDA guidance shortfall.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited FY2026 Adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$3.2M – $3.8M.”

surprises.description: Liquidity was much thinner at quarter-end: cash and receivables were about $1.4 million, versus $4.1 million at March 31 in the preview. This leaves limited near-term balance-sheet resources while the company is still prioritizing the Defiance facility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The balance sheet is thin, with roughly $1.4 million of cash and accounts receivable … as of June 30, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash plus receivables was $4.1M at 3/31/26,” and the preview flagged “Liquidity and the Defiance facility” as a key issue.

surprises.description: Defiance construction costs rose more than anticipated, and the company now expects to use a new mortgage and equipment financing rather than an equity raise. The preview flagged liquidity and the facility but did not anticipate this cost escalation or financing approach.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Construction costs have risen more than anticipated, requiring a new mortgage and equipment financing rather than an equity raise.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Liquidity and the Defiance facility” and noted that the facility had “already slipped once.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $1.8 million, about 29% below the post-recall consensus of $2.54 million. The $734,000 customer credit from the recall more than offset gross U.S. product sales, making the reported shortfall materially worse than the preview’s consensus baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue was $1.8 million”; “A voluntary recall … triggered a $734,000 customer credit that more than offset gross U.S. product sales in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $2.54M” (post-recall Q2 2026 estimate).

surprises.description: International revenue reached $2.1 million, but the preview expected $2.3–2.6 million. It still grew 21% year over year on demand, yet came in below the expected range and below Q1’s $2.2 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International revenue grew approximately 21% year-over-year to $2.1 million, driven entirely by demand with immaterial FX impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The full preview's expectation is $2.3–2.6M”; Q1 international revenue was “$2.2M.”

surprises.description: The original CGuard delivery system’s FDA approval moved from the expected Q3 2026 timing to Q4 2026. The preview had specifically flagged a Q3 approval and U.S. re-entry as the expected timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FDA approval timing for the original CGuard delivery system slipped from Q3 to Q4 as management adopted more conservative regulatory timeline assumptions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided to Q3 2026 approval and a Q3 U.S. re-entry.”

surprises.description: Management announced a nearly 20% workforce reduction with about $9 million in annual savings, a larger cost-reduction action than the preview’s discussion of pausing headcount additions. The savings are partly offset initially by a $900,000–$1.2 million restructuring charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A workforce reduction of nearly 20% initiated in Q3 is expected to save approximately $9 million annually, with a $900,000-$1.2 million restructuring charge in Q3 and the full run-rate benefit visible in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said it would pause headcount adds pending FDA clarity”; the preview said to watch whether OpEx came in below Q1’s $14.7M as evidence “the hiring pause is real.”

surprises.description: The quarterly loss per share was smaller than expected: $0.17 versus the consensus loss estimate of $0.183 per share.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $14.3 million ($0.17 per share).”

in_line: The recall-related customer credit and inventory impairment were close to the preview’s flagged estimates: the preview cited about $700,000 for customer returns and about $650,000 for inventory impairment and remediation; the reported figures were a $734,000 customer credit and a $612,000 inventory impairment.
Liquidity was close to the preview’s estimate: cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities were $30.4 million, versus an expected roughly $29–30 million at the preview’s assumed burn rate.
The Prime 80 / TCAR approval timing remained within the preview’s expected H2 2026 window: management expected FDA approval in Q4 2026.

surprises.description: Nuvve's gross margin fell to 2.6% from 26.1%, and product and service margins excluding grants turned negative at -14.5%. The preview did not forecast margin pressure or the Troy write-down, low-margin hardware mix, and elevated warranty costs behind it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margins collapsed to 2.6% in Q2 2026 from 26.1% a year ago,” hurt by a “$1.2 million write-down on the Troy project,” low-margin hardware sales, and warranty costs; excluding grants, product and service margins were “-14.5% versus +11.6%.”

surprises.description: Cash at quarter-end was $0.5 million, below the preview's $0.8–1.5 million base-case range and at the preview's bear-case threshold. The shortfall came despite $1.2 million raised through stock and warrant exercises and $1.4 million of new debt.
surprises.fact_evidence: Cash was “$0.5 million as of June 30, 2026 (plus $0.3 million restricted),” down $1.4 million sequentially; the company raised $1.2 million through stock and warrant exercises and took on $1.4 million in new debt.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case expected “Ending cash at 6/30/26” of “$0.8–1.5M”; its bear case was “under $0.5M.”

surprises.description: Operating cash use was $3.6 million, above the preview's base-case estimate of $2–3 million in burn. This points to a worse cash draw during the quarter than the preview assumed.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “used $3.6 million in operating activities during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case assumed “burn of $2–3M.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $1.23 million came in just below the preview's $1.3–1.8 million base-case estimate, although it exceeded the preview's bear-case threshold. The preview said there was no reliable consensus, so this is a modest miss against its own estimate rather than a consensus miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 2026 revenue was “$1.23 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's own base estimate was “$1.3–1.8M”; it also stated, “Revenue (Q2) … Consensus: None reliable.”

surprises.description: Nuvve raised capital during the quarter rather than following the preview's base-case assumption of no new capital. The funding partly offset cash burn, but it included new debt as well as stock and warrant issuance, and the preview did not establish that the terms were workable.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company raised “$1.2 million through issuance of common and preferred stock and warrant exercises” and took on “$1.4 million in new debt” to partially offset cash burn.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview's base case specified “no new capital”; its bull case anticipated financing “with the print on workable terms.”

in_line: Megawatts under management increased, consistent with the preview's note that management had cited growth, though the preview provided no numeric expectation.

surprises.description: Sidus reported that it joined the Russell 3000, Russell 2000, and Russell Microcap Indexes in the June reconstitution, a development the preview did not mention. The call said this expands institutional-investor eligibility and is expected to improve trading liquidity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sidus joined the Russell 3000, Russell 2000, and Russell Microcap Indexes in the June 2026 reconstitution,” expanding institutional investor eligibility and expected trading liquidity.

surprises.description: The preview focused on the Fortis platform’s TRL-9 path and potential near-term customer evidence, but the call put full commercial availability in early 2027 and said integration and customer qualifications are still underway. That introduces a commercialization timeline and remaining gates the preview had not specified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full commercial availability of the Fortis VPX platform is anticipated in early 2027,” subject to “final integration and customer qualifications currently underway.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted the “Fortis Maxima TRL-9 path” and said a paying hardware customer or purchase order would support recurring-revenue evidence, but gave no commercial-availability date.

in_line: Q2 revenue was approximately $583,000, within the preview’s $0.4–0.6 million base scenario; the preview also said a sharp year-over-year decline was likely, and revenue fell 54%.
June 30 cash was $166.5 million, within the preview’s estimated $165–175 million range.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was approximately $3.57 million, inferred from H1 revenue of $7.6 million less Q1's $4.03 million. That was about 6% below the preview's roughly $3.8 million base case, though above its bear-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: H1 2026 revenue reached $7.6 million; Q1 2026 revenue was $4.03 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: About $3.8M (+47% YoY, −6% QoQ)”

surprises.description: RaceControl fell short of the preview's operating benchmarks: H1 subscription revenue was 18% of total revenue versus a stated target of at least 22%, and its $2.9 million ARR implies a run rate of about $242,000 per month, below the preview's $250,000 MRR marker. The disclosure of 40,500 paid subscribers and 349% H1 revenue growth is strong, but the preview gave no expected subscriber count.
surprises.fact_evidence: “RaceControl subscription revenue grew ~349% year-over-year to approximately $1.4 million in H1 2026, now representing 18% of total revenue”; it was “running at approximately $2.9 million in annual recurring revenue” with “over 40,500 paid subscribers,” all acquired organically.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Look for MRR above $250K, subscription share of at least 22%, and any first-ever disclosure of subscriber count, ARPU, or churn.”

surprises.description: Le Mans Ultimate engagement was stronger than the preview's flat-to-slightly-down CCU picture suggested: April was the game's highest-ever month for average daily active users. The reported sales of more than 0.5 million base games and 1.2 million DLC pieces also provide positive traction not quantified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “April marking the highest-ever month for average daily active users”; the game had sold “more than 0.5 million base game units and over 1.2 million individual DLC pieces since launch.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Steam concurrent users are flat to slightly down” and “Le Mans Ultimate averaged about 3,243 CCU in Q2 versus 3,355 in Q1.”

surprises.description: H1 gross margin expanded by 5.9 percentage points to 84.7%. The preview focused on revenue durability and declining revenue per CCU but did not set a gross-margin expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanding to 84.7% from 78.8% a year earlier.”

surprises.description: The company retired all Class B super-voting shares, giving all outstanding shares equal voting rights. The preview discussed the buyback and governance issues but did not anticipate this change in voting rights.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retired all Class B super voting shares, giving all outstanding shares equal voting rights.”

in_line: Management deferred detailed plans for the new game title and long-term project to the Q3 earnings call, as the preview's base case expected.

The preview already reported the $3.7 million Driven Lifestyle repurchase and the $1.2 million revolver draw with maturity extended to February 2028; those items were not new surprises in the call facts.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $2.5 million, below the preview’s $2.7–3.0 million build and $2.96 million consensus. Revenue came entirely from staking, so the preview’s question about advisory or platform revenue produced no disclosed Q2 revenue from those activities.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $2.5 million, entirely from staking.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My Q2 build… total revenue of $2.7–3.0M”; the preview also listed “Q2 FY2026 Consensus” revenue of “$2.96M” and asked for “Advisory revenue with a dollar figure.”

surprises.description: The net loss was $30.3 million, worse than the preview’s estimated $20–22 million loss, although far smaller than Q1’s loss. The reported loss was driven largely by non-cash digital-asset fair-value losses, as the preview anticipated, but the total loss was greater than its estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reported a Q2 2026 net loss of $30.3 million ($0.38 per share)… driven largely by non-cash digital asset fair value losses.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “That implies a net loss of roughly -$20M to -$22M, or about -$0.36/share.”

surprises.description: Average net staking yield was 6.14%, below the preview’s expectation that yield would hold near 6.9%. It nevertheless exceeded the Solana network average by 46 basis points, a relative advantage not specified in the preview’s Q2 expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average net staking yield was 6.14% APY in Q2 2026, outperforming the Solana network average of 5.68% by 46 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “yield holds near 6.9%.”

surprises.description: G&A jumped to $11.1 million, including $6.8 million of nonrecurring severance tied to the PoNS divestiture. The preview expected the divestiture to be a cost-savings item but did not anticipate this large severance charge; management said G&A should normalize toward Q1 levels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 G&A expenses jumped to $11.1 million from $3.3 million a year earlier, including $6.8 million of nonrecurring severance from the PoNS divestiture, with management guiding G&A to normalize back toward Q1 levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said PoNS should appear “only as discontinued operations and as a cost-savings item.”

surprises.description: The company secured a roughly 0.5 million SOL institutional stake commitment, with initial validator revenue expected in Q3. This was a new source of prospective revenue beyond the preview’s discussion of named partnerships and the need for disclosed advisory revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured its first institutional third-party stake commitment of roughly 0.5 million SOL, with initial validator revenue expected to be recognized in Q3 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether named partnerships would produce “advisory revenue with a dollar figure” in Q2 and noted they had “produced no disclosed revenue so far.”

surprises.description: The company completed an $8 million strategic institutional raise led by Mirae Asset with Hashkey Capital. The preview emphasized limited cash and questioned the capacity to fund buybacks, but did not anticipate this financing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed an $8 million strategic institutional raise led by Mirae Asset with Hashkey Capital.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “Cash $4.4M against roughly $5M quarterly G&A” and questioned whether the buyback authorization was “largely symbolic”; it did not mention a new raise.

surprises.description: The PoNS divestiture generated a $3.1 million gain, an additional positive result beyond the preview’s expectation that the sale would remove a cash-consuming business and provide cost savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “divested the cash-consuming PoNS medical device business for a $3.1 million gain.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected the PoNS divestiture during Q2 and described it as a “cash-savings item,” but did not anticipate a $3.1 million gain.

surprises.description: The company acquired a Hong Kong regulated trust company for $2 million, a transaction not anticipated in the preview. The facts provide no detail on its expected contribution, so the shareholder impact is unclear.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “acquired a Hong Kong regulated trust company for $2 million.”

in_line: SOL holdings were about 2.3 million across all categories, broadly matching the preview’s cited 2.30–2.33 million external figures and close to the 2.37 million figure from the prior-quarter call, though above the 2.07 million reported in the 10-Q.

The mNAV discount persisted: the reported 0.81x was between the preview’s estimated 0.65x on basic shares and 0.94x on fully diluted shares. The preview had flagged the discount and share-count basis as key issues.
The PoNS business was divested during Q2, as the preview expected.

surprises.description: Q4 sales of $115.4 million beat the preview’s roughly $109.5 million consensus by about 5%, though they were close to the company-guidance level. The preview had identified revenue at or above $113 million as a key catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net sales were $115.4 million,” up 0.7% year-over-year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Consensus was “~$109.5M”; the catalyst checklist highlighted “Revenue at or above ~$113M.”

surprises.description: The company reported a debt-free balance sheet with $16.7 million in cash, rather than the debt-funded Q4 balance sheet the preview anticipated after the buyback. This is a meaningful balance-sheet outcome compared with the preview’s assumed revolver borrowing.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “maintained a debt-free balance sheet with $16.7 million in cash” and generated “over $47 million in free cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Q4 is the first quarter with debt; the revolver is about $55M” and modeled an assumed “~$30M revolver draw.”

surprises.description: GAAP operating margin reached 14.2%, far above the roughly 7.1% margin level anticipated, because tariff refunds added 780 basis points. The adjusted margin was 7.1%, so the unusually high GAAP figure reflected a large refund benefit rather than stronger underlying profitability.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 GAAP operating margin of 14.2% was inflated by a 780 basis point benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds,” while “adjusted operating margin” was 7.1%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q4 operating-margin guidance as “Similar to Q3 (≈7.1%).”

surprises.description: Flexsteel is exiting Home Styles, a roughly $12 million ready-to-assemble business with below-average gross margins—an unanticipated portfolio change. Management said excluding it, fiscal-year sales growth would have been closer to 6.5%–7% and Q4 growth about 2.3%, better than the reported growth rates suggest, though the exit also removes revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is “exiting its Home Styles ready-to-assemble product category,” which contributed “roughly $12 million in fiscal 2026 sales at below-average gross profit margins”; excluding it, FY growth would be “closer to 6.5%-7%” and Q4 growth “about 2.3%.”

surprises.description: Despite beating revenue consensus, management described demand as sharply weakening: average prices rose about 10%–11% while unit volumes declined, and backlog was down 11.8% sequentially. The preview warned that a Q4 sales figure with a 10-handle could signal weakening demand, but sales came in above $115 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 sales reflected “a sharply weakening demand environment”; “Average pricing rose approximately 10%-11%” with unit volume declines, and backlog was “down 11.8% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said, “Anything with a 10-handle would suggest demand weakened during the quarter,” and highlighted revenue at or above ~$113 million as confirming guidance.

surprises.description: Q1 guidance puts operating margin at 6.5%–7.0%, with the midpoint below 7% because of supply-chain inflation. The sales outlook is still for 1%–4% growth, so it avoids the preview’s feared below-flat revenue outcome, but the margin range reaches the preview’s identified risk threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q1 FY2027 guidance calls for sales of “$111 million to $115 million (1%-4% growth)” and operating margin of “6.5%-7.0%, pressured by supply chain inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a “revenue guide below flat with margins under 7% is the highest-risk outcome” and noted fuel, energy, and ocean-freight cost pressure hitting Q1.

surprises.description: The preview’s year-over-year comparison showed adjusted operating margin falling from 9.0% to an expected roughly 7.1%. The call noted that the prior-year quarter had a 160-basis-point foreign-currency benefit, making the comparable underlying decline much smaller than the headline year-over-year comparison implies.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The prior-year Q4 adjusted operating margin included a 160 basis point foreign currency benefit, making the year-over-year margin decline less severe on a comparable basis.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Operating margin 7.1%, versus 9.0% adjusted in the year-ago quarter.”

in_line: Q4 adjusted operating margin was 7.1%, matching the preview’s Q3-like margin expectation of approximately 7.1%.
Q4 sales were close to the company-guidance level of approximately $114.6 million, even though they beat the lower consensus estimate.
The dividend increase was expected: the preview flagged an increase to approximately $0.20 per quarter, and the call reported $0.20 per share.

surprises.description: The preview expected construction to begin by the end of Q2 2026, but New Era said it had only just obtained the county permits and expected grading to start in the coming weeks. The permits de-risk the project, but the grading start is later than the preview’s milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “obtained its construction permits” and “expects to begin site grading in the coming weeks”; management framed the permits as “meaningfully de-risking the project.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Phase 1 construction to begin by end of Q2 2026”; the preview also said to confirm whether “groundbreaking happened as guided this quarter.”

surprises.description: The Macquarie facility has $270 million undrawn, as expected, but $240 million of that amount is contingent on securing a final lease. That makes most of the stated undrawn capacity conditional rather than immediately available for the Phase 1 funding need.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$270 million undrawn” on the facility, “though $240 million of that … is contingent on securing a final lease.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Of the $290M Macquarie facility, $20M is funded and $270M is available”; the preview also said Phase 1 needs roughly $180M and called for monitoring “any new draws that do not require new equity.”

surprises.description: Phase 2 capacity rose from approximately 450 MW to 550 MW, lifting combined Phase 1 and Phase 2 gross capacity to roughly 757 MW versus the approximately 650 MW previously contemplated. The preview did not flag this expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Phase 2 capacity was increased from approximately 450 MW to 550 MW”; combined gross capacity is “roughly 757 MW versus the ~650 MW previously contemplated.”

surprises.description: New Era gained the opportunity to negotiate the Phase 1 power purchase agreement in its own name, and management said the contract is substantially in final form pending approvals. This is progress on a power contract that the preview did not identify, though it is not evidence that the separate hyperscaler lease has been signed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In early July, New Era gained the opportunity to negotiate the Phase 1 power purchase agreement in its own name”; the contract is “substantially in final form pending approvals.”

surprises.description: The company said Phase 1 can use adjacent behind-the-meter generation without ERCOT interconnection or an air permit, keeping it outside Texas’s Batch Zero queue. That is an unanticipated project advantage; the stated Q4 2027 power target still falls within the preview’s broader 2H 2027 window.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Phase 1's 207 MW draws from existing adjacent behind-the-meter gas generation requiring no ERCOT interconnection or air permit,” positioning it “outside Texas's Batch Zero queue” and supporting “a targeted Q4 2027 initial power timeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “First power for the TCDC site targeted for 2H 2027.”

surprises.description: New Era closed a 54-acre corridor acquisition, taking owned land to 492 acres, while saying the first two phases need less than half of that acreage. The preview did not mention this land addition or the resulting capacity to accommodate further development.
surprises.fact_evidence: “closed the acquisition of a 54-acre corridor, bringing owned land to 492 acres”; Phase 1 and Phase 2 together require “less than half of that acreage.”

surprises.description: Management described a substantially enlarged leadership team, with hires from major cloud, data-center, and technology companies, and said the team is positioning New Era to grow beyond TCDC. The preview identified the new senior executives but did not anticipate this broader hiring or expansion push.
surprises.fact_evidence: “significantly expanded its leadership team with hires from Microsoft, AWS, TikTok, CoreWeave, Switch, and EdgeConneX,” positioning the company “to pursue growth beyond TCDC.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “New CEO Charlie Nelson (effective July 1), Ted Warner as President and CFO, and Jose Rodriguez as COO” as the new team for the first filing.

surprises.description: Management presented Governor Abbott’s call for stronger data-center oversight as a competitive advantage, saying TCDC already meets the standards and has drawn interest from essentially every major potential tenant. The preview did not flag this regulatory development or management’s claim that it benefits the project.
surprises.fact_evidence: Governor Abbott’s directive was cited “as a competitive advantage”; management said TCDC “already meets the standards” and has attracted interest from “essentially every major potential tenant.”

surprises.description: Management outlined raising capital for the larger multibillion-dollar build at the asset or JV level after lease execution, targeting roughly 80% debt financing, and said parent liquidity covers multiple years of operating burn plus the Phase 1 equity contribution. This is a more detailed funding plan than the preview provided, although the debt target depends on a lease and is not described as committed financing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Project capital for the larger multi-billion dollar CAPEX is to be raised at the asset/JV level after lease execution, targeting roughly 80% debt financing,” while “parent liquidity covers multiple years of operating burn and the Phase 1 equity contribution.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Phase 1 needs roughly $180M” and flagged liquidity and Macquarie draws as key issues to watch.

surprises.description: Cash rose to $84.8 million despite capex and burn, with the increase driven largely by cash-paid exercises of $2-struck warrants. The cash level clears the preview’s $60 million watchpoint, but the warrant-funded source was not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company ended Q2 with “$84.8 million in cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash,” an increase “despite CAPEX and burn,” driven largely by “the exercise of $2-struck cash-paid warrants.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “Watch for cash above $60M” and to check ATM usage, noting management’s “no material near-term dilution” framing.

in_line: Cash was above the preview’s $60 million watchpoint: the company reported $84.8 million at quarter-end.
The Q4 2027 initial-power target remains within the preview’s stated 2H 2027 target window.

surprises.description: StreamX reported $146,000 of gold lease income, including about $134,000 earned in Q2. That was below the preview’s $0.4 million consensus estimate, but above its base-case expectation of $0.0–$0.1 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “StreamX recognized its first-ever revenue of $146,000 in Q2 2026” in gold lease income, with “approximately $134,000 earned in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 Consensus” revenue was “$0.4M”; the preview’s base scenario expected “$0.0–0.1M.”

surprises.description: Management said a first significant institutional GLDY allocation is expected in Q3 2026 and repeatedly framed it as the key inflection point. The preview anticipated possible inflows through distribution channels but did not identify a specific institutional allocation or timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “repeatedly guided to the first significant institutional GLDY allocation arriving in Q3 2026 as the key inflection point.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described “inflows from new distribution channels” as a potential driver, while saying it found “no quantitative guidance.”

surprises.description: The silver product launch has been pushed from Q3 2026 to 2027, delaying the second commodity product that the preview viewed as a possible sign of a revenue ramp.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “delayed the silver product launch from Q3 2026 to 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called “a named launch date on the Aug 17 call” the clearest sign of a revenue ramp and listed a “dated silver launch” in its bull scenario.

surprises.description: The company reported $41.8 million of total liquidity and no debt, but only about $19.5 million was immediately available; the rest included a loan, a locked-up investment, and physical gold inventory. Despite the lower immediately available amount versus the preview’s estimated cash balance, management indicated substantially longer runway than the preview’s roughly two-quarter estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$41.8 million in total liquidity with no debt, but only ~$19.5 million is immediately available”; cash burn was “~$1.6 million per month in Q2,” expected to fall to “~$1.1 million per month in Q3,” with “roughly 18 months of runway on immediately available funds and ~3 years on total liquidity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Cash of $28–32M” and inferred “roughly two quarters of runway.”

surprises.description: StreamX disclosed that it owns about 91% of GLDY, leaving only about 9% in external ownership. The preview focused on ounces and near-zero net inflows, but did not anticipate that the reported reserve was so heavily seeded with company capital.
surprises.fact_evidence: “StreamX (including exchangeable shares) holds about 91% of GLDY,” leaving “external ownership [at] only ~9% (about 280 ounces), as the company seeded the reserve with its own capital.”

surprises.description: Management introduced GLDC, a permissionless, fee-free gold token backed by yield-bearing GLDY, creating a potential additional revenue line not discussed in the preview. The cited revenue potential is illustrative rather than guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: GLDC is “backed one-to-one by yield-bearing GLDY”; management said “a 3.5% reserve rate could generate ~$3.5 million annually per $100 million of GLDC,” noting this is “illustrative, not guidance.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed that material weaknesses in internal controls remained unremediated and that disclosure controls were not effective, and it changed auditors. The preview did not flag these governance and reporting-control issues.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Material weaknesses in internal controls remained unremediated as of June 30 and disclosure controls were concluded not effective”; the company “switched auditors from CBiz to EisnerAmper.”

surprises.description: A board-authorized buyback of up to 10 million shares, capped at $2 per share, was disclosed despite the preview’s focus on possible dilution; no shares had been repurchased yet, so the authorization had not resulted in actual buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: There is “a board-authorized buyback of up to 10 million shares (max $2/share) with no shares yet repurchased.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “New equity issuance” as a key metric to watch and said any new ATM or shelf takedown would be dilutive.

in_line: GLDY assets under management were broadly flat at 3,111 ounces, close to the preview’s derived estimate of about 3,118 ounces and its base case of roughly 3,120 ounces.

surprises.description: Home Depot reported $47.9 billion of sales, above the preview’s $47.5 billion consensus. The roughly $0.4 billion beat was a modest upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 sales rose 5.7% year-over-year to $47.9 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $47.5B (range $47.0–47.5B)”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $4.92, well above the preview’s $4.71 consensus and the top of its cited range. The beat was meaningfully larger than the preview’s expectation of a modest EPS beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS was $4.92, up 5.1% from $4.68 a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | $4.71 (range $4.71–4.73)”

surprises.description: Total comps of 1.7% exceeded the preview’s assumed 1.0%–1.5% range, and comps strengthened over the quarter; management also said Q3 began in line with Q2 demand trends. This was better than the preview’s base-case comp expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total comp sales up 1.7%”; “May +1.2%, June +1.5%, July +2.3%”; “Q3 has started consistent with Q2 demand trends.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable sales: Not found … Derived ~+1.0% to +1.5%; treat as an assumption”; catalyst: “Comps versus ~+1.2% and transactions versus –1.3%.”

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 gross-margin pressure to ease to better than roughly 65 basis points of decline, but management said pressure excluding the tariff refund was about 120 basis points. The refund substantially masked that underlying cost and acquisition-mix pressure, with management describing a timing shift and expecting Q4 margin to be roughly flat year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding the tariff refund, gross margin faced about 120 basis points of pressure”; “tariff refunds to be fully offset by unplanned cost pressures over the year, creating a Q2-to-Q3 timing shift”; “Q4 gross margin expected to be roughly flat year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said Q2 pressure would continue but not to the degree of Q1, with H2 returning to roughly flat”; “Hitting the 33.1% full-year bridge needs Q2 better than about –65bp.”

surprises.description: Home Depot received a large tariff refund that the preview had not anticipated; instead, its tariff discussion focused on potential exposure to new duties taking effect after the call. The refund reduced Q2 cost of goods sold and added about 145 basis points to gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $730 million in IEEPA tariff refunds late in June, of which $685 million reduced Q2 cost of goods sold and boosted gross margin by roughly 145 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Section 338 tariffs” taking effect the morning after the report and said HD would likely be asked to “size COGS exposure.”

surprises.description: Online sales grew 11% for a fifth consecutive quarter of double-digit growth, supported by higher traffic and conversion. The preview did not identify this as an expected source of strength.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Online sales grew 11% year-over-year, marking the fifth straight quarter of double-digit growth, supported by higher traffic and conversion.”

surprises.description: The call described broad merchandise and Pro-channel strength: 13 of 16 departments had positive comps, Pro outperformed DIY, and SRS comps were above the company average with positive comps in every vertical. The preview did not set expectations for these results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “13 of 16 merchandising departments posted positive comps, Pro outperformed DIY, and SRS comped above the company average with positive comps across all verticals.”

in_line: Fiscal 2026 guidance was reaffirmed, as the preview expected: flat-to-2% comp growth, 2.5%–4.5% total sales growth, roughly 33.1% gross margin, 12.4%–12.6% operating margin, and flat-to-4% EPS growth.
Comp average ticket rose 2.8%, essentially matching the preview’s 2.7% estimate.

surprises.description: DocGo widened its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA loss guidance to $17–$22 million, far worse than the prior $5–$10 million loss range the preview cited. Management attributed the change to slower-than-expected cost cuts and lower first-half gross margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year adjusted EBITDA loss guidance to $17-$22 million,” citing “slower-than-expected cost cuts and lower gross margins in the first half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 adj. EBITDA: –$5M to –$10M”; the preview also said a Q2 print of –$8M or worse would make that guide hard to hit.

surprises.description: DocGo announced its largest-ever acquisition, agreeing to buy virtual care provider Hicuity Health, which the preview had not anticipated. Hicuity had about $65 million of trailing-twelve-month revenue and $4.5 million of adjusted EBITDA; the deal includes assumed debt and equity issuance.
surprises.fact_evidence: DocGo “signed a definitive agreement to acquire” Hicuity, its “largest acquisition to date”; Hicuity generated approximately “$65 million” in trailing-12-month revenue and “$4.5 million” in adjusted EBITDA. DocGo will assume about $52 million of debt and issue equity equal to 2% of fully diluted shares, with a possible additional 3.5% earnout.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $73.4 million fell short of the preview’s roughly $75.4–$75.6 million consensus estimate. The year-over-year decline reflected migrant-project wind-down, although organic revenue excluding migrant and SteadyMD contributions grew about 5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue fell to $73.4 million from $80.4 million a year earlier due to migrant project wind-down,” while “excluding migrant and SteadyMD contributions, organic revenue grew about 5% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 revenue consensus was “$75.35M” or “$75.57M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin was 30.5%, below the preview’s expectation that it would recover above 32% after temporary SteadyMD labor pressure. Management also cited higher field wages and fuel costs, with fuel at $4.27 per gallon versus $3.16 a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated adjusted gross margin declined to 30.5% from 31.6% year-over-year,” pressured by “higher field labor wages, fuel costs rising to $4.27 per gallon from $3.16, and temporarily lower SteadyMD margins from aggressive hiring.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had described the SteadyMD labor drag and fuel costs as temporary, with “relief guided after Q2,” and that a print “above 32% supports that view.”

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash was below the preview’s $50–$56 million base case: total cash and equivalents including restricted cash was $48.1 million. Available cash also fell to $25.2 million from $35.7 million quarter-over-quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total cash and equivalents including restricted cash fell to $48.1 million from $59.9 million quarter-over-quarter, with available cash dropping to $25.2 million from $35.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “$50–56M ending liquidity” and identified ending liquidity as a key item to watch.

surprises.description: DocGo disclosed a new financing commitment of up to $50 million from Perceptive Advisors, with the term loan set to replace its existing asset-backed credit line. This was not forecast in the preview and comes alongside the Hicuity deal’s assumed debt and equity issuance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Perceptive Advisors committed up to $50 million of additional financing to DocGo in multiple tranches,” with the first $12.5 million funded upon execution of a pre-closing management services agreement; “the term loan will replace DocGo's existing asset-backed credit line.”

surprises.description: Management introduced a potential 2027 Medicare reimbursement risk from a proposed CMS rule, but said the exposure is limited: about 2,000 patients could be affected, while most of DocGo’s 55,000 monitored patients are in unaffected cardiac implantable-device programs. The preview did not flag this issue.
surprises.fact_evidence: A proposed CMS rule “could eliminate Medicare RPM reimbursement in 2027,” but management said “only about 2,000 patients face potential risk” and the “vast majority of its 55,000 monitored patients” are unaffected cardiac implantable-device patients.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EBITDA loss was slightly worse than the preview’s expected range: $6.3 million versus the preview’s buy-side estimate of $4–$6 million and base case of $5–$6 million. It nevertheless improved nearly 40% sequentially, so the miss against the lower end of expectations was small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA loss improved nearly 40% sequentially to negative $6.3 million from negative $10.3 million,” aided by a corporate reduction in force that cut annual SG&A by approximately $4.5 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s derived buy-side range was “–$4M to –$6M”; its base scenario was “$(5)–$(6)M.”

in_line: FY2026 revenue guidance was narrowed to $305–$310 million, within the prior $300–$315 million company range and broadly in line with the preview’s $305.1 million consensus estimate.

Management still expects to reach a positive adjusted EBITDA run rate exiting 2026, excluding Hicuity, consistent with the preview’s focus on a back-half recovery—although the full-year adjusted EBITDA loss guidance was materially worsened.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was below both preview estimates: $12.6 million versus $12.98 million and $13.59 million. That was a shortfall of roughly 3% to 7%, rather than the preview’s flat-to-down modestly outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $12.6 million, down 7% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $13.59M” and “Revenue (alt.) | $12.98M”; the preview described the estimates as “~flat YoY” and “About -4% YoY.”

surprises.description: Retina revenue fell to $6.5 million, well below the preview’s roughly $7.5 million base case and down from $8.0 million a year earlier. The preview expected retina to improve sequentially, so the reported weakness was a key shortfall and the source of the total revenue decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retina decline from $8.0 million to $6.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Retina revenue vs. ~$7.5M base case” and the base scenario expected “Retina improving sequentially.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was only 34.2%, far below the preview’s 39%–41% base case and its 40%+ bull case. It was also essentially unchanged from the 34.5% year-ago level, rather than delivering the anticipated margin improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin was essentially flat at 34.2% versus 34.5% a year earlier,” with glaucoma probe gains offset by softer retina system margins and cost pressures.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario projected “39–41%”; the bull scenario projected “42%+”; the preview also called out “Gross margin at or above 40%.”

surprises.description: Glaucoma probe growth was much stronger than the preview’s already-positive expectation: volume rose about 35%, and underlying growth remained above 15% even after excluding relocation-related pre-orders. G6 product-family revenue also grew 19%, across every operating region.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cyclo-G6 probe volume rose approximately 35% year-over-year to 17,700 units”; excluding pre-orders, “underlying glaucoma probe growth was still over 15%”; G6 family revenue “grew 19%” with growth “spanning every operating region.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Two straight quarters of double-digit probe growth” would be the strongest datapoint and the bull scenario assumed “probes +15%.”

surprises.description: GAAP EPS was much worse than expected, at a loss of $0.07 per share versus preview estimates for a loss of $0.01 to $0.02. The adjusted EBITDA result also turned negative, though the preview had no adjusted EBITDA consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $1.3 million ($0.07 per share) from $1.0 million ($0.06 per share), and adjusted EBITDA turned to a $0.4 million loss versus $21,000 income a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (GAAP) | $(0.01)” and “EPS (alt.) | $(0.02)”; the preview’s base scenario projected “$(0.01) to $0.00.”

surprises.description: Cyclo-G6 system placements fell sharply to 18 from 35, with management citing EMEA order timing and competitive pressure on console placements in the GmbH business. The preview emphasized recurring probe growth but did not flag this degree of weakness in placements.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cyclo-G6 system placements fell to 18 units versus 35 in the prior year,” driven by “order timing in EMEA and competitive pressure on console placements in the GmbH business.”

surprises.description: Management added that relocation-related safety-stock buildup is expected to pressure cash through 2026, with the benefit reversing into a tailwind in 2027. The preview focused on the current cash balance and positive cash-flow commitment but did not anticipate this near-term cash drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Headquarters relocation-related safety stock buildup is expected to pressure cash through 2026 before reversing as a tailwind in 2027.”

in_line: The company reaffirmed its FY2026 revenue guidance of $51 million to $53 million, consistent with the preview’s expected reaffirmation; the guidance also excludes Middle East revenue, as the preview noted.
Cash was $4.7 million, within the preview’s expected $4.3 million to $4.8 million range, and the company reported positive cash flow.
Full-year adjusted operating expense guidance of $19 million to $19.5 million matched the preview’s stated range.

surprises.description: Keysight reported Q3 EPS of $3.07, far above both the $2.46–$2.48 consensus and the preview’s inferred $2.60–$2.70 buy-side bar. That is a much larger beat than the preview’s normalized-beat scenario anticipated.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $2.47 as the print bar”; “A normalized beat puts the buy-side EPS bar at ~$2.60–$2.70.”

surprises.description: Q3 orders reached $2.91 billion, well above the preview’s roughly $1.9 billion threshold for maintaining the acceleration story. Book-to-bill exceeded 1.1 for a second straight quarter, while management also reported an all-time-high pipeline and highest-ever monthly funnel intake.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 orders reached $2.91 billion”; “Book-to-bill has exceeded 1.1 for two straight quarters, with the sales pipeline at an all-time high and highest-ever monthly funnel intake reported last month.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Below ~$1.9B (book-to-bill under 1.1x) would undercut the acceleration story”; “Orders ≥ $1.9B and book-to-bill ≥ 1.1x.”

surprises.description: Q4 guidance was substantially above the preview’s implied bar: revenue of $1.930–$1.950 billion versus about $1.82 billion, and EPS of $3.34–$3.40 versus about $2.80. The outlook implies FY2026 revenue growth of 32%, above the prior “high-20s%” framework, and EPS growth of about 60%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 guidance calls for revenue of $1.930-1.950 billion” and “EPS of $3.34-3.40”; “implying full-year FY2026 revenue growth of 32% and EPS growth of ~60%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 FY26 revenue/EPS guide vs. the ~$1.82B / ~$2.80 implied bar”; prior guidance framework was “high-20s%” FY26 revenue growth.

surprises.description: Q3 operating margin reached 33.2%, well above the preview’s implied 27.9% blended margin and above Keysight’s stated long-term target range of 31%–32%. This was the opposite of the preview’s concern that the capex ramp or mix might dilute incremental margins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin expanded 820 basis points year-over-year to 33.2%, surpassing the long-term target range of 31%-32%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus implies ~27.9% blended operating margin”; “Watch whether manufacturing-test mix and the $200M capex ramp dilute incrementals.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $1.846 billion exceeded the $1.75 billion consensus and the preview’s $1.78–$1.82 billion normalized-beat range, as well as the high end of company guidance. The reported 36% growth was also above the preview’s 29.4% consensus-implied growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Revenue of $1.846 billion grew 36% reported (31% core), exceeding the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q3 revenue consensus of “$1.75B”; whisper revenue of “$1.78–$1.82B”; company guidance of “$1.73–$1.75B.”

surprises.description: Commercial Communications delivered $1.06 billion of revenue, up 56%, versus the preview’s $910 million and 41% growth expectation. It also had its first-ever $1 billion quarter, with wireline revenue exceeding wireless for the first time.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The commercial communications business posted its first-ever $1 billion quarter at $1.06 billion revenue (up 56%), with wireline revenue exceeding wireless for the first time.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Commercial Communications (consensus $910M, +41%)”; “Deceleration into the mid-30s with a slowing order book would be the bear trigger.”

surprises.description: Management said near-term revenue over the next two quarters will be governed by supply, not demand, particularly because incoming component parts are constrained. The preview emphasized demand and order-book risks but did not anticipate supply availability limiting revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Supply chain, not demand, [will] be the governor of near-term revenue over the next two quarters, particularly due to constrained incoming component parts.”

surprises.description: Acquisition integration was completed a quarter ahead of schedule, with 80%–90% of the $100 million synergy pool expected to be at run-rate exiting FY2026 and another roughly $50 million of synergy contribution expected in FY2027. The preview had flagged the synergy target but not this accelerated integration timing or the incremental FY2027 contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Acquisition integration completed a quarter ahead of schedule”; “80%-90% of $100 million in cost synergies expected to be realized on a run-rate basis exiting the fiscal year,” with “~$50 million incremental synergy contribution expected in FY2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “>$100M cost synergies reiterated.”

surprises.description: FY2026 revenue was $402 million, below the preview's cited $443.2 million consensus, though that figure was flagged as stale; Q4 revenue of $100.9 million also came in below the preview's $108 million base case, but above the cited low estimate of about $95.8 million. Overall, revenue was weaker than the preview's base expectation, with substantial uncertainty in the estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 net revenue fell 21% year-over-year to $100.9 million,” and “full-year revenue declined 12% to $402 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My own base case is about $108M revenue”; FY26 revenue consensus was “$443.2M,” with the caveat “Stale: implies a ~$142M Q4 versus 9M actual of $301.0M.”

surprises.description: Management withheld formal FY2027 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance. The preview said management had planned to update guidance at Q4 and warned that a second withdrawal would be damaging, so the continued lack of guidance was a negative outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company will not provide formal FY2027 revenue or adjusted EBITDA guidance,” citing tariff impacts, China and Middle East conditions, and macroeconomic uncertainty.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said it would update at Q4. Reinstatement signals confidence; a second withdrawal would be damaging.”

surprises.description: Although reported Q4 product gross margin was 31.7%, $5.8 million of EPA tariff favorability lifted it; excluding that benefit, adjusted product gross margin was just 17.5%, well below the preview's 27% threshold for evidence that the cost program was reaching the P&L.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 product gross margin of 31.7% was inflated by $5.8 million of EPA tariff favorability; excluding this, adjusted product gross margin was only 17.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything under 27% would suggest the cost program is not reaching the P&L.”

surprises.description: Orders remained weaker than the preview's helpful benchmark: Q4 book-to-bill was 0.9, below 1.0, and full-year book-to-bill was 1.1. Backlog was about $313 million, down from the $356.2 million reported at the prior quarter, adding to the concern that order weakness could impair the FY2027 revenue base.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year book-to-bill ratio was 1.1,” with “Q4 book-to-bill at 0.9 and backlog of approximately $313 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “above 1.0x would help” and warned that “Two more quarters of order decline would impair the FY27 revenue base.”

surprises.description: Transformation initiatives generated over $20 million of FY2026 bottom-line improvements, exceeding the $12 million target, with roughly $15 million of additional annualized benefit expected in FY2027. This was a stronger quantified cost-program result than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Transformation initiatives delivered over $20 million in bottom-line improvements in FY2026, well above the $12 million target,” and are expected to generate “roughly $15 million of incremental annualized benefit in FY2027.”

surprises.description: The TCW transaction includes a covenant holiday through December 2027, a specific lender concession not described in the preview's account of the $55 million recapitalization. That added covenant relief is a favorable additional term.
surprises.fact_evidence: The transaction includes “a covenant holiday through December 2027.”

in_line: The TCW recapitalization was described as a $55 million deal, including a $15 million cash investment, consistent with the preview's description of the announced $55 million TCW transaction and its $15 million investment.

surprises.description: The preview called for an update on how Jaguar would satisfy the Nasdaq Panel by September 1, but the call facts report no Panel outcome or compliance plan. The stated webcast theme was strategic focus and catalysts, without a reported answer to this urgent listing question.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call theme was “transformation, near-term catalysts and sharp strategic focus”; the provided call facts report no Nasdaq Panel update or plan.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Nasdaq Hearings Panel outcome. The Panel retained jurisdiction through 1 Sep 2026”; the catalyst checklist asks, “What is the plan to satisfy the Panel by 1 Sep?”

surprises.description: The preview specifically sought a current cash and runway update, given the $3.79M quarter-end cash balance and expected cash needs. The reported financial recap included no specific figures, and the call facts provide no updated liquidity or runway answer.
surprises.fact_evidence: The CFO delivered a Q2 financial recap, but the call facts say it included licensing-related topics “without presenting specific figures”; no cash or runway update is reported.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “What is the cash position and runway today? Anything short of a specific answer is a bear signal.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted undisclosed subsequent-event transactions as a reason for the delayed 10-Q and expected clarification. The call facts mention a corporate development from earlier in the year only as an illustration of strategy, with no reported details on the subsequent-event transactions.
surprises.fact_evidence: Lisa Conte “referenced a corporate development that occurred earlier in the year to illustrate the company's strategy”; the provided call facts report no details about the material subsequent-event transactions.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Undisclosed ‘material subsequent event transactions.’ This was the stated reason for the NT 10-Q”; the checklist asks, “What are the material subsequent event transactions that delayed the 10-Q?”

surprises.description: The preview flagged the proposed Series Q exchange and its potential share issuance as a key dilution issue, but the call facts report no update or explanation of the exchange. The only stated financial-recap detail is that licensing-related topics were covered without specific figures.
surprises.fact_evidence: The call facts report no Series Q exchange update; the CFO's recap included licensing-related topics without specific figures.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlights the “4 Sep special meeting / Series Q exchange” and asks the call to address the remaining exchange proposal.

surprises.description: The preview sought confirmation of MVID NDA timing, the SBS-IF readout window, and the remaining Future Pak milestone amounts and triggers. The call facts report no pipeline timing or milestone update, despite describing the webcast as focused on near-term catalysts.
surprises.fact_evidence: The webcast theme was “transformation, near-term catalysts and sharp strategic focus,” but the call facts report no MVID, SBS-IF, or Future Pak milestone specifics.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The checklist asks to “Confirm MVID NDA timing and SBS-IF Phase 2 readout” and identify “the remaining Future Pak milestone amounts and triggers.”

surprises.description: Net signed contracts rose 5% year over year, modestly exceeding the preview’s flat-to-positive bar for the seasonally weakest order quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net signed contracts rose 5% year-over-year to 2,508 units ($2.5 billion), driven by community count expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Flat-to-positive units would be a strong signal.”

surprises.description: The Q4 gross-margin outlook was 26.0%, below the roughly 26.3% management had previously guided and the preview expected to be reaffirmed—a 30-basis-point shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 guidance projects … 26.0% gross margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided Q4 to about 26.3%” and the bull scenario called for “Q4 26.3% reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Management reported that the sales environment remained subdued in the first 2.5 weeks of Q4, adding a near-term demand caution that the preview did not specifically anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management noted the sales environment remained subdued into the first 2.5 weeks of Q4.”

surprises.description: The company raised its FY26 buyback projection to $700 million from the $650 million target in the preview, while buying back about $231 million in the quarter—above the preview’s roughly $212 million-per-quarter H2 pace requirement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year 2026 stock repurchase projection to $700 million from $650 million and returned approximately $231 million to shareholders in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Buyback target: $650M” and “Hitting the $650M target requires about $212M per quarter in H2, versus $175M in Q2.”

surprises.description: The company lowered incentives to about 7.5% of gross sales price, below the preview’s 8.0% plateau expectation; it also said roughly 30% of communities raised prices.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Incentives declined to approximately 7.5% of gross sales price from about 8% over the past year, and roughly 30% of communities saw price increases during the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Incentives at 8.0% of gross sales price, flat for four straight quarters” and the bull scenario assumed “incentives 8% or lower.”

surprises.description: The company raised its full-year average delivered-price outlook to $995,000–$1 million, adding about $53 million in revenue; the preview did not specify an expected FY26 average-price range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year average delivered price to $995,000-$1 million (adding ~$53 million in revenue).”

in_line: Q3 deliveries were 2,662, essentially matching the preview’s approximately 2,669 expectation; home-sales revenue of $2.6 billion was within the $2.60–$2.62 billion consensus range.
Q3 adjusted gross margin of 25.6% was 35 basis points above the 25.25% company guide, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a roughly 25–40 basis-point beat and its 25.4–25.6% base case.
Q3 EPS of $2.97 was within the preview’s $2.95–$3.05 base-case range, though slightly above the cited consensus estimates of $2.89–$2.93.
The company remained on track for 480–490 communities in FY26 and reaffirmed similar 8–10% community growth into FY27, as the preview highlighted.

surprises.description: Lowe’s moved from the preview’s expected full-year guidance affirmation to the bottom of its prior ranges: about $92 billion in sales, flat comps, 11.6% adjusted operating margin and $12.25 adjusted EPS. These are the low ends of the prior ranges, rather than cuts below those ranges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management cut full-year 2026 guidance to the bottom of its prior range,” now expecting “~$92 billion in sales, roughly flat comps, ~11.6% adjusted operating margin, and ~$12.25 adjusted EPS.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EPS guide ($12.25–12.75). Affirmation is the base case. A cut is the main downside risk”; the base scenario also says “FY guide affirmed.”

surprises.description: Comparable sales rose just 0.2%, below the preview’s roughly 0.5–1.0% expectation and the higher bar set by Home Depot’s results. The monthly pattern deteriorated after June, with July comps down as competitors used tariff refunds to cut prices in seasonal categories.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable sales rising just 0.2%”; monthly comps were “May down 0.4%, June up 1.7%, and July down 1.2%,” with July hurt by competitors “using tariff refunds to aggressively cut prices” in seasonal categories.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comparable sales: ~+0.5–1.0% (buy-side inference)”; the preview also said the bar was “effectively above published consensus after HD’s +1.3% U.S.” comps.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS beat the $4.22–$4.26 consensus range, and the beat was not explained entirely by tariff refunds: even excluding the $0.11 benefit, EPS was above expectations. The refund nevertheless contributed to reported earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS was $4.40 (GAAP $4.27), which included an $0.11 benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds, and exceeded expectations even excluding that benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS: $4.22 (some feeds $4.26).”

surprises.description: The near-term outlook was weaker than the preview’s expectation that transactions would improve later in FY26: Q3 comps are expected to track the flat full-year outlook, adjusted EPS is expected to be about 7% lower year over year, and Q4 is implied to be negative. The Q4 comparison includes a temporary drag from last year’s winter storm.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for comps in line with the flat full-year outlook and adjusted EPS approximately 7% below prior year, with Q4 implied to be negative partly due to a ~50 basis point drag from cycling last year's winter storm.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the H2 bridge “depends on transactions improving” and flagged that if Lowe’s dropped its May comment that “transactions will improve later in FY26, the H2 bridge loses support.”

surprises.description: The ticket-up, transactions-down pattern the preview raised as a possibility was more pronounced on transactions: comparable transactions fell 2.1%, versus Home Depot’s 1.0% decline, while Lowe’s comparable ticket rose 2.3%, below Home Depot’s 2.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comparable average ticket rose 2.3% while comparable transactions fell 2.1%,” with the transaction decline concentrated in DIY weather-sensitive outdoor and seasonal categories in Southern geographies.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A similar pattern at LOW would mean the recovery is inflation and mix, not returning customers”; the preview cited Home Depot’s “Ticket +2.8%, transactions −1.0%.”

surprises.description: Sales came in slightly below the preview’s consensus range, despite year-over-year growth of 8.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 sales reached $26 billion, up 8.3% year-over-year.”

surprises.description: Management described added pressure on FBM and ADG from weak residential construction, with ADG fully exposed and FBM substantially exposed. The preview noted that their organic growth and margin contribution were unknown but did not flag this construction exposure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FBM and ADG face heightened pressure from soft residential construction (ADG 100% exposed, FBM 45% exposed).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “First real FBM/ADG scorecard. Organic growth and margin contribution are still undisclosed.”

surprises.description: Online sales remained exceptionally strong, growing 15.7% for a second consecutive quarter above 15%, and customers using the Mylow AI agent converted at triple the rate of non-users. The preview gave no Q2 online-sales or Mylow conversion expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Online sales grew 15.7%, the second consecutive quarter above 15%, with customers using the Mylow AI agent converting at triple the rate of non-users.”

in_line: Adjusted operating margin declined 62 basis points, within the preview’s expected 60–80 basis-point decline; the call attributed pressure to FBM/ADG dilution and elevated fuel and transportation costs.

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP revenue was $633 million, about $17 million above the preview’s roughly $616 million non-GAAP consensus. That is a clear beat, although the preview’s separate $630.9 million estimate was for GAAP revenue and is not directly comparable.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 non-GAAP revenue was $633 million, up 7% year-over-year and above implied guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue (non-GAAP) | ~$616.3M | ~+3.6%”

surprises.description: Fiscal 2027 GAAP EPS guidance of $7.33–$7.38 was above the preview’s roughly $7.20 statutory consensus and its $7.00–$7.15 base scenario. The preview’s bull case began at $7.20, so the guide is above even that stated threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 guidance calls for … GAAP EPS of $7.33-$7.38 (5%-6% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 consensus EPS | ~$7.20 statutory”; base scenario: “EPS $7.00–7.15”; bull scenario: “EPS at or above $7.20.”

surprises.description: Management said Q1 FY2027 non-GAAP revenue growth would be modestly below the low end of the full-year range, an early-quarter slowdown the preview did not flag. Management attributed it partly to moving the Connect conference into Q2 and to timing of one-time items.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 non-GAAP revenue growth [is] to come in modestly below the low end of the full-year range,” driven by “a 1% impact from shifting the Connect conference into Q2 … plus timing of onetime items.”

surprises.description: Core wins reached 58, modestly above the preview’s commitment of more than 55 and a record for the company. The preview had identified core wins as a key item to watch but did not anticipate the record result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A record 58 competitive core wins in fiscal 2026,” up from 51 the prior year.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Full-year core wins. Target is above 55, versus 51 in FY25; 43 through nine months.”

surprises.description: The preview did not set expectations for the mix of core wins, but management reported a pronounced increase in deals combining core, digital banking, and card, alongside a larger share of sales from new contracts. This points to stronger cross-selling and new-contract mix than the preview discussed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trifecta deals … rose to 59% of the 58 core wins versus only 39% of 51 deals last year, and new contracts reached 60% of sales versus 45% the prior year.”

surprises.description: The preview did not forecast payment-network activity, while management reported 45% year-over-year growth across Zelle, RTP, and FedNow. Each of the three networks also grew, rather than the result being attributable to just one named network.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Payment transaction volume across Zelle, RTP, and FedNow grew 45% year-over-year, with Zelle adoption up 25%, RTP up 24%, and FedNow up 29%.”

surprises.description: The preview did not discuss Banno signings or user growth. Management reported 219 full-year signings, up 24%, and more than 15.8 million registered users, up 11%, providing an additional indicator of digital-platform momentum.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Banno Digital platform now serves over 15.8 million registered users (up 11%), with full-year signings of 219 (up 24%).”

surprises.description: Treasury-management deal activity was not addressed in the preview. Management said the business set a record with 45 deals, up 25%, and reported an average client asset size of $2.1 billion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Treasury management set a record with 45 deals (up 25%) at an average client asset size of $2.1 billion.”
