surprises.description: The preview did not discuss capital returns, while the company reported distributing more than its full-year free cash flow through buybacks and dividends. Buybacks also reduced the share count by 4%, and year-end debt was just $40 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2026 free cash flow rose 31% to $539 million, and the company returned 122% of free cash flow to shareholders via $448 million in buybacks (4% share reduction) and $170 million in dividends, ending with just $40 million in debt.”

surprises.description: For FY2027, management identified near-term margin pressures from normalizing self-insured medical costs, cyber and frontier-model investments, and the EC 2030 data-center consolidation project, while saying margin upside may come later in the year. The preview had discussed cost pressures around Q4 but did not flag these FY2027 drivers or this within-year margin pattern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management … flagged near-term margin pressure from normalizing self-insured medical costs, cyber/frontier model investments, and the EC 2030 data center consolidation project, with margin upside possible later in the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q4 was expected to be the weakest print, citing “medical benefit cost normalization, cloud-migration spend, and higher commissions.”

in_line: Full-year non-GAAP revenue growth was 7%, in line with the preview’s expected 6.6%–7.1%.
Full-year non-GAAP operating margin was 24%, within the preview’s cited 23.9%–24.1% FY26 guide.
FY2027 non-GAAP revenue growth guidance of 6.3%–7.3% was broadly around the preview’s approximately 6.5% Street expectation.

surprises.description: BEEM reported a GAAP loss of $0.14 per share, versus the preview’s consensus estimate of a $0.20 loss. The loss per share was about 30% smaller than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss narrowed to $3.1 million ($0.14 per share)”

surprises.description: First-half results included a $1 million noncash provision for credit losses on a balance owed by one customer, which BEEM is still trying to collect. The preview did not flag this charge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half results absorbed a $1 million noncash provision for credit losses tied to a single customer balance, which the company is still working to collect.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses were $4.5 million, below the preview’s roughly $5.0 million threshold for supporting the cost program. The comparison with last year is partly affected by a $1.4 million stock grant included in prior-year opex.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses fell to $4.5 million from $5.9 million a year ago (which included a $1.4 million stock grant), reflecting roughly $0.5 million in first-half cost reductions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP opex at or below about $5.0M would support the cost program.”

surprises.description: BEEM said Europe now generates roughly as much revenue as the United States, and cited European EV sales growth despite weakness in the U.S. market. The preview did not identify this regional balance or European demand as an expected driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Europe now generates roughly the same amount of revenue as the United States,” and management cited “European EV sales up 35% year-over-year despite US market weakness.”

surprises.description: BEEM reported more than $0.5 million of drone and robotics orders booked in a single week, in a battery and energy-storage segment it called its fastest-growing. The preview did not anticipate this order activity or these end markets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Battery and energy storage is the fastest-growing segment, with over $0.5 million in drone and robotics orders booked in a single week,” targeting “drones, robotics, AI data centers and weapon systems.”

surprises.description: The preview cited expected rent savings from the Yuma move but described labor savings as unquantified; management said Yuma labor costs are about 75% of San Diego rates. This adds a specific labor-cost comparison beyond the preview’s stated expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The relocation of manufacturing from San Diego to Yuma, Arizona is expected to save approximately $2.7-3 million in rent over the 5-year lease, plus labor costs at about 75% of San Diego rates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The company cites $2.7M of lease savings over five years, plus unquantified labor savings.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $8.6 million, consistent with the July pre-announcement of more than $8.5 million; the preview’s older ~$7.5 million consensus was superseded by that announcement.
GAAP gross margin of 17.8% was within the announced 15–18% range.
June backlog of $5.4 million was in the preview’s anticipated $5–6 million range after substantial conversion of backlog into shipments.

surprises.description: BILL’s FY27 core revenue growth guidance of 11%–14% falls below the preview’s 13%–14% buy-side bar at the low end and has a 12.5% midpoint. Management also identified a 3-point year-over-year growth headwind from spend-and-expense dynamics and bank channels.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 core revenue guidance of $1.669B-$1.719B implies 11%-14% growth,” including “3 points of year-over-year growth headwind.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side bar is roughly 13–14%”; the preview also said “11–12% supports the bear case.”

surprises.description: Q4 net customer adds were far below the preview’s roughly 3,800–4,000 expectation. Management’s expected Q1 recovery to 2,500–3,000 would still be below that benchmark, with restructuring and a narrower ideal-customer focus cited as reasons for the shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company added only ~1,800 net new customers in Q4,” and Q1 is “expected to recover to 2,500-3,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q4 guidance “slightly below 4,000,” a checklist of “~3,800 or more,” and Q3 net adds of “~4,100.”

surprises.description: Q4 non-GAAP operating margin reached 23%, well above the roughly 19.5% implied by the preview’s consensus operating income and revenue estimates. The margin also expanded sharply year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating margin reached 23%, expanding 860 basis points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “Non-GAAP operating income” of “~$84M” and total revenue of “$430.5M,” implying an operating margin of about 19.5%.

surprises.description: Management said FY27 growth is expected to reach its trough in Q2, revealing a specific within-year slowdown that the preview did not identify. This adds a near-term timing concern beyond the weaker annual growth range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 FY27 is expected to mark the trough of the year's growth trajectory.”

surprises.description: The call provided a more concrete profitability outlook than the preview had available: BILL expects to exceed the Rule of 40 exiting FY27 and generate well over $125 million of GAAP profit for the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects to exceed the Rule of 40 ... exiting FY27” and “generate well over $125 million of GAAP profits for the full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “management deferred Rule of 40 and GAAP margin content from Investor Day to this call” and modeled roughly 25%–26% FY27 non-GAAP margin from expected savings.

surprises.description: BILL disclosed substantial Q4 buybacks, including about $300 million repurchased and roughly 15 million shares retired since Q3, while $400 million remains authorized. The preview flagged buyback pace as relevant but did not anticipate a specific execution amount.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Repurchased ~$300 million of stock ... in Q4,” retiring “~15 million shares (nearly 14% of shares outstanding) since Q3,” with “$400 million remaining” on the authorization.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that “How much of the $1.0B authorization was executed in Q4 affects the FY27 EPS bridge.”

surprises.description: Core revenue came in modestly above the preview’s implied consensus, though the reported growth rate was within the company’s previously guided range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 core revenue grew 16% year-over-year to $400.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview put core subscription and transaction revenue consensus at “~$397M (implied)” and company guidance at “$392 – $402M (+13–16%).”

surprises.description: BILL reported strong AI invoice-financing growth alongside substantially improved expected losses, a risk-and-growth update not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI-driven invoice financing saw both volume and revenue grow ~30% year-over-year in FY26 while the expected loss rate improved by more than 50%.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed strong adoption and cross-product indicators that the preview did not set expectations for: more than 175,000 businesses use AI agents, joint AP and spend-and-expense customers grew 35%, and multiproduct customers had 111% net revenue retention.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Over 175,000 businesses are now using BILL's AI agents,” joint AP and spend-and-expense customers “grew 35% year-over-year,” and existing multiproduct customers showed “net revenue retention of 111%.”

in_line: Restructuring savings were broadly in line with the preview: about $110 million in gross savings and roughly $30 million reinvested, leaving an approximately $80 million net benefit versus the preview’s estimated $80–90 million net savings.

surprises.description: ADI guided Q4 revenue to $4.3 billion, well above the preview’s derived $4.0–4.1 billion expectation and even above its $4.15 billion bull trigger. The accompanying outlook was for 52% operating margin and $3.86 EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 guidance calls for revenue of $4.3 billion (+/- $100 million), operating margin of 52%, and EPS of $3.86 (+/- $0.15), implying continued sequential growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Derived consensus for the October quarter is roughly $4.0–4.1B”; “A guide of $4.15B+ is the bull trigger.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue reached $4.02 billion, beating the roughly $3.92 billion consensus and edging above the $4.0 billion high end of company guidance. The preview’s bull case had included revenue up to $4.05 billion, so the result was a modest beat rather than an outcome beyond that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 FY2026 revenue reached a record $4.02 billion, exceeding the high end of guidance while growing 11% sequentially and 40% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus (~Aug 14, 2026): ~$3.92B”; company guide “$3.90B ± $100M”; bull scenario revenue “$3.98–4.05B.”

surprises.description: Q3 EPS of $3.45 beat the preview’s $3.33 consensus, although it was at the high end of company guidance and only the bottom of the preview’s bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 EPS hit a record $3.45, up 12% sequentially and 68% year-over-year, at the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS” consensus was “$3.33”; bull scenario was “$3.45–3.55.”

surprises.description: Management’s Q4 gross-margin outlook was stronger than the preview’s expected roughly 72.5% Q3 margin and its focus on whether pricing could hold margins at 73% or higher: it now expects Q4 gross margin to rise about 150 basis points to roughly 74%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Q4 gross margin to rise ~150 bps to about 74%, back near 2022 peak levels, driven by favorable mix, higher fixed cost absorption, and price adjustments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q3 adjusted gross margin consensus at “~72.5%” and said “Holding 73%+ would signal pricing strength.”

surprises.description: The data-center contribution to communications was much more emphatic than the preview’s framing of data-center performance as potentially in line: data center was 80% of communications revenue, while optical and power each grew more than 100% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Data center now represents 80% of communications revenue, with both optical and power businesses each growing more than 100% year-over-year in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “data center in line” in its base scenario and identified communications growth as a key test of the AI-power case.

surprises.description: ADI’s inventory position improved more than the preview’s risk-focused setup suggested: days inventory fell from 168 to 156, and distributor channel inventory moved below the 6–7 week target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Distributor channel inventory fell below the 6-7 week target and days inventory declined to 156.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Days of inventory 168 (elevated); channel weeks 6–7 (lean)” and warned about “the risk of double-ordering.”

surprises.description: Management raised its long-term view of analog-industry growth beyond the 5%–7% model it had used since 2021, and described fiscal 2027 as a brisk-growth year. The preview did not anticipate a change to that long-term growth framework.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management signaled potential for double-digit annual analog industry growth for years, raising expectations above the prior 5%-7% long-term model set in 2021, and expects a ‘brisk growth year’ in fiscal 2027.”

surprises.description: Management said its 2030 data-center and energy revenue opportunity had more than doubled in just a year, and projected roughly 2x OCS revenue in 2026 with similar growth targeted in 2027. The preview had not flagged these specific opportunity and OCS-growth claims.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management's 2030 data center and energy revenue opportunity has more than doubled versus its assessment just one year ago, with OCS revenue set to roughly double in 2026 and targeting similar growth in 2027.”

in_line: Automotive grew 16% year over year, meeting the preview’s key test of whether ADI could deliver sustained double-digit automotive growth; the preview noted FQ2 growth of 2% and said double-digit growth would broaden the cycle.

surprises.description: TJX’s 4% comparable-sales growth beat the preview’s 3.2% consensus estimate, though it matched the preview’s +4% base-case scenario. The increase came from both higher average basket and more customer transactions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 consolidated comparable sales rose 4%, above plan, driven by both higher average basket and increased customer transactions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consolidated comp: +3.2%” consensus; the preview’s base scenario was “Comp +4%.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted pretax margin reached 11.9%, above the preview’s 11.4–11.5% guide-based expectation and its 11.7–11.8% base case. Adjusted gross margin rose 70 basis points, largely because of tariff-related merchandise-margin favorability, despite the preview viewing direct tariff P&L impact as minimal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted Q2 pretax profit margin was 11.9%, up 50 basis points year-over-year, with adjusted gross margin of 31.4% (up 70 bps) largely driven by tariff-related merchandise margin favorability.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pretax margin: 11.4%–11.5%” company guidance and “margin around 11.7–11.8%” in the base scenario. The preview also said, “Direct P&L impact appears minimal” for tariffs.

surprises.description: Marmaxx, TJX’s largest division, comped only 1%, well below the preview’s 2.7% consensus expectation. Management attributed the miss to self-inflicted, correctable merchandise-mix execution issues.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marmaxx, TJX's largest division, comped only 1% versus 6-7% at the other three divisions, with management attributing the shortfall entirely to self-inflicted, correctable merchandise-mix execution issues.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus comp is +2.7%” for Marmaxx.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted diluted EPS of $1.22 beat the preview’s $1.18 consensus estimate (or $1.19 in some sources) and was described as well above plan. The beat was modest against the preview’s $1.21–$1.24 base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted Q2 diluted EPS was $1.22, up 11% versus last year and well above plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS” consensus: “$1.18 (some sources $1.19)”; the base scenario projected “EPS $1.21–$1.24.”

surprises.description: Q3 guidance introduced a near-term slowdown signal: adjusted EPS is expected to rise only 2–3%, while adjusted pretax margin is expected to decline 30–40 basis points. The preview gave no Q3 estimate; TJX cited higher fuel and freight costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance implies a margin pullback, with adjusted pretax margin of 12.3-12.4% (down 30-40 bps) and EPS of $1.30-$1.32 (up just 2-3%), pressured by higher fuel and freight costs.”

surprises.description: Inventory growth was less pronounced per store than the preview’s most recent figure suggested, and management characterized the position as well placed for buying opportunities rather than emphasizing markdown risk. Inventory rose 7% overall but only 2% per store, versus +7% per store at Q1 end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Balance sheet inventory rose 7% (up 2% per store), which management views as well-positioned amid abundant buying opportunities across a network of ~21,000 vendors and 1,400+ buyers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Inventory per store +7% reported (+6% constant currency) at Q1 end”; the preview said management’s framing of inventory—“well-bought inventory versus markdown risk”—mattered.

surprises.description: TJX raised its long-term store target by 500 and plans to accelerate annual store growth from 3% to 4% starting next year, an expansion plan the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “TJX raised its long-term store target by 500 units to 7,500 stores and plans to accelerate annual store growth to 4% starting next year (from 3%).”

in_line: The FY27 adjusted EPS guide was raised to $5.15–$5.20, within the preview’s base-case expectation of $5.15–$5.25. It reaches, but does not exceed, the preview’s stated buy-side threshold of about $5.20 or higher.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was about $560,000, far below the preview's $1.34 million consensus estimate. It was within the preview's $0.5–$0.9 million base-case range, but roughly 58% below consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue rose to approximately $560,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $1.34M | TradingView/Zacks-derived, Aug 2026”; the preview's base case was “$0.5–0.9M.”

surprises.description: ClearSign booked six M-Series burner orders, including five large M1 units for two top-tier Permian Basin customers. The preview's base case anticipated smaller revenue and said hard backlog disclosure was unlikely, so these concrete bookings were a positive development beyond that baseline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Since the prior call, the company booked orders for 6 M-Series burners—about 10-12% of its roughly 50-proposal pipeline—with 5 large M1 units going to two top-tier Permian Basin customers.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Silence is the base case” for a hard backlog number and described the base scenario as “Parts and smaller revenue only.”

surprises.description: The 36-burner Texas project is on hold because the customer has not resolved its financing. The preview identified the Texas equipment phase as a timing question and potential revenue, but did not flag customer financing as a reason for a hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 36-burner Texas process burner project is on hold due to unresolved customer financing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “timing of the Texas 36-burner equipment phase” as a catalyst to watch and described the project as potential equipment revenue “not yet booked as firm orders.”

surprises.description: Management described a path to a $6–7 million run rate from midstream and flare products alone, with double-digit-million annual revenue feasible as process burner installations activate. The preview highlighted uncertainty about the second-half revenue shape but did not provide or anticipate this specific run-rate outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management sees a path to a $6-7 million run rate from midstream and flare product lines alone” and “views double-digit-million annual revenue as feasible as process burner installations activate.”

surprises.description: One three-burner order used a licensing and royalty structure: it reduces revenue per unit because the customer manufactures the burners, while preserving the same profit-margin dollars. The preview did not anticipate this different route to fulfilling an order.
surprises.fact_evidence: “One of the 3-burner orders was structured as a licensing/royalty deal where the customer manufactures the burners from ClearSign drawings, reducing revenue per unit but preserving the same profit-margin dollars.”

in_line: Gross margin was approximately 41%, matching the preview's apparent 41% figure and its base-case range of 35–45%.
The Gulf Coast 26-burner startup remained on track for October, as the preview's base case expected.

The July private placement was already described in the preview; the reported approximately $1.7 million proceeds and approximately $11.6 million pro forma cash do not represent a new financing surprise.

surprises.description: The preview used Q3’s 7.0% gross margin as the benchmark and viewed a margin above 8.5% as a potential upside trigger. Unifi reported roughly 10% gross margin, well above that benchmark.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross profit swung to $14.3 million (roughly 10% margin)” from a gross loss of $1.1 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3's 7.0% is the benchmark” and “above ~8.5% as a re-rating trigger.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was expected at roughly $6–7 million, with $6 million or more described as the bull-case threshold. Unifi delivered $8.2 million, exceeding that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved by $12.3 million year-over-year to $8.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$6–7M (implied, not published)” and “A Q4 print of $6M+ is the bull math.”

surprises.description: The preview already knew of the roughly $60 million real-estate sale but said net proceeds and cash taxes were unknown. Unifi said tax leakage should be minimal because of NOL carry-forwards and that the proceeds could leave it essentially bank debt-free by calendar year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: The sale is “for $60 million,” with “minimal tax leakage due to NOL carry-forwards”; management said it could make the company “essentially bank debt-free by the end of the calendar year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net proceeds are not yet known. Watch fees, cash taxes” and the sale was expected “with proceeds to retire debt.”

surprises.description: The preview did not provide a full-year free-cash-flow expectation. Unifi reported $21.5 million for FY26, more than $50 million better than FY25.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year free cash flow reached $21.5 million, an improvement of over $50 million versus fiscal 2025.”

surprises.description: Revenue was expected to be about $141.1 million. Unifi reported $144.2 million, a modest beat, and year-over-year growth was 4% rather than the preview’s implied 1.9%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 consolidated net sales rose 4% year-over-year to $144.2 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales ~$141.1M” and “Consensus implies +1.9% YoY.”

surprises.description: The preview did not flag a delay to Unifi’s REPREVE mix target. The call said the target of 50% of fiber sales had been pushed out to 2030, indicating a longer timeline than investors were alerted to in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “REPREVE's target of 50% of fiber sales has been pushed out to 2030.”

in_line: The roughly $60 million real-estate sale agreement was already known from the preview; the expected transaction itself was confirmed.
Brazil was flagged as “pretty strong” for Q4, consistent with the reported segment strength.
The preview highlighted Asia’s contraction and tariff uncertainty; the call likewise described Asia as challenged and the current quarter as difficult on revenue.
The preview expected Q4 revenue of at least $138 million as a key threshold; reported sales of $144.2 million cleared it.

surprises.description: The preview said the key Q1 question was whether Wolfspeed would guide to its first sequential growth quarter, but gave no Q1 revenue estimate. Management guided to $140–160 million of Q1 device revenue versus about $106 million of Q4 device revenue, signaling substantial sequential growth in devices; the guidance does not establish growth in total revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 FY2027 guidance calls for device revenue of $140 million to $160 million”; Q4 device revenue was “~$106 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The question is whether management guides to the first sequential growth quarter in over two years.”

surprises.description: The preview called for a credible path toward gross-margin breakeven but had no revenue threshold. Management newly estimated that Wolfspeed needs roughly an $800 million annual revenue run rate to reach breakeven gross margin, with the exact point depending on mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A roughly $800 million annual revenue run rate is needed to reach breakeven gross margin, though the exact point depends on product mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for a credible path toward breakeven gross margin.”

surprises.description: AI data-center revenue grew 20% sequentially in Q4, below the 30% Q3 growth rate mentioned in the preview, although it more than doubled for FY2026 and became Wolfspeed’s fastest-growing end market. The preview flagged quantification as important but did not specify an expected Q4 growth rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI data center revenue grew ~20% sequentially from Q3 to Q4 and more than doubled from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2026, becoming the company's fastest-growing end market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said AI data-center growth was “about 50% QoQ in Q2 and 30% in Q3” and that it had “never given a dollar figure. Quantification would matter.”

surprises.description: Q4 cash generation benefited from a sharp fall in gross capex and a $41 million inventory reduction. The preview flagged FY2027 capex and cash as issues to watch but did not anticipate these specific cash-flow contributors.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross capital expenditures fell sharply to $5 million in Q4 from $38 million in the prior quarter, and inventory reduction contributed a $41 million benefit to operating cash flow.”

surprises.description: Management identified a refinancing opportunity in roughly $630 million of first-lien debt carrying about 16% interest, saying it could meaningfully reduce the company’s quarterly operating cash burn. The preview discussed cash-flow breakeven but did not identify this specific refinancing lever.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First lien debt of roughly $630 million carries ~16% interest, representing a major refinancing opportunity that could meaningfully reduce the company's $54 million quarterly operating cash burn.”

surprises.description: Holders voluntarily converted $46 million of convertible notes to equity in Q4, saving about $1 million in annual interest. The preview flagged potential convertible dilution, but did not describe a conversion or its interest savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Holders of $46 million of convertible notes voluntarily converted debt to equity during Q4, saving approximately $1 million in annual interest expense.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “potential convertible dilution (about 44M shares against 52M outstanding).”

in_line: Q4 revenue was $150 million, at the midpoint of the $140–160 million guidance and in line with the preview’s $150 million consensus estimate.

Q4 adjusted non-GAAP gross margin was negative 19.9%, within the preview’s implied range of roughly negative 18% to negative 21%; management also continued to cite factory underutilization as the primary margin constraint, as the preview anticipated.
Adjusted EBITDA of negative $62 million was within the preview’s expected range of roughly negative $55 million to negative $62 million.
Operating expenses of $62 million were close to the preview’s roughly $61 million estimate and the prior guidance for roughly flat sequential spending.
Q1 guidance still called for negative non-GAAP gross margin, consistent with the preview’s expectation that gross margin would remain negative.

surprises.description: Coty said sellout has trailed category growth for several quarters, contributing to lower sell-in and inventory swings. The preview discussed weak prior-quarter results but did not flag this persistent sellout shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Coty's sellout has been trailing category growth for several quarters, driving lower sell-in and inventory swings.”

surprises.description: Elevated oil prices are costing Coty about $20–30 million, an unflagged cost headwind in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Elevated oil prices between $90 and $100 are costing Coty roughly $20-30 million.”

surprises.description: Management described a shift away from Coty's historically sell-in-focused culture by making sellout and market share key bonus measures. The preview did not anticipate this compensation change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Coty has restructured its fiscal 2027 bonus system to make market share and sellout a key KPI, alongside sales and a strong EBITDA component,” marking a shift from its “historically sell-in-focused culture.”

surprises.description: Coty said CoverGirl and Sally Hansen have substantially narrowed their U.S. performance gap to the market, with Sally Hansen now growing ahead of its category. The preview did not flag this brand-level improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CoverGirl and Sally Hansen have substantially narrowed the gap to market, with Sally Hansen now growing ahead of the category,” driven by equity-building advertising rather than promotions.

surprises.description: Coty plans to cut 20% of its on-shelf SKUs and expects no material sales impact, while aiming to reduce returns and obsolescence costs. This specific operational plan was not in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Coty plans a 20% SKU reduction on shelf,” which management expects “without material sales impact” while reducing returns and obsolescence costs.

surprises.description: Management put a roughly $30 million tariff refund forward as possible upside, though it remains unconfirmed. The preview noted tariff pressure on margins but did not mention a potential refund.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A potential ~$30 million tariff refund remains a possible but unconfirmed upside.”

surprises.description: Coty set a target to return its underlying portfolio, excluding Gucci, to growth in fiscal 2028, supported by innovation intended to benefit core brands. The preview highlighted the Gucci revenue cliff in FY28 but did not mention this growth target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Coty targets returning its underlying portfolio (excluding Gucci) to growth in fiscal 2028,” relying on innovation with “halo effects on core global brands like Burberry and Hugo Boss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “the revenue cliff falls in FY28” and asked Coty to confirm how FY27 guidance treats Gucci revenue.

surprises.description: Coty said its cost-savings and restructuring program alone is intended to offset the financial impact of Gucci's departure. The preview identified the Gucci revenue cliff but did not describe this specific offset target.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Coty intends for its cost-savings and restructuring program alone to offset the financial impact of the Gucci license departure,” targeting savings in allocated overhead, manufacturing, distribution, and central functions.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted that Gucci's revenue cliff falls in FY28 and asked Coty to confirm how FY27 guidance treats the license.

in_line: Coty framed FY27 as a transition year, targeting EBITDA and free cash flow close to FY26 rather than growth. This was broadly consistent with the preview's FY26 EBITDA base of about $840 million and its base case of a wide FY27 outlook, though the preview did not state a specific consensus FY27 target.

Management expects Q1 FY27 sellout to remain similar to the prior two soft quarters before improving sequentially, consistent with the preview's base scenario of a weaker first half followed by improvement in the second half.

surprises.description: The reporting delay was not resolved by a routine filing: Solésence filed a Form NT 10-Q and is restating historical financials because indirect manufacturing costs were allocated improperly in inventory costing. Management said the issue does not affect cash flows or operations, but the restatement is more serious than the preview’s base case of a discrete, non-restatement explanation for the delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Filed a Form NT 10-Q and is restating historical financials due to an inventory costing methodology error involving improper allocation of indirect manufacturing costs,” though management says it “does not affect cash flows or operations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... Delay explained by a discrete, non-restatement item”; the preview also flagged a restatement as a bear-case risk.

surprises.description: Gross margin was 31%, above the preview’s roughly 28% base estimate and management’s 30% floor, rather than the 25–27% result the preview identified as a credibility concern. The margin held near the prior-year level despite substantially lower revenue, which management attributed partly to improved labor efficiency.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin held roughly steady at 31% versus a restated 32% a year earlier,” despite 25% lower revenue, “signaling improved labor efficiency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base estimates ... gross margin about 28%”; management had a “30% floor” for 2026, and the preview said “another print at 25–27%” would be a credibility issue.

surprises.description: Management gave a stronger growth outlook than the preview’s base case of demand around $13–15 million per quarter: it now expects full-year 2026 revenue to exceed 2025 and projects about $35 million in the second half, its strongest second half ever.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management now expects full-year 2026 revenue to exceed 2025, with the second half projected at approximately $35 million, the strongest second half in company history.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: Demand near the $13–15M quarterly level”; the preview also said to watch whether full-year framing changed.

surprises.description: Despite the expected Refy charge, the reported net loss was smaller than the preview’s modeled loss: Solésence lost $158,000 versus an estimated loss of about $400,000. The year-over-year swing also reflected the absence of the $1.4 million ERC payment received in Q2 2025.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 swung to a net loss of $158,000,” partly due to a “one-time $938,000 charge related to Refy” and “the absence of a $1.4 million ERC payment received in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My base estimates ... net loss about $0.4M.”

surprises.description: The company reported $64.9 million in shipped and on-hand orders for 2026 as of August 17, versus $60 million at the same point in 2025. The preview discussed demand and OTIF recovery but did not anticipate or provide an order-book expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “As of August 17, shipped and on-hand orders for 2026 totaled $64.9 million, up from $60 million in the same period of 2025.”

surprises.description: Solésence launched a scalp-care segment in July, including a dry shampoo/SPF combination and an allantoin-based treatment using Whisper technology, targeting an estimated $3 billion market. This new product area and market opportunity were not previewed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company launched a new scalp care segment in July,” targeting an estimated “$3 billion addressable market,” with a dry shampoo/SPF combination product and an allantoin-based treatment using its Whisper technology.

surprises.description: Management described the FDA’s approval of the non-mineral BEMT sunscreen platform as an opportunity, planning combination products with Solésence’s mineral and boost technologies. The preview did not discuss BEMT or this product strategy.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company views the FDA's recent approval of the non-mineral BEMT sunscreen platform as an opportunity rather than a threat,” and plans combination products pairing BEMT with its proprietary mineral and boost technologies.

in_line: Q2 revenue was $15.3 million, close to the preview’s roughly $15.0 million model estimate and above its stated $15 million sequential-revenue watch point; the 25% year-over-year decline was also close to the preview’s modeled 26% decline.
The $938,000 Refy charge was in line with the preview’s expectation of an approximately $0.9 million charge in Q2.

surprises.description: AAP reported adjusted diluted EPS of $1.03, well above the preview’s $0.80–$0.81 consensus. The roughly 27% beat was substantially larger than the preview’s bull-case EPS range of $0.95–$1.05 might have suggested as an upside scenario, not the base expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS rose to $1.03 from $0.69 a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS” consensus was “$0.80–0.81.”

surprises.description: Sales were below consensus and comparable sales declined slightly rather than growing about 2%, with the shortfall driven by DIY weakness: low-single-digit Pro growth was more than offset by a larger-than-expected low-single-digit DIY decline. This was weaker than the preview’s expected comp moderation and its base-case positive comp range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales were $2 billion with a slight comparable sales decline,” as “low single-digit Pro channel growth was more than offset by a larger-than-expected low single-digit DIY decline driven by tighter household budgets in the last 4 weeks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Net sales consensus was “$2.03–2.04B”; comparable sales consensus was “~+2%”; the base scenario expected “Comps +1.5–2.5%.”

surprises.description: The reported 5.6% adjusted operating margin was above the preview’s roughly 4.5% expectation, but it included IEEPA tariff refunds; excluding those refunds, margin was 4.3%, 20 basis points below expectation. Gross-margin expansion included both a substantial refund contribution and merchandising gains, rather than being purely recurring improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating margin was 5.6%, but excluding IEEPA tariff refunds it was 4.3%”; adjusted gross margin expanded “approximately 240 basis points to 46.2%,” with refunds contributing “130 basis points” and merchandising initiatives “roughly 110 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview put adjusted operating margin at “~4.5%” and said to watch “whether expansion comes from merchandising (durable) or from LIFO and supply-chain timing (not durable).”

surprises.description: AAP raised its full-year adjusted EPS range by $0.20 at both ends, but the new $2.60 floor remained below the preview’s roughly $2.70 floor marker. The company also said roughly $100 million of interest income aided the guidance, an earnings source not highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year EPS guidance was raised to $2.60-$3.30, aided by roughly $100 million of interest income.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior guidance was “$2.40–3.10”; the preview said “lifting the floor toward ~$2.70” was a likely upside catalyst and that a flat reaffirmation would read as caution.

surprises.description: Same-SKU inflation accelerated to about 4% in Q2 from 3% in Q1, and full-year inflation is now expected at about 3%, roughly 100 basis points above original plans. That is worse than the preview’s expectation of inflation near 3% against a 2–3% plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Same-SKU inflation stepped up to approximately 4% in Q2 from 3% last quarter” due to motor-oil and petroleum-product price increases; “full-year inflation [is] now expected at about 3%, roughly 100 basis points above original plans.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Same-SKU inflation is running near 3% versus the 2–3% plan.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow turned positive year to date at $120 million, a sharp reversal from the $201 million outflow in the same period last year and the first positive result in two years. The preview had flagged the need for an H2 cash inflection after a $75 million Q1 outflow, but did not have a full-year FCF estimate; AAP also reaffirmed approximately $100 million of full-year FCF guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated $120 million of year-to-date free cash flow,” versus “a $201 million outflow last year,” marking positive free cash flow “for the first time in two years”; FY FCF guidance was reaffirmed at “approximately $100 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FCF was −$75M in Q1. Against ~$300M capex, the H2 cash inflection needs to show up here.” The preview said FY2026 FCF guidance “could not be obtained.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $3.25, above the $3.09 consensus and the preview’s roughly $3.16 whisper, and $0.10 above the high end of Nordson’s Q3 guidance. The earnings beat was stronger than the preview’s base case of $3.10–$3.18.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS reached a record $3.25, up 19% year-over-year and $0.10 above the high end of guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus” adj. EPS was “$3.09”; the whisper implied “about $3.16”; the base scenario was “$3.10 – $3.18.”

surprises.description: Q3 sales of $818 million substantially exceeded the $779 million consensus and even topped the preview’s bull scenario of $800–$810 million. This was a stronger sales result than the preview’s base case of $780–$792 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Record Q3 FY2026 sales of $818 million, up 10% year-over-year, including 12% organic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue consensus was “$779M”; the bull scenario was “$800M – $810M” and the base scenario was “$780M – $792M.”

surprises.description: Nordson raised FY26 sales guidance to $3.035–$3.075 billion and adjusted EPS to $11.80–$12.00, above the preview’s prior ranges of $2.930–$3.010 billion and $11.30–$11.80. The new ranges lift both the floor and the top end of the prior outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year guidance to sales of $3.035-$3.075 billion and adjusted EPS of $11.80-$12.00.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Prior FY26 guidance was “$2,930M – $3,010M revenue and $11.30 – $11.80 EPS”; the preview asked whether management would “raise the floor or only narrow.”

surprises.description: Backlog growth accelerated to 35% year over year, well above the 18% growth reported in Q2 and the preview’s 20%+ bull-case marker. The increase was broad across segments and gave management visibility into FY27.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog grew 35% year-over-year, driven broadly across all segments … providing visibility into fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Backlog +18% YoY” in Q2 and used “backlog +20%+” in its bull scenario.

surprises.description: ATS sales reached $220 million, far above the $190.9 million segment consensus and the preview’s bull-case threshold of $200 million. The segment’s 31% organic growth was also well ahead of the consensus growth expectation of 11.5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advanced Technology Solutions delivered an all-time record $220 million in sales, up 28% (31% organic).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: ATS revenue consensus was “$190.9M (+11.5%)”; the bull scenario specified “ATS above $200M.”

surprises.description: ATS EBITDA margin reached a record 30%, exceeding the preview’s expectation of about 27% or higher and its bull-case threshold of 28%+. This was a stronger margin result than the operating-leverage case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: ATS EBITDA margin expanded “to a record 30% from 24% a year prior.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “A margin of about 27% or higher supports the operating-leverage story” and set “margin of 28%+” in the bull case.

surprises.description: Medical and Fluid Solutions sales were $231 million with 11% organic growth, beating the $224.4 million segment consensus and its expected 2.3% growth despite a 6% headwind from the divested contract manufacturing business.
surprises.fact_evidence: MFS “posted record sales of $231 million with 11% organic growth” despite “a 6% headwind from the divested contract manufacturing business.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: MFS revenue consensus was “$224.4M (+2.3%).”

surprises.description: MFS produced record EBITDA of $88 million at a 38% margin despite the preview’s concern that regulatory-driven product change costs would weigh on margins. The results indicate that the anticipated near-term margin headwind did not prevent a record outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: MFS posted “record EBITDA of $88 million at a 38% margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Management flagged regulatory-driven product change costs as a near-term headwind. Q3 is when that is tested.”

surprises.description: IPS grew 3% organically, whereas the preview interpreted its 3.7% revenue consensus as implying roughly flat to slightly negative organic growth. The segment therefore avoided the weak organic result the preview considered possible.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Industrial Precision Solutions grew just 3% organically.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the IPS consensus “implies roughly flat to slightly negative organic growth.”

surprises.description: Free cash flow conversion was 144% of net income, materially above the preview’s expectation of sustained conversion above 100%. Nordson also reported a fifth consecutive quarter above 100% conversion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was $237 million, representing a 144% conversion of net income and the fifth consecutive quarter above 100% conversion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Sustained conversion above 100% is expected.”

surprises.description: Management said ATS growth should normalize toward mid-single digits in FY27 after the current peak, tempering the strong backlog and FY27 visibility story. Management also said North American chip-infrastructure investment has not yet generated Nordson orders, leaving that activity as potential upside rather than current demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects “ATS growth to normalize toward mid-single digits off a peak in fiscal 2027,” and said North American chip infrastructure investment “has not yet generated Nordson orders,” representing future upside.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described backlog as “the main signal for … the FY27 setup” and said “operating momentum supports a beat,” but did not anticipate a specific FY27 ATS growth normalization rate.

surprises.description: Nordson reported net debt of about $1.6 billion, leverage of 1.7x, and a year-over-year reduction of more than $5 million in net interest expense aided by a new commercial paper program. The preview did not discuss debt, leverage, or this financing development.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt declined to approximately $1.6 billion with leverage reduced to 1.7x, and net interest expense fell over $5 million year-over-year aided by a new commercial paper program.”

in_line: IPS EBITDA margin was flat at 35%, consistent with the preview’s description of management defending margins rather than expanding them amid tariff and input-cost pressures.

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted EPS growth exceeded 19%, well above the preview’s expected 7.4%–8.8% growth, while adjusted operating income rose 17.4% versus the 7%–10% guide. The operating-income result included a roughly 750-basis-point benefit from $2.9 billion of tariff refunds; excluding that benefit, growth was at the top of the guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating income rose 17.4% and adjusted EPS increased over 19%”; Q2 operating income included “a ~750 basis point benefit from approximately $2.9 billion in tariff refunds”; excluding this, underlying OI growth was “at the top end of the 7%-10% guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS: $0.73 (Barchart) or $0.74 (CNBC & BofA)”; “Adj. operating income guide: +7% to +10% cc.”

surprises.description: Walmart raised its full-year outlook rather than leaving it unchanged: sales guidance moved to 4%–5%, operating income to 7%–8.5%, and EPS to $2.80–$2.87. The preview expected the existing sales and EPS ranges to be reaffirmed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year sales guidance was raised to 4%-5% (from 3.5%-4.5%), operating income guidance to 7%-8.5% (from 6%-8%), and EPS to $2.80-$2.87 (from $2.75-$2.85).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 revenue guide: $731.1–738.2B (+3.5–4.5% cc)” and “FY27 adj. EPS guide: $2.75–$2.85”; the preview said “No raise has come after Q1” and described reaffirmed guidance as the base scenario.

surprises.description: Walmart U.S. comps came in at 2.6%, below the preview’s roughly 3.5% expectation. Management attributed 125 basis points of drag to maximum fair price drug regulation and put underlying core comps closer to 3.5%, so the reported shortfall was largely tied to that regulatory effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Walmart U.S. comp sales rose only 2.6%, hurt by a 125 basis point drag from maximum fair price drug regulation, with management framing underlying core comps closer to 3.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Walmart U.S. comp ex-fuel: ~3.5%.”

surprises.description: Management guided to only 2%–4% operating-income growth and EPS of $0.62–$0.64 for Q3, and asked investors to view Q2 and Q3 together because price reinvestment is concentrated. The preview gave no Q3 estimate, so this was a newly disclosed near-term slowdown despite the stronger Q2 result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q3 operating income growth of just 2%-4% and EPS of $0.62-$0.64, urging investors to view Q2 and Q3 together (averaging ~10% OI growth per quarter) due to concentrated price reinvestment.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a roughly 20-basis-point operating-income headwind from the Vibe acquisition being absorbed into guidance. The preview did not mention this acquisition-related cost.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guidance now absorbs … roughly 20 basis points of OI headwind from the Vibe acquisition.”

surprises.description: Walmart U.S. had deployed more than 11,000 rollbacks, up from about 7,200 in Q1, and management said the pricing push creates temporary deflation before the sales benefit arrives with a lag. The preview did not anticipate this specific scale or timing of the price investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Walmart U.S. deployed over 11,000 rollbacks (up from ~7,200 in Q1)”; management warned this “creates a temporary deflationary effect with a lagged sales benefit.”

in_line: Enterprise net sales grew 5% in constant currency, at the top end of the previously issued 4%–5% guidance.
Excluding the tariff-refund benefit, adjusted operating-income growth was at the top end of the previously issued 7%–10% guidance.
Advertising and membership remained around the strong pace the preview highlighted: global advertising grew 38% versus 37% in Q1, and global membership income grew nearly 17% versus 17.4% in Q1.
Elevated fuel costs were a pressure as the preview anticipated; the call quantified more than $2 billion of incremental fuel-related costs and noted a softer consumer, especially in June.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $8.2 million, slightly above the roughly $7.9 million implied by consensus and management’s prior guide. This was a modest beat after the prior quarter’s large revenue miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 revenue was $8.2 million,” up 25% sequentially.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $7.94M” consensus; management had guided to “about 20% sequential revenue growth” from the $6.6M Q3 base, or “roughly $7.9M.”

surprises.description: The company forecast Q1 FY2027 revenue falling to $6–7 million from Q4’s $8.2 million, before recovering to $8–9 million in Q2. The preview did not give a Q1 forecast, so the near-term decline is new negative guidance rather than a miss against a stated estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company guided Q1 FY2027 revenue down to $6-7 million before rebounding to $8-9 million in Q2 FY2027.”

surprises.description: Cash ended the quarter at only $0.3 million, underscoring a tighter immediate liquidity position than the preview quantified. The preview had highlighted covenant, borrowing-base, and financing risks, but did not state an expected quarter-end cash balance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Flux ended the quarter with only $0.3 million in cash and cash equivalents, down from $0.4 million in the prior quarter.”

surprises.description: Management said gross margin would not get back above 30% until quarterly revenue reaches $12–14 million, setting a substantial revenue hurdle for margin recovery. The preview expected Q4 margin around 27–29% but did not flag this recovery threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Margins won't return above 30% until quarterly revenue reaches $12-14 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 gross margin is an estimate” of “~27–29%”; the preview noted the company “does not guide to margin.”

surprises.description: Flux obtained Hyster-Yale certification across Class 1, 2, and 3 forklifts and reported selling to the four largest OEMs, broadening its qualified customer reach beyond the preview’s focus on declining revenue and backlog. The preview did not anticipate this certification milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Flux received Hyster-Yale certification for all Class 1, 2, and 3 forklifts,” and “now sells to the top four OEMs representing over 60% of the North American market.”

surprises.description: Flux entered robotics through a global technology company’s testing deployment of more than 70 C48 batteries, with potential to scale to hundreds annually. This new vertical and customer deployment were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Flux entered the robotics vertical with a large global technology company that has deployed over 70 of its C48 batteries” for testing, “with potential to scale to hundreds of units per year.”

surprises.description: An OEM white-label customer raised its yearly order commitment by 50%, a favorable customer-volume development absent from the preview. The report does not quantify the revenue impact, so the size of the surprise is moderate rather than large.
surprises.fact_evidence: “One OEM white-label customer increased its yearly order commitment by 50%.”

surprises.description: Flux launched AI-driven SkyBMS 3.0 as a foundation for future software-attached recurring revenue, a new potential revenue model not discussed in the preview. Management cautioned that it remains a hardware add-on, not a standalone product.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company launched AI-driven SkyBMS 3.0 as a foundation for future recurring software-attached revenue,” though “it remains a hardware add-on rather than a standalone product.”

surprises.description: Operating expenses fell 33% year over year in Q4 and 28% for the full year, a substantial cost reduction not quantified in the preview. This is favorable for limiting losses, although Q4 still produced a net loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating expenses were cut 33% year-over-year in Q4 and 28% for the full year,” with full-year opex “falling to $19.2 million from $26.8 million.”

in_line: Full-year FY2026 revenue was $42.1 million, close to the preview’s $41.83 million consensus and consistent with the expected roughly 37% annual decline.
Q4 EPS was a loss of $0.11 per share, within the preview’s expected loss range of $0.10–$0.11 per share.
Q4 gross margin was 27.4%, within the preview’s estimated 27–29% range and essentially flat sequentially, as expected.

surprises.description: Fresh bread volumes fell 9.5%, far worse than the preview’s base-case expectation of a 3%–4% volume decline; management said the weakness also caused Q2 to miss the company’s own expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 results missed the company's own expectations,” driven by continued fresh packaged bread weakness; “Fresh bread volumes declined 9.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario expected “Volume −3% to −4%.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed significant new business wins in both away-from-home and retail branded segments, with benefits beginning to phase in during Q3 and Q4. The preview did not flag these wins as a potential source of improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company has secured significant new business wins split across both away-from-home and retail branded segments, with benefits phasing in during Q3 and Q4.”

surprises.description: Management said inflation is expected to rise notably in 2027, with remaining exposure to oil, diesel, and indirectly resin and packaging despite most commodities being hedged for the rest of 2026. The preview did not flag this forward cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Most commodities are fully hedged for the balance of 2026,” but exposure remains in “oil, diesel, and indirectly resin/packaging,” with “inflation expected to tick up notably in 2027.”

surprises.description: Management acknowledged that Flowers is underpenetrated in fast-growing sourdough, protein, fiber, and half-loaf formats, and that consumer preferences have moved ahead of its innovation pipeline. Sourdough is a roughly $1.3 billion subcategory, but DKB currently offers it only on the West Coast, with broader rollout still planned.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company is “underpenetrated in fast-growing segments like sourdough, protein, fiber, and half-loaf formats,” where “consumer preferences have shifted ahead of the innovation pipeline”; sourdough is “roughly a $1.3 billion” subcategory, while DKB offers it “only on the West Coast.”

surprises.description: Management said additional cost savings should provide about a $20 million tailwind entering 2027, on top of roughly $200 million in costs already removed. This was not identified in the preview as a prospective earnings tailwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company has “removed roughly $200 million in costs over recent years” and took further measures “expected to deliver about a $20 million tailwind entering 2027.”

in_line: The expected near-term caution was reflected in management’s outlook: Q3 sales are expected to decline year over year, with more stabilization in Q4. The preview’s base case anticipated a cautious second half.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $1.5 million, about 11% below the $1.682 million consensus estimate. That was a meaningful miss against the only usable headline estimate in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue fell 52% year-over-year to $1.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $1.682M”

surprises.description: Gross margin stayed around 49%, rather than moving toward management’s mid-60% 2026 target. The preview’s base case anticipated at least a partial recovery, so the lack of progress was a sizable shortfall.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin held roughly flat at about 49% versus the previously guided mid-60% range,” with B2C product revenue falling to under 19% of total revenue from about 35% a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The CFO guided gross margin toward the mid-60% range over 2026”; the base scenario expected “margin partly recovers.”

surprises.description: The senior secured notes were fully extinguished after quarter-end, but doing so involved substantial dilution: the holder converted $5.5 million of principal and received about 1.58 million additional shares to settle penalties and damages. The preview flagged conversion risk, but not this scale of share issuance or the full extinguishment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The senior secured convertible notes were fully extinguished after quarter end,” with $5.5 million principal converted into about 721,000 shares and approximately $8.2 million of floor penalties plus $412,000 in liquidated damages settled via about 1.58 million additional shares.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Dilution from convertible notes”; “Check the cover-page count and subsequent-events note for conversions after 6/30.”

surprises.description: A major B2B customer disruption was reported that the preview had not flagged: AI-related sales disruption at Eastern Standard coincided with a 41% B2B revenue decline and a swing from operating income to an operating loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “B2B revenue declined 41% to $1.22 million and swung to an operating loss of ~$103,000 (versus $70,000 income prior year), driven by AI-related sales disruption at largest agency Eastern Standard.”

surprises.description: Despite the company’s weak cash position, it reported acquisition progress: a seller-financed LOI for a business with roughly $4 million of trailing adjusted EBITDA and a reduction in another deal’s upfront cash requirement from $3.5 million to $1.3 million. The preview described LOIs as being pursued as capitalization improved, but did not anticipate these financing terms or this progress.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed a letter of intent for a 100% seller-financed acquisition with roughly $4 million in trailing-12-month adjusted EBITDA, targeting an October 1 close,” and renegotiated another deal so its upfront cash requirement fell from $3.5 million to $1.3 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: As of July 23, the LOIs were retained “to pursue as its capitalization improves.”

in_line: June 30 cash of $251,000 was below the preview’s bear-case cutoff of $400,000.
The company retained going-concern disclosures, consistent with the preview’s base case and its warning that substantial doubt had already been disclosed in Q1.

Stockholders’ equity was below Nasdaq’s $2.5 million threshold at June 30, consistent with the preview’s base case that equity would remain short; the preview also identified negative equity as a bear-case possibility.

surprises.description: Q2 comps were expected around 7% by consensus and guided at 6%–7%, but came in at 10%—also above the preview’s 8%–9% base case. That is a roughly three-point beat against consensus and continues the second quarter of double-digit growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 comparable store sales grew 10%, marking the second consecutive quarter of double-digit comp growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 FY2026 Consensus” comps “~+7%”; company guidance “+6% to +7%.” The preview also said the “Base” scenario was “+8% to +9%.”

surprises.description: Q2 EPS of $2.66 was far above the $1.92 consensus and the company’s $1.85–$1.93 guidance range. The unusually large beat included the unexpected tariff refund, but still substantially exceeded the preview’s expectations for the quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net income of $851 million ($2.66 EPS) versus $508 million ($1.56 EPS) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS” consensus “$1.92”; company guidance “$1.85 – $1.93.”

surprises.description: Ross reported $253 million, or about $0.60 per share, in tariff refunds—an upside item the preview identified as uncertain and excluded from guidance. The refunds accounted for 405 basis points of the 625-basis-point gross-margin improvement, making them a material contributor to the quarter’s results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 results included $253 million (~$0.60 EPS) in tariff refunds, which contributed 405 basis points of the 625 basis point gross margin improvement.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Tariff refunds are excluded from guidance. The CFO withheld them citing ‘ongoing uncertainty.’ Any disclosed credit would be upside.”

surprises.description: Ross raised full-year EPS guidance to $8.61–$8.77, well above the preview’s expected raise to roughly $7.85–$8.00. The new range includes about $0.60 per share of tariff benefit, but the raise still exceeds that benefit alone relative to the prior $7.50–$7.74 guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year EPS guidance to $8.61-$8.77 (including ~$0.60 tariff benefit).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “The Street appears to need a raise to about $7.85–$8.00” and listed full-year guidance of “$7.50 – $7.74.”

surprises.description: Even excluding the tariff refunds, Q2 operating margin expanded 205 basis points year over year, with merchandise margin up 110 basis points. That indicates stronger underlying margin performance than the preview’s expected operating-margin range of 12.8%–13.0%, which depended on continued merchandise-margin expansion amid freight pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding tariff refunds, Q2 operating margin still expanded 205 basis points year-over-year, with merchandise margin up 110 basis points.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 operating-margin consensus at “12.8% – 13.0%” and said “Operating margin in the 12.8% to 13.5% range depends on whether merchandise margin keeps expanding.”

surprises.description: Revenue reached $6.3 billion, modestly above the preview’s $6.12 billion consensus. The roughly 3% beat was smaller than the surprise in comps and EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 sales rose 13% to $6.3 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue” Q2 consensus: “$6.12B.”

surprises.description: Ross raised its 2026 store-opening plan from 110 to 115 locations, an increase not identified in the preview’s expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised 2026 store openings to 115 locations (up from prior 110 guidance).”

surprises.description: Quarter-end inventory was up 18%, a material operating metric not addressed in the preview. The increase was partly tempered by lower packaway inventory as a share of the total and management’s report that in-store turns remained strong.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Quarter-end inventory increased 18%, with packaway declining to 36% of total inventory from 38% a year earlier, while in-store turns remained strong.”

in_line: Comps were still driven primarily by customer transactions rather than higher basket size, consistent with the preview’s note that Q1 growth came mostly from transactions and its warning that a shift toward ticket-driven comps would be a concern.
Freight pressure from higher fuel costs remained a headwind, as the preview had flagged elevated fuel prices pressuring freight through 2026.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $484 million, about 8% below the $528.3 million consensus, and full-year revenue of $1.79 billion also fell below the preview’s $1.83 billion consensus and the company’s prior guidance range. OSI attributed the Q4 shortfall primarily to about $50 million of security deliveries deferred beyond year-end because of Middle East conflict-related delays.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year fiscal 2026 revenue of $1.79 billion finished below guidance, with Q4 revenue of $484 million down approximately 4% year-over-year, primarily due to ~$50 million of security deliveries deferred beyond year-end from Middle East conflict-related delays.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 Revenue: $528.3M”; “FY26 revenue: $1,830M”; prior FY26 guidance was “$1,825M – $1,867M.”

surprises.description: Fiscal 2027 revenue guidance of $1.875–$1.93 billion came in below the preview’s $1.94 billion consensus and below its expected $1.92–$1.97 billion base-case range. Management also said growth should be strongest in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OSI issued fiscal 2027 guidance of $1.875-1.93 billion revenue (5-8.1% growth) … with growth expected to be strongest in the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus is $1.94B revenue”; the base scenario expected “FY27 guide $1.92–1.97B.”

surprises.description: The Q4 operating cash flow concern proved much better than the preview’s threshold: OSI generated $182 million, well above the $120 million level below which the preview said receivables concerns would return.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company generated record Q4 operating cash flow of $182 million and $276 million for the full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything below about $120M of Q4 operating cash flow would reopen the receivables concern.”

surprises.description: OSI collected $159 million from its largest Mexico customer during Q4, more than the roughly $74 million the preview expected to be collected just after quarter-end. The receivable nevertheless remained substantial at $190 million at year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OSI collected $159 million from its largest Mexico customer in Q4, reducing that receivable balance from $345 million (40% of total AR) to $190 million (25% of total AR), with further collections expected in fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “About $74M of a large Mexico receivable was collected just after quarter-end.”

surprises.description: The fiscal 2027 adjusted EPS guidance midpoint was about $11.31, below the preview’s $11.44 consensus, although the company’s range extends above consensus. This was less optimistic than the preview’s base-case expectation of $11.25–$11.55 only at the low end of the range, rather than at the midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of $11.13-11.49 (7.5-11% growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus is … $11.44 EPS”; the base scenario expected “$11.25–11.55.”

surprises.description: The year-end backlog was about $1.9 billion, below the preview’s watch level of at least $2.0 billion, even though it was a record.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ending fiscal 2026 with a record backlog of approximately $1.9 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for at least $2.0B”; the catalyst checklist also called for “Backlog of at least $2.0B.”

surprises.description: OSI’s margin performance was stronger than the preview’s focus on a roughly 21% security margin alone suggested: all three divisions expanded margins, and company-wide adjusted operating margin rose 200 basis points to 17.7%. Healthcare’s adjusted margin reached 10%, a sharp turnaround from 1% a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 company-wide adjusted operating margin rose 200 basis points to 17.7%, with all three divisions expanding margins”; healthcare “expanded dramatically to 10% from just 1% a year earlier on ~5% revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted healthcare adjusted operating margin was “negligible” in Q3 and focused on security segment margin of about 21.0%; it gave no expectation for a company-wide margin increase or a healthcare recovery of this scale.

surprises.description: The Mexico security revenue headwind is expected to fall sharply in fiscal 2027: it reduced fiscal 2026 revenue by nearly $150 million, but management expects less than $25 million of impact next year. The preview flagged Mexico disruption and collections but did not anticipate this quantified easing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Mexico security headwind, which reduced fiscal 2026 revenue by nearly $150 million (including ~$20 million in Q4), is expected to moderate to less than $25 million in fiscal 2027, concentrated in the first half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “Mexico collections stalled” and listed Mexico among the issues to watch, but provided no fiscal 2027 estimate for the revenue headwind.

surprises.description: OSI repurchased about $123.6 million of shares in Q4, a notable change from the preview’s expectation that no buyback authorization or capital-return program was in the models. The preview described a buyback authorization as a possible narrative shift; the call reported actual repurchases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “OSI repurchased ~565,000 shares at ~$219 for $123.6 million in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A buyback authorization would be a clear narrative shift. None is in the models I reviewed”; the preview also said “no repurchase program discussed.”

surprises.description: The preview anticipated a roughly $200 million CBP IDIQ award to confirm as additive, but OSI reported two five-year sole-source contracts with ceilings of about $200 million and $85 million. The added award expands the opportunity, although only a portion of delivery orders is in fiscal 2027 guidance and most revenue is expected in fiscal 2028 and beyond.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CBP awarded OSI two five-year sole-source IDIQ contracts (ceilings of ~$200 million and ~$85 million), but only a portion of delivery orders in hand (including a $21 million task order) is included in fiscal 2027 guidance, with the majority of revenue expected in fiscal 2028 and beyond.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Confirm that the $235M homeland-defense radar award and the Aug 17 $200M CBP IDIQ are additive.”

surprises.description: Management’s fiscal 2027 free-cash-flow outlook was strong: it expects free cash flow to exceed 100% of net income, a conversion target not specified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects fiscal 2027 free cash flow to exceed 100% of net income.”

in_line: Q4 non-GAAP EPS of $3.78 was essentially in line with the preview’s $3.76 consensus; full-year adjusted EPS of $10.35 was also essentially in line with the $10.36 consensus.
Security segment adjusted operating margin of 20.8% was essentially in line with the preview’s estimate of about 21.0%.

surprises.description: BJ’s adjusted EPS was $1.36, well above the preview’s $1.16–$1.17 consensus range. That is roughly a 16%–17% beat, substantially larger than the preview’s bull-case EPS of $1.22–$1.27.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS was $1.36… and ahead of expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS $1.16 (Zacks) / $1.17 (MarketBeat).”

surprises.description: Q2 net sales of $6.1 billion exceeded the preview’s $5.89–$5.97 billion consensus range. The preview’s bull scenario reached $6.00–$6.10 billion, but the reported result was still above both consensus estimates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales rose 15.9% year-over-year to $6.1 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue: $5.89B (Zacks) / $5.97B (MarketBeat).”

surprises.description: Merchandise comps grew 3.1%, above the preview’s roughly 2.5% consensus and the base-case range of 2.3%–2.8%. Traffic and ticket contributed roughly evenly, rather than growth being mainly ticket-driven as in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Merchandise comps grew 3.1%, driven by a roughly even balance of traffic and ticket”; BJ also cited its “18th consecutive quarter of traffic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comps ex-gas vs. ~2.5% consensus”; the base scenario projected “+2.3% to +2.8%,” while Q1 growth was described as “mostly ticket-driven.”

surprises.description: BJ raised its full-year adjusted EPS range to $4.60–$4.80 instead of reaffirming the prior $4.40–$4.60 range, moving the low end up by $0.20. The preview identified unchanged guidance as the base case and a higher floor as the clearest bullish outcome.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $4.60-$4.80 (from prior range) largely due to fuel outperformance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reaffirmation is the base case”; “Raising the floor is the cleanest bull signal.” The prior range was “$4.40 to $4.60.”

surprises.description: Fuel was not just a source of sales: fuel profit dollars were ahead of plan and a major contributor to the earnings beat. That was better than the preview’s explicit caution that fuel revenue could be strong while fuel profit disappointed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comp gallons grew 10.5% while the broader industry saw fuel gallons decline approximately 5%,” and “strong volume plus favorable gas price pullback drove fuel profit dollars ahead of plan as a major contributor to the earnings beat.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Fuel is low-margin, so revenue can beat while profit disappoints.”

surprises.description: Membership fee income reached $136 million, above the preview’s estimated $132–$135 million, and grew 9.9%, above the preview’s 7%–8% deceleration watch level. BJ also reported a record 8.5 million members.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Membership fee income grew 9.9% to $136 million, reaching a record 8.5 million members.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Membership fee income ~$132–135M”; “Watch for deceleration below about 7–8% or any renewal-rate softness.”

surprises.description: Management said membership fee income growth should slow toward a roughly 6% exit rate by year-end as the fee increase laps. The preview anticipated moderation, but this stated exit pace is below its 7%–8% watch level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects MFI growth to moderate from ~10% toward a ~6% exit rate by year-end as the fee increase laps.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for deceleration below about 7–8%”; the preview also said growth “must moderate after the Jan 2025 fee increase is lapped.”

surprises.description: Digitally enabled comps grew 30% and reached roughly 19% of the business, a notable operating result not addressed in the preview. Management also said digitally engaged members spend more and renew at higher rates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Digitally enabled comp sales grew 30% (64% on a 2-year stack) and now represent roughly 19% of the business, with digitally engaged members spending more and renewing at higher rates.”

surprises.description: The Texas expansion was tracking more than 30% ahead of membership plan, with all four gas stations ranking in the top 30% of the chain for gallons. The preview did not flag this performance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Texas expansion is tracking more than 30% ahead of membership plan, with all four gas stations ranking in the top 30% of the chain for gallons and two in the top 10%.”

surprises.description: BJ disclosed a plan to remove about 20% of SKUs over the next few years, a significant assortment change not anticipated in the preview. The call facts do not specify the expected financial effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Plans to remove about 20% of SKUs over the next few years.”

in_line: The merchandise gross margin rate declined about 20 basis points amid price investments, with tariff refunds nearly exhausted. This is consistent with the preview’s warning to focus on underlying margin pressure as tariff refunds fade; the facts do not provide a separate ex-tariff margin figure.
BJ maintained its 2%–3% full-year comp club sales growth guidance excluding gasoline, consistent with the preview’s base case of full-year guidance being reaffirmed unchanged.

surprises.description: Q4 sales appear to have exceeded the $222.8 million consensus: Display Solutions generated $164 million, or 70% of total LSI sales, implying total sales of about $234 million. That is above the preview’s base range and within its bull range.
