surprises.fact_evidence: “All three late-stage NDAs have been submitted”: BBP-418 has a “November 27, 2026 PDUFA with priority review and no adcom,” encaleret has a “May 8, 2027 PDUFA with priority review,” and infigratinib targets approval in mid-2027.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described the preferred investment as funding “three upcoming launches,” but did not state that all three NDAs had been submitted or give these review timelines.

surprises.description: Management framed encaleret as a potential additional blockbuster for a roughly 200,000-patient U.S. and EU opportunity, while its Phase III trial had begun screening and top-line results were expected in roughly 18 months; the preview did not flag this opportunity or timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management framed encaleret's chronic hypoparathyroidism opportunity of “~200,000 patients in U.S. and EU” as a “potential additional blockbuster”; the Phase III RECLAIM trial “having begun screening” with top-line results expected “within roughly 18 months.”

surprises.description: Management put a much larger long-term commercial scale on the portfolio than the preview discussed, projecting over $10 billion in risk-adjusted revenue and saying acoramidis could reach worldwide blockbuster status in 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The portfolio supports over $10 billion in risk-adjusted revenue ($8 billion post-Phase III),” and management “guided to acoramidis reaching worldwide blockbuster status in 2026.”

surprises.description: Management said operating results should remain stable for several quarters before trending toward breakeven by late 2027, providing a concrete timeline but indicating that breakeven is not expected immediately.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “expects stable operating results for several quarters before trending toward breakeven by late 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch “any framing of operating leverage” and characterized its base case as a revenue beat with “EPS miss on launch spend,” but gave no breakeven timeline.

in_line: The $1 billion preferred equity investment had already been disclosed as having closed July 1 in the preview; the call’s confirmation and the resulting approximately $1.7 billion cash balance were consistent with that expectation.
Gross-to-net remained within the 30%–40% range, consistent with the preview’s focus on whether gross-to-net or other commercial indicators softened.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $227.9 million, above the preview’s $219 million base scenario. The preview cautioned that its $121.49 million consensus figure was stale, so the gap to that estimate is less reliable as a measure of surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated revenue surged 126% year-over-year to $227.9 million in Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (50%) | Revenue ~$219M”; the preview also says the $121.49M consensus “appears to be carry-over estimates from the Q1 2026 period.”

surprises.description: ATS revenue reached $182.8 million, above the preview’s $173 million base scenario and well above the $150 million level it said would break the “new plateau” narrative. It also grew 18% sequentially from Q1, rather than falling below that threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ATS segment revenue jumped 230% year-over-year to $182.8 million and grew 18% sequentially from Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base (50%) … ATS ~$173M”; “A print below about $150M would break the ‘new plateau’ narrative.”

surprises.description: Management said Q2 ATS performance was exceptional and forecast a sequential revenue decline in Q3. That tempers the preview’s focus on whether the Q1 run-rate would hold, even though management still expects more than 100% year-over-year ATS growth in both Q3 and Q4.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 ATS performance was exceptional and unlikely to repeat, guiding to a sequential revenue decline from Q2 to Q3 2026”; ATS is “still expected to deliver more than 100% year-over-year growth in both Q3 and Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ATS revenue vs. the $154.6M Q1 base. This is the number that sets the stock”; the preview says political advertising pacing for H2 and Q3/Q4 commentary matter.

surprises.description: ATS operating expenses rose sharply, with management attributing the increase partly to cloud computing and AI investment. That contrasts with the preview’s bull-case assumption that management would sound unhurried about infrastructure costs, although ATS still produced a roughly 22% operating margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ATS operating expenses rose $13.9 million (85%) year-over-year, equating to roughly $56 million annualized, driven by cloud computing, AI investment, sales commissions and new hires.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull case assumed management “sounds unhurried about infrastructure costs”; the bear case flagged “a cloud-cost guide that rises.”

in_line: ATS operating margin was approximately 21.9% ($40.0 million operating profit on $182.8 million revenue), essentially matching the preview’s roughly 22% base-case expectation.
Media revenue was down just 1%, broadly in line with the preview’s expectation of flat Media revenue.
There was no reported progress on the Televisa/Univision renewal, consistent with the preview’s expectation that continued silence was possible.
The company declared a $0.05 per-share Q3 dividend, matching the quarterly dividend amount already noted in the preview.

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin was 49%, well above the preview’s concern about a drop below 35% and above the company’s 35–40% full-year guidance band. The preview did not give a Q2 margin estimate, so this is a strong quarterly result rather than a direct comparison to a quarterly forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded nearly 20 percentage points to 49%” from 29.4% a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A decline below 35% would breach the FY guidance band.”

surprises.description: Revenue reached the company’s $18.5 million floor, but came in below the preview’s $19 million catalyst threshold. The preview also cited conflicting consensus figures, so this is a small shortfall against the more bullish threshold, not a miss against the company floor or the base scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue increased 137% year-over-year to $18.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue at or above $19M”; the preview also states company guidance was “Floor ≥$18.5M” and gives a base scenario of “$18.5–19.5M.”

surprises.description: Management offered a partial H2 bridge: roughly 60% of full-year revenue is expected in H2, with Q4 the largest quarter. It also said about 70% of guidance revenue is locked in and expected limited H2 OpEx growth; the preview had asked for an H2 bridge but the call facts do not give quarter-by-quarter amounts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly 60% of full-year revenue” is expected in H2, “with Q4 anticipated to be the largest quarter”; “Approximately 70% of guidance revenue is already locked in”; limited expected OpEx increase in H2.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether management quantifies H2 by quarter”; the preview says reaching guidance requires H2 revenue of “$50.7–55.7M.”

surprises.description: The quarter produced positive adjusted EBITDA of $1.0 million, a record for Q2, even as the preview focused on whether the company would soften its full-year EBITDA target. The full-year target was reiterated, as expected, but the quarterly profit was not forecast in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA improved by $4.2 million to a positive Q2 record of $1.0 million,” versus a $3.2 million loss a year earlier; full-year guidance was reiterated at “over $5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether management quantifies H2 by quarter or softens the ‘>$5M’ EBITDA language.”

surprises.description: The company reported substantial buybacks and said it had begun opportunistically selling ETH to fund them. The preview flagged ETH liquidation for buybacks as a possibility to watch, but did not report that it had occurred or give a buyback scale; selling treasury assets to repurchase shares is a mixed development.
surprises.fact_evidence: GameSquare repurchased “more than 8.8 million shares for about $4.1 million” since the program began, including 2.8 million in Q2 and 1 million in July; it “has begun opportunistically liquidating ETH to fund buybacks.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ETH treasury policy. Further liquidation to fund buybacks would change how the market views the company.”

surprises.description: TubeBuddy’s AI ideation tool was already driving subscriber gains and unusually strong paid conversion among users who activate it, with nearly 88–90% SaaS margins. The preview did not flag this product or provide a comparable expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The tool drove “roughly a 10% increase in new subscribers since July”; feature-activating users converted to paid subscriptions at “about 10 times the rate” of non-activated users, at “nearly 88–90% SaaS margins.”

in_line: GameSquare reiterated full-year 2026 guidance of $85–90 million revenue, 35–40% gross margin, and adjusted EBITDA above $5 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the guide could be held.
The August 13 shareholder vote on a potential reverse stock split was already flagged in the preview.

surprises.description: The preview expected Q2 revenue of $57.20 million, but GEN reported $55.7 million, about 2.6% below consensus. Revenue grew only 1.2% year over year versus the preview’s expected 3.9% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue rose just 1.2% year-over-year to $55.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue, Q2 … $57.20M” and “+3.9% y/y.”

surprises.description: GEN’s loss per share was wider than expected: the preview listed consensus of $(0.08), while the call reported $(0.14) per share. The net loss also widened year over year, to $4.6 million from $1.7 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss widened to $4.6 million (negative $0.14 per share) from a $1.7 million net loss (negative $0.05 per share) a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (Class A), Q2 … $(0.08).”

surprises.description: The preview said Q2 restaurant-level margin needed to reach roughly 10% to keep the H2 target credible; GEN reported 11.3%, above that level, and said it had improved sequentially from 7.4% in Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Restaurant-level adjusted EBITDA fell to $6.3 million (11.3% of revenue) from $9 million (16.3%) a year ago, but improved sequentially from 7.4% in Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 needs to reach roughly 10% for the 15% to 15.5% H2 target to look credible.”

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s expectation that easing commodity pressure could allow COGS recapture, COGS rose to 39.1% of revenue. GEN attributed most of the food-cost increase to the new CPG business, with the remainder from commodity inflation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cost of goods sold jumped over 5 percentage points to 39.1% of revenue, with 81% of the $3.2 million food cost increase attributable to the newly added CPG business and the rest to commodity inflation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said commodity pressure ‘eased considerably’ in Q2, so COGS recapture is the most likely source of upside.”

surprises.description: GEN disclosed a nonbinding offer to sell only its U.S. restaurant operations and related leases for approximately $100 million, while retaining all of its CPG business. The preview did not anticipate this potential transaction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GEN received a nonbinding letter of intent from a nationwide multi-concept restaurant operator to acquire only its U.S. restaurant operations and related leases at a valuation of approximately $100 million, while GEN retains 100% of its CPG business.”

surprises.description: The CPG update was substantially stronger than the preview’s already-due disclosure: revenue grew sharply, the retail footprint expanded, and management raised its 12-month run-rate target to $35–$40 million from the prior $20 million-plus target. The preview cited 800-plus supermarkets and expected hard numbers, but did not anticipate this scale of run-rate increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The CPG division's revenue grew 341% sequentially from Q1, with June being the biggest month at over $2 million in revenue and products placed in nearly 2,000 retail doors nationwide”; “Management raised its forward 12-month CPG revenue run rate guidance to $35 million-$40 million based on current sales alone, up from the prior $20 million+ run rate target set in March 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “This is the first deadline for hard numbers on revenue, margin, and door count. Current footprint is 56 SKUs and 800+ supermarkets.”

surprises.description: Management described additional potential CPG upside from fresh prepared and cooked meals, a category excluded from its new $35–$40 million run-rate guidance. Buyers indicated the category could generate twice the sales of frozen products, an opportunity the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The $35-$40 million run rate excludes any contribution from the fresh prepared/cooked meals category, which buyers indicate could generate double the sales of frozen products.”

surprises.description: The preview listed guidance for 5 to 7 new restaurants in FY26, while management now described development as near maintenance levels and expects to complete its fifth and final restaurant transfer in Q3. That points to a more limited development posture than the preview’s cited opening plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GEN reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $215 million-$225 million and expects to complete its fifth and final restaurant transfer in Q3 while keeping development near maintenance levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Other guidance from the Q1 call: 5 to 7 new restaurants in FY26, and about a $250M exit run-rate.”

in_line: GEN reaffirmed FY2026 revenue guidance of $215 million–$225 million, matching the company range cited in the preview.
GEN drew on its line of credit to fund CPG, consistent with the preview’s note that management expected to draw on credit for that purpose.

surprises.description: The preview treated silence on the strategic review as the base case and identified a signed letter of intent as the major positive milestone. GoPro instead said inquiries have come from defense, consumer, and financial sectors and that the process is in its later stages, although it did not announce a deal.
surprises.fact_evidence: The Board authorized a process in May to evaluate a potential sale or other strategic alternatives, inquiries spanned defense, consumer and financial sectors, and management said it is in the later stages of the process.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Silence is the base case. A signed letter of intent would be the largest positive binary.”

surprises.description: GoPro reported a record subscriber attach rate of 69%, up from 54% a year earlier, while retention remained at 67%. The preview flagged subscribers and subscription revenue for attention but gave no attach-rate or retention expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company's subscriber attach rate hit a record 69% in Q2, up sharply from 54% in the same period last year, while retention held steady at 67%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Subscription revenue and subscriber count (2.26M at Q1).”

surprises.description: GoPro launched its Mission 1 compact cinema cameras in May and said the interchangeable-lens Mission 1 PRO ILS is scheduled for September. The preview did not anticipate these product launches or timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GoPro launched its new Mission 1 Series compact cinema cameras (Mission 1 PRO and Mission 1) in May, with pricing starting at $499 for existing subscribers”; “Mission 1 PRO ILS … is set to launch in September 2026.”

surprises.description: GoPro is offering a limited-time $100 discount on the new Mission cameras, an unanticipated promotional push to build awareness and sell-through.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is offering $100 off Mission 1, Mission 1 PRO and Mission 1 PRO Grip Edition for a limited time, signaling a promotional push to drive awareness and sell-through.”

surprises.description: GoPro expanded distribution for its new cameras at major retailers including Best Buy, Walmart, B&H, and Adorama, but acknowledged that worldwide retail representation remains incomplete. The preview did not set expectations for distribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GoPro expanded distribution of its new cameras through Best Buy, Walmart, B&H and Adorama globally but acknowledged it still lacks full retail representation worldwide.”

surprises.description: The AGV co-developed motorcycle helmet remains on track and has achieved ECE 22.06 safety compliance, a development the preview did not mention.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The tech-enabled motorcycle helmet co-developed with Italian brand AGV remains on track and recently achieved ECE 22.06 safety standard compliance.”

surprises.description: GoPro announced a MAX2 360 camera firmware upgrade adding 10-bit color, GP-Log, and 200 Mbps recording, and said the product earned the company a third technology and engineering Emmy Award. Neither update was anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The MAX2 360 camera received a June firmware update adding 10-bit color with GP-Log and 200 Mbps recording bit rate, and won GoPro its third technology and engineering Emmy Award.”

in_line: GoPro again withheld forward-looking guidance, consistent with the preview’s note that guidance had been withdrawn in May.
Management provided no additional detail on margins, sell-through, or second-half results, broadly matching the preview’s expectation of limited updates during the strategic review.

surprises.description: The preview framed a third FY26 EPS raise as the bullish outcome and a reaffirmation as neutral to negative, but AECOM instead lowered its FY26 guidance to $4.05 EPS at the midpoint, with NSR of about $7.3 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $950 million. The company attributed the reduction to the project charge and lower NSR growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “revised its full-year guidance to approximately $7.3 billion NSR, $950 million adjusted EBITDA, and $4.05 EPS at the midpoint, reflecting the CM charge and lower NSR growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adjusted EPS guidance. A third raise is the bull signal; a bare reaffirm is neutral to negative.” The preview also gave prior FY26 guidance of “$5.90–$6.10.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on cash and growth risks but did not flag a large charge tied to a troubled project. AECOM recorded a $337 million pretax charge that reduced EPS by $1.99, primarily because delivery of a large P3 design-build construction management project was delayed.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AECOM recorded a $337 million pretax charge in Q3 2026, primarily due to a delay in delivering a large P3 design-build construction management project, reducing EPS by $1.99.”

surprises.description: Even after the charge, AECOM said its underlying FY26 outlook was intact and raised its adjusted EBITDA margin target. That is better than the preview’s neutral-to-negative base case of guidance being narrowed rather than raised, although it does not undo the reported guidance cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding the charge, AECOM reaffirmed its prior guidance of ~$7.65-7.7 billion NSR, $1.29 billion adjusted EBITDA, and $6.00 EPS, and raised its adjusted EBITDA margin target to 17.4% from 17%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario anticipated “Guidance narrowed rather than raised”; it described a third raise as the bull signal and a bare reaffirmation as neutral to negative.

surprises.description: The preview highlighted cash generation as a key risk but did not anticipate roughly $500 million of further cash burn from the two troubled projects in the first half of FY27. AECOM also expects that burn to increase debt and interest costs and constrain near-term buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The two troubled P3 construction management projects will drive continued cash burn totaling roughly $500 million across the first two quarters of fiscal 2027”; higher debt is expected to raise FY27 interest expense by “$30-35 million year-over-year,” while “share buybacks will be constrained near-term.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called for attention to “Free cash flow vs. the ~$400M FY26 target” and described cash as “back-end loaded,” but did not mention this project-related FY27 cash burden.

surprises.description: AECOM disclosed that it is pursuing $600–650 million in claims on the two projects, an unanticipated potential recovery, while cautioning that this is only a fraction of the total amounts being claimed against third parties. The disclosure leaves the possible offset to project losses uncertain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AECOM is pursuing claims of $600-650 million on the two projects,” which management said “is only a fraction of the total amounts being claimed against third parties.”

surprises.description: International had contracted in the prior quarter, and the preview flagged its return to growth as a key test. Instead of remaining negative, the segment grew NSR by 4%, posted a 14.3% adjusted operating margin, and grew backlog 28%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The International segment returned to growth with 4% NSR increase and a 14.3% adjusted operating margin,” with double-digit growth in Australia, high single-digit growth in the U.K., and backlog up 28%.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called International NSR and margin “the sharpest contradiction in the story” after Q2 International NSR was “–3% constant currency,” and listed “International turning positive” as a bull-scenario driver.

surprises.description: The preview did not identify the scale of AECOM’s project-specific pipeline expansion. Management reported roughly 30% growth in both U.S. Water and Department of War pipelines, alongside data-center and defense demand supporting its long-term growth algorithm.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Key pipeline expansions include roughly 30% growth in both U.S. Water and Department of War pipelines,” alongside strong data center and defense-related demand supporting the “5%-8% long-term organic growth algorithm.”

in_line: Backlog remained strong rather than breaking below the preview’s key 1.0x book-to-burn warning level: AECOM reported an all-time-high backlog, 13% year-over-year growth, and a 1.6x book-to-burn (1.8x in the Americas). The preview had highlighted record backlog and a long streak above 1.0x as expected strengths.

surprises.description: Investors were looking for a payments contribution and a ramp in Exodus Pay, but Monovate’s European card issuance remains constrained after a Bank of Lithuania inspection, which management said is gating both Monovate growth and Exodus Pay adoption. Exodus is pursuing TixiPay to restore issuing licenses, but that depends on Bank of Latvia approval and a new issuing arrangement is targeted only for Q4 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Monovate's card issuance in Europe remains constrained following a Bank of Lithuania inspection,” and restoring it is “gating both Monovate growth and Exodus Pay adoption.” Exodus is acquiring TixiPay pending Bank of Latvia approval and is “targeting a new issuing arrangement in Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said two months of payments revenue at a $36M+ annualized run rate implied about $6M and flagged whether management would “quantif[y] the H2 payments ramp”; it also identified “Exodus Pay and UFC monetization” as a catalyst.

surprises.description: Q2 produced a net loss of $18.6 million and an EBITDA loss of $21.5 million, despite adjusted EBITDA being a smaller $6.7 million loss. The preview expected elevated Q2 costs, but the reported scale was driven by about $17 million of transaction-related incentives and $5.8 million of professional-services costs—large one-time items it had not quantified.
surprises.fact_evidence: Net loss was “$18.6 million, driven largely by one-time acquisition and restructuring costs”; adjusted EBITDA was a loss of $6.7 million versus an EBITDA loss of $21.5 million. One-time Q2 costs included “approximately $17 million in transaction-related incentives and $5.8 million in professional services.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “expect an elevated Q2 cost line” because Q2 included acquired costs and purchase-accounting amortization, while the workforce reduction’s restructuring charge was expected in Q3.

surprises.description: Monovate reported substantial transaction-volume growth, a positive operating datapoint beyond the preview’s revenue estimate: about $900 million of Q2 gross transaction volume and $1.8 billion year-to-date, with normalized core-client volume up 60% quarter over quarter and growth above 50% year over year excluding one large client.
surprises.fact_evidence: Monovate processed “$1.8 billion in gross transaction volume year-to-date (roughly $900 million in Q2),” up “60% quarter-over-quarter on a normalized basis” across its core client base. Excluding one large client, volumes grew “over 50% in the first half of 2026 versus the prior year.”

surprises.description: The announced workforce reduction was already known, but the expected timing of its savings moved forward: the preview’s base case assumed savings on track for 2027, while management now expects the full $10–13 million annualized run rate by Q4 2026.
surprises.fact_evidence: Exodus reduced its team by approximately 25%, expects “$10-13 million in annualized operating expense savings,” and expects the “full run rate in place by Q4 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base scenario assumed “savings on track for 2027” and said the savings “do not help Q2 operating expenses.”

surprises.description: Monovate contributed $5 million of Q2 revenue, somewhat below the preview’s roughly $6 million implied payments-revenue estimate. The shortfall was limited: the preview had identified less than $4.5 million as weak, and the reported contribution was above that threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q2 revenue was $26.2 million, including “$5M from Monovate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said that two months at a $36M+ annualized run rate “implies about $6M,” and that “a figure below $4.5M would be weak.”

surprises.description: The call reported 1.4 million monthly active users, below the preview’s cited Q1 MAU figure of 1.5 million, although management characterized legacy metrics as roughly flat quarter over quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: Legacy metrics were described as “roughly flat quarter-over-quarter, with 1.4 million monthly active users.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “MAU held at 1.5M” in Q1 and flagged funded users and MAU as metrics to watch.

in_line: Total Q2 revenue of $26.2 million was close to the preview’s approximately $26.5 million consensus estimate.
Legacy swap volume was $1.13 billion, above the preview’s roughly $1.0 billion stabilization threshold; the preview had already noted weak crypto conditions.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $22.7 million, above both the $22.5 million top of company guidance and the $21.45 million consensus estimate. The preview’s base case was around $21.3 million to $21.8 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $22.7 million” and “exceeded the company's guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Company Q2'26 guide: $20.5M – $22.5M”; “Consensus: $21.45M.”

surprises.description: Management raised FY2026 revenue growth guidance to 3%–5% from 2%–4%, rather than reaffirming the prior range. This is a positive change, although the preview noted that sell-side revenue consensus was already around or above the prior range’s top.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year revenue growth guidance to 3%-5% (from 2%-4%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance (reaffirmed May 12): revenue growth +2% to +4%”; “Sell-side FY26 revenue consensus of about $90.7M sits at or above the top of the company's range.”

surprises.description: Q2 adjusted gross margin was 57%, at the bottom of guidance and below the preview’s roughly 58% consensus and 59%-or-higher catalyst threshold. The preview had flagged whether margin pressure was real as a key debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted gross margin declined to 57%” and was “pressured by higher CMT and China sales carrying lower margins.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. gross margin” consensus “~58%”; “Adjusted gross margin of 59% or higher.”

surprises.description: The company cut its full-year adjusted gross margin outlook by 100 basis points, rather than leaving the prior 58%–60% range unchanged. Management attributed the reduction to product mix shifting toward lower-margin CMT products and higher China sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year adjusted gross margin guidance was cut by 100 basis points to 57%-59% (from 58%-60%) due to product mix shift toward lower-margin CMT products and higher China sales.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance (reaffirmed May 12): … adj. gross margin 58% to 60%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA of $1.7 million was above the preview’s roughly $1.5 million consensus and at the high end of the company’s outlook, despite the preview’s flat year-over-year consensus expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA came in at $1.7 million, up 11% year-over-year and at the high end of the outlook range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA” consensus “~$1.5M”; implied year-over-year change “flat.”

surprises.description: The preview warned that a second consecutive quarter of operating cash burn could intensify liquidity concerns. First-half operating cash use was $0.3 million versus Q1’s $0.7 million use, implying a modest Q2 operating cash inflow rather than another quarter of burn; however, quarter-end cash was still only $6.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash used in operations was $0.3 million in the first half”; Q1 operating cash flow was “-$0.7M”; the company ended the quarter with “only $6.5 million in cash.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash and free cash flow. A second straight quarter of burn from a $7.1M base would raise liquidity concerns.”

in_line: FY2026 adjusted EBITDA growth guidance was reaffirmed at 6%–10%, as in the preview’s prior guidance baseline.

Project Viking was reported on track against the preview’s stated $3 million of expected 2027 savings and $4 million annually thereafter; the preview had flagged timing slippage as something to watch.

surprises.description: Harrow reported Q2 revenue of $70.7 million, slightly below the $71 million company-guidance floor and below the preview’s $76 million midpoint. Management also said first-half revenue was lighter than expected, largely because of Vevye and AIHESO revenue timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $70.7 million” and “first-half revenue to approximately $115 million, which management admitted was lighter than expected largely due to Vevye and AIHESO revenue timing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 revenue: $71M – $81M (midpoint $76M)” and consensus estimates of “$71.75M,” “$70.99M,” and “$70.35M.”

surprises.description: Despite the first-half shortfall, Harrow kept its $350–365 million FY26 revenue and $80–100 million adjusted EBITDA guidance. That leaves roughly $250 million of revenue for the second half, weighted toward Q4—a more back-end-loaded path than the preview’s $230–245 million H2 estimate, while avoiding the trim anticipated in its base scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reiterated full-year guidance of $350-365 million in revenue and $80-100 million in adjusted EBITDA, implying a substantial second-half ramp to approximately $250 million in revenue weighted toward Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated “H2 revenue of $230–245M”; its base scenario expected “FY revenue trimmed to ~$340–355M,” and it said reaching guidance required a “43–52% YoY increase” in H2.

surprises.description: Q2 GAAP gross margin was 71%, comfortably above the preview’s roughly 64% caution threshold after Q1’s 61%. Management also expected gross margin to move back toward the high 70s in the second half.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP gross margin was 71% in Q2 but is expected to trend back toward the high 70s in the second half as AIHESO's revenue cycle normalizes and product mix improves.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Anything below ~64% would suggest pricing actions are not flowing through.”

surprises.description: AIHESO posted record demand of 65,477 units, up 44% sequentially, and management cited a roughly 25% net price improvement effective July 1 and gross margins above 90%. The preview gave no such product-level growth, pricing, or margin expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AIHESO reached record quarterly unit demand of 65,477 units (up 44% sequentially, 34% YoY) with a ~25% net pricing improvement effective July 1 and gross margins exceeding 90%.”

surprises.description: The Tervaia deal was already known, but management newly quantified an expected 2027 revenue contribution of more than $30 million, accretive economics, and assumed exclusivity through 2034—specific upside not supplied in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is acquiring Tervaia for $30 million upfront funded by cash on hand, with self-funded contingent milestones, expecting more than $30 million in 2027 revenue, accretive economics, and assumed product exclusivity through 2034.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted “A $30M upfront payment for TYRVAYA, announced Aug 6 and funded from cash on hand,” but gave no revenue, accretion, or exclusivity details.

surprises.description: Management said the acquired product is expected to add roughly $20 million in annualized SG&A once fully integrated, a significant added cost that the preview did not identify. It said integration costs would weigh on early quarters but not reduce 2026 earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Tervaia acquisition is expected to add roughly $20 million in annualized SG&A once fully integrated, with some integration costs weighing on early quarters but not pulling down 2026 earnings.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview mentioned the $30 million upfront acquisition payment but did not flag additional annualized SG&A.

surprises.description: Harrow disclosed a specific GMELT regulatory timetable: a pre-NDA FDA meeting in early Q4, an NDA targeted for the first half of 2027, and potential approval and launch in 2028. The preview did not flag this milestone or timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GMELT secured a pre-NDA FDA meeting for early Q4 with NDA submission targeted for the first half of 2027, potential approval in the first half of 2028, and commercial launch later that year.”

in_line: Vevye prescriptions continued to grow after the copay-assistance change: prescriptions were up 21% sequentially, and branded dry-eye market share rose to 14.6% from 7.8% a year earlier, consistent with the preview’s expectation that prescriptions would keep growing.
Q2 adjusted EBITDA was negative $1.2 million, near the preview’s checkpoint that Q2 should be close to breakeven after Q1’s negative $12.7 million.

The preview expected the Tervaia/TYRVAYA upfront payment to be funded from cash and highlighted the lack of an equity component; management said the $30 million upfront payment was funded from cash on hand.

The preview warned that sales-force costs could pressure EBITDA; management reported Q2 SG&A of $53.3 million and said base SG&A should remain approximately flat for the rest of the year, excluding Tervaia additions.

surprises.description: CorMedix raised its FY2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $125–140 million, rather than simply maintaining the prior $115–135 million range. The new range is $5–10 million higher at its endpoints.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $125-140 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 adjusted EBITDA guidance of “$115–135M” and said maintaining the May raise was a scenario to watch.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $101.9 million exceeded the $96.04 million consensus estimate by about $5.9 million. It landed within the preview’s bull-case revenue range, but above the stated consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue reached $101.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus $96.04M.”

surprises.description: DefenCath revenue was $66.1 million, above management’s pre-release indication of about $60 million for the quarter. That is a stronger Q2 result than the preview’s stated pre-guidance implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DefenCath sales of $66.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management pre-guided Q2 DefenCath to ~$60M.”

surprises.description: The Phase 3 ReSPECT study met its primary endpoint, a clinical milestone the preview did not flag. Mundipharma is expected to submit the sNDA in Q3 2026, with FDA action anticipated in the first half of the following year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Phase 3 ReSPECT study met its primary endpoint of non-inferiority in fungal-free survival at day 90”; Mundipharma is “expected to submit the sNDA in Q3 2026.”

surprises.description: CorMedix signed a multi-year supply agreement with another large dialysis organization, bringing its contracts to all five top U.S. dialysis providers. The preview focused on post-TDAPA volumes but did not anticipate this additional commercial agreement; the initial pilot covers a couple hundred clinics, with potential expansion in 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Signed a multi-year supply agreement with an additional large dialysis organization,” giving it “commercial contracts with all 5 top U.S. dialysis providers”; a pilot of “a couple hundred clinics” starts in Q3 2026.

surprises.description: Diluted EPS of $0.29 was above the preview’s $0.26 consensus estimate, despite the reported income tax expense and non-operating mark-to-market items.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income was $26.0 million ($0.29 diluted EPS),” with “$12.7 million in income tax expense and $4.2 million in non-operating mark-to-market items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (Q2) … Consensus $0.26”; the preview noted that the basis was unclear.

surprises.description: A $4.2 million insurance reimbursement credit reduced reported G&A, including $2.7 million related to prior-period legal fees. The credit flattered the quarter’s expenses, while management indicated the underlying expense run rate was higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “G&A benefited from a $4.2 million insurance reimbursement credit (of which $2.7 million related to prior-period legal fees), artificially lowering expenses and implying a higher underlying run rate.”

in_line: FY2026 revenue guidance of $325–345 million and DefenCath revenue guidance of $175–195 million were reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the May guidance would be maintained.

July DefenCath orders tracked in line with the post-TDAPA forecast: volumes stabilized with larger players and small-player attrition was expected, with DefenCath tracking to the mid-to-upper part of its guidance range.

surprises.description: Hallador’s Q2 loss was much worse than the preview’s roughly $0.10-per-share loss anchor: it reported a $15.2 million net loss, negative $2.9 million adjusted EBITDA, and negative $23.9 million operating cash flow. The company attributed the results to outage-related downtime and high power-purchase costs, rather than the expected recovery to a thin positive gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net loss of $15.2 million”; “Adjusted EBITDA turned negative at -$2.9 million”; “operating cash flow swung to -$23.9 million”; results were “driven by outage-related downtime and high purchase power costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2'26 EPS | –$0.10”; the base scenario expected “Partial availability recovery, thin positive gross margin.”

surprises.description: The Turtle Creek gas project’s estimated cost fell to below $800 million from below $900 million last quarter, and commercial operations were pulled forward to the second half of 2028. The preview discussed the project and its funding, but did not anticipate a lower cost estimate or an accelerated timeline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Turtle Creek gas project's estimated total cost has been lowered to below $800 million (roughly $1,700/KW), down from below $900 million last quarter, with commercial operations pulled forward to the second half of 2028.”

surprises.description: Hallador disclosed a new three-year capacity agreement alongside the anticipated 12-year deal: the two agreements total about $1.1 billion, and the three-year deal is priced at roughly twice historical contracted capacity pricing. The preview discussed the 12-year agreement but did not flag the additional deal or its pricing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Two landmark capacity agreements signed in 2026 (a 3-year and a 12-year deal) total approximately $1.1 billion in contracted revenue, with the 3-year deal priced at about 2x historical contracted capacity pricing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The 12-year deal is capacity-only.”

surprises.description: Management said it aims to fund Turtle Creek with little to no equity dilution, using equipment financing and structured or traditional debt. That is more reassuring than the preview’s concern about a potentially dilutive follow-on, though the financing plan remains an aim rather than a completed funding package.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management aims to finance Turtle Creek with little to no equity dilution using equipment financing and structured/traditional debt.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any framing toward project-level debt, a partner, or contracted offtake would be the most constructive thing management could say”; “A follow-on at current prices would be poorly received.”

surprises.description: Liquidity fell from $97.5 million at Q1 to $84.2 million, while bank debt rose from zero to $45 million after a term-loan draw. This adds pressure to the liquidity and covenant-headroom issue the preview highlighted, although it gave no specific balance-sheet forecast.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total liquidity declined to $84.2 million (from $97.5 million at Q1), and bank debt rose to $45 million after drawing the delayed-draw term loan, up from zero at March 31, 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Liquidity and covenant headroom” was a key metric to watch, with Q2 described as the “first test quarter, ahead of roughly $450M of turbine-related spend.”

surprises.description: Management expects generation volumes to improve sequentially in Q3, but warned that year-over-year comparisons will be difficult because Q3 2025 had unusually favorable power-market conditions. The sequential improvement is consistent with the preview’s recovery expectation; the specific year-over-year caveat was not flagged there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects generation volumes to improve sequentially in Q3 but flagged a challenging year-over-year comparison due to unusually favorable power market conditions in Q3 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Merom would return with ‘higher availability’ and be ‘better positioned heading into the peak summer demand period.’”

in_line: Management’s expectation of sequentially higher generation volumes in Q3 is consistent with the preview’s expectation that Merom would be better positioned after its outage.

surprises.description: Q2 EPS was $4.11, far above the preview’s $2.25–$2.35 consensus range, but $1.65 per share came from a tariff refund. Excluding the refund, EPS growth was about 20% year over year—better than the preview’s expected 10%–14% growth, but a much smaller beat than the headline suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GAAP and adjusted EPS reached $4.11 versus $2.05 a year ago,” including “a $1.65 benefit from a $994 million pretax tariff refund”; excluding refunds, EPS “rose approximately 20%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS” consensus was “$2.25–2.35 (+10–14%)”; the buy-side bar called for “EPS above $2.40.”

surprises.description: Full-year EPS guidance jumped to $9.90–$10.90 from $7.50–$8.50, exceeding the preview’s call for a move toward roughly $9. However, excluding the $1.65 tariff-refund benefit, the guidance midpoint increased only $0.75 from the prior midpoint, so the underlying upgrade was much more modest than the headline range implies.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year EPS guidance was raised from $7.50-$8.50 to $9.90-$10.90,” but excluding the tariff-refund benefit “the guidance midpoint rose only $0.75.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “a move toward $9” would be needed and described a bull scenario with FY EPS raised to “~$8.75–9.00.”

surprises.description: Target raised full-year net sales growth guidance to around 5%, one percentage point above its prior 4% outlook. The preview described the prior 4% guidance but did not anticipate this additional increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year net sales growth guidance was raised to around 5%, one percentage point higher than the prior outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Company guidance was “Net sales growth about 4%.”

surprises.description: Underlying operating-margin improvement was stronger than the preview’s stated full-year threshold: management now expects a roughly 50-basis-point increase excluding refunds, versus the preview’s expectation of at least 20 basis points. In Q2, margin was up about 70 basis points year over year excluding the refund, despite a higher SG&A rate.
surprises.fact_evidence: Full-year operating margin excluding refunds is guided to “about 0.5 percentage points above last year's adjusted rate of 4.6%”; Q2’s 9.6% rate included 3.7 points from refunds, leaving underlying margin “roughly 70 basis points higher year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Operating margin was expected to be “up 20bps or more versus 2025's 4.6% adjusted.”

surprises.description: Management said apparel and home growth was only flattish and that it was not satisfied, describing home as a multiyear turnaround. The preview did not flag this weak category performance or an extended home recovery as an issue to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Apparel and home showed only flattish growth”; management “is not satisfied” and described home as “a multiyear turnaround.”

surprises.description: Target said it would resume share repurchases in the second half after having paused them. The preview did not discuss a resumption of buybacks or otherwise set an expectation for repurchases.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company plans to resume share repurchases in the back half of the year, having paused them.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $6.7 million, well below even the preview’s lower consensus estimate of $15.5 million (and far below the alternative $45 million estimate).
surprises.fact_evidence: Datavault AI reported Q2 2026 revenue of only $6.7 million, predominantly from its acoustics group.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Revenue consensus: $15.5M; alternative: $45.0M.

surprises.description: Management kept the $200 million full-year revenue target, as expected, but specified that Q3 should bring only a modest bump and that a very significant jump is pushed to Q4. That ramp depends on launching the exchanges in mid-September after Fiserv integration, a specific operational condition the preview did not identify.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects a modest revenue bump in Q3 and a “very significant” jump in Q4, contingent on launching its exchanges in mid-September once Fiserv integration is completed.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue of at least $200M, back-half weighted, tied to tokenization contracts and to passage of the CLARITY Act.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed $2.5 billion of intended token issuance under signed contracts, representing $213 million in fees, but none of those fees has yet appeared in reported revenue. The preview linked the annual target to tokenization contracts but did not anticipate this disclosed fee pipeline or the gap between signed fees and recognized revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: Signed tokenization contracts total $2.5 billion in intended token issuance, representing $213 million in fees ($160 million banking/licensing and $61 million pure-margin technology fees), though none has yet appeared in reported revenue.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue of at least $200M, back-half weighted, tied to tokenization contracts.”

surprises.description: The preview listed closing CyberCatch among Q3 goals, but management said the $94 million all-cash deal is expected to close in Q4. BankWise and NIACS were also announced as acquisitions, while management said major acquisition activity is now largely concluded.
surprises.fact_evidence: Datavault announced acquisitions of BankWise, CyberCatch (a $94 million all-cash deal closing in Q4), and NIACS, and said it believes major acquisition activity is now largely concluded.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The Q3 goals included “closing CyberCatch and NYIAX” and “a bank acquisition.”

surprises.description: The preview highlighted uncertainty over how the CyberCatch purchase would be funded. The call instead disclosed a $60 million Q2 raise used primarily for the Available Networks/Quest structure and roughly $200 million of expected 2026 liquidity from several sources to fund the network rollout, but did not specify CyberCatch’s funding mechanism.
surprises.fact_evidence: Datavault raised $60 million in Q2, primarily to fund its initial payment into the Available Networks/Quest token structure. Management cited roughly $200 million in expected 2026 liquidity from BTC sales, Vivisol/Silex receivables, a $120 million non-dilutive Silex rev-share deal, and the morning’s financing to fund the Available network rollout.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash and the funding of the $94.5M CyberCatch deal” was the most important disclosure to watch; management had cited “more than $250M of available funding,” with the source undisclosed.

surprises.description: The expected share count rises from the preview’s 855.6 million to approximately 1 billion, with another 45–50 million shares to be issued for BankWise and the morning’s financing. The shares are also expected to remain below $1, indicating substantial dilution alongside the financing activity.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management expects approximately 1 billion shares outstanding at a $0.855 stock price, with an additional 45–50 million shares to be issued for BankWise and this morning’s financing.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Shares outstanding 855.6M.”

surprises.description: Despite the preview’s expectation that a Nasdaq extension would require a formal reverse-split commitment or that a reverse split would be needed, management said an equity exemption allows the company to remain listed through February without one and said it would not execute a reverse split.
surprises.fact_evidence: The stock faces Nasdaq delisting risk for trading below $1, but management has an equity exemption allowing it to remain listed through February without a reverse split, which it is refusing to execute.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The options are a second 180-day extension (which requires a formal commitment to a reverse split) or a reverse split.”

surprises.description: Management made a new, very large Project Questrel revenue claim: over $10 billion at completion, split 50-50 with Available Networks. It also said $1 billion in coins had already been minted and some sold to a Fortune 500 company, though the call did not report revenue from the tokenization contracts.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company projects Project Questrel could generate over $10 billion in revenue at completion, with a 50-50 revenue split, and claims it has already minted $1 billion in coins and sold some to a Fortune 500 company.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed a “$1B Project Qestrel deployment” among Q3 goals.

surprises.description: The call disclosed a share-swap chain that converted 50 million Datavault shares into $150 million of Phoenix Asia Holdings stock, intended to enhance the balance sheet and support Genius Act compliance for the exchanges. The preview did not mention this transaction.
surprises.fact_evidence: A share-swap chain converted 50 million Datavault shares for Vivisol shares into $150 million of Phoenix Asia Holdings stock, intended as a balance sheet enhancement to achieve Genius Act compliance for its exchanges.

in_line: Management reaffirmed FY26 revenue guidance of $200 million, consistent with the preview’s expectation that guidance was at least $200 million and back-half weighted.

surprises.description: Q4 organic sales growth was 5%, above the preview’s expected 2–3%. The quarter was also the strongest of FY26, rather than merely continuing the roughly 3% full-year pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The fourth quarter deliver[ed] the strongest performance at 5% organic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Organic net sales growth: ~+2–3%” for Q4.

surprises.description: Q4 diluted EPS was $0.39, above the preview’s $0.31–$0.32 consensus range. The preview had described consensus as near the top of the implied guidance range, not a result as high as $0.39.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 EPS jumping to $0.39 from $0.09 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS: $0.31–$0.32” for Q4.

surprises.description: FY27 operating-margin guidance of 12.7%–13.5% is above the preview’s preliminary 12.5%–13.0% framework. The top of the range is 50 basis points higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its operating margin outlook to 12.7%-13.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Preliminary: … 12.5–13.0% adj. operating margin.”

surprises.description: FY27 EPS guidance has a $3.225 midpoint, slightly above the $3.18 consensus the preview called the core issue, although the $3.10–$3.35 range also allows for an outcome below consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS of $3.10 to $3.35 on ~368 million shares.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 adjusted EPS guide vs. $3.18 consensus”; the preview also said EPS at or below $3.18 in its base scenario.

surprises.description: Travel Retail returned to positive territory in June and July, a stronger near-term turn than the preview’s focus on Middle East and travel-retail disruption as a sales and EPS drag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Travel Retail, about 15% of reported sales, returned to positive territory globally in June and July for the first time in three years, led by double-digit growth in Hainan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “about 2 points of Q4 sales drag” from “Middle East and travel-retail disruption” and identified “travel retail worse than assumed” as a bear-case risk.

surprises.description: FY26 diluted EPS reached $2.51, above the preview’s $2.43 FY26 consensus and the company’s previously stated $2.35–$2.45 guide. The call’s diluted EPS figure and the preview’s adjusted EPS estimate are not necessarily like-for-like.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS grew 66% for the full year to $2.51.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS: $2.43” consensus and company guide of “$2.35–$2.45.”

surprises.description: FY26 operating margin was 11.2%, above the preview’s 10.7%–11.0% adjusted-margin guide. The call’s operating-margin figure may not be directly comparable to the preview’s adjusted measure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating margin expanded 320 basis points to 11.2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY26 “Adjusted operating margin” guide of “10.7%–11.0%.”

surprises.description: The company said full annualized PRGP savings benefits are expected to flow through in FY28, later than the preview’s stated focus on FY27 benefit realization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The PRGP restructuring approvals concluded as of June 30 with $823 million in fiscal '26 cumulative charges, and full annualized savings benefits are expected to flow through in fiscal '28.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “watch FY27 benefit realization” from PRGP savings.

in_line: FY26 organic sales growth was 3%, in line with the preview’s approximately 3% organic-growth expectation for the full year.
FY27 organic net sales guidance of 3%–5% matched the preliminary range in the preview.

surprises.description: The preview flagged H2 2026 ARDS data as a timing to watch, but MiNK now guides to a preliminary randomized readout in H1 2027. The preview also noted that some coverage already pointed to early 2027, so the delay is less unexpected than a clear H2-to-2027 shift might otherwise be.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management guided to “a preliminary randomized readout in the first half of 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reaffirmation of H2 2026 preliminary ARDS data”; the preview also said “Some coverage now points to early 2027.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case expected the Aug 6 lung-injury update to be supplemented by one or two more patients, but the call described the same initial two treated patients and their day-28 outcomes. There was no additional patient outcome or control-arm information in the reported update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Initial run-in data on the first two treated patients showed they were alive and fever-free at day 28 with improved oxygenation and ARDS resolution.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected “the Aug 6 content [to be] restated with one or two more patients”; the preview said “the bar now is more patients and any control-arm information.”

surprises.description: MiNK specified that its first named-patient access program is paid and is operating in Brazil, resolving the preview’s open question about whether access would be free or paid. However, revenue from the initial patients is to be reported in the Q3 update, rather than being confirmed in this Q2 update.
surprises.fact_evidence: “MiNK launched its first paid named-patient access program for agent 797 in Brazil, with revenue from initial patients to be reported in the Q3 update.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called first named-patient revenue “the wildcard,” asked “whether revenue is recognized,” and said “First revenue would be a real change in the story.”

surprises.description: The call introduced a plan to ask the FDA to convert the randomized phase 2 into a seamless phase 3, with 28-day mortality as the primary endpoint. The preview did not flag this regulatory-development plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management plans to seek an FDA meeting in the coming weeks to convert the randomized phase 2 into a seamless phase 3 study, with 28-day mortality as the FDA-driven primary endpoint.”

surprises.description: MiNK reported a 77% disease control rate and durable survival in a subset of patients in PD-1 refractory gastroesophageal cancer, an efficacy update not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In phase 2 PD-1 refractory gastroesophageal cancer, agent 797 combination therapy showed a 77% disease control rate with durable survival in a subset of patients.”

in_line: Cash ended Q2 at $8.8 million, within the preview’s $7.0–9.5 million estimate range and its $7.5–9.0 million base scenario; it was above the preview’s point estimate of about $7.8 million.
The $3.1 million net loss and $0.62 per-share loss were broadly within the preview’s estimated $2.5–3.5 million net-loss range and $0.51–0.72 per-share loss range.

surprises.description: The preview expected the Q2/H1 FY2026 results call, but the call was opened as Gorilla Technology Group’s “First Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call.” The materials therefore identify a different reporting period than the preview anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: The operator opened “Gorilla Technology Group, Inc. NASDAQ GR First Quarter 2026 Financial Results Conference Call.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview is titled “GRRR (Gorilla Technology) Q2/H1 FY2026 Earnings Preview” and identifies the quarter as “Q2 / H1 FY2026 (quarter ended June 30, 2026).”

surprises.description: Bookings far exceeded the preview’s bar for a strong quarter: Q4 bookings were $660 million, nearly double the prior record, and backlog rose to a record above $1.9 billion. The preview said bookings had the potential to be the strongest of the year and flagged below $300 million as a demand concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY26 bookings hit a record $660 million, up 93.1% year-over-year and nearly double the previous record,” with a “2.28 book-to-bill ratio”; “Record total backlog reached over $1.9 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management said Q4 bookings ‘have the potential to be the strongest of the year.’” The preview also said “Bookings below $300M would be read as a demand slowdown.”

surprises.description: FY27 revenue guidance came in above the Street’s $1.05 billion expectation: management said revenue would approach $1.1 billion, or approach double-digit growth. That is a modestly stronger outlook than the preview’s expected 9.1% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “For FY27, management guided revenue approaching $1.1 billion (approaching double-digit growth).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 revenue / EPS | Consensus $1.05B (+9.1%) / $1.51.”

surprises.description: FY26 free cash flow fell short of the preview’s expectation that Q4 would generate about $60–80 million and put full-year cash flow roughly flat to up versus FY25. Full-year free cash flow was only $68 million; given the preview’s reported nine-month total of $39.8 million, Q4 was about $28 million, though still positive.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year free cash flow (down from $119 million).” The preview reported 9M FY26 free cash flow of “+$39.8M.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 FCF of about $60–80M would put FY26 roughly flat to up.”

surprises.description: Management expects FY27 free cash flow conversion of only about 35%, well below the company’s 50% target. The preview highlighted the 50% conversion target but did not flag a lower FY27 conversion outlook or an unusually large Q1 cash outflow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 free cash flow conversion is expected to approach only 35%, below the 50% target, with Q1 anticipated to be a larger-than-normal cash outflow due to early material receipts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management's medium-term target is above-market growth, low-to-mid 20% adj. EBITDA margin, and about 50% FCF conversion.”

surprises.description: The revenue picture was more geographically uneven than the preview indicated: domestic sales grew organically, but international sales fell about 15% because of a temporary contract-manufacturer delivery slowdown. The expected unwind over the next couple of quarters limits how permanent the weakness appears.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Domestic revenue, representing 85.8% of FY26 sales, grew 13% organically, while international sales declined roughly 15% due to a temporary contract-manufacturer delivery slowdown expected to unwind over the next couple of quarters.”

surprises.description: Mercury raised its long-term organic growth target to low double digits, making the target more specific and higher than the preview’s general description of above-market growth. It maintained its low-to-mid-20s adjusted EBITDA margin and 50% free cash flow conversion targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its long-term targeted organic revenue growth to low double digits while maintaining adjusted EBITDA margin targets in the low-to-mid 20s and 50% free cash flow conversion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management's medium-term target is above-market growth, low-to-mid 20% adj. EBITDA margin, and about 50% FCF conversion.”

surprises.description: The company reported a substantial revolver payment and lower net debt, whereas the preview raised the possibility of further tuck-in M&A after SolderMask. The reported capital allocation instead included a $150 million debt payment; the materials do not indicate whether this changes M&A plans.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net debt was reduced to $227 million (down 19.5% year-over-year), aided by a $150 million payment against the revolving credit facility.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any shift in capital deployment. SolderMask (closed 3/3/26) suggests appetite for tuck-in M&A.”

in_line: Q4 adjusted EPS was $0.37 versus the preview’s roughly $0.38 consensus, within the preview’s stated ±2–3% precision caveat.

Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin was 16.7%, within the preview’s derived 16.5–17.5% range; it was below the 18% level the preview said would suggest the mix drag was clearing, but above the level below 16% that it flagged as evidence the problem persisted.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $114.4M, well above the preview’s $100–104M working range, and FY26 revenue of $381.3M exceeded the $370.9M estimate. Marine propulsion grew 20% and land-based transmission 26%, while industrial sales declined modestly; the preview did not provide segment forecasts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 revenue reached a record $114.4 million, up 18.3% year-over-year (15.9% organic), with full-year sales of $381.3 million.” Marine propulsion sales grew 20% and land-based transmission sales grew 26%, while industrial sales declined modestly.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 FY26 revenue… Consensus… $100.35M…; ~$104.0M implied”; “Working range ~$100–104M.” FY26 revenue consensus: “$370.9M.”

surprises.description: Q4 gross margin came in at 26.3%, substantially below the preview’s roughly 29% base case and below its 28% downside-warning threshold. The reported contraction was attributed to mix, tariff dilution, and comparison against a favorable prior-year adjustment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 gross margin contracted approximately 600 basis points to 26.3% due to product mix, tariff dilution (60 bps impact), and a prior-year $3 million favorable one-time adjustment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base… gross margin around 29%”; “30% or higher suggests mitigation is working. Below 28% suggests tariffs and mix are hurting.”

surprises.description: Cash generation was stronger than even the preview’s bull-case threshold: Q4 free cash flow was $17.2M versus the bull scenario’s “above $10M.” Net leverage also improved to 0.5x, though the preview did not set a leverage expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 free cash flow was $17.2 million and net leverage improved to 0.5x (from 0.8x a year prior), with net debt of $13.8 million and trailing EBITDA of $29.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bull… FCF above $10M.”

surprises.description: Defense was a larger share of backlog than the preview’s roughly 15% figure: it reached 17%, with the defense portion growing 53% in the quarter. This was stronger backlog-share momentum than the preview’s reported 20% year-over-year increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Defense now comprises 17% of total backlog, with the defense portion of backlog growing 53% in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Defense was about 15% of total backlog, up 20% YoY.”

surprises.description: The identified defense pipeline was lower than the preview’s stated $50–75M range: management cited $30–50M as of June 30. That is a notable reduction in the pipeline figure supporting the defense-growth thesis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A defense project pipeline of $30-50 million as of June 30th.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$50–75M identified pipeline.”

surprises.description: Fiscal 2027 CapEx was guided above $20M, with spending tied to a new Finland facility, the ARFF product-line move, and machine tools. The preview anticipated unquantified FY27 commentary, not a specific investment program or spending level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 CapEx is guided to north of $20 million to fund the new Finland facility, the ARFF product line move to Lufkin, Texas, and new machine tools.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No numeric quarterly or annual guidance”; the base scenario expected “unquantified FY27 commentary.”

surprises.description: Oil and gas had become a meaningful source of Q4 revenue, exceeding 10% of sales and reaching its highest share since Q4 FY24, with e-frac deliveries and more expected. The preview had no oil-and-gas-specific expectation, though weak North American orders appeared as a bear-case risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Oil and gas represented a little over 10% of Q4 revenue—its highest share since fiscal Q4 2024—with roughly two e-frac spreads delivered and more coming.”

in_line: Q4 EPS was $0.64, but about $0.17 came from a tax benefit, implying roughly $0.47 excluding that benefit—broadly in line with the preview’s upper adjusted-EPS estimate of about $0.49–0.50, despite the preview’s conflicting lower estimate.

Six-month backlog was $178.3M versus $179.5M in the prior quarter, broadly within the preview’s $178–188M base-case range and above its roughly $170M downside level, though just below the $180M watchpoint.
The 25% quarterly dividend increase to $0.05 had already been announced and was noted in the preview.
The FY2030 targets of $500M revenue and 30% gross margin were reiterated, matching the targets cited in the preview.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue of $16.5 million was well above the preview’s $14.65–$15.00 million consensus range, and growth was 18% rather than the 5%–8% implied by that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue grew 18% year-over-year to $16.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus (Investing.com) $15.00M”; “Consensus (MarketBeat) $14.65M”; “Implies +5% to +8% YoY.”

surprises.description: The company swung to $3.5 million of GAAP net income, versus the preview’s expectation of a GAAP loss per share. The call also reported record adjusted EBITDA, though the preview had no EBITDA consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Swung to GAAP net income of $3.5 million versus a net loss of $1.8 million in Q2 2025”; “strongest adjusted EBITDA to date at $3.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GAAP EPS” consensus: “-$0.205” and “-$0.165.”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached approximately 59%, exceeding the preview’s 46%–49% guided band; even excluding the $1.1 million tariff refund, it was about 52%. Management said low-50s margins are sustainable as recurring revenue grows.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin rose to approximately 59% (52% excluding a $1.1 million tariff refund benefit)”; management “views low-50s as sustainable as recurring revenue grows.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin: 46%–49% guided band”; “Q1 printed 48%.”

surprises.description: Recurring revenue was $13.7 million, comfortably above the preview’s $12.7 million watch level, and grew 20% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recurring revenue up 20% to $13.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Recurring revenue needs to hold at or above about $12.7M.”

surprises.description: Procedure volume was 58,682, up 13% year over year, exceeding the preview’s 54,000-or-more threshold and showing a stronger pace than the 3.3% growth cited for Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Procedure volume reached 58,682, up 13% year-over-year and 8% sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Procedures of 54,000 or more”; the preview cited Q1 procedures of “54,094 worldwide, +3.3% YoY.”

surprises.description: U.S. procedure market share rose to 24.1%, above the preview’s 23.4% hurdle.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. procedure market share increased to 24.1% from 23.4% in Q1 and 21.4% in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “U.S. share needs to move above 23.4%”; the catalyst checklist also called for “U.S. share above 23.4%.”

surprises.description: The call added a favorable utilization comparison not covered in the preview: LENSAR systems performed substantially more procedures than the national average for installed systems.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LENSAR systems performed 31% more procedures than MarketScope's national average for installed systems.”

surprises.description: Management introduced a seasonal caution for Q3, saying it is historically the weakest quarter for cataract procedures because of holidays and summer vacations; the preview had not flagged this near-term volume risk.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 is historically the seasonally weakest quarter for cataract procedures due to holidays and summer vacations.”

surprises.description: Management said income and EBITDA may vary as operating expenses normalize higher toward historical levels. The preview noted that Q1 opex was unusually low but did not identify this explicit near-term earnings variability warning.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Expects income/EBITDA variability as operating expenses normalize higher toward historical levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 opex was flattered by the absence of merger costs”; the preview called for extracting the “clean SG&A and R&D run-rate.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a plan for modestly higher commercial spending, including LENSAR’s first-ever direct presence at ESCRS to expand in Europe. This adds a spending commitment the preview had not anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management plans to modestly increase commercial spending, including a first-ever direct presence at ESCRS in Q3 to expand in Europe.”

in_line: ALLY placements met the preview’s clean-print threshold exactly: 10 systems were placed versus a stated bar of at least 10. The backlog ended at 13, slightly above the preview’s 12-or-more threshold.
Cash ended at $13.6 million, above the preview’s $12 million watch level.

surprises.description: The preview’s rough Q2 revenue base was about $42 million, but FutureFuel reported $78.7 million. That is a much larger result than the preview’s estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue surged 120.7% year-over-year to $78.7 million in Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My rough Q2 base (my own estimate, not a sourced figure): revenue about $42M.”

surprises.description: The preview estimated an adjusted EBITDA loss of about $7 million, but FutureFuel reported positive adjusted EBITDA of $11.8 million and net income of $11.4 million. The quarter therefore moved from an expected loss to profitability on both measures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $11.8 million versus a prior-year loss of $11.4 million”; the company also “swung to net income of $11.4 million” from a $14.2 million loss.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My rough Q2 base (my own estimate, not a sourced figure): … adjusted EBITDA about ($7M), EPS about ($0.22).”

surprises.description: The preview expected hedge losses to be partly offset, but biofuel gross profit reached $10.1 million, including a $9.1 million benefit from selling physical inventory above hedge levels. That favorable inventory-versus-hedge effect also offset a prior-quarter hedging loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Biofuel segment gross profit reached $10.1 million versus a $13.5 million gross loss a year earlier, aided by a $9.1 million benefit from selling physical inventory above hedge levels that offset a prior Q1 hedging loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “hedge losses partly offset”; the preview also called for scrutiny of “the size of the Q2 derivative mark.”

surprises.description: The preview treated cash above about $20 million with the revolver untouched as a bullish threshold, while highlighting the risk of continued cash depletion. FutureFuel reported $34.3 million in cash and no revolver borrowings, comfortably above that threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company held $34.3 million in cash with no borrowings on its $35 million revolver.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash at or above about $20M with the revolver untouched reads as bullish”; the preview also highlighted “roughly $34M and then $29M of quarterly depletion.”

surprises.description: The preview cited about $19 million committed for 2026 45Z monetization, while management now expects $22 million in gross proceeds in the second half. Management also described the credit proceeds as recurring annually through 2029, extending the stated horizon beyond the preview’s FY2026 focus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company expects $22 million in gross proceeds from monetizing Section 45Z clean fuel credits in H2 2026 (about $3 million in Q3 and $19 million in Q4), recurring annually through 2029.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “FY2026 45Z credit monetization … About $19M committed to Freepoint.”

surprises.description: The preview did not mention the extension of the 45Z credit through 2029 or the reduction in SAF’s credit. Management said these changes level competition for biodiesel, adding a favorable policy development beyond the preview’s discussion of the existing 45Z commitment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The 45Z credit was extended through 2029 while SAF's credit was cut from $1.75 to $1.00 per gallon, leveling competition for biodiesel.”

surprises.description: Management identified elevated soybean oil and other raw-material costs as a near-term headwind, a cost pressure not raised in the preview. Management added that a return of commodity prices toward historical means could provide upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Elevated soybean oil and raw material input costs remain a near-term headwind, though management sees potential upside if commodity prices revert to historical means.”

in_line: Chemicals reached gross profit, as the preview’s bull scenario anticipated, and utilization was 65%, above the preview’s roughly 60% watch level.
The general direction of higher renewable-fuel mandates was already flagged: the preview said the EPA’s final RFS rule raised 2026–2027 RVOs.

The customer-funded capacity expansion is broadly consistent with the preview’s existing customer-funding expectations, including the Batesville commitment of $25 million in 2026 and up to $17 million in 2027.

surprises.description: Q4 diluted EPS was $0.71, far below the $1.30 consensus and even below the preview’s $1.17–$1.30 estimate range.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 fiscal 2026 net income fell to $8.4 million ($0.71 per diluted share) from $13.5 million ($1.15 per diluted share) a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Diluted EPS $1.30 (range $1.17–$1.30)”

surprises.description: Q4 gross margin fell to 15.7%, sharply below the roughly 18.3% estimate and the preview’s 17.5% downside threshold. The reported quarter included $2.7 million of recall costs as well as higher claims, freight, and manufacturing inefficiencies.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 gross margin contracted to 15.7% from 18.1%, hurt by $2.7 million in recall-related costs from third-party dry milk powder, higher customer claims, freight, and manufacturing inefficiencies.”
