surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin ~18.3% (estimate)” and “Sub-17.5% would break the FY26 margin-expansion story.”

surprises.description: Despite the weak profit result, Q4 sales reached $280.4 million, above the $274.9 million consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 sales growth to $280.4 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales $274.9M.”

surprises.description: The full-year EPS estimate was about $5.85, but reported FY26 diluted EPS was $5.26, a meaningful shortfall even though it increased from the prior year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year fiscal 2026 net sales reached a record $1.2 billion, up 6.2%, with diluted EPS rising 4.6% to $5.26 from $5.03 in fiscal 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 EPS (implied) ~$5.85.”

surprises.description: Full-year net sales came in at $1.2 billion, above the preview’s $1.17 billion estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year fiscal 2026 net sales reached a record $1.2 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue $1.17B.”

surprises.description: Q4 total volume turned positive, up 1.4%, after five consecutive quarters of declines—better than the preview’s concern that volume could relapse to a 4% decline or worse.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 marked a return to volume growth (up 1.4%) after five consecutive quarters of decline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A relapse to −4% or worse would suggest Q3 was a contract-manufacturing timing effect.”

surprises.description: Contract manufacturing volume rose 12.6%, supported by a significant new snack nut customer, extending the strength of that business beyond the timing concern raised in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Contract manufacturing volume up 12.6% driven by a significant new snack nut customer.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 total pounds were flat Y/Y… Commercial ingredients rose 14.3% and contract manufacturing rose 16.5%.” The preview cautioned that Q3 strength could be “a contract-manufacturing timing effect.”

surprises.description: Company shipments outperformed a weak snack nut and trail mix category: private label snack/trail shipments rose 3% and Fisher snack/trail rose 15%, contrasting with the preview’s concern about consumer and private-brand declines.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The snack nut and trail mix category declined 7% in volume and 3% in dollars in Q4, but the company's private label snack/trail shipments outperformed, rising 3%, and Fisher snack/trail rose 15%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consumer fell 4.5% in Q3 and private brand fell 5.3%” and “several Fisher and Southern Style lines declined.”

surprises.description: Management put a figure and timeline on the Elgin bar-line opportunity, estimating over $300 million in potential new growth over three to five years; the preview focused on startup costs and early distribution rather than a quantified growth opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company estimates over $300 million in potential new growth from its new high-speed bar lines at Elgin, which management expects to be realized over a 3-to-5-year timeline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch startup costs in COGS, capex, and any first protein-bar distribution commentary.”

surprises.description: Cost pressure was expected to remain a near-term issue, but the call specified that higher input, freight, fuel, and resin costs were reducing Q4 profitability by a couple million dollars and pricing offsets would not arrive until Q2 FY27.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Higher input, freight, fuel, and packaging resin costs reduced Q4 profitability by roughly a couple million dollars, with pricing offsets not expected to materialize until Q2 fiscal 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case assumed “Pricing +5–7%, volume roughly flat; margin up modestly on easy comp.”

surprises.description: The CEO succession was not flagged in the preview: Jeffrey Sanfilippo will step down in October to become Executive Chairman, with COO Jasper Sanfilippo taking over as CEO.
surprises.fact_evidence: “CEO Jeffrey Sanfilippo will step down in October to become Executive Chairman, with his brother and current COO Jasper Sanfilippo succeeding him as CEO.”

surprises.description: Raw nut and dried fruit inventory costs were up 12.1% year over year, above the 10.5% increase noted at the prior quarter and consistent with greater cost pressure than that earlier reading suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The weighted average cost per pound of raw nut and dried fruit inventory rose 12.1% year-over-year, driven by higher pecan and almond acquisition costs partially offset by lower walnut costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Inventory cost per pound was up 10.5% Y/Y at quarter-end, with pecan costs the main driver.”

in_line: The annual dividend increase to $0.95 and the $1.05 special dividend had already been declared before the release; the preview reported both and their combined $23.6 million total.

surprises.description: The preview said the buy-side wanted Q2 adjusted operating margin in the 7% range or better; management guided to 4.0%–5.5%, well below that threshold. The prior-year quarter also included a 110-basis-point warranty benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management guided Q2 sales to $500-$520 million (down 1% to up 2% ex-divestitures) and adjusted operating margin of 4%-5.5%, versus a prior-year quarter that included a nonrecurring 110 basis point warranty benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side wants a guide in the 7% range or better to confirm that the Q4 margin is structural.”

surprises.description: Q1 adjusted operating margin was 3.9%, below the preview’s 4.0%–5.5% company guidance range and the 4.8%–5.0% margin implied by consensus. The preview expected the result to land in the upper half of the band.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated adjusted operating margin declined to 3.9% from 4.8% a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating margin | 4.0% – 5.5% | Implied ~4.8%–5.0% (my derivation) | Consensus EPS implies the upper half of the band.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS came in at $0.43, below the preview’s $0.49–$0.50 consensus range. The preview’s bear scenario was $0.38, but its base case was $0.50.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of $0.43 versus a GAAP loss of $0.06.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | Not guided quarterly | $0.49 (Benzinga) or $0.50 (TradingKey).”

surprises.description: Retail written same-store sales rose 3%, turning positive and exceeding the preview’s base scenario of flat to down 2%. This was a stronger improvement than the preview’s Q4 baseline of down 2% suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retail segment written sales grew 16% with same-store written sales up 3%, a significant sequential improvement from Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Retail written same-store sales –2%, improving from Q3”; the base scenario expected “SSS flat to –2%,” while a positive print “would be the first in several quarters.”

surprises.description: Management disclosed a major distribution transformation and a $90–$110 million FY2027 capital-spending plan, described as the largest investment year for the project. The preview did not flag this planned investment or network overhaul.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 capital expenditures are expected at $90-$110 million, the largest investment year for the distribution transformation that will cut distribution centers from 15 to 3 hubs, reducing mileage 20% and square footage 30%.”

surprises.description: Management said La-Z-Boy’s EIPA tariff refunds are much smaller than competitors’ refunds, limiting its ability to fund promotions while competitors reinvest theirs. The preview discussed tariff-driven price increases but did not flag this relative disadvantage in promotional capacity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company noted its EIPA tariff refunds are significantly smaller than industry peers, limiting its ability to fund promotions as competitors reinvest refunds.”

surprises.description: DICK'S cut full-year consolidated non-GAAP EPS guidance to $11–$12 from $13.50–$14.50, rather than raising guidance as the preview expected. The midpoint fell from $14.00 to $11.50.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management cut full-year consolidated non-GAAP EPS guidance sharply to $11–$12 from the prior $13.50–$14.50 range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus expects a raise to the low end of sales and EPS”; the preview characterized a cut as “the bear case.”

surprises.description: Foot Locker’s full-year outlook swung from expected operating profit to a projected loss, with comps also now expected to decline or be flat instead of grow. This was substantially worse than the preview’s expectation of roughly flat-to-positive quarterly comps and the prior full-year growth outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The full-year Foot Locker outlook was slashed to an operating loss of $40–$80 million from prior guidance of $110–$150 million in profit, with pro forma comps now expected at negative 2% to flat versus prior 1.5%–3% growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited prior Foot Locker full-year comp guidance of “1.5–3.0%” growth and expected Q2 comps of “~ -1% to flat”; its base scenario expected “Foot Locker flat to +1%.”

surprises.description: Foot Locker’s Q2 comps fell 3.6%, well below the preview’s roughly -1% to flat buy-side mark, and the business recorded a $31.9 million operating loss. The comp result was notably weaker than the market’s already cautious expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Foot Locker business posted a Q2 operating loss of $31.9 million with pro forma comps declining 3.6%, hurt by weak launches, legacy silhouette softness, and a more challenging EMEA environment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Foot Locker comps ~-1% to flat” and “The buy-side has marked this to about -1%”; “-3% or worse would break the turnaround narrative.”

surprises.description: Consolidated non-GAAP EPS was $3.53, below the preview’s $3.77–$3.80 consensus range. The shortfall was about 6%–7% versus expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated non-GAAP EPS fell to $3.53 from $4.38 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed adjusted EPS consensus of “$3.77–3.80.”

surprises.description: DICK'S lowered its full-year operating margin outlook and now expects gross margin to decline slightly, with the most pressure in Q3. That is a weaker forward margin picture than investors hoping for a narrowing of the margin dilution flagged after Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lowered operating margin guidance to 10.6%–10.9% from 11%–11.4%, with gross margin now expected to decline slightly and pressure most pronounced in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “Gross margin dilution. Q1's -328 bps non-GAAP hit drove the stock lower. Watch whether dilution narrows.”

surprises.description: The full-year effective tax-rate assumption rose to about 29%, adding an estimated $0.35 per share of EPS pressure. The preview did not flag this tax-rate headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The full-year effective tax rate was raised to approximately 29% (up ~200 bps), unfavorably impacting non-GAAP EPS by roughly $0.35 due to persistent EMEA marketplace conditions.”

surprises.description: Net sales were $5.59 billion, modestly below the preview’s $5.64–$5.65 billion consensus despite the large reported year-over-year increase that included Foot Locker.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated net sales rose 53.2% to $5.59 billion, including a $1.74 billion contribution from Foot Locker.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed net sales consensus of “$5.64–5.65B.”

surprises.description: DICK'S core comps grew 4.9%, ahead of the preview’s 4.1% expectation. Growth included both higher average ticket and more transactions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DICK'S core business delivered Q2 comp sales growth of 4.9% (total sales up 5.6%), outpacing the broader industry by nearly 200 basis points, with growth in both average ticket (+3.6%) and transactions (+1.3%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “DICK'S Business comps +4.1%.”

surprises.description: DICK'S business gross margin expanded 79 basis points, rather than showing the ongoing margin dilution that had been a key concern after Q1. Merchandising margin rose about 150 basis points, with the company citing its media network, GameChanger, and tariff refunds as offsets to promotional pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “DICK'S business gross margin expanded 79 basis points year-over-year (merch margin up ~150 bps), driven by DICK'S Media Network, GameChanger, and tariff refunds offsetting promotional pricing pressure.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted “Gross margin dilution” after Q1’s “-328 bps” non-GAAP decline and said to watch whether it narrowed.

surprises.description: DICK'S received about $59 million in tariff refunds, with $21 million benefiting non-GAAP results, and reinvested the benefits in competitive pricing. The preview did not anticipate this earnings benefit or its use to support pricing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received approximately $59 million of tariff refunds in Q2, of which $21 million benefited non-GAAP results, and management reinvested these benefits into competitive pricing.”

surprises.description: Fast Break store expansion exceeded the preview’s roughly 250-store back-to-school target, and management now expects more than 300–350 stores by year-end.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company surpassed its back-to-school goal of ~250 Fast Break stores globally and now expects north of 300–350 by year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Fast Break had about 100 stores at Q1 and was “targeting about 250 by back-to-school.”

in_line: DICK'S maintained full-year comp sales guidance at 2.5%–4%, the range cited as standing guidance in the preview.

The total Foot Locker integration-charge estimate remained within the preview’s expected $500–$750 million envelope: management projected charges up to $750 million, with $516 million recognized to date.

surprises.description: Deere reported diluted EPS of $5.10, above the preview’s $4.67–$4.85 consensus range, and total net sales and revenues of $12.608 billion, above its roughly $12.4–$12.5 billion estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net sales and revenues up 5% to $12,608 million and net income of $1,379 million or $5.10 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) | $4.67 – $4.85”; “Total net sales & revenues | ~$12.4 – $12.5B.”

surprises.description: Model year 2027 early-order results are trending up mid-single digits, stronger than the preview’s expectation of flat-to-slightly-higher orders and above its low-single-digit threshold for challenging the bear case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Model year 2027 early order program results are trending up mid-single digits year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management's expected flat-to-slightly-higher FY27 orders”; “Growth above low single digits would challenge the JPMorgan bear case.”

surprises.description: Production & Precision Ag’s full-year sales outlook was cut to down approximately 10% as South America and Europe softened further. The preview flagged regional weakness and PPA margin risk, but did not anticipate this specific sales-guidance cut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year sales guidance was cut to down approximately 10% due to further softening in South America and Europe.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified South America weakness as a risk, including a bear case in which “Brazil weakens beyond the -15% industry assumption,” but did not state a PPA full-year sales outlook.

surprises.description: PPA’s 13.2% Q3 operating margin exceeded the preview’s 12.5% consensus, despite the weaker sales outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Production & Precision Ag net sales fell 6% to $3,998 million with 13.2% operating margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “PPA operating margin | Consensus is 12.5% against an 11–13% full-year guide.”

surprises.description: Deere received an additional $110 million in tariff refunds in Q3, although the preview said the prior quarter’s one-time refund would not repeat. The refunds brought the FY2026 total to $382 million and reduced expected FY2026 net tariff exposure to about $750 million, below the preview’s roughly $900 million figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Deere recognized $110 million in incremental tariff refunds in Q3, bringing FY2026 refunds to $382 million”; net FY2026 exposure is “roughly $750 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The prior-quarter refund “does not repeat in Q3”; tariffs were “~$900M net after refunds.”

surprises.description: The tariff outlook also includes a higher burden beyond FY2026: net exposure is expected to rise to around $1 billion in FY2027, creating a year-over-year headwind.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net tariff exposure is expected to rise from roughly $750 million in FY2026 … to around $1 billion in FY2027, creating a year-over-year headwind.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a tariff-cost revision could affect FY2027 EPS, but gave no FY2027 net-exposure figure.

surprises.description: Small Ag and Turf’s full-year operating-margin outlook was raised to 14.5%–15.5%. The preview anticipated strength in small ag but did not specify or forecast a margin-guide increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Small Ag and Turf outperformed with Q3 sales up 12% to $3,383 million and an 18.4% margin, prompting a raised full-year operating margin guide of 14.5%-15.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bull” scenario: “C&F and small-ag strength to persist”; no small Ag and Turf margin guidance was specified.

surprises.description: Equipment Operations cash-flow guidance improved to $5–$5.5 billion from the prior $4.5–$5.5 billion outlook carried in the preview, lifting the low end of the range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Equipment operations cash flow outlook improved to $5-5.5 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Operating cash flow (Equipment Operations): $4.5 – $5.5B.”

surprises.description: Deere said See & Spray factory installation is expected to nearly double to about one-third of North American sprayers on order, while more than 40% of planters are taking advanced technologies. The preview did not discuss these adoption metrics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “See & Spray factory installation expected to nearly double to about one-third of North American sprayers on order and over 40% of planters taking advanced technologies like ExactRate and ExactShot.”

surprises.description: Deere is producing slightly below retail demand in both PPA and C&F to keep dealer inventories healthy heading into 2027, while model year 2023–2024 high-horsepower used-tractor inventory is down nearly 40% year over year. The preview did not set expectations for this inventory and production approach.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Modestly underproducing retail demand (a couple of percentage points in both PPA and C&F) to position dealers with healthy inventory heading into 2027”; high-horsepower used tractor inventory is “down nearly 40% year-over-year.”

in_line: FY2026 net income guidance was raised to $4.75–$5 billion, broadly in line with the preview’s anticipated upward narrowing to about $4.8–$5.0 billion.

surprises.description: Smucker reported an $0.84-per-share tariff-refund benefit in Q1 and expects about a $0.60 net benefit for the year, while reinvesting the difference in administrative costs, marketing, and McCalla preproduction. The preview did not flag this sizable one-off benefit or its planned offset.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received an $0.84 EPS tariff refund benefit in fiscal Q1 and expects roughly a $0.60 net benefit for the full year, reinvesting the difference into administrative costs, marketing, and McCalla facility preproduction expenses.”

surprises.description: Underlying COGS inflation is now expected to run about 100 basis points higher than initially expected, mainly because of freight and some commodity and ingredient costs. That adds cost pressure beyond the company’s initial outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Underlying COGS inflation (excluding green coffee tariffs) is now running at mid-single digits, about 100 basis points higher than initial expectations, driven mainly by freight and some commodity/ingredient costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “about 100 basis points higher than initial expectations”

surprises.description: The preview expected mid-single-digit green coffee deflation and sequential price decreases beginning in Q2. Management instead said sustained deflation and key commodity thresholds have not materialized, reversed a contemplated list-price decline, and plans to pass deflation to consumers through trade promotions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company reversed a previously contemplated coffee list price decline, instead passing deflation to consumers via trade promotion since key commodity thresholds and sustained deflation have not materialized.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Guidance assumes mid-single-digit green coffee deflation”; “sequential price decreases starting in Q2 as green coffee costs pass through.”

surprises.description: Smucker reached its 3x leverage target in Q1, ahead of schedule, and is on track to repay about $500 million of debt this year. Management also said it now has flexibility to begin contemplating share repurchases, which the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Smucker achieved its 3x leverage ratio target in Q1, ahead of schedule, and is on track to pay down about $500 million of debt this year while gaining flexibility to begin contemplating share repurchases.”

surprises.description: The full-year Uncrustables growth outlook increased from mid-single digits to high-single digits. The preview did not identify a comparable brand-growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised the Uncrustables growth outlook from mid-single digits to high-single digits for the full year, following the brand surpassing $1 billion in sales last fiscal year.”

surprises.description: Coffee volumes were strong in Q1, better than the preview’s base case of low-single-digit volume/mix declines. Management nevertheless retained a low-single-digit decline outlook for the full year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Coffee volumes are still guided to decline low single digits for the full year despite Q1 volume strength.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “volume/mix down low-single-digits as guided”

surprises.description: Management expects frozen handheld and spreads margins to step back slightly over the next few quarters as McCalla preproduction costs rise. That is a near-term segment margin headwind not called out in the preview’s gross-margin-expansion outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Frozen handheld and spreads margins may take a slight step back over the next few quarters as McCalla, Alabama preproduction expenses increase to support Uncrustables capacity expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin expansion: about 300bps”

surprises.description: Management gave a weak Sweet Baked Snacks outlook: down low single digits for the year, with sharper declines in the first two quarters and only a more flattish back half. The preview flagged the segment’s trend but did not forecast this pattern of declines.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sweet Baked Snacks (Hostess) is expected to be down low single digits for the full year, with the first two quarters down more sharply due to lapping SKU rationalization and persistent convenience-channel traffic pressure, and a more flattish back half.”

in_line: Full-year coffee volumes remain guided to decline low single digits, consistent with the preview’s base case of low-single-digit volume/mix declines.

surprises.description: SelectQuote guided FY27 revenue to $1.35–1.45 billion, far below the preview’s $1.74 billion consensus estimate and expected 5.6% growth; the midpoint implies a 14% decline. Management attributed the outlook to MA approved policies falling 10–15% and Healthcare Services revenue falling 10–15%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 revenue guidance of $1.35-1.45 billion implies a 14% decline at the midpoint,” with MA approved policies “expected to fall 10-15%” and healthcare services revenue “down 10-15%.”

surprises.description: FY27 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $90–115 million falls short of the preview’s $120–140 million buy-side bar, with even the top of the company’s range below the expected range. The guide is near the preview’s warning that a figure near $100 million would signal structural impairment, despite planned margin expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA is guided to $90-115 million with roughly 60 basis points of margin expansion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side bar is roughly $120–140M in EBITDA”; “A guide near $100M would signal structural impairment.”

surprises.description: FY26 revenue was $1.62 billion, about $30 million below the $1.65 billion consensus estimate, although it remained within the company’s $1.61–1.71 billion guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full year fiscal 2026 revenue totaled $1.62 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue | $1.65B”; company FY26 guidance was “$1.61–1.71B.”

surprises.description: FY26 adjusted EBITDA reached $109 million, exceeding the top of the $90–100 million guidance range by $9 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA of $109 million beat guidance of $90-100 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 ... Adjusted EBITDA $90–100M.”

surprises.description: Management projected FY27 operating cash flow of $60 million-plus, ahead of the preview’s buy-side bar of more than $50 million, and also forecast about $50 million of free cash flow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects to approximately double operating cash flow to $60 million-plus in fiscal 2027 and generate about $50 million of free cash flow.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The buy-side bar is roughly $120–140M in EBITDA and OCF above $50M.”

surprises.description: SelectQuote reported more than $30 million of annualized run-rate expense improvement from AI, technology, process changes, and organizational rightsizing—an additional cost-improvement program not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company identified over $30 million of annualized run-rate expense improvement, driven by AI, technology, process improvements, and organizational rightsizing.”

surprises.description: Healthcare Services is expected to approximately double its margins in FY27, adding a profitability tailwind even as the segment’s revenue is forecast to decline; the preview had focused on reaching a $40–50 million EBITDA run rate, not this margin expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA is guided to $90-115 million with roughly 60 basis points of margin expansion, supported by healthcare services margins expected to approximately double.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said management had committed to a “$40–50M EBITDA run-rate ‘in the very near term.’”

surprises.description: The new Olathe pharmacy facility is delivering about 30% better shipment efficiency than legacy sites and is expected to handle a much larger share of enrollments and members after this AEP, supporting a long-term low-double-digit segment EBITDA margin target. These operating gains and the target were not covered in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The new Olathe, Kansas pharmacy facility is achieving about 30% shipment efficiency gains versus legacy sites” and is expected to support “a long-term low-double-digit EBITDA margin target for the segment.”

in_line: Healthcare Services exited FY26 at a nearly $50 million annual EBITDA run rate, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a $40–50 million run rate in the very near term.

FY26 operating cash flow improved $44 million year over year, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a significant year-over-year improvement; the facts provided do not state actual FY26 operating cash flow against the $25–35 million guide.

Senior delivered a 26% adjusted EBITDA margin for a fourth consecutive year of mid-20% margins, providing the durability signal the preview identified as a key issue. FY27 margins are expected to decline but remain above the 20% target.

surprises.description: The preview estimated Q2 adjusted EBITDA at about $1–2 million in its base case, with even its bull case at about $4.5 million. CTRN reported $5.5 million, with a 320-basis-point margin expansion; first-half adjusted EBITDA of $19.4 million also exceeded all of fiscal 2025.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBITDA reached $5.5 million,” improving by $6.6 million year over year, with adjusted EBITDA margin “expanding 320 basis points to 2.6%.” First-half adjusted EBITDA was $19.4 million, “exceeding the company's total EBITDA generated in all of fiscal 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The preview's base case is about +$1–2M”; the bull scenario estimated “~$4.5M.”

surprises.description: Gross margin expanded more than the preview’s base case expected, despite fuel surcharges remaining a headwind. The reported 40.6% was also above the preview’s 40.5% level for a “clean beat,” though below its bull-case estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin expanded 60 basis points to 40.6%,” driven by higher merchandise margin and lower shrink, “partially offset by rising freight from fuel surcharges.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario estimated “~40.3% (+30bps)” and said fuel could offset merchandise gains; the catalyst checklist said “Above about 40.5% would be a clean beat.”

surprises.description: CTRN reduced its 2026 new-store plan to about 20 from 25, while increasing planned remodels to 60–65 from 50. This shifts the near-term store investment mix; the preview’s expectation of about 40 new stores in 2027 was reaffirmed, as expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “New store openings for 2026 were trimmed to ~20 (from 25) due to timing, while remodels were increased to 60-65 (from 50); management reaffirmed plans to accelerate to 40 new stores in 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview flagged “confirmation of about 40 new stores in 2027 (vs. about 25 in 2026).”

surprises.description: Beyond the prior statement that it was evaluating acquisition opportunities, the board authorized a $100 million shelf registration for potential acquisitions or strategic investments. Management said there was no immediate financing need, so the authorization adds a new potential funding avenue without indicating an imminent transaction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The board authorized a $100 million shelf registration for potential acquisitions or strategic investments,” alongside an existing $40 million share repurchase authorization; management “stressed no immediate financing need.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview noted management was “evaluating ‘synergistic acquisition opportunities’” and flagged “any M&A detail” as a capital-allocation item to watch.

in_line: Q2 revenue of $211.6 million and comp sales growth of 10.5% were already pre-announced in the preview.
The raised FY26 guidance of 9%–11% comp growth and $38–$42 million adjusted EBITDA matched the preview’s base-case expectation of $38–$42 million and +9%–11% comps.
Management reaffirmed plans for about 40 new stores in 2027, as the preview flagged as a point to confirm.

surprises.description: Q2 sales were $169.8 million, above the preview’s $164.2–$165.5 million range, with growth of 4.9% rather than the expected 1.5%–2.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 fiscal 2027 sales rose 4.9% year-over-year to $169.8 million.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $0.54 substantially exceeded the preview’s $0.35–$0.36 expectation. The quarter included a $0.11-per-share duty-refund benefit; even excluding it, EPS was about $0.43, still above the expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS more than doubled to $0.54”; “including a $0.11 per share benefit from IEEPA duty refunds.” Adjusted operating profit was also $15.1 million versus $7 million a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS | $0.35 – $0.36”; “Adj. operating income | ~$10M – $11M (implied).”

surprises.description: Gross margin reached 59.4%, well above the preview’s implied 55.5%–56.0%. Even excluding the duty refunds, margin was 57.5%, with management attributing the improvement to pricing and favorable channel/product mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded to 59.4% from 54.1%, but excluding the IEEPA refunds it was 57.5%, a still-strong 340 basis point improvement driven by pricing and favorable channel/product mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Gross margin | ~55.5% – 56.0% (implied)”; the preview also said “Above 56% suggests the gain is structural.”

surprises.description: Although Movado still withheld a full-year outlook, it provided a new directional forecast of mid-single-digit sales growth for the rest of the fiscal year. The preview anticipated continued withholding and identified any reinstated outlook as a potential narrative event, so this is partial rather than full-year guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company discontinued providing an annual outlook, instead guiding to mid-single-digit top-line growth for the remainder of the fiscal year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The company has given no FY27 guidance”; “Whether an FY27 outlook is reinstated”; “FY27 outlook reinstatement or continued withholding.”

surprises.description: Movado announced a Kate Spade watch launch for next fiscal year as an expansion of its Tapestry partnership, a product and partnership development not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Movado will launch Kate Spade watches next fiscal year, expanding its long-term partnership with Tapestry.”

surprises.description: Management said it expects to recover another $6.8 million of previously paid IEEPA duties, but will not recognize the gain until it receives the cash. The preview did not mention this additional potential recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company still expects to recover a remaining $6.8 million in previously paid IEEPA duties but will not recognize the gain until cash is received.”

in_line: Movado continued to withhold a full-year outlook, consistent with the preview’s expectation that it might continue withholding FY27 guidance.

Management’s warning that the gross-margin benefit from lower-duty legacy inventory is temporary, with H2 margin guided to 55%–56%, was consistent with the preview’s concern that the tariff-timing benefit would fade.

surprises.description: BBW cut FY2026 revenue guidance to $500–$525 million from $530–$550 million and pre-tax income guidance to $60–$68 million from $72–$78 million, well below the ranges investors were watching. Management cited weak traffic and the loss of the Walmart program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered full-year revenue guidance to $500-$525 million (from $530-$550 million) and cut pre-tax income guidance to $60-$68 million (from $72-$78 million), citing weak traffic and the loss of the Walmart program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue guidance ($530–550M): held, narrowed, or cut.”

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $115.3 million, below the preview’s $120.8 million consensus and just below the cited consensus range’s $116.2 million low end. The reported 7.2% year-over-year decline was also steeper than the preview’s implied decline of about 2.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 fiscal 2026 total revenue fell 7.2% year-over-year to $115.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $120.8M (range $116.2M–$121.3M) | $124.2M | Implied Y/Y about –2.8%”

surprises.description: Commercial growth guidance fell from at least 20% to essentially flat. The preview described Commercial as a growth bright spot and identified Walmart’s rollout as the swing factor; the call said the inability to repeat last year’s multi-million-dollar Walmart order and slower wholesale opportunities drove the downgrade.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Commercial segment growth guidance was slashed from at least +20% to essentially flat, driven almost entirely by the inability to repeat last year's multi-million dollar Walmart order and slower-than-expected wholesale opportunities.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Commercial growth guided at 20%+ for the year”; “Commercial is the growth bright spot”; “Walmart's 1,500-store rollout is the swing factor.”

surprises.description: E-commerce was still down, but its 15.6% year-over-year decline moderated from the 26.1% decline in Q1, a better sequential trend than the preview’s open question about whether the decline would deepen or moderate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “E-commerce demand declined 15.6% year-over-year on soft web traffic, though it improved sequentially from Q1.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “E-commerce trajectory. Is the –26.1% decline moderating or deepening?”

surprises.description: The summer trend collection underperformed because products such as slushy plushies and berry goods were less customizable, prompting promotions that contributed to gross-margin contraction. In contrast, the highly customizable Chummy Shark sold out; the preview did not flag this product-specific split in demand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The underperforming summer trend collection (slushy plushies, berry goods) was less customizable and drove weaker traffic”; “highly customizable products like the Chummy Shark sold out”; gross margin “contracted 340 basis points to 54.2%, driven by occupancy cost deleverage and increased promotional activity to clear underperforming summer trend products.”

surprises.description: The Halloween launch produced the company’s highest non-Q4 sales week and third-highest U.S. e-commerce week ever, signaling improved Q3 trends, but sales were still slightly below prior expectations. The preview did not discuss this launch or set an expectation for it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Halloween launch delivered the highest non-Q4 sales week in company history and the third-highest US e-commerce sales week ever, signaling improved Q3 traffic and sales trends despite still being slightly below prior expectations.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Despite still being slightly below prior expectations.”

in_line: Q2 pre-tax income was $11.6 million, essentially in line with the preview’s estimated $10.5–$11.5 million range.

surprises.description: Fiscal 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $333 million, below the company’s $345–350 million guide by $12–17 million. That was a meaningful miss against the preview’s central test for the year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA was $333 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA inside $345–350M” and “Company FY26 guide… Adj. EBITDA $345–350M.”

surprises.description: The initial fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA range of $340–360 million did not reach the preview’s $375 million bull-case threshold, and its upper end only reaches the level the preview said would point to structural erosion if the guide were below it. Management called the guidance deliberately conservative.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company guided fiscal 2027 adjusted EBITDA to $340-$360 million… describing the guidance as deliberately conservative.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 EBITDA guide: ≥$375M supports the bull case; <$360M points to structural erosion.”

surprises.description: June same-store sales fell 7%, sharply below the preview’s expectation for Q4 comps at or above zero. Management attributed the decline to record World Cup viewership and the NBA finals drawing people to watch sports at home, and estimated a $7–12 million revenue hit from this one-time event.
surprises.fact_evidence: “June comped -7% due to record World Cup viewership and NBA finals driving at-home sports viewing, costing an estimated $7-12 million in revenue, a one-time event not repeating next summer.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FQ4 same-store sales at or above 0%, with California improving.”

surprises.description: Fiscal 2026 revenue was $1.245 billion, slightly below the preview’s $1.25 billion consensus and the company’s $1.250 billion low end of guidance, although the gap was small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total revenue grew 4% to $1.245 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 revenue | $1.25B (+4.3%)” and “Company FY26 guide | Revenue $1,250–1,260M.”

surprises.description: Capital spending came in at $114 million, down from $141 million the prior year, and the fiscal 2027 budget falls further to $90 million. The preview flagged capex and free-cash-flow progress but gave no capex forecast, so this is a newly reported cost-reduction trajectory rather than a miss against a stated capex estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Capital expenditures fell 19% to $114 million (from $141 million and $194 million in prior years) and are budgeted at $90 million for fiscal 2027, potentially settling in the $70-80 million range longer term.”

surprises.description: The events business showed a reversal after losing roughly $40 million of revenue over three years: it was positive for four consecutive months, and the December-quarter backlog was up 10% versus down 30% a year earlier. The preview did not flag this recovery.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The events business, which lost roughly $40 million in revenue over three years, turned positive for four consecutive months, with December quarter backlog tracking up 10% versus down 30% a year ago.”

surprises.description: Management said marketing spend had risen from $17 million to $30 million and impressions from about 75 million to 350 million, but engagement was weak enough to prompt a shift toward more targeted, higher-return spending. The preview did not anticipate this evidence of weak engagement or the change in marketing approach.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Marketing spend rose from $17 million to $30 million (1% to 2.5-3% of revenue), lifting quarterly impressions from ~75 million to ~350 million, but weak engagement prompted a shift toward higher-ROI, more targeted spending.”

surprises.description: Management plans to shed roughly 10 mostly post-IPO acquired properties in fiscal 2027 to improve leverage, while saying only two or three centers are currently EBITDA-negative. The preview did not mention a planned property exit program.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects to shed roughly 10 mostly post-IPO acquired properties in fiscal 2027 to improve leverage, with only two or three centers currently EBITDA-negative.”

surprises.description: Water-park attendance faced weather-related pressure, including an approximately 60% decline in one month at Raging Waters Los Angeles. Higher per-capita spending and lower payroll partly offset the attendance weakness; the preview anticipated summer water-park earnings but did not flag this operating volatility.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Water park per-capita spending rose 15-20% while payroll fell mid-single digits, though attendance was pressured by weather, including a ~60% attendance decline in one month at Raging Waters Los Angeles.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “About $18M of EBITDA is expected ‘this summer,’ mostly landing in FY27 rather than FQ4.”

in_line: The timing of water-park summer earnings broadly matched the preview: management said roughly 80% of summer earnings would land in the fiscal 2027 September quarter, while the preview expected most summer water-park EBITDA to fall in FY27 rather than FQ4.

surprises.description: Q2 EPS was $2.48 versus the preview’s $2.00 consensus. About $0.25 came from tariff refunds, but even excluding that benefit EPS was roughly $2.23, still above consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: EPS increased 33% to $2.48, including approximately $0.25 benefit from tariff refunds after related reinvestments.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus (Q2 FY26): $2.00 (+7.5%)”; the preview’s bull scenario put core EPS at “$2.15–2.25.”

surprises.description: Same-store sales grew 3.5%, well above the preview’s derived 2.2–2.5% estimate, with traffic up 2% and basket up 1.5%. The traffic gain was notably stronger than the consumer-pressure concerns highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Same-store sales up 3.5% driven by 2% traffic growth and 1.5% basket growth, marking the fifth consecutive quarter of traffic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Same-store sales: ~2.2–2.5%”; the preview also said Walmart cited “consumers stretched by higher gas prices.”

surprises.description: Net sales of $11.3 billion modestly exceeded the $11.17 billion consensus estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales rose 5.2% to $11.3 billion.”

surprises.description: Gross margin expanded 127 basis points, far above the preview’s expected 35–40 basis points. Tariff refunds contributed 81 basis points net of reinvestment, while lower LIFO and improved shrink and damages also helped.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 127 basis points to 32.6%, including an 81 basis point benefit from tariff refunds net of reinvestment, aided by lower LIFO, shrink and damage improvements, despite higher transportation costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus implies roughly +35–40bps of gross margin expansion to ~31.65–31.70%”; the preview said the prior-year shrink tailwind was “largely lapped.”

surprises.description: Dollar General raised full-year guidance substantially above the preview’s existing range and scenarios: EPS is now $7.80–$8.00, while sales and same-store sales ranges also moved higher.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year fiscal 2026 guidance to net sales growth of 4%-4.3%, same-store sales growth of 2.5%-2.9%, and EPS of $7.80-$8.00.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Existing FY26 guidance was sales growth of “+3.7% to +4.2%,” same-store sales of “+2.2% to +2.7%,” and EPS of “$7.20–$7.45”; the preview’s bull scenario was a raise to “$7.35–$7.55.”

surprises.description: The company plans to restart repurchases in Q3 and buy up to $700 million in the second half, much earlier than the preview’s expectation of no 2026 buybacks and ahead of the 2027 timeline in its framework.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Dollar General will resume share repurchases in Q3, buying up to $700 million of stock in the second half funded with cash on hand, ahead of the initial 2027 timeline in its long-term framework.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No share repurchases planned” for FY26; the preview called out “any refund-funded reversal” as a possible narrative shift.

surprises.description: Management described a stronger shrink-and-damage margin contribution outlook than the preview’s lapping concern suggested: it now expects about 50 basis points of expansion on the 2025 base, in addition to more than 80 basis points already achieved in 2025, and said this exceeds original targets.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Shrink and damages are now expected to add about 50 basis points of gross margin expansion on the 2025 base, on top of 80-plus basis points achieved in 2025, exceeding original targets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the prior-year shrink tailwind was “largely lapped” and highlighted that shrink had contributed “only 28bps” in Q1 versus 61bps a year earlier.

surprises.description: Trade-down among customers earning $100,000 or more accelerated from sporadic visits to everyday shopping, an upside development amid the preview’s concerns about stretched consumers. The continued strain on low-income core customers tempered the picture.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Trade-down momentum accelerated among customers earning $100,000-plus, shifting from sporadic to everyday shopping, while low-income core customers face continued strain from stubborn inflation and volatile fuel prices near $4 per gallon.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to “Watch trade-in from $100k+ households” and described consumers as “stretched by higher gas prices.”

in_line: The preview anticipated that tariff refunds could be recognized in Q2 and cautioned that they could lift reported EPS relative to underlying operating results; the call reported an approximately $0.25-per-share benefit and said most refunds were received in Q2.

surprises.description: Burlington’s Q2 adjusted EPS was $2.37, $0.18 above the $2.19 consensus and above the $2.05–$2.20 guidance range. The call also cited a $0.64-per-share tariff-refund benefit, so the headline beat included a substantial one-time contribution.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EPS was $2.37” and was “above the guidance range of $2.05-$2.20”; the call also cited “a $0.64 tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS” consensus was “$2.19”; guidance was “$2.05–$2.20.”

surprises.description: Q2 comp sales were +2%, below the preview’s +3–4% expectation, though within Burlington’s +1–3% guidance. The comp came entirely from higher basket size, with transactions flat, and was further pressured by 1.5 percentage points of cannibalization.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Comp store sales rose only 2% (midpoint of the 1%-3% guidance), pressured by an elevated 1.5 percentage point cannibalization headwind”; “Q2 comp was driven entirely by higher basket size with flat transactions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Comp store sales” consensus was “~+3–4%,” described as “Above high end” of guidance; the preview also said “A comp of 4% or better supports the share-gain story.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBIT margin expanded 100 basis points, well above both the preview’s roughly 50-basis-point consensus and Burlington’s 30–60-basis-point guidance. Merchandise margin, supply-chain leverage, and SG&A leverage all contributed to the outperformance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 adjusted EBIT margin expanded 100 basis points to 7%, well above guidance of 30-60 basis points,” driven by “a 70bp merchandise margin gain, 20bp of supply chain leverage, and 50bp of SG&A leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gave operating-margin guidance of “+30 to +60 bps” and consensus of “~+50 bps.”

surprises.description: Total sales grew 11%, modestly below the preview’s +11.8% consensus expectation, although growth was within Burlington’s +10–12% guidance. Store openings helped total sales growth outpace the +2% comp.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total sales grew 11% while comp store sales rose only 2%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed net-sales consensus of “$3.02B (+11.8%)” against guidance of “+10% to +12%.”

surprises.description: Burlington received about $55 million in tariff refunds, an amount not included in its prior guidance, and identified a $0.64-per-share refund benefit in the quarter. It plans to reinvest the refunds in sharper pricing during Q3 and Q4, leaving the full-year earnings impact neutral rather than retaining a lasting earnings benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received approximately $55 million in tariff refunds in Q2” and “plans to fully reinvest them into sharper pricing across Q3 (40%) and Q4 (60%), making the full-year earnings impact neutral”; the call also cited a “$0.64 tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Burlington “excluded any refund from guidance,” noted that “Sources do not give a company figure,” and said to watch “whether it is reinvested in price.”

in_line: The full-year adjusted EPS guide was raised to $11.77–$11.97, with a midpoint of $11.87—approximately the preview’s $11.84 Street estimate and consistent with its expectation that guidance would move up. The full-year comp and sales outlooks also moved to +3–4% and +10–11%, respectively.
Comp-store inventory was up 11%, matching the inventory level highlighted in the preview; reserve inventory was a lower share of total inventory, at 43% versus 50% a year earlier.

surprises.description: The preview expected a roughly $6–7 million funding shortfall against the January 2027 tanker payments, with equity issuance expected to continue. Management said the $39.78 million obligation is already fully covered by cash, which had reached $48 million by the end of July.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company faces a $39.78 million CapEx obligation for two product tankers due in January 2027, which management says is already fully covered by cash”; cash “further [climbed] to $48 million by end of July 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “$39.8M in capex is due in January 2027 for two MR product tankers, against $33.2M of cash. On the Q1 call, management said equity issuances will continue.”

surprises.description: Voyage revenue was $24 million, above the preview’s $18–20 million estimate range. That is about 20% above the top of the range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 voyage revenues rose 124% year-over-year to $24 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Voyage revenues | $18–20M”

surprises.description: Fleet-wide TCE reached about $40,300, above the preview’s estimate of roughly $33,000–$35,000 per day. The reported rate was about 15% above the top of that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The fleet-wide TCE rate rose 145% year-over-year to $40,300 in Q2 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Daily TCE | ~$33–35k”

surprises.description: Q2 EBITDA was $12 million, above the preview’s approximately $8–9 million estimate for adjusted EBITDA. The comparison is approximate because the preview specified adjusted EBITDA while the reported fact says EBITDA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 EBITDA reached $12 million versus negative $3.7 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA | ~$8–9M”

surprises.description: Net income was nearly $10 million, versus the preview’s $6–7 million estimate. The result exceeded the top of the estimate range by about 43%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income swung to nearly $10 million”; adjusted net income was “$9.8 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net income | ~$6–7M”

surprises.description: Quarter-end cash of $33.2 million was above the preview’s roughly $30 million estimate, though the gap was relatively small.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company's cash balance climbed to $33.2 million by end of June 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash + time deposits | ~$30M”

in_line: Bank debt was $0, as the preview expected; it stated “Bank debt: $0” and described the vessels as unencumbered.

surprises.description: Dollar Tree raised FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $7.70–$8.05 from $6.70–$7.10, a much larger increase than the preview’s base-case expectation of $6.85–$7.20. The new range includes about $0.60 of net tariff-refund benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year guidance was updated to ... adjusted EPS of $7.70-$8.05, including an approximately $0.60 net tariff refund benefit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EPS guidance raised to $6.70–7.10”; the base scenario expected it to be “nudged to $6.85–7.20.”

surprises.description: Q2 gross margin expanded 850 basis points, far above the preview’s bull-case threshold of 100 basis points or more and its bear-case expectation of less than about 50 basis points. Tariff-related items alone contributed 680 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin expanded 850 basis points to 42.9%, including a 680 basis point benefit from tariff-related items.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the bull case required “gross margin expands by 100 bps or more”; the bear case had “margin expansion below about 50 bps.”

surprises.description: The company received a substantial tariff refund, contrary to the preview’s assumption that guidance excluded refunds and that none would be received. The refund and related items contributed $1.31 to reported diluted EPS after reinvestments and duties.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company received $383 million in tariff refunds (benefiting gross profit by $369 million)” and “$1.31 came from the net impact of tariff refunds, reinvestments, and certain duties.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management ... assumes no tariff refunds”; the preview also said refunds “would be reinvested, not dropped to EPS.”

surprises.description: Excluding the tariff-related net impact, implied underlying EPS was $1.39, above both the $1.00–$1.15 company outlook and the preview’s $1.11–$1.12 consensus. This was a meaningful beat even apart from the refund-related reported EPS uplift.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Implying underlying EPS of $1.39 versus the $1.00-$1.15 outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS ... Consensus $1.11 ... or $1.12.”

surprises.description: Sales and comparable-store growth exceeded the preview’s consensus, with comps also above the top of company guidance. Net sales were near the top of the expected range, while the comp beat was more pronounced.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 net sales grew 7% to $4.9 billion with comparable store sales up 3.7%, exceeding guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Net-sales consensus was “$4.85B ... or $4.86B”; comparable-store-sales consensus was “+3.1%,” against company guidance of “+2.5% to +3.5%.”

surprises.description: Traffic turned positive, avoiding the negative reported result the preview identified as a key downside risk, but at +0.4% it was below the +1.4% Q2 foot-traffic reading cited in the preview. The traffic signal was therefore better than the downside concern but weaker than the alt-data reading.
surprises.fact_evidence: Comparable sales included “traffic +0.4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A reported traffic figure that is still negative would undercut the alt-data read”; Placer.ai data cited in the preview showed “Q2 foot traffic up 1.4%.”

surprises.description: Dollar Tree disclosed a sharp split in category performance: consumables comps were much stronger than discretionary comps. The preview did not provide segment-level expectations, so the divergence was not anticipated there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consumables comped 5.8% while discretionary comped 1.6%.”

surprises.description: A helium shortage unexpectedly constrained sales, costing an estimated $15 million, or about 30 basis points of comp. This was a newly disclosed operating headwind not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A helium supply shortage [was] estimated to have cut total sales by about $15 million or roughly 30 basis points of comp.”

surprises.description: Management reported that stores classified as needing improvement had fallen from about half the fleet at the prior October Investor Day to about one-third, indicating broader execution progress that the preview did not discuss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Stores in the ‘opportunity for improvement’ category declined from about half of the fleet at last October’s Investor Day to about one-third today.”

surprises.description: Multi-price penetration had increased by about 400 basis points to 17% of sales, a concrete level of progress beyond the preview’s general mention of multi-price conversions as a possible comp driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Multi-price penetration rose approximately 400 basis points year-over-year to 17% of total sales, helping drive ticket growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The bull scenario said “multi-price conversions comp above the chain average,” without specifying a penetration level or increase.

in_line: FY26 net-sales guidance remained at $20.5–$20.7 billion with comp growth of 3%–4%, matching the previously stated company range in the preview.
Q2 repurchases were $605 million, close to the $595 million reported for Q1; the preview flagged buyback cadence as important but did not provide a specific Q2 estimate.

surprises.description: The preview’s base case put comps at +3.5% to +4.5% and revenue at $1.90B to $1.93B; WSM reported +6.2% comps and $1.96B of revenue. The comp result also reached the preview’s bull-case threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 comparable brand revenue grew 6.2%” and “total revenue up 6.7% to $1.96 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: $1.90B to $1.93B (comps +3.5% to +4.5%)”; “Bull: At least $1.95B (comps at least +6%).”

surprises.description: Pottery Barn was expected to post a +2.3% comp, but its Q2 comp was +5.1%, a notably stronger result on the brand the preview singled out as the key furniture-cycle read.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Pottery Barn 5.1%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pottery Barn comp (Q2) … +2.3%”; “PB is the main furniture-cycle read.”

surprises.description: WSM raised its full-year comp range to 4%–6.5% from 2%–6% and its operating-margin range to 17.8%–18.2% from 17.5%–18.1%. The company said the raise was operational and excluded any IEEPA refund benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised full-year fiscal '26 guidance on both ends” to comparable brand revenue growth of “4% to 6.5% (up from 2%-6%)” and operating margin of “17.8% to 18.2%”; the raise was “purely operational” and excluded tariff refunds.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY26 comps guidance of “+2.0% to +6.0%” and operating margin of “17.5% to 18.1%,” and said “the question was the size of any raise.”

surprises.description: Gross margin came in below the preview’s roughly 46% level associated with mitigation ahead of plan: it was 45.5%, down about 160 basis points, with tariff-driven merchandise-margin pressure only partly offset by efficiencies and occupancy leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 gross margin fell approximately 160 basis points to 45.5%,” driven by a “230 basis point merchandise margin decline from tariffs,” partly offset by 70 basis points of efficiencies and leverage.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A print above roughly 46% would suggest mitigation is ahead of plan”; the preview also flagged Q2 as the peak tariff-impact quarter.

surprises.description: The preview anticipated that an IEEPA recovery might be a non-recurring GAAP item but did not quantify it. WSM received $200 million, recognized $174 million into income, and reported a net pretax GAAP benefit of about $117 million, with another $29 million expected to flow through Q3 gross margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Received $200 million in IEEPA tariff refunds (including interest), recognized $174 million into income,” reimbursed $47 million to vendors and $10 million to employee 401(k)s, “netting ~$117 million pretax GAAP benefit,” with “an additional $29 million to flow through Q3 gross margin.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any IEEPA recovery would likely be a non-recurring GAAP item”; FY26 guidance “assumed no tariff refunds.”

surprises.description: The preview flagged SG&A leverage as an issue to watch but gave no expected result; WSM reported about 100 basis points of leverage, driven largely by employment expense leverage from payroll and incentive-compensation discipline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “SG&A leveraged approximately 100 basis points to 28.2% of revenue,” including “120 basis points of employment expense leverage.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “SG&A leverage and buyback pace” were listed as a key issue to watch.

surprises.description: The preview did not flag the scale of B2B growth; WSM reported a record-volume quarter, with B2B up 14.5%, including 20% growth in contract and 12% in trade.
surprises.fact_evidence: “B2B grew 14.5% to a record volume quarter, with contract up 20% and trade up 12%.”

surprises.description: WSM reported a specific Q4 headwind that the preview had not anticipated: about 150 basis points from anniversarying the prior-year shrink-accrual benefit. Management also warned that fuel costs would continue to pressure results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged a Q4 headwind of ~150 basis points from anniversarying last year's shrink accrual benefit and warned of continued fuel cost pressure.”

surprises.description: Merchandise inventory increased only 1% year over year despite revenue growth of 6.7%, a favorable inventory outcome not addressed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Merchandise inventory was up only 1% year-over-year against 6.7% revenue growth.”

surprises.description: WSM paid $90 million in dividends, a 15% increase, but made no share repurchases in Q2. The preview highlighted repurchase pace as an important EPS lever, but did not specify an expected level of buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Paid $90 million in dividends (15% increase) but did not repurchase shares in Q2, retaining ~$1.1 billion in buyback authorization.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “With a roughly $28B market cap and strong free cash flow, the repurchase pace is the main lever on EPS.”

surprises.description: The emerging brands’ double-digit growth was not anticipated in the preview, which did not discuss their results.
surprises.fact_evidence: “All emerging brands (Rejuvenation, Mark and Graham, GreenRow) posting double-digit growth.”

in_line: The preview identified Q2 as the peak quarter for tariff pressure; management said tariff impacts are expected to moderate as WSM laps prior-year tariffs beginning mid-Q3.
Diluted EPS was $2.10, within the preview’s practical bar of roughly $2.10–$2.15, though the published $2.05 consensus was for adjusted EPS and is not directly comparable to the reported diluted EPS.

surprises.description: Hormel cut its fiscal 2026 organic net sales growth outlook to 1%-2% from 1%-4%, citing weaker market and consumer conditions. The preview presented the prior range as reaffirmed guidance and did not anticipate a sales-growth reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company lowered its full-year organic net sales growth expectation to 1%-2% from a prior range of 1%-4%, citing weaker market and consumer conditions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales: $12.2–$12.5B, organic growth +1–4%” and the preview described the full-year guidance as “reaffirmed at Q2.”

surprises.description: Hormel raised and narrowed its adjusted EPS range, lifting the low end by two cents to $1.45 while keeping the $1.51 high end. That is a modestly better outcome than the preview’s base case of reaffirming the full range, though short of its bull-case range of $1.47-$1.51.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hormel raised and narrowed its fiscal 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $1.45-$1.51 from the prior $1.43-$1.51.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: ... full $1.43–$1.51 range reaffirmed without narrowing”; the bull case was “FY guide narrowed to $1.47–$1.51.”

surprises.description: Q3 organic net sales fell 2% year over year, whereas the preview’s consensus estimate anticipated slightly higher net sales. The comparison is not exact because the preview cited total net sales while the reported figure is organic net sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 organic net sales declined 2% year-over-year, driven by portfolio shaping actions, softer commodity markets, and a pressured consumer.”

surprises.description: Q4 adjusted EPS is now expected to be about $0.37 at the midpoint, below the prior expectation of about $0.40. This tempers the positive full-year EPS guide revision.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 EPS is now expected at ~$0.37 at the midpoint versus a prior ~$0.40 expectation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q4 EPS is now expected at ~$0.37 at the midpoint versus a prior ~$0.40 expectation.”

surprises.description: Q3 adjusted EPS was $0.37, a one-cent beat against the preview’s $0.36 consensus estimate and at the top of its base-case range. The preview described the quarter as potentially noisy, so this was a modest beat rather than a large departure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 adjusted EPS was $0.37, up 6% versus last year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS | Q3 FY26E: $0.36”; the base case was “Adj. EPS $0.35–0.37.”

surprises.description: Adjusted operating margin reached 9%, despite the preview’s concern about fuel, logistics, and utilization pressure; the preview said holding margin near 9% would be a positive surprise. The reported margin expanded 60 basis points year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating margin expanded 60 basis points year-over-year to 9%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 carries the full 13-week impact of the fuel spike ... plus elevated logistics and above-plan commodity costs”; “Holding margin near 9% would be a positive surprise.”

surprises.description: Retail volumes fell by a high-single-digit percentage. The preview highlighted a hoped-for positive branded Retail organic-growth signal and only a 1.4% year-over-year decline in Retail segment profit; the reported volume decline was notably weak, though about half was attributed to portfolio exits and other actions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Retail volumes fell high single digits, with about half of the decline tied to the whole-bird turkey divestiture, private label snack nut exit, and contract manufacturing.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus has Retail profit down 1.4% Y/Y”; “Look for ... positive branded Retail organic growth.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed an impairment of Hormel’s Indonesia minority investment, an adverse one-off not flagged in the preview. No amount was provided, so the size of the earnings impact cannot be assessed from the supplied facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ... recorded an Indonesia minority investment impairment.”

surprises.description: A one-time legal-entity transition depressed SPAM export sales, an unanticipated temporary sales headwind not discussed in the preview. The call facts do not quantify the effect.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A one-time legal entity transition depressed SPAM export sales.”

in_line: Foodservice continued to grow organically and profit growth outpaced sales, consistent with the preview’s expectation of positive Foodservice sales and faster profit growth.

surprises.description: Q4 sales were $396.7M, about 4.9% above the $378.3M consensus and above the preview’s bull-case range of $380–392M. That was a substantial upside gap against a preview that warned consensus was near the top of the implied guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 2026 net sales grew 5% to $396.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | $378.3M (range $378.0–378.7M)” and the bull scenario had “Q4 revenue” of “$380–392M.”

surprises.description: FY27 guidance was above the preview’s main benchmarks: the sales midpoint is about $1.575B versus $1.55B consensus, and the EPS range of $3.41–$3.59 is above the $3.32 consensus even at its low end. The preview’s base-case EPS range was $3.05–$3.25, with its bull case starting at $3.30.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2027 guidance calls for net sales of $1.55-1.6 billion (midpoint ~4% growth) … and adjusted diluted EPS of $3.41-$3.59.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 consensus: Revenue of $1.55B (+3.2%) and EPS of $3.32 (+8%).” The preview’s base scenario gave EPS of “$3.05–3.25” and bull scenario “$3.30 EPS.”

surprises.description: Q4 profitability also exceeded the preview’s earnings benchmarks. Adjusted EBITDA rose 29%, implying about $64.3M from the reported $14.3M increase, versus roughly $60M consensus; adjusted diluted EPS rose 35%, above the $0.73 consensus based on the prior-year $0.57 result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA increased 29% (up $14.3 million), with adjusted diluted EPS up 35%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | $0.73” and “Adj. EBITDA | ~$60M (derived).”

surprises.description: Management’s Brazil assumption was more cautious than the preview’s discussion of expected therapeutic-claim approvals during the transition: FY27 guidance includes only minimal Virginia mycin sales, with approval treated as upside. That leaves most of roughly $27M of FY26 sales unassumed in the coming year rather than signaling a material conversion already built into the plan.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management assumed only minimal Virginia mycin sales in Brazil for fiscal 2027 after ~$27 million in fiscal 2026 sales, treating regulatory approval … as potential upside.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has said it expects therapeutic-claim approvals during the transition. The key number is how much of the $26M converts to therapeutic labels.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a Chicago Heights facility closure with sizeable eventual savings, but those benefits are mostly delayed until FY28 and beyond and come with roughly $20M of cash costs and capex, plus undetermined non-cash write-offs. The preview did not flag this restructuring or its costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The planned closure … is expected to generate $15-20 million in annual adjusted EBITDA benefit, mostly in fiscal 2028 and beyond, with only minimal benefit in fiscal 2027”; costs are “roughly $10 million in cash costs plus about $10 million in capex,” with additional non-cash write-offs undetermined.

surprises.description: Despite the stronger full-year and FY27 outlook, management expects Q1 FY27 EBIT growth to be negative because of the higher SG&A base from infrastructure investments. The preview cited positive FY27 EPS growth consensus but did not flag a weak first-quarter earnings profile.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects Q1 fiscal 2027 EBIT growth to be negative due to a higher SG&A base carried forward from infrastructure investments, before turning positive for the remainder of the year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 consensus: Revenue of $1.55B (+3.2%) and EPS of $3.32 (+8%).”

surprises.description: Management forecast a meaningful FY27 free-cash-flow improvement as the acquired MFA inventory build slows sharply, a more constructive outlook than the preview’s focus on persistently weak cash conversion. The FY26 result itself remained weak, but the expected inventory build falls from $86.3M to $25–30M.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow was only $10 million in fiscal 2026, weighed down by an $86.3 million inventory build for the acquired MFA portfolio, but management expects significantly greater free cash flow in fiscal 2027 with inventory build limited to $25-30 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “TTM free cash flow only $13M”; the preview said weak Q4 cash conversion would put earnings quality “at the center of the thesis.”

surprises.description: FY26 sales modestly exceeded the preview’s $1.50B consensus and the top of the raised guidance range, reaching a record $1.518B. The beat was smaller than the Q4 upside but still above the full-year bar.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fiscal 2026 delivered record net sales exceeding $1.5 billion ($1,518 million).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 full year: Consensus is $1.50B revenue” and raised guidance called for sales of “$1.46–1.50B.”

in_line: FY26 adjusted EBITDA of $255M landed at the top of the preview’s cited $247–255M guidance range.
FY26 free cash flow remained weak at $10M, consistent with the preview’s warning about low trailing free cash flow and cash-conversion risk.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $42.4 million, below the roughly $44.0 million consensus and the $44.8 million the preview said was needed to meet the company’s FY2026 revenue floor. The shortfall was modest relative to consensus but widened the gap to that floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 fiscal 2026 net revenue fell 23.1% year-over-year to $42.4 million” and “declined 3.1% sequentially from Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | ~$44.0M (range $43.4–44.4M)” and “Q4 needs about $44.8M revenue” to hold the $185M floor.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS came in below the preview’s roughly $0.13 consensus and the $0.15 it estimated was needed to meet the FY2026 guidance floor.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 adjusted net income dropped to $1.4 million ($0.11 per diluted share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | ~$0.13 (range $0.12–0.13)” and “Q4 needs … about $0.15 adj. EPS” to hold the $185M floor.

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $2.7 million, below the preview’s estimated $3.5–4.0 million range, and its margin fell year over year. This was a meaningful miss against the estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 adjusted EBITDA fell to $2.7 million (6.5% of revenue) from $4.8 million (8.7%) a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | ~$3.5–4.0M (estimate).”

surprises.description: Revenue fell 3.1% sequentially rather than stabilizing around flat, as the preview’s base case anticipated. The decline was much smaller than the preview’s bear-case $4–5 million step-down, but it still showed that the sequential slide had not stopped.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q4 revenue “declined 3.1% sequentially from Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base scenario expected “Roughly flat sequentially”; the preview also said “a further step down of $4–5M” would suggest weakening.

surprises.description: Management said it does not expect trends to turn positive until fiscal Q3–Q4 2027, with difficult comparisons in Q1 and Q2. That points to a longer wait for improvement than the preview’s stabilization-focused discussion suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management “flagged difficult comparables in Q1 and Q2 of fiscal 2027 and does not expect trends to turn positive until fiscal Q3-Q4 as new strategies take effect.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the key question whether “sequential revenue has stabilized” and said “a slowing decline is the condition for any stabilization story.”

surprises.description: Gross margin was 78%, below the 79.0% reported for Q3 in the preview and down from 79.9% a year earlier. Product mix, inventory obsolescence, and shipping and warehouse costs weighed on the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin declined to 78% from 79.9% year-over-year due to product mix shifts, higher inventory obsolescence, and increased shipping and warehouse costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported “GAAP gross margin 79.0%” for Q3 FY2026.

surprises.description: Despite the revenue and order declines, subscription revenue remained above 75% of sales and customer retention improved year over year. This was a favorable customer-quality signal not anticipated in the preview’s focus on falling active accounts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Subscription-based revenue remained strong at more than 75% of total revenue, and customer retention metrics improved year-over-year despite some subscribers pausing orders.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview highlighted active accounts at 109,000 as a leading indicator and said a print below about 105,000 would make stabilization hard to argue.

in_line: No formal FY2027 guidance was issued. The preview explicitly considered deferring guidance to October as a plausible base-case outcome.
The quarterly dividend remained $0.05, matching the preview’s stated dividend.

surprises.description: AI Cloud revenue was $70.5 million, well above the preview’s $50 million watchpoint and even the $60 million level used in its bull scenario. This was a stronger quarter for AI Cloud than the preview’s threshold implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue was $137.2 million (including $70.5 million AI Cloud revenue)”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AI Cloud revenue at or above $50M”; bull scenario: “AI Cloud above $60M”
