surprises.description: IREN said ARR had risen from roughly $0.5 billion at the end of Q4 to $1 billion after Microsoft accepted Horizon 1. The preview already expected the more-than-$4-billion exit-2026 target, but did not anticipate this near-term ARR milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “IREN exited Q4 with roughly $0.5 billion of ARR, reached $1 billion today after Microsoft accepted Horizon 1”

surprises.description: The company described a substantial funding runway for its GPU buildout: $6.5 billion of GPU financing secured in three months, $14 billion of cash and committed financing, a target for another roughly $8 billion of GPU financing, and unencumbered data centers available as collateral. This is more concrete financing capacity than the preview’s funding-and-dilution concern anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “secured $6.5 billion of GPU financing over three months”; “has $14 billion of existing cash and committed financing”; “targets an additional ~$8 billion of GPU financing”; “holds 100% of its data centers unencumbered as future financing collateral”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Funding and dilution. A new equity or convertible raise announced with the print would be a negative catalyst. Management has ~$5.8bn of Dell GPU purchases for Microsoft alone, plus Sweetwater and the 1.2GW 2027 build.”

surprises.description: Customer prepayments are expected to fund 45%–55% of GPU CapEx, and management said that, combined with 90% GPU financing, the funding model requires relatively little equity. The preview highlighted dilution risk but did not describe this customer-funded mechanism.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Recent customer prepayments are funding 45%-55% of GPU CapEx, and combined with 90% GPU financing this creates a funding flywheel requiring relatively little equity.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Funding and dilution. A new equity or convertible raise announced with the print would be a negative catalyst.”

surprises.description: IREN guided to approximately $25 billion–$30 billion of FY27 CapEx, with data-center and GPU CapEx expected to rise 15%–20%. The preview discussed major buildout commitments but gave no comparable CapEx outlook, so the stated investment scale was not anticipated there.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 CapEx of approximately $25 billion to $30 billion, with data center and GPU CapEx expected to rise 15%-20% for ongoing and new deployments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has ~$5.8bn of Dell GPU purchases for Microsoft alone, plus Sweetwater and the 1.2GW 2027 build.”

surprises.description: Contract pricing had risen sharply: about 125% for three-year deals and 70% for five-year deals since November, with recent three-year deals above $20 million per megawatt and discussions near $25 million. The preview did not flag this pricing improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “3-year contract pricing has risen about 125% since November while 5-year pricing is up about 70%, with recent 3-year deals exceeding $20 million per megawatt and active discussions near $25 million per megawatt.”

surprises.description: Q4 net loss was $684 million, with $450.4 million of noncash impairments on decommissioned mining hardware and another $102.1 million fair-value decrease on hardware held for sale. The preview anticipated mining-related revenue decay and flagged possible BTC fair-value swings, but did not anticipate these large hardware charges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net loss of $684 million, largely driven by $450.4 million of noncash impairments on decommissioned mining hardware plus a $102.1 million fair value decrease on mining hardware held for sale.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch hashrate, BTC mined, and whether any BTC on the balance sheet creates fair-value swings in GAAP EPS.”

surprises.description: Management expects Q1 cash SG&A to increase by approximately $40 million–$50 million sequentially as it makes growth investments ahead of revenue. The preview did not flag this near-term cost increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 cash SG&A is expected to increase approximately $40-50 million sequentially due to growth investments ahead of revenue.”

surprises.description: IREN said more than $4 billion of ARR is expected by the end of the December quarter and is already under contract, with that contracted amount representing less than 10% of its 5+ gigawatt secured-grid portfolio. The target itself was expected; the additional scale of secured but still unmonetized capacity was not highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “expects more than $4 billion of ARR by the end of the December quarter, all already under contract”; “The $4 billion of contracted ARR is derived from less than 10% of the company's 5+ gigawatt portfolio of secured grid connections”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Exit-2026 AI Cloud ARR: ‘>$4bn’ reaffirmed or hedged?”

in_line: Q4 revenue of $137.2 million was close to the preview’s roughly $137 million midpoint and within its $132.3 million–$142.3 million consensus range.
The more-than-$4-billion exit-2026 AI Cloud ARR target was reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s central expectation.

surprises.description: Medtronic reported $9.8 billion of Q1 revenue, above the preview’s realistic $9.55–$9.65 billion bar. The gap was meaningful even against the preview’s higher, guide-implied range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 revenue reached $9.8 billion” and beat expectations.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The realistic bar is closer to $9.55–9.65B”; the company-guide-implied estimate was “$9.56–9.66B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $1.45 exceeded the preview’s $1.40–$1.42 base case and its $1.44 bull-case threshold. The preview expected a possible raise to full-year guidance, but not this size of quarterly EPS beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS of $1.45,” coming in “$0.06 above the guidance midpoint and Street estimates.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Base scenario: “$1.40–$1.42”; bull scenario: “≥$1.44.”

surprises.description: Cardiac Ablation Solutions grew 88% worldwide, substantially exceeding the preview’s concern that growth could decelerate below 45% and surpassing the prior quarter’s 78% growth despite a harder comparison. It also passed $2 billion in trailing-12-month revenue ahead of schedule and gained 9 U.S. share points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cardiac Ablation Solutions delivered 88% worldwide growth (139% in the U.S.), surpassed $2 billion in trailing 12-month revenue ahead of schedule, and gained 9 points of U.S. share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 FY26 was already ~+50%, so the comp is harder. Deceleration below ~45% is the most likely source of a de-rate”; Q4 FY26 growth was “+78% worldwide.”

surprises.description: The Q1 tariff burden was much lighter than the preview’s estimated $75 million hit: refunds nearly offset tariffs paid, leaving only a slight net headwind. Management also said no future refunds are included in guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Tariff impacts were a slight net headwind as refunds nearly offset tariffs paid,” and “no future refunds are embedded in guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s FY27 framework included a “~$250M tariff COGS hit, $75M of it in Q1.”

surprises.description: Q1 adjusted operating-margin expansion was only 10 basis points, below the preview’s estimated 40–70 basis points. Management also expects about 50 basis points of full-year expansion, down from the prior 60-basis-point expectation, citing reinvestment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted operating margin rose 10 basis points to 23.7%”; full-year expansion is expected to be “~50 basis points,” a “slight reduction from prior 60 basis point expectations due to reinvestment.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q1 non-GAAP operating margin was estimated at “~24.0–24.3%” and “+40–70 bps” year over year; the preview said “Needs +40–70 bps of Y/Y expansion to keep the FY +60 bps credible.”

surprises.description: Medtronic disclosed quantified margin benefits from the planned MiniMed separation—about 50 basis points to gross margin and 100 basis points to operating margin—with only about a 20-basis-point growth cost. The preview had identified quantified separation accretion as unmodeled upside.
surprises.fact_evidence: The separation “will lift gross margin by ~50 basis points and operating margin by ~100 basis points, while costing only ~20 basis points of growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Any quantified accretion is unmodeled upside.”

surprises.description: Medtronic announced a previously unanticipated $700 million investment and distribution agreement for Cornerstone’s Sentire surgical robotics system in select non-U.S. markets, with material revenue and margin contribution expected from FY28. The sizable near-term investment is paired with prospective longer-term returns.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company announced a $700 million strategic investment and distribution agreement” with “material revenue and margin contribution expected starting FY28.”

in_line: Organic revenue growth was 13.7%, but roughly 670 basis points came from the extra selling week, leaving underlying growth near 7%. That is within the preview’s expected clean-growth range of ~5.5–7% and above its 6.5% threshold for supporting the FY27 acceleration story.

The full-year guidance action was broadly in line with the preview’s expectation that Medtronic would raise guidance: organic revenue guidance rose 50 basis points to 7.25%–7.75%, and EPS guidance moved to $5.94–$6.00 from $5.90–$6.00.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $56.0 million, above the preview’s $53.0 million consensus estimate, and the year-over-year decline was 7.3% rather than the preview-implied 12.3%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Fourth quarter revenue declined 7.3% to $56 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $53.0M (implied −12.3% Y/Y)”

surprises.description: Consolidated same-store sales rose only 0.1% in Q4, well below the preview’s 2.0–2.5% base-case range. The full-year increase was also modest at 0.9%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consolidated same-store sales rose only 0.1% in Q4 and 0.9% for the full year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … Consol. SSS | +2.0–2.5%”

surprises.description: The preview identified positive traffic as an important signal, but Supercuts’ Q4 growth was still price-led: traffic remained down about one point. This indicates the anticipated traffic improvement had not materialized in that key brand.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Supercuts Q4 growth of 2.6% came primarily from higher average ticket, as traffic was still down about one point.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Traffic versus price in same-store sales. Positive traffic in any brand is the most important qualitative disclosure.”

surprises.description: The preview’s closure scenarios suggested that fewer than about 50 net closures in Q4 could indicate the cycle was ending. Although the 199-salon net decline for FY26 is roughly consistent with that quarterly pace, management expects FY27 closures to remain similar to FY26 levels, pointing to continued elevated closures rather than a clear end to the cycle.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects fiscal 2027 closures to be similar to fiscal 2026 levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Under about 50 net in Q4 suggests the closure cycle is ending.”

surprises.description: Company-owned salon adjusted EBITDA increased by $800,000 to $2.8 million despite a reduction in labor margin. That was better than the preview’s downside scenario of company-owned margins giving back gains, although the segment’s 4% same-store sales growth was mainly pricing-driven.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Company-owned salons posted 4% same-store sales growth driven mainly by pricing, and improved segment adjusted EBITDA by $800,000 to $2.8 million while reducing labor margin through pay plan adjustments and scheduling discipline.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bear … company-owned margin gives back gains.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed a $7–8 million excess-cash-flow sweep payment expected in September. The payment will reduce cash as well as debt, a specific near-term cash use the preview had not identified.
surprises.fact_evidence: “An excess cash flow sweep payment of $7-8 million [is] expected in September to reduce cash and debt.”

surprises.description: The closed franchise salons were unusually low-volume locations: they averaged $136,000 in unit volume, about $364,000 below top-quartile salons. This suggests the closures were concentrated among substantially weaker units, a detail not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Closed locations averaging just $136,000 in unit volume, roughly $364,000 below top-quartile salons.”

surprises.description: FY26 adjusted EBITDA was $32.8 million, above the preview’s $32 million threshold for keeping the year above that level. The preview did not provide an actual Q4 adjusted EBITDA figure, so the quarterly result cannot be compared directly with its Q4 range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Regis finished fiscal 2026 with … $32.8 million of adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A print of $9.0M or more keeps FY26 above $32M.”

in_line: FY26 unrestricted cash from operations rose to $13.5 million from $5.4 million, fulfilling the preview’s expectation of a meaningful increase versus FY25.
Refinancing remained in progress rather than being announced, matching the preview’s base case that refinancing would still be underway.

surprises.description: Gap raised its FY26 adjusted EPS outlook to $2.35–$2.45, above the preview’s expected reaffirmation of $2.30–$2.40. The increase came despite the preview’s emphasis on tariff and operating-cost uncertainty.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Raised its full-year adjusted EPS outlook to $2.35-$2.45 (up 10%-15%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case expected Gap to “reaffirm $2.30–2.40” and the catalyst checklist said investors wanted a “reaffirmation.”

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin was stronger than the preview’s expected flat-to-down result: it rose 20 basis points year over year and reached 41.4%, above the preview’s 40.7%–41.2% consensus range. Merchandise margin increased 80 basis points, with some of the benefit offset by fuel costs.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted gross margin rose 20 basis points to 41.4% with merchandise margin up 80 basis points, though 30 basis points of tariff benefit was largely offset by higher fuel costs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected gross margin of “~40.7–41.2%” and company guidance of “Flat to –50 bps y/y.”

surprises.description: FY26 sales guidance was narrowed at the lower end: the new 1%–1.5% growth range has the same low end but a lower high end than the preview’s expected reaffirmation of 1%–2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company narrowed full-year net sales growth guidance to 1%-1.5%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview expected Gap to “reaffirm $2.30–2.40 and +1–2% sales.”

surprises.description: Q2 net sales declined 2% year over year, a somewhat weaker rate than the preview’s roughly 0.6%–1.1% expected decline, although the reported $3.7 billion matched the dollar consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 net sales declined 2% year-over-year to $3.7 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited “~$3.70B” consensus and expected sales growth of “–1.1% y/y”; company guidance was “Flat to –1%.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS of $0.52 modestly exceeded the preview’s consensus figures of $0.48–$0.50, even though EPS declined from $0.57 a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS fell to $0.52 from $0.57 a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Q2 adjusted EPS consensus of “$0.50 (Zacks); $0.48 (StockStory).”

surprises.description: Athleta remained a significant weak spot, with comps down 12% and management expecting similar trends for the full year. The preview’s key brand debate centered on Old Navy and did not flag this degree of continuing weakness at Athleta.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Athleta remained the weakest brand with comparable sales down 12%, and management guided to full-year trends staying similar to the first half.”

surprises.description: The company gave a positive Q3 outlook—sales growth of 1.5%–2.5% and gross-margin expansion of 25–75 basis points—alongside meaningful sequential improvement at Old Navy in August. The preview highlighted substantial uncertainty around second-half tariffs and margins but did not anticipate this quarterly outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for net sales up 1.5%-2.5% with gross margin up 25-75 basis points,” and “Old Navy is showing meaningful sequential improvement in August.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called the post-Section 122 tariff rates the “main driver of H2 gross margin” and expected the company to be “monitoring” tariffs.

in_line: Old Navy comps declined 4%, consistent with the preview’s expected down-low-single-digit result and its base case of a 2%–4% decline.
Total comparable sales were down 1%, in line with the preview’s expectation of roughly –1% to 0%.

surprises.description: Cango's Q2 revenue was about $50.8 million, below the preview's $65–75 million base case and within its $50–60 million bear case. Bitcoin mining revenue was about $47.4 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue was approximately $50.8 million, with about $47.4 million from Bitcoin mining.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “Revenue $65–75M”; “Bear” scenario: “Revenue $50–60M.”

surprises.description: Cango mined 656 Bitcoins, well below the preview's base-case range of 850–950 and even below the bear-case threshold of 750. This was a sharper volume shortfall than the preview's downside scenario anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: The preview's reported-results section states “Coins mined 656”; its scenario table gives “Base” of “850–950” and “Bear” of “<750.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “BTC mined 850–950”; “Bear” scenario: “<750.”

surprises.description: The company ended Q2 at 27.58 EH/s of combined hashrate, below the base-case exit range of 30–33 EH/s. Management said it deliberately rightsized mining operations, explaining the lower capacity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company deliberately rightsized mining operations, ending Q2 with self-mining hashrate of 19.84 EH/s and lease hashrate of 7.74 EH/s for a combined 27.58 EH/s.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base” scenario: “Exit hashrate 30–33 EH/s.”

surprises.description: Although the preview focused on cash cost, Cango reported an all-in cost of $98,405 per Bitcoin, above recent Bitcoin price levels. That indicates substantially worse full-cost economics than the cash-cost figure alone suggests.
surprises.fact_evidence: “All-in cost was $98,405 per Bitcoin, exceeding recent Bitcoin price levels.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cost per coin must fall below revenue per coin for mining to be cash-positive.”

surprises.description: Cango recorded about $51 million of impairment and disposal losses on mining machines, a substantial one-off drag on its $81.6 million continuing-operations net loss that the preview did not flag.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net loss from continuing operations was approximately $81.6 million, driven primarily by about $51 million in noncash impairment ($42.9 million) and disposal losses ($8.5 million) on mining machines.”

surprises.description: The crypto fair-value loss fell to $4.1 million from $151.8 million in Q1, with management attributing the improvement partly to a newly implemented Bitcoin hedging program. This sharply reduced a major loss driver highlighted in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Loss from fair value changes in crypto assets narrowed sharply to $4.1 million from $151.8 million in Q1, aided by a newly implemented Bitcoin hedging program.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview identified “Bitcoin hedging” as a key issue and cited Q1's “$151.8M fair-value loss on crypto assets.”

surprises.description: The hedge was described as short-term BTC-denominated loans sized to roughly one to two months of production, with about $8 million of short-term debt at quarter-end. The preview asked how much of the treasury was hedged and at what strikes, but the reported details instead emphasized the loan structure and risk-management purpose.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The hedging program is structured as short-term BTC-denominated loans sized to roughly one to two months of production, with around $8 million in short-term debt at quarter end, used for risk management rather than speculation.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “How much of the 1,056 BTC is hedged, and at what strikes, determines whether CANG still trades as a bitcoin-beta instrument.”

surprises.description: Cango signed its first AI infrastructure customer contract, a concrete commercial milestone, but said initial Q3 revenue would be modest and immaterial. The preview expected Q3 revenue recognition but emphasized the need for evidence of a meaningful contracted scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company signed its first AI infrastructure customer contract after June 30, with revenue recognition expected to begin in Q3 but described as modest and immaterial initially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management has committed to Q3 recognition. Any slip removes the main bull argument. Look for a disclosed dollar figure and contracted MW, not another progress update.”

in_line: Average cash mining cost was $73,313 per Bitcoin, within the preview's base-case estimate of approximately $72,000–$75,000.
AI revenue recognition remained on the expected Q3 timeline; the Georgia site was completed for up to 3 MW in early July, with GPUs arriving on site.

surprises.description: Q4 revenue was $102 million, about $6 million above the preview model’s ~$96 million estimate. The quarter grew 14% sequentially, faster than the modeled 7% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 FY2026 revenue was $102 million, up 14% sequentially from $89.6 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My model (Q4 FY26): Revenue ~$96M (+7% Q/Q, -13% Y/Y).”

surprises.description: Instead of the expected near-breakeven result, KTCC reported a $34.3 million Q4 net loss. The loss included a $28.4 million non-cash deferred-tax valuation allowance and an $8.4 million distressed-receivables write-off.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net loss was $34.3 million ($3.16 per share), including a $28.4 million non-cash valuation allowance against deferred tax assets and an $8.4 million write-off of distressed customer receivables.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net income ~breakeven. EPS ~$0.00 to $0.02”; management had said it felt “strongly that we'll be in the black bottom line” in Q4.

surprises.description: Adjusted gross margin was 8.3%, below the preview’s 9.0% estimate, so margin improvement fell short of the level the preview said was needed to support a return to profit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 gross margin improved to 7.8% (adjusted 8.3%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. gross margin ~9.0%”; the preview also highlighted “Adjusted gross margin of 9.0% or better.”

surprises.description: More than $60 million of new program awards were secured in Q4, including a data-center program worth $40–45 million per year. The preview expected new wins to be announced but did not anticipate awards of this stated scale.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company secured over $60 million in new program awards during Q4, including a $40-45 million/year data center program in Mexico.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “New program wins announced with the print.”

surprises.description: Supply-chain financing constraints delayed about $10 million of Q4 shipments. Management said they would move to future quarters rather than represent lost revenue, but the preview did not anticipate a financing-related shipment delay.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Supply chain financing constraints forced the company to delay approximately $10 million of shipments in Q4, which will shift to future quarters rather than being lost revenue.”

surprises.description: Management described the company as liquidity-constrained, said it was evaluating additional capital sources, and declined to provide Q1 FY2027 guidance. That left near-term visibility and funding more uncertain than the preview’s expected FY2027 framing and ramp-timing discussion suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management is liquidity-constrained and evaluating additional capital sources, including customer capital-sharing partnerships and leveraging unencumbered foreign assets, while declining to provide Q1 FY2027 guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY27 framing on the call, including the Q2 FY27 ramp timing”; the preview also said to “Watch for credit facility amendments, covenant waivers, or going-concern language.”

surprises.description: Vietnam-based revenue more than doubled sequentially, showing a sharper near-term ramp than the preview’s mention of doubled capacity alone indicated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Vietnam-based revenue more than doubled sequentially in Q4, driven by medical device and consumer products programs.”

surprises.description: The call put the completed China wind-down savings at about $4 million annualized, or roughly $1 million per quarter, somewhat below the preview’s estimate of about $1.2 million per quarter.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The completed wind-down of China manufacturing operations is expected to generate approximately $4 million in annualized savings in FY2027, measured against the first three quarters' run rate.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “China manufacturing ceased in April 2026 (about $1.2M per quarter of savings).”

in_line: FY2026 revenue was $386.7 million, close to the preview model’s ~$381 million estimate.

surprises.description: The preview flagged negative-margin professional services as a margin concern but did not indicate that Rory Read would take over the area. On the call, Read said he would lead services on an interim basis to accelerate improvements, suggesting a direct management intervention in that business.
surprises.fact_evidence: Rory Read said he would lead the services organization on an interim basis to accelerate improvements in the services area.

surprises.description: The preview did not anticipate a change in sales leadership. Sprinklr announced Tom Addis as its new Chief Revenue Officer.
surprises.fact_evidence: Rory Read announced the addition of Tom Addis as Chief Revenue Officer.

surprises.description: The preview did not mention a board appointment. Sprinklr announced Jordi Ribas as a new member of its Board of Directors.
surprises.fact_evidence: Rory Read announced Jordi Ribas as a member of Sprinklr's Board of Directors.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $2.61, below the preview’s roughly $3.00 in-house estimate and slightly below the $2.66 headline consensus, although it was within the preview’s wider $2.58–$2.74 consensus range. That made the result weaker than the preview’s expectation of an EPS beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted profit of $580.2 million ($2.61/share).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “My estimate is ~$3.00”; consensus estimates listed at “$2.66,” “$2.74,” and “$2.58”; the base scenario expected “Beat on EPS.”

surprises.description: Q2 VLCC TCE of $152,700/day came in well below the preview’s $181,700/day booking benchmark and the roughly $165,300/day implied by its 9% ballast-day haircut. The preview specifically flagged realized VLCC TCE as a test of that haircut.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 TCE rates reached $152,700/day for VLCCs.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “82% of Q2 VLCC days were booked at $181,700/day”; “The model haircuts the $181,700 VLCC booking by about 9%”; “Realized VLCC TCE against the $181,700 booked.”

surprises.description: Q3 VLCC bookings covered 86% of days, far more coverage than the preview’s roughly 50% base expectation and its 55%+ bull-case threshold. The $156,900/day rate itself was within the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “86% of Q3 VLCC days already booked at $156,900/day.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: … on ~50%”; “Bull: … on >55% of days.”

surprises.description: Frontline sold two roughly 10-year-old VLCCs for about $270 million and returned the proceeds as a special dividend rather than reinvesting them. The preview anticipated possible asset sales and full adjusted-EPS payout, but did not anticipate this specific sale-proceeds distribution or the reported price as the highest achieved for that generation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Sold 2 VLCCs (~$270 million total, ~$135 million each for ~10-year-old ships) at the highest price achieved for that generation and paid the proceeds out as a special dividend rather than reinvesting.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch for further asset sales and any shift between buybacks and dividends”; “Any cut below full payout … would likely be read as negative.”

surprises.description: The call quantified a particularly low fleet cash breakeven—about $23,900/day—against much higher current TCE rates, a level of operating cushion the preview did not set out as an expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The fleet's estimated 12-month average cash breakeven is about $23,900/day … against far higher current market TCE rates.”

surprises.description: At August 28 rates, management estimated $2.3 billion of potential cash generation, or about $10.35/share, with a 24% cash-flow yield; the preview provided no comparable cash-generation estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Cash generation potential at August 28 rates is $2.3 billion (~$10.35/share), implying a 24% cash flow yield,” with scenarios of $3.1 billion if rates rise 30% and $1.5 billion if they fall 30%.

surprises.description: Liquidity was reported at $1.2 billion, including a $901 million undrawn revolver, with no meaningful debt maturities until 2030. The preview cited about $945 million of cash and substantial newbuild commitments, but did not anticipate this liquidity and maturity profile; the figures are not directly comparable because the reported liquidity includes the revolver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Strong liquidity of $1.2 billion in cash and equivalents (including $901 million undrawn revolver) with no meaningful debt maturities until 2030.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The company has ~$925M of newbuild commitments and ~$945M of cash.”

surprises.description: Frontline cut its weighted average interest-rate margin by about 52 basis points, from 178 to 126 basis points, a financing-cost improvement not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reduced its weighted average interest rate margin by approximately 52 basis points, from 178bps to 126bps.”

surprises.description: The call said the order book amounts to about 40% of the commercially active fleet once roughly 166–167 non-trading vessels are excluded, versus 33.5% of the total fleet, and described the active-fleet measure as approaching 2008–2009 levels. The preview did not flag this potentially significant supply overhang.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The VLCC order book stands at ~33.5% of the total fleet but nears 40% of the commercially active fleet once ~166-167 non-trading … vessels are excluded, approaching 2008-2009 levels.”

surprises.description: The call reported an 82% fall in crude exports from inside Hormuz and a 35% drop in China crude imports, alongside a 23% rise in VLCC idling days that tightened effective supply. The preview identified Hormuz reopening as a key debate, but did not anticipate these quantified trade-flow and fleet-inefficiency effects; lower oil flows and tighter effective shipping supply point in different directions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Crude oil exports from inside the Strait of Hormuz fell 82% and China crude imports dropped 35% … while VLCC idling days rose 23% as inefficiencies and longer trade routes tightened effective fleet supply.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Hormuz commentary. The Strait of Hormuz has been closed since 28 Feb 2026, briefly reopened around 17 Jun, and was effectively re-closed in early July”; “CEO Lars Barstad's view on reopening timing is the main binary risk.”

surprises.description: Management described oil majors seeking two- to three-year VLCC charters and 2028 U.S. Gulf-to-Asia FFA rates near $100,000/day, indicating market pricing for sustained disruption well beyond the current quarter. The preview treated longer disruption as a possible bullish scenario, but did not cite this longer-dated charter demand or FFA level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Long-term charter demand has deepened with oil majors seeking 2-3 year VLCC deals, and 2028 FFA paper (TD22, U.S. Gulf to Asia) is trading near $100,000/day, signaling expectations that disruptions persist.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bull: … management signals longer disruption.”

in_line: The Q3 VLCC booking rate of $156,900/day was within the preview’s $150,000–$175,000 base-case range, even though the proportion of days booked was much higher than expected.

surprises.description: U.S. revenue accelerated to 13.1% growth from 1.5% in Q4, well above the preview’s 3–5% base-case expectation. New U.S. pump sales grew over 20%, new prescribers rose 24%, and competitive conversions doubled year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. growing 13.1% (up from 1.5% in Q4)”; “U.S. new pumps sold grew over 20%”; “new MiniMed prescribers up 24%”; “competitive conversions in the U.S. have doubled versus a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case called for “U.S. +3–5%,” while its bull case required “U.S. +8% or more.”

surprises.description: Organic growth excluding the extra week was in the low double digits, above the preview’s 8% bar and its estimate that consensus implied only about 3–5% underlying growth. The extra week accounted for roughly 4–6 points of the reported 15.8% organic growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 organic growth was 15.8%”; “An extra week … contributed roughly 4-6 points”; “excluding it, organic growth was low double digits versus 8.7% in Q4.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said an “explicit ex-week organic number of 8% or more” would support the bull case and estimated consensus embedded “about 3–5% underlying growth.”

surprises.description: Total new pump sales were 34,000, up only 7.7%, below the preview’s 45,000–50,000 level for a good quarter and also below the approximately 42,000 reported in Q4. This contrasts with the stronger U.S. pump growth and prescriber metrics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q1 new pumps sold of 34,000 (up 7.7%).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to check new pump sales “against the ≥45–50k NPS level” it treated as good; it also cited “~42k in Q4.”

surprises.description: Q1 adjusted EBITDA margin was 9.9%, well below the 16% full-year target and Q4’s 18.4% margin. Management attributed about 230 basis points of pressure to investment pulled forward and a nonoperational FX charge; even excluding those items, Q1 margin would have been 12.2%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 adjusted EBITDA was $83 million (9.9% margin), reduced ~230 bps by an $8 million pull-forward of investment and a $12 million nonoperational FX remeasurement charge; excluding these, margin would have been 12.2%.” Management reaffirmed approximately 16% for the year, with “most improvement weighted to the second half.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited Q4 adjusted EBITDA margin of “18.4%,” a FY27 margin guide of “~16%,” and flagged that “a Q1 margin below the ~16% guide would suggest the FY guide is front-loaded.”

surprises.description: The company raised its FY27 organic revenue growth outlook by 0.5 percentage point, to approximately 10.5%, rather than simply reaffirming the approximately 10% guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised its full-year fiscal 2027 organic revenue growth outlook to approximately 10.5% from prior guidance of approximately 10%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed FY27 organic revenue growth guidance as “~10%” and framed the possible action as a “Raise, reaffirm, or cut.”

surprises.description: Revenue of $843 million beat the $828.4 million consensus estimate, but fell short of the preview’s $850–860 million base-case scenario. The result therefore landed between the stated consensus and base-case expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue was $843 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed revenue consensus of “$828.4M” and a base-case scenario of “$850–860M.”

surprises.description: MiniMed Flex received its CE Mark ahead of target, a timing milestone the preview did not specifically anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “MiniMed Flex received CE Mark ahead of target.”

surprises.description: The MiniMed Fit patch pump’s FDA 510(k) filing came ahead of schedule, with the company targeting a full U.S. launch by summer 2026 and initial capacity for 20,000 patients; the preview did not flag this filing milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The MiniMed Fit patch pump 510(k) was filed with FDA ahead of schedule, targeting a full U.S. launch by summer 2026 with initial manufacturing capacity for 20,000 patients.”

surprises.description: Enrollment in the U.S. pivotal trial for the Vivera fully closed-loop algorithm was completed ahead of schedule, an unanticipated pipeline timing update in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Vivera fully closed-loop algorithm completed U.S. pivotal trial enrollment ahead of schedule.”

in_line: The extra week contributed roughly 4–6 percentage points of growth, broadly in line with the preview’s estimate of approximately 4.3–6.5 points.
Management reaffirmed the approximately 16% FY27 adjusted EBITDA margin outlook, matching the preview’s cited guidance.

surprises.description: Dell reported Q2 non-GAAP EPS of $7.04, far above the preview's $4.91 consensus estimate. The gap was much larger than the revenue beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS jumped 203% to a record $7.04.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS ... Consensus $4.91.”

surprises.description: Full-year guidance jumped to $192 billion of revenue and $25.50 of EPS, well above the preview's expectation of another, much smaller raise; Dell also lifted its AI server revenue outlook to $74 billion from about $60 billion. The scale of the revision exceeded even the preview's bull-case ranges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year revenue guidance was raised by $25 billion to $192 billion (up ~70%), with FY EPS of $25.50 (up ~150%) and AI server revenue expected to triple to $74 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus expects another raise, so the debate is the size”; the preview's bull case was “FY27 raised to about $175B and EPS $19+.”

surprises.description: AI server orders reached $60.9 billion, dramatically above the preview's concern that a quarter below $20 billion would signal digestion. This was also a record quarter for orders.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company booked a record $60.9 billion in AI server orders in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “A sub-$20B orders quarter would read as digestion”; the preview cited prior-quarter AI orders of “$24.4B.”

surprises.description: The AI backlog reached $95 billion, far above the prior $51.3 billion and well beyond the preview's expected range of roughly $50–53 billion. Instead of being flat or merely growing modestly, the backlog surged.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Exiting with a record $95 billion AI backlog.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AI backlog ... roughly flat at $50–53B” in the base case; the preview cited a prior-quarter backlog of “$51.3B.”

surprises.description: ISG operating margin recovered to 15%, substantially above the preview's base expectation of about 11% and even above its 12%+ bull-case threshold. The preview had highlighted margin recovery as the key test after Q1's 10.5% margin.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ISG ... operating margin expanding 620 basis points to 15%, driven by scale and favorable storage/product mix.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ISG operating margin vs. 10.5%”; the base case expected “about 11%” and the bull case “12%+.”

surprises.description: Dell raised its full-year revenue outlook to $192 billion, and Q2 revenue of $47 billion was also above the $45.1 billion consensus estimate. The quarterly revenue beat was meaningful but smaller than the EPS and guidance surprises.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 revenue rose 58% to a record $47 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue ... Consensus ~$45.1B”; company guidance was “$44.0–45.0B.”

surprises.description: ISG revenue reached $31.8 billion, above the preview's $29.8 billion estimate, with 89% growth versus the preview's roughly 75% growth expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ISG revenue grew 89% to a record $31.8 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ISG revenue ~+75% growth” and consensus “~$29.8B.”

surprises.description: Traditional server and networking revenue surged 122% to $10.5 billion, with demand exceeding supply and Dell gaining more than 10 points of share in two quarters. The preview did not anticipate this scale of traditional-server growth or share gain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Traditional server and networking revenue surged 122% to $10.5 billion, with demand outstripping supply and the company gaining over 10 points of traditional server share in two quarters.”

surprises.description: Dell returned a record $4.3 billion to shareholders in the quarter, including $2.2 billion more than in Q1. The preview noted Q1 returns but did not anticipate a new quarterly record or this sequential increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company returned an all-time record $4.3 billion to shareholders in Q2 ... up $2.2 billion sequentially.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited that Dell “Returned $2.1B to shareholders in Q1.”

surprises.description: Full-year operating expenses are expected to be only about 8% of revenue, a company-record low attributed to modernization-driven operating leverage. The preview did not flag this unusually low expense ratio.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Full-year operating expenses are guided to approximately 8% of revenue, the lowest level in the company's 42-year history, reflecting significant operating leverage from modernization.”

surprises.description: Dell reported 26% storage growth and a sixth consecutive quarter of Dell IP demand growth above the market, a positive segment trend not anticipated in the preview's estimates or key debates.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Storage revenue grew 26% to $4.9 billion, marking the sixth consecutive quarter of Dell IP demand growth above market.”

surprises.description: The AI factory customer count exceeded 6,500, with more than 3,300 customers added in the last three quarters. The preview had cited more than 5,000 customers in Q1 but did not anticipate this further expansion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “AI factory customer count surpassed 6,500 with over 3,300 added in just the last three quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview cited an AI customer count “above 5,000 (+50% in six months)” in Q1.

in_line: CSG revenue grew 20%, matching the preview's expectation of approximately 20% growth.

surprises.description: Q2 LINZESS U.S. net sales were reported at $582.3 million, far above the preview’s expected $288–292 million. The reported figure is also difficult to reconcile with the stated full-year guidance, but it is the figure in the call facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LINZESS delivered Q2 2026 U.S. net sales of $582.3 million, up 14% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “LINZESS U.S. net sales vs. ~$288–292M.”

surprises.description: Ironwood raised its full-year outlook: LINZESS sales guidance moved above the prior $1.125–1.175 billion range, revenue guidance rose to $460–485 million, and adjusted EBITDA guidance increased to greater than $310 million. The preview identified a guide raise as a bull trigger; the scale of the LINZESS guidance increase is modest, while the revenue and EBITDA updates also improve the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ironwood raised full-year 2026 guidance, now expecting LINZESS U.S. net sales of $1.15-1.2 billion”; “Full-year 2026 revenue guidance was raised to $460-485 million, and adjusted EBITDA guidance to greater than $310 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance: revenue $1.125–1.175B LINZESS U.S. net sales; FY adjusted EBITDA above $300M”; “FY26 guidance action. A raise is the cleanest bull trigger.”

surprises.description: Q2 LINZESS prescription demand grew 4%, a little below the preview’s +5% comparison point. However, year-to-date demand remained at 5%, and the company raised its full-year demand-growth expectation from low-single-digit to mid-single-digit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “LINZESS TRx volume grew 4% year-over-year in Q2 and 5% year-to-date, prompting a raise in full-year demand growth expectations from low-single-digit to mid-single-digit.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EUTRx demand vs. +5%”; “Q1 was +5% Y/Y.”

surprises.description: Q2 total revenue was $113 million, slightly below the preview’s primary consensus estimate of $114.8 million and below its $114–120 million base range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 delivered … $113 million in total revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $114.8M”; “Base | Revenue | $114–120M.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed that the original STARS trial was intended to use 5 mg but actually delivered 3.5 mg because of dosing errors. STARS II will use 3.5 mg to match the delivered dose, with an improved kit designed to prevent a recurrence—new information that adds a trial-execution concern as well as a mitigation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “STARS II uses a 3.5 mg dose to match the actual delivered dose in the original STARS trial (intended to be 5 mg), with an improved delivery kit developed after root cause analysis to prevent prior dosing errors.”

surprises.description: The company reported a favorable long-term-extension result for apraglutide: more than one in five patients had achieved enteral autonomy, with roughly 90% of STARS patients rolling into the extension. The preview flagged the trial program but did not anticipate this result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “In the STARS-EXTEND long-term extension study, more than 1 in 5 patients achieved enteral autonomy as of January, with roughly 90% of STARS patients rolling over into the extension.”

in_line: The company repaid the $200 million convertible notes at maturity using cash on hand, as the preview expected.
Year-to-date LINZESS demand growth of 5% matched the preview’s +5% comparison point.
No 2027 bridge was provided in the facts; the preview’s base case expected no 2027 numbers.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was far above the $86M–$88M company guide and the roughly $87M–$88M consensus, rather than landing near the preview’s expected range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue reached a record $99.3 million” and beat the quarter’s guidance.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | $87.33M (Zacks) / $87.67M | $86M – $88M”; the preview said consensus was inside the guide.

surprises.description: Amtagvi revenue substantially exceeded its $79M–$81M quarterly guide, rather than merely coming in within the range as the preview’s base case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Amtagvi revenue hit a record ~$91 million,” well above the $79M–$81M guidance range.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed Amtagvi at “~$79M – $81M (implied)” and said its base case had “Amtagvi in guide.”

surprises.description: Gross margin recovered much more sharply than the preview’s expected 45%–50% range: it reached 56%, setting a new high rather than just recovering to the prior 50% peak.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Gross margin reached an all-time high of 56%, up from 41% in Q1 and above the prior peak of 50%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case expected “gross margin 45% to 48%”; it described 50% as “achievable or exceedable” and framed 46%–50% as the key range to watch.

surprises.description: Instead of simply reaffirming the $350M–$370M full-year revenue range, management said it expects to raise the range in a separate Q3 announcement, citing strong Q3 performance to date. The formal range has not yet changed.
surprises.fact_evidence: Management is “reviewing and expects to raise full-year 2026 total revenue guidance” via a separate announcement during Q3, citing “very strong Q3 performance to date.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview called reaffirming the $350M–$370M range “the base case” and said the guidance “needs roughly $192M to $212M in 2H.”

surprises.description: Iovance reported new LUN-202 progress and a Q4 data update that the preview did not flag: enrollment is nearing completion, with the trial aimed at a lung-cancer opportunity management described as roughly seven times the size of advanced melanoma.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The LUN-202 non-squamous non-small cell lung cancer trial is nearing complete enrollment with a Q4 data update expected,” targeting an opportunity “roughly 7x the size of advanced melanoma” and an sBLA in 2027.

surprises.description: The call disclosed an unpreviewed FDA Fast Track designation for lifileucel in two soft tissue sarcomas, alongside an early pilot response result that could support this additional opportunity.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FDA granted Fast Track designation for lifileucel in two soft tissue sarcomas,” supported by a pilot study with a “50% objective response rate in the first 6 evaluable patients.”

in_line: The ATC network exceeded 95 centers and remained on track for at least 110 by year-end, consistent with the preview’s 95–100 near-term watch range and 110-plus year-end target.

surprises.description: The preview modeled Q2 AFFO at about $0.31 per share, with a reasonable range of $0.30–$0.33; COLD reported $0.35, above even the preview’s $0.34 bull-case threshold. This was a clear upside surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 AFFO came in at $0.35 per share,” the fourth consecutive quarter of meeting or exceeding analyst consensus.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “AFFO/share | ~$0.31 (modeled, not published)” and “A reasonable live band is $0.30–$0.33”; the bull case was “$0.34+.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case assumed occupancy was roughly flat, but physical occupancy rose by nearly 300 basis points year over year and more than 200 basis points sequentially, against the usual flat-to-down seasonal pattern. That was a stronger improvement than expected.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Physical occupancy rose over 200 basis points sequentially and nearly 300 basis points year-over-year, defying the typical flat-to-down Q1-to-Q2 seasonal pattern.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case assumed “Occupancy roughly flat.”

surprises.description: COLD raised its full-year AFFO guidance instead of maintaining the existing range, lifting the midpoint by $0.04 despite estimated dilution from the EQT joint venture. The preview treated reaffirmation as the base case.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company raised full-year AFFO guidance to $1.26-$1.32 per share, a $0.04 midpoint increase, after absorbing an estimated $0.05 of dilution from the EQT joint venture.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: FY2026 AFFO/share guidance was “$1.20–$1.30”; the preview said “Maintained is the base case” and its base scenario assumed “guide reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Same-store revenue guidance fell to $2.03–$2.09 billion, about $230 million below the prior range cited in the preview. The company attributed the reduction to the EQT JV, so the lower reported range is a surprise but is not necessarily a comparable deterioration in underlying operations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Reported same-store revenue guidance was lowered by ~$230 million to $2.03-$2.09 billion due to the JV.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Same-store revenue guidance was “$2.20–2.27B.”

surprises.description: Full-year same-store NOI guidance came in well below the preview’s cited range: $660–$695 million rather than $735–$785 million. The provided facts do not specify the reason for this reduction.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Same-store NOI is now guided to $660-$695 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Same-store NOI guidance was “$735–785M.”

surprises.description: Interest expense guidance is now $155–$160 million, below the preview’s expected $170–$180 million range. This is a favorable reduction relative to the stated expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: The updated guidance includes “interest expense of $155-$160 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Interest expense guidance was “$170–180M.”

surprises.description: The preview expected a $305–$320 million impairment tied to Ahold Delhaize facilities; the reported charge was slightly smaller and was tied instead to winding down Lancaster and Plainville, which are now listed for sale. The lower charge is modestly favorable, while the facility and sale details differ from the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A noncash impairment charge of $298.8 million was recorded in Q2 tied to winding down the Lancaster and Plainville automated facilities, which are now listed for sale.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: A “pre-announced $305–320M non-cash impairment on the Ahold Delhaize automated facilities lands in Q2.”

surprises.description: The physical-to-economic occupancy gap narrowed by 240 basis points to 860 basis points. The preview focused on economic occupancy but did not set an expectation for this gap, making the reported narrowing an additional favorable operating detail.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The gap between physical and economic occupancy narrowed 240 basis points to 860 basis points,” which management views as a healthier, more sustainable long-term level.

in_line: The EQT JV received regulatory approval and is expected to close in Q3, consistent with the preview’s expectation of a Q3 close; the planned debt repayment and roughly three-quarters-of-a-turn leverage reduction are also broadly consistent with the preview’s expected move toward approximately 6.2–6.3x leverage.

The cost-savings plans were broadly in line with the preview: it anticipated a roughly $30 million SG&A cut and a further program exceeding $25 million; the call cited about $30 million in annual savings plus an additional $25 million in SG&A savings by Q1 2027.

surprises.description: Investors had positive Q2 diluted-EPS estimates and the preview warned that the Finance of America sale might produce a book gain. Instead, Onity reported a net loss, with about $33 million of pretax costs from the reverse asset sale, the Rithm subservicing transfer, and unfavorable asset fair-value adjustments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Onity reported a Q2 2026 net loss that included approximately $33 million of pretax costs” from the sale, transfer, and “unfavorable market-driven asset fair value adjustments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) | MarketBeat $0.95 | Investing.com $2.23” and “Any book gain will appear in GAAP results.”

surprises.description: The preview’s base case anticipated servicing returning to profit, albeit subdued. Instead, servicing adjusted pretax income fell more than 60% year over year as lower rates drove MSR runoff nearly 80% higher, indicating substantially greater pressure than that base case implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Servicing adjusted pretax income declined over 60% year-over-year as lower interest rates drove MSR runoff up nearly 80% versus the prior year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The base case assumed “Servicing profitable but subdued”; the preview also flagged runoff above Q1’s “$99M” as a key risk.

surprises.description: Although Onity guided to the low end of its 10%–15% full-year adjusted pretax ROE range, it said it was currently operating around 9%—below even the range’s floor. The preview discussed whether the low end could be achieved, but did not anticipate a current operating rate below the stated range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Guiding to the low end of its full-year 2026 adjusted pretax ROE range of 10% to 15%, currently operating around the 9% range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q2 needed “roughly $20M of adjusted pretax income for the low end of guidance to look credible.”

surprises.description: Onity reported $35 billion of first-half subservicing additions, exceeding guidance. The preview did not identify this as an expected outcome, making the reported overdelivery a positive surprise.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half subservicing additions of $35 billion exceeded guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “First-half subservicing additions of $35 billion exceeded guidance.”

surprises.description: Servicing growth was stronger than the preview had highlighted: total servicing UPB rose 10% year over year against industry growth of 3%, with $76 billion of additions net of runoff despite planned transfers and client MSR sales.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total servicing UPB grew 10% year-over-year versus industry growth of 3%, with servicing additions net of runoff of $76 billion despite planned Rithm transfers and client MSR sales.”

surprises.description: Onity reported a 51% refinance recapture rate, up 3 percentage points and above the ICE industry average, alongside doubled home-equity volume and more than doubled second-lien volume. These origination and retention metrics were not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Refinance recapture rate improved to 51%, up 3 percentage points year-over-year, exceeding the ICE industry average, with home equity product volume doubling and second lien volume more than doubling.”

surprises.description: Onity completed a $10 million buyback and authorized another $20 million, signaling active repurchases even though the preview identified deleveraging MSR debt as management’s stated first priority for the Finance of America proceeds.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company completed a $10 million share buyback and reauthorized an additional $20 million buyback,” citing shares priced below book value.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management's stated priority is deleveraging MSR debt first.”

in_line: The FY2026 adjusted pretax ROE guidance was steered to the low end of the 10%–15% range, matching the preview’s base-case expectation of guidance reaffirmed at the low end.
The Finance of America reverse-mortgage sale had closed in Q2, as the preview expected.

surprises.description: The preview said Americas SOI needed to be around $100 million to show the quarter was recovering; instead, the Americas reported a $10 million operating loss. That is a substantial shortfall against the level investors were watching.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Americas posting a $10 million loss.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “It needs to be above about $100M”; the base scenario expected “Americas about $90M.”

surprises.description: The preview looked for a free-cash-flow inflection and visible progress toward a year-end working-capital inflow, but management expects a $200–300 million cash burn for 2026 and says the burn will continue into 2027. The Q2 cash use improved materially, but the outlook indicates the cash-flow recovery will take longer.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Free cash flow to be a burn of $200 million to $300 million in fiscal 2026 with continued but moderating burn into 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The year-end working-capital inflow needs visible progress in Q2”; the base scenario anticipated “FCF inflection reaffirmed.”

surprises.description: Unit volume declined 4%, better than the roughly 10% decline cited in the preview’s Q2 guidance discussion. The preview’s downside case was triggered by volume worse than 10% down, so the reported decline was materially less severe than that concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Unit volume declining 4%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview described Q2 guidance as “units down about 10%” and its bear case as “Volume worse than -10%.”

surprises.description: Sales of $4.3 billion were above the preview’s working consensus of about $4.15–4.20 billion, though the preview also listed a higher $4.33 billion estimate. The result was therefore a modest beat against the working range, not a clear beat against every cited estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales were $4.3 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working consensus: revenue about $4.15–4.20B”; the preview also listed estimates of $4.12B and $4.33B.

surprises.description: Despite the weak volume and operating backdrop, Consumer OE grew and market share increased in every region; larger rim sizes also gained 4 percentage points. This runs counter to the preview’s concern about structural share loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Consumer OE grew and market share increased in all regions despite weak OE production backdrops,” and “18-inch-and-above rim sizes rose 4 percentage points year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Americas SOI needed to show the quarter was not “structural share or price loss.”

surprises.description: The preview focused on Americas weakness but gave no Asia Pacific outlook; the call reported that Asia Pacific expanded SOI to $63 million and raised its margin by 330 basis points. That was a notably strong regional result alongside losses in the Americas and EMEA.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Asia Pacific expanded SOI to $63 million (12.7% margin, up 330 bps).”

in_line: Total segment operating income was $36 million, within the preview’s estimated Q2 SOI range of roughly $30–70 million.
Adjusted EPS was a loss of $0.61, essentially matching the preview’s working consensus of a loss of about $0.60.
The expected H2 raw-material headwind was about $200 million; management maintained that outlook, while noting a roughly $20 million Q3 increase.
The expected Fayetteville SOI benefits were reaffirmed: roughly $90 million in 2027 and $270 million annually from 2028 onward.
Management reaffirmed its full-year SOI outlook of roughly $600 million or slightly higher.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $731.1 million, above the preview’s $713.1 million consensus estimate and even above the top of its cited $706–$713 million range. That is a roughly 2.5% beat versus the consensus figure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue was $731.1 million”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 revenue … $713.1M (range $706M to $713M)”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA came in at $206.1 million, substantially above the preview’s own ~$180 million Q2 model, though close to the ~$208 million quarterly run-rate the preview said was needed for the full-year guide.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $206.1 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Preview models ~$180M (own estimate, not consensus)” and “The FY guide needs about $208M per quarter for Q2 through Q4.”

surprises.description: The company kept its full-year guidance ranges, as the preview’s base case expected, but management now expects results toward the lower end of both ranges rather than simply reaffirming them without qualification.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is maintaining its full-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance ranges but now expects to finish toward the lower end of both.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base … FY guide reaffirmed unchanged” and “FY26 guidance action. A silent reaffirm should be treated skeptically given the H2 math.”

surprises.description: Disney Solitaire rose to $142.4 million, up 15.5% sequentially, despite a meaningful reduction in marketing. The preview identified Q2 as the first read after user-acquisition spending was cut, with its base case expecting the title to hold rather than clearly grow.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Disney Solitaire generated $142.4 million, up 15.5% sequentially … growing even as marketing spend was reduced meaningfully.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Disney Solitaire revenue. $123.3M in Q1 … Management cut user acquisition spend after a ‘front-loaded’ Q1, so Q2 is the first read without that support”; base scenario: “Disney Solitaire holds.”

surprises.description: Management gave a more pronounced second-half warning for Super Play: it expects titles including Disney Solitaire to decline sequentially, alongside a roughly 70% reduction in Super Play marketing versus the first half, with the biggest cut in Q3. The preview discussed prior acquisition cuts but did not anticipate this scale of spending reduction or an explicit sequential-revenue decline outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Super Play titles, including Disney Solitaire, will see revenue decline sequentially in the second half”; “Overall Super Play marketing investment is being cut by roughly 70% in the second half versus the first half, with the largest step-down concentrated in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management cut user acquisition spend after a ‘front-loaded’ Q1, so Q2 is the first read without that support.”

surprises.description: Management reported softening consumer sentiment and inflation pressure on discretionary spending, including a steeper-than-typical demand step-down from May to June. The preview did not flag this demand deterioration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management flagged softening consumer sentiment and inflation pressure on discretionary spending, observing a steeper-than-typical demand step-down from May to June.”

surprises.description: User activity weakened: DAU fell to 8 million, down 9.1% year over year, while daily paying users fell 2.9% to 367,000. The preview cited Q1 DAU of 8.6 million, down 4.4% year over year, but gave no Q2 forecast for these metrics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Average daily active users down 9.1% year-over-year to 8 million and daily paying users down 2.9% to 367,000.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “DAU 8.6M (down 4.4% YoY).”

surprises.description: Bingo Blitz declined 5.6% sequentially and 9.5% year over year, with weakness concentrated among players acquired in the last 12 months after a shift away from incentive-driven channels. The preview did not discuss this title or forecast a decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bingo Blitz revenue fell to $145.1 million, down 5.6% sequentially and 9.5% year-over-year, with declines concentrated in players acquired in the last 12 months after a shift away from incentive-driven acquisition channels.”

surprises.description: ARPDAU rose 16.1% year over year, accelerating from the 8.0% growth cited for Q1 in the preview, even as DAU and paying users weakened.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ARPDAU rose 16.1% year-over-year.”

in_line: D2C revenue was $286.9 million versus $291.8 million in Q1, a modest 1.7% sequential decline, broadly consistent with the preview’s warning that softer DTC traffic was a concern.

surprises.description: Commerce.com cut FY26 revenue guidance by $18 million at the midpoint and non-GAAP operating income guidance by $12.5 million at the midpoint, rather than reaffirming the ranges. Management attributed the reduction roughly equally to a deliberate partner-ecosystem decision and more cautious new-account booking assumptions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company cut full-year 2026 revenue guidance by $18 million at the midpoint (to $336.5-344.5 million) and non-GAAP operating income by $12.5 million (to $28-34 million), driven roughly evenly by a deliberate partner ecosystem decision and more cautious new account booking assumptions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Reaffirming the full range again reads as low conviction”; the preview also said narrowing toward the lower half “would point to a weaker outlook.”

surprises.description: The Q2 non-GAAP operating income result was well above the preview’s base case and the top of company guidance: $8.1 million versus guidance of $4–5 million. Non-GAAP operating margin also expanded nearly 400 basis points year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP operating income of $8.1 million beating the high end of the $4-5 million guidance range,” with “non-GAAP operating margin expanding nearly 400 basis points year-over-year to 9.6%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s base case was “$5M – $6M” of non-GAAP operating income; its bull case was “$7M+.”

surprises.description: Weakness was specifically concentrated in B2C replatforming, where merchants took longer to decide how to approach AI and agentic discovery. That demand hesitation was not described in the preview, while B2B, Feedonomics, and product intelligence were said to show no material weakening.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Softness is concentrated specifically in B2C replatforming, where longer sales cycles reflect merchants deliberating over AI/agentic discovery strategies, while B2B, Feedonomics, and product intelligence showed no material weakening.”

surprises.description: BigCommerce Payments GMV was running more than 30% ahead of internal plans, with adoption extending to select performance-plan merchants and larger accounts. The preview had no disclosed attach rate and treated a quantified Payments update as useful, so the reported pace and expanded adoption were positive new information.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BigCommerce Payments GMV is running more than 30% ahead of internal plans since its U.S. launch,” with “adoption expanding to select performance plan merchants and larger accounts, plus a UK launch planned later this year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “No attach rate has been disclosed. Whether management gives a number is itself a signal”; “A quantified number helps the story.”

surprises.description: GMV grew 14%, including 17% growth in B2B, but platform activity was growing faster than revenue because B2B carries less card-based payment volume and partner revenue share. This points to weaker revenue conversion of activity than the GMV growth alone might suggest.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GMV grew 14% year-over-year to nearly $8.8 billion, with B2B GMV growing a stronger 17%, but platform activity is growing faster than revenue because B2B carries lower card-based payment volume and less partner revenue share.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP gross margin fell 170 basis points sequentially, less than the preview’s 200-basis-point-or-more compression concern, but management identified higher hosting expense from AI crawler and agent traffic as the main cause and said it deliberately kept that traffic open.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP gross margin declined sequentially from 77.4% in Q1 to 75.7% in Q2, driven primarily by higher hosting costs from increased AI crawler and agent traffic that management deliberately chose to keep open.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If gross margin falls another 200bps or more, the margin story weakens.”

surprises.description: NRR improved to 95.8%, slightly above the preview’s 95.5% estimate, but remained below the 96% level the preview identified as the first clear sign of cross-sell improvement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenue retention improved sequentially for the third consecutive quarter to 95.8%, up from 95.4% in Q1 2026.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview estimated NRR at “~95.5%” and said “A print above 96% would be the first real sign that cross-sell is working.”

in_line: Q2 revenue was $84.5 million, within company guidance and broadly in line with the preview’s approximately $85 million consensus estimate.
Ending ARR of $360.5 million was close to the preview’s approximately $361 million estimate.

surprises.description: Peloton’s FY27 revenue guidance implies a 3.9% decline at the midpoint, versus the preview’s expectation of roughly flat revenue around $2.43 billion. Management also framed FY27 as a transition year, with revenue acceleration tied to new-category launches starting in fall 2027.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 revenue guidance of $2.3-2.4 billion implies a 3.9% year-over-year decline at the midpoint,” and management framed FY27 as “a transition year” before revenue acceleration starting fall of calendar 2027.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street expects roughly flat revenue (~$2.43B).”

surprises.description: FY27 adjusted EBITDA guidance has a $480 million midpoint, below the preview’s roughly $504 million Street expectation and below its stated $490 million negative-surprise threshold. The $435–525 million range leaves meaningful downside to that midpoint.
surprises.fact_evidence: “FY27 adjusted EBITDA guidance of $435-525 million reflects a 7% increase at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Street expects … adj. EBITDA ~$504M”; the preview also says “A guide below ~$490M EBITDA would be a negative surprise.”

surprises.description: Q4 revenue came in above both consensus and the high end of the implied company range, rather than merely landing within the expected range. It also delivered a second consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 revenue of $608 million beat the high end of implied guidance by $6 million and marked the second consecutive quarter of year-over-year revenue growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | Q4 FY26 Consensus | $597.0M (range $587.5–612.0M)”; the implied guide was “$581.6–601.6M.”

surprises.description: Net churn rose to 2.2%, above the preview’s 1.4% level that would reopen the bear case and above Q3’s 1.2%. Management attributed about half the increase to a one-time payment-reactivation algorithm change and half to lingering price-increase effects, with the algorithm change reverted and FY27 churn expected roughly flat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q4 net churn rose 37 basis points year-over-year to 2.2%,” with “roughly half attributed to a one-time payment reactivation algorithm change (since reverted and normalizing) and half to lingering price-increase effects”; “full-year FY27 churn is expected roughly flat.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Churn above 1.4% would reopen the bear case”; the preview also listed “Q4 churn against 1.2% in Q3.”

surprises.description: FY26 adjusted EBITDA was slightly below the company’s own guidance range, despite growing year over year. This is a small shortfall relative to the preview’s expected $470–480 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Peloton delivered … $468 million adjusted EBITDA (up 16% YoY).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gives FY26 guidance of “adj. EBITDA $470–480M.”

surprises.description: Peloton accrued a $23.8 million legal contingency for a jury verdict concerning third-party media-player patent infringement, an unexpected Q4 charge. Management said it does not expect a material ongoing royalty impact.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company booked a $23.8 million legal contingency accrual in Q4 tied to a jury verdict over third-party media player patent infringement, though it does not expect material go-forward royalty impact.”

surprises.description: Peloton reported its first full fiscal year of positive net income and operating income, a profitability milestone the preview did not specifically forecast. This contrasts with the small FY26 adjusted EBITDA shortfall to guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Its first full fiscal year of positive net income ($63 million) and positive operating income ($161 million).”

surprises.description: The call reported strong FY26 free cash flow, which the preview did not give an expectation for: $378 million, up 17% year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$378 million free cash flow (up 17% YoY).”

surprises.description: Peloton said more than half of monthly active users engaged with Peloton IQ in Q4, and that it had become the most-interesting feature for prospective customers. The preview did not flag these adoption metrics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Peloton IQ engaged more than 50% of monthly active users in Q4 and is now the #1 feature of interest among prospective customers.”

surprises.description: The company disclosed that 316,000 members own multiple connected-fitness products, up 20,000 year over year, and that these members churn at lower rates. The preview did not identify this as an operating metric to watch.
surprises.fact_evidence: “316,000 members now own multiple connected fitness products (up 20,000 YoY) and churn at lower rates.”

in_line: The preview expected refinancing and buyback consideration; management has begun a refinancing process and said excess cash could go toward buybacks once it is completed. No buyback authorization was reported.
The preview flagged the Commercial Series launch timing; management said the new bike and treadmill series will launch in the coming months.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $1.92, above the preview’s consensus range of $1.68–$1.72 and above its base-case range of $1.72–$1.80. It did fall within the preview’s bull scenario of $1.85–$1.95.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP adjusted EPS was $1.92, up from $1.68 in the prior-year quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adjusted EPS” Q2’26 consensus: “$1.68 – $1.72”; base scenario: “$1.72 – $1.80.”

surprises.description: The company cut full-year revenue guidance to $825–$855 million, from the preview’s expected guidance of $865–$895 million. The new range is also below the preview’s $869.9 million consensus, with lower Nuscenta pricing cited as a driver.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nuscenta franchise revenue fell 24% year-over-year to $35.2 million due to lower net pricing on authorized generics, prompting a downward revision to full-year total revenue guidance of $825-855 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue” company guidance: “$865M – $895M”; Q2 preview also gives “FY26 revenue” consensus of “$869.9M.”

surprises.description: Full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance fell to $445–$470 million, below the preview’s $475–$500 million company guidance. The reported outlook implies essentially flat EBITDA despite projected revenue growth, a weaker earnings trajectory than the prior guide implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $445-470 million implies essentially flat performance versus 2025, despite 8% projected revenue growth at the midpoint.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. EBITDA” company guidance: “$475M – $500M.”

surprises.description: Nuscenta fell 24% to $35.2 million, with lower net pricing on authorized generics cited as the cause. The preview flagged post-exclusivity erosion and channel destocking as key risks, but did not anticipate or quantify this reported decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Nuscenta franchise revenue fell 24% year-over-year to $35.2 million due to lower net pricing on authorized generics.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said to watch for “Nucynta loss of exclusivity” and “Q2 channel destocking ahead of generics,” and described a need for management’s “first quantified H2 and 2027 erosion curve.”

surprises.description: Astaris full-year revenue guidance was raised to $65–$75 million, above the preview’s expected $60–$70 million for the rest of 2026. The call also reported $12.9 million of initial revenue from about a month and a half of sales, for which the preview gave no estimate.
