surprises.fact_evidence: “Alta narrowed its full-year adjusted EBITDA guidance to $167.5–$177.5 million, cutting the upper end by $5 million due to delivery timing uncertainty rather than weaker demand.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Whether FY26 guidance holds. Management already cut once in May. A second cut on a levered balance sheet is the main downside catalyst. A narrowing toward the upper half would be a strong positive signal.”

surprises.description: Material handling showed more operating resilience than the preview’s caution about converting bookings into revenue might suggest: backlog reached about $143 million, its highest since 2023, and adjusted EBITDA rose about 13% year over year despite lower revenue. Revenue conversion was not yet evident, but bookings and profitability remained strong.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Material handling backlog rose to approximately $143 million, its highest level since 2023”; “Material handling delivered $19 million of adjusted EBITDA, up about 13% year-over-year despite lower revenue.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Material Handling bookings converting to revenue. Q1 MH revenue fell 4.7%, but bookings rose about 20%”; “a weak HY quarter is not automatically weak for ALTG, but it limits enthusiasm.”

surprises.description: Ecoverse had one of its strongest quarters since acquisition, with adjusted EBITDA rising to $2.8 million from $1.1 million as tariff-related margin pressure eased. The preview did not identify this business or recovery as a likely development.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ecoverse posted one of its strongest quarters since acquisition, with revenue rising to $22.8 million and adjusted EBITDA growing from $1.1 million to $2.8 million as tariff-related margin pressure subsided.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA of $48.6 million was within the preview’s modeled range of approximately $48–$52 million.
Free cash flow guidance of $100–$110 million was reaffirmed, in line with the preview’s stated guidance.

surprises.description: Arrow reported Q2 revenue of $10 billion, above the preview’s $9.45 billion consensus and the company’s $9.75 billion guidance high end. That is a clear upside revenue beat, though below the preview’s bull scenario.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue reached $10 billion” and was “exceeding guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists consolidated sales consensus of “$9.45B” and company guidance of “$9.15B – $9.75B.”

surprises.description: Non-GAAP EPS of $5.45 substantially exceeded the preview’s $4.45 consensus and the guidance high end of $4.52. The gap was much larger than the preview’s base case of about $5.00.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS surged 124% year-over-year to $5.45, above the guidance range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview lists non-GAAP diluted EPS consensus of “$4.45” and guidance of “$4.32 – $4.52”; its base scenario is “~$5.00.”

surprises.description: Global Components sales reached $7.4 billion, above the preview’s roughly $7.0 billion midpoint and $7.2 billion guidance high end. Its 11% sequential growth also far exceeded the preview’s implied expectation of about 5% sequential growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Global Components sales grew 11% sequentially to $7.4 billion.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gives Global Components guidance of “$6.80B – $7.20B (mid $7.00B)” and says it implies “about +5% sequential growth off Q1's $6.64B.”

surprises.description: Although growth was still primarily volume-driven, price inflation contributed roughly one-third of sequential Global Components growth. That is more price contribution than the preview’s volume-not-price framing led investors to watch for, and memory had risen to a low-double-digit share of segment revenue from the previously cited mid-single-digit share.
surprises.fact_evidence: Revenue growth was “driven primarily by unit volume growth,” with “price inflation contributing roughly one-third of sequential Global Components growth”; memory was “a low double-digit percentage” of Global Components revenue.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says Q1 growth “was driven by unit volume growth, and it was not driven by pricing,” notes memory was “only a mid-single-digit percentage of revenue,” and says to listen for whether that “volume-not-price language holds.”

surprises.description: ECS took a $27 million charge on underperforming multiyear contracts with a strategic partner, reducing ECS operating margin by 100 basis points year over year; management expects smaller additional charges in the second half. The preview did not flag this contract issue or the prospective charges.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ECS took a $27 million charge on underperforming multiyear contracts with a strategic partner,” cutting ECS operating margins “by 100 basis points year-over-year,” with “additional but smaller charges expected in the second half.”

surprises.description: ECS backlog grew more than 75% to an all-time high, alongside strong compute, business applications, and security product growth. The preview noted positive book-to-bill trends but did not anticipate this scale of ECS backlog growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ECS backlog grew over 75% year-over-year to an all-time high,” with compute “+51%,” business applications “+26%,” and security “+21%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says book-to-bill was “well above parity in all three operating regions” and flags possible softening as a bearish tell.

surprises.description: Q3 non-GAAP EPS guidance has a $4.93 midpoint, slightly below the preview’s roughly $5.00-plus bar, and implies a sequential decline from Q2’s $5.45. The shortfall versus the preview’s threshold is small, but the sequential drop is explicit.
surprises.fact_evidence: Q3 non-GAAP EPS guidance is “$4.83-$5.03,” “implying a sequential earnings decline from Q2's $5.45.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says Arrow would need to guide Q3 to “$5.00+ in non-GAAP EPS” to keep pace with Avnet’s trajectory.

surprises.description: Q3 ECS revenue guidance is only 2% higher year over year, a much slower growth rate than the company’s overall Q3 revenue outlook. Management attributed the comparison to lapping a large partner addition from last year rather than a change in business trajectory; the preview did not provide an ECS Q3 expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “ECS Q3 revenue guidance of $2.1-$2.3 billion (up only 2% YoY) reflects lapping a large partner addition from last year rather than a change in business trajectory.”

surprises.description: Management said the supplier relationship departure affected roughly $700 million in revenue, rather than the reported $1.4 billion, and should have no impact on ECS revenue, margin, or profit because alternatives are available. This reassurance was not covered in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: The departure “impacted roughly $700 million in revenue (not $1.4 billion as reported)” and is “expected to have no impact on ECS revenue, margin, or profit due to alternative solutions.”

surprises.description: Share repurchases increased to $43 million from the prior quarter’s $25 million pace, as the preview specifically asked whether buybacks would step up. The company also reported more than $1 billion of year-to-date operating cash flow and lower debt and leverage.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company generated “over $1 billion in year-to-date operating cash flow,” reduced gross debt by “~$650 million YoY to $2.2 billion,” improved adjusted leverage “by over a full turn to 1.75x,” and repurchased “$43 million in shares.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says to watch “whether buybacks step up from the Q1 pace of $25M.”

in_line: Q3 consolidated revenue guidance has a $9.9 billion midpoint, essentially matching the preview’s roughly $10 billion expectation.
Global Components operating margin of 5.4% was close to the preview’s expectation that it would be down from Q1’s 5.5% on seasonal mix.
Book-to-bill ratios remained above parity in all three regions, consistent with the positive levels cited in the preview.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $70.9 million, about 13% below the roughly $81.2 million consensus preview. No flight equipment sales occurred, despite the preview saying consensus assumed 2–4 units; the result was within the preview’s bear-case revenue range, but below the central expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue fell to $70.9 million” and this was driven primarily by “the absence of flight equipment sales”; the prior-year quarter included $33.4 million of sales across eight engines.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q2 revenue” consensus “~$81.2M”; the preview also said “Consensus assumes 2–4 units” and gave a bear-case range of “$63–75M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was a loss of $0.09 rather than the preview’s $0.11 consensus estimate, a $0.20-per-share shortfall and a swing from expected profit to a loss. The company also reported a $5.6 million net loss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted loss per share of $0.09”; the company posted “a net loss of $5.6 million” versus net income of $8.6 million a year earlier.
surprises.expectation_evidence: Q2 “adj. diluted EPS” consensus was “~$0.11”; the preview’s base case was “$0.04–0.12” and bear case was “−$0.05 to $0.02.”

surprises.description: Gross margin fell to 22.9%, below even the preview’s bear-case expectation of 26–27%, rather than showing the anticipated improvement from startup costs rolling off. Lost high-margin equipment sales and startup costs at Goodyear and Millington weighed on the result.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Overall gross margin fell to 22.9% from 32.9% due to lost high-margin equipment sales and startup costs at Goodyear and Millington.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Below 27% would push the expansion narrative out” and set the bear case at “gross margin 26–27%.”

surprises.description: The preview warned that liquidity below about $35 million would make the balance sheet central; available liquidity ended at $34 million, crossing that threshold. Year-to-date operating cash use was $33.5 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date cash used in operating activities was $33.5 million,” leaving “available liquidity of just $34 million” ($2.2 million cash and $31.8 million revolver availability).
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said “Availability below about $35M would shift the discussion from growth to the balance sheet,” compared with Q1 availability of $41.8 million.

surprises.description: The preview’s liquidity concern contemplated feedstock purchases continuing if asset sales did not occur, but Q2 acquisitions instead fell sharply to $5.6 million from $27.1 million. Management attributed the cut to pricing discipline in a highly competitive market, which limits near-term cash deployment but also means less feedstock was acquired.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Feedstock acquisitions dropped sharply to $5.6 million in Q2 from $27.1 million a year ago due to pricing discipline in a hyper-competitive acquisition market.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview warned: “If Q2 has no asset sales while feedstock purchases continue, availability becomes the central topic on the call.”

surprises.description: Core revenue excluding flight equipment sales declined 4.2%, as lower USM sales more than offset growth in leasing and MRO. That is weaker than the preview’s expansion framing and expectation for modestly higher TechOps, even though the reported TechOps revenue itself grew.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding flight equipment sales, overall revenue declined 4.2% year-over-year as lower USM sales offset growth in leasing and MRO.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said expansion initiatives were expected to “exceed the incremental $50 million revenue expectation” and described the base case as “TechOps modestly higher.”

surprises.description: Goodyear was operating at under 20% of available capacity, with 84 stored ex-Spirit aircraft still awaiting maintenance work. This points to a much slower current utilization of that operation than the preview’s broader expansion narrative suggested, although the aircraft could provide future work.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Goodyear is operating at under 20% of available capacity with 84 stored ex-Spirit Airlines aircraft awaiting maintenance work.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said expansion initiatives were expected to “exceed the incremental $50 million revenue expectation” and identified the MRO ramp as a key issue.

surprises.description: Management reported a secured $35 million 737 sale and several expected engine sales, plus 17 engines in work that are expected to exit repair in coming months. The concrete pipeline is a positive development versus the preview’s statement that management had not committed to asset sales, though the expected closing window of late Q3 or early Q4 is consistent with its warning about later-quarter timing.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management secured a $35 million 737 aircraft sale to the U.S. Marshal Service plus several engine sales expected to close in late Q3 or early Q4,” and “has 17 engines in work expected to exit repair over the coming months.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said consensus required whole-asset sales “that management has not committed to by quarter” and warned that “Language pointing to Q4-weighted asset sales is a warning sign.”

in_line: TechOps revenue rose 8.7% to $33.8 million on the Millington CRJ program ramp, broadly matching the preview’s base-case expectation for TechOps to be modestly higher.

Leasing revenue grew about 50% year over year to $12.4 million, with 18 engines and three 757 freighters on lease; the preview had flagged leasing and the existing 18-engine/three-freighter fleet as important, and did not set a higher quarterly fleet target.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $73.2 million, below the preview’s $78.13 million consensus, and fell 25% year over year versus the expected 20% decline. The reported shortfall was attributed to both weak demand and a customer tariff-refund accrual.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue fell 25% year-over-year to $73.2 million, hurt by a customer tariff refund accrual and continued demand weakness in both end markets.”

surprises.description: A non-recurring $5.1 million tariff recovery lifted adjusted EPS to $0.34 per share, far above the preview’s $0.03 consensus. Without that recovery, adjusted EPS was about $0.04, close to consensus, and the recovery is excluded from full-year guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A non-recurring $5.1 million tariff recovery boosted adjusted EPS to $0.34 per diluted share and is excluded from full-year guidance”; excluding it, the company reported adjusted EPS of “~$0.04 per share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. non-GAAP diluted EPS | $0.03”

surprises.description: A new smart-thermostat platform for a major HVAC OEM had already begun mass production, with additional Q4 volume requested. That provides concrete evidence of a program ramp beyond the preview’s open question about whether thermostat and HVAC OEM programs would convert to shipments.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A new smart thermostat platform for a major HVAC OEM began mass production with additional Q4 volume requested.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Watch whether thermostat and HVAC OEM programs convert to shipments”; the bull case “needs a named HVAC OEM ramp with a shipping date.”

surprises.description: Liquidity was stronger than the preview’s Q1 snapshot suggested: UEI ended Q2 with $32.4 million in cash and $11.6 million in net cash, with no borrowings on its U.S. credit line. The preview had cited $29.8 million in Q1 cash and $23.2 million drawn on lines of credit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $32.4 million in cash, $11.6 million in net cash, no borrowings on its U.S. credit line, and available borrowing capacity of $48.7 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Cash $29.8M; lines of credit $23.2M drawn”; the preview flagged that “a flat or lower revolver would reduce risk.”

surprises.description: The CEO uncertainty resolved with an unexpected leadership change: interim CEO Rick Carnifax stepped down on the call date and CFO Wade Jenke became CEO. The preview identified a permanent CEO appointment as a high-variance possibility, not a consensus expectation.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Interim CEO Rick Carnifax stepped down effective August 6th, with CFO Wade Jenke appointed as the new CEO.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Permanent CEO or strategic alternatives: Richard Carnifax has been Interim CEO since July 2025. A permanent appointment or strategic review is the highest-variance item and is not in consensus.”

surprises.description: UEI disclosed a new IP lawsuit against Amazon, a legal development the preview did not discuss. The shareholder impact is unclear from the provided facts.
surprises.fact_evidence: “UEI filed a new IP lawsuit against Amazon the day of the call.”

surprises.description: The Roku litigation has a court date scheduled for 2027, putting a specific timeline on a legal matter the preview did not mention. The eventual outcome and shareholder impact are not given.
surprises.fact_evidence: UEI “continues litigation against Roku, which has a court date scheduled for 2027.”

in_line: Full-year 2026 adjusted non-GAAP EPS guidance was reaffirmed at $0.45–$0.65, as the preview expected; the tariff recovery is excluded from that guidance.
Adjusted EPS excluding the one-time tariff recovery was about $0.04 per share, close to the preview’s $0.03 consensus.
Adjusted gross margin excluding the tariff recovery was about 27%, at the low end of the preview’s 27–28% base-case range.
Further opex cuts were a key part of the preview’s expected earnings bridge; adjusted non-GAAP operating expenses fell $6.2 million year over year.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $156 million, above the preview’s $147.4–$149 million consensus range and just above the company’s $155 million guidance ceiling. The result was stronger than the preview’s base-case range of $152–$156 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue reached a record $156 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Consensus (varies by source): ~$147.4M – $149.0M”; company Q2 guidance was “$145M – $155M.”

surprises.description: Arlo raised FY26 revenue guidance to $580–$600 million from $550–$580 million. That was a larger lift than the preview’s central question of whether management would raise guidance or only nudge it.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to total revenue of $580-$600 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 revenue: $550M – $580M”; the preview asked “Whether management raises the revenue guide or only the EPS guide.”

surprises.description: FY26 non-GAAP EPS guidance rose to $0.90–$1.00 from $0.75–$0.85, above the preview’s roughly $0.81 consensus and prior guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to… non-GAAP EPS of $0.90-$1.00.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 non-GAAP EPS: $0.75 – $0.85”; consensus was “~$0.81.”

surprises.description: Q2 non-GAAP EPS of $0.28 topped the preview’s $0.20 consensus and $0.23 guidance ceiling, but a $0.07 tariff-refund benefit accounted for much of the beat. Excluding it, EPS was $0.21—still ahead, but only slightly above consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS was $0.28… but included a $0.07 benefit from an $8 million tariff refund; pro forma EPS excluding the refund was $0.21, still ahead of guidance and consensus.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Non-GAAP EPS… Consensus… $0.20”; company Q2 guidance was “$0.17 – $0.23.”

surprises.description: Arlo added roughly 298,000 paid accounts, above the preview’s roughly 250,000 expected net adds and its 230,000 warning threshold. The preview had also noted 318,000 adds in Q1, so the Q2 result was strong but below that prior-quarter pace.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Arlo added roughly 298,000 paid accounts in the quarter, bringing total paid accounts to 6.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Paid account net adds vs. ~250K”; the preview said “Net adds below about 230K would be a warning sign.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance was $140–$150 million, below the preview’s roughly $150 million consensus at the midpoint, though the top of the range reaches that estimate. Management also said it would reinvest an anticipated approximately $6 million tariff refund in growth rather than pass it through to earnings.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for total revenue of $140-$150 million… planning to reinvest an anticipated ~$6 million tariff refund into growth initiatives rather than dropping it to the bottom line.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q3 revenue guide vs. ~$150M consensus.”

surprises.description: Services revenue grew 19%, just below the preview’s expectation that services growth would be above 20%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Service revenue of $93 million (60% of total) growing 19%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management’s FY guide assumes services growth above 20%.”

surprises.description: Lifetime value per paid account rose about 15%, supported by subscription renewals that management said were better than forecast. That renewal strength was not quantified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lifetime value per paid account rose about 15% year-over-year to $967… and better-than-forecast subscription renewals.”

surprises.description: Management announced an Arlo Secure 7 launch for September with advanced AI threat-assessment features and a higher-priced subscription tier expected to lift ARPU and ARR. The preview did not identify this product and pricing launch as a catalyst.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Arlo will launch Arlo Secure 7 in September, introducing advanced AI threat-assessment features and a new higher-priced subscription tier expected to lift ARPU and ARR.”

in_line: The preview flagged memory-cost increases and uncertain tariff-relief timing as risks to product gross margin. Product gross margin was positive 1% with tariff refunds but negative 11.6% pro forma, and management expects it to remain negative; the direction of underlying product-margin pressure was consistent with that preview concern.

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.91, far above the preview’s $0.62–$0.66 estimates. GAAP EPS was also $0.67, above the preview’s $0.37 GAAP estimate and $0.51 estimate with an unspecified basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS rose to $0.91 from $0.85 year-over-year”; GAAP net income was $30.3 million versus $31 million, while GAAP EPS was $0.67 versus $0.64.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS | $0.66” and “Adj. EPS | $0.62”; the preview also lists “EPS | $0.51 (Basis not stated)” and “EPS | $0.37 (−42% YoY) … appears to be GAAP basis.”

surprises.description: Revenue exceeded the preview’s consensus estimates, coming in at $183.9 million versus estimates of $179.92 million and $182.06 million. Growth was 5% year over year, above the preview’s consensus-implied 3.2% growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue grew 5% year-over-year to $183.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $179.92M (+3.2% YoY)” and “Revenue | $182.06M.”

surprises.description: BAQSIMI sales declined 3% despite strong prescription growth, rather than meeting the preview’s cited flat-to-low-single-digit growth outlook for 2026. Lower prices from rebates and 340B discounts more than offset the volume gain.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BAQSIMI net sales fell 3% to $45.5 million despite ~17% prescription growth,” as lower selling prices from higher rebates and 340B discounts reduced sales by about $8.1 million versus a $6.9 million unit-volume gain.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “BAQSIMI now guided to ‘flat to low-single-digit’ growth for 2026”; the preview also says to watch “whether the May 1 price increase and 340B remediation show up.”

surprises.description: BAQSIMI exceeded its contract-year sales threshold, triggering an unflagged $100 million payment to Eli Lilly in Q3. The preview discussed BAQSIMI sales pressure but did not mention this contingent payment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “BAQSIMI generated $178.3 million in net sales in its third contract year, exceeding the $175 million threshold and triggering a $100 million milestone payment to Eli Lilly due in Q3 2026.”

surprises.description: Amphastar disclosed an FDA warning letter for IMS, which accounts for about one-third of corporate sales; the preview had not identified this regulatory issue. Manufacturing and shipping continue without a required shutdown, limiting the immediate disruption described on the call.
surprises.fact_evidence: “IMS, which represents about one-third of corporate sales, received an FDA warning letter tied to a December 2025 inspection but continues manufacturing and shipping without a required shutdown.”

surprises.description: The IMS warning letter also brings several quarters of additional remediation expense and redirects capital spending away from the Amphastar facility—costs and a capex shift not anticipated in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “IMS remediation is expected to increase expenses by $2 million to $3 million per quarter for several quarters, with capex redirected from the Amphastar facility.”

surprises.description: The company accelerated share repurchases to about $45 million in the quarter, above the preview’s cited $29.5 million in Q1 repurchases and beyond its general expectation of continued buybacks.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company accelerated buybacks, repurchasing roughly $45 million of shares in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview notes “$29.5M of share repurchases in the quarter” in Q1 and flags “Buyback pace; continued repurchases are a visible signal.”

in_line: Management reaffirmed full-year 2026 corporate sales guidance of mid-single-digit to high-single-digit growth, as the preview described that outlook and identified reaffirmation versus a reset as the key issue.

The new ipratropium product contributed $8.4 million in sales and was approaching its targeted market-share range. The preview expected a disclosed first-full-quarter contribution but provided no revenue estimate for comparison.

Sequential profitability improved through margin expansion, broadly consistent with the preview’s expectation of partial margin recovery. The facts provided no Q2 gross-margin percentage, so the preview’s specific 44%–47% or roughly 47% margin tests cannot be assessed.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $30.5 million, well below the $37.04 million consensus estimate. Revenue was essentially flat year over year, though excluding $4.3 million of non-recurring Spanish return-to-service work, it grew 16%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue was $30.5 million, essentially flat versus $30.8 million a year earlier,” and “excluding $4.3 million of non-recurring Spanish scooper return-to-service work, revenue grew 16% year over year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | $37.04M” and “~+20% Y/Y implied.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $8.1 million, materially below the preview’s $12–14 million estimate and down from $10.8 million a year earlier.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA declined to $8.1 million from $10.8 million in Q2 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | No published consensus”; “Preview’s own estimate: $12–14M.”

surprises.description: Common-stockholder loss per diluted share was $0.13, worse than the preview’s $0.03 loss estimate. The company also reported a $0.5 million net loss, rather than the roughly $1 million of net income the preview said was consistent with consensus.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Loss attributable to common stockholders of $7.6 million ($0.13 per diluted share)” and “a Q2 net loss of $0.5 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (diluted) | -$0.03”; the preview also says “Consensus EPS of -$0.03 is consistent with positive net income of about $1M.”

surprises.description: Bridger left its full-year guidance unchanged rather than raising it or narrowing it toward the high end, despite the preview identifying a raise as the bar investors were watching.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Bridger reiterated full-year 2026 guidance of $135-145 million in revenue and $55-60 million in adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance action. Bridger guides annually, so guidance is the main event. The bar is a raise, not a reiteration”; the base case also anticipated guidance “narrowed to the high end ($140–145M), not raised.”

surprises.description: The two newest Super Scoopers leased for Portugal were committed later than expected, and management plans to move them to the U.S. after the season unless European commitments improve. That indicates weaker or later European utilization opportunities than the preview’s description of the Portugal lease as weighted to Q3 suggested.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The two newest Super Scoopers leased to Europe’s DaVinci for Portugal were committed later than expected,” and management plans to “reposition them to the U.S. after the season for higher-value opportunities absent stronger European commitments.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The Portugal deal is a lease to Avincis through mid-October, which is capital-light but finite and weighted to Q3.”

surprises.description: The U.S. Forest Service awarded task orders covering four Super Scoopers for 160 days each, the longest guaranteed task orders in Bridger’s history. The preview did not flag these orders, making this a positive operational development.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The U.S. Forest Service awarded two 160-day task orders covering four Super Scoopers—the longest guaranteed task orders in Bridger’s history”—with activation “on a staggered basis into October and November.”

surprises.description: Interest expense rose to $6.6 million from $5.7 million, with management attributing the increase to additional fleet-expansion borrowing and short-term revolver use during heavy maintenance. The preview flagged liquidity and financing concerns but did not anticipate this specific increase in interest expense.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Interest expense rose to $6.6 million from $5.7 million,” reflecting “an additional $25 million drawn for fleet expansion plus $10 million in short-term revolver borrowings during Q1 heavy maintenance.”

in_line: The $58 million Texas A&M King Air 360 contract is expected to run over three years, with deliveries starting in 2028 and little to no margin-generating revenue in 2026, consistent with the preview’s expectation that the award would contribute mostly in FY27–29 rather than act as near-term run-rate revenue.

The numerical full-year guidance remained at the previously stated $135–145 million revenue and $55–60 million adjusted EBITDA ranges; the surprise was that management did not raise or narrow those ranges.

Cash was $7.2 million, below the preview’s $12 million concern threshold, consistent with the preview’s warning about a low cash balance. The call also cited roughly $75 million of remaining credit facility availability and a delayed-draw feature of up to $100 million.

surprises.description: Revenue was $744.3 million, above the preview’s $716.35 million consensus and its $690–720 million base case, reaching the preview’s $740–760 million bull-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total operating revenue and other income increased 89% year-over-year to $744.3 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue | Consensus (varies by source) | $716.35M (Investing.com, Aug 2026)” and the base case was “$690–720M.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS of $2.50 was just above the preview’s working consensus band of $2.41–$2.49, though it remained within the preview’s base-case EPS range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 net income attributable to common shareholders was $47.4 million… or $2.50 per diluted share.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Treat $2.41–$2.49 as the working band”; the base case was “$2.35–2.60.”

surprises.description: Growth was not limited to Mercury: excluding Mercury, managed receivables rose 26% to roughly $3.8 billion, and the company added a record 790,000 customers, with active accounts up more than 1 million year-over-year excluding Mercury. The preview flagged originations and Mercury’s contribution as questions, but gave no directional expectation for this level of non-Mercury growth.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding Mercury receivables rose 26% to roughly $3.8 billion”; “record 790,000 new customers”; “active accounts up more than 1 million year-over-year excluding Mercury.”

surprises.description: Direct mail acquisition was a weak spot: higher solicitation volume raised acquisition costs and originations lagged plan, although digital originations were ahead of plan. The preview flagged originations and marketing-spend framing, but did not anticipate this channel split or the cost pressure.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Direct mail solicitation volumes are up over 50% year-over-year, raising customer acquisition costs and leaving direct mail originations behind plan, though digital originations are running ahead of plan.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview listed “Purchase volume and new account originations” and “2H26 interest-expense and marketing-spend framing” as items to watch.

surprises.description: ROE reached 28.1%, above the preview’s expectation of sustained mid-20s returns; management tempered that strength by saying ROE should revert toward 20% as the company delevers, with capital actions possible if it remains in the high 20s.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Return on average equity reached 28.1%, materially exceeding the company's long-term target of 20%”; management expects “ROE to revert toward 20% as the company delevers, with capital actions possible if it stays in the high 20s.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “ROE against the 20% target. Sustained mid-20s would matter for the multiple.”

surprises.description: Management expects delinquency and charge-off rates to rise slightly next quarter, citing partial-quarter Mercury comparisons and mix shifts. The preview focused on whether Q2 credit normalization was seasonal or cyclical but did not flag this additional near-term increase.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects delinquency and charge-off rates to rise slightly next quarter due to partial-quarter Mercury comparisons and mix shifts.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The question is whether the Q2 normalization is seasonal or cyclical.”

surprises.description: A $5.5 million favorable Mercury-related contingent-consideration adjustment still boosted Q2, whereas the preview said the EPS beat needed to come from net margin dollars rather than another favorable mark. The adjustment was smaller than the roughly $13 million Q1 benefit discussed in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: “A $5.5 million favorable adjustment to Mercury-related contingent consideration boosted the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The beat needs to come from net margin dollars rather than another favorable mark.”

in_line: Interest expense was about $123 million, essentially flat with Q1’s $122.8 million and consistent with the preview’s warning that quarterly interest expense would remain elevated through 2026.
The combined principal net charge-off rate was 17.7% and up only modestly sequentially, consistent with the preview’s focus on Q2 credit normalization rather than a clearly severe deterioration.

surprises.description: Adjusted diluted EPS was $0.80, above the preview’s roughly $0.75 estimate. The gap was about 7%, despite the preview’s warning to distinguish adjusted from GAAP EPS.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted diluted EPS hit a record $0.80.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “EPS (adjusted diluted) | ~$0.75”

surprises.description: Revenue of $973 million fell short of the roughly $985.7 million consensus. The company attributed a one-time $15 million reduction to CMS billing-anomaly adjustments; the corresponding expense reduction largely offset it, leaving EBITDA impact immaterial.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $973 million”; “A one-time $15 million revenue reduction tied to CMS billing anomaly adjustments for ACO REACH 2025 was largely offset by a corresponding expense reduction, resulting in an immaterial EBITDA impact.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total revenue | ~$985.7M”

surprises.description: Commercial medical costs were running slightly above expectations in outpatient specialties, even though the overall year-to-date trend was slightly better than the 5.2% full-year assumption. This was a less favorable pocket than the preview’s focus on holding the overall trend near 5%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Year-to-date medical cost trend is running slightly better than the 5.2% full-year assumption, with Medicare favorable and Medicaid in line, but commercial trending slightly above expectations in outpatient specialties.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “If Astrana holds near 5% while peers run near 7%, that supports the bull case. Hedging language about utilization would point to the bear case.”

surprises.description: Net leverage reached 2.26x after $92 million of debt retirement, and Astrana said it met the sub-2.5x Prospect commitment in half the promised 24-month timeframe. The preview noted leverage of 2.3x and a year-end target, but did not flag this earlier commitment milestone.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net leverage fell to 2.26x on a trailing 12-month basis after retiring $92 million of debt, surpassing the sub-2.5x Prospect commitment in half the promised 24-month timeframe.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net leverage 2.3x pro forma TTM, down from the prior quarter”; “net leverage at or below 2.0x by year-end 2026.”

surprises.description: Full-risk arrangements were slightly more advanced than the preview’s approximate mix: 81% of capitation revenue and 42% of membership, versus about 80% and 40%, respectively.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Roughly 81% of capitation revenue and 42% of membership now come from full-risk arrangements.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “About 80% of Care Partners capitation revenue and about 40% of owned membership are now full-risk.”

surprises.description: Astrana reported a 210-basis-point year-over-year G&A improvement, expects G&A to exit 2026 at roughly 6% of revenue, and said Prospect synergies are tracking to the high end of the $12 million–$15 million range. The preview did not set expectations for these cost and synergy metrics.
surprises.fact_evidence: “G&A improved approximately 210 basis points year-over-year, with the company expecting to exit 2026 at roughly 6% of revenue and Prospect synergies tracking to the high end of the $12M-$15M range.”

surprises.description: Management said it would reinvest mid-to-high single-digit millions—about three-quarters of its outperformance—into payer contracts, provider partnerships, and expansion markets, rather than simply retaining all of that outperformance. The preview did not anticipate this capital-allocation choice.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company is reinvesting mid-to-high single-digit millions (about three-quarters of its outperformance) into new payer contracts, provider partnerships, and expansion markets in Texas and Hawaii.”

surprises.description: Astrana reaffirmed mid-to-high-teens organic EBITDA growth for 2027 despite Medicaid work-requirement changes beginning January 1, 2027. The preview discussed Medicaid enrollment assumptions as a guide issue but did not anticipate this specific reassurance about the 2027 outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management reaffirmed medium-term mid-to-high teens organic EBITDA growth, including for 2027, despite Medicaid work-requirement changes starting January 1, 2027.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management called that low end a ‘stacked downside case’ built on Medicaid and exchange enrollment assumptions that have since proven too conservative.”

in_line: Adjusted EBITDA was $69 million, near the high end of the $65 million–$70 million quarterly range and close to the preview’s roughly $68 million implied consensus.

The full-year adjusted EBITDA range was raised at the low end to $255 million while retaining the $280 million high end, consistent with the preview’s expectation that management would raise the $250 million low end.
The overall year-to-date medical cost trend was slightly better than the 5.2% full-year assumption, consistent with the preview’s focus on whether Astrana could hold near 5%.
Full-year revenue guidance of $3.8 billion–$4.1 billion was reaffirmed, consistent with the preview’s $4.00 billion consensus falling within the range.
Free cash flow guidance of $105 million–$132.5 million was reaffirmed, matching the range identified in the preview.

surprises.description: Net revenue was $117 million, about 14% above the $102.27 million consensus, and grew 23% year over year versus the preview's 7.7% implied growth. This was a substantial acceleration from the revenue pace investors were expecting.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net revenue up 23% to $117 million”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $33 million, well above the preview's roughly $23–25 million estimate, and the 28.2% margin was also above the roughly 24% run-rate the preview said was required. The record EBITDA margin came despite a 150-basis-point gross-margin decline from mix.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 51% to a record $33 million, achieving a record 28.2% adjusted EBITDA margin on net revenue”; “Gross margin declined 150 basis points in Q2 due to a mix shift”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA (derived) | ~$23–25M”; “Q2 adj. EBITDA margin vs. ~24% required run-rate.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $2.07, far above the $1.30 consensus and contrary to the preview's implied 13.3% year-over-year decline; instead, adjusted EPS grew 38%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS grew 38% to $2.07”

surprises.description: Willdan raised rather than merely reaffirmed its full-year outlook: the new ranges are $415–430 million net revenue, $103–107 million adjusted EBITDA, and $5.00–5.15 adjusted EPS, each above the prior range. The implied 25% full-year EBITDA margin is also higher than 2025's 21.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to net revenue of $415–430 million, adjusted EBITDA of $103–107 million, and adjusted diluted EPS of $5.00–5.15, implying a 25% full-year EBITDA margin versus 21.8% in 2025.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Raised FY26 guidance to $410–425M net revenue, $100–105M adj. EBITDA, and $4.90–5.05 adj. EPS”; preview said to watch whether the company would “reaffirm, raise, narrow, or trim” that range and described reaffirmation as the base case.

surprises.description: The company disclosed three notable new awards totaling about $212 million: a $110 million LADWP solar streetlight expansion, a $53 million City College of New York plant upgrade, and a $49 million five-year SoCalREN contract. The preview flagged bookings as a catalyst but did not anticipate these specific wins.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Notable new contract wins since the last call include a $110 million LADWP solar streetlight expansion (half already authorized), a $53 million City College of New York plant upgrade, and a $49 million five-year SoCalREN contract.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “New bookings or backlog” was a catalyst to watch; the preview cited prior wins and the July 15 Encina award but gave no expectation for these awards.

surprises.description: A $5.3 million tax benefit boosted GAAP EPS, a larger quarterly benefit than the $1.3 million disclosed in Q1. The preview noted an approximately zero FY26 effective-tax-rate projection, but did not anticipate this size of Q2 benefit.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP EPS increased 53% to $1.58 … aided by a $5.3 million tax benefit”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 disclosed a $1.3M tax benefit and a projected ~0% FY26 effective tax rate.”

surprises.description: Net debt was $33 million, or 0.3x trailing EBITDA, below the 0.6x leverage level the preview reported after the Burton-related revolver draw. The expected year-end revolver repayment remains conditional on there being no further acquisitions.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The balance sheet carries only $33 million net debt (0.3x trailing EBITDA) with $165 million in total liquidity, and management expects the revolver to be fully repaid by year-end absent further acquisitions.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Leverage rose to 0.6x net debt / TTM EBITDA after a $30M revolver draw”; management expected the revolver to be fully repaid by year-end.

surprises.description: The deferred-tax-asset cushion was reported at $34 million, above the preview's roughly $28 million figure, and management said it survives the June 2025 sunset of the 179D provision. That is a somewhat larger stated cushion for the tax transition than the preview described.
surprises.fact_evidence: “$34 million in deferred tax assets that survive the June 2025 sunset of the 179D provision.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The ~$28M of deferred tax assets is the cushion.”

in_line: APG was projected to nearly triple year over year to roughly $75 million, consistent with the preview's expectation that it would more than double or approach tripling in 2026.
Management still expected to repay the revolver by year-end, in line with the preview; the call qualified that expectation as applying absent further acquisitions.

surprises.description: CART reported $10.35 billion of GTV, above both the $10.10–$10.25 billion company range and the roughly $10.2 billion consensus estimate. The 14% growth rate also exceeded the preview’s 11–13% guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 GTV reached $10.35 billion, up 14% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “GTV | Company guidance (Q2) $10.10B – $10.25B (+11–13%) | Consensus ~$10.2B.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA was $313 million, beating the $290–$300 million guidance range and roughly $298 million consensus. At about 3.0% of GTV, it also cleared the preview’s 2.95% watch level and its 3.0% relief threshold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA rose 19% to $313 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA | Company guidance (Q2) $290M – $300M (+11–15%) | Consensus ~$298M”; “A print at or above 3.0% would ease the Q1 margin concern.”

surprises.description: Advertising and other revenue reached $297 million, above the $283–$291 million guidance range and roughly $289 million consensus; growth of 16% also exceeded the guide’s 11–14% range. The advertising investment rate rose to 2.9% from 2.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Advertising and other revenue grew 16% year-over-year to $297 million, outpacing GTV growth and lifting the advertising investment rate to 2.9% from 2.8% a year earlier.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Advertising & other revenue | +11–14% ($283–291M) | ~$289M”; “Ads & other at or above $291M, the top of the guide.”

surprises.description: Q3 GTV guidance has a $10.425 billion midpoint, just above the preview’s $10.4 billion bull-case threshold. However, management also said it would widen guidance ranges and now expects to land at the midpoint rather than beat the high end as it had historically, tempering the implication of the outlook.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 2026 guidance calls for GTV of $10.3-$10.55 billion (14% growth at midpoint)”; management “now expects to land within the range at the midpoint, rather than beating the high end as it had done historically.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bull” scenario: “Q3 GTV guide ≥ $10.4B”; the preview also flags “Q3 guidance on GTV and adj. EBITDA” and a buy-side GTV benchmark “about 3% above consensus.”

surprises.description: Operating cash flow and free cash flow rose sharply after weak Q1 cash flow, but management attributed much of the jump to collecting a large accounts-receivable balance in the quarter, making the improvement appear partly timing-driven.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating cash flow surged 143% to $493 million and free cash flow jumped 156% to $480 million, largely driven by a large accounts receivable balance collected in the quarter.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview reported Q1 “operating cash flow $268M (-10% YoY)” and listed cash flow among the prior-quarter weak spots, but gave no Q2 cash-flow forecast.

surprises.description: Transaction revenue grew, but fell to 7.2% of GTV from 7.3%, indicating weaker transaction monetization as a share of GTV. The preview had raised pricing cuts and their possible take-rate impact as a key debate, but did not forecast this metric.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Transaction revenue grew 13% to $746 million but slipped to 7.2% of GTV from 7.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview asked whether pricing cuts were retailer-funded or Instacart-funded and said that this “determines take-rate impact.”

surprises.description: GAAP net income fell 4% even as adjusted EBITDA rose 19%; management attributed the decline primarily to higher stock-based compensation after moving the first vesting date of annual equity grants from August to May. The preview provided an EPS estimate but no expectation for net income or this vesting change.
surprises.fact_evidence: “GAAP net income fell 4% to $111 million, primarily due to higher stock-based compensation from shifting the first vesting date of annual equity grants from August to May.”

surprises.description: Customer activation reached its fastest year-over-year growth rate since 2022, a favorable demand signal not covered by the preview’s specific operating expectations.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Instacart activated net new customers at its fastest year-over-year growth rate since 2022.”

surprises.description: Found rate and perfect order fill rate both improved for a 16th consecutive quarter, an operational-quality improvement the preview did not address.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Improved both found rate and perfect order fill rate for the 16th consecutive quarter.”

in_line: Gross profit as a share of GTV was 7.3%, down from 7.5% a year earlier—the second consecutive year-over-year decline, matching the preview’s flagged risk. The preview’s cited prior-quarter level was 7.2%.
Orders grew 9%, above the preview’s warning threshold of below 8%; the preview had identified user growth as the key order-growth driver.

surprises.description: WSC reported Q2 revenue of $612 million, about 4.5% above the preview’s $585.4 million consensus and company frame. The beat also exceeded the preview’s bull-case range of $598–608 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 2026 revenue was $612 million” and beat company guidance of approximately $585 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Revenue $585.4M”; the preview also gave a bull scenario of “$598–608M.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.28, above the preview’s $0.246 consensus and even the top of its bull-case range. This was a positive per-share result despite reported diluted EPS being flat year over year.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS $0.28”; diluted EPS was flat year-over-year at $0.26.
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EPS $0.246”; the bull scenario was “$0.28–0.31.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EBITDA reached $228 million, $5 million above the preview’s approximately $223 million company frame. The beat was modest and remained within the preview’s base-case range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $228 million (beating the $223 million outlook).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA ~$223M (company frame).”

surprises.description: The adjusted EBITDA margin was 37.2%, below the preview’s roughly 38.1% implied margin and below its 37.5% level that it said would break the temporary-cost explanation. The decline was about 500 basis points year over year, worse than the preview’s implied 420-basis-point decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA margin fell to 37.2%, a roughly 500 basis point year-over-year decline driven by upfront investment costs, revenue mix, and higher SG&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. EBITDA margin ~38.1%”; the preview said “A print below ~37.5% would break the ‘temporary cost’ story.”

surprises.description: Full-year guidance moved up rather than remaining at the preview’s existing levels: revenue rose by $50 million to approximately $2.3 billion and adjusted EBITDA rose to approximately $920 million. The EBITDA increase was comparatively small, from the preview’s $915 million level.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance by $50 million to approximately $2.3 billion” and “increased adjusted EBITDA guidance to approximately $920 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY2026 guidance: Revenue ~$2.25B”; “Adj. EBITDA ~$915M.”

surprises.description: Net CapEx guidance rose to approximately $375 million from the preview’s $325 million level. The increased reinvestment coincided with Q2 adjusted free cash flow of only $55 million, a near-term cash-flow trade-off management tied to demand-driven fleet investment.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Net CapEx guidance was raised to approximately $375 million”; “Q2 adjusted free cash flow” was “$55 million” as the company reinvests “over half its capital generation into demand-driven fleet.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “net capex ~$325M.”

surprises.description: Despite growth in total revenue and modular activations, combined leasing revenue across modular, storage, and VAPS was essentially flat year over year excluding the World Cup. That points to a weaker underlying leasing inflection than the preview hoped activation growth would support.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Excluding the World Cup, combined leasing revenue across modular, storage, and VAPS was essentially flat year-over-year in Q2.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said a third consecutive quarter of modular activation growth was “needed … to support the leasing inflection.”

surprises.description: Enterprise account revenue grew 21% year over year, and management said newer offerings are expected to exit 2026 at roughly a 20% growth rate. The preview did not flag these businesses as an expected growth source.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Enterprise account revenue grew 21% year-over-year” and newer offerings “are expected to exit 2026 at roughly a 20% growth rate.”

in_line: Modular activations rose for a third consecutive quarter, as the preview specifically looked for a third consecutive quarter of activation growth.
Management quantified the World Cup contribution, addressing the preview’s call to quantify its Q2 impact.

surprises.description: AMN reported Q2 revenue of $673 million, above both the $626 million consensus and the $635 million top of company guidance. Labor-disruption revenue was $25 million rather than the $10 million assumed in guidance, but even excluding that $15 million excess, revenue was about $648 million—above the guidance range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 consolidated revenue was $673 million,” “6% above the high end of guidance”; “Labor disruption revenue came in at $25 million versus the $10 million assumed in guidance.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “Revenue | $620M – $635M | $626M (Zacks)” and “Q2 guidance includes only about $10M of disruption revenue.”

surprises.description: Adjusted EPS was $0.77, far above the preview’s $0.22 consensus estimate, despite the preview expecting a year-over-year decline.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EPS jumped to $0.77 from $0.30 a year ago.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “Adj. diluted EPS … $0.22 (Zacks)” and “About −27% YoY.”

surprises.description: Reported adjusted EBITDA margin of 10.9% was well above the preview’s 6.7%–7.2% guidance range, but about $27 million of non-recurring items lifted the margin by 370 basis points. Excluding those items, the margin was about 6.8%, roughly in line with guidance rather than a comparable underlying beat.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Adjusted EBITDA reached $73 million (10.9% of revenue)”; “roughly $27 million in non-recurring items … added 370 basis points to EBITDA margin and are not expected to repeat in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “Adj. EBITDA … 6.7% – 7.2% margin.”

surprises.description: Nurse and Allied revenue grew 11% and was 12% above consensus, with travel nurse and allied volumes both growing faster than the preview’s stated 5% buy-side threshold. The preview had identified whether volume could offset rate normalization as a key debate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Nurse and Allied segment grew revenue 11% to $422 million (12% above consensus), with travel nurse volume up 6% and allied volume up 7%, the highest growth rates in four years.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “the buy side reportedly wants at least 5% YoY” volume growth and “the bull case needs volume growth to offset rate declines.”

surprises.description: Q3 revenue guidance of $640 million–$655 million was above the preview’s base scenario of $628 million–$636 million, with the top of the range also above its bull-case threshold of $650 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q3 guidance calls for consolidated revenue of $640-655 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview scenarios: “Bull | $638M – $650M” and “Base | $628M – $636M”; it also says “Q3 guide above $650M” is a bull-case driver.

surprises.description: The Q3 outlook includes only $7 million–$8 million of strike revenue, substantially below the preview’s rough estimate of $20 million–$35 million for the Brigham and Women’s/MGB strike. That estimate was explicitly described as the preview author’s own estimate, not company guidance.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Only $7-8 million of strike revenue is embedded in the Q3 outlook.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “My rough estimate is $20M – $35M of Q3 revenue, but this is not company-disclosed.”

surprises.description: Travel nurse orders strengthened sharply: they turned positive in May and were up about 40% year over year by early August. That provides a stronger forward volume signal than the preview’s open question about whether underlying volume growth would hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Travel nurse orders turned positive in May and by early August were up about 40% year-over-year and 20% higher than August 2024, supporting projected double-digit Q3 volume growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “The stock now depends on whether the underlying business is growing” and “the bull case needs volume growth to offset rate declines.”

surprises.description: Technology and Workforce Solutions revenue fell 15%, with language-services pricing down 8% despite flat volume, and management expects pricing pressure to continue through 2026. The preview did not flag this segment-specific pricing decline or its expected duration.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Technology and Workforce Solutions revenue declined 15% … with language services pricing down 8% year-over-year while volume was flat, and management expects continued pricing headwinds through 2026.”

surprises.description: Cash ended Q2 at $362 million, above the $175 million expected, partly because of $117 million in strike-related client deposits. The balance and low leverage were cited as capacity for M&A, although no transaction was announced.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended the quarter with $362 million in cash (well above the $175 million expected due to $117 million in strike-related client deposits) and a low leverage ratio of 1.5x, signaling capacity for M&A.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Call: “well above the $175 million expected.”

surprises.description: Kaiser’s contract, which expires at the end of 2026, is now in a competitive RFP process. The preview had flagged Kaiser contract commentary as a risk, but the call’s confirmation of a competitive process makes the renewal exposure more concrete.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The Kaiser contract expires at the end of 2026 and is now in a competitive RFP process.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Preview: “Kaiser is about 22% of revenue, so contract commentary is also a risk.”

surprises.description: Management lowered its 2027 international nurse growth expectations toward single digits, citing embassy appointment backlogs and travel bans. The preview did not flag this downgrade or these constraints.
surprises.fact_evidence: “International nurse growth expectations for 2027 were lowered toward single digits due to embassy appointment backlogs and travel bans.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: Call: “growth expectations for 2027 were lowered toward single digits.”

in_line: Excluding the roughly 370 basis points from non-recurring items, Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin was about 6.8%, within the preview’s 6.7%–7.2% guidance range.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $210.8 million, about $6 million below the preview’s working consensus of roughly $217 million. Management attributed the decline to unusually strong IDR-driven revenue realization in the year-ago quarter; revenue per visit is now about $4,000–$4,200 and management expects that level to persist, rather than describing the shortfall as a new eligibility reversal.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 total revenue fell 13.6% to $210.8 million” due to “unusually strong IDR-driven revenue realization in the 2025 comparison period”; net revenue per visit “normalized to roughly $4,000-$4,200” and management expects this level to persist.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview gives a “Working consensus ~$217M” and flags “Claim-eligibility reversals” as a key risk.

surprises.description: Hospital visits grew much faster than the preview’s near-flat same-hospital trend suggested: same-hospital visits rose 6.3%, compared with 0.6% in Q1. This is a positive update on the core hospital activity the preview identified as a key concern.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Hospital visits grew 9.6% to 49,962 in Q2 2026 with same-hospital visits up 6.3%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview says Q1 same-hospital visits were “+0.6%” and calls out that “Same-hospital revenue and visits” were “near flat in Q1.”

surprises.description: A renegotiated Halo MD contract materially lowered costs, including a retroactive benefit, and management expects total contract services costs to be 25%–30% lower going forward. The preview anticipated arbitration-cost normalization after Q1’s elevated costs, but did not flag this contract change or the scale of the savings.
surprises.fact_evidence: The renegotiated contract shifted arbitration fees to a “pay-on-collected basis retroactive to 2024,” contributing about $38.4 million to a $49.6 million decrease in facility operating costs; total contract services costs are expected to be “25%-30%” lower going forward. Q2 adjusted EBITDA rose 25.7% to $90 million.
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said Q1 arbitration costs were 35% of arbitration-related revenue and management had guided costs back to 24–26% “in coming quarters.”

surprises.description: Management reported substantial IDR activity and strong outcomes despite the preview flagging declining submissions. It said 50%–60% of claims continue to go through IDR, with more than 85% of award determinations won and average collections above 80%.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company continues submitting “50%-60% of claims through IDR,” winning “over 85% of award determinations” with an “average collection rate over 80%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview’s catalyst checklist says “Management flagged declining submissions in Q4 2025.”

surprises.description: The final federal IDR rule reduced CMS administrative fees sharply, producing an additional $4.3 million of quarterly cost savings that the preview did not anticipate.
surprises.fact_evidence: The final federal IDR rule cut CMS administrative fees “from $115 to $15 per party,” contributing about “$4.3 million in cost savings for the quarter.”

in_line: Three hospital openings in H2 2026—West Little Rock, San Antonio, and Jacksonville—matched the preview’s expectation of three H2 openings; management also maintained its 3–5 hospitals-per-year pace.

surprises.description: Q2 orders were $28.9 million, below the preview’s $35 million bogey and ending three consecutive quarters above $30 million. The preview’s base case was $33–37 million, so actual orders also fell below that range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Total Q2 orders were $28.9 million, down 9% sequentially but up 4% year-over-year, ending three consecutive quarters above $30 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Bogey: at least $35M”; base scenario: “Orders $33–37M.”

surprises.description: Backlog fell to $45.4 million, well below the preview’s $52 million bogey and below the base-case range of $52–54 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Backlog stood at $45.4 million, down 12% sequentially but up 20% year-over-year.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 exit was $51.8M. Bogey: at least $52M”; base scenario: “backlog $52–54M.”

surprises.description: The Alfamation material weakness was not yet described as remediated: management expected remediation to be effective by fiscal year-end, later than the preview’s expectation that it had already been remediated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company disclosed a material weakness in internal controls at Alfamation tied to the Q1 restatement, with remediation expected to be effective by fiscal year-end.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The company expects to report a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, but believes it has now been remediated.”

surprises.description: Auto EV orders declined sharply after four strong quarters, a reversal not anticipated in the preview’s broad expectation that demand would hold.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Auto EV orders declined 67% sequentially after four strong quarters.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Base: Demand holds”; “Bull: Demand holds.”

surprises.description: Semi orders were unusually strong, rising 56% sequentially and reaching their highest intake in six quarters, despite the weak overall order total.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Semi orders surged 56% sequentially and 64% year-over-year, the strongest semi order intake in six quarters.”

surprises.description: The balance sheet was stronger than the preview’s Q1 snapshot suggested: Q2 ended with substantially more cash and less debt than the preview had cited for Q1.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The company ended Q2 with $22.1 million in cash (up $6.4 million), $62 million in total liquidity, total debt of $6.2 million, and a low leverage ratio of 0.8x trailing-12-month adjusted EBITDA.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 operating cash flow was −$3.3M with $12.9M cash against about $8.5M debt.”

in_line: Revenue was approximately as expected after the July 31 pre-announcement: the preview cited preliminary revenue of about $35.0 million, versus reported Q2 revenue of $35.3 million.
Gross margin was approximately in line with the already disclosed preliminary result: the preview cited about 40%, versus reported gross margin of 40.5%.
Full-year guidance matched the July 31 revision already described in the preview: revenue of $135–140 million and gross margin of approximately 43%.
The quarter’s earnings were consistent with the preview’s expectation of roughly breakeven results: it estimated non-GAAP EPS of about $0.04–0.06, and reported diluted EPS was $0.04.
The material weakness being tied to Alfamation was consistent with the preview’s description of the control issue as arising from Alfamation’s ERP implementation.

surprises.description: Q2 revenue was $292.9 million, above the preview’s working consensus of about $272 million and above its highest cited estimate of $274.7 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 revenue reached $292.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Working midpoint” revenue was “~$272M”; published estimates were “$269.2M” or “$274.7M.”

surprises.description: Shipments were $281.5 million, below revenue of $292.9 million, breaking the preview’s highlighted expectation that shipments would keep outpacing revenue.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Shipments of $281.5 million,” versus Q2 revenue of “$292.9 million.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Management guided shipments to keep outpacing revenue”; shipments below revenue “would break that commitment.”

surprises.description: Single-wafer cleaning, Tahoe and semi-critical cleaning revenue fell 14.2%, a steeper decline than the 5.5% Q1 decline cited in the preview; newer SPM products contributed minimally.
surprises.fact_evidence: The group’s revenue “fell 14.2% to $133.0 million,” reflecting “minimal contribution from newer SPM products.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: The preview said the line “fell 5.5% YoY in Q1” due to a transition into new SPM tools, and warned that “steepening declines” would make growth more concentrated.

surprises.description: Management flagged tighter component supply and lead times that could extend to six months, potentially constraining second-half shipments—an operational risk not identified in the preview.
surprises.fact_evidence: Component supply was tightening, with lead times extending “from 4 months to potentially 6 months,” potentially constraining second-half shipments; key suppliers had not raised prices so far.

surprises.description: First-half purchase orders rose 105% year over year, with heavier emphasis on newer products across all categories; the preview had not identified this order surge.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half 2026 orders (POs) increased 105% year-over-year, with a heavier emphasis on newer products across all categories.”

surprises.description: Customer concentration improved sharply: just one customer accounted for at least 10% of first-half revenue, compared with three such customers representing nearly half of revenue a year earlier; the preview did not flag this development.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Only one 10%+ customer at 12.7% of first-half revenue versus three 10%+ customers representing 49.9% in first-half 2025.”

surprises.description: ACM reported orders for its panel-level horizontal plating tool, including a production order in Mainland China and an evaluation system for a new Asian customer—commercial progress the preview did not mention.
surprises.fact_evidence: The company “received orders for its panel-level horizontal plating tool,” including “a production order in Mainland China” and “an evaluation system for a new customer in Asia.”

surprises.description: ACM ended with more than $1.0 billion in net cash, including about $300 million in the U.S., after completing a $150 million registered direct offering in May; the preview did not discuss this balance-sheet development.
surprises.fact_evidence: ACM “strengthened its balance sheet to over $1.0 billion in net cash (including ~$300 million in the U.S.) following a $150 million registered direct offering completed in May.”

in_line: The FY2026 revenue guidance floor rose from $1.08 billion to $1.125 billion while the $1.175 billion ceiling stayed unchanged, matching the preview’s base scenario of guidance “narrowed upward with ceiling unchanged.”
Gross margin was 46.0%, in line with the preview’s focus on holding at about 46% and within the company’s 42%–48% long-term target range.
ECP and advanced packaging were expected growth drivers; the call reported ECP, furnace and other technologies up 167.7% and advanced packaging revenue (excluding ECP) up 153.3%.

surprises.description: Sales were $8.8 billion, above the preview’s ~$8.45 billion estimate and above the top of its $8.3–$8.6 billion range. Organic growth was also 3.8%, slightly above the preview’s ~3.5% estimate.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 sales rose 4.6% year-over-year to $8.8 billion,” including “3.8% organic growth.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Net sales | ~$8.45bn (range $8.3–8.6bn)” and “Organic growth | ~+3.5%.”

surprises.description: Diluted EPS was $3.39, above the preview’s ~$3.25 estimate. The preview estimate was adjusted EPS, while the call fact is reported as diluted EPS, so the comparison is not on an explicitly identical basis.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Diluted EPS increased 5.3% to $3.39.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. diluted EPS | ~$3.25 (range $3.15–3.35).”

surprises.description: Ferguson raised its full-year sales outlook from low-to-mid single-digit growth to mid-single-digit growth, rather than reaffirming the existing guide as the preview’s base case anticipated.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Ferguson raised full-year 2026 guidance, now expecting mid-single-digit sales growth (up from low-to-mid single digits).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 net sales growth: low-to-mid single digit”; the preview also said “Reaffirm is neutral.”

surprises.description: The company raised the low end of its full-year operating-margin range to 9.5%, from 9.4%, while leaving the high end at 9.8%. This is a smaller upgrade than the preview’s bullish scenario of narrowing the range to 9.6%–9.8%.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Lifting the low end of its operating margin range to 9.5%-9.8%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 adj. operating margin: 9.4%–9.8%”; the preview said “Narrowing to 9.6%–9.8% is the most bullish outcome.”

surprises.description: U.S. residential returned to growth at 2%, a better result than the preview’s assumed low-to-mid single-digit decline and its downside concern of a 4% or worse decline. HVAC was particularly strong, although Ferguson Home and Fire & Fabrication declined.
surprises.fact_evidence: “U.S. residential returned to growth, up 2%, powered mainly by HVAC customer group growth of 11%”; “Ferguson Home declined 1% and Fire & Fabrication fell 13%.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The FY guide assumes a low-to-mid single-digit decline. Any step to −4% or worse pressures the margin bridge.”

surprises.description: The preview warned that price inflation was flattering revenue; instead, inflation eased to low single digits and Ferguson returned to volume growth. That points to a healthier source of growth than the preview’s price-versus-volume concern implied.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Returning to volume growth as inflation eased to low single digits.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Q1 price inflation was mid-single digit, above the low-single-digit expectation, driven by tariffs. Price is flattering revenue.”

surprises.description: The reported operating margin was 10.7%, above the preview’s ~10.4% adjusted-margin estimate, though the call reported a 10-basis-point year-over-year decline rather than the preview’s estimated 20-basis-point increase. The measures are not explicitly stated on the same adjusted basis, and gross margin was down 20 basis points.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Operating profit grew 2.9% to $932 million at a 10.7% operating margin (down 10 basis points), and gross margin held at 31% (down 20 basis points against a tough comp).”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Adj. operating margin | ~10.4%” and “~+20bp.”

surprises.description: The call disclosed a substantial first-half cash-flow decline tied to working capital and tax timing; the preview did not identify this cash-flow pressure as an expected issue. Operating cash flow was down about $400 million year over year, with free cash flow around $500 million.
surprises.fact_evidence: “First-half operating cash flow fell ~$400 million year-over-year to $716 million due to working capital investments in HVAC and large projects plus tax payment timing, yielding free cash flow of ~$500 million.”

surprises.description: Management indicated stronger near-term growth than the preview specified: it expects Q3 organic growth above Q2 and said the July exit rate outpaced the quarter. This adds a constructive second-half trading signal beyond the preview’s discussion of the back-half margin requirement.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Management expects a slightly stronger second half with Q3 organic growth above Q2, supported by a July exit rate that outpaced the second quarter.”

surprises.description: FloWorks was already announced and its Q3 close was expected, but the call added that the deal is immediately accretive to adjusted EPS and includes ~$45 million of expected synergies. The preview had flagged accretion timing as an open question without stating an expectation for accretion.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Acquire FloWorks for an enterprise value of ~$1.6 billion (~10x EBITDA including ~$45 million of expected synergies), immediately accretive to adjusted EPS and expected to close in Q3.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “The $1.6bn deal (announced Jul 13, 2026) raises the question of whether FY guidance includes it”; “get accretion timing and funding mix.”

surprises.description: FloWorks will take net debt-to-EBITDA to approximately 1.8x, while the preview cited a 1.0x starting point. The resulting leverage remains within Ferguson’s stated 1–2x target, but the preview had also identified a slowdown in buybacks to fund the deal as a possible negative; management said buybacks would resume once leverage returns to the low end of the range.
surprises.fact_evidence: “The FloWorks deal will raise net debt-to-EBITDA from 1.3x to approximately 1.8x”; management “plans to resume buybacks once leverage returns to the low end of its 1-2x target range.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Pro-forma leverage starts from 1.0x”; “A slowdown in buybacks to fund FloWorks would be read negatively.”

in_line: FloWorks was expected to close in Q3 2026, consistent with the call’s expected Q3 closing.

surprises.description: N-able cut full-year 2026 ARR guidance to $562–565 million from the preview’s expected $581–586 million, and revenue guidance to $539–542 million from $554–559 million. The reduction is substantial across both measures.
surprises.fact_evidence: “N-able lowered its full-year 2026 guidance, now expecting ARR of $562-565 million (4-5% reported growth) and revenue of $539-542 million, citing go-to-market leadership transition and pressures in UEM and EDR markets.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “FY26 guidance (set May 7, 2026, unchanged): Revenue $554–559M”; “Total ARR $581–586M.”

surprises.description: Q2 ARR was $544 million, below the preview’s $555–558 million consensus estimate. Constant-currency growth was 6%, at the bottom of the preview’s expected 6–7% range, so the reported ARR level was the more notable miss.
surprises.fact_evidence: “Q2 2026 ARR was $544 million, growing 6% year-over-year in constant currency.”
surprises.expectation_evidence: “Total ARR… Consensus ~$555–558M”; “Q2 constant-currency ARR growth… likely around 6–7% cc.”

surprises.description: Renewals weakened in N-able’s largest annual renewal cohort, concentrated in UEM and EDR, and management said this drove the net new ARR shortfall and guidance cut. The preview flagged UEM/EDR-related security-incident risk, but did not anticipate this deterioration in renewals.
